_childDocuments_.review: Gloomhaven delivers the turn-based top-down dungeon crawler experience through the limitations of a ~10 card deck. Your deck diminishes over the course of the dungeon, using cards for actions or movement. Taking excessive damage will also cost you cards, sometimes more than half your deck in a single turn if you are very unlucky, which can make your run very short.The idea of fusing movement and actions into a limited set of action cards is novel, but ultimately given the games aggressive RNG this will mean most players will exhaust their turns part way through a dungeon. There are certain classes with the ability to restore discarded cards, which my party relied on heavily.The game itself is designed to be punishing, but mostly not in a way that can learned or overcome. In our experience, rolls typically skew unfavorable. Using one of your ~10 cards for an action doesn't mean it will happen, often you will fail a dice roll and just waste one of your precious cards. Our party began at Normal difficulty, and after failing to clear the first mission more than 6 times, we tried other missions, and also failed all of those. Eventually we began periodically lowering the difficulty which allowed us to finally progress. There appears to be a massive disparity between the games easiest difficult and all other difficulty settings. Ultimately we had to choose between an unchallenging easy difficulty and an unassailable Normal difficulty. As you progress the game does become somewhat manageable as you can afford items and unlock new cards.The game also has "encounters" which occur between dungeons. They involve a bit or story followed by a binary choice. Regardless of the choice, most encounters will hurt your party, either by taking away your progress towards action points, money, or giving your party a debuff at the start of the next dungeon. There is no way to predict which choice will provide what detriment, the only way to learn this is through experience and repetition. There is also a chance that encounters can benefit a party, but these appear to be extremely uncommon.Playing with friends, the game needs to be reset roughly every other dungeon due to technical issues such as desync, crashes, and other bugs. The game has a dedicated bug report menu, which our host used frequently. The game does not allow players to rejoin mid-turn: you have to wait until turns are over, so the host ends up having to play many of other players moves. Rejoining is not a guarantee that users will be able to retake control of their characters and we experience several soft locks where our only solution was to kick all players and stream the hosts perspective in a voice call.I write this review after having narrowly completing an escort dungeon by one turn before exhausting our last standing players deck. We are not sure if it was a deliberate design choice or buggy pathfinding AI, but the NPC we were required to escort would not move if any enemies anywhere in the dungeon were positioned in a doorway space. It took many turns during the session to even understand how to get them to move, as they just stood by at the entrance turn after turn.The game is not bad, I personally think the aesthetic of the game is wonderful. The dungeons feel somewhat underwhelming in design, but the game definitely captures a tabletop map and deck game motif. The abilities are varied and choosing which card to play definitely involves understanding, strategy, and a degree of chance. It definitely involves a different mindset. The games story is largely driven by each dungeon, episodic and sparse. The game does provide art and narration.This is perhaps one of the few games where I do not feel a sense of accomplishment when overcoming difficulty, and unfortunately felt strongly enough to leave a negative review. It's a nice game if you're a glutton for punishment, but I do not think most people would find this game enjoyable. The game will roll the dice, and bad rolls are extremely punishing and will make your experience short.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very accurate digital remake of the board game.  The characters are the same and have the same cards and abilities although some have not yet been added.  The enemies are also familiar and the AI is fully automated so dungeons play much faster.  In the beta they recently added perks which are essential for certain classes. _childDocuments_.review: Honest Review,A lot of people don't understand early access. Which is just people not understanding game development and most of the critiques come from that blinded view. For example one guy didn't understand the durability system on some items. While this can suck, it is a balance system on items and characters in general since they have a shared gold pool as well. This system is just for the adventure mode which is just a small campaign mode really and not the main story/campaign.The game is fun, and very challenging in its current state. It is not a 1 to 1 with the board game right now as there is no campaign mode(story mode) at the moment, which is expected as that is going to take a lot of time as the campaign in the board game is quite extensive. There are bugs as with all games and they will take some working to fix but if you send in support tickets/report them on the discussion post under bugs they seem quite receptive and the patches seem to fix a lot of bugs if you look through the latest patch notes.Overall, for a gloomhaven experience/strategy/turnbased rpg combat, the game passes with flying colors. Again, it's not the campaign/story mode and if that's all you want then you should wait and multiplayer will also be released later. If, however, you want to support a fun game with much promise and an active indie studio through my personal experience has been quite friendly purchase now. In the long run you'll probably save yourself 20-50% of the final product cost as with all Early Access games.I hope this review helps someone. Overall the game is highly recommended and look forward to the progress being made to the point I can experience the story with a few friends and wonderful graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: Completely formatted to be a chore to play. There is no "undo" button so if anyone accidentally mis-clicks, then you have to live with the decision. We have played multiple scenarios where the players barely hit and basically didn't play. If you want to have a good time, don't spend money on this and buy the board game instead. At least there you can take back a decision and not have to start the game over again.

Now you need to move 5 squares to open a door and for instanceonly have movement 3. Bummer you now need to use a card that you cannotuse and don't get back. Oh fun.I really fell like a wait or even the usage of 1 card should be allowed.All this sucks the fun out of the game for me. _childDocuments_.review: From a technical standpoint, other than some weird UI decisions, this implementation of the boardgame is very well done and really takes a lot of the fiddly bits away.  There is room for improvement, but it is otherwise a solid board game adaptation and true to the real thing.  However, I feel like sometimes poetry can sum up your feelings on a subject better than anything else can.  So here's one about Gloomhaven the game, regardless of medium:, by Al BundyWhen hooters jiggle around and I find nickels on the ground, I care. When a Mustang engine purrs and the bathroom is not hers, I care. When the pitcher's on the mound and the wife is underground, I care. But when I've been playing this for days, I will kill anyone who stays. I swear.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely my favorite online boardgame, and one of the most fun and challenging tactical games I've ever played.  The biggest improvement over the physical copy is that pets can't try to eat the pieces while you're playing.  Scratch that, everything's a huge improvement: the game plays faster, shuffling decks isn't as fiddly, ally and enemy cards are very easy to flip through, and sources of error in calculation and enemy movement are greatly reduced.  Also, soothing Scottish accents.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Can't speak about Multiplayer.Not knowing the board game single player was somewhat tough to begin, but the card mechanics etc are soon learnt and one is very soon drawn into this game's somewhat tough tactical combat. Replayability is mainly using different class combinations, items, enhancements and card combos, the bulk of which are unlocked as one progresses through the game. RNG does play a part too, especially in combat where it can be quite cruel. Characters don't so much die but become exhausted and disappear from the scenario one's playing and are available again for any retry or the next scenario if the rest of the crew make it through; so there's no perma death or serious repercussions for a wipe out and the characters get to keep gold and XP etc they gained prior to the wipe. In that sense the game's user friendly. But it's a tough tactical game none the less. Unfortunately the characters are the bog-standard generic fantasy types with very little new about them for players of fantasy dungeon crawlers. Same can be said of the animations - the standard fare whose novelty wears off rather quickly. Music is pleasantly unobtrusive and weirdly makes my canary start singing; so anything that keeps her happy deserves a thumbs up despite the game's somewhat minor failings.

_childDocuments_.review: The game difficulty was a bit high at the start. You'll spend a few hours figuring out how to make your cards last for the whole map. I found the random encounters to be annoying and often devastating to the final outcome of the destination dungeon. The handicaps are no joke.It's a good game, but this is not a casual strategy game. You gotta have the patience to play a dungeon many times before finding the right combination of luck and skill the squeeze by.Not a game I'd recommend, because the difficulty to start is frustrating enough to walk away from the game. It requires strategy guides and forums to really get a good grasp on the game....and I think it's a bit presumptuous of the programmers to assume that people will be infatuated with this title, like it's the 2nd coming of Magic: The Gathering. I don't know many people that are willing to dedicate that much time to a title.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Gloomhaven with the physical game and on TTS, so I wasn't expecting to want to play through the whole thing again when the Digital game left Early Access - boy, was I wrong. _childDocuments_.review: I would say this is better than the board game. Why? Well, let's be realistic. You and your friends decide to get together for the first time in months to play some board games. You've got one night to throw in all of the games you've been wanting to get to for like seven years. Gloomhaven is agreed upon by everyone but Todd. Todd wanted to play Twilight Imperium. It takes you 2.5 hours to learn how to play. It takes you another 30 minutes to physically set the game up. It's going smoothly and then someone forgets to move a monster. You have to back track five moves or have that nagging feeling that you're playing the game wrong because of one mistake. It's cool. You get over it. Someone forgets that they aren't invisible anymore. Or they're muddled. Or they're stunned. The cycle continues. You lose the scenario. Todd flips the table and decides he's going to divorce his wife. All because of Gloomhaven the board game. With the digital version you don't have to invite your friends over. You don't have to deal with Todd and his drinking problem. You don't even have to pretend you have friends for this example. You can just purchase the game via steam and go right on playing. Sure there's a tutorial, but it's useful to go through once. And it can frustrating to become fully exhausted in a dungeon, but you don't have to keep track of tiny pieces or physical cards. Plus that's something you would deal with in the board game anyway. And better yet you can play solo, as a guild master, or build a campaign. Or if you forgive Todd because you've known him since middle school and he's always been there to help you move, you can invite friends to play without being in the same room.See? Better than the physical board game.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far the hardest table top game I have ever played. First, it was hard to understand the mechanics, then tactics came into play but after that (and with the help of my smarter comrades) the game really opened up for me. It's challenging. It's beautiful. It makes you use your brain for once. The amount of content quest-wise and character-wise is huge. Can't be certain, but I reckon it may take up to 300 hours to try out every max level character with all perks and cards unlocked and beat all 95 scenarios.I would especially like to note the work of the narrator. Boy did he deliver an outstanding performance! And yes, as many before mentioned, it's better with friends. You will fight, argue about choices and laugh at your stupidity, basically having a great time. There's one technical issue though that could ruin the fun: the game is VERY sensitve to your internet connection so if you have a bad one prepare yourself for frequent disconnects.Other than that, highly recommend and do hope to see more content soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a turn-based strategy game like you're used to from xcom, blackguards, etc. This is a board game. As such it works differently to most computer-based games, but it works well. It's a high-concentration game, where (especially on harder levels) you tend to just scrape by scenarios if you play well. Especially enjoyable with 1-3 friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: The Guildmaster update of this game is the game I wanted when I first bought in.  It now teaches the player about how Gloomhaven works and automates many tasks that improve the experience from tabletop.  Although I have 26 hours currently, I only have four or five with this new version.  I am enjoying the storyline and unlocks.  There are still a few issues with powers not being 100% clear until you have played the character enough to know why you can't pull someone objectively closer, for example, when they are not closer in hex count.   My largest negative is that twice I have had an occasional dropout that corrupts the map and takes you back a couple of hours.  I learned to go to the main menu once I did anything I cared about and force a save.Positives:* introduction to the six mercenaries that gives you a feel for play style* open campaign where you can time your access to unlocks such as improved powers, characters, and equipment.* has been very accessible for me to jump on, play two scenarios, then hit the road.  The game keeps track of all the little things for me.Negatives* Some powers not 100% clear in the difference between "reality check" and game terms* Not much explanation for unlocks; you take your best guess on some things* There have been a couple of time-consuming dropouts.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Was already a fan of the Gloomhaven board game and got this to play through on my own. The game is still fantastic and now I don't have to set up or tear down. It's fast with satisfying visuals and sound effects. I wish there was some more variety in that regard, like where the scoundrel still throws knives when a bow is in the card description. Small things. Also, the rules can be heavy so it's nice to have the game keep track of things and do all the maths. The rough part is that it's utterly unforgiving once choices have been made even if I think and undo would have not impacted the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent adaptation of possibly the best tactical dungeon crawling board game ever. The myriad of classes all play very differently providing lots of different play styles. The main campaign from the board game and the additional Guildmaster mode provide an enormous number of different scenarios with different goals and uniqure challenges. Play multiple characters yourself or gather some friends and strategize together to determine the best way to deal with the monsters and environmental difficulties. The multiple difficulty levels provide a range from somewhat challenging to nearly impossible. For first time players, the Guildmaster option is a little easier, the campaign comes out swinging with difficult and somewhat unforgiving scenarios when you're ready to see what you are made of. Would highly recommend Discord or another voice server for multiplayer. While you aren't supposed to explicitly describe what you are doing discussing how early or late you are going and what you are generally doing is both allowed and often essential in beating many of the scenarios.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful adaptation from the board game and I cannot wait for the full campaign to be released. The beginner trainer is an awesome addition that should really help new players understand the basics as well as introduce the different beginner classes. The only negative is the fact that there is no "back" or "Undo" action for anything. I get that this helps keep the integrity but for small things like maybe not selecting all of the possible enemies for an attack or loot action (the selection of these is sometimes a little wonky) or if you forget to take a health potion at the end of a character turn or miss the click to use an element and you realize right after... it's like ah man, this stinks! as this was never an issue on the tabletop version. But again, overall this is an amazing game that I'd highly recommend and hope to play with friends in the future. This digital version will likely make the game far more approachable to casual players as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent, near perfect port of the game. For those who play the tabletop version this means non-of the long preparation time or time-consuming pieces and parts management. For those who have been curious about the board game but intimidated by its size and complexity, this game has the same experience and feel of the game, but being digital, it feels easier to manage. For those unfamiliar with the game, it is one of the best (if not the best) dungeon crawler-type games. What makes this game unique is that the table top version has a persistent campaign, where your actions and previous dungeon crawls have an impact on the game and reveal new characters that you unbox and bring into the game only after completing certain missions and events, with more items available for purchase by your characters and the town of Gloomhaven  prospers with your actions. In other words, the tabletop version of the game is a port of a typical role-play adventure video game, with a campaign and scenarios, which in turn means that it ports perfectly into a video game. Honestly, the video game may end up encouraging you to experience the board game. Great graphics. Clear and useful tutorial that truly teaches you the mechanics of the game. Nice score. 10/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: After carefully monitoring Gloomhaven's early access for over 2 years I decided to purchase it during the last patch before the 1.0 release. I am an avid board game player and have bought the physical game. What's most interesting to me, is that I actually did NOT enjoy the board game for various reasons. That being said, you would probably expect me to dislike and not recommend this game for the above reason. The funny thing is, the digital implementation of Gloomhaven made things a lot of easier for me and made me realise that one of the most frustrating things about the board game is actually the setup and tear down time which spanned from 30 minutes to 1 hour (excluding the hour length games). Suffice to say the digital game has none of that issue, therefore it makes Gloomhaven a much more desirable experience!Gloomhaven is a long campaign game, dungeon crawler with minatures, card management and RPG elements amongst other things. Yeah...it's complicated. You gather your party of 2-4 merchenaries (characters), each and every one of them dinstinct from one another. Each character has their own personal deck of cards that represent their abilities in the game. They also have a personal gold stash, aditionally, they also have personal equipment that they purchase and do not share. Each character also has a personal goal; A card that you draw uppon creating your character that represents their ultimate dream, their life goal. Uppon completing that (and trust me it will take some time) your character actually retires, effectively granting you unique one time bonuses such as new unlockable chacters but also deleting themselves! Despair not though, as the game has a deep legacy system that allows you to upgrade and enhance the character class, allowing you to begin a new character of the same class with increased power and perks! It's all an organic experience that makes you "feel" that you are not a player in a game revolving around you, but rather a guest in a fully fledged world!The campaign fearures numerous scripted scenarios, each and every one of them offering a unique challenge that you must overcome as a group. It is worth noting that the scenarios are handcrafted and extensively playtested in the board game, so there is a pretty good storytelling with pretty solid difficulty curves. The digital game also features Guildmaster mode, which is essentially a freestyle adventure mode, having the same rules but randomized dungeons with no story involved.Gloomhaven is a dark fantasy adventure that resonates better at older players. It's dark theme and it's complex mechanics are a lot to take in, but in return for investing your time and brainpower at it, it unfolds a beautiful world like a rose blossoming it's petals. It's many systems have a most organic feeling, like picking a character and embarking on an adventure with your friends. It's digital implimentation is far superior to the physical board game and I can only assume that it will get even better as time goes by. If you are looking for a deep engrossing experience with dark fantasy theme and superbly handcrafted gameplay involving minatures (character models digitaly), you need not look any further. Gloomhaven has been the number 1 board game of all times for a long time and we can finaly enjoy it for about 1/4 of it's physical price, with the added perks of the digital adaptation. If you enjoy a good challenge, be sure to enter this grim world and leave your mark uppon the city of Gloomhaven!Pros:A deep, dark, fantasy world +Personal characters that feel alive +Mechanics that feel organic +Handcrafted scripted scenarios +Lot's of different enemies to best and overcome +Lot's of uniquely different characters to unlock and master +New character/enemy models that really elevate immersion +A character-unique customizable card system +A legacy system that allows you to leave your mark +Rewards progress constantly +Guildmaster mode +Various difficulties that even scale with playercount +Digital implimentation saves your precious time +Insane replay value that doesn't really ever end +Insanely good price compared to physical game +Multiplayer +Cons:User Interface could be better -Animations could be better -Requires a lot of brainpower -Can be stressful -Requires patience -Mistakes are usually unforgiving -No rewind for moves -Verdict: A dark handcrafted fantasy world that begs to be explored! 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: ***SPOILER FREE REVIEW***Gloomhaven is one of the best board games ever made.  Period.  The game plays as a dungeon crawler and uses a Card based action system that is simple to explain but extremely nuanced in its complexity.  Each round you play two cards and then, when it's your turn in initiative, perform the top action of one card and the bottom action of the other.  It's that simple but there are ten thousand reasons why it is actually more complex than that.  Which top action do you choose (for you are not locked in to an action until you perform it)? What do you target with your attack?  What is the enemy doing?  What are your allies doing?  Should you use one of the game's many powerful items?  Should you use all of your items in one bombastic turn thus sacrificing yourself in a white, hot blaze of glory?  The possibility space is nearly unlimited and thus this game's main mechanic is just perfection.  I simply cannot rave about it enough.  You NEED to play this game!So, all this digital version has to do is adapt the board game faithfully without any game breaking glitches.  Gloomhaven digital does succeed at that but not perfectly.  I've played a lot of this game by now and I would say one out of every dozen play sessions something goofs up.  That's only a 8.33% failure rate but still, it can be frustrating.  Most frequently it just requires a reboot but occasionally my play group and I have lost progress.  Never huge amounts of it but we have lost multi hour long play sessions to the ether forcing us to replay scenarios.  So, do I recommend the game?  Yes, I do.  I would also recommend that you, or someone in your play group, back up your saves.  Speaking of play groups, this game is enhanced greatly by playing it with others.  I would still recommend the game if you are forced to play it alone but it's worth playing at a slower pace just to accommodate friend's schedules.  Good luck friends!-B9

_childDocuments_.review: A bare-bones version of the board game that captures the magic of the card-driven action system I've come to love, but every other aspect of this game is grossly underdeveloped.  The sheer amount of work required to elevate this project to something functional and fulfilling is staggering to think about.Scenarios (the combat events of the game) are engaging but horribly imbalanced.  Serious play testing is needed, especially on harder difficulties.  Playing scenarios grants you gold and exp which can then be used to empower your heroes.  The sad part is that - at the moment - gold is almost entirely useless. Items available in the shops are nearly worthless and, worst of all, uninteresting.  Not to mention the infuriating item decay system.  Items you aquire break after a short time, even when unused.  Gaining new cards after leveling remains satisfying and meaningful, but even this system needs an overhaul.The UI is gross.  Reading your cards is time-consuming and frustrating in the game's current state.  I can only read the text of one card at a time when selecting from a hand of 10-11.  Inexcusable. Attack modifiers, a major source of tension in the board game, are displayed microscopically.  Embrace the board game aesthetic and display them on colored cards that flash up after every attack. The current system only leaves players confused and frustrated.  Even if you love the board game, skip this.  In it's current adolescent state it's just not worth your time.  Darkest Dungeon, Icarus, Slay the Spire, and many others scratch this same itch in a far more effective way.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially did not recommend Gloomhaven, because it was missing so much interaction, and so faithful to the board game that it wasn't truly enjoyable as more than a spare moment of play. The changes that have been made to date, give the user a better experience in general. The flow of the game has been improved. There is now multiplayer, and there seems to be enough that deviates from the board game, to even out the change in experience.  These developers, have truly taken our time, and feedback in a way that is respectful to us. You can wait for the campaign; however, as it is, you are able to experience the game without too much of the early access rough edges.  Below is the original review, in which I did not recomend the game:I love the tabletop version of Gloomhaven. It is an exceptional in person experience, with too many chits, rules, and exceptions to be properly tracked. And it is glorious. This is a nearly one to one digital recreation of the tabletop experience. It's good, except a video game experience and tabletop experience focus on completely different aspects for enjoyment.  Unfortunately the camaraderie, and joint experience that makes Gloomhaven (Tabletop) so good, is not present here. Instead it has become a slogging dungeon crawling experience, that is far too slow, and does not provide the peaks and enjoyment of traditional GH.  A tabletop game is half about the game, and half about the way the game makes you interact with others. This is a solo experience, to it's detriment.Hopefully the experience will be refined to accomodate the shift from Tabletop to Digital by the time it is released as a 1.0.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the most important part out of the way first: this is a 1:1 recreation of the tabletop game with fancy graphics. The various tags like "RPG" ad "Strategy" are accurate in this context, but if you come here expecting a "video game adaptation" of Gloomhaven, you're going to find it stiff, limited, and disappointing.If, like me, you came here for a digital conversion of Gloomhaven, you're going to be thrilled. The eye-candy makes the game crisp and easy to follow, all the rules and updates are there and interactively explained. And the game a LOT of the bookkeeping for you. No more lengthy setup and pack down, no fumbling through rulebooks to resolve edge cases, no forgetting a step or losing a piece. This automation takes solo mode from "technically possible but boring as hell" to a legitimate way to enjoy the game, and makes multiplayer run super smooth - perfect for groups that can meet up online more often than in person.In short, I can 100% recommend this as a way to experience Gloomhaven the tabletop game, alone or with friends, and Gloomhaven is something that deserves to be experienced. The game itself is lengthy, with oodles of content, branching mission paths that require more than one playthrough, and the new Guildmaster mode is a great learning experience that massively expands on even that. Just be aware that this is a digital board game and may fall short if you're expecting the scope of a "videogame".

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice adaptation of the physical game, without all the painful setup. It is difficult for newcomers, but that's mainly due to the shear number of cards/abilities you are given right off the bat, and less the complexity of the game mechanics themselves. Come with a nice "Guildmaster", which is separate and easier than the campaign, to ease you into things a bit. However, Guildmaster can still feel overwhelming at first because of the huge amount of cards you start with.One thing I would suggest for the developers is to add the functionality to immediately undo an action, rather than restarting the round. Yes, this makes a difficult game more forgiving, but I've found myself accidentally clicking the wrong half of a card a few too many times.

_childDocuments_.review: this game can give a very negative first impression as the difficulty of the 'normal' level is off the charts hard for anyone who is not very familiar with the board game.  It is just excessively difficult and after failing the first missions over and over I think a lot of people will just stop playing and trash the game - that is what i almost did.  But I sucked it up and after reading a ton of complaints about the difficulty I bit the bullet and did 'easy mode'...  That is much more what I expected 'normal' to be -  and it is not easy at all, but i can do most scenarios in less than two tries.  It is like buying a chess program that only has AI setting for GM. I know, white knights will point out a video showing someone crushing the hardest difficulty, but i can point them to Magnus Carlson crushing GM level chess... most players are not Magnus.... As a new person to the 'world' it should be common sense to play 'normal' difficulty and win the early battles in a try or two. I think they are really doing the game a disservice by making the early game so difficult. I recommend the game because if you can stomach playing 'easy mode' it offers a lot of content and is a good value for the price - but i can also see giving this a big thumbs down as the first impression is terrible.  it also suffers from the tight restrictions on card use making it a must that you highly optimize every card decision - but the first run of 'dungeons' you will not have a perfect optimal move path etc. and so it is very punishing for first time thru a level as you will fail often due to running out of cards toward the end.

Read some guides posted on steam 2 x over before starting to play and watch youtube videos. (I really wish I found these before playing)Recommendations:Neural Net Games (all of his videos are awesome)MandatoryQuest (this guy is amazing and scientific with his approach)ChistopherOddUseful links:2. _childDocuments_.review: It is only appropriate that one of the most ludicrously ambitious board games ever should get one of the most ambitious ports ever. It is far better than I'd have dared hope for - combining faithful translation of the board game, excellent UX, and decadent 3d graphics. The departures from the board game are all good choices: resolving AI ties with randomness instead of player choice, replacing a couple abilities that would have made the interface much worse, etc. In addition, it is both wonderful and kind of insane that they added an entirely new semi-random campaign mode ("Guildmaster"), that is arguably better than the original's campaign.I do have some criticism. Better "undo" support would have been fantastic. It would also have allowed removing some of the "comfirm action" buttons. I also wish they supported harder difficulties than +2 out of the box, but since they have provided modding support, it's not too big a problem.Playing Gloomhaven has never been easier. Overall, wow, great job Flaming Fowl!!

_childDocuments_.review: Information is WAY too front-loaded. I didn’t find it “too hard” personally - I have seen replies to similar reviews saying to “lower the difficulty” but the difficulty is not the problem. I finished the first few fights on my first attempts and I wasn’t even playing on the lowest difficulty.The problem is that it feels very tedious and unfun to make decisions without any internalized, intuitive basis for doing so. In your first encounter with your first two characters you already have access to something like 40 distinct abilities (20 different cards each representing two options). When you’re just starting you essentially have to read through all your 30-40 abilities every turn to make decisions, while also remembering all the core mechanics you just learned from the 10 or so tutorials (which take a couple hours to finish, as others have pointed out). There's no chance given to build "reflex" or "intuition" for what an ability/card does.I can see this game being fun and tactically engaging if you really knew all your possible actions and the interactions off by heart, but the game gives you no chance to gain that intuition. I don’t really have a suggestion for doing so exactly. I wish you could start with fewer cards but the burning mechanics makes that infeasible.I am someone very familiar with and fond of "information-heavy" games, and I'm writing this because I think the game is very deep and interesting tactically, but I think most people will be immediately turned off for this same reason that I did.

_childDocuments_.review: The negatives first:- They really need to implement a "side game" to play and steal/win gold from other players while waiting between decisions of other players to bring down the bogging of wait time. Would add to the whole mercenary mentality of not trading items or gold freely, too. Or some other kind of mini games that you can play to make the wait time between actions a little easier on group playing.- Also, theres a lot of redundant ways to view your cards/team cards leftover, but its fairly unecessary where they could implement something more useful.- High learning curve, so can be discouraging for casual gamers (not that im complaining personally)- Voice acting the events and adding a vote feature would be really nice, as wellOtherwise, for the positives, to end on a nice note:Beautiful animations, beautiful graphics, and the game definitely appeals to taking a different approach to playing turn based tactics. The music and sound effects are clear and really add to the atmosphere of the game. If you get past the high learning curve and different approach to how you "win", its easily enjoyable. The UI is also smooth and great as far as approaching a "board game" as a video game. I love it.Would I recommend the game? Yes, but only if you're fine with constantly min maxing your scenario losses. Once you have that mind frame, losses arent as discouraging anymore, since theyre more like possible gold and xp advances more than lost time, and can actually be rewarding in their own way (essentially, losses are more of a grind)....But please add some minigames so I have something to do without windowing my game while I wait for other people to make their move : )All that being said, Im the kind of "gamer" that enjoys a challenge, solo or group. So, this is up my alley.8.5 out of 10 easily, potentially 9 even.

_childDocuments_.review: I came to Gloomhaven after putting tens of hours into the physical board game. It was a great way for me and my friends to play and enjoy the game without having to nail down a time for us all to be in the same place. I can honestly say that I enjoy the digital version more than the physical. Pound for pound, the digital version of the game captures all the things that are great about the board game, save maybe the sheer awe that is instilled by the depth and complexity that the board game evokes upon playing. If you like the board game, you will like this game. Period. Nothing of value is truly lost, and one major negative aspect of the physical game is removed: set-up. That's right. No more 45 minutes of set-up for an hour session, segueing into another 15-20 minutes of clean up. That alone makes it worth it, because there are times with the board game that I felt I spent more time setting up than actually playing.For those that haven't played the board game, Gloomhaven is a tabletop tactics game set in a unique fantasy universe. The lore is deep enough to be interesting and the mechanics are where it really shines. Completing scenarios always feel like you're accomplishing something to progress and the variability in play style is impressive to me. There's a lot of card and inventory management and forward-thinking required. It's definitely not a mindless game, and it punishes mistakes handily and without mercy. So be prepared! You're going to lose. Quite a bit. Unless you have some virtuosic command of the game, it will deliver several defeats to your doorstep. If you don't like losing, or get easily frustrated by a couple of random sequences resulting in your total demise, then stay away. BUT. If you don't mind getting bodied here and there, and enjoy learning and growing your playstyle while unlocking cool treasures and characters, this game is tirelessly rewarding as well.I highly recommend with the caveat that its hard as hell and doesn't care who knows it.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this because it was on sale and wanted a different type of RPG. If you like massively micromanaging, this is for you. Some quests are inexplicably stupid like an NPC ghost that moves 2 spaces a turn will basically make your "mage" die before the end of that quest because they just move so stupidly slow. Also, that ghost can die to a trap on the ground, so if you don't have a scoundrel (mine retired before I did this quest) then you'll need to get one to do that quest. It is an interesting concept and I did not know anything about the history of this which is what many other reviewers glowed about. I simply just hated the stupidly small things and I don't like repeating stuff more than once or twice before it just becomes stupid. My time is too valuable to be wasting on nonsense. It was different than most of the classical rpgs I love to play, so if you are into that, give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I haven't played the tabletop game so I can only judge this as a video game, not as an adaptation.✔️ Excellent tactical depth - each choice you take during a battle can have huge consequences on its outcome, and the game has some surprisingly astute combat mechanics I have seen nowhere else.✔️ Incredible balance - while every action counts, it is possible to win often, but expect most victories to be very close ones.✔️ The graphics are very beautiful, with a particular care given to the environments that not only have a tabletop feel to them, but are also varied, crisp, and detailed.✔️ Smart character build customization with a unique deckbuilding mechanic. Like for the battles, each choice you take can impact your gameplay in a major way, and synergies between abilities (and characters) are many!✔️ The world is rich and detailed, filled with intrigue, factions, strange creatures, and surprising events.✔️ Despite the game's focus on tactical combat, the narration still offers an interesting amount of player choice.✔️ Full voiceover of the narration.✔️ Nice music.✔️ Flexible difficulty options that allow anyone to experience the game.💭 Some people I know complain about some degree of "sluggishness" in the game, due to the fact that the time between turns of a given player may be somewhat long, especially in full groups of 4. Personally it doesn't bother me, since the tactical sharpness of the game requires some degree of maintained attention in order to avoid fatal misplays, but it wouldn't have been fair if I didn't mention that.Overall I ABSOLUTELY recommend this game to any fans of turn-based based RPGs and other tactical battle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I've tried really hard to learn and enjoy playing this game, but most of the time it ends up being more frustrating than fun to play.As others have written, this game has a really steep learning curve and it is very challenging. I knew this going in so I played all the tutorials and also spent hours reading the very extensive manual for the physical version. It was still confusing to play but I gradually learned at least the basics.What no amount of preparation could prepare me for is the incredibly steep learning curve. I don't mind a challenge but this game is over the top difficult. And when I finally start to make some progress the game throws me some absurdly difficult scenarios. For a game where grinding is pretty much pointless, the difficulty balancing is very poor. Grinding is pointless because as you increase in level the scenarios scale to become more challenging. You get very few rewards for completing a scenario - a tiny amount of money and maybe an item that you still have to buy (you only get the ability to make a tiny number of each item).You do have the ability to upgrade your card abilities, but the cost of absurd. This may be the single worst design decision in this game. After playing 30-40 hours I have around 500 gold. This will allow me to upgrade perhaps 3 cards with a very minor upgrade. The better upgrades can cost upwards of 300 gold so you won't be using this feature very much. Worse, it seems that in the Guildmaster mode you can't sell these card upgrades, even at a loss. Apparently there is a way to sell the upgrades at 75% of cost, but this may only be in the Campaign (I'm playing in Guildmaster). I wouldn't know, the game leaves a lot unexplained and there is only one save so you can't learn by doing.The game is so hostile to beginners I'm surprised it is so highly rated. I will say that when you play a scenario that offers a reasonable challenge (reasonable here still means tough, I sometimes win with only one character who is not exhausted), the game can be really fun. When get get a few of these well balanced scenarios in a row I start to think I've finally caught on to the game. Then I struggle to find another scenario of the many available that I stand the slightest chance at and go back to disliking the game and wanting to stop playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the game, that is the board game. Played countless hours with that one and around 1.5k with the digital version. While I prefer the real thing, playing campaigns is a tedious job, setting up scenarios, not making mistakes during the plays etc, is not easy, you need a pretty big table and a reliable group who doesn't abandon the campaign. The digital version helps with this a lot, no more setup, no more mistakes etc, I think it looks pretty nice , I'm even ok with the controls. It was quiet buggy at the beginning but most of them were fixed. There is one thing that ruins the game for me though, and I can't look over it, and that is the rate of pulling curses and misses on high brutal+ difficulty. I played the game a lot of times, but I'm still enjoying it with a friend and we still enjoy playing it on very high difficulty, however it looks like the developers using different algorithm to decide what cards we pull from the attack modifier on different difficulty. This is prety damn annoying. And I'm talking about pulling a miss with 1-2 characters out of four, for about 4 rounds every turn. Now, according to the rules, whenever you pull a miss, you supposed to reshuffle the deck, the chances to pull 4 misses for several turns continuously.. well they are very low, but somehow it keeps happening on every scenario with us. The enemy also seem to pull every single curse from their deck when they have 4-5+ curses. It's just really not realistic, and even if you put Maths on the side, I played a lot with the physical board game, it's not happening. This ruins the game for me, I want to finish it on Brutal and Deadly but even with a deck, with no negative modifier other than the miss, I pull a miss 5 times in a row... BS.Not sure how it is implemented, but it really feels like on higher difficulty, the algorithm is different, which is just stupid, you have increased damage and HP for enemies and traps, just stick to that, introduce more difficulty levels with even more damage + hp, but changing the "luck" element of the game is a joke.I really want to recommend the game because the rest is ok or really good, but I had enough. Luckily Frosthaven is out!

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the boardgame, and it is one of my favorites.  We played over the course of 18 months, and it was an amazing adventure.  When this online version was first released with early access, it was not like the boardgame, and it was definitely a work in progress.  Now, it is very similar to the boardgame, and while it has its positives, there is one massive issue, and that is the RNG.  When pulling combat modifier cards, you start with six +0, five +1, five -1, one +2, one -2, one 2x, and one Null, thus twenty cards total.  So the odds of pulling one of these cards (initially and after a reshuffle) are as follows; 30% +0, 25% +1, 25% -1, and 5% each for the +2/-2/2x/Null.  But, over the course of twenty battles in a couple recent games I played, this is what I pulled: -2/Null 60%, -1 25%, +0 10%, +1 5%, and +2/2x 0%.  I understand how RNG works.  Yes, this could have been a fluke, and yes I will continue to collect stats.  But 12 out of 20 pulls with a 5% chance of pulling the -2 or Null card?  The odds of that occurring are astronomically low.  I don't need an easy mode or an "I win" button, but I need to enjoy the game.  But when I'm taking my time, planning my attacks, and the entire round is zeroed out repeatedly, its just not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Campaign mode for this game doesn't have Easy difficulty and when you ask for help community pile on you with "Git Gud". EDIT: Turns out, It is expected from the player to start playthrough in the Guildmaster game mode while there is no such emphasis via in-game tooltip or help. There is enormous difference between Easy difficulty in Guildmaster and Campaign game modes (at least it should not be called that way in the Campaign).Also, the game crashes very often for me. Good news, dev team is still working on the game, so there is a glimpse of hope that crashes as well as abysmal difference between Easy difficulty will be fixed in the future.Do not waste your money & time unless:A) You're aware of the table game and actually played it;B) By the time you read this review devs actually reballanced easy difficulty for story mode and released update.P.S. _childDocuments_.review: A bit shallow in terms of choice.The game showered me with text wall tutorials, which I read. It explains the most mundane things that you can figure out in game, like moving the camera. Few really important mechanics (like AoE rotation or element building/consumption) are only explained in tutorials (separate game mode). UI design also complicates things in some places, until you get used to it.Going onto gameplay part, I played with a friend on normal difficulty and it became very clear that the game is not winnable by playing safe. Depending on your class/setup you have a fixed amount of turns to finish a dungeon with. Unless you rush through, you run out of cards and fail. That matters because you get quite a lot of strategic choices you cannot take (like breaking enemy line of sight to lure them into traps).I don't think it's a good game to play alone. Co-op makes it redeemable and I can see myself playing a few more games. If I do end up changing my mind, I will update this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended.To those who own the physical game: the early access has only adventure mode for now, stop comparing it to the almost flawless play experience that is the campaign mode, its a mode that is different and has some bugs or things that are in need of reworking, but that is just normal in such a massive game with tons of rules and crazy situations with skills, etc.To those who dont own the physical game or dont know how to play: Dont complain about the lack of a tutorial please...this game is massive, and quite well known. I dont own the physical game and was only available to play it with friends via tabletop simulator, and had to read the manual a lot, and forums on rules clarifications, and there are plenty of youtube how to play videos and walkthroughs... _childDocuments_.review: It is early access and there are bugs that I am confident will be fixed in time but it is enjoyable to play and relatively easy to pick up on. There is a very detailed tutorial on how to play but I just decided to hop in and wing it. There were some things that I was took me a few times to figure out; specifically timing around using items or elements and such but I was able to eventually figure them out. It is pretty intuitive. _childDocuments_.review: Gloomhaven was designed as a co-op game, but the co-op is a buggy mess. There are constant disconnects regardless of who is hosting. I searched on Google, Reddit, and Steam to look for a solution, but all I see are posts from other people complaining about the same issues.That said, if you're only planning to play single player, then the above problem is a non-issue. Outside of the constant co-op disconnects, the core game is actually a solid adaptation of the board game.Edit: I found a janky workaround to the multiplayer desync issue.  Rolling the game back to the pre-crossplay patch version solves it. (In other words, the desync issue was caused by the last patch.)To roll back, go to the game's properties, then click beta, then choose the "Pre Cross-Play" beta.

There are some bugs, but developers are patching it up, most encountered got fixed.Reason we stopped playing this is stability.Host together with one player on the same home network, third connects from outside. _childDocuments_.review: I like it.Solid digital conversion of the elements found in the Gloomhaven board game, and the plans beyond Early Access include a direct conversion of the board game campaign - which is great, since I can look at running individual campaigns outside of the physical board game group I run. There's a lot of misinformation around, but two *important* things keep coming up in reviews as cons, so let me clear some up (based on reading through Dev info):1. The current EA build is limited to Adventure Mode, which is randomized and not indicative of the board game2. Items in Adventure Mode have a degradation timer for scenarios, but this *will not* be present in the campaign modeCurrently there's work being done on adjusting UI, fixing bugs, testing and the like. But, compared to other EA games I've tried, this is a solid and fun experience overall. My recommendation: If you like (or love) Gloomhaven, get involved and take part in EA. It will help the Devs and the game.If you're kind of interested, get involved and take part in EA. Gloomhaven has a way of reeling you in and revealing layers of interest.If you're not interested, watch some videos, do some research about the board game and then decide. Either way, I'm liking it, and I think the EA cost was well worth the experience/fun so far. Plus, the game will be increasing in cost on full release, so saving now for a solid digital conversion of the board game later is a bonus for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I am an owner and regularly scheduled player of the Gloomhaven tabletop version and was part of the Frosthaven Kickstarter project, so my review comes from experience with the source material.Having said that, I am *highly* impressed by how they have not deviated from this source material.  The cards are all there.  The cards all work precisely as expected.  The items all work precisely as expected.  The combat hasn't been altered.  What I mean to say is, this is a 1:1 digital recreation of the material found within the box, minus the campaign which I know they are working on implementing for full launch.I am highly enjoying this Guildmaster mode, even though it offers the only deviation from the 1:1 expectation in that not all items are available, you don't get EVERY card unlocked as you level up but rather choose only one, and the bonus objectives that grant you extra gold or unlocks is different.  The campaign promises the same experience as the box, however, so I'm not at all worried about this.As it stands, this game is in early access, and thus incomplete.  If you are looking to enjoy a digital Gloomhaven stroll while waiting for the campaign to come online, then you'll love it.  The rules are all handling by the background and are only unforgiving in that there is no room for mistakes.If, however, you are looking for a digital retelling of the Gloomhaven narrative?  You wont yet find that here.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: This is a 1to1 conversion of the tabletop version of Gloomhaven. Right now it has a very barebones "adventure mode" that lacks the magic and charm of the original's campaign. Eventually the campaign and other characters will be added later in development. For those that have never played the original, it is an incredible experience, with some of the most engaging and exciting combat of any table top dungeon crawler. This game promises to be an excellent substitute for those that don't have a few faithful friends to go through the massive campaign or a swole enough  body to lift the massive game box. Warning: As of this writing, there is no tutorial, and Gloomhaven is not exactly like much of anything else. Most of what is going on is explained in the compendium, but for those unfamiliar with how the table top version functions this is going to prove confounding until better guidance is implemented or you go read how to play the table top version. In particular, pay attention to what cards are "burned" when used vs those that are only discarded.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is as smooth, dynamic, and so beautifully balanced - exactly like the original board game. Honestly I prefer this to the board game which I LOVED and put a few hundred hours into. I can foresee enjoying the digital game version just as much - it's so much faster, pretty intuitive once you get used to the controls, exciting to have less information about the rest of the scenario maps... everything feels exactly like the board game. They did an excellent job with putting it online. I've also done Co-Op a little bit, which has been very well done and also is just like the original board game. I largely had to stop playing the board game after my cat started hunting pieces of the game hah!... so I've been waiting for the digital version - 50 hours in and I've only done a a handful of scenarios, so much more content and character classes to explore - 10/10, highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to say it, but the majority of negative reviews come down to one thing.  The inability to "git gud".  Gloomhaven at it's heart is NOT a friendly game.  It is not a game you pick up in 20 minutes like 99% of all PC games out there.  The way the game flows is very deliberate and requires a very strategic approach.  When do you use loss cards, when do you take damage vs lose a card?  When do you heal vs do damage to reduce future incoming damage... If you have never played the boardgame, expect a steep learning curve until you truly understand the mechanics.  Despite a digital format, it is still the boardgame at heart.

_childDocuments_.review: Gloomhaven is unique. If you've delved deep into the world of board games, so be it in actual board games or discovering them through Tabletop Sim, such as I did, you will find that there are many, many imaginative, interesting and strangely complex games out there. Of them all that I tried, Gloomhaven outdoes, outshines, outperforms in every aspect. As a tactical, turn-based RPG, it has half the industry to compete with, and yet, it manages to do everything right. From the smallest system of using cards instead of dice, to every unique scenario mechanic, Gloomhaven is never lazy nor boring with its design. It always considers what every other game is doing, and introduces its own thing that defies the norm, so be it in lore, setting and mechanic. You would think that by saying this, the game is astoundingly complex and it would have a rule book the size of a barn. No, not quite - the rules are intuitive, predictable, and easy to memorize to the point that you will never forget the basics. Not quite perfect, as there is some fiddling with some unintuitive mechanics that will require to check what manner of event happens where, or at least make you question how do you have line of sight through a solid wall. Overall, Gloomhaven is one of the best co-op, campaign-based RPGs I've played in my life, and it might be one of the few games I don't mind paying full price for. I do hope it continues to get updated, as there are still some avenues the game can be improved, in performance, content and graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: Though still early access, the game has a lot of options, strategy, customization, and gear.  The small limit of cards a party member has in battle makes each battle very tactical.  Only found one character so far (spell caster) that can recover burned cards.  The longer battles force you to use the weaker (non-burned) cards so that you still have options late into the battles.  This is a very deep game and even in early access would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awful.  I feel like I'm playing against the games developers, not the game itself.  It's filled with terrible mechanics and bad decisions that completely suck the fun out of the game.  For example.Your characters will randomly deal ZERO damage with their attacks and this happens a lot.  Seriously, I'm not even joking here, you'll attack, and then randomly your damage will get reduced to zero.  This is utterly frustrating every time it happens.Also, this game is 100% dungeon crawling, but your characters have a limited number of actions they can perform total in a dungeon.  Once you've used every one of your possible actions, your character is removed from the dungeon as if they had died.  They don't respawn, they're just done.  You could be at full helath and poof you vanish because you don;t have any actions left.  If all your characters go poof this way, or just die, you lose.  Now get this, due to the limited number of actions the dungeons are really small, like 3 rooms max.  In a game entirely about dungeons, no dungeon has more than 3 rooms.  Why would you ever design a game like this.TLDR Game is garbage.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much a work in progress.  Pros:-Does not follow board game story line; you can play this to get your fix or try things out without spoiling a first play thru.-Looks and sounds great.-Plays like Gloomhaven.-Character selection is currently very limited; does not yet include all of the basic starting classes even. -Some card effects, notably "push", multi-target and element consuming effects don't seem to function yet.-The game balance is way off, as the scenarios are RNG created.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: It's extremely difficult at the start and gets easier as the game goes along. The multiplayer is a bit screwy and occasionally missions will bug out. Some missions are just way harder than others. It's a board game and you have to be prepared to accept a huge amount of abstraction in terms of how things work.But the tactical depth is just so good. You have to pick two cards to play each turn and you can't pick them again until you've run out. Each card has a move, an attack and an initiative value so planning what to do and when to do it is just ridiculously rich in tactics. If you like the rich strategy here the game is gigantic. 17 classes, 95 missions and then a bunch more missions in Guildmaster which I've barely touched. Turn based strategy is a wide genre so I can't guarantee if you like games like Civilization or even Wildermyth you'll like this. I love it though and this is either going to redefine tactics games going forwards or just be an evergreen cult classic.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: At first I was frustrated with crashes and connection issues with a friend.  We overcame that but this game was incredibly difficult to learn... maybe the hardest to learn of any turn based rpg I've ever played. What hooked me after alot of frustration was the progression of the characters I created only to find out once I really started enjoying and understanding my character, they get RETIRED and you CAN'T play the anymore.I guess that makes it replayable to an extent as it unlocks another new character class for you to refill the spot but it ends up being a much lower level character with none of the equipment or buffs you worked so hard to achieve on the previous character.Not my kind of game -- the gameplay itself is actually kind of annoying and it's only appeal to me was the character progression -- which the game kills as soon as it gets going intentionally.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: It became apparent that due to the complexity of the rules and gameplay dynamics, each turn plays out like solving a puzzle which is not what I was into. Also the tutorials don't teach you how to play.  They briefly explain several gameplay mechanics then drop you in a scenario and if you can't figure it out, the game doesn't (during the tutorial mind you) help you figure out what the problem is. Just fail and repeat. Which normally wouldn't be an issue but again, due to the complexity of the gameplay dynamics is more difficult than it should be.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: this game really frustrates me. I found the controls really weird. You can restart rounds, but only at certain points, which feels kind of arbitrary to me. You can just be unlucky at times and it is possible to deal no damage at all, because there is no mechanic to prevent to draw x0 attack modifiers all the time.Then there is a bug, that after some turns the camera rotates. Sometimes it's often, sometimes not. It's also still unclear to me, in which cases you can attack 'through the wall' or around a corner. I miss an ingame wiki or encyclopaedia, where the basic game rules are explained.And please fix this rotation bug, this is so annoying, especially because the rotation always happens, while manual rotation is blocked, so you have to wait some time to rotate back!Also there is one thing I am not yet certain of: If you are bad, then you can grind your way through the levels.. but as you gain levels, the game also becomes harder. _childDocuments_.review: tl;dr : Overall this is a great bang for the buck game.Very true to the boardgame. You do not have to know the board game to enjoy though.If you like turn based fantasy play, this is for you. If you have a friend or three to join youyou'll have a great time. The art is easy on the eyes and the maps mostly intuitive whennot deliberately puzzly.Think turn based strategy solo or with friends (cooperative only).  That will be full of difficultchoices, and laughable mistakes. Along with a few mistakes that make you made at yourself.But when you one hit and elite drake and three of your friends cheer... It's magical too.Speaking of magic it's a card based system of play. you have a limited size deck, too manycards and always a few regrets. You will want a crowbar for one more card. Which is another sign this is a good game.  Your spells, stabs, hacks, and heals are all in the cards. How and whenyou choose them is the game play.The campaign story has arcs, sides to pick, quests to fail and then succeed, and decent voice overs forthe story reading. I'd list cons and problems but they are few and if i listed the ones that weretwo months ago, they are mostly fixed now. Dev team is still making improvements, and regular updatesas of Q4 2021. With more planned into 2022. I could go on but other reviewers have gone into detail better. Overall this is a great bang for the buck game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really glad to stumble upon this game. Prior to the release of Gloomhaven on Steam i had no idea that a tabletop version had existed. What really makes this game different is that every character has a deck of cards in which they choose 2 for their turn. As you progress in the game you will level up which in turn allows you to add new cards to your characters deck, you also can equip items in each of your characters slots. As you progress through the game you will also free up more spots to take more companions with you rather than the starting of 2 characters only. _childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - Gloomhaven is still in early access, but is looking promising. As a fan of the board game, I wish certain features inherent to that version were playable already, but since they're not, I find myself enjoying what is available, but getting bored of it after a time. I am excited to see what the community comes up with for custom rules and mods, and how the dev team handles common "house rules" that exist among players today. What's there (12/30/2019): All 6 starting characters, (almost) all cards, basic game play in adventure mode (preconfigured/randomized dungeons), some items, some enemy types, some tilesets, some bosses, some road events. All of this enables what feels more like a proof-of-concept or sandbox style game play. Probably a necessary (or at least useful) step in the development. Money and items are pooled for the whole party. Dungeon configurations are unknown until you enter the dungeon and/or open a door. (An impossibility for the physical version of the game since the players have to know how to set up the scenario - somewhat increases difficulty, but not to an unfair degree). A party (of up to 4, after killing the adventure mode bosses) consists of unique characters whose progress and level dictate nothing for another party. Characters belong only to the party they are created in, and cannot join another party. This means that there is no drop in/drop out for characters. Once you unlock the third character slot - if you want a 3 person party, you have to make a new party (and everyone starts at level 1). Repeat for the 4th slot. What's missing (12/30/2019) - Campaign mode and all of its progress - Character levels, card enhancements, city levels (meaning starting a new character will always start at level 1),  city events, all non-starting character classes, retirement goals, dungeon goals, various items, item blueprints (these wouldn't make sense outside of campaign mode), the rest of the various 'some...' things listed above, etc... I'm sure there are a few things I'm forgetting, but if it has to do with the campaign or campaign progress, expect it not to be there at the moment. Also, custom rulesets and mods, and multiplayer mode are all supposed to be added in during Early Access, but are not available yet. Summary: This is a great start. If you enjoy the progress you obtain in the board game, like the city leveling, card enhancements, character level/progress carry-over, then early access will currently leave you wanting. Assuming development continues to progress, I have high hopes for Gloomhaven. A suggestion to the Devs: Build in basic communication features for Multiplayer mode. Possibly in-game voice chat. Allow me to see other players' mouse cursors, maybe allow players to show cards (helpful for new players).

_childDocuments_.review: Was excited for a cheaper and more accessible option than the physical version. Well, cheaper is exactly what I got.Multiplayer has frequent desync issues (the host's data not transferring in full or correctly) even after it takes 10 minutes for other players to load in. The solution is for the non-hosts to delete any local save data in LocalLow and the host to re-sync on Steam.There's apparently plenty of soft-locks where missions are unwinnable because the game is broken: My group got stuck on Infernal Throne (Scenario #21) and in trying to find a solution, found posts reporting the bug in 2021 but with no solution from the community and much less from the devs. With my own knowledge of Unity3D, I believe it should have been an easy fix.The graphics are so-so.The narration is top notch, but it's all one guy.Gameplay is **hard** but house rules + mods make it more casual-friendly and a tolerable challenge.The events are the same as in the physical game. I don't know how much, if any, of the narrative content here is unique.All the localizations are player-made mods, which means quality will undoubtedly vary.Whole game ends up feeling cheap and flimsy with just as much time wasted debugging it as getting clobbered in 1-2 hr long dungeons.It's a cheap way to learn the rules of Gloomhaven but it's not guaranteed to be playable. The physical version might be >$100 USD but at least it works.

_childDocuments_.review: was originally a tabletop game that has now been developed into a digital version. This is a faithful representation of the board game with a few balancing differences, quality of life improvements, and a few tweaks. Whilst this version improves on some of the critiques that the original board game had, there are some newfound problems that can’t go overlooked.• Heavily strategy focused• Diverse range of Mercenaries that have their own strengths and weaknesses• Numerous unique monsters• Multiple levels of difficulty to suit newcomers and seasoned veterans• High replay value• Over 100 hours worth of content• A big learning curve to overcome• Scenario 1 is make or break for newcomers• Playable tutorial doesn’t explain some of the more valuable rules#• UI can be very crowded• Bugs and performance issues here and there is not for the faint-hearted. Don’t come into this game expecting it to be another RPG you can haphazardly stumble through and win. Admittedly, it’s a steep learning curve to climb, one that may cause players to become frustrated and give up. There’s an intricate set of mechanics that requires a lot of strategic thinking, planning, and improvisation to triumph in . Gathering knowledge about how this game works, and figuring out some nuance mechanics is what will give you the edge, which sometimes you need. Are you still here? Great, let's talk about the game.At the start of the campaign, you’ll be greeted with six mercenaries that you can choose to form a team. Each of them has their own play styles that they specialise in, but also have downfalls that need to be considered. From a weak but powerful mage to a hard-hitting but slow Inox Warrior, there is a surprisingly diverse group to pick from. Every class has a set number of cards they pick to build their deck. The cards mostly have unique actions on them for each class, but at low levels, there isn’t much to be excited about. For such a small roster to select from, there are various different teams you can build. Part of the fun is finding new combinations and strategies between the original six and how their actions can complement each other. That being said, no Mercenary wants to be diving in dungeons forever, they want to move on with their retirement goal at some point.Once a Mercenary has achieved their retirement goal, they will leave the team. You’ll be awarded a new class for your efforts, and can recruit another Mercenary if you wish. Although it's difficult to let go of the characters that you’re used to playing, it's a core element of the game. The new classes are far more powerful than the original six. It takes some time to become accustomed to your new recruit before you realise their full potential. So, what do you say to a bit of good old-fashioned dungeon delving?Every scenario you encounter has a goal to achieve in order to win. Most of the time it’s simply ‘kill all enemies’ or kill a specific enemy, which leaves a lot to be desired. However, mowing down enemies is still satisfying nonetheless, almost feeling like a delicate puzzle that could fall apart with a few wrong moves.At the start of each round you’ll pick two cards from your deck of cards with each Mercenary you control. The actions of cards can vary widely depending on what class you play. Usually, the top action is an attack of some kind, and the bottom is movement. Once the enemy card has revealed itself and your turn rolls over depending on initiative order (number in the middle of the card, the lowest goes first). You then use the top action on one card, and the bottom action on the other. These are then placed in a discard pile and the cycle continues. Once you are unable to play a pair of cards on your turn, you’ll have to rest to get them back. However, upon resting you’ll be forced to  a card, which makes it unavailable for the rest of the scenario. The number of cards you have represents your longevity in the scenario before you become exhausted.You’ll find most cards have average damage or movement, but there are far more compelling actions that might catch your eye. Massively devastating singular attacks or huge AOE attacks that apply a status effect to all targeted enemies. Whilst these are extremely valuable, they do come at a cost. Burning them after use. This forces you into a balancing act, whereby burning powerful cards early on, though might prove useful in the short-term, will jeopardise your longevity in the scenario. Consequently, making you exhaust faster. really does push you to get the most out of every action that you play. You need to be aggressive, but also mindful of how monsters will act. Every scenario is tight to win and only gives you a small amount of leeway (depending on the difficulty). It will punish you if you attempt to play it at your own pace. Whilst the first scenario is notoriously difficult for new players, it sets you up for how the game is going to play. It’s a steep learning curve that you can’t overcome with pure luck, it requires a lot of tactical movement and strategy.For such an extensive campaign, you’ll encounter a multitude of different monsters, all with their own attack deck and unique actions. There are only about four to six cards in each deck, so it's possible to memorise each monster deck and attempt to predict what they do next. Some enemies such as cultists can summon the living dead, whilst others such as the demons have a shield value that soaks up damage before you can deplete their health.Upon completing a scenario, you’re more than likely to be rewarded with experience. As each character levels up, you’ll gain stronger cards to add to your deck, which further diversifies each class. It does feel like a chore however when you have to choose a card to burn when your deck gets more streamlined with better cards. You’ll also gain perks that modify your attack deck (a deck that you draw every time you attack that modifies your attack) by removing negative cards (-1, -2), adding positive cards (+1, +2), or including new cards altogether. This allows you to streamline each modifier deck and, once again, adds even more variety to each class as they’ll have unique perks available to them.Whilst the digital version handles a lot of the automation that you would usually control in the tabletop version, there are new problems that need to be addressed. There are still bugs and performance issues throughout, the playable tutorial leaves valuable information out. Crowded areas make it difficult to figure out who you’re attacking, occasional soft locks, and so on. These don’t necessarily break the game by any means, but become annoying to deal with. isn’t a game for everyone. It takes a while to wrap your head around, but it seems some people are bashing their heads against a wall playing this game. Whilst the digital version makes it more accessible, it doesn't do itself any favours with annoying bugs, performance issues, and an average tutorial. Overall, I’d only recommend  if you're willing to put in the time and dedication to learn the game.
