_childDocuments_.review: 1989 - Mechwarrior 1995 -  Mechwarrior 21999 - Mechwarrior 32000 - Mechwarrior 4Welcome to Mechwarrior 5!Battletech: Long Tradition. 1985 Battletech was born. 1986 Mechwarrior was born. Both started an unprecedented triumphal procession.In a short Time the whole Franchise was growing faster then a Locust on Nitro. Books, a Cartoon TV Series, Comics,  Tabletop, Merchandise AND OF COURSE the Gaming Universe.Battletech is a science Fiction Space Opera that deserves a TV Series.Someone said to me: Hey Battletech is like Game of Thrones in Space!I said: No, it is NOT. Game of Thrones is like Battletech in Fantasy.As you can i see, i´m a huge Battletech Fan since 1988 as i bought the First (Decision at Thunder Rift) of 61 Books. I have a huge Battletech/Mechwarrior Collection. simply passion. So much for the Introduction, dear Reader. Mechwarrior 5 was long awaited. 20 Years after Mechwarrior 4 it is Time to climb back into the Cockpit.The Year is 3015. Humankind colonized Space and founded a Stabound. After Betrayal and a fatal Civil War everything went to hell and 5 Houses remain. You are the Son of a Mercenary Leader. Speaking of Betrayal, yes your Father died because of one. Betrayal is a Tradition in the Battletech Universe. And Revenge. My first thought was: Decision at Thunder Rift! The First Battletech Book. And yes, it casted a big smile on my Face, the Story is a Homage to it. Okay it is not the GRAY DEATH LEGION from the Book itself, but i got Goosebumps.But don´t expect too much, the Story is a typical Vengeance Story like in MW4. After a nice done practical Tutorial you found yourself in Space, just with a Ship and 2 Mechs and are fleeing.Here starts your Mercenary Career, so welcome to the first Day of your new Life..... or the Rest? Who knows?You can wander around your Ship, what is for the First Time very impressive. When you stand in front of your giant Mechs in the Hangar, thats a Moment where a Fan like me gets a Fangasm.  OH .... MY .... GOOOOOD!!!!! Oh please i want one on my own at home, to go to work with.No more Parking or traffic Problems!Well, that is something i never experienced before, just to mention that i never played "Mechwarrior Online" if you can do it there, too. I´m a PVE not PVP Player, so i didn´ttry it. What i like is Coop Playing and that is something we have here. You can invite Friends to help you on your Missions. they took Control of your other Pilots and their Mechs. Of course you can help your Friends, too. Nice done, you can see if a Mech was into Battle.Your first Mission. You have a light Mech and are launching out of the ship. Here awaits you the WING COMMANDER PROPHECY Effect. First Mission, many, maaaaany Enemies. No laming and easy 3 Enemy Units Mission, no there are 19 Units + Turrets if you dont destroy the nearby Generator. All you need to come directly into the Gameplay. Shooting, Jumping, Runing, Aiming and just having Fun.THAT was a great Feeling like coming Home. That Mission was really easy. Just Tanks, no Mechs.The controlling of your Mech can be specified. Your Mech can run forward while the Torso is left or right. Well, that was something new for me, because in older Games the Torso went mostly Back in Front Direction. I found myself walking elsewhere while i tried to shoot my Enemies. Thanks God, there is an Option in the Menu that makes that Walking/Torso Direction easier. Yup. Assign your Weapons to Groups and use them as a Ticket to scrapyard for your Enemies. Have 2 Important things in Mind. You have limited Ammo and Heat. Weapons produce Heat and If you have too much you can make Fried Eggs on your Console,shutting down your Mech, making you the Sandbag for your Enemies. For you: Hit them hard. No Arms, no Weapons, no Legs, no moving, no Head, no Mech. Aim and don´t shoot blindly, that spare you much money and maybe your Life.You have all Kind of Enemies. Mechs, Air and Ground Attackers. First blow the lower Ones to hell, because small livestocks do also much Damage if you don´t took care of them. That brings me to the Enemies itself.Second Mission, first Enemy Mech. Oh i was so excited. There he came ...... and run in Circles around me. What the.... He was very fast, of course it is a light Mech, but he was not the best Aimer. Didn´t get any Damage, aimed at his legs and there he went to Dirt. To be honest. The AI of BOTH Enemies AND Companions is really, really questionable.But hey, this is Old School. I want Fun in a Big Mech and not highly ambitious Enemies. This Mechwarrior, this is Fun!But 2 Golden Rules if you want to survive!1) Never have an ally in your Back. They shoot at the Enemy, no matter if you are in the Middle. Remembering the Moment, where i scraped that Urbie Mech, while my Back Armor went down like Cheese Slabs. Thought to myself, the Urbie can shoot around the Corner? Oh no, its that damn Jenner of my OWN TEAM behind me!2) Never give your allies a Chance to go into the Constructions you have to defend! That Brontodinosaurs moved everything you must defend into the Ground, just to reach the Enemy if the way is shorter to reach them...... Yes, i have a Headache momently because after a Manouver like that, i hammered my Head on the Table.......One funny thing, there are spawning enemies. Me and my Lance was running happy over the wide Meadows, a Message came in, telling of an ambush. Just in that Moment a Tank spawned in Front of me and i was not able to stop and BAM. Was like having an insect under the Shoe.  Yeah, he was not alone, but hey, one Enemy less. Another Option i liked is the Tonnage Reduction. Before your Missions, the Tonnage is limited. So choose wisely if go for example with one Heavy or with 2 Medium Mech on your Metal Date. It would be so lame if you can go out evertime with 4 100 Ton Mechs. Hey, this is not a STEINER SCOUT LANCE Game, this is Mechwarrior 5!!! Are we ♥♥♥♥♥♥ or are we Mechwarriors!?!?!?! This is Old School! Hell yeah!But there is on thing i have my problem with. The Soundtrack.I´m a big BIG Fan of Game Soundtracks, especially Mechwarrior Soundtracks, owning them all but this is the First i didn´t like that much. A Game with much crashing Metal deserves a Heavy Metal Soundtrack, but ..... no. In all the Years, the Music fit in perfectly into the Games, giving you always the Feeling sitting in a big Mech. This Time some of the Tracks are blowing me out of my Cockpit instead of going with me into Battle.  Come on! Say it. I know you want to say it. Are we ♥♥♥♥♥♥ or are we Mechwarriors?Yeah, yeah, yeah. XDThe Tracks for themselves are great, but some doesn´t fit into the Game in my Opinion. If you want Modern great Mechwarrior Tracks then have a listen to Timothy Seals Tracks on You Tube. Most Tracks are remixed from the Past, but in a really great Way. Sorry, Devs, your Soundtrack is cool but i listen more to Mr. Seals Music in the Back. Maybe you should have a listen to him if you are making another Mechwarrior. You´re still here, dear Reader? Thank you for your power of endurance.Well, Mechwarrior 5 is not perfect, i know. But it is pure Fun. For Fans like me and also for new Player. I really enjoy it and i´m so damn happy with that Game. Also because i have my absolute Favourit Mech inside. The MARAUDER!!!! Controlling since 1988. Was very sad, after loosing him because of Rights Trouble, was so happy getting him back having a Tear in my Eye seeing him in the Game, because that is not awkward ..... that is Passion. True Passion.Thank you, dear Reader, for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechwarrior 5: Mercenaries is a decent entry in the Mechwarrior single-player game library. If you enjoy mech-themed games, and the Battletech universe, you will probably find some enjoyment in this title. Overall, a 6.5/10 title in my opinion. - 5/10 - One of the biggest flaws in this game is the mapping and environments. The terrain on most tilesets looks quite half-assed: it's lumpy, blobby, and due to the procedural nature of maps, often disjointed and unappealing. The bases and city environments are nice, but they are repetitive (if you've seen one version of it, you've seen all the versions of it.) The skyboxes on certain levels are very cool (floating asteroids around a moon) but the rest is barely passable. - 8/10 - The models used for the mechs are polished, and very appealing. They are visually distinct, and have the appropriate sense of scale. There are very few models I'd consider sub-par (mostly the tanks and VTOLs that the player cannot use), so this is where the game tends to shine. I wish there were more variety in terms of styling of the mechs - they all have very similar visual themes in terms of how they are modeled/represented, which breaks the illusion that these are junky 100-year old mechs pieced back together from remanufactured parts from disparate parts of the galaxy. - 5/10 - The general rendering and particle effects of various weapons and explosions are rather lacking. Missiles in particular look like glowing fireballs arcing through the sky. The gauss cannon particle effect from firing the weapon 'sticks' to the weapon, rather than hanging in a fixed point in space. Destruction effects, barring those applied to VTOLs, are lackluster as well - being neither all that realistic or flashy. - 9/10 - The work Sean Kolton put into this soundtrack is excellent. The music is high-quality, and quite atmospheric when it ramps up in the middle of a battle. I wish there was more! Though not a comment on the quality of the music itself, when entering a mission there seem to be bugged audio queues that result in, say, the Main Menu music playing during a high intensity fire fight. - 7/10 - Overall, the voice acting work is good enough. Ryanna, the ops commander, will be the voice you hear most often. Her lines are well-done, and easy to understand. Commander Mason, the character that you play, is a bit stilted and flat though. Generic NPC voice acting seems fine. After playing 100 hours of the game, the voice acting gets repetitive though. - 6/10 - Most of the sound effects for weapons firing/hitting are good, but nothing special. Autocannons tend to have the best sound effects while firing/impacting, while the gauss sound effects tend to be flat. Pulse lasers are probably a little too heavy on the bass. - 4/10 - Over the course of the campaign, you'll play out Commander Mason's story, which is largely a cut-and-paste revenge plot with Bad Guys(tm) and The Real Bad Guys(tm). The 'villians' are poorly developed and feature a few recurring characters, none of whom meet the bar as 'interesting' or 'memorable.' Thoroughly unambitious and bland, but a requirement for a single player game. - 6/10 - Career Mode cuts out the main story, and benefits from it overall. This mode is more of a 'freelance' mercenary style game, with a few scripted/special missions. (Those missions are also available in Campaign mode.) Take contracts, shoot mechs, salvage mechs, and use bigger and better and cooler toys. - 6/10 - The majority of the game takes place on the battlefield, with you in command of a lance of mechs. There are 6 mission types that are repeated in general, exempting scripted missions. Mechs control well, and the specific mechanics of mech combat (twisting, weapon groups, destroying components on enemy mechs) are executed well-enough. Heat management is poorly implemented - a linear scale for heat management results in quite a lot of downtime. Jump Jets are fun, but not overly useful. When playing with AI-controlled lancemates, tougher missions can be an exercise in frustration; they don't engage targets intelligently, and the controls for directing one's lancemates are quite barebones and not always effective. The AI, both enemy and friendly, really falls apart in urban environments and close quarters situations as mechs and vehicles struggle to navigate down straight roads. - 7/10 - Designing and refitting mechs is another key part of the game, and it is executed well enough. There are some outright bad mechs you may come across, which can't really be improved with a redesign (though they're in the minority.) Typically there are always meaningful choices to be made, and customizing mechs to work as a team in your lance and to suit your gameplay style is a lot of fun. There are some options that I'd wish for - such as being able to modify the engine in mechs - that would be an added bonus, but modders have added some of this in. - 7/10 - Anything can be fun with friends, and MW5 is no exception. The Coop gameplay helps mitigate the poor performance of AI lancemates by having actual, human pilots that can focus fire on mech components, and act with independent thought! Sadly, there is no mode that accommodates players using their own pilots/personally designed mechs from their own saves to help form a company. Non-hosting players also can't view the starmap or mech cold storage by default either, which I find to be a detriment to quality of life. Still, coop is where the game shines.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid Mechwarrior game. Never thought I was going to see another after Mechwarrior 4. So needless to say I was really excited upon seeing this.The game is surprisingly simple. Everything might look a bit overwhelming to a first time player in the series, but it really is quite simple to figure out.Nothing fancy to the game. Pick a contract and get to it. Just glorious action stomping around in huge robots smashing everything in your path. Graphics are really good. Sound is great.Music is great.Tons of Mechs to pick from with multiple variants. Finding the best variants of those mechs is in and of itself a challenge.Missions are rather repetitive with very light story which doesn't help to alleviate how repetitive they become  if you do every single high reward contract and a few of the randomly generated contracts on the side (so you don't waste your economy just going from 1 side quest to the next).Balance of difficulty seems wonky. I fought 90-95 difficulty rating where there were just hoards of tanks, VTOLs and light-medium mechs and then fought 70-80 difficulty missions where loads of assault class mechs spawn. The drop ton limits really didn't help for any of that when you expected an easier time on lower difficulty rating and end up getting obliterated by a lance nearly double your weight and twice the firepower.RTX looks good, especially in a city where you see reflections, but it absolutely murders performance. I played with it on high on an RTX 3060 and got around 25-30 frames most games. With it off i got over 120-150.Other than that, this is a solid Mechwarrior game. It could do with more polish, but from what there is now, it is looking good.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my all time favourite franchises, and I’ve played most of the major games over the last 20 years, either piloting my own mechs in MechWarrior 2,3,4 and MW Online, or commanding entire lances in the strategy games MechCommander 1,2 and Battletech.In MechWarrior 5, the player commands a mercenary company and must hire pilots, salvage, buy and repair mechs, manage the finances, take contracts, and then step into the cockpit of your favourite mechs to lead your lance in exciting real time combat.•	Each type of mech can be equipped with a different combination of laser, ballistic and missile weapons. Your weapon loadout can be customised in the mechlab, along with the mech’s ammo, heat sinks, armour and jump jets.•	The mechlab works slightly differently in every game, and while this version has some restrictions on which weapons each mech is allowed to equip, I’ve been able to make some very effective builds. I especially like that this game is very generous with ammo, one ton lasts a long time, which frees up space for extra heat sinks and armour.•	Most missions allow you to bring a lance of up to four mechs of any size, with the only restriction being the tonnage limit for the whole lance.•	Friendly AI is good. While you can order allies to attack specific targets, I don’t feel like I need to babysit them, they usually do something useful without me having to micromanage their orders.•	In addition to enemy mechs, most missions include vehicles such as tanks, SRM/LRM carriers and helicopters, as well as base defence turrets, which gives you a sense of scale and power as your mechs tower above them and destroy them in a couple of shots.•	Some missions feature a battle already in progress when you arrive, which feels like you’ve been dropped into a warzone. During other missions the enemy will constantly bombard the area with artillery until you locate and destroy the launchers.•	Mission objectives are repetitive, usually either destroy buildings, defend buildings, or kill waves of enemies, however the combat itself stays enjoyable over time as the enemy fields increasingly bigger mechs, and you acquire new mechs to pilot.•	Difficulty is quite well balanced. You’re heavily outnumbered on most missions, and quite often more reinforcements will arrive after you complete the objectives, at which point I usually just make a run for the extraction point. I’ve completed most missions on the first attempt but my mechs usually need significant repairs afterwards.•	The star map contains hundreds of planets, divided into territory controlled by the great houses. Missions take place on planets located in conflict zones. As well as the main story missions you can take contracts working for the great houses against each other, or against smaller factions like bandits or other mercenary companies. •	Your company needs money to do everything including repairing mechs, buying components, paying pilot wages, and travelling to different planets. Completing missions allows you to earn c-bills and salvage. The more often you work for a specific faction, your reputation with them will increase, leading to greater rewards.•	Each pilot has stats showing their skill using the different weapon types, evading enemy fire and managing heat. These stats will increase during missions, but when their mech is heavily damaged the pilot could be injured or killed.•	Main story takes a while to get going, but gets more interesting in the later stages.•	With both expansions installed there’s a lot of content. After 44 hours I haven’t completed the campaign yet, and looking around the star map I can still see around 20 “high value contracts”, each of which have a short story taking place over a few missions. •	Controls work great on mouse and keyboard.•	Graphics are fantastic. Long time fans will be able to recognise the different mechs just by looking at them. Environmental destruction is impressive, as trees set on fire and buildings fall apart when hit by stray weapons fire.•	I haven’t noticed any bugs or crashes so far.•	While my framerate drops a bit on urban maps with lots of buildings, I never felt like it affected my aim with precision weapons like autocannons and ppcs. Performance on maps with wide open space is fine.•	If you lose internet connection while playing, a message pops up on screen requiring you to click dismiss, but the game doesn’t pause. There is no reason for this to happen while playing in single player.MechWarrior 5 is a great game, fans of the series will definitely enjoy it, and there’s enough content to buy the game and both expansions at full price or a small sale. This is also a good place to start if you’ve never played these games before.

_childDocuments_.review: MechWarrior is at its best when you’re fighting other ‘mechs, testing your own build against theirs and either succeeding and moving on to the next challenge or going back to the drawing board to rebuild. This loop is missing from MechWarrior 5 for one key reason: poor AI, both for enemies and yourself.Mechs in MechWarrior each have their own role. Ideally, you would figure out the best combination of different roles for completing different missions. The reality is that roles are a worthless consideration because your AI teammates are only capable of four behaviors: attacking a single target, moving to a specific location, holding their fire, and following you. Many mechs in the game make use of long range missiles at the expense of extra armor, intended to be used as snipers. If you order the AI to attack enemies in one of these mechs, they will automatically charge to a pre-set range of not very far and begin circling the enemy, and die like a ♥♥♥♥♥.This behavior is problematic because the enemy AI’s numbers are inflated to make up for their lack of intelligence. Not too far into the game, you will often have to go up against 5 times the tonnage of your own team because otherwise you’d always win. But, because your AI are also incapable of doing anything except for charge and circle, it becomes virtually impossible to beat missions outside of using exploits or getting lucky.Outside of combat, the interactions you have with the greater world and the factions you work for have little consequence. The world map  change, but not due to any kind of player action. The story is uninspired filler and is more used as a way to bridge scripted missions together than to encourage you to keep playing. Speaking of missions, there are about 5 or 6 types that get repeated, and they all effectively boil down to defending a circle, destroying a mech, or destroying buildings. It gets old, fast.Presentation-wise, it’s mostly good. The sound effects for the mechs are weighty and powerful. The models for all of the units are impeccably detailed, even changing to reflect battle damage which you can inspect closely after each mission. Level textures are usually high resolution, and the character models look good… except for Fahad, your repairman, who’s missing some polygons on his head.As far as I know, MechWarrior 5 is the  first-person mech sim on Steam that has come out in the last 30 years, besides its free-to-play predecessor MechWarrior Online. As someone who has been searching for this kind of game for years, I cannot recommend MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries to anyone. On the surface, it is a very promising game, but it fails to deliver at its most important aspect and then buries that aspect underneath a tacked-on career mode. I really wanted to learn to like this game, but after picking it up again and giving it another go, I just wish I hadn’t.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long time since I last played a MechWarrior Game, MechWarrior 3 to be precise. But from my adventures in Turn Based Strategies in recent years led me to BattleTech, which then led me to MechWarrior Online, and now here I am on MechWarrior 5.Correct, I've only played 6 hours so far so take this review as you will, but so far I am not disappointed.  The formula is much from what I remember - take contracts, earn money, fix your Mechs with that money, buy new Mechs, hire new pilots, buy new and better weapons, take contracts, the cycle goes on. The first few missions will have you taking out mostly small armoured vehicles and Light Mechs with a couple of Mediums thrown in now and again, but I assume the game progression will introduce the Heavies and that's when the action heats up like a thousand PPCs being shot at the same time.It's a lovely game to look at and the destruction animation is satisfying, and it sounds quite immense in the middle of battle. Nice to hear an 80's / 90's heavy rock soundtrack that will probably be familiar to players of the older games. Too early to tell if the story has any meat on the bone, but a fairly straightforward affair so far. It also has Co Op! Invite buddies into your Lance to help you out on missions. Crucially, £25 is a super fair price for the base game, £40 if you go for the whole lot. If you're a fan of the older games, or are somehwat curious of what MechWarrior still has to offer after all of these years, I feel MW5 pushes a lot of those dials that will get you into the Mechy groove.If you're still not convinced, give MechWarrior Online a go first - its a Free to Play game that will give you a good insight into the world of MechWarrior.

_childDocuments_.review: Playtime is not accurate - offline on a steam deckI am also not a longtime Battletech fan, so I'm coming at this more from the perspective of someone who just likes mech games.Mechwarrior 5 has you as the leader of a mercenary company, traveling around the galaxy to take on jobs from a host of different factions.  The game has a campaign and a "career mode".  The campaign takes you through a set of specific missions on top of the travel and job-taking, Career Mode takes out the campaign and lets you just roam around.  While aboard your ship you perform all the administration of running your mech company - repairing your machines, changing loadouts, travel, and choosing contracts/missions.  Once you've picked what you want to do, you'll deploy with your "Lance", a squad of four mechs.You'll then have to lead them through the mission, designating targets and pulling them around for different maneuvers, while fulfilling whatever the objective of your contract was.  Objectives vary; you may end up destroying a base, chasing down a convoy, dueling another lance, really all the basic sort of things you could imagine doing if you had a bunch of mechs to screw around with.  Contracts come with a brief negotiation phase, where you can through your reputation with a faction determine how much money you'll get paid, how much salvage you can claim after the mission is done, damage coverage, and/or air support.  In battle, mechs handle a lot like tanks.  If you're on a controller, you use the left stick to increase/decrease throttle, moving always in the direction your legs are pointed.  The right stick controls your torso, and different mechs have different aptitude for turning and looking around (there is one, for example, which can rotate 360 degrees while moving).  Your weapons are assigned to weapon groups, and through a panel for that you can configure which keys fire what, as well as setting up "chainfire", which fires each weapon once in succession.  There are a few types of weapons.  Ballistic weapons consume ammo, generate little heat, and do all of their damage upon a successful hit.  Energy weapons have infinite use, but generate much more heat, and for the most part they fire for a set period of time, meaning your damage potential can go down if you can't keep a lock.  Missile launchers, depending on the type, may lock on or may be fired blind, and come in different-range variants. At first it feels very slow - even with a very quick mech, it plods and stomps and takes forever to turn around.  In comparison to other mech games, this is much closer to an Armored Core than a Gundam.  You won't be flying around chopping up zakus, there's no Nineball defying the laws of physics.  In Mechwarrior you're going to take a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of punishment and have to trust that your machine will hold together while you get ♥♥♥♥ done.  You might come out of a mission missing both your arms and hobbling, and the more damaged you are the more expensive it's going to be to get fixed back up.  This gets pretty detailed too in a way I appreciate - for example, ammunition is stored in the mech and you choose where it goes.  If that section of your mech takes a gnarly hit, your ammunition can catch fire and explode, which could end you then and there.Designing your mech's loadout is fairly simple and mostly intuitive - there's a mechlab screen where you choose where to slot different weapons and accessories.  At first these options are very limited, but as the game progresses/time passes, you find more varied options of stuff you're familiar with and whole new things.  There's more to it than the beginning of the game lets on.The game has a timeline and sits within the Battletech universe's big timeline.  I'm not very familiar with it, but in checking out different bits and pieces, if you're into lore and having a big context for what you're doing, seems like Battletech's got that for sure.  For someone who isn't familiar (like me), it's pretty cool to stumble into such a detailed and meaty setup for a game.  There is a *ton* of material if this is your thing. One thing I did not like was the soundtrack.  It's extremely generic, very "autozone commercial".  I ended up turning it off until I found some replacements for it.  It's not badly put together, it doesn't sound horrible for what it is.  It's just not very interesting.  That said, with the music turned off, you can hear more of the sounds of the game and that actually can be pretty cool.  Definitely cool when all there is are environment sounds and the thud, thud, thud of your squad's footfalls.The game had several pieces of DLC which I think were integrated in a pretty neat way.  They come up as optional quests, big contracts that entail long periods of time in service to a faction/person/etc.  You're given plenty of notice they are available and the game will remind you when the time comes to make a decision, which I appreciate.  It is really enjoyable, once you get your footing and a nice roster of mechs, to just roam around finding what kind of ♥♥♥♥ you can get into.  There's a decent variety of mission types and lots of little bonus things come up along the way - rumors of a long lost mech derelict somewhere, people contacting you because they knew your family, setting up deals and bigger mission chains.  The generic missions sometimes exist as multi-mission operations, with big payouts and lots of opportunity for salvage/capture.There is a form of balance to these missions, the tonnage limit.  Your mechs have weight, and missions will have a specific weight total you need to either be at or below.  if you exceed the tonnage limit you take penalties to your payout and salvage, increasing the more over the limit you get (you can, depending on what you're facing, choose to exceed the limit and just take the penalty).  There's also a difficulty rating and reputation recommendation for different missions/areas, to help you gauge what you can and can't do. As you go along, time passes (literally, days go by and eventually, months, then years).  As the years roll on, you start to encounter new and different things, which I'm assuming lines up at least loosely with how things progress in the greater Battletech timeline.  New mechs, weapons, and accessories will start appearing, you'll start salvaging new things, it's got a cool way of bringing those things into play without really announcing it to you.  There is a news feed that gives you information about them, sometimes there are actual product announcements and such.All in all, I've had a wonderful time with this game, especially the Career Mode.  It's a ton of fun to jump into it, figure out along the way how different stuff works, and then start checking out Battletech stuff to see how it all fits together in the world.  There's also a modding community, and because this ultimately draws from a tabletop game that means a *ton* of content and mechs derived from those materials.  There are mods to make the mechlab more complex and closer to the tabletop game; others generate new mission types and expand the possibility space with respect to things like allied forces being sent to help, enemy merc bands staging an ambush, so on and so forth.If you're playing on a steam deck, the game works great as it is.  There are mods which massively help out performance without changing the visual fidelity, too.  Mods are very easy to install, they mostly go into a single folder and you can enable them in a menu in-game.  Very much recommended, especially if you're a fan of games that play around with war machines - if you're into tanks, I think you'll really like this.  But too, if you're more of a general fan of mechs like me, this one provides a unique vision/approach and backs it up with a healthy bit of management/strategy on top.

_childDocuments_.review: Preface: I played the EGS version over a year ago. A lot has changed since then and the Steam release, but it looks like a lot has stayed the same.The first video game I can ever remember playing was MechWarrior 4: Mercenaries, on my dad's 4:3 lime green AlienWare desktop-replacement. It had to be ~2003. I also was an avid MechWarrior: Online player, with an account worth >$500. I have been waiting for a new, proper MechWarrior title for 17 years.This isn't it. This is a soulless arcade shooter with laughably half-assed features mixed with mechanics that have no place in a mech game. Why is there a level-up system; do my lasers magically start making less heat because I have killed more mechs? Why are there artificial drop limits; shouldn't I be able to field an assault lance to roll over a tiny outpost if I feel like it, even if its expensive? Why do enemies spawn <500m away from me? Why is the AI such god awful trash, feeding my heavy lance kills by trying to tank all four of us in one light mech? Why do enemies spawn infinitely, in super isolated locations without any other structures, drop ships, or plausible reinforcements around?The sad thing is the wasted potential. The mechs are beautiful. The IP is amazing. The mech-to-mech combat is satisfying (when the enemy isn't braindead). The mercenary company management aspect has been done before and is always incredibly fun, and yet despite there being a solid foundation here it doesn't every really... click.There are mods to fix a lot of issues, but none of them are compatible with the Steam version currently; also, "modders will fix it" is a toxic mentality that enables games like this.If you want a good mech shooter, go look for a copy of MW4:Mercs. It's old enough to buy a beer in the US and its still the better game by far. Stay far, far away from anything these devs make; they are genuinely the most incompetent and mediocre video game company I have ever seen.-a MechWarrior fan

_childDocuments_.review: As one might expect, I am a Battletech fan. However despite technically my first contact with the setting has been Mechwarrior 2 as a child, back then I was too young to figure out how to even get the game to run, so beyond having distinct memories of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' Betty reading out the names of certain 'mechs for me which back then sounded really strange and funny to me, my big interest only has developed in recent years. So while this technically is not my first Mechwarrior game .. in practice it pretty much is.In terms of story and flair between missions there isn't all that much, unfortunately. Your crew and lancemates might as well not exist outside of missions, and the story is neither groundbreaking nor presented to you in a grand way. For the most part it's just conversations happening in front of you with writing that may quickly sound like something no one would naturally say in such a situation. During missions there is some radio chatter here and there, but there, too, the story usually gets more told to you than shown. The DLCs have gotten better at it, both with more meaningful stories and more engaging presentations of them. A majority of story missions play out like regular missions with perhaps an extra step here and there, properly crafted missions that feel like the terrain has an actual purpose are more rare (but more common in the DLCs).As a whole, replayability has been pushed to the fore-front at the cost of meaningful content.The answer to the question "is it fun to stomp through buildings and punch a tank with your 3-stories tall 100 ton heavy 'mech?" is obviously yes. And that is a stellar point of Mechwarrior 5. No matter if you try to skillfully shoot the cockpit to watch the enemy topple over lifelessly, if you literally disarm them by blowing off their arms, or chew through their centre torso to destroy the engine and watch the whole thing blow up, this game successfully makes it fun to fight in, with, and against battlemechs. Various mission types favour different types of gameplay, at times also offering alternative approaches. Unfortunately however the general tendency is heavier is better as on higher levels the amount of infinitely spawning heavy and assault lances of the enemy meaning you may need a lot more firepower and armour to get through it all. The only way around that is either gimping yourself for added challenge, aiming for combat zones that are of lower difficulty..or mods.Personally I have played this game vanilla for quite some time, before buying my first DLC (Heroes of the Inner Sphere). The game stands well enough on its own without mods and is perfectly playable without community patches or similar mods, unlike certain other games. Ultimately however mods absolutely enhance your experience, may it be purely visual stuff like shaders, unlocked camos, something a bit less vanilla but mostly on brand like adding a couple mechs (shoutout to  which is pretty much always installed for me), or going a bit more deeper and influencing core mechanics. And this is where  or YAML comes into play.YAML is a double-edged sword. On the one hand the added freedom by giving MW5 a mechlab that is more closer to MWO and..what you'd generally just expect and want, but it also heavily blurs the lines between mechs. Some minor quirks and a difference of 5 tons aside, with YAML a Rifleman and Jagermech for example can turn out extremely similar, resulting in some mechs basically just being the same one as others, just with different looks. So while this does enable you to make a mech more your own thing and even turn pretty bad mechs like the Cicada which by default uses so much tonnage on its engine that you cannot even fully max its armour without running out of spare tonnage into fun and usable machines, a lot of flair of variants and chassis may get easily lost. A great example for a mod that is technically awesome to have but that may easily decrease how much fun you end up having. Hence why most people tend to recommend doing a playthrough without YAML first and then checking it out. is another notable mod. While it does have some quirks that may not be to your liking, ultimately the increased variety in potential mission types adds a lot of fun. Stronghold Defense being my personal favourite added by the mod.Overall there are a lot I could go through, and perhaps I will do so in the future in a guide or something. But the ultimate takeaway is that the game itself is fine without mods, but adding them definitely may improve your experience.As a whole, the base game itself is serviceable. But the DLC do add various things that you may want or feel are missing from it. , , and  all add some mechs and a standalone storyline, each definitely more well crafted and presented than anything in base game. The priority and ranking of which of these is better than the others is absolutely up to personal taste, so if you had to choose only one of the three it can be tough to recommend one over the other.  adds a career more which is a more sandbox-y freeplay variant along with some other stuff. Overall people seem to agree that if you only buy one DLC, it likely ought to be this.  is by far the weakest DLC which does little more than expanding on the then newly introduced melee system with some weapons and mech (variants). It can be nice to have, but you won't really miss out by skipping it either.If you ever see Mechwarrior 5 on sale it is likely to be worth your money. Especially if you intend to pick up any DLCs as they do add up in cost.

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games that needs a Neutral button.I have been deeply embedded into the Mechwarrior/Battletech universe for years and despite the game's flaws (and issues with the developer), this game does scratch that Mechwarrior itch, so for that reason alone, I give it a thumbs up.For those wanting more details, rather than Pro/Cons, I will simply list what I find to be notable here:1. Finally, a return to open space travel to go wherever you want in the Inner Sphere. Something that hasn't been available since Mechwarrior 1; released back in 1989! Seriously, it took 32 years to figure out how to get this back in? Makes you think it must be Lostech.2. Nice graphical dropship that you can wander around in to look at your mechs and otherwise do absolutely nothing in. A lot of detail put into a cosmetic that you'll look at for all of 2 minutes before getting bored and never look at again except for when you're forced to for 'story reasons' because it wants you to walk to the other side of the ship to talk to 1 person that you could have just spoken over comms with. This is something that could have been put to a lot better use or just eliminated entirely.3. Totally destructible environments! Except for when it isn't. So, because a building has more than 1 level, you can't destroy or walk thru it, but yet you can walk thru a wall that's built with the full intention to handle mech weapon fire, like it was made of paper?4. Lots of big, stompy, classic mech designs with multiple variants available that you can customize! Except, sadly, the customization options are Extremely limited; even more so than Mechwarrior Online. Where MWO limits by weapon type (energy, ballistic, missile), MW5 has this, but also restricts by weapon size and the variant's original loadout. Meaning; if the mech originally had only 1 Medium laser for energy weapons, you can only replace it with another Medium laser variant or downgrade to single Small laser variant. You wouldn't be able to upgrade to a Large Laser variant if you were able to make out the tonnage difference elsewhere. Add to that, extremely excessive refit times when doing doing the changes, or even repairs. You take a single small laser hit and the mech takes a week to repair? At least in the Battletech PC game, you're provided the ability to upgrade your mech bay for faster times; in MW5, it is purely based on your location.5. Official mod support! Great for fixing issues overlooked or features that are otherwise questionable (such as the customization restrictions) and of course adding weird things no one would ever have intended. While there are some very good mods available that make the game much more like what it could be, a game shouldn't need to rely on mods to actually make it a good game (Master of Orion 3 anyone?).6. Mission difficulty. If you're looking to just walk thru missions, you won't. Certainly not the higher rated & story missions at least. Mission difficulty is a little on the excessive. Go into a mission rated for 200 tons using 300 (thx to mods) and you still get beaten up something harsh. Making you wonder how you would have even survived with 200. Part of this relates to the random spawning (noted below) and poor ally AI though. You decide to take a light and give AI an assault and you still out damage them by more than triple, there's an issue.  7. Mech Melee! You can finally punch those annoying Locust in the face when they try to swarm your Atlas, and it's exactly as satisfying as this sounds. And yet, mechs still don't fall over when losing a leg? Again, something that was actually available way back in MW1. More Lostech code perhaps?8. Co-Op! Really the highlight of the whole game. Actually being able to go on the missions with friends makes everything better, most especially since the ally AI is only marginally ok at best. And yet, you can only invite if you know the person, no lobbies or LFG broadcasts. Add to that, there's no voice support. How can you add online co-op and not allow a way for people to talk to each other thru the game?! Should not need to rely on 3rd parties (I.E. Steam, Discord, etc). Add to that, invitees are also limited to only whatever the host has available for mechs to play. Some sort of basic VS would have been nice as well, but I imagine PGI would think that would compete too much against their Mechwarrior Online game.9. Loot crating. While I have nothing against random salvage, this is clearly a Console idea and not at all very Mechwarriory. I mean, how many giant mech sized crates are you just going to find laying around; and sitting inside someone's house no less?10. Random spawning. This is honestly what I find to be the worst part of the game and almost ruins it for me. Again, clearly a Console thing. While recent updates have minimized this a bit, it's still not great. Popup turrets literally just pop up every 50 yards. Not to mention mechs or tanks that may suddenly appear out of no where. What's the point in providing players Airstrikes as an option on missions if the enemy units aren't going to appear inside a base until after you're already entered the base yourself?11. Lackluster story. Similar to the Battletech PC game story; it's just sort of there. By no means do you have any reason to care about or even push through it other than whatever cool rewards you might get from the missions. Ironically, also much like MW1. Although the movie cut scene narrations are nice.12. Mech repairs. You have industrial zones that are otherwise peaceful (no missions available on them) that you're able to repair with relative ease. When trying to repair on a combat world though, you're struck with a premium on them which increases both the cost and the time to repair/refit. This premium can range anywhere between 20%-150% (mostly based on location difficulty). I get there being an increase in a warzone, and I'm fine with that. However, it's a little excessive for a mech to be unavailable for a week just to repair a single plate of armor when you only took damage to 1 location from a 1 small laser. Just to replace 1 single heatsink with 1 double heatsink takes 8 days, and that's on an industrial world outside of combat. In some warzones, that mech becomes unavailable for almost a month!13. Controls are pretty much standard fair with past Mechwarrior games as well as Mechwarrior online. Although there are some options missing, like no InfraRed view; just Nightvision which is practically useless most of the time. It's important to note for new players that, unlike other mecha games like Titanfall or War Robots, the Mechwarrior series has always been more a simulator game play style, not an action run and gun game. So torso and legs move independent of each other and no 1 button strafing, for example. For anyone unsure on controls, I recommend trying Mechwarrior Online first, since it's free. The controls are virtually the same and has training grounds to mess around in without getting into a player match.What it all comes down to is, if you like giant mecha combat, it's definitely worth buying, but only on sale. Especially since the DLC is a must as they fix some of the inherent problems in the base game. After that, mods are also almost a requirement on top of that for it to be the game it really should have been.

_childDocuments_.review: The first Steam game, and the first MechWarrior or BattleTech game, I feel like I wasted my money on. Seriously, after over two years you'd think they'd have done 'anything' to improve the AI and not have your teammates require constant attention while the OpFor dog piles you with a dozen 'Mechs, tanks, and VTOLs. I've enjoyed BattleTech, MechWarrior, and MechCommander going 'way' back, and this has to be the most unfinished game of them all. I don't mind 'hard', but I do mind when I get slaughtered regardless of how well I play or how many times I replay the scenario because my lancemates are idiots, or I'm smothered in obscenely accurate artillery barrages I can't outrun. I feel like i'm in a closed Beta and the Devs have their fingers firmly in their ears. At least the current BattleTech has a range (with Mods) from 'arcade fun run' up through 'realistic challenge' to 'crap, this is hard'. This horror show sucks all the fun right out of running a Merc company. I'll be playing BattleTech and wishing I'd dropped the $75 I wasted on this on something fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechwarrior 5 is an exercise in single player frustration. There is a good game waiting to be found but that is buried underneath horrible AI behavior that cancels out much of the fun factor of MW5. I can only recommend picking the game up for the co-op career mode to play with friends.  Example AI Issues:1. AI teammates are constantly running through objects and are incredibly slow to respond to attack orders, sometimes breaking off and running in the opposite direction of the enemy you tag for attack for no reason. 2. Friendly fire. The teammate AI can inflict more damage to the player mech. A option should be included to turn friendly fire off. (There is a mod on the Workshop to fix this)3. The enemy AI will ignore your AI teammates and focus fire on the player, not disengaging until significant damage has been inflicted by the AI teammates. Minor Issues and gripes (updated 6-02-21): 1. To unlock Co-op you must play trough a portion of the single player campaign. Luckily its only a few missions before that occurs. 2. Randomly the game stops at a loading screen when traveling to a plant and will never progress. The game must be force closed and restarted.3. The Mech Lab is streamlined to the point of being overly restrictive and crippling one of the reasons Battletech is a popular IP, freedom to create unique customized variants of a mech. Weapons are now assigned to particular slots that only supports a particular size of weapon. For example: Small Energy, Medium Energy, Small Missiles, Large Missiles, etc. The fact that PGI didn't design the MW5 Mech Lab around their existing Mechwarrior Online Mech Lab system is perplexing. 4. NPC Enemy Mech weapon loadouts are too similar. (Why do all the Urbanmechs have burst AC weapons?!)5. Travel between planets is far too expensive. (There is a mod on the Workshop to fix this)6. Cosmetic customization is lacking for the Inner Sphere DLC. Limited Mech patterns, the inability to add custom merc company logos, the "Commander" portrait cannot be changed or customized and the dropship color cannot be changed. Hopefully the community will mod these in, but it shouldn't have to.7. The NPC characters on your dropship have a creepy mannequin stare, don't move and have the lip sync quality of a ventriloquist dummy. 8. No photo mode or ability to hide the UI. The game is begging to be visually captured and shared. Positives:1. MW5 has been streamlined from a hardcore sim to balanced accessibility for newcomers, which will expand the fanbase and hopefully renewed interest in the franchise on a wider scale.2. The planet environments are varied and stunning to look at. 3. The battlemechs are satisfying to pilot and the tonnage difference is felt in game.4. The weapons are also satisfying to use.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was a little kid, my Dad would bring me along to practice with his band. While they rehearsed at a band-mates house, I would be set up in the space's owners office with a computer that was decked out for Mechwarrior 2. He had joysticks and surround audio set up around the room.The feeling of piloting a mech like that, in my childhood eyes, was beyond belief. I grew to love giant robots because of this moment, and still cherish a lot of different aspects of Mech genres. I, sadly, never really stayed in touch with Mechwarrior as it went through it's own legal troubles and went through a lot of ups and downs as a brand. Also, growing up without a computer to play MW on did not help.As we came along, years later, when MWO was first in Beta.... I was having the multiplayer mech experience I always really wanted before, but couldn't find at the time, now that I had a gaming PC of my own. MWO was a good time, but obviously was flawed, and it was driven through a lot of struggle both over bad development choices, and toxic/picky player base. Emphasis on the player base. MWO was the first time I had ever really interacted with the batteltech/mechwarrior fan base on anything more than a very casual curiosity for awhile. They weren't the worst community I had been a part of, but they really were never satisfied with whatever PGI was doing with MWO. It could have been a positive choice, or a bad, they still would not have liked it. Coming into MW5 development and reception, I see why the game got based on release day. While many complaints of MW5 were valid, you could just see usual reactions from the MWO community. The AI wasn't bright, missions sometimes got glitchy, and other buggy things that affected the immersion of what would be a Mech simulator. It did not help that they first released this on Epic gamestore, which only drove more harsh response. I decided to wait till it came to Steam.Eventually after the updates came out I shelled out the cash to get the full game with all current DLC. Memories of my childhood, at my dad's band-mates, came flushing back into my head when I dropped onto that battlefield. While flawed, it whisked me back away through my fantasy of smashing and stomping through war-zones, while shooting large weaponry. The kestrel lancers DLC really helps the gameplay out (it's a good time.), and steamworkshop mods help fine tune the experience to the players. Audio, animations, and even game events do get buggy, I will admit, but nothing game breaking. I also gotta say, playing this with friends for the Co-Op modes is a hella good time. I wouldn't say it's the best game, and far from a triple A style title, in my eyes. But if you're willing to just relax and do some shooty/stompy, you will enjoy yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had this game since it released on Epic Store. When I first played it back then I was underwhelmed to say the least. _childDocuments_.review: Advertising for the Steam edition of this game framed it as a fresh release, or even a re-release. This is partially justifiable, as the game has been markedly improved over its original Epic launch state. The UI is better organised, sounds improved, new features and assets added. Notably, enemy AI and spawns are now more consistent with prior entries - no more swarms of Cicadas, and there is a greater emphasis upon non-mech combatants at lower levels. Combined arms is now relevant.Mechwarrior 5 is certainly not a bad game to satisfy your Battletech or mech combat needs. It provides a palpable sense of scale, and your salvo of LRM-20s will feel powerful. The story is bad - but I don't think any Mechwarrior story has ever been more than serviceable at best. It's like stories in pornography - it's more setup than purpose.Ignoring whatever (totally legitimate) qualms you may have over PGI's handling of the business side of this product, the game itself is not amazing, but it's not the dumpster fire some make it out to be.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Having clocked close to 100 hours previously in MW5, nothing drastic has changed. PGI sold-out fans to go on another platform to grab their money bag then sell out once they made their profit. Even after nearly two years, the game still has numerous issues with AI, pathfinding, balance and customization, among others. The missions seem to be an endless repeat, just with different characters. As a long-time Mechwarrior and Battletech fan, it is sad to see the lore was not used effectively and instead, MWO was used as a template for simplicity's sake with regards to mech customization. Many of these problems can be fixed with mods, but ask yourself, before you buy it, is it worth all the headaches that come with mod-related issues? Currently priced too high for what you get, the campaign, even with DLC, will put you about 30-40 hours, but by the last 10 hours, it is very grindy. This game is not complete without mods; pick it up from a key reseller like Fanatical for a better price or wait for a sale.Full Review:So before I say anything, I wanted to thank all the beta testers at Epic for this game. I also wanted to let everyone know that I was an original backer of this game but got a refund due to the unacceptable switch to EGS and the ensuing debacle. The radio silence surrounding this game was unacceptable, with long periods of no news, then a sudden delay just because another game will supposedly steal MW5's proverbial thunder. The last time I checked, even now, it wasn't on the bestseller list. There are reasons for that, this is the lowest rated Mechwarrior title historically, and it shows.The AI is slightly better, but without mods to correct the AI pathfinding issues, both friendly and enemy mechs will run in circles around each other until one dies. In addition, pathfinding is still very poor, as friendly mechs still crash into buildings. This makes defence missions very difficult, as the buildings get damaged every time your lance mates run into them. Until you get a mod to fix the spawning issues, it is more of a horde shooter than a Mechwarrior game. Until you get a mod to fix the customization issues in the mech lab, you have no reason to pick anything but the heaviest mech. All of the mechs per class move at the same speed, with few exceptions. Light mechs are supposed to be used to outmaneuver the enemy, but you have no incentive to do so. Medium mechs are supposed to be well balanced etc. You will need a mod to fix the market limitations as well, as some mechs are super hard to find; I could go on.It begs the question that if non-professional modders can do these things, why couldn't PGI do them? The catch 22 now is because PGI delayed the game for so long to steam; many of the modders won't update their mods anymore. It is a huge blow to the game. For the DLC content, the missions you complete to get your mech upgrades are poorly done in some cases. Destroying tracked vehicles was particularly terrible, as only super-heavy tanks count. Some of the missions you need jump jets, but it isn't mentioned in the briefings at all. There are spawning issues as well where only 9/10 enemies show up, and you have to restart your mission as you cant complete it. On launch, even running without mods, this still comes up. Cold storage also didn't work when your saves were transferred at launch, though this was fixed. After all this time, I wonder how all these bugs still exist. There is very little polish, so where did all the money they made from selling out to EGS go? Thanks, PGI.The only thing that saves it is that the mech portion of the game is fun, minus how repetitive it is. More mission variety is needed, and more options overall. I give this game a 6/10. Unfortunately, you likely won't play it after you go through it once; only mods can save you. In the future, I hope another company can do the Mechwarrior franchise right.

_childDocuments_.review: This game leaves a lot to be desired. While it provides the core experience of piloting a giant mecha and smashing things to pieces the title falls short in several places.The core gameplay is satisfying. Walking through a building and watching it collapse feels good and always works the way it should. Firing the weapons and watching them impact enemy mechs tickles the brain. A large enough variety of mechs are featured that you'll always be able to have fun in a quick skirmish or while you're hunting around the Inner Sphere for that coveted mech to add to your lance. The maps in this game are procedurally generated. While this is obvious the first time you see a square little city dropped in the middle of a wasteland, it gets the job done. The variety of mission types is acceptable enough to hold your interest. This game admittedly lacks a lot of the gameplay choices Mechwarrior 4 had throughout their missions leading to a lot of the contracts feeling shallow and repetitive.A lot of the downsides of this game revolve around the poor AI of your lancemates and a boatload of cut or unimplemented features to support this game releasing on consoles. Advanced zoom, a staple from MW4 is not present, Infantry enemies were cut to support performance, mechs do not have separate walk or run animations, third person locomotion does not sync with first person cockpit bob, mechs do not have inverse kinematics to ensure their feet line up with the terrain.It's very frustrating how little control you seem to have over your AI lancemates. You cannot tell them to fire from a position, go to a position if you do not have line of site with it, prioritize destroying buildings (unfortunate as several mission types revolve around this), prioritize a type of unit such as battlemechs, VTOLs, or tanks etc. Ultimately, you're left to do almost everything yourself while these idiot bots snipe at the enemy.This game is saved mostly by co-op and mods. Co-op play is a blast and I've put almost 100% of my gameplay time into this with at least one friend. Several mods either fix or restore features that should have been in the base game. TT_Rulez in particular makes the AI much smarter.While I ultimately would recommend the game if you're a fan of the Mechwarrior series or the Battletech universe, a lot of mech chassis and the entire career gameplay mode is locked behind the Heroes of the Inner Sphere DLC. While I would describe the other three DLCs of MW5 as optional, Heroes of the Inner Sphere feels essential to the core gameplay experience which is very unfortunate as it almost doubles the price of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid Mechwarrior game, though not necessarily an amazing one.In terms of stompy mech action with lots of pew-pew and glitzy detonations, it does a good job of keeping the monkey part of the brain entertained. If you are looking to point a target reticle at something, shoot lasers at it and watch some detonate off, it is a perfectly good time.That being said, the vanilla experience has some significant flaws: Friendly AI is usually moronic and make sub-optimal use of whatever mech you give it (better with mods, more on that later), the missions start feeling pretty same-y\repetitive by 15-20 hours in (your mileage may vary), the universe feels static (your actions don't really change anything in the game universe) and the variety of mech customization is limited.There are two things, however, that can make this game great: playing with a friend (who shouldn't suck as much as the AI does) and mods. A friend that can effectively coordinate with you allows you to take on significantly more challenging missions than when you have the AI derping around. As for mods, everything from mech customization, to AI improvements, to new mission types, and much more: mods can bring it to the table. While this isn't praise for the game developers, it is an element that makes the game that much more involved and worthy of your time.If you don't like modding (or don't like that you need them to make the game truly good) and your friends have failed you in drawing aggro and target selection too many times, the game will be pretty hit-or-miss, so consider your purchase wisely.

_childDocuments_.review: There are tons of mechs that can be kitted out in tons of ways, and they’re all a lot of fun to drive. The campaign is expansive, complex, and reactive, though at times it can also be aggravating and directionless. The mission structure can also feel a little repetitive after a while, but a variety of exciting environments serve to mitigate this. And casually plowing directly through a row of high-rises in an Atlas? Well, that never gets old.8.5/10Some Tips:Get some mods, the game has some issues that can be easily fixed for a massively improved experience.Turn on some level of aim assist. It's very difficult to aim while moving and managing your torso and leg positioning, and even the low setting with help a lot with keeping you on target, especially with lasers.Positioning is incredibly important in fights; you can't just slug it out until you get into heavy and assaults, and even then it's dangerous.Present your tougher sides to targets unless firing. The centurion for instance has more armor on his left arm because of the shield, so you should rotating your torso to present that side towards enemy fire as much as you can.Pay attention to where your components are so you know what to protect and how to position.Ammo will explode if hit by weapons, and take out the section its in. If that's a side torso, the arm attached comes off too. If it's center torso, you die. Don't ever put ammo in the CT.Look for where your targets have their weapons, watch where the beams and projectiles come from. Targeting and destroying enemy weapons is a massive part of combat; don't just fire center mass, blow off arms to weaken them and legs to slow them.Losing a leg cripples you, losing both kills you. Same for enemies.Keep moving, the AI has more trouble hitting you at speed. They are still hideously accurate still though, which is one of the aforementioned issues. Mods can balance this.Lancemates are really bad though and will regularly be worthless, unless you, yes, get mods.I always put a negotiation point into damage costs, and the rest into salvage unless I need a fast cash injection. Salvage will always end up being more valuable in the long term.Check your weapon groups! You don't want to alpha strike (fire everything at the same time) all the time.Specialize your mechs. Focus on close combat and high armor (heavy acs, srms) mid range (lasers and mrms), or long range (ac/2, lrms, ppcs). If you have a spread of different ranged weapons, you're going to be weak at all ranges. Your lancemates can cover the other ranges.You don't always need to max out armor. It helps when you're new and learning positioning, but the best defense is destroying enemy arms and weapons. If you can lose a ton or two of armor and add another laser or missile rack, you will potentially be way better off. Dead mechs can't shoot at you.Don't overdo it on ammo. I promise you you do not need 80 shots on that ac/20.Don't bring what you can't afford to lose. That brand new level 3 large pulse laser is really dope yeah, but if you get your arm blown off it's gone forever. Hope you can find another one! That said, don't be afraid to use your good stuff. Just think about the mech it's going on and the mission ahead (torso slots are usually way, way safer than arms, demolition missions tend to be cqc slogs, etc).Check industrial zones on the regular. They populate with rare weapons and mechs, as well as Hero Mechs. The hero variants are great; always have higher armor and structure, as well as unique perks and bonuses coupled with rare and powerful fittings.Flank flank flank flank. Rear armor is always weaker that front, even if it's maxed. Get behind a mech and go ham on it and you'll drop it in no time. Same goes for you though, so pay attention to your positioning.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend the game, but I do have some reservations about it.  I get together with some old Marine Corps buddies for "MechWarrior Wednesdays" that we drop together and see how much mayhem we can cause throughout the inner sphere for a couple of hours.  If you spend too much time in single player and march through the game, it will get old very quickly, as the missions are somewhat repetitive.  However, I got the DLC, and the kestrel lancers DLC adds many more special missions, that bring something sorely needed to the table.  I do feel that Piranha dropped the ball on this pretty badly.  They have here an opportunity to really build a massive universe, with huge potential for not only storytelling, but allowing the player to feel like they can make an impact on what is happening... but it just doesn't do that.  If we are involved in an assassination mission, how has that impacted the local politics?  If we are involved in a major offensive for one faction over another, do we see borders move?  If they are, I am not aware of it.  The AI is rather stupid...  they definitely should have spent a lot more time on the AI than they did.  But as it stands... Kestral Lancers is a MUST, to get the deeper missions with more excitement.  But all in all, I'd tell you to limit your play so you don't run into a boredom wall, and then you should enjoy your time in MW5.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechwarrior 5 is a strategic first person shooter in which the player pilots gigantic mechs to assault groups of tanks, hovercraft, and other mechs. The mechs handle well and can be tuned to suit different playstyles. While the combat is generally well done, the player is faced with ever crueler tests of endurance as the game proceeds, not aided by the incompetence of the bot teammates. Overall, the combat and customization are pretty good, but can often be undermined by the progression and mission balancing. It’s decent, and is probably a lot of fun if you can get three or four players together in co-op.You pilot a battlemech. While they vary in size and weight, all mechs are capable of trampling armored vehicles and plowing through buildings. It takes time for the mech to change course, but the torso can be rotated to face a 180 degree area while the legs march along, meaning that your movement rarely interferes with your shooting. The majority of your targets are large to the point that they’re easy to hit even at long range. You, in turn, have a hard time fully avoiding hits.Much of the skill in piloting your mech comes in the form shifting these unavoidable hits across your armor evenly. A mech is defeated if its head, center torso, or both legs are destroyed, with enemy pilots additionally retreating if all their weapons are shot out. What this means is that you only need to deal enough damage to destroy one or two components to kill an enemy. If you’re skilled, you can take four or five times the damage before going down by spreading incoming damage across the whole mech. Combat has a slower, more intentional pace to it while maintaining a sense of pressure under fire.Mechs can be equipped with a number of weapons for combat, each with their own pros and cons. All weapons generate heat that can disable the mech if it hits a critical point. Lasers are typically light and don’t require ammo, generating large amounts of heat instead. Autocannons are heavier guns with a slow fire rate, their range being however far you can lob the shot. SRMs are short ranged missiles that do lots of damage and generate a lot of heat. LRMs can lock on to targets at extreme range and attack indirectly if an ally spots the enemies. Lastly, any mech is capable of ramming enemies and many can punch.While different mechs are limited in exactly what weapons they can bring, there are still choices to be made regarding how much armor and ammo to equip; which armament to choose and how many heat sinks it needs to function smoothly. This culminates in a wall of guns that you can group by range, ammo type, or any arbitrary category that makes sense to you. Shooting works well with a number of different weapons each with their own tradeoffs.The story follows a mercenary company led by commander Mason and their quest for revenge against the company that killed their former leader. While the story is present, it’s just really there to add some unique missions every now and then. It’s mostly an excuse to beat stuff up, and it does a fine job of that.While bot squadmates are better than none at all, they seem to be terrible at aiming, provided they even shoot at the enemies. They can’t be given complex orders, and will normally follow the player if not stuck or sitting completely still. Their only saving grace is that their minimal presence in combat inclines the enemies to focus their fire on the player instead. With this in mind, the game is balanced around the player’s team fielding three or four  pilots each mission. Good luck.Starting from the fourth story mission, a player can host a co-op game on their save file and invite other players to control mechs in their lance. Players, naturally, leap above and beyond the low bar set by the bots, being much more capable gunners and competent tacticians. While players are fully capable in combat, they’re very limited in their permissions outside combat. The only privilege co-operators are allowed is the ability to alter mech loadouts and order repairs. However, they cannot:This system makes decision making a pain in group play. The co-operators need to sit around and pester the host if they want anything at all. While it’s better than bots, it’s not perfect.The company is capable of deploying one lance (four mechs) per mission with its dropship. Once the mechs are on the ground, the player will work to complete the mission objective.Once the objective is complete, the dropship will return for extraction. Reaching the dropship will end the mission, with rewards determined prior to the mission with the player balancing payment, damage insurance, and salvage opportunities.While the mission structure never really changes, missions are kept fresh by a variety of well made maps and a large roster of mechs. Each map offers differing terrain and environments better suited to various mechs and weapon types. Mechs will have different effective ranges, movement speeds, and playstyles. The centurion is reliably average with a variety of weapons and decent armor. The urbanmech is a slow turret that’s only good for trading hits while defending a fixed position. The rifleman is a long range specialist wielding autocannons, distinct from something like the catapult which primarily employs LRMs. Mechs vary wildly in their playstyles and must be approached differently in combat, keeping missions interesting.There is no skillful duel with another master pilot, nor well planned assaults on entrenched foes. Instead, harder missions are only ever longer slogs where the player’s lance plows through one, two, and eventually as many as six full lances on its own. Remember, the player can’t avoid damage so much as shift its impact. Loadout optimization and mechanical mastery can only take a player so far without the capacity to employ any kind of tactics or more mechs.Facing ever crueler odds, quality equipment could give the player a much needed edge in missions. Unfortunately, the player is not able to consistently acquire rarer weapons or mechs no matter how much money they have. That’s all up to whatever limited stock the market just happens to have on hand. With how easily equipment is lost, especially on the player’s mech, it’s hard to justify using rare weapons like gauss guns in real missions. Further, players can’t meaningfully seek heavier mechs with the brute force to clear longer missions. It’s frustrating at times.Generally, the mechs convey a great sense of both weight and power while handling well. The shooting can be quite satisfying with meaningfully different ways to disable foes. Finally, combat is paced slow enough to allow for more strategic play while maintaining reasonable times to kill. Unfortunately, it’s partially sabotaged by the incompetence of the bot pilots and the constant slogs through stacked odds. All in all, it’s decent.

_childDocuments_.review: If I played a game for over 500 hours that I did not in some way enjoy, I would need my head examined. OK, maybe I need it examined anyway, but.....here is my take on Mechwarrior 5.Disclaimer: I am a Battletech nerd. I watched Robotech when it first hit the US. I had the original board game. I still have all the old Tech Manuals. I have played every Battletech game starting with The Crescent Hawk's Revenge to MW5. Unless it sucks, I am going to like a Battletech game.What works in MW5: Mercenaries is the FIGHTS. Jumping into the cockpit of a Mech and blasting things has to be the core of any MW game. It is done very well here. Pretty scenery, varied maps, nice Mech models, exciting weapons fire models that look almost real, smoke, explosions, and the list goes on - all done well. While occasionally there can be a graphical glich (such as a Spider moving one way jumps, lands facing another direction and then kinda speeds off in that direction, then starts moving normally), the player driven combat part of the game is amazing.What does NOT work as well is the campaign/career part of the game. One of the biggest problems is getting enough salvage points to claim bigger Mechs so that you can go after bigger contracts, including taking on some of the harder campaign missions. I cannot count how many times I was 1 or 2 salvage points short trying to claim a nice Mech that once fixed would have enabled me to move on to bigger contracts. I ended up in my second playthrough using a mod that increased the salvage points per negotiating point that made it better, but not great. The tonnage limits on missions I understand were there to make the missions at least a bit challenging, but then why can I only have a dozen Mechs ready for action at any moment? I understand the concept or you have limited space in your Dropship, but this is a giant pain in the ass as it makes doing multiple mission contracts almost impossible. Since repair costs and times are so ridiculous you cannot repair moderately damaged Mechs in time to use them for the 3rd/4th mission and you cannot have 16 Mechs ready to go. Do not even think about taking unrepaired Mechs into a mission as they will get popped in no time. Basically, I had to use another mod to modify this part of the game to make it playable as well. In parts of the game where you have to speak to your crew, there is a pointless setup where you have to run around your ship to get to the crew member just to get a clip of dialog and then you can move forward with the campaign. Overall - fun game, frustrating details that two mods have made much more tolerable. Worth picking up on sale.
