_childDocuments_.review: Yet another indie roguelite that didn't need to be a roguelite.Randomized dungeons are the meat of the game. Unfortunately they're just a slog for you to retry several times until you harvest enough resources to get mathematically good enough to clear it. Nothing significant is different about each run; you neither receive new experiences from repeated attempts, nor do you gain mastery by studying specific challenges. It's just there to spread thin content over a longer playtime.There is good handcrafted content to be had though! Exploring the overworld and bespoke dungeons used to get between the randomized ones is rewarding and well built. Specific rooms you always find in dungeons have good puzzles that are satisfying to solve the first time (though you'll be repeating them many more times than is welcome). This could have been a solid, brief, linear experience; the devs are obviously fans of the genre and seem to know how to conjure Link to the Past magic when they put their minds to it.I feel like lots of games like this (Towerclimb, Scourgebringer, Children of Morta) aren't confident enough in what they're actually trying to do; they're worried about the quantity of content they're delivering and not sure that just the quality of it will  make sales. Adding roguelite elements is an obvious way to pad out a smaller game and make the player spend more time with each batch of content. Making a good roguelite means making a good loop, though; the game needs to actually be about dying and retrying, needs to be about the core mechanical gameplay that the player will be interacting with for hours. A Link to the Past was not fun because its combat was good; it was fun because of the giant world to explore, the constantly shifting context of the enemies and environments, and your evolving and expanding toolset with which to interact with both of those things. Repeating content works against all of those goals, and unfortunately Ruins doesn't offer up anything compelling to justify why you're repeating it.All that said, it's dirt-cheap and has local multiplayer. If you're a megafan of the 2d Zeldas and need a little romp with your friends, it might be worth trying it out.

_childDocuments_.review: So we get quite a few of these co-op adventure games each year. Just a few months ago we had The Survivalists, which I did end up enjoying and recommending despite its issues. Now we’ve got Rogue Heroes, the next contender within that very genre, and let’s just say that it also is not without its issues.This is a game that will have you going through procedurally-generated dungeons and taking out a bunch of enemies within – along with the usual loot and roguelite progression. However, this is also a co-op focused game and if you’re playing it as such, you’ll be doing a lot of combat with your friends scattered about the same room. This is where the problems begin to appear.For one, there’s contact damage when touching any enemy. That’s not bad in itself, but this is on top of the fact that every time you hit an enemy, there is a pretty sizeable knockback. So, as my friends and I quickly discovered, you’ll be taking a lot of damage from someone accidentally hitting an enemy at just the right angle to send it hurtling towards a teammate.There’s also the extremely limited attack range – enough so that you have to almost be on top of some enemies to actually be able to hit them. This is remedied a bit in that you can upgrade your attack range in-between runs, but even after spending most of my jewels upgrading it, it’s still pretty close and the fact that most enemies move around a lot means you’ll be doing a lot of accidental contact damage to yourself while trying to line up attacks. And the hitboxes definitely don’t help either. They’re not all bad, but there are definitely a few that are larger than their sprites would suggest.You have your one basic attack, a secondary slot for a bow, wand, or other item, a class-specific ability, and that’s it. 90% of your combat is going to be pressing the same basic attack, so you’ll need to be close to enemies even if you’re playing a completely different class. Imagine my disappointment when I unlocked the ranger only to discover that you’re not even given a bow and have to find one yourself in the dungeon only to then realize that it does about the same damage as your basic attack but with the added negative of running out of ammo.The combat really just isn’t satisfying until much later once you’ve got a bunch of upgrades backing it up. It’s the opposite of something like Hades or even the recently released Skul: The Hero Slayer, where the combat is immensely satisfying right from the get-go and only gets better from there. The fact that there are so many mechanics that actively harm co-op players doesn’t help either and honestly it wasn’t until I played the game singleplayer that I was able to beat the first boss.The combat is not even my main issue with the game - the bugs and technical issues are actually more of a problem right now. Rogue Heroes is a co-op game with both local and online options, but n actual play, only the local co-op works - the online co-op unfortunately makes the experience almost unplayable. That is because there is a massive desync issue, with each player seeing something different on-screen and never quite being synced up.Treasure chests only appearing for one player, HP and item amounts differing depending on whose screen you’re looking at, and even entire puzzles that flat-out don’t work for others because only one player can see the interactable objects – it’s pretty bad across the board. One of the worst examples being from the first boss fight. I would hit this weak spot to stun it, only for my friends to ask me why I haven’t stunned it yet – as the fact that the boss was stunned did not appear on their screens.For what it’s worth – I did reach out to the publisher and was told that the desync issue was being worked on. However, I was also told that each desync was a standalone issue and to fix they would need specifics of when and where each happened. Given that this happened to me dozens upon dozens of times, it might be a while before all of these desyncs are cleared up, but at least the team is working on it.I also had an issue where my HP upgrades disappeared entirely until I upgraded them again, an issue where my speed as a ghost was permanently locked to the speed I was moving at when I died, a sound bug where the knight’s leap ability would play the wrong sound effect, and even the game’s revive totem straight-up not working and consuming my friend’s skull – leaving me unable to revive them.I didn’t have any crashes or fps issues – it ran perfectly at 1440p and 60 fps, although it unfortunately cannot go higher than 60. The controls are also fine both on controller and keyboard and mouse, the latter of which can be configured. The only issue I have there is that the controller has the ability to automatically attack in whatever direction you hold the right stick, whereas with keyboard and mouse you have to constantly click to attack.Boring and unsatisfying combat is one thing, but being a co-op game and not having functional online co-op just doesn’t do it – and that’s just one of the technical issues. The graphics, music, and roguelite elements are at least nice, although not enough to carry the experience. I really hope the bugs and such can be fixed up in the future, but it will likely take more than that for me to come back to the game.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: While the roguelike formula doesn't exactly work PERFECTLY with the Link to the Past game mechanics, it is a solid game for what it is. A lot of the overworld aspects and side quests are nice, and sometimes are even more engaging than the actual dungeons themselves. While the roguelike aspect of the procedurally generated dungeons is nice, I also feel like that is where some of the game's design falls a bit flat. The puzzles generate based on the items you have in your possession, so if you don't have a hammer for instance, you won't get puzzles that rely on use of the hammer. Unlike LTTP, the item you get from dungeons is gotten at the end after clearing the boss. It's a sacrifice that had to be made to ensure the procedurally generated dungeons work, but also robs that satisfying feeling of progression and meaningful puzzle solving a lot of the LTTP dungeons had. The only real mandatory puzzles are for boss keys, and the rest are usually just for extra gems for upgrades. All in all, the game is solid, but the core gameplay loop does get a little stale after a little while due to the roguelike nature getting in the way of the consistent well thought out dungeon designs that drive that feeling of meaningful progression like in LTTP. Having more static puzzle rooms like those that house the boss key generated throughout the dungeon (for example key rooms having static puzzle layouts), putting some items in guaranteed rooms in a dungeon you'd need to find in order to gain access to the boss door (for example needing the grapple hook to clear a chasm in the room with the first dungeon boss door or something), just a bit more consistency to the dungeons to make exploring feel more meaningful rather than just optional for grinding gems would have probably made for a more solid experience. Multiplayer does help make the game more fun than solo, but it doesn't fix some of the issues due to some of the concepts that could have used a little more polish. Overall, definitely worth picking up and playing if you have some friends and enjoy the classic LTTP style gameplay (works with remote play together so only one of you actually needs a copy), but you might need to take a break around the halfway mark so things don't start getting a bit stale and come back to it with a fresh mindset.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes is exactly as advertised. It feels like Zelda and it’s a roguelite. It plays and looks like how I remember older Zelda’s behaving. The overworld is the same every time, but when you enter any of the main dungeons, the layout changes every time, as with all roguelites. In the dungeon, you earn gems, which can be used to buy permanent upgrades for your character, again, as is pretty standard with roguelites. However, the balance does seem to be off in that gems were extremely easy to get. If you’re playing this game as a roguelite, you will be disappointed as there really is not much reason to enter a dungeon after beating it and most dungeons can be beaten in a few tries. By the end of the game, we were blasting through everything without much trouble at all. This probably can be fixed by just not spending your gems or choosing to play the game on a harder difficulty. On the other hand, playing this as a Zelda knock off is a lot of fun and the randomly generated dungeons was a nice touch. They still contained puzzles as you would expect in a Zelda style dungeon, although none of them were particularly difficult to figure out.Something that was difficult to figure out at times was where to go next. A few times we got lost trying to find how to get from the dungeon we just defeated into the next dungeon, especially towards the end of the game. Navigating the vast number of items was also really bad. Manually cycling through 10s of items takes too much time and I found the quick access wheel to not work great most of the time.It’s really nice that you can play coop with friends, but sometimes that is a bit buggy. It’s also really annoying how any time anyone opens their inventory or does something similar, it pauses the game for everyone. It would also be nice if we could all explore on our own, at least within the village where we upgrade our characters. Being in the middle of browsing a shop or selecting an upgrade and having a friend leave makes you leave as well, which gets annoying fast.Overall, Rogue Heroes is not the most polished game, but it’s still a lot of fun, especially with friends.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with a great concept -- marrying The Legend of Zelda with the rogue-light death-and-power-up model -- but a few downfalls in execution.The core gameplay is solid; you explore a constant overworld, and venture into procedurally-generated dungeons to fight monsters and get loot. Then you die, revive in town, and spend your crystals on stat boosts so you can do better next time. There are eight character classes (all but one of which are unlocked through play), but they're not massively different; they have different stats and each one has a special ability, but the basics of gameplay don't change. There's also a whole bunch of stuff to do on the side, and this leads into one of the game's main weaknesses.Other than the core dungeoneering, the game's systems are pretty thin. There's a farming minigame, but it's almost entirely bereft of content; you dig holes and plant seeds, then you water them, and you can sell the crops for gold -- which currency is almost never used. There's no challenge and no long-term goal, merely a daily "water the plants" grind for money. Fishing is even worse; the fishing minigame itself has inexplicable controls, and completing the fishing quest requires endless grinding for three rare spawns.The overworld is fun at first, but it seems like the developers ran short of ideas as they went along. The initially-accessible area has lots of paths to explore and secrets to find, but the later areas are much more linear and plain. Worse still, there are areas of the world map (and one accessible dungeon) that are still entirely unfinished, either unpopulated or populated by obvious placeholder mobs, complete with "under construction" signs. There are landmarks identified on the map that cannot be reached. This is not an early-access game, mind you; it's been in full release for almost a year, and is in version 3.0.Still and all, gripes aside, the core game is a lot of fun. If you like the Legend of Zelda, and you like leveling up, you'll have a good time with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: There's very little to do outside of the four main dungeons, virtually all of the other interactions in the overworld seem to be puzzles that always reward you with a spherical (a collectable that allows you to further invest in your class skills) or some sort of fetchquest. The dungeons themselves are enjoyable, but when a player dies (and it can happen easily and often), they're often forced to sit out for 5-10+ minutes until the surviving players can bring their skull to a shrine to resurrect them. Often times players will die in a way such that their skull is stuck in a small area and can't be brought to a shrine at all for the rest of that run. This forces the players to have to decide whether to exile that player indefinitely or restart the run. The mechanic itself has some promise but it's poorly implemented as-is. Some of the dungeons have soft locks that will end your run by locking you in an area you can't leave, so your only option is to self-destruct to end the run.The town buildings/interactions all basically amount to different upgrades, and certain types of upgrades (health vs damage vs stamina etc) are arbitrarily separated into different houses so you have to coordinate with your friends to make a circuit to spend your gems after each run, which can be kind of a chore because  you all have to visit each building together rather than splitting up.The devs are very much done with the game; do not expect any bugfixes or patches. It was fun for a short bit with friends. Get it on a major sale if for some reason you don't want to play Four Swords.

_childDocuments_.review: Many modern games have a crisis of fun - they are technically impressive, but they heap on layers of stupid garbage that you don't want to do and which isn't fun (10 minute opening cinematics, season passes, obtuse crafting mechanics, and other generally Ubisoft crap). This game is different. They have studied the work of gaming's Classical Masters and paid attention to their teachings. They have gazed upon the pixelated Sistene Chapel that is Zelda: A Link to the Past and have applied its lessons admirably.The gameplay in Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos is immediately engaging and fun. The controls are tight, the combat and puzzles feel rewarding, the exploration provides plenty of "aha!" moments, and even when you die you feel like your dungeon crawl was a worthwhile endeavor. Above all else, this game is FUN. It remembers what this medium is actually about, and it doesn't stand in the way of a good time. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another addicting game that you could easily pour hours of gameplay into with friends, Rogue Heroes is a cute rpg action dungeon crawler. It is reminiscent of classic Zelda games; in that you have to solve puzzles with friends in order to progress through the dungeons. The visuals are very simplistic and cute (I’m sure this design choice was made so that connections and gameplay would be better and honestly, it was a great decision). You can pitch in together to build the town, or hoard your gems for the development of your character’s skills and other attributes. Playing with friends progresses the town a lot faster than if you play alone and it also makes the experience with going through the dungeons a bit better (when you die). But that being said, due to the limit of visibility (since you share the same screen with others you’re playing with), sometimes doing a dungeon run solo may be easier honestly. I recommend this game just for the fact that it is one of the nicer and friendlier games that you could play with friends. It is an engaging and fun game to play, and its cons definitely don’t take away from it being the gem that it is.@Indie_Diva_Mina

_childDocuments_.review: This game has all the assets to potentially make it a fun, enjoyable, and all-in-all decent if not even great rogue-lite game. However, it messes up badly in online co-op.Constant bugs and de-sync happen for example:The story in itself is rather shallow and superficial, however, that is not necessarily a bad thing. To be honest I was more driven by the gameplay (fighting in dungeons and saving gems to upgrade my character's class and skills) than the plot. However, despite being a rogue-lite game, the rooms are NOT generated randomly. Rather a certain set of very few rooms exists per dungeon making them repetitive and very quickly boring.I wanted to love this game, I really did but these bugs ruined not only the flow of the game but also its experience. Furthermore, this project seems to have been abandoned by the developer since the last update/patch is dated 7th June 2022 (!!). If you plan to play this game in online co-op with your friends: don't. It's a waste of your time and money. As for single-player I give this game a neutral score. However, wait for a sale before you decide to buy it for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Eh. This is a weird one.**Coop**+ Some rooms require cooperation to solve puzzles which can be cool- The game pauses if only one of the player pauses the game. It's very disruptive when you just want to check the map or do other stuff in the menu- Some puzzles are very boring and repetitive- You can get soft locked in some dungeon rooms- Sometimes will desync. Nothing too bad while I was playing tho, mostly enemy positions but they most of the time are doing the same actions on both screens. Didn't happen too much.- Bombs are useless because other players always catch them accidentally. It's a mechanic used for some puzzles. Can be fun at first, but grows old fast.**Story**- Basically inexistant.- Sidequests feel empty. They exists but have no real meaning / rewards...**Combat system**- Stamina system is bad. Using your sword will use your stamina, but there's no point for that because the enemies become invincible a couple seconds after receiving a hit. You also have less attack speed the less stamina you have. Some other weapon also use a lot of stamina along with ammo, so your kiting capabilities are limited AND if you kite, you won't have stamina left to attack with your sword.- Weapon level up: A lot of them cost a lot and feel useless. For instance, your sword starts with 100 units of range, and each range upgrades increases it by... 1 unit. There are similar upgrades for attack speed and other weapons. Since  enemies in dungeons deal so much damage, you mostly need to upgrade your max health...- No balance at all. Overworld enemies are super weak. Dungeon monsters are super strong compared to the overworld... Enemies deal much more damage and have more health. - Dungeon bosses deal almost no damage and is much easier to beat than almost any small enemy in the dungeon. Their attack pattern can be interesting, but you receive so little damage that you end up just tanking most of the hits.- You get so many regenerative items by slashing plants or destroying pots that it removes a lot of the difficulty in the game.- Character class system is pretty useless: They have nothing that make them feel too unique, only 1 simple ability and base stats are changed+/- The traps. THEY'RE EVERYWHERE!!! Be ready to develop trust issues**Sounds**- Only ambiance music. I feel like another kind of music would have been more fitting+ I guess sounds effects are good**Graphics:**+ Actually pretty good. Of course almost all the graphics are based on / inspired of Zelda: alttp, but I liked it.- Tried to be a Zelda: alttp clone with online capabilities. Feels like the devs changed their mind halfway and decided to add every systems they could think of. In the end, most of the systems feel wrong.- Difficulty is very unbalanced- Combat system is based on stamina and is disappointingI really wanted to enjoy the game but it just felt wrong. Still found the motivation to finish the game with a friend.

_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable "Link to the Past" feeling dungeon crawler. The open world exploration along with the changing dungeons are a welcoming addition to this top down graphics style. The classes feel unique enough to vary builds and they offer several tech-tree style upgrades / leveling systems. You will find yourself deep in a dungeon with a bag full of goodies actually wanting to die just so you can rush back to town and level up! _childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes is a playable, competent game with good fun to be had with friends. It's by no means a great game but it is not a hard recommend if you've got a couple friends you want to spend a bit of time clearing dungeons with.The Good -- Lots of potential progression to keep each run feeling valuable for a long time- Gameplay is solid- There's enough game chaos to create lots of fun, interesting moments without being overwhelming- Music and sound never got old- Large open world with lots to explore. There are gates but it didn’t feel overly restrictive most of the time- Dynamic puzzles that change depending on the number of players was neat- Scratches the Zelda-esque itch with some of its own variety and uniquityThe Bad -- The game does not evolve much after 3 or 4 hours. Advancement is there but its mostly just increasing stat points.- Pause menu is shared, even across online multiplayer. If one player wants to change their inventory selection or check the map, it pauses all players. This can end up being very frustrating and our group tended to just stay out of the menus as much as possible, even though that gimped us on occasion.- Classes are only vaguely different. Superficially, each class has a different ability and strengths/weaknesses but, realistically your upgrade path will do significantly more to define your play style than the class you choose.- Farming is mostly useless considering how big a deal the game tries to make the mini game. By the time we had the farm and all the requirements to actually use it we were half way through the game and once you have the farm it takes FOREVER to grow and sell your crops. Needing to individually water an entire field every time you return from a dungeon for a couple coins every 6th dungeon run was not at all worth it.The Other -- Exploration was fun but generally underwhelming. The main collectable is an item that lets you keep a percentage of your gems when you enter a dungeon (you have to give up any remaining gem currency each time) and, after collecting around 50 of them, we were only at 17-ish percent you get to keep. And, since its use it or lose it, you're always going to spend as much as you can before starting your next dungeon. Since you'll always start your next run with <200 gems, 17% at the end of the game only equates to keeping 20-30 gems which is less than the drop from a single enemy. Feels like the collectable needed either no in-game reward to just be a side thing you could do as an achievement or a much more meaningful reward like +17% more gems collected.- Quests can be confusing. We constantly had a quest to 'craft a shovel' even though we had already crafted a shovel to use the farm but we found there were places in the world that appeared too dense/thick to dig. Never could figure out how to build the shovel the quest wanted.- Keyboard remapping wouldn’t stick. Change a couple of the commands to use additional mouse buttons but they would only last through that session, restarting the game reset the keybinds.We did enjoy the game and played to the final boss but have no real incentive to continue playing. $20 for ~15 hours of co-op gameplay isn’t bad if you can excuse some of the game's shortcomings :)

_childDocuments_.review: An indie LoZ-like, so much LoZ that that name essentially describes the entire thing. However it has horrendous balancing across the many classes and tools to where most of them are useless or active handicaps to use, multiplayer is obscenely bug-ridden with all kinds of constant issues plaguing it throughout, and it even commits the cardinal sin of prominently using royalty-free music in areas where having its own OST would suit it better.And yet, I can't help but enjoy it. It's such an obvious passion project and made by a minuscule 2-man team at that, which makes the sheer scope of the game impressive enough to overshadow its countless faults.This is the kind of product that makes you genuinely look forward to whatever comes next.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is actually fun, the puzzles are there with some puzzles being more reaction based and some requiring a little bit of thinking. In solo, the game functions as intended.The main issue most players may come across is the multiplayer that is definitely enjoyable but also comes with a potential game breaking bug. It can be avoided but with the irony that the multiplayer of this game works best when the host of the game has computer specs that isn't too powerful.If the host has a PC with powerful specs, the game will have a high likely chance to encounter the game breaking bug for clients that joins the room.The bug occurs upon exiting certain caves, the game will teleport all players to the top most left corner of the map. While the clients will be stuck with a black screen, the host would be able to move as usual. However, this comes in variation as sometimes it will teleport the players to some inaccessible parts of the map leading to players being stuck in the middle of nowhere. At this point, if the host closes the room or the game, the clients will recover from the black screen. If this issue occurs, it's best to get any of the clients who had a black screen to host the game instead.Probably has something to do with computers with powerful specs loading the map faster than the clients, which lead to the bug.Overall it's an enjoyable game, the different classes has it's place in the team, beating up mobs and bosses with friends as a team is a plus so long the game breaking bug is worked around / resolved in time to come

_childDocuments_.review: Fun gem, buy it - The bomber class bonus is great! Played this game at PAX and as a Demo. Very happy to see the full game release on steam. Simply put, the game is what you expect: a mix of "Secrets of Grindea" / "Zelda" / "Stardew". Players build up and customize a small town using gems found in dungeons. The newly unlocked structures of your town open the doors to many quests that will send you all over the map. Combat is fun and caters to a variety of play styles through their class system. There are loads of dungeon puzzles for both multi-player and single player. Steam muti-player works great and most in-game communication is via 'emojis'. Bosses are fun and the grind for coins and gems is enjoyable in the same way "Enter the Gungeon" was. Menu interface, is for the most part, easy to use and understand. The game plays much better on controller however.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a beautiful 2D pixel-art world and has a lot of potential for being a good co-op game (main purpose of getting it) but with some issues I experienced while trying it alone first, I ended up refunding the game. Their are reviews that had longer playtime and have a better perspective of other bugs/multiplayer issues, but focusing on only what I experienced in my short time playing. (sorry for a long list, but hope it helps) If at least some of these bugs were fixed then my recommendation could change, but for now this is my take on it.1. When attacking, the direction you attack is inconsistent. Although it appears you attack in whichever direction you're facing (which can be an issue on its own depending on the game/how it is implemented) it sometimes attacks in completely different directions, and if you are moving by pressing 2 different keys (ex. pressing W and D to move North-East) the game will randomly decide which of the two directions to attack, instead of in the direction being moved every time, which for me is a personal game killer of not having full control over attacks in a game that focuses on attacking enemies. And although the game is sort-of designed to be like this where only WASD are directions to attack in, enemies can attack in all directions most of the time, which is the main reason I'm pointing this out.2. Stamina regen rates are very inconsistent. Whenever you attack and deplete your stamina, the game randomly decides if the stamina will regenerate within 1-2 seconds, while other times it seems to take as long as 5 seconds before it even starts to refill, which is a very odd bug.3. In the dungeons, sometimes a puzzle to be able to access an area/treasure will be designed so that if you are not careful and/or once you activate something, you can be effectively soft-locked out of an entire area of the dungeon, losing access to possible rooms/loot. I am more forgiving of this issue because dungeons are generated as you play, but is still an issue because if it can block you off from things in general, that means their is a chance the dungeon layout will just block you from continuing, effectively ruining your run.4. It is not stated clearly that any gems you gather within the dungeon will be lost upon re-entering a new dungeon, costing me a lot of gems that could of been used on something useful, but I decided to save up towards another item. This mechanic is one that I actually love in games, but is annoying that it leaves you to discover it on your own.4a. Adding onto this, for some reason any gold earned, which is another currency, is able to be kept no matter what unlike gems, adding to the confusion of this mechanic being within the game but not explained initially or in the description/trailer of the game.5. The damage traps deal is very inconsistent. In one room, an arrow trap may deal about 10-12 damage, but in the room next door on the same floor/run, it deals 20+ damage now. If it was at least another floor within the dungeon it would make sense, but changing it from room to room is a very weird move.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos is a great game, and one I would highly recommend to anyone looking for a short puzzling adventure game. It brings back memories of Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventure. However, to call this a roguelike is misleading. The only roguelike aspect in this game is the layout of the dungeons. Everything else in this game will be the same every time you play it. The art style brings a lot to the game. The classes all have cute outfits and enemies designs are fun. I have played this game both multiplayer and single player, and both of these modes have various pros and cons to them. The single player is very nice to quickly access your inventory, change out runes or potions, check the map, access quests, and generally has a faster-paced play. That being said, playing with 4 people is a much more enjoyable experience. The different classes feel like they should offer a lot of versatility to how one plays the game, but they do not unfortunately. Some, such as the mage and the reaper, feel like they are just strictly better than others, given that their ability allows them to avoid all damage. It would be nice if the different classes had more unique aspects. The same can also be said about the weapons. After having upgraded the bow, bomb, wand, grapple hook, and sword, only the sword is a viable weapon. It does far more damage and has no limited ammunition or mana cost. There are a number of problems with the game though. The mage can clip through walls sometimes, making it impossible to progress. The fire boss will die to the fire vents in multiplayer, which is entertaining to watch, but makes the dungeon anticlimactic. If a player leaves the match, they cannot join back in without restarting the whole lobby.After having completed this game, I was left wanting more. More side quests, more to explore. Despite the problems I've mentioned, it is a lot of fun and a game that I would recommend to all my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really, really, really fun. Instantly addicted.It's like Zelda: Link to the Past, Terraria, and Stardew Valley had a rogue-lite baby that's multiplayer.It's challenging but not overly frustrating.  The graphics are smooth, fluid, and really cute.  The hero characters are just adorable.I was initially skeptical that a game like this with a $20 price tag would be worth it, but it is absolutely worth every penny and if what I said above sounds intriguing, you won't be disappointed.  The only issues I have with it are as follows:Wand and bow aiming/targeting are wonky sometimes. Sometimes you aim your cursor at a nearby enemy, and then try to shoot the one across the room instead, usually hitting some object between you rather than that target, wasting the arrow and the magic power (which, in longer runs, doesn't get replenished very well).Finding/getting to certain areas is a bit frustrating.  Townspeople give you quests and tell you generally what to do and where to go, and there is a very, very basic quest log, but getting back on track without googling or looking up a guide is a chore.  Quest details could be a bit more ...well...detailed. The farm could use a little bit of an overhaul. Such as a way to water multiple plots instead of one at a time (if there is a way and I am missing it, tell me so).  Also, you can remove all the twigs and boulders on the farm, then move away a screen and come back and they're all back again in random spots.  That's tedious.Other than those very minor complaints, this game is a 9.5/10 and worth your time and money!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to start by congratulating the developers on making my current autistic obsession. I've wanted a multiplayer Link to the Past for years, and I'm overjoyed to finally have it. Nintendo did make a game that fits that description, but I've never played, and you probably haven't either, at least not with multiplayer, since it required you to have as many GBAs and link cables to hook up to your GameCube/Wii for that number of people playing its multiplayer mode, including player 1. Rogue Heroes has local and online co-op for up to 4 people right away. It also a variety of different classes, several different weapons inspired by some of the more iconic items from Link to the Past, like the hookshot, bombs and wands, and procedural-generated dungeons. It's worth noting that the individual rooms appear to have been deliberately designed, while the enemies, items, certain details of the puzzles and the overall layout of the dungeons are randomized. Conversely, its overworld appears to be entirely designed, even down to enemy placements, and has a number of secret chests with special upgrade items hidden in plain sight to reward thorough exploration or behind item-oriented progression gates. There's side quests given by charming NPCs, many of which become available based on how much you build up your town. This game has a lot to do.All that said, while the game is extremely fun for me, there are some important criticisms that might sway you one way or the other. The minor criticism I have is of the music. It's all royalty free stuff, which tells me that the devs couldn't afford a composer to make the whole soundtrack, but the tracks chosen lean more toward being "atmospheric," rather than exciting and adventurous, which might take the wind out of some peoples' sails, since the music is such an important part of a Zelda-style game's appeal. The major criticism is how the game feels like it was designed around multiplayer primarily, and then adjusted haphazardly to facilitate single-player runs. It's hard to describe the feeling of playing by yourself in detail, but, basically, a lot of the puzzles that felt clever and team-oriented with 2-4 players are still used in singleplayer but often take longer to execute the solution (a lot of pushing blocks onto pressure plates, for instance). There's also no mechanic to replace the resurrection mechanic available with multiple people. In multiplayer, if someone dies, you can pick up their skull and take it to a special shrine to bring them back. As far as I've seen, there's nothing like this in singleplayer, which makes playing by yourself even harder, since one death is an immediate end to your run. I haven't personally been too frustrated by this fact for it to affect whether I like the game or not, but your mileage may vary. It's worth noting that there are bottles in this game that you can fill with potions, which can alleviate the difficulty.The tl:dr is that the game is incredibly fun with 2-4 people, but falters a bit as a singleplayer experience (though not enough for me personally to stop liking it), and the music is boring.  Update! I've figured out how to change the in-game music, and it was much easier than I initially thought. You simply take whatever music you want, convert it into .wma format using a wide variety of tools that can be found with a quick google search (I've been using . After that, you rename to the new .wma file to match the name of the specific song you want to replace in "...steamapps\common\Rogue Heroes\Content\Audio\Mp3", and you're done. The new audio will replace the original song, play based on the same triggers and automatically loop. To test this, you can replace the file "Music - Juniper.wma," which is found in the previously mentioned folder. This is the name of the song that plays over the start screen. Some quick warnings: if the new audio file you're using isn't properly formatted and the original audio file is missing, the game will crash on startup, and I recommend that you make backups of the audio files you plan on replacing before doing so. the biggest problem with this method is that the audio files that're being replaced are named in ways that are not helpful for intuiting the context of where the song will be played in-game. For instance, the song "Juniper" plays over the title screen, "Arid Foothills" plays while in caves and "Morgana Rides" plays while exploring the first dungeon. I'm considering making a proper guide explaining all of this once I beat the game.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr; This is not a "stay away from this game" recommendation. From what I've played so far, it's not a BAD bad game. It's just a bit... all over the place? Considering it's pretty cheap when on sale you can probably get enough bang for your buck before it bores. It's got nice art, the music is meh, and the core gameplay is okay. That said, it also feels unfinished and empty. I hate overly long reviews because who's gonna read them anyway. But to list some of my gripes in more detail:- I'm not sure if it wants to be a roguelike/lite, a zelda clone ("inspired" by Zelda is understating it, it basically rips 80% of the gameplay elements from it), or a dungeon crawler. - Most dungeons are procedurally generated, with a set of rooms that is chosen from for each dungeon. But the puzzly rooms just feel tedious, because it's just a bit of back and forth to press switches. Especially after you have completed them earlier already they're just boring- As said: it feels unfinished and unpolished in some places; for example, the town is much larger than the amount of stuff you can build, and most of the skill "trees" just contain multiple of the same items to inflate how fleshed out they are (the shovel upgrade tree just consists of like 6 "dig X% faster!"...). I'm not even sure what the point is of the whole southwest area, it's just a lot of empty space and an optional dungeon.- The "farming" minigame is extremely tedious and unnecessary.- Overworld pathing is frustrating at times. - The amount of grind counters is excessive (destroy X rocks! shoot X arrows! kill X {monster type} monsters! etc.- There's an annoying bug where enemies may "spawn" into the wrong elevation of the level (like Zelda it's got an upper and a lower level). In order to kill them you need to be on the same elevation, At least one run I had to abandon because an enemy spawned wrong and I couldn't kill it and I needed to kill all enemies to unlock a door.

_childDocuments_.review: I have not experienced the online co-op issues many are reporting. I have played mostly singleplayer and some co-op over the internet utilizing Parsec without any issues in that regard. This game satisfies a simple 2D zelda-esque itch pretty well. Playing it co-op make sit much more interesting as you run around with your friends through the overworld and dungeons with a generally bright and clean art style tying everything together. I do think the game is well worth the cost overall and recommend it for a reasonably fun 2-4 player game if you're doing couch or steam remote play/parsec co-op. That said, I have a few small criticisms.1. All the classes are sword wielders. Magic user, witch, thief, ranger. You're using a sword as your go-to weapon. Your class may modify a sub-weapon when you unlock it but those subweapons require ammo or mana to use and just are overall weaker than swinging the sword as a high damage melee class.2. After the first dungeon, the second dungeon is comparatively difficult to get to. You'll be doing a lot of quests back and forth to and from a swamp to town to get items and leads on where to go next until you finally manage to do some minor dungeons to get to the next big dungeon/shrine. This is okay, but it's very different from all but walking out the first gate of town into the first dungeon, so the pacing is a bit off in that regard.3. The subweapons are unlocked pretty quickly for some, and obtusely for others. You'll get a wand, boomerang (you never use this in my experience) and bomb pretty quickly. Other stuff will take longer and you never really need those items outside of the grappling hook which is required for puzzles. Need a bomb for a puzzle? The game provides unlimited bombs nearby, so why get bombs on your own?4. Incremental leveling and shop building. You have to spend your gems to unlock shops and homes in town, opening quests and upgrade trees. Unfortunately, you're going to be farming a TON of gems. Upgrades are in the realm of 1-10 points of things early on, like 1 sword damage or 5 health. You unlock more trees for higher amounts of these things but the upgrade trees are very flat and plain and not at all entertaining. You aren't getting new abilities so much as getting 0.5% better with each unlock.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game. It feels like the developers were Link to the Past fans and thought, "I want more of that, but be able to play with a few friends." The progression feels much like that, I'm having fun exploring the world with each new item I'm able to get. And grinding the first dungeon doesn't feel grindy because of the procedural generation. So it's fun to go back to that same dungeon again and again to build your inventory and expand the town.Being able to work on your character in single player and then join or invite friends is a strong point of this game. I don't mind hopping into a friends game to go back to one of the first dungeons to solve the puzzles and clear the rooms. The dungeon bosses are just difficult enough to make the fight exciting without being a slog. When two of your mates have died to the boss and it's down to you and one other, and the teamwork pays off, it's satisfyingThere are a few issues in the co-op mode. A little jank. But I wouldn't say that makes it unplayable. There have been some trees and bushes invisible to some players, and a couple spots impassable by one or two of the players in a group. But it gets reset when another player can just go to the next part of the map and the teammate is automatically teleported there. I found it only a minor inconvenience and I do hope they try to resolve this with a future update. None of those same issues seem to arise in the single player.I've seen far more broken multiplayer play in AAA game titles. This game is well worth the time and money to play IMO. Forty dollars well spent for me and the other copy I bought for my partner.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this as part of my humble bundle monthly.  This is  fun game to play at home with my kids since it has 4 player local coop.  It is very similar to the old 4 swords game I used to play on my ds years ago.  It's nice not needing 4 devices to play, nintendo really needs to re-release 4 swords on switch.Anyway this game has the added bonus of being a roguelite, so it's fun to build the town and upgrade your heroes in between each run of the dungeon.  The puzzles are a lot harder on coop since you need each activate switches individually and the more players you have the less blocks you can use.  The different classes are fun and there are lots of unique upgrades for them.  There are also plenty of generic upgrades that work to upgrade all classes.  You must unlock all the tools to use any of them on the overworld.  In the dungeons you will find whats needed for each run and the dungeon floors are randomized so its not always the same.  I am still on the first dungeon so it's not that easy to beat.  The boss was almost a bullet hell type fight so you are running around a lot.  Definitely an easier game while playing solo, but so far the kids aren't bored.   I usually do some single player to make my character stronger so I can carry them a bit easier.  So far I have only had one bug where the screen goes blank and I have to force quit the game but so far that's on happened once.  Pretty much bug free experience for me so far which is refreshing since most games these days release littered with bugs making them almost unplayable.  It's nice to pick up a game immediately and not have to mod it to make it work.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was $20. I would say it is worth that price.It drew me in with its Link to the Past aesthetic and gameplay and it tickled my nostalgia bone very nicely. So if you don't mind spending $20 for several hours of gameplay and enjoyed Link to the Past, this game is worth it.I will say I am a little disappointed though because before I bought the game, I believed there was more to it than there actually is. I saw the classes as something that would be fun and exciting to play with, but nope. Classes might as well be aesthetic choices because they only provide some intensely minor bonus to one thing and change your dash/run mechanic a bit. The starting guy is the best character until you get Knight, then it becomes the best character because its passive is the most useful (he takes less damage). That about sums up the classes. I had initially imagined how fun it would be to play a Witch or Mage casting spells, but none of that really happens or matters. There are no spells really, just a wand item that everyone gets through play and anyone can use and you just choose between Fire, Ice, or Missile plus two others that really serve no purpose in combat. They cost magic power to use and no one has magic regeneration, so there really isn't a point to being a mage or witch because they don't really offer anything that you can't get as a Knight. The broom ability was kind of cool, but it only lasts 2 seconds and has a looong recharge time and honestly it wasn't needed because the only traps it actually lets you avoid are the obvious floor spikes that are trivial to avoid anyway. It doesn't let you fly over fire or ooze or anything else on the ground, it will hurt you anyway.I also believed that each dungeon would be procedurally generated for unlimited play and that isn't really true either. They layout seems to change each time, but there are only so many rooms in each dungeon and you'll very quickly see them all and know how to complete them and how they work, so it doesn't really have unlimited replayability and I found that disappointing as well.It's a nice little game that had the potential to be really outstanding but fell short of that. But i'd say it is worth $20, and definitely worth getting if it ever goes on sale if you're a fan of Link to the Past.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all this game as a Roguelike is NEAT...Second it is not noticeable immediately, but this game is a gem...at the beginning while you explore and try to unlock places, it makes you stupid because you don't understand some dynamics, after you get the grips of it, (i'm talking in particular of 2nd dungeon), you enjoy spending the time in it.Nothing extremely new to the genre, except that instead of focusing only on dungeons and bosses, there is also a big exploration element on the game, to find the path to those dungeons from your village or teleporters.There are no armors, or better, the armos in the wardrobe will change your character; you level up your stats by leveling up your village time by time you complete dungeons and loot crystals.Luckily at death there's no loss of statistics, you will revive at your house at the village keeping the crystals you looted to power up yourself.The game is NOT EASY...is it very rogue and probably like me you are going to die many times...There are several little puzzles to solve scattered around the dungeon in order to loot everything, like displacing a column, moving a block onto a tile or lighting fires.This is not a game for casual players, been playing online with stoners and we couldn't solve the puzzles cause they were confused at the point to sabotage continuosly.I reccomend this game, is nice, you just need the right company.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic and surprisingly fun to play. I see a lot of negative reviews, so I'd like to counterbalance that with my perspective on the matter.First and foremost, I absolutely love co-op couch games with a shared screen option. I play this game with my girlfriend, and we are both fans of Zelda. In terms of look and feel, this game is clearly an homage to the SNES version: A Link to the Past, which I used to play endlessly in the past.I consider this game to be a well-executed casual multiplayer Zelda look-alike with a lot of Roguelike elements. The game offers a delightful dose of retro hack & slash action. It is fun playing together with friends (or in my case, my girlfriend) on the couch, exploring dungeons in a well-designed world, building a village, and even doing some farming and fishing. It's an easy-going game.Multiplayer on one screen works really well. The shared screen option has been well thought out. You are forced to play intuitively and make decisions together. The screen moves smoothly with each player, and when someone goes off-screen, everyone is teleported to the same starting location. A neat detail is that puzzles are seamlessly adjusted for a game with 1 to 4 players. If someone dies, the rooms change to fit the puzzle with the new number of players.Occasionally, you have to wait a bit for each other's selection screen, like when brewing a potion or placing a weapon in your quick-select wheel. However, these moments are few. I can imagine patience wearing thin if your partner takes ages to spend gems in the village while you wait. Luckily, we don't have that problem because we play a style where we shop around aggressively and quickly make all our purchases. We don't bother meticulously calculating how to optimize our character's stats. Because that's not really necessary. Sure, you can theoretically build up your character, and there are plenty of upgrades available. However, for us, it's perfectly fine to enter a shop after a dungeon and without much thought, boost our stamina, weapons, or strength and continue playing.In that regard, it's essential to know what expectations you have for the game. After the first dungeon, I let go of the notion that it would offer a complex challenge where we have to finely balance our characters to progress further, as in Vagante (a fantastic Roguelike Co-op). Its just a simple game, at some point we increased the difficulty, but we still rushed through the game, slaying all creatures, discovering secrets, upgrading our characters, and yeah… having a blast!Of course, I also notice the flaws and missed opportunities. Additionally, many players encounter bugs, which is naturally frustrating, especially if you can't proceed and lose progress. Fortunately, I haven't experienced any of that so far. My most significant criticism is the lack of a quick-select option for various potions and the different runes in your staff. I'd also prefer to see 3 or 4 super well-balanced characters instead of the current 8 or so characters without much added value.The variety of monster movement could use improvement, and I miss seeing monster strengths and weaknesses in relation to all available weapons. It's as if the basic framework and complete artwork for a unique Rogue-Zelda-like game are in place but not entirely matured. There seems to be a certain lack of depth. Did the developers need an extra six months or a year? Or... perhaps the game was intentionally kept more straightforward? Maybe it just doesn't have to match the immense amount of finely balanced roguelikes on Steam.All in all, with the right expectations, the right nostalgic fondness for old SNES games, and a friend or partner to play with, this game is definitely worth it. It's clear that a lot of attention and love were poured into this game. The world is imaginative, the gameplay is smooth, and the music is great. I just really enjoy this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this as an action roguelike to play with my girlfriend. There was way too much of an emphasis on puzzle solving than I expected. I don't mind some puzzles, but the visual presentation made solving the puzzles frustrating. I couldn't tell if blocks were raised of lowered, or if something was a pushable block or the space where the block was supposed to go. It often wasn't clear what the goal of the puzzle was anyway. Most of our time playing was spent just trying random solutions to one puzzle. Finally, once we realized there is no way to save & quit mid-run (you have to kill yourself or lose all progress) we decided to refund it. I also don't think the roguelike elements added anything to the game. It would have been better as just an ARPG without roguelike elements where you can save your progress and come back later to puzzles that stumped you, instead of them being gone forever once that run ends.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is done purely from the perspective of single player (only thing i got to say about multi is that it is buggier then single according to other reviews)Short Version:A fun, roguelike rpg style game that is similar to zelda: a link to the past (except you use your gems/rubies to upgrade your character). In order to keep upgrading your character you need to build your town (which you also use gems for and other things as well). BUT, you will encounter some bugs here and there as a heads up.Longer Version:A fun roguelike that is very similar to Zelda: A link to the past except unlike in zelda, you upgrade your character in a more traditional rpg style type way with the gems you find (your currency as well) is used to upgrade your character/build your town.That being said, there are some features that are in this game that are not very common to the roguelike/lite genre.Such as here they are (along with some extra info): 1. When ever your character hits an enemy, your character takes a step forward, and since contact damage is a thing in this game, you must becareful not to just spam your attack if your close to an enemy.2. There is stamina in this game, as such, after a certain amount of weapon swings, you will tire and attack slower until you just wont be able to attack until you let it build back up again (both blocking and attacking with your sword which all classes do takes up stamina).3. The artwork for the game is somewhat deceiving. Their is no sexes in this game per say. No clear definition of male or female. One could argue that when you change to a certain class, you change sexes to match eg, knight makes you male, witch makes you female ect. But id say your character is just a unisex sprite at the end of the day, neither being male or female. This feature may matter to some, and to others it wont, just tossing this timbit of info out there in order to cover every base i can for a proper review.4. The bugs. You will encounter bugs in this game. More so in multiplayer as opposed to single player but they are there in single. Patch's are few and far between and the game is done in terms of sales (not even in the top 8 pages, last i checked i checked the top 13 and didint see it anywhere), as such, dont expect any bugs you find to be fixed in a timely fashion. They are patching the game (most recent june 7th that fixed the  catacombs bugged that prevent you from even really giving it a solid go, the cata is one of the games 2 infinite dungeons as a heads up, this patch took them 2 months and a bit to do but also brought some more bugs with it lol but at least nothing game breaking from what ive seen so far), just not often.5. This game is also a bit light on the story side. Again to some this might be an issue, to others it wont be. Their is  dialogue but nothing i would classify as an in-depth story with lots to read.6. This game can be played with either a controller or mouse/keyboard. The keys for mouse/keyboard can be rebinded easily enough, however rebinding the controller keys is a nightmare that can only be done via controller layout (and even then it doesint exactly work properly via this method, it is possible to really royally mess up the controls for the controller via this method and have no real way of resetting it back, spent a good 2h on it myself and managed to somewhat get what i wanted rebinding controls this way, you have been warned, dunno if its cause i use a logitech controller with xnput or what, but damn what a nightmare lol)7. Also, sometimes, the game will have VERY small plateform's with a stair leading up to it with enemies waiting for you, depending on the class and what resources you have access too, it can be VERY hard to not take damage sometimes depending what type of enemies are on so said platform (the catacombs, the games last infinite dungeon can be VERY ugly for these types of situations).8. You can choose from a couple of different difficulty settings and change them on the fly and it will take effect off the bat (or should at least). So if you having difficulty, you can just pause the game and lower the difficulty on the fly (im not sure if this applies to the catacombs since i know it records what difficulty the game was on when you die, thus i dont know if it locks the difficulty, havent tested it yet)9. There is no new game + feature in this game.Other then that, the last question that needs to be answered is "Will i get at least 1 hour of fun/entertainment/gameplay for every dollar i spend on this game". To that i say, if you pay full price for this game, you should most likely even if you skip both infinite dungeons. If you give both infinite dungeons a go, then for sure. Game costed me around 20 bucks (bought it on sale) and after using some guides to find some of the power sphere's (another way to upgrade your character, there is lots and some are not ease to find) and giving both infinite dungeons a solid go, i ended up with 32 hours in the game by the time i was mostly finished with it. i definitely got my money's worth and suspect anyone into games such as this will as well (and if this game isint for you, assuming you didint spend alot of time trying to rebind your controls like i did, you will easely find that out with in the first hour and 45 mins of game play and can just get a refund).Over all, i give this game, a 7 out of 10 and definitely recommend but it might be wise to wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: 5 hours in, and I simply don't get the hate that this game gets. Being a fan of the older Zelda games, including the original and A Link to the Past, I can honestly say that this is the best ALTTP clone I've ever seen. It initially seemed a little too straightforward of a game - the first dungeon is discovered very quickly, and bears a fairly punishing level of difficulty. I died a lot trying to complete it. I didn't get a whole lot out of it at first, but the third floor started to feel more like a proper Zelda dungeon to me, as I was starting to get a good grasp of the mechanics of the game.The real magic started while trying to get to the second dungeon - the world opens up more, and getting to the dungeon is a proper puzzle in and of itself. This felt SOOO much like ALTTP, and was one thing that really hit the mark of a proper Zelda game - you go questing about before you can even reach the point of getting to a desired dungeon, and it hit all of the nostalgia marks just right. I forgot that this wasn't a Zelda game at that point. Playing this with my kiddos is an absolute delight. I always wanted to play Four Swords, but never found people to play it with. This scratches that now decades-old itch beautifully. The lovely thing about it is that the game plays beautifully whether single or multiplayer. Every now and then, I run into a puzzle that cannot be completed by one player alone, but it seems like those are few and far between (that, or maybe I just don't have the right items or abilities yet). I haven't experienced almost any of the bugs that so many players have reported. I saw a bit of a bug where running along the corner of a wall yielded some glitchy movement in one specific spot, but I haven't had a single issue since. Playing with my kids hasn't yielded any issues so far. On the note of multiplayer, the developers did something REALLY smart with players who have died - their ghost can possess pots and plants and throw them at enemies. They can also trigger traps to keep you from getting hurt, or as my son did, alert me to traps on the floor I didn't see.  Even if it takes a while to revive the other players, they can still interact in a meaningful way with the game as a whole. I loved that my son could still play, even though he struggled to not die. All in all, I really don't get the poor reviews this game has gotten. I enjoy it quite a bit, and perhaps that's all that matters.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game. It's like a mix of zelda world exploring with roguelike randomized dungeons. Both the world exploring and the dungeons are well done. While I do recommend this game, I do have a few gripes. My first gripe is please, Please, PLEASE, make it so that you can pause the game or open your inventory in coop without forcing your coop partner(s) to also pause their game. There's no reason for this. All it does is automatically make you a ♥♥♥♥ every time you want to look at the map, because doing so prevents your friend from doing anything. They only thing you can do when your partner is in their menu is open your own menu, which then prevents them from doing anything when they are done with their menu, and it's just an endless cycle. The coop elements otherwise work great for the most part. Both the host and client can perform most actions, and moving off a tile automatically moves the other players to the next tile, which is already way better than many coop games. There are a few minor glitches/desync issues in coop but nothing game breaking. The most annoying one I came across is that some achievements don't unlock properly if you play as a client.Next, a fairly large issue with the game right now is balancing. Generally in a game like this you would expect to jump into the first dungeon and immediately be completely obliterated by the enemies, because you don't have any upgrades yet. You then play the dungeon a few times, get gems to purchase upgrades, and learn the enemies better, and eventually unlock the second dungeon. So far, this is all exactly how things play out in Rogue Heroes. The problem starts after you beat the first dungeon. Basically, at that point, the game stops being hard. You would expect the second dungeon to be hard again, until you level some more, and so on for the third and fourth dungeons. But after my friend and I beat the first dungeon, we beat every dungeon thereafter on the first try, often without even dying (if your coop partner dies in a dungeon you can revive them at a revival totem). Even the "endless dungeon" that you unlock after beating the game is extremely easy, and only gets easier as you purchase all the upgrades (although I have to admit I'm kind of glad of this, because otherwise getting the "reach level 25 of the endless dungeon" achievement would be a huge pain in the neck). The balance isn't so bad that the game ceases to be fun. The dungeons are only part of the game (the rest is exploring the world map). But I do hope the devs can improve it. I don't think it's a fundamentally broken aspect of the game. I really think this can be fixed by just tweaking some aspects of the progression. Finally, the game feels somewhat unfinished. Actually, I think it's unfair to say it's unfinished, because the game has a lot of content and you can get to the end of it. The problem is that the devs seem to have had a lot of ideas that didn't really go anywhere, but they still included them all in the game for some reason. There are tons of mechanics/items/etc in the game that either do nothing or are at best are used exactly once. This leaves you feeling very confused about what something does, until you finally realize that the devs just never fleshed that particular thing out. I would love to see some of the ideas actually fleshed out, but I would also suggest to the devs to just remove the things from the game that don't do anything. I would honestly rather see the devs focus on polishing the things that do work (and in particular, fixing the balance issues and coop glitches I mentioned above, or cleaning up the inventory system). There are already plenty of things in the game that are fleshed out. It's really bad to add half baked stuff to a game. Either flesh it out completely, or don't include it at all. All these things do is confuse the player before they figure out they don't actually do anything, and disappoint them when they do.For example, at one point you get a special item that changes the layout of the world. But, unless I missed something, it's only ever used twice: once immediately after you obtain it, and once in a single randomized dungeon room. I was rather expecting the item to change the world map, and maybe force you to re-explore some areas that you previously couldn't access. But instead all it does it clog up your already difficult to use inventory (which is itself only difficult to use because you have to use the scroll wheel to scroll through 20 different items because actually opening your inventory to select something would PAUSE your friend's game, but I digress). There are dozens of similar instances of this, which I'm not going to enumerate here.To be sure, I do recommend this game, especially for coop. But if you play it do be aware of these issues. Don't over-grind past the first dungeon, because the game is already easy enough at that point. And be aware that if you come across a item/mechanics that confusingly doesn't seem to do anything, it's probably because it actually doesn't do anything. The game is still new, so with any luck, the devs will patch the issues I mentioned.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a 'meh' recommendation here. I'm going with a thumbs down in the most tentative, mild way imaginable. This game has fantastic potential, but there's a lot holding it back.  Visually the art style feels more like it's going for Earthbound instead of Zelda. The lack of deep shadows and brighter highlights on objects, characters, and enemies lends to the world having a bland flatness to it.  Certain tools have alternate visuals, while others don't. The world itself feels like it should be large and vast, but it's mostly trees and hills forming linear paths through areas.  I spent most of my time wishing there was an audio mod to put something catchy from A Link to the Past just to try to give some actual energy to the score. There are no catchy tunes, the music is just as subdued as the visuals, sadly. The good thing is that it IS just subdued, nothing will be grating your ears. It's just not stand out or catchy.  There are a few core gameplay elements. Each is a solid foundation, but doesn't reach the point where it needs to be to truly stand on its own. The class system lets you get threads for different cloaks to become a different character class. Unfortunately, the game doesn't give you much documentation on what each secret little feature a class has. On top of this, there isn't enough mechanically different in those classes to make them stand out as a unique play experience. Outside of different stats, the only thing that changes is a special ability button which is just a movement ability, and a few passive abilities. (The Ranger is good with bows, Mage cases spells cheaper, Reaper auto-crits after a certain number of kills) . The problem is that in most cases your standard sword and shield will be so good that there is no point in using anything BUT your sword.  Changing a classes default weapon, even just aesthetically, would help give a more unique feel. In general the buffs each class provides needs to feel tangible or provide a distinct mechanical difference. Maybe give the thief two knives that he can stab instead of a sweeping sword, or make the knight's shield a tower shield that can reflect projectiles automatically.  Allowing players to power-up their classes the same way that everything else is built up would allow for builds to be made would help diversify each class from each other.  There are some redundant tools, and some tools that are used fairly often. The lack of a quick selection wheel or even a favorites wheel to let you quickly pick tools on the fly is something that needs to be added, badly. The boxing glove feels pointless when the mallet can do the same thing, the lens of truth stand in is only used about 4 times, whereas the hook shot is used in just about every dungeon tile set at some point. Magic spells and arrows may as well be the same thing with different colored sprites.  Diversify what some items do while giving different mechanics to them. Make bombs clearly go up and over things when thrown, instead of having it be vague. This way players always know what they can throw over an edge, and what will just hit a railing. Make spells each do something different. Fireball is fine, but why not add in a spell to clone your character for a bit, or an AOE repulsion shield that vanishes after it hits a certain number of enemies. Specialized Classes and their tool of choice should absolutely feel like an outright superior option to the basic sword attack.  Rangers should be able to fire a fan shot of arrows, or a super shot for example.  The only point to exploration is to tidy up a few side quests to flesh out your town, and to find places to dig so you can gather more stones. All the stones do is allow you to keep a percentage of your gems when entering a dungeon. The problem is that it's totally counter-intuitive to do that. In any circumstance you're going to be powering up your character after a dungeon anyways, so you SHOULD be going into that dungeon with next to no gems. Other than that there are hints to a story in the world here and there, but beyond a few quick romps in very brief caves or dungeons the world feels dead and devoid of incentive to explore. Some very minor tools like the boxing gloves can be used in only a few areas and are world exclusive, but there should absolutely be more to discover than that.  The stones need to have an actual purpose that could be tied to player power progression, or unlocking secret areas in the world that lead to unique cloaks, cosmetics, tools, or lore. More areas should be created to flesh out the story of the world and add in extra personality. Use more design assets than trees to shape the layout of the world while experimenting with other methods of moving around. The frog whistle was an absolutely brilliant concept that made the swamps stand out from everything else, it made that biome feel incredibly unique.  There are only 4 main dungeons with a fifth 'endless' dungeon. In comparison Zelda: A Link to the Past (The game this one feels most inspired by) has 12 or so dungeons, each with their own tool, mechanic, and theme. The problem is that the developers banked so much on repeated treks through the same 4 dungeons that it lost the plot in terms of why Zelda Dungeons are so fun to do. In the end you can break down a dungeon's purpose into 4 goals. Get a key, get a bigger key, Get from Point A to Point B,  or get gems. Dungeons (outside of the endless one) are only ever 3 floors, Even by the time you get to that third floor you may be pretty bored of where you are after your third or fourth trek through the same tileset.  There need to be more dungeons and more tilesets. New dungeon mechanics and puzzle mechanics, and more goals than just those same four goals. Setting dungeons up so that they dynamically create obstacles that need to be overcome in the same way the puzzles change dynamically based on the number of players could add some extra flare. Maybe one part of the dungeon is flooded and it needs to be drained by a series of puzzles in another area in the dungeon, for example. The bosses also need a complete redesign and rework, both visually and mechanically. Very bare bones with multiplayer actively gouging out a lot of the story scenes as well. You miss the entire point of the plot if you start the game multiplayer for the first time. There are no major story beats that change the world or really make your adventure seem like an adventure. You just go to four dungeons, beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of some very very bland bosses Fun fact: I played the game entirely in muti-player and after entering the final dungeon accidentally went right in to fight the final boss without even knowing there was a dungeon component attached. We just went in, beat the final boss, saw credits, and that was it. The only reward is an unpredictable energy attack from your sword. It only fires out sometimes, so it's not even useful as a combat tactic. Sometimes it's the first slash, sometimes the fifth, who knows. Beyond that and just a "Hooray, you did it" type of ending summary, that's it. The game was on sale for 14 bucks so i grabbed it. I played about 13 hours, so that was about a dollar of enjoyment per hour. Based on the price of a movie, it's entirely worth it at that price. But there's nothing making me want to come back to the game and keep enjoying it, and that's where the rogue-like elements of a game SHOULD be doing their job to keep you pulled in and playing. Sadly , Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos just leaves you thinking "What's the point?" and moving on to the next game.  I'm looking forward to what the devs can do in future updates. But for now, i'm done.
