_childDocuments_.review: While the game has some excellent aircraft and very fun and interesting physics, by the time you get to the mid- and upper-tier grinds, many players become exasperated by obvious problems with matchmaking, balance, and goofy AI influence that seems to supersede actual human-player skill to the point where some players complain about "rigged matches" that often seem programmed to inexorably favor a certain outcome. This is merely some players' perception and the "official" stance is to strenuously deny any such bias (after all, to what purpose? who knows); but player perception is what it is, and if such a mindset exists out there in the mainstream, obviously something is triggering it, and therefore matchmaking, AI shortcomings, and win-loss dynamics should be addressed and refined.Devs don't seem inclined to listen to feedback on these types of matchmaking & AI & balance issues, instead opting for bells-and-whistles "updates."  Let's face it -- some players will happily pay $ and/or grind endlessly for shiny new objects and trinkets. Problem is, there's a recognizable concern with a somewhat lacking online population (at least on the NA server) including a known steady bleed-off of experienced players due to disillusionment and frustration with game dynamics and with suggestions/complaints apparently falling on deaf ears. I'm at the permanent rage-quit stage myself (or at least "semi-permanent"). Side note: I had initially posted a glowing review of this game but after a long slog of it, the bloom is off the rose. The earlier positive version is pasted below for posterity; unfortunately I am now one of the negative reviewers with "an axe to grind."=======================Let me preface by saying I simply do not understand the mixed reviews; I suspect many of the negative reviewers have an axe to grind because -- let's get it straight -- this game is obviously a bunch of fun on more than a few levels.The flying dynamics and flight control are right up my alley as the game leans more toward arcade-style than simulator --  but the physics are still complex and interesting; you need a basic grasp of aerodynamics and "control-surface" principles if you want to get your dogfighter or ground-attacker to behave effectively, and it will challenge your spatial awareness, reflexes, and targeting skill. But again, the "arcadey" style of flying is more to my liking as I'm not a hardcore fan of full-blown simulators -- I played "Freelancer" and even "Heroes of the Pacific" a heck of a lot more than "IL-2 Sturmovik," if you catch my drift. For me it's about having fun, not gritting your teeth and wiping sweat from your eyes. (Not to say that "IL-2" isn't outstanding in its own right, not to mention groundbreaking and "the" benchmark for dogfight-themed flying simulators.)Airplane models in this game are gorgeous and painstakingly detailed, the sheer number of different planes is amazing, the weapons feel right, and there are a lot of reasons to keep coming back for more. I became addicted rather quickly -- even flying the tier-1 biplanes is quite fun, right out of the box.

_childDocuments_.review: Like all Wargaming games, and MMOs in general, I need you to hear massive, deafening klaxons in your hears when considering getting into a game like this.This game is not fun. It is not fair. Games like these are inherently addictive. But this is all true for any MMO, really. The particular reason I give a thumbs down for WoWP is simple: The game is dead. At the lower tiers, even during peak gaming hours for the server, you'll probably be the only non-bot in the match. Even at tier 8+ you'll be lucky to have three other real players in a 14v14 match. There is no variation to the gameplay when all you have to work with is bots. Bots never surprise you. There are no tense matches. And without that fundamentally addictive component that every MMO relies on, you WILL get bored of this game and go off to War Thunder in search of plane combat instead. It's a damn shame because if you're like me, and prefer arcady combat to semi-realistic simulation combat, then this game is better than War Thunder's plane-mode. But without real players, there is just no reason to play more than a match a week when you get the random hankering for a dog-fight. Honestly, it's a wonder that Wargaming hasn't shut down the servers yet.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played War Thunder's flight simulator, you'll like the mechanics of this game. It's a bit easier, but still requires skill. There's no forward marker, so you really need to aim carefully. The tier system is nice keeping only tiers 1 above or below your plane's rank. This allows for players to be able to have a better flight experience when planes are grouped within the same tiers vs. War Thunder's "put all these tiers into one game" method. The lower tiers (I-IV) seem fairly easy to me, but that could just be my experience from War Thunder being transferred over. I've only so far have gotten into tier V, and the skill of the players are much more challenging at this point bringing more exciting air battles.What I also like about this game is that it acts more like a MOBA compared to War Thunder. In War Thunder, you have a selection of airplanes from a country to choose from during game play. If you happen to lose all your planes in a short period of time, the experience is not very exciting. In World of Warplanes, you choose one plane and you're on cool down if you die, like in LOL. I feel like I get more enjoyment out of flying the crafts and dog fights because, in some modes, you simply go back in until the game ends.One thing to note is that there are nightly maintenance server checks. During this time period, I like to go back to War Thunder until the servers are back online.If you want a more realistic experience with flight and develop more professional skills, I would play War Thunder. The realism in how the planes fly are considered into the experience, requiring a bit more understanding in the plane you are flying and how it maneuvers. However, if you're new to flight simulators and WWII aerial dog fights, start with World of Warplanes. It's a bit easier in my opinion, and the enjoyment, whether win or lose, is mostly positive.

Every aircraft has it's own physics, load out, etc. You may love a light fighter but hate a heavy fighter.But, the game a has a ways to go, I think the dev lost sight of "early access" and jumped in the deep end working on pay content when there are still a number of things to address. There are a few German Heavy fighters that are far too powerful and are used to simply ram an enemy to destroy them and no harm to them. Sometimes the physics on a plane go cross eyed and the plane just ends up flipping direction or becoming unpredictable.lastly "services" and "upgrades" can be confusing. I have a service with a ! next to it with nothing for me to do, no clue if it's working or not because there is no feedback. There are "player points" which are just experience point but they don't show now many you have and can only see how much more you need in order to "research" something. It's just kind of annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: It needs more players (Right now as of this review the daily peak is 260), but this game is still very much playable and a hell of a lot of fun. Now, if you're looking for an ultra-realistic flight combat sim where you can put on a flight mask and bomber glasses and all that ♥♥♥♥, go play War Thunder. This is a no sweat zone. Arcade-y aerial combat and a decent progression system that, with time, can take you from WW1 planes, to WW2/modern planes with bombs and rockets and machine gun turrets on the back! I also like the slight rpg element with the modules and parts. They're a welcome gameplay element that imo don't really hurt the pvp all that much. Starting out can be slightly jarring, but if you hit alt and look around your ui, things should clear up a bit (more like fill up, but I'm a fast learner, tbh.) Also, hitting F1 allows you to look at which objective you are best suited for (i.e. Attack Fighters and Bombers are pretty good for Garrisons, but fighters and Multipurpose fighters are better at defending them). I'll allow comments on this review and I wanna see if yall would like my in-depth tutorial, although the in-game one is pretty helpful if you pay attention.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. It is more arcade style than sim, but if you are looking for ww2 air combat games that thrill, this is a good one. It is not difficult to learn and you can be dogfighting in no time at all. Very good graphics and mouse/ KB control. you won't need to spend lots of $ on accessories like a flight stick and head tracking programs. It is also free to play. Having said that, not all good things come free. You have the option of buying currency in the game to help accelerate upgrades and research into better aircraft. These folks have to pay bills and eat too. So, I don't mind dropping a few dollars every now and then to them. The choice is yours. At least try it for a few days and decide for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice little flight arcady game, easy to get into especially because the game has well made mouse+keyboard control for those without a joystick. it still retains a rest feeling that you are flying a real plane though. Gameplay has also a strategic component of taking control of special zones that drive the battles so be aware that it's not only necessary to become a good pilot but also to keep a good look on what's happening on the map, especially when flying bombers of ground attack aircraft. Oh yes, there are 5 aircraft classes: fighters, multi-role fighters, heavy (two engine+) fighters, bombers, ground attack aircraft where each has a distinctive gameplay. also the tech tree has over 200 planes in it and each has its little individualities - many of which have taken to the air in reality but also some interesting paper projects as you would except from a WG game.Oh, don't mind my low play time: i just wanted to test access via steam and normally play via my wargaming account. If you have one i recommend using that since some currencies and premium account are shared with the other WG titles, and world of tanks isn't on steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Dead but clawing its way out of the grave, very slowly, if you don't mind playing against bots with the chance you might run into 1-3 actual humans per match, then it's good. It's a fun game to throw on if you have some time to kill. The grind is okay, you start unlocking tier 7 planes at about the 10 to 15 hour mark depending on wins, kills, etc. It's got a pretty decent line up of planes, BF 109's, P51's, A6M's, Spitfire's, and that's only some of the fighters. _childDocuments_.review: Overall a good game. When compared to other similar games, I found it a little less focused on realism and more on an arcade feel. That is not a criticism. The default controls limit control to a "point and shoot" style of play. Your damage is measured by a health bar. You can take damage to specific areas of your aircraft, but as long as your plane's HP is above zero, such damage gets repaired pretty quickly. Stalls are very forgiving, and all movement is very fluid. Additionally, the current community is really healthy. In the early tiers, players are fairly entry level, and the later tiers have decent players.Your play is quickly rewarded and progressing to better planes is very quick. When compared to war thunder, there are a handful of features that are not included. As mentioned early, the game seems to aim to be accessible to new players, and thus has no "realistic" or in depth controls or game modes. The game does not offer any historic scenarios to play through, and only has a zone capture match type. (no massive death match) Aside from the absence of game type customization, this game is wonderful. If you haven't played an aerial combat game before, this game is a perfect introduction to the genre. However, there is so much more complexity, skill, and strategy to be found in very similar hat this game does not offer.
_childDocuments_.name: World of Warplanes

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game and its setup. Being able to use fighters, bombers, etc. and upgrade with experience is awesome.However, my only issue with this game is that only two buddies can play together at a time. At the moment, you can invite one other friend to join you in a game and they will be on your team. I think the game makers should allow up to 8 friends to be invited and play, with the game setup that any group of 3 or more will randomly and evenly be placed on the two different teams. This would allow more friends to play together, but not allow them to join the same team and completely dominate. It would still be pretty fair to new comers because they would also have some good players on their team, not just against game veterans. The game would be more fun to play with and against friends than to only play solo or on a team with only one friend.

_childDocuments_.review: So what do I think of World of Warplanes on Steam...I enjoy it greatly except for the following bugs that have obviously been around for ages: - Matchmaking will start the match leaving you at the Matchmaking "waiting clock", the match is already starting, you are just staring at the clock counting up. You quickly realize if the clock shows up without a line under it with an estimated time that you have been bugged. You have to quickly Ctl-Alt-Del and choose Task Manager. End the WoWP task and then reload game. Veterans of this bug can spot it and be back in match by end of count down timer.- Dropped at end of match bug. You will randomly be disconnected from the server after the battle result screen and clickcing "return to hanger" and have to reload the game. This happens about 1 out of 10 matches. - Aiming recticle gets off center bug. I have had this happen twice where you respawn in game and your aiming circle is of to the side instead of directly in front of you.. No fix that I have found but to reload game. _childDocuments_.review: Not as cooperative as world of tanks, but also your teammates aren't calling you names.   Much more than world of tanks, skill and situational awareness rewards big time.   In world of tanks you can go back and play newbies and still get smoked.   However when I need to feel good, i go back and play newbie pilots and rack up 16 kills routinely.   THat tells me that my skill has increased and that it matters.   There are, as in most games, those who have overly powerful and unrealistic aircraft because they paid top dollar for them.   There are also unachievable missions with rewards that only those who have no life can achieve in the allocated time.    I did like one type of challenge where you gain small rewards as you go, the Christmas mission was fun.    Also there is a VERY unrealistic tactic of large aircraft ramming small aircraft and surviving.    Not sure why they allow that, and it is annoying for those who like realistic dogfights and bombing.      I am also a quite motion sick with most first person shooters, but can play this all day if I use the keypad ( the mouse for controls gets me sick).   Recommend this for its overall realism, its beauty, and its pure thrill (chasing or being chased)

Is the planes you grind for and get the good old fashion way will never compete with certain Pay 2 Win planes. Nearly identical planes with less engine horse power end up having much better altitude performance than your plane. Dont get me wrong 50 bucks for a plane is insane, but don't use me for fodder for them with no chance of getting the exact same performance from the same plane. The German Spit V out perfroms the Euro Spitfire V in altitude perfomrance by nearly 20 points. name: 112 Operator
detailed_description: 112 Operator allows you to manage emergency services in any city in the world! Dispatch units, take calls and face situations caused by weather, traffic or changing seasons. Help the city survive escalating events like riots, organized crime, terrorist attacks, cataclysms, natural disasters and many more! Danger has escalated Help on a scale bigger than ever before. The sequel of the award-winning 911 Operator lets you act on many, completely different levels - from taking care of a single neighborhood to coordinating several operators’ work in the world’s biggest metropolises. Full 3D visualization will give you the inside view of your units’ actions. Choose from over 100 000 areas, such as districts, municipalities, and tens of thousands of real cities from all over the world. To all units: a storm is coming… Face the dynamic weather, based on authentic, historical data. Watch the incidents change as day or night comes, traffic increases and seasons pass. Watch out for extreme conditions that may lead to cataclysms and natural disasters. Try to tame big wildfires spreading across the map. Weather isn’t your only problem though - be careful when dealing with terrorist attacks and gang wars. 112, what’s your emergency? Take calls from people in various situations, needing emergency services’ help. You never know who’s on the other side of the line - you might hear a frightening murder story, maybe you’ll have to instruct someone on performing CPR, or keep your nerves while encountering an annoying prankster. It’s my job, ma’am... Choose one of the European cities in completely new Career mode and find out if you’ll manage to climb up to the very top of an operator’s career ladder. Follow the commands of your supervisors and see your actions affecting people you’re in charge of or those who need your help. Sometimes your mistakes will only be followed by a reprimanding e-mail, sometimes they’ll influence your own life. You can also play special scenarios in any city in the world, or make your own rules in the Free Game mode. We need backup! Command the best specialists, using technologically advanced equipment and vehicles. Decide what to use - a SWAT team, Search and Rescue helicopter, or maybe riot gear? When your units arrive at the scene, command them in the tactical view that gives you the full image of the situation. NEW FEATURES IN 112 OPERATOR: 25 times bigger, expandable maps of REAL CITIES with 3D buildings entirely new set of emergency calls and large events completely redesigned campaign mode, with objectives system, emails, and a story day&night, weather, seasons and traffic now influences the duty and the incidents happening new fire mechanic, that can consume entire areas and require dozens of units region specification - gameplay will vary depending on a country legislation and district characteristics (slums / business / residential /industrial / forest etc) new OnSite situation visualization that shows the action precisely and intuitively new team members - doctors, sergeants, dogs, robots, and others! additional dispatchers, that you can assign to districts for help! redesigned equipment, now packed up in entire gears

_childDocuments_.review: 112 Operator - A Gripping Emergency Services Simulation112 Operator, the sequel to the well-received 911 Operator, brings a whole new level of depth and challenge to the world of emergency services simulation. Whether you're a fan of strategy games, simulations, or just want a unique gaming experience, this title provides hours of gripping and thought-provoking gameplay.At its core, 112 Operator puts you in the shoes of an emergency services dispatcher, handling a wide range of incidents and crises, from medical emergencies and fires to police interventions and search and rescue missions. The game's scenarios are incredibly diverse and offer a realistic glimpse into the world of first responders. You'll be tasked with managing resources, making life-or-death decisions, and coordinating your teams to save lives and maintain public safety.The game's replayability is impressive, thanks to its random events and the wide variety of scenarios you'll encounter. No two shifts are the same, and the game's sandbox mode allows you to customize your experience to suit your preferences. The challenges and intensity increase as you progress, ensuring that 112 Operator keeps you engaged and tested throughout.The inclusion of real cities and maps adds an extra layer of immersion to the game. Planning routes, considering traffic conditions, and identifying the optimal locations for your bases and units are all part of the strategy. It's a small touch, but it makes a significant difference in the realism of the gameplay.The game's mechanics are deep and intricate, but they can also be a bit overwhelming for newcomers. Learning the ropes and managing multiple emergencies simultaneously can be a challenging task. While this complexity might be intimidating at first, it's also one of the game's strengths, as it provides a genuine simulation experience for those who appreciate depth and strategy in their games.On the downside, the game's graphics and audio are serviceable but not particularly impressive. The focus is clearly on the gameplay and mechanics, which is where 112 Operator truly shines.In conclusion, 112 Operator is a captivating and challenging emergency services simulation game that keeps you on your toes with its diverse scenarios, real-world maps, and complex mechanics. It's a must-play for fans of strategy and simulation games, and even newcomers can find immense satisfaction in mastering its intricacies. While it may not be the most visually stunning game, its depth and immersion more than compensate for any graphical limitations. If you've ever wondered what it's like to manage emergency services, 112 Operator is a thrilling and educational experience well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I am 32 years old.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the predecessor a lot and so was looking forward to playing 112 Operator. The game definitely does not disappoint. Gameplay is pretty much the same but they added some new features which are quite nice. The one I liked most was the summary of each case at the shift's end, with an explanation of what was done correctly and what was done wrong. The predecessor often had me guessing why I was losing reputation points. Now it seems clearer and the system also seems more balanced. In 911 operator I often kept losing points like crazy while in 112 Operator I never lost a shift. I also like that you can play in your home city. It's a different feeling when you know the street names and map and I admit I was thrilled to even find my house on the map. It's a nice feature to have the hometown option. Another good feature is that you can click on the different incident locations and see what is currently happening - that helps to find why there is a holdup and to rectify it. You also get emails, which are a variety of games tips, scenario-relevant tips or reactions ("Thanks for saving my baby yesterday"), which all adds some more liveliness.There are also some new storylines and calls, all done well. Some things I didn't like. One is that the interface is less clear, at least to me. I find it harder to see which unit is available (in spite of the useful option to show little symbols right on the cars on the map) and to locate units in the lists, etc. This mainly becomes an issue when you have to deal with the whole city and a countless number of units. Location symbols sometimes also overlap with other symbols and cars. The useface was in some ways far less user-friendly and I often couldn't locate the relevant symbol or accidentally called a unit away again because there were so many units on the map that I clicked the wrong one. Active units/symbols are marked by a thin white lining, but later in the game it's just too much and all too small. Another thing I didn't like is that there's just one scenario. You have different cities, yes, but each city gives you the same scenario. You start with one city district and then more and more districts get added. Towards the end you have the situation mentioned above: far too many units and too many events. I like fast-paced games but here it ended up in a mindless clickfest and took a lot of the fun away. I preferred the different shorter scenarios of the predecessor. Still, why the game has its weaknesses, it's fun to play and I'm enjoying it.

_childDocuments_.review: While I obviously haven't actually played the game for 170 hours, I feel like I've played enough to form an informed decision. The game is solid. In a lot of areas it clearly surpasses 911 operator, in some ways it feels smaller to its predecessor, and in some, it duplicates it, sometimes to the detriment, unfortunately.Let's start with the good. The maps are a LOT bigger, and you can pick them to your heart's content. Great improvement compared to 911 operator, where not long into the game you just didn't have any room to expand. New vehicles and equipment make sense, they  can and will definitely help in demanding situations. Being able to pick disasters is a great quality of life addition imho, would love to see more of those added though.Now the bad. The one that jumped out at me first was the calls. Feels like there are a lot fewer of those. In 911 operator the calls felt a lot more impactful. There was more space to make a wrong call (kitchen fire anyone?) and calls repeated itself, so you couldn't just memorise the right answer. It was more interactive, whereas now it feels like each custom call gets flagged once you receive it, and you can't get it again. That might be just my luck with calls, but there it is.Second part of bad, is the mixed-bag-bad. Things that are bad because they don't feel enough tied-in into the game. Let's start with the vehicles. Yes, it's great to have more vehicles, and thus more tools to deal with situations. Unfortunately, a lot of the vehicles have very few uses as of now. Like the ladder truck for the firefighters. When I'm playing in a 600k city, I'd expect to get a lot of use out of them. In reality, I very rarely get to use them to their intended purpose and they end up being just another truck I send to a broken hydrant. Then, there is the expansion, which despite being a great addition to the game, has a massive problem. Once you start expanding, you'll end up with the core of the city filled with infrastructure, and the outskirts, that have barely any, despite being a much larger area to cover. If you get flooded with 2-3 calls for the same service in the back country, you WILL time out, simply on the basis of that one police car having to go all the way back to the city to drop off the suspects, or that fire truck you strategically placed there having to go for a refill. It would be fine if the incident frequency adjusted for each sector, but it doesn't feel like it does, or at least it doesn't do it enough. Being able to build your own infrastructure would be a massive help in this respect, cause it gets really irritating when you are pretty much forced to buy a boonies district with 4 fire stations, but the closest hospital or police station is 3 districts away.In summary, 112 is better than 911 operator. That much is clear. What it now needs though, in my opinion, is connecting all the pieces that are there and delving deeper. More calls. More development of infrastructure. More opportunities for niche equipment. It's a thumbs up, but there's still plenty left to do.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy 112.  It's an excellent successor to 911.   The layouts are a lot nicer and I enjoy having new cities and all the campaigns to do so there is quite a bit of content for the price.  Plus if 911 has taught me anything, there will be lots more content to come.  I love the large maps and how you build up your districts.  I love how interactive the dev team is with everyone so issues are addressed pretty quickly. Though I find the incidents come in quite fast even on easy, there is a sense of realism to it as you prioritize calls.  Building money for equipment is my largest gripe.  I don't want to use cheat codes so i wish this was a bit more balanced.  It wasn't until the last few duties in the campaign that I could afford the higher end items.   I'm hoping in future updates that there will be more calls and content added.  I finished one campaign and now I'm doing another in another city and it's, so far, the same calls and same major events.  That makes it feel a bit repetitive.Overall, none of this has deterred me from playing and continuing to play.  It’s a fun game and easy to lose hours on end in it.

Suddenly you get a call to dispatch "everything you have" to the airport because of an emergency plane arrival while there is also a mob ravaging through your streets and then one of your police units got wiped out because in this mess of incidents & calls you made a mistake and sent poor Officer Doofy with standard police gear and his trusty searchdog Woofie to the scene of a gangwar. Oops.

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: I backed 112 Operator on Kickstarter, and have been playing since Closed Alpha. TL;DR: I recommend 112 Operator, especially if you're a fan of 911 Operator.All the features and events from 911 Operator and its DLCs are there, e.g. earthquake, blackouts, search request, etc. So what about the new features promised in-this game? For those new to this game, there's not much music playing in-game, but it's a good thing since the prompts for calls and events would pop up often especially when you have half the area open to you, and moreso if you have radio chatters (they don't overwhelm the popup sounds though). However, the star of the game are the voice actors. It feels weird the first time playing 112 Operator to find the VAs all speak with an American English accent. It will be great if we can have more European-sounding VAs, but it's understandable given the cost of recording voices. Once one get past this fact and drill into the voice acting themselves, they're quite great. The aforementioned 112 Operator of course is the same VA from 911 Operator and Radio Commander, which is no stranger to some. The people who record the callers themselves have done an astounding job in bringing that human emotion to play, e.g. when that caller is on the verge of tears finding his girlfriend OD-ed. The sounds are also decently mixed, e.g. the call in the storm, the train call, etc. Not much left in some of the latest builds as far as I am aware. There's the very rare issue of units somehow stuck / not working when handling a dispatch. Balancing still feels a bit off (e.g. sometimes it takes too long for police units to stop a speeding car, police effectiveness vs armed gunmen, etc.), but it's nothing that can't be fixed.Despite the issues, I feel like I have got my money's worth and did not regret backing the game. Looking at some of the things the devs put in the Kickstarter pledge, I'm tempted to see where the devs would take 112 Operator next (hint: please give us water events :v). If you're a fan of 911 Operator, then I highly recommend 112 Operator, since it builds so much of what 911 Operator has that it can feel difficult to come back to 911 Operator. If you're new to this type of gameplay, I would recommend you watch a couple of videos to see if this game is right for you. If it is, then I feel the pricetag, especially at launch, would not deter you from this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I played 911 Operator and now - 112 Operator. There are many improvements in the game indeed - spreading fires, weather, subordinates, etc. These are good. What I don't like is that you are "forced" to acquire new districts - after 3-4 games, the game becomes unmanagable. The recruited dispatchers do stupid re-assignments of tasks (something that happens in real life, too, I guess), but the number of accidents compared to 911 Operator is uncontrollable. If I play 30-minutes game, I spent 25 of those "on pause", as the incidents are so frequent that I simply cannot focus on the gameplay... The interesting phone calls feel much less as percentage due to this. There are also some nasty bugs (I was able to extinguish fire after emergency plane landing "before" it crashed). Also, money is a big problem - units are too expensive, equipment is too expensive, and even after 20-30 duties, I cannot save enough for a fire helicopter. In short, 112 Operator vs. 911 Operator: more complex, more things to think about, but has some issues with several small bugs and balancing the gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: This is everything 911 Operator was plus a lot more. Not much else to say really. Both this and it's predecessor are great titles where you are given emergency responder assets and must manage them accordingly. There are little narrative driven scenarios sewn into emergency phone calls, adding some flavor to each level. The big difference with this one is you can chose a real life map to play on, which is a nice novelty (I grew up in Sydney and it was nice to dispatch units around an area I was familiar with). The one criticism I have is that the additional content adds more, but creates a less defined experience compared to the previous title.There are no other games like 911 and 112, even with that in mind, the price is a big steep for what you get. Luckily, these titles are on sale often and worth a shot if you find the premise interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Feeling very frustrated but game is still recommended... but it needs some optimisation and tweaking still unfortunately.Long time player of 911 Operator and have been waiting all week for this release. Very impressed overall - it has a smart layout, good graphics, excellent sounds and so far everything has worked without problem. What I find frustrating after 3 hours of play is that the game is just a clicker... you're not given any time to decide which is the best resource to send to each incident. You basically just find the nearest appropriate unit and send them. This is a real shame because half the fun is watching the units arriving on scene and observing their actions. I'm playing on the second level of difficulty and am about 25% through the campaign. I'm finding myself pausing the game just so I can work out which resources are available and whether that particular resource is carrying my upgraded equipment or not. Improvements required:1) Reduce the number of incidents early on (namely the bike thief ones... time consuming, low priority ones)2) Make it clear whether we're actually meant to get to all calls or not... 3) The outside help is available but you have nowhere near enough funds to ask for help4) The Berlin map has only one police station so all the units have to travel all the way to the south to process criminals5) Units with an arrested person can still respond to another scene... this isn't realistic but if you choose to maintain realism you lose that unit for a lot of time6) There's no quick way of identifying which units are free and ready to respond. (I know I can click the units option in the left menu and look for the question marks but I wish I could filter by availability) 7) There's no explanation as to what the 'priority' button does in the left menu8) The search missions are attention-intensive which only increases the stress. Plus you can use any unit which isn't realistic. (Surely police, or specific SAR team only?)That's everything so far. In summary, it's too stressful and therefore I'm struggling to enjoy the shifts. I recognise it's a game designed to demonstrate the stressful environment of a call taker but this is over the top.

_childDocuments_.review: 112 Operator is a game that puts you in the shoes of an emergency dispatcher, fielding calls and directing responders to save lives and keep the city safe. It's a game that will test your multitasking skills and decision-making abilities, but it's also a lot of fun. Let's take a closer look at the pros and cons of this thrilling game:Pros:Cons:Overall, 112 Operator is an exciting and engaging game that will keep you on your toes. With its unique gameplay, realistic graphics, and sense of urgency, it's a game that's worth playing. Just be prepared for a bit of a learning curve and some repetitive tasks.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a vast improvement over its 911 predecessor. Many of the suggestions placed for 911 Operator were implemented in this iteration of the game. While the 112/911 calls have retained their repetitiveness at times, they have more than made up for it with better voice acting and far more emergencies to deal with in a given day. What also makes the game even more fun is that instead of being limited to a specific region in a city, they take a city as a region and divide it into districts.  Over time the game increases difficulty exponentially as you take care of far more emergency services and deal with far more emergencies. This makes for a far more challenging, but fun game. Keep in mind, I was only play in normal mode, and they have added a hard difficulty and an expert difficult where there are no pause options and are unable to save unless you completed the day. You also suffer far harsher penalties at the higher difficulties.Finally, the game adds campaign mode for several cities across Europe. In addition, you retain the ability to play in every city in the world, big or small. This makes the game infinitely repeatable because each district has its own weather patterns! (Yes they added weather patterns specific to each region. This affects the probability of experiencing weather-specific emergencies like fires, snowstorms, power outages, etc.) TL;DR, the game got far more difficult, but in a fun way. The game also lets you take control of far more districts in a city. Weather patterns also available. Far more types of emergencies to deal with. Extremely addicting.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game on the winter sale for 50% off. Still think I paid too much at 15$.I played 911, I appreciated it. Mostly for its originality, not going to lie. I made some research and decided to place 112 in my wishlist until it was on sale as it wasn't a good sequel. It is a clone to the original with so little added to the game that they could have made a free update on 911 and then released the DLC this game has. Nobody would have complained and it would only be logical considering what you get.Fans of 911 will feel at home here. There is actual polish in the map interface now. Police vehicles return to their original deployment point after each interception which is very refreshing... But ambulances and fire fighters don't. Just... Why? They added it for the police AI code but not for the other two? Can't give out any logical answer on this one, but his is one of those "improvements" which could easily have been a free fix on the original. There is also a huge gap in AI when you get your vehicles stuck in snow (or in a storm I guess), as they completely "forget" what they were doing after they are done getting unstuck. I believe it wasn't the case in 911, tho I'd need to recheck that to be sure. More toward the initial point, the gameplay is completely identical to 911 except that there is more voiced dialogues with unfortunately many from 911 reused. From the little I played so far, they actually focused their efforts in trying to make transition between two "shifts" more interesting by adding drama and information pop via emails and a new information interface. Considering that's about the only thing really new from its predecessor please consider that you are paying a premium price only for this.One huge downside is that the purchasing UI has been changed to the point it is clearly worse than 911. I didn't exactly have much of a problem playing or using it at all but since I did play 911 I knew what I was doing. It still took me fiddling around to be able to find what I was looking for and I have to admit that  what I was looking for in the first place I simply might not have found it at all. I believe it might be one of the direct sources of why there is currently so many negative reviews on this subject.Finally, I often end up not posting reviews at all when the game is neutral as there is no such options in Steam. What really made me automatically reject this title is the fact that you absolutely  an internet connection to be able to play the single player portion of the game. This is simply a pure sign of lazy developers and a big pet peeve of mine. If you played 911 before then you know and should expect to have to connect to a server to retrieve a more local map of your own area that you might want to play in, which is fine. I'm not complaining about this at all, but instead of the fact that even the single player campaign is going to require you to fetch those maps even tho they should already be fully included in the campaign. Please also note that the scale of the game is much bigger than 911 and as such only major cities of a relevant minimum size are included now, then subdivided into smaller maps which are slowly added to your "play ground". This make most local maps I used in the past in 911 simply to be "not found" as they probably didn't bother making them in the first place.Final verdict: pure pass unless you are a huge fan of 911 and want to throw money toward lazy devs in the faint hope they make something better next time.

That has gotten to be the exception in society where the loudest mouths are the law enforcement and public safety hating leftists.You use maps of cities all over the world and it will detect where you are to suggest there. The maps are not always accurate as bodies of water are added here and there so that water rescues can be done, etc.Different cities will have different main problems which appear somewhat accurate. Some cities muggings will be very common, some might have high murder rates, sexual assaults, or whatever. I start with the smallest base city (where I live is not a base city but much larger than the smallest default city) to get used to a smaller population first. I'm not sure if can limit the area you are dispatcher for yet. Personally I'm too old to handle large areas as there is too much to keep track of.Dispatching is pretty good. _childDocuments_.review: I was very excited about this game, when they first announced it, but after 7 hours, all their promises seems to be false: They promised a new traffic system, which I thought was about to have rush hours, traffic jams, where you have to find new routes for your units. Instead, the units get slower, right before they reach some incidents, but its such a small amount, that it doesn't matter at all. The new fire mechanic seems to be a thing to have just in the campaign. I played several freeplay duties, but I've never encountered with it, not even when I was playing in a rural area, with heatwave on. The fire spreads, but if you ignore it, somehow its just disappear.The weather system gives you special events, and you have to leave units behind. For example, you can't use motorcycles or horses during blizzards.There are lots of new units, but why? I find them unnecessary. From the police, the only two units you are gonna use, is gonna be a patrol car, and a police van. Every other police units are literally useless. Its the same with the medical units, and the fire units are the only ones, where there are some diversity between units, and is worthy to buy more type. The campaign is good, but its just neverending. 30 duties on the same map is a bit repetitive, but its really good to present all the game mechanics, which are the good things from 911 operator, with all the DLC-s.The maps are definitely bigger, and 911 operator seems to be a claustrophobe experience after playing with 112 operator.Even though, we usually don't have enough units to cover even the half of some cities, because we will get such a ridiculous amount of money after a duty, that it's just nerve-racking. The devs probably wanted us to make decisions, and prioritizing during freeplay too, that's why we have much more calls, and we have to ignore some. It's a bit unrealistic, to have that many calls, that we have in the game, even on easy mode, but I actually like it. Every duty is filled with stress, and I love to see that I solved everything I was able to, and have a 80-90% efficiency, but i'm not able to play more than two duties, because its just too intense. If there would be a normal mod, with less calls, but with some challange, it would be really good. At this point, I enjoy playing this game, but it still need to be polished. It could be worthy with a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty addictive game. There's the police, medical and fire services, each with their own vehicles. With the Water Operations DLC you even get access to amphibious vehicles and boats for water ops. For the police branch you can hire dogs that will give you a bonus when searching for suspects, or a robot that will help you out with a bomb defusal. The gear of each person that you hire can be customisable and each gear item will provide their own bonuses to certain activities. There's also voice-acted 911 calls that you have to respond to and provide them with basic first aid advice if needed.Definitely pick up the Water Ops DLC. The Last Duty and Pandemic Outbreak adds an interesting touch, but I find the pandemic events to be hell of a chore since staff members need to undergo quarantine if they're exposed without PPE.One big plus that I really like about this game is that you can play a game in your own city. Search for your town or city name when creating a free game and it will download a map of it, complete with 3D models of the buildings. It's cool to see the silhouette of MBS while fighting a huge wildfire at MacRitchie.If you like micromanagement, it's an excellent game for you.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: 112 Operator is all about exactly that, a simulation where you're a dispatcher for the 112 Emergency Line and if you like to try out the stress and mayhem that these good people go through on the daily, you're welcome to try.You are a 112 Emergency Hotline operator, whose job sounds quite easy at first when you're introduced to your desk and given a headset. Then the calls come in and you're basically just swarmed to the core... Someone lost their puppy? They call you, someone broke up with their wives? They call you... Someone is about to commit a mass shooting, they call you and it's up to you to talk them out of it. This is exactly the kind of game that makes you go like: "Wow thank God I'm not American" lol.Anyways, gameplay is quite simple, it's the execution that sometimes is too.. complicated. The whole game takes place in a map where you control a bunch of security units, you know; ambulances, police cars and firefighting units. Your job is to deal with incidents that happen throughout the city accordingly, if they pop up in white it means there are injured people in need of medical car so send in your ambulances, if they pop up in red it means the incident requires firefighters and finally blue means there are miscreants that need to be arrested about or witnesses that need to be questionned. Sometimes incidents pop up in all three colors, so you have to send one unit of each kind and sometimes, ONE police car is not enough if there are shots fired. Other than these mundane incidents that need taking care of, your job is to respond to calls and resolve them accordingly as well as deal with calamities that hit your city, such as earthquakes or forest fires.The game really does its best at making you think and act like an operator... I mean, I just talked some crazy bastard into letting two girls he'd kidnapped go unharmed; then I sent in the police to arrest him. How cool is that? The only con I've found so far is the game is not replayable at all... Apart from a bunch of predetermined scenarios (and more from DLCs), the campaigns are really flat, and at some point you'd be hearing the same phone conversations and the same calls coming in over and over, and it just gets super boring at some point. In the end, I gotta say it's a great game if you want to feel like you're making a change in society... You know, a game for a fat couch potato who games all day like yourself to feel like you're a superhero.

_childDocuments_.review: A few years ago I bought a game on impulse called "911 Operator". Not knowing anything about it or what to expect, I was hooked on its mixture of strategic gameplay and somewhat authentic emergency management setting. Then they announced the sequel, 112 Operator. Now it is here and it is fantastic.The premise is the same. You are working in a center based around answering emergency calls. The first game had its focus in North America, hence the 911. This game shifts the focus to Europe where the code is 112. Despite the core gameplay being the same, there's many improvements. For instance, the campaign mode is more fleshed out. In the original you just moved from city to city, doing a good job, with occasionally a major event happening. This one gives you a choice of several European cities and that is where you remain the whole campaign. Except this time events are more frequent, you get e-mails about your progress, and storylines progress through the various calls. One of the main ones you'll find deals with a serial killer, as people will call reporting finding victims and possible suspects. Now of course this does lead to a bit of immersion breaking. I chose to play in Moscow, and despite all the Russian names for staff and cities, everyone speaks perfectly good English over the phone. It does throw you off a bit but it isn't totally detrimental. The voice work on the various calls has been improved. Some of the lines on the calls in the first game were a little strange. I mean you aren't going to get top notch voice acting here but it's remarkably well done. And there is more variety as well. Best played with headphones though because some of them can be loud and creepy if someone doesn't know that you're playing a game.Other things that have been improved are the map of the various cities, as now you can see 3D representations of buildings instead of just flat maps. You get wide areas to handle, as instead of a single city you'll get a whole area, slowly unlocking piece by piece as you progress. The addition of Operators allows you to assign one of them to a district to handle stuff automatically so you do not get too overwhelmed. It's also much easier to equip your staff as there are now sets of equipment to buy, as opposed to deciding in the first game if you give someone a pistol and a vest, or an attack dog and a computer (as an example.) Also, dogs are no longer classified as weapons and can be hired independently, which is neat. The best feature of the original was of course the ability to play in just about any city or town in the world, and it is still here in this version. However several difficulties are tied into campaign progress and completion, and a lot of the story events seem to happen in the 'free play' mode as well. Right now its not truly a sandbox. But it is there.As of this writing they have recently released the Steam Workshop which should allow for some interesting additions to the game. All in all its a very solid game but also a bit niche. If the idea of handling police and fire and ambulance services doesn't appeal to you, you might not like it. But there's a lot to enjoy for strategy and simulation fans here. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I thought 112 was an improvement over 911; new content, game mechanics and a nice UI facelift. How wrong I was!As you advance and get promoted you can hire dispatchers, who btw are horrible at their job. The game tells you that this makes you able to focus on the most important/urgent tasks. It may sound good, but it doesn't work well in practice. From this moment on, the game is ruined by mainly two things:1.Incoming emergency calls gets replaced by internal/operator calls, which I absolutely don't care for! It really sucked the life out of this game! The calls was what made this game so great; take incoming calls, analyze the situation, answer/ask questions, and then act with the proper response.2.Incidents now pops up like it's the end of the world. It's complete chaos! Like a game of whack-a-mole. The list gets long and unmanageable and there's no sort feature either. So, the whole "focus on the most important incidents" goes out the window.Managing the dispatchers is also tedious. It's so hard to distinguish them just from the profile picture and it doesn't tell you the name when you hover over them.BTW: There's a very annoying "Check Out More Games..." ads screen when you start AND exit the game, which requires you to click the "OK" button to continue. There's no way to disable this. The devs really should have included a checkbox for "don't show this again".

Should you prioritize the stabbing incident over some guy who burned himself on the stove at home? A house is on fire and all you have is one free fire truck in the area, that kitty in the tree is gonna have to sort its own problems out.Then there's the callers, naturally most are reasonable, sane, if not panicked people...Then there's the hair pulling frustrating citizens who refuse to give you an address, or hold up the line just to get their phone unlocked, or just will. Not. Listen, to any instruction you give.It's an exhausting experience that will leave your faith in humanity, and public funding programs shattered....And I love it, because I know 911 operators, and they basically agree this is exactly how it's like, though, as one of the loading screen tips tell you, with far, far less useless calls...But still enough to give you an idea of what it's like.So buy it.Now.Or I'll buy 30 horse police units and send them to your in game house's location.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played and reviewed 911 Operator (9O) recently, knowing I owned 112 Operator (1O) as well, I figured I may as well play it too. As far as I'm aware, it's essentially the same, but having looked at the store page and some reviews, its made some improvements on the original. Hopefully enough that I enjoy this game more than its predecessor, even if it shifts from a US centric perspective.  Overall, not much has changed from the gameplay of 9O. Your primary task is still responding to 911 calls and directing emergency vehicles to the proper incidents. The main difference I saw was in packaging, as the presentation is more advanced here. Icons still show up on the city map, outlining the basic issue and what's needed, but clicking on them shows more information than before. In the previous title, all you'd see was a brief text summary of what was going on. However, with 1O, you get a visual representation of the emergency responders, involved people, and important objects such as vehicles. Another important change is when progressing in the Campaign, you're assigned more territory to cover, as long as you meet certain objectives. You'll certainly notice a difference between handling a few dozen districts compared to the starting amount of three.  Since 1O is still a form of resource manager, its controls were largely the same and worked just as well from how they were in the first game. Unless I completely missed them in 9O though, 1O adds more control features on how you direct units, giving the player more finesse and options. One I used often was having the first units to arrive at an incident wait for the last police car to show up before heading in. It's much more effective for three police cars to handle a drug lord's base instead of each one barging in on arrival and waiting for back-up.  1O comes much closer to a story throughout the Campaign then 9O did. Unfortunately, there isn't really a well-defined main character, even though he has a daughter. It's honestly a little odd to me how close they approach the idea of giving this person some character, including a soap opera scene no one would take seriously, but by the end you still know next to nothing about the guy. Either way, it progresses through this character's career as a 911 dispatcher, rapidly gaining new responsibilities and unlockables, such as overseeing other dispatchers. It's more of a small guiding factor to direct your game progress than a story though.  There's not much to change from one game to the next, when a large amount of what you see is a city map, and I didn't notice improvements in things like icons or character portraits. On that note though, even if it's not be a big deal, having simple visuals showing what's taking place at emergency sites is considerably more clear and interesting than one or two sentences of text. Watching firefighters clear away debris while the ambulance team waits to rush in and aid the injured helps me better understand how these roles interact with one another. I was a bit surprised when I heard some basic music playing, which was one of my complaints from 9O. Radio chatter wasn't a welcome substitute to tunes for me, and though it's not very pronounced, it still breaks up monotonous silence better than recycled dialogue between different parties. There's still a bit too much of that for my taste, as they repeat so often, but it might help set the ambiance for those who'd get immersed in this game. Plus, the radio static didn't seem as screechy this time. As a trade-off, the voice-acting wasn't any better compared to 9O, as some of the deliveries seemed worse to me.  🌟 Shortly after starting 1O, I recognized improvements in the game's aesthetic and gameplay compared to 9O. One thing I enjoyed was how it made progression in the campaign much more clear and relevant to my performance. 🌟 There's greater variety in the 911 calls you field. It helps the game from getting as repetitive.  ❌ Later in the Campaign, I got really sick of the constant new incidents I'd have to address. I thought that was part of the reason I assigned all of the dispatchers, to remove some of the mundane tasks not needing my input. Unless there's a corresponding emergency vehicle in their district though, they seemingly won't send them over. ❌ With how large the map becomes, this would be difficult to play on a smaller screen. ❌ The load times are pretty slow for a game this basic. 🔍 If you're unclear on whether a police intervention will need a transport, looking at the icon as the police handle the suspect will clear it up. A ticket or money symbol means they'll leave once the ticket is issued, but handcuffs indicate they'll haul the perp to jail. 🔍 When progressing in the Campaign, you'll want to reserve a decent amount of money in case one of the upcoming objectives includes buying a specific vehicle. 🔍 I switched the action to fast forward, and when a new incident popped up, I'd slow the action down so I could process them.  Frankly, I came into 1O doubting that it'd change enough from the first game for me to enjoy this one. I knew that it was going to be similar gameplay, which is the most crucial element, so why would my opinion sway that much? However, the developers must have taken player feedback into account with this release, because almost every issue I had in the first was resolved in some way, including things I hadn't thought about that much. Slowly diminishing the amount of 911 calls the player has to screen so they don't need to worry about making dozens, if not hundreds, of made-up crises was pretty sharp. Taking stead of an entire city's emergency services definitely makes up for not answering calls personally, as you've so many pans in the fire to fret over. It did get a bit annoying at times, but with the refined design compared to 9O, I think people would like this game significantly more. A single playthrough of the campaign is pretty short though, so I'd hold off for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It's predecessor seemed much more enjoyable to me. The idea of being able to customize kits to buy for your units to specialize and/or expedite basic tasks seems great but never really plays out, because the map size WILL increase over time and you will be spending all your money on additional units to cover the area accordingly with basic units. There will be very little room to specialize in the end or making use of those specialized units. Even if you did manage to get a fully equipped SWAT-team in one of those fancy trucks -you know the ones you would send to a gang-war, a hostage situation and stuff like that- you probably never will. Those cars are extraordinarily slow and will take half a day to cross the city. And even if you did send it, you will probably have sent any free units in the direct vicinity anyway, who will have solved the problem before the SWAT-team even arrives. So you will send them to parking violations and administering speeding tickets anyway...because they were closer than other units. And this happens all the time. Let's say you bought one of those bomb-robots and there is a threat of a bombing. Of course you would like to use it but it is probably very far away and/or the squad having it is resolving another situation and will probably not arrive on time anyway. So you will just send whoever is available. And even if you insist to send them and only them: good luck finding that specific unit. If it is a basic patrol car you will probably spend a minute or two looking for the right one and then again they might be busy resolving another issue and can't be sent right away.The specialization is a neat concept but the player is far better off getting more and more units for a map that is getting bigger and bigger by adding additional districts every few duties. Having so many units means upgrading these kits will be extremely expensive. So what do you do? Get more basic units instead of course! They will do just fine without the gadgets. Trying to get a decent coverage of specialized units is of course even more expensive and might be something achievable in the "endgame" when there are no additional districts to be thrown at you but starting out you are probably better off just ignoring this avenue. You will also learn that some of the vehicles are not worth their money. Once again: the most basic car is the best option here with the exception of a couple of motorcycle squads for police for chasing and minor incidents and helicopters for search missions and single transports and maybe those pickups for the fire brigade because they can be used to give you more time before the big trucks arrive. There are several more options but....yeah. Useless to me.So in the end bigger is not always better. It's still an enjoyable game for the most part but the idea with adding districts every few duties does nothing for me. Never got the idea of employing more operators by myself as well. Who ever needed those? Hired one because the game told me so. Don't know what he does but costs a lot of money I could be spending on basic units. The devs just really, really wanted to hammer these concepts in but they don't really add much to the game in my opinion. Just to set it apart from 911 I guess, but it is basically the same game with a really huge mod like XCOMs Long War.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the sequel to 911 Operator. You play the protagonist from the first game, but depending on the country you choose to play in, his name and everyone else change. You pretty much got promoted from serving as operator in America to an operator in the country you chose. You progress from operating one district to multiple district as you play through the campaign. You even get a backstory with family and enemies. This game plays almost exactly like 911 Operator but they added some more features to increase to complexity of the game.PROS:- You play the protagonist from the first game with same voice actor and consistent backstory- Animations are included even though there is probably only 2-3 scenes- Added new features compared to 911 Operator (More equipment, Assistant operators, Emails)- Difficulty increases as you play through the campaign (Compared to 911 where it varied through states)- Similar fun event calls to 911 Operator- Detail to the city (If you zoom in you can see the city outlines which makes it interesting to see with the units moving around)CONS:- Difficulty increases too fast (More districts start getting added to your play every 3-4 rounds)- Assistant operators are not too helpful (They can help direct units if you miss them, but most of their assignments just get thrown back to you)- Game gets tedious late game (1 event roughly every 2 seconds) that you can't really even enjoy being an operator or even reading what the issue was in the first place- Progression is too fast you can't really prepare for much (Not enough money to buy resources to use)- Last 2 rounds can be annoying since you will fail the round if you do the main call events wrong.The game was definitely an improvement compared to 911 Operator.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game wants to be two games at the same time. For me, this fails and the game is much less fun than it could have been.On the one hand, you can do a lot of micromanagement: Select a unit, an employee, and equipment for the employee. Each of those choices has advantages and disadvantages in the different types of emergencies you have to handle (a fire fighting truck needs a lot more time to free people from a stuck elevator than the technical truck). Depending on the weather and the events in the cities, you can plan ahead which incident you want to specialize on.On the other hand, once you are in duty, the game is a stressful (in the positive sense) experience. There a lot of incidences, and you have to solve them quickly.The problem is, in duty, you just have no time to search for your technical squad across the city. And you pretty much realize that sending the nearest vehicle to the incident does the job reasonably well. Also, while there are different icons for the different vehicles, there are no visual clues who sits in the vehicle: Answering the question: Where is my police vehicle with the bomb defusion specialist? takes a lot of clicks – time the game doesn't give you. Having several vehicles located at the same station: Good luck selecting the correct one when under stress …It would have been a nice game if you had the time to really use the micromanagement part. But due to the stress during duty, you end up selecting the always same vehicle with random employees and somewhat random equipment. Or it would have been a nice game if it focused on the duty phase without the complicated setting up of units.Also, as soon as a got all districts, the game rendered itself unplayable due to freezes after every button click in mission setup.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10: Great fun despite feeling overwhelmed at times. The ability to add custom gear to every type of first responder is a brilliant late addition to the game. The rating was originally a nine, but a point had to be deducted because off-road (and amphibious vehicles with the ) do not automatically take advantage of their capabilities when waypoints are set. (Intermediate waypoints are possible, but  does not make it clear exactly where amphibious vehicles may embark or debark on land.)Ol' Il Pallino has a confession to make:  He's never played  going into , so this review most likely won't be helpful for players who wonder how both games compare. The selling point for  is obviously the feature that allows players to play sandbox games in any city in the world. Campaigns, however, are limited to a handful of cities in Europe and the gray area that is Istanbul, Turkey. Both the sandbox and campaign start with a story of the player becoming an emergency dispatcher managing a single district through a probationary period, and after three shifts, the player presumably does well enough to unlock more regions on the map (the player gets to pick which regions in sandbox mode) and also gains more units and personnel along the way. (New vehicles may be purchased once unlocked.  Equipment may also be purchased for police, medical, and fire units to perform specialized tasks or to simply make units more skillful.) As the player progresses, the situations become more hectic, but if the player knows anything about unit and resource management (and you probably do, or else you wouldn't be reading this review) the player should have no problem staying on top of tasks no matter how overwhelmed the player feels seeing icons appearing on the screen requesting any combination of police, medical, and/or fire units, and all in real time.The graphics are almost entirely limited to the player looking at a monitor with a city going to hell in a handbasket. There are exceptions, and one in particular in a campaign scenario set in London when a disaster occurs.The sounds are all realistic enough, and it's not just blips from a computer, the sound of sirens, and radio transmissions!  Special events often lead to sounds that the player can hear outside while sitting behind their desk, and admittedly, ol' Il Pallino once had a bomb squad fail to disarm a bomb, and an explosion was heard in the background.Just like it's predecessor,  Operator is an original concept for a game, and is perfectly sound in regards to everything a unique game should be.  There are growing pains, but nothing that will leave the player singing Early Access Blues.ASSuming the player isn't being overwhelmed, the option to watch situations unfold is possible, although watching a bunch of red dots fight fires or white dots providing medical care likely won't interest the player, blue dots engaged in violent situations with criminals are always fun to watch.No tutorial exists for  besides tool tips that pop up between missions. A game as complex as  really needs a spoonfed style of tutorial, and admittedly, ol' Il Pallino made several mistakes in allocating people (and equipment) to a bomb squad.The game is anything but precise when it comes to assigning waypoints to units on a street for having an extra unit cut-off an escape route for a fleeing criminal, or to have multiple police units arrive at an expected violent crime scene at the same time.Unit names do not appear on the respective icons on the map, which is a huge problem for the aforementioned idea of having more than one type of unit use a common vehicle.  This once resulted in ol' Il Pallino sending a bomb squad to a druglord's house when he thought he was sending a SWAT team, and as expected, things got ugly! If the player is playing at the highest difficulty level (in which the pause button is removed) the player is going to be spending precious time trying to locate a specific unit while new emergency situations are spawning.One of the most annoying features in  is that the player is expected to hire out a subordinate dispatcher for one of the areas on the map.  At first the player may think they'll be shifting their problems onto someone else, but fact in the matter, is that dispatchers are going to whine more than a spoiled rich girl about how they need more of something. (More units in the case of dispatchers, and if there's a special event or disaster going on, the player better be ready to mute their computer!)Once again, it's going to look fishy that a game receives ol' Il Pallino's stamp of approval while the negatives outweigh the positives. (In both numbers and in passion.) Make no mistake,  is an amazing game, and no telling where players may spot a situation happening if they're playing a sandbox mission in their own town. (Ol' Il Pallino once had to dispatch a police and a medical unit to a house one street away from his own!) With the ability for games to take place anywhere, who wouldn't want to play missions in places like Truth or Consequences, New Mexico or that infamous town in Austria beginning with the letter "F"?A word of caution: The further the player progresses, the more empathy they'll build with their computer.  Both the player and their computer will feel the strain from being worked to their very limit! (Especially if a player doesn't have a computer that significantly surpasses the recommended RAM and CPU requirements.)This review made possible through the generosity, consideration, and contribution of  and the developer/publisher. Email contact@dnbmedia.co for requests & promotions.

_childDocuments_.review: It would be nice if there was a "possibly recommend" option, because it's hard to give a definite yes or no to 112 Operator.  In its current state, the game is more stressful and frustrating than fun.  But the developers are constantly improving it, and the biggest issues may get sorted out over the next couple months.  For now though, it's hard to justify the asking price, unless you're a fan of extreme micromanagement.Anyone familiar with 911 Operator will have no problems jumping in to the sequel.  The core gameplay is pretty much the same: incidents pop up across the map, and units need to be dispatched to resolve them.  Occasionally a 112 call will come in, and you have to talk the caller through an emergency situation while deciding which type of units to send out, if any.The maps in 112 Operator are much larger than the previous game, and there are now several districts to handle at once.  This makes unit management more challenging, since it takes nearly half the shift to send a unit from one side of the map to the other.  There are also objectives to be completed, such as prioritizing vandalism or drug-related calls, which adds to the challenge.Unfortunately, the biggest flaw in this new approach is the sheer number of incidents that come up during a shift.  The developers have said this is by design, since they want players to be overwhelmed with incoming calls.  It's easy to see what they were going for, but it doesn't really work out the way they were intending.  Unless you pause every few seconds, shifts quickly become a non-stop cacophony of noise, with multiple requests coming in at the same time and voice clips all talking over each other.  The constant stream of incoming incidents makes it hopeless to try and prioritize anything at normal speed - in the time it would take to read through the call description, find the best-equipped unit with the most efficient travel path, and then dispatch them to the target location, four more incidents will have popped up.Outside of pausing every time an incident comes in, the only way to get through a shift is to just mindlessly send whatever unit is closest and immediately move on to the next one.  There's no easy way to visually distinguish between low-priority and high-priority incidents, or those that require special equipment, and some of the incidents are way more resource-intensive than they should be.  (For instance, a bicycle theft requires police units to be dispatched to both the thief and the victim.)  You can't even focus during the 112 events, since incidents continue to come in while you're trying to work through the dialogue, and there's no way of pausing during a phone call.The developers seem to be very receptive to feedback, so it's possible these issues will be fixed in later patches.  If the number of incoming incidents is better balanced, and some UI and quality-of-life changes are implemented (such as having different colors for high-priority calls, or giving the units localized dialects instead of everyone having American accents), 112 Operator could be an enjoyable followup to 911 Operator.  However, in its current form, it feels more like a step down from the previous game.

_childDocuments_.review: Strangely satisfying, 112 Operator is a game that puts you in control of the firefighters, paramedics and law enforcement of a city of your choice.You are in charge of managing vehicles, gear and facilities and hiring staff for your emergency services. Depending on the difficulty settings you'll have troubles attending to all of them in time, so the game can be quite stressful! The coolest feature is that the game automatically detects where you are and automatically generates a map for your city! You can also choose cities throughout the world, though. You also have scenarios and a campaign. All game modes are fun and have their own flair.The biggest downside is that sometimes you'll be forced to pick up a 112 call and conduct a conversation with the caller. At the beginning they are interesting, but this feature gets old very quickly. I wish you could disable that.Achievements are great with one exception: "Somewhere in the north" is VERY random and luck-based. The other scenarios are fun, some are hard, but that's part of achievement hunting. No Linux port but worked without a hiccup on Proton (thanks Valve!)
