_childDocuments_.review: You can view my VR experience review & gameplay here: You can play The Sojourn in VR by using the Unreal Engine Hack. Simply type "-vr" in the game launch options (right click on game listed on steam library, then left click on Properties, it's in the general tab). As usual though, with the Unreal Engine VR hack, menus do not render, also pop-up messages. There's also minor issues with reflective spots on surfaces from the sun light.However, those issues do not really effect the experience (maybe the pop-up messages since they do have helpful tips, but you can figure it out). The menu is easy to navigate, especially with a gamepad (just click on A on Xbox One). The game is pure eye candy in VR. It looks almost like native VR. The reflective objects thing is very minor in this game as it's only a few spots & does not effect gameplay at all. Most of the game looks perfect. Game is running on the Unreal Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting steady 60 fps. No stutters of any kind. Smooth gameplay. If you already own this game and have a VR headset, it's a no-brainer to try it out. The Sojourn is better than the vast majority of VR puzzle games. Even if you don't own this game, I recommend getting on sale just for the VR. I don't think the developer will break the VR as I don't foresee any future updates. I bought this game for about $6 USD from a 3rd party website.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! Some of the chapters were extremely challenging but these brains are happy :) I was looking for a fix for The Witness and The Talos Principle for quite some time and The Sojourn is definitely it. Of course this game is also very different and stands alone beautifully. Amazing visuals, solid story and fantastic wisdom bits that you will want to write down. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: A good and long puzzle game with puzzles that make you think. There are 60 levels in total with most of them containing two puzzles. One puzzle allows you to proceed to the next level and the second is optional. You can come back to the optional puzzles after you beat the game. New game mechanics are introduced around the 20th and 40th levels. The combination of mechanics can sometimes make things quite tricky, but at the same time you get better at solving everything with practice.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the concept and had high hopes here. At first it was fun. However, the puzzles are extremely repetitive, and in many cases overcomplicated for no reason, and plain boring. I very often had a situation where the puzzle was almost done, but a small detail was missing - however to get there and change it, I had to redo most of the puzzle from scratch.All of it is basically a remix of the same concept over and over again. There are 4 "worlds" which means the scenery changes slightly, and there are a few mechanics introduced one by one, but that's it.The puzzles way too often are closer to annoying than hard, the walking speed is terribly slow, the "dark world" adds a flamey border around the screen which just obscures half of it and makes the game uncomfortable, and some of the mechanics are a real pain (like when you have to go on a thin ledge backwards, without being able to see where you're going, while having to point the camera exactly at one specific point because if you lose that point from your sight, the ledge vanishes).The visuals are nice for the first 15 minutes before you get bored of seeing the exactly the same ledges, just rearranged a bit differently - but that's about it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: bit of a let down. most puzzle are kinda linear. no too difficult.pace is really slow. story is... something?The 'wisdoms' you can unluck are just simple sayings written a bit more cryptic and mystical... i don't see any relation to the rest with it either.I like puzzle games but i can't get myself to finish this. just too plain boring.pretty but shallow
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked games like , , but wanted something more relaxing and a bit simpler, you might enjoy this title.It's a simple game of teleportation-based puzzles, set in the usual sky island environment. The scenery is what you'd hope for from the Unreal engine, pleasing and not too distracting.It's definitely worth having if you want to put yourself in a relaxed mood, without going to sleep in the process.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: The game still launches Steam VR and the developer has not fixed this for over a year. The lack of responsiveness on this simple fix reeks of amateurism.Aside from that The Sojourn is great: the visuals and music are really nice and do a good job of setting the tone of the game. The walking speed feels slow at first but I do think it helps force you to soak in the experience which is the standout element of this game, and the set pace does help in some puzzles by letting you know that sometimes you're definitely not going to be fast enough on foot to make a timed section and need to find another way instead of trying to be faster. Also I'm not sure why there's a jump since it's barely a hop and isn't used in a single (intended) solution but whatever.The difficulty is pretty perfect for me, nice to have a game where I don't have to rack my brain or  look up a guide if I'm stuck, just listen to some music and mess around with some easily-digestible mechanics. The last chapter does get difficult though, but it's a nice challenge to wrap up the game. Rotating the beam tower is backwards, not the way people want to rotate, watched a few videos and saw people also doing it backwards each time on controller and keyboard. What makes the puzzles so good is there is no fluff or red herrings, just a clean and precise puzzle with walkways and barriers in specific orientations that help keep a player on track by clearly showing what you are intentionally blocked from interacting with in certain spots which guides you to looks for other interactions. Really appreciated that there was no platforming or reaction-based elements, just a pure 3d puzzle game. The star of the show is the visuals. Really like how the eye gets bigger in the final section. Unfortunately there is no level select and you cannot backtrack, so once you beat the game your only option to continue playing is to start completely over.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: This is a definition of a borderline recommendation. I will talk about the puzzles, but let’s start with the narrative. It is not true this game has none. There' no less narrative here than in, say, The Witness, Antichamber, or Manifold Garden (all of which are phenomenal, imho). There’s more, in fact. You follow the path of the game’s protagonist through a set of stone-like sculpture compositions. Plus, you can collect, I’d guess, about 30 “merits” by solving optional puzzles, that provide supposedly profound insights related to where you are in the “narrative”. However, all of that is just primitive or flat out bad. I mean, here is one of the insights you are given after solving an optional puzzle:“The truth is hidden in a maze of lies. Lose yourself among the walls of uncertainty to fight your way through endless doubt.” if you thought that was iffy, have a look at those:“Wearing your truth on the sleeve is brave, even if others mock you for it.” (said every single fanatic, bigot, and conspiracy theorist ever) or“Forbidden fruits are forbidden because someone said so, not because they are bad for you.” (even heroin or pedophilia?). Now, you may think those teachings are actually correct. And you’re not alone! I personally found these and many other “merits” the game proudly provided an insult to human intellect.Anyways, puzzles. They are actually quite good. However, contrary to some other games, the pull you’re feeling from the game, for me at least, was getting weaker the more I progressed, when in best games it tends to be the opposite. Simply there is something off with these puzzles. They are like work. They are not the ones you’d solve while modeling the situation in your head, before falling asleep. They are novel, no  doubt about it, but the thinking required gets laborious and solving the puzzle is not rewarding at all. I personally gave up after about 50 puzzles and simply watched the important remaining scenes on YouTube. With that said, these puzzles are the only reason why I gave this a “Recommended” evaluation. They served as a decent distraction, even if at the end were not going anywhere for me. Buy at a discount, disregard the infantile teachings, and you may find it worthwhile.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very beautifully slightly low poly game; with, for me personally, a very refreshing way of puzzling.I do not think its a game that you could play in one sitting, but its very well suited for playing for 2-3 levels at a time, and then resuming your other activities.I've seen quite a few people complain that there is no rewards..GUYS. This game is a reward in itself. Beatiful design, amazingly soothing OST.If you have no patience, don't get the game. Just don't.If you do, and you love puzzles, get this gem!
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: My scores/reviews are almost always based on having bought the game at close to the "lowest historical price" on steam at time of purchase.Quick score: 5/5Notes: This game is insanely undderated on steam and should have way more positive reviews, I wouldn't rate it quite as high as something like Portal or Talos Principle but maybe 1 tier below.3 small complaints/issues#1 there isn't a run button and the walking speed is just a bit slower than I would prefer. Not a ton, but a 25% increase would be nice.#2 There were a handful of puzzles where after solving I'm not quite sure if i was abusing game mechanics or it was intended, and there was another handful of puzzle where I definitely abused game mechanics to complete them. This is because the game is designed around line of sight, angles, and a grid tile. However the game sometimes feels a little loose when it comes to determining what exact tile you are on, as well as sometimes being able to activate things slightly around corners or above walls. This is just the result of poor testing in most cases. I would say this was a noticeable issue on about 10% of the levels.#3 Your reward for completing the challenges is essentially just a fortune cookie or "words of wisdom". Would have liked to seen maybe some actual game related lore/worldbuilding or snippets of some kind lol.---------------------------------------Visuals are great, mechanics are unique (AFAIK), and the puzzles are generally good. Took me about 16 hours to 100% and I think I'm pretty decent at puzzle games. Though a couple of those hours may have been AFK. In terms of difficulty I would say the game is pretty average overall. There are some pretty difficult stages, but generally most stages will be completed in under 15 minutes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Sojourn is similar to Portal and Talos Principle. It doesn't quite live up to those titles but it's still a good game. I won't comment on the story as it's pretty cliche. It starts out easy and boring but eventually picks up in difficulty after a couple of hours. This will make it hard to judge if you should refund since the first couple of hours are less enjoyable. It's definitely worth a buy if you enjoy puzzle games and don't focus too much on the story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I had to go for the less than an hours play refund. If I'd persevered then maybe it would have improved but there was no obvious story line and the game play was linear and gave no indication that this would change at any time. The world looked really beautiful and I was looking forward to exploring but you have to follow these light fairies around all the time. The puzzles were just a variation on a theme and got boring very quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: This is a challenging first person puzzle game.  The puzzles are unique and deserve a 10/10!  This involves many portal techniques.  If you like first person puzzle games, this is the one!  The only bizarre part is the artwork and statues tell some silent story that's pointless, but it sort of grew on me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Positive:- Beautiful visuals. In the first two areas I spent more time looking over the edges and into the background to admire the scenery than acutally solving the puzzles.- New puzzle elements which complement/expand the main light/dark mechanic are introduced gradually and they all use different game mechanics (distance walked, timing, holding and moving objects, temporary and persistent binary state changes, line of sight, etc.)- The visual effects and HUD make it very clear what is happening in the puzzles and what is required to solve them.Neutral:- There are no built-up rewards except progressing from one puzzle to the next, and the bonus challenges don't have any rewards either until you complete all of them. So the game is for those who simply enjoy solving a puzzle.- The bonus challenges are inside the puzzle levels themselves and they unlock after solving the main puzzle (i.e. another part of the level and a second goal are revealed, but the original level remains). Unfortunately they are very inconsistent in terms of how difficult they are, how much new elements they add to the level and how much backtracking is required. There are also real bonus levels at the end of each area and they do a much better job at offering a more difficult bonus puzzle.- In the first area the puzzles are all put into one environment and after reaching the end of one, you go through a door to the next without any loading. You also see how much of the area you did and have left from the stars on the door. There are only small walking sections between the areas. So I was walking through this city environment solving puzzles to get to the end, and I was excited by the progression and expected the game to go on like this ... but then from the second area on they put in awfully simple and small level hubs where you complete 4-5 challenges and then walk to the next hub. Towards the end it's just a linear set of doors to the challenges. Very disappointing.Negative:- I have no idea what the story is supposed to be. A game this focused on puzzles doesn't need a story so there shouldn't have been an attempt at creating one, because it turned out to be confusing and distracts from the puzzle experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: The Sojourn is a comparatively expansive first person puzzle game where you embark on a journey to learn the merits of life. The game has over 50 puzzles that are mostly presented as their own little levels that you enter through portals and such.In every puzzle, your objective is to get to the end and release a small caged ball of light. To do that, you manipulate the powers of dark and light. You enter the dark world through specific platforms or gates and, while in it, you can swap places with statues to open gates via switches or move around, make walkways appear and manipulate darkness rays. Switching between darkness and light to handle the various facets of the levels is very fun and the game is, overall, very fair. Most puzzles are on the manageable side, but there are quite a few headscratchers too. The levels are small enough, though, to never be frustrating or unfair. The mechanics slowly expand over the course of the game and it is just the right length to not get too repetitive.I can't find much fault with it, but if I had to criticize something, it would be the lack of the run button (though it would probably break some puzzles). The artstyle is clean and the soundtrack is surprisingly good. If you are a fan of first person puzzle games in the vein of Talos Principle and the like, then The Sojourn is another excellent title to play and a definite recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: There are some amazing puzzles in this game, a great game IMO if you like first person type puzzles like The Talos Principle or Portal. Some are on the easy side for sure but (for me) there are definitely some nice, satisfying head-scratchers.Also: absolutely gorgeous.Only complaint: the walking is too slow/no sprint button, but that may have been because you could cheese some puzzles that way.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting puzzles, a decent addition to the 'first person puzzler' genre, but something about it just makes me bored playing after only 20-30 minutes, so I have to play it in smaller chunks. Maybe it's the slow movement speed and the inability to sprint (which is required for the puzzles to work), or the sterile environment with story notes so vague they might as well not be there. Regardless, the puzzles are quite clever and include optional difficulties, which are quite fun to tackle. It's not as strong as The Talos Principle series or the Portal series, but it's good enough to play and recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: After the first hour I was sure I was going to give this a bad review, but it picked up. Overall the game lacks the exploration that one usually expects from a game like this, and the fact that it is just puzzle after puzzle with tiny bits of story is what stops this from being a great game. The puzzles in the second half are pretty good though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Very good puzzles based on original concepts. I wouldn't say it is similar to The Witness as many reviewers have done. The Witness is a masterpiece on many levels. The Sojourn does not reach that level, but it is still good. One notable difference between the two games is that the structure of the games is very different. The Sojourn is essentially a series of "puzzle chambers" (although these chambers are actually outdoors) connected via a mostly linear progression system where once you solve one chamber you have a very short path the the next one. Sometimes there are mini-hubs where you can choose which of say 5 chambers to try next, but you need to complete all of them to proceed to the next mini hub. So unlike the Witness, The Sojourn has no single large seamless world to explore, and there are no interconnected puzzles that span multiple areas/chambers.The music of the Sojourn is very nice. I think it was all Classical style with lots of haunting Cello. And the environments you move through between puzzles and within puzzle chambers are generally beautiful, and yes, the art style is sometimes reminiscent of that of The Witness.There is an artsy story told via statues that you come across between puzzle chambers that didn't make a whole lot of sense to me or maybe I did not really care enough about about to try too hard to understand. It seems like a vaguely philosophical story about "the journey of life" as far as I can tell. The statues don't speak or present any text or anything like that.Aside from the main puzzles in chambers that you need to complete in order to progress, there are optional challenges. Usually these optional challenges are in the form of secondary objectives in a puzzle chamber that appear after you have solved the primary puzzle. In a few cases, an optional challenge is essentially given it's own puzzle chamber. Solving these optional challenges yields a scroll with some pearl of wisdom written on it. Some of the pearls are are better than others and let's leave it at that.In the end, the reason I give this game a solid thumbs up is that it is is series of puzzles solved in first person view, and the puzzles are fresh, often challenging (but not ridiculously hard), and the environments and music are very pleasant to be in. Finally, to give you an idea of the difficulty and length of game: I completed every puzzle including all the optional challenges in 22 hours without needing any help. I would say I am a pretty seasoned puzzle game player.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Well-made puzzle game, where the aim is to figure out how to move from A to B using various mechanics, most of which are in the trailer. No control issues, no bugs, music didn't get annoying and game ran smoothly!Like other reviews have said better than I, the main focus of the game is puzzles, there is a little story, but mostly the reward for completing a puzzle is another puzzle. That's fine, it's just not everyone's cuppa tea. Did get a little repetitive at times, but was a good brain workout without being impossible.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. The puzzles are simple but then can be really tricky. You really have to think how to solve them with the tools provided. The music is nice and the scenery is lovely. I missed doing the first 2 of the scroll challenges as I went through the door and it auto saved  and I couldn't get back, so be aware to complete what you want before moving on.Edit: I have found there is a garden of merits near the end where you can try to complete all the merits you missed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: There's not much substance other than the puzzles.The puzzle mechanics are very solid and synergize well, though I don't think they were utilized to their full potential.Felt like the developers were holding back on using too many of the mechanics in the same puzzle to make it easier to manage.A bare-bones but polished experience. I do recommend the game if you need yet another first person puzzle crack fix after playing The Talos Principle or The Witness.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game if you're into puzzle games. In the beginning the puzzles seem way too easy, but eventually they will become quite difficult. Very nice visuals, but unfortunately the storyline isn't very clear. If you like games with a lot of variation, you probably won't like this game. But if want to relax and do some puzzles you'll love this one!
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better first person puzzle games that I played.What strikes me most about this game is that all the levels are small. There are only a few puzzle elements per level. Yet, most of the levels succeed in being challenging. Some of the levels are real head-scratchers.Everything about this game feels good. The game has the right level of difficulty. The environments look nice. The effects and the changing environment in between the puzzles make the trip worthwhile. The sojourn tries to tell a story with static human figures you encounter. All together it's a wonderful journey.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: You like pure puzzling? Then you'll probably like this. Not much else to say here, it's what it says on the label - disregard the 'Adventure' tag though, unless your bar for interesting narratives is very low.A bunch of puzzles and another bunch of optional challenges make for a fairly long journey (if you want) through some pretty environments - you wouldn't wanna play this game just for the graphics or the bare-bones story though, so you can just try the first bunch of puzzles and see if you like it, because it'll stay that way with some new elements popping up every now and then.If you like the visual style but not necessarily the gameplay, you might like RiME or The Witness instead. Maybe Etherborn, which has a similar lack of narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I received the game from a friend because of an event that we do where we give eachother random games.The game looked pretty good but I hoped for a few more mechanics to solve puzzles. The puzzles were pretty challanging but the story was minimal. I was kinda sad when I completed the first floor of the academy towerish just to find a few more statues of dudes and more doors that I had to complete.Its still a good game if you like to solve puzzles :D
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game with one of the more unique puzzle mechanics I have seen. Puzzles are are challenging especially the later ones in each world although some of it is more from a long list of operations to do. The story is generic and has no bearing on the puzzles whatsoever. It’s there just for flavour.Overall there is nothing wrong with this game and its stand out is its unique puzzle mechanic. Puzzle design and story are all normal.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Great overworld and flashy visuals make me want to keep playing this game. The puzzles are the perfect length. Just when they start to get too long, you move to the next hubworld and reset the length. There is no story, just a visual telling through statues. The best I can tell the story is white=good, purple=bad. Disintegrate your body to feed trees and scare away the bad purple people.Most puzzles are fairly short, but have a bonus component that adds a few more steps. Your reward for completing this bonus is a scroll with some outdated philosophical proverb that is written in computer font and looks super out of place. Has absolutely nothing to do with the game/story. From a game perspective, it feels more like a punishment than a reward when picking these up. Really detracts from the design of the world. But I still 100%'ed it anyway because I can't help myself. I wish they would just replace these scrolls with gold stars or something simpler to make it feel more rewarding and less confusing.Whoever decided this game doesn't need a sprint function should honestly be beaten really badly. The puzzle mechanics are nice and require a bit of thought to work out, but there is so much backtracking every time you mess up by accidentally walking a foot in the wrong direction. And sometimes there is just intentional backtracking to loop through some areas. All the while you are moving extremely slowly. It can take literal minutes to get back to a state from 2 seconds ago because you have to do some back and forth trading of inputs. Perhaps an actual time rewind mechanic would be better though, and it would really fit into this game's visual theme. But I would gladly settle for a sprint function. They could easily make it work with other game time/distance mechanics. Perhaps simply disabling it while the time components are active.Only thing that I was left feeling really confused about is the game duration. I saw all these reviews at 20-50 hours and I easily 100% achievement beat the game in 8 hours?
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like to be negative, but, in my experience, this game had very little in the way of redeeming qualities.The "plot" is hardly even an original idea, let alone a story worth telling over the course of an entire game.The proverbs prattled throughout the game, while fine when taken on their own, are increasingly self-important and self-righteous as the game goes on.The puzzles were challenging, but repetitive and unrewarding.The underlying philosophy of the game seemed extremely juvenile and lacking in perspective, considering the "antagonists" of the game were mostly just people doing their jobs, while the "savior" protagonist lacks any experience in their individual fields, and is himself a privileged student of their very principles. It calls to mind the all too many opponents of reason who see bad things happening and blame "the system" while having no insight into what is actually going on and being unable to provide any viable solution. The game is also subtly critical of theism and capitalism, which I can't hold against it, but it sure didn't help.Speaking of which, without going into detail, the optional collectible scrolls are made entirely counter-intuitive to the plot by the implication that they are the teachings of the wise old ruler.The symbolism is cliche and heavy-handed, mainly consisting of blindfolds and seeds.It is also never made clear what the player's role in any of this is, where or when the game is set, or how the puzzles or the settings of the puzzles relate to the plot. The only other thing that moves during the story portions are the lights that guide you through the environments, but they are never related to anything either. I was hoping it would be like The Unfinished Swan, which has little plot throughout the game (although much more than this), but is tied together at the end. The end of this game, however, is as vague as the rest.All this being said, the game has been solely marketed as a puzzle game, which it was. The puzzles may have been the only part with true originality. A group of people must have put a lot of effort into making these puzzles and designing new elements for each stage of the players progression, which I can sincerely appreciate. However, the half-measure inclusion of a skeletal plot and implied character progression obscured the puzzles as the focus of the game and made the experience, in all honesty, a drudgery. Had the game not been so coyly offered a plot, I simply would not have played it, and the target audience would have been more effectively reached.In truth, the reason I played this game is because it looked like the game RiME, which I personally loved and remains one of my favorite games of all time. if you are like me, and sought more in the way of character progression and original story elements, I highly recommend playing that game instead.Before posting this review, I've gone back and looked at the store page. I didn't pay full price, but It is an atrocity that they charge $25 for this, what amounts to a Candy Crush style puzzle game. It certainly is not a "captivating tale of light, darkness, and the nature of reality."
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: 98% of your time would be solving puzzle and moving to the next puzzle. Puzzle that good for the first time then it get boring, repetitive and monotonous real fast. Only buy if you really into puzzle and know that you solve puzzle only to get the next puzzle in this game. There is no objective, bonus, or story for you to get it in this game.Tl;dr ONLY PUZZLES
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Repetitives and (mostly) easy puzzles one after another combine with some glitches (no answer on the forum). Not finished yet but if I do it will really be because I don't like to let something unfinished.The pseudo philosophical nonsense doesn't help at all.I paid half the price. Let say I paid the graphist designers at least.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I am unable to play this game without getting sick and nauseous because there is no FOV option. I wish I could have given the game one more try, but I'm really having trouble. Sad considering how intriguing the puzzles seemed. To clarify: this game's FOV is REALLY low by default, making it extremely difficult to play. I was able to play other games without a FOV setting, but this one is excruciating.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very pretty and the puzzles are interesting and challenging. However, they're essentially the same puzzle over and over and over until you want to throw the computer out the window. There's some semblance of a background story, but it's vague and ephemeral, and it has little to no bearing on the player's actions. After playing it for 55 hours - admittedly, a lot of the time I put the laptop down and watch something on tv because it's so dreadfully boring - all I can say is "please, for the love of all that's good and holy, end already!" I saw the mixed reviews before purchasing it, and I bought it anyway because it was on sale. I would not recommend getting this unless it's practically free and you're aware that you might either end up abandoning it halfway out of boredom or finish it out of spite (as I am).
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: $25 for this game is robbery.  For over an hour, I literally just walked around and followed directions on the screen.  Absolutely nothing whatsoever like the descriptions, videos, etc shown.  There are no "puzzles," puzzles aren't the same as "follow what the screen is telling you to do, then walk forward at 0 mph." Terrible, boring, and WAYYYYYYYYY overpriced.  I kept wondering when something was going to happen, when the "tutorial" was going to end and when the game would finally start.  For nearly an hour and a half.No thanks.  I submitted a refund request - don't waste your money unless you have really bad insomnia or something.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: It's a rather good puzzle game. Mechanics are pretty unique and the devs surely have made some tricky puzzles out of them.However, lack of a re-do feature is such a pain in the ass. If you have played The Talos Principle, it's not too hard to imagine walking through all levels without ever rewinding. Once you make some irreversible mistake, the only option left is to start over. It's a such fun killer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: If you're really into puzzle games, particularly first-person ones that are very light on plot, this is worth checking out. Keep in mind, however, that, while the game isn't long, it sure can feel like it is. The story that does exist is told in the abstract, through imagery, rather than dialogue. The puzzles themselves - as you'd expect - get progressively more complex until they add a new mechanic. I feel no shame in admitting that there were quite a few stretches where I just had to put the game down, step away, and come back to it later to spare what remaining brain cells I have left. Later, I'd come back to the game refreshed, realize I missed a key element, and continue trodding through. Environmentally, the game can be rather soothing, with its placid scenery and light music. All in all, it's a game I feel accomplished in completing, but it was most definitely a trudge.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Very well made, very polished puzzle game that looks quite good and has good art design. However, the core puzzle mechanics and the telling of a subtle obscure story by inference don't match up. My main critique is that everything is so slow, from the walk speed to the puzzle reactions to the level transitions, but the puzzles are so easy that it becomes frustrating that you cant get through them quicker. I started the game clearing all the bonus puzzles but they became tedious and I was impatient so mainlined the main path instead, and even then i was very close to uninstalling this game multiple times before the end. The best puzzle  mechanic was saved until the last, the one where you had to maintain your gaze with the eyeball. Guys, you should have introduced this one far far earlier than what you did because I was ready to quit but this got me through to the end. It was the only puzzle mechanic that gave me an "a-ha" moment the entire game.I can't recommend this game when there are so many others out there that do everything better. Not really sure who this is for, puzzle enthusiasts will probably find it too easy, while theres not enough going on outside of the puzzles for a puzzle novice/casual.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: It's a decent puzzle game. The graphics are good and the music is nice, but the game is quite dry. It's pure puzzles and nothing else. There is no story, there are no distractions of any kind, so it does become quite monotonous about half-way through and just feels like a chore.Maybe get it if you really like puzzle games, but I did not enjoy my time with it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing I noticed about this game was it has awesome lighting and great atmosphere; that the graphics were simple yet stunning. The next thing I noticed is that the noises are fantastic. Then I realized the game had great music. Once I started getting to actual levels, the way each level is built upon entering is really cool and well done. The architecture and design of the areas surrounding the levels is really pleasing, and the different look of each environment in light and dark is awesome.The puzzles consist of two worlds, light and dark, which the player must navigate, using different gimmicks, to reach the end point of each level. Gimmicks are introduced at steady pace; one that felt just right for me. The difficulty curve is really slow and it makes this an enjoyable experience. Occasionally, the game made my brain hurt because of the amount of things I was tracking, but for the most part, it's quite straightforward. Not too challenging, but challenging enough to be fun and rewarding. As I entered the fourth area, the levels started to take more time to complete, but ultimately, the game didn't provide the same end game experience that many puzzle games do for me. Where I'm stuck on a handful of levels I can't beat, and I end up abandoning it post ending, but without hitting 100%. Which isn't to say that is bad about other puzzle games, more a comment on this being a laidback puzzler that can be easily completed.The game presents asort of story through the use of statues. It was a bit confusing at first, but I started to follow it as the game progressed. It's an interesting way to present a story. Very little context through only a few still shots. This is more than most puzzle games offer, so it was welcomed.My only gripe. I REALLY wish this game allowed you to tweak walk speed on a slider in the menu that would tweak the rest of the game's time-based functions accordingly. The speed was just painfully slow at times, especially when struggling a bit on a level.The price point of the game is fair on a slight sale. It took me about 14 hours to complete the game 100% with no hints. Asking price is a little steep for the hours the game takes, but if you really need a first person puzzler and can't wait for a sale, it's worth it. Otherwise, wishlist it and wait for sale, even a small one is fair, and makes the game a no-brainer to pick up.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: It's middling - okay - nothing special. Got it on sale and still kinda feel iffy about it.Music's comfy at least. Ambience kinda ruined by the dumb text explaining mechanics and the cheesy life advice on the scrolls.Already getting to be too many puzzles with razor thin timing, which is a crappy crutch to lean on design-wise in what otherwise seems to be billing itself as a relaxing puzzle game.It scratches the itch but it could be so much better.Graphics nice enough and hasn't crashed yet.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Nice little puzzle game. But at the end it becomes a bit of a drag (for the last 7ish levels). Also sometimes during the game there are a few levels which dont really feel like introducings something new but only prolonging the game.All in All except for the level where you can get the 40th merit of life the levels are constructed well (the one I mentioned can cause a soft lock which forces you to restart the level and you have to do quite some walking in it so it can be very frustrating).Still very much worth the money if you want to spend a 12 hours or so puzzling and looking at some nice scenery.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: A peaceful, yet fairly challenging puzzle game that takes you into a strange journey. Each challenges you go through contains some piece of advice about life, you get to see the beauty in this game.Truly, this game is definitely a work of art and knows how to make a good puzzle game along with it. Recommend it to those puzzle lovers.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game and recommend it with a caveat. Although the puzzles/challenges change as you progress with added features and complexity as many games do, the basic premise and structure remains the same. After a while, and there are lot of puzzles/challenges, I was ready for it to be over. Game mechanics were great, no glitches, graphics are very well done, easy to navigate and views were very smooth. Glad i played it and liked that I could stop, come back, take as long as I needed on a challenge or start it over.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game.It's a good puzzle game, various enough to stay interesting throughout the whole journey. The puzzles can be tough, sometimes, but never hardcore; bonus puzzles unlocks after completing the levels and those can be quite hard.Graphics are truly gorgeous, there's a lot of work in creating the world. Only, sometimes I thought they were... well, too much. I mean, I wasn't really paying attention to what was outside the game stage, so I felt like there was a lot of effort into making... backgrounds (but maybe it's just me).Also, the mute story is too obscure, something about truth and revelations. I don't really like this kind of narrative: if you want to tell a story, make it clear; otherwise, just go for the puzzles.So... buy it or not? I'd say yes, if you're looking for a good first person puzzle and if you like carefully crafted worlds.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this in hopes of having a calming puzzle game to indulge myself into. I can honestly say that I was not disappointed. Having %100'd the game, I can say, with certainty, that the time was well-spent.I would compare this game to The Witness, in terms of its overall vibe, graphic style, and allure. If you're looking for a thought-provoking puzzle game, please sincerely think about buying.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge portal 2 and puzzle game fan, the logic and level design in this game are beautiful. The dark world reminds me a lot of lightmatter which is another fantastic puzzle game. The abstract story so far is very interesting and mysterious. The puzzles are challenging, but not difficult enough that you start to feel stuck. I WISH this game had a level editor because I can think of so many cool uses for these statues to interact with each other. I highly recommend this game to any puzzle fan out there.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for an extremely challenging game filled with complex puzzles that demand a detailed and deep understanding of the many game mechanics....this game probably won't quite meet your expectations. However, if you are looking for a moderately challenging, relaxing, and beautiful game you will probably enjoy The Sojourn.Personally, I found this game to be right about the perfect difficulty. Most of the levels were just challenging enough to keep me mentally engaged, but not too difficulty so that they became frustrating or tedious. Most of the levels only took me about 5-10 minutes to solve, but many offered and additional optional/secondary more difficult challenge.In addition, I thought the game did a good job with its pacing/difficulty curve. New mechanics were introduced often enough to keep things fresh, but not too often to become overwhelming. I also appreciated how the new mechanics were gradually integrated with older mechanics with increasing complexity. This helped me have a firm understanding of each of the mechanics by the time I was presented with some of the more complex challenges.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sojourn

_childDocuments_.review: Traverse a thought-provoking puzzle game and its immersive color-drenched world of light and shadow. The Sojourn takes place in a mysterious land, where lights guide you forward and the world reveals itself to be full of challenges. Overcome these intricate and ever more demanding obstacles to uncover the nature of reality.

name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark
detailed_description: Feature List • 9 unique cases, the likes of which you’ve never seen before (not a guarantee) • Uses both pointing and clicking technology • Music from Thomas O'Boyle, a totally-living composer, definitely not undead • Photo-Realistic* Pixel Rendering (*Depends on your definition of photo-realism) • 1 mail-in rebate per customer on exorcism services for hauntings resulting from play • A brief recap of the events of 'The Darkside Detective' for anyone who hasn't played it and doesn't want to About the Game Delouse your room with sage and pack up your travel-sized ouija board, it’s time to re-enter Twin Lakes - America’s 34th most haunted city. Join Detective McQueen as he puzzles his way through 9 chilling cases, risking life and pixelated limb to solve the macabre mysteries that plague the poor town. Twin Lakes is a cursed city. Less cursed than say, “Demons are tearing it apart” but more cursed than “always loses its keys” or “often steps in puddles”. It’s roughly in the middle of the cursed scale, is what we’re trying to say. Cursed enough that it’s a nuisance. Cursed enough that somebody has to deal with it… That’s where The Darkside Detective comes in. Whenever you hear a bump in the night, feel a tingle up your spine, or smell something fishy, Detective Francis McQueen isn’t far behind. No, he doesn’t smell of fish - it’s a phrase, come on... Picking up after the events of The Darkside Detective, McQueen has to save his usually-present (in body, if not mind) sidekick Officer Dooley from the Darkside, so the two can get back to what they do best - investigating the city’s many strange, often paranormal, always paradoxical goings-on. Join them in this frighteningly funny point-and-click adventure as they investigate nine more standalone cases bringing them to a carnival, the local retirement home, an amateur wrestling circuit and even as far away as Ireland as they do what they can to keep the Darkside at bay. Like how this sounds? Try the first title.

_childDocuments_.review: Although released roughly 4 years after the original  the experience was pretty fresh for me as I played the first game only early this year. Moving forward I'll be focusing on  as a sequel so if you're interested in the series in general head back and read my review of the original game.The sequel is a blast! We pick up exactly where we left off: Dooley is still missing and McQueen is desperately trying to find him. The first case focuses on this so that the two protagonists can once again join forces and continue solving cases of the paranormal. 6 of them are available at the moment with the 7th referred to as "coming soon". Wrestling, cursed castle in Ireland, high school reunion, fun park - everything that needs to be made fun of. The concept is the same. McQueen is very helpful in saying what should our next step be while Dooley is pretty much useless but at least he always has better (=worse) puns at his disposal. Exactly for this reason it is recommended to examine everything and talk to everybody even if it does not advance the story as for the jokes alone it's worth it. Still no voice acting but the eerie soundtrack perfectly makes up for it.If you fancy laughter and point-and-click adventures in lieu of AAA games Darkside Detective (and its sequel) is perfect for you.

_childDocuments_.review: The first "Darkside Detective" game (which is very good, and you should play it) was less of a point-and-click adventure than a delivery system for jokes, mostly of the dad variety. What puzzles it contained were rudimentary, though this actually helped to keep the ten-gags-a-minute pace going before tedium could set in. Its sequel "A Fumble in the Dark" upgrades the difficulty level to, oh, I'd say somewhere just north of "still extremely easy." As I suspect no one is playing these games for their brain-busting quality, this shouldn't be much of a deterrent to purchase for any but the most died-in-the-wool PnC nerds.The bigger issue with this sequel is that it tries  hard to be funny all the time, especially in an ironic self-aware way that was largely missing from the original, that it ends up feeling much less inspired. I found myself  the gags more often than I actually laughed at them. And maybe this is just a "me" thing but I've always been annoyed at point-and-click games with too much dialogue-per-click. Here, a simple click on almost any object can result in a back-and-forth dialogue that carries on for ten lines or so,  disrupting the flow of what is still, at the end of the day, supposed to be an exploration game. Worse, many of the gags rely upon recall of "Darkside Detective" lore from the original release that I'd long since forgotten; most of these flew over my head.That bit of grouchiness out of the way, I still recommend "A Fumble in the Dark" to anyone looking for an amusing way to turn their brain off, preferably in 30-minute sessions while the humor remains fresh. It retains a good deal of the series' charm, and I hope that the developers come back for a third installment -- but only after making something different in-between, in order to recharge their considerable talents.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Often, it is hard for a sequel to a great game to live up to player expectations. I am happy to report that this new romp with Detective McQueen and Officer Dooley is just as well done as the original. It is fun and incredibly entertaining.A Fumble in the Dark is a pixelated throwback to the Sierra-style games that many of us older folks know and love. It has great characters, a good story, dialog that will keep you laughing, and (often) ridiculous 'find and use' inventory solutions. Throw in an intuitive interface (inventory is dragged and dropped with no 'verbs' required) and a few not-too-difficult mini-games and you have old style adventure gaming at its finest.The game is divided into six stand-alone cases to solve. Each involves the 'dark side' with supernatural events to investigate. Your progress is auto-saved quite often. In addition, you can explicitly save your game. There appears to be one save slot, per case.  Once a case has been completed, you can move on to the next. Later, you can reopen any case o pick up missing achievements without disturbing the status of other cases. I highly recommend A Fumble in the Dark. Even if you are not a fan of classic adventures, this one is worth your time!
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the first Darkside Detective game, you'll be likely to enjoy this one.If you didn't enjoy the first Darkside Detective game, you probably won't.It really is as simple as that.The game starts out a bit slower than the first in terms of easily relatable jokes, but it picks up nicely as you go through the cases.Silly, irreverent, weird- just what I expected from this game.The puzzles are a bit more complicated in terms of steps needed to be taken (more back & forth), but none of them are terribly difficult. None of them are exceptionally easy easy either- you will need to think about things- but none of them are going to break your brain. Much.Some achievements are unmissable story-related achievements. Some are missable and require things to be done in a specific order or a specific number of times. Click everything,talk to everyone- repeatedly. hover over the entire scene to make sure you did not miss any interactable items- some of which may not appear until you visit a location again or again again.Some dialogue options and jokes only show up if you go back and talk to people every time you see them.Expect a lot of cheese. And politics- the devs do not hide their views, just like in the first game. But it is all very tongue-in-cheek. I recommend playing through without using a guide first- you may get some achievements without understanding what you did and how you got them. I found this enjoyable. There are guides to help if you missed achievements, or want a step-by-step walkthrough. I did need a guide to get the one achievement I had missed during my first playthrough. You can play each case separately- they are all stand-alones.  You choose- step-by-step walkthrough if you only want to play each case once,or just playthrough and replay any cases that you missed an achievement in. 2 cases are shown on the case list that are not available to play yet,so there will either be an update or 2, or the devs enjoy trolling players, hard. Probably both.Good, silly game when you need some laughs. worth full price, for sure, IMHO.

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Darkside Detective is bringing back the classic indie flavor of out-of-the-box thought processes and storytelling, mixed with a fantastic yet simplistic style of gameplay.Hey, kids . . . remember back when indie games weren’t shy about creating weird game designs and stories?  Well, it seems like Darkside Detective is trying to bring that weird awesomeness back with a more refined traditional style of gameplay.In this game, you get to play as a desperate Police Detective trying to solve cases that are out of the scope for most cops; cases that require a bit more open-mindedness and belief in the extraordinary. Well, I am talking about Ghosts, Realms, Demons, and everything creepy in between. The game is all about looking beyond the scope, looking for nitty gritty details, puzzles that require keen attention, and so on. The game is a bit on the dialogue-heavy side, so if you’re not into that, you have been warned. But I must say that dialogues in this game are very well thought-out; charming, witty, and clever. The game obviously is not serious, but it’s kinda funny to see it tries to create some form of tension.Plot: Ah! Twin Lake City is a beauty of a place cursed with a demon infestation (along with a variety of otherworldly creatures). As the curse starts to affect the city more and more, the demand for someone with skills to deal with this kind of infestation grows. Here’s where our protagonist, Detective Francis McQueen, comes into play, specializing in dealing with all the otherworldly drama. Case after case, Detective McQueen takes on the toughest of the tough. Until that one ill-fated day when, while working with his longtime partner Officer Dooley, an unknown event occurred and Officer Dooley was sucked into a different realm far away from human contact. Having running dry on leads, Detective McQueen starts looking for new leads to discover the whereabouts of Officer Dooley. Taking some time off his official duties to dedicate maximum effort to Dooley’s case, McQueen manages to pull Dooley back to his earthly realm.As the days go by, more and more such mysterious cases land on the floor, and who better to manage them other than Detective McQueen.Gameplay: The game doesn’t mess around, with just a brief glimpse of a short yet fantastic animated storyboard which pretty much sets the tone for the first case... There are currently seven such cases, and I am very much hoping to get some more.Each case takes about 20-25 minutes to complete if you’re not in a rush or you’re not paying attention. This is fair enough, considering how well the game has been scripted, and combined with its simplistic gameplay, it’s a win-win situation.The cases sort of progress episodically; when a case comes by that’s slightly spooky, McQueen gets called in for help.As you interact with NPCs on each case, you start to gather up all the necessary information at a snail’s pace. Most interactions are pointless with little information to be collected, but immensely amusing to see NPC’s trying to create some false tension, or making unfunny comments, being jerks to each other. And here’s where the star attraction comes into play, the gameplay itself. Simplistic point and click style of gameplay, full of witty dialogue and nothing much to do other than to go back and forth in scenes to collect items, information, and complete puzzles. There’s a fair bit of backtracking going on in this game, but nothing to get stressed about.  It’s very manageable as you collect information and items from one scene and go to the next to get some more info, while getting the items to interact with each other or with NPC’s. The game features a few unique sets of puzzles; nothing too crazy, mostly items interacting with each other and NPC’s to figure out their purpose. Basically object inventory puzzles, logic puzzles, circuit connection puzzles, etc. Most of the puzzles are either no-brainers or mildly tedious. World design: Darkside displays a fantastic assortment of Pixel Graphics Motion art.  From rooms to streets, everything was pretty much in good shape, contributing to the game's overall charm (although certain things could’ve been improved visually, like the cop car).Music and sound effects: The game features a pretty interesting background tune, trying to simulate some sort of creepy theme; I found it rather funny and enjoyable.I wish I could say the same for the other sound effects; some are okay but others outright disappointing; a little more of something would’ve been nice.Positive: + Fantastic cases to be solved+ Fun and simplistic style of gameplay + No-brainer fun puzzles + Pixel Graphics Motion art+ Enjoyable background tune + Splendid Witty dialoguesNegatives: -  Most dialogues are pretty pointless and distract from the game - Some puzzles are rather tedious- Certain sections of the artwork could’ve been improved - Short game, could use some more casesA super retro indie game that doesn’t takes itself seriously.  It’s pretty funny to see characters trying to create some form of tension . . . well, they tried. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: This is everything I wanted out of a second Darkside Detective season.  The first game has a special place in my heart and is among my favorite adventure games.  It is a great series for newcomers to the point and click genre.  If you are not familiar, Darkside Detective is a spooky comedy developed by a small Irish team featuring  a straight-laced detective and his lovably dim cop partner as they investigate supernatural disturbances in and around the fictional city of Twin Lakes.I use the term "season", because Darkside Detective is broken up into distinct standalone cases, making it perfect for popping in and out at your leisure over a long period of time.  It's great for streaming, too, if you are into the Twitch scene.  The first game launched with six completed cases, and every few months the developers dropped a new case, bringing it up to a total of nine.  It appears similar plans may be in the works for A Fumble in the Dark.In DSD2, the boys are back, and the game's current six cases take us to places like a haunted carnival, a demonic wrestling match, and a perfectly normal nursing home where nothing at all strange is happening.Fumble in the Dark is an A+ continuation of the magic formula used in the first game, but with improvements across the board.  The writing is just as funny (if not funnier!).  If anything, the art has gotten even better.  The six currently available cases are a bit longer and more varied than the average case from DSD1, and it feels like Spooky Doorway made conscious efforts to improve puzzle design as well.While the original composer from DSD1 did not return for the second game, the new composer Thomas O'Boyle had big shoes to fill and did a phenomenal job in maintaining the feel of the original game while putting his own spin on it.If you are new to the series, go ahead and buy the bundle with both of them.  Just do it, and thank me later.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is one of the games that made me wish steam had a more neutral option for reviews.That said, I definitely didn't enjoy this game as much as the first one. I'd suggest playing the original Darkside Detective if you have any interest. And honestly, frankly, skipping this one. I enjoyed it, but the puzzles in this game were a lot more of a pain in the ass than the original. In the first game, I wouldn't say I hit any major stumbling blocks in solving any of the cases. Most of the logic made sense, things were well foreshadowed in their use, and the layout of puzzles did a good job making sure you didn't have to backtrack too much.This game definitely is a step down in puzzle design. Several steps down in my eyes, honestly. There were multiple points in this game where I ended up completely stuck with no idea how to progress. Multiple times where I felt like I was pixel hunting for something that wasn't properly signposted, or a lack of context clues left me with zero idea how to proceed. I had to look up guides at points for over half the mainline cases. I don't like referring to guides if I can avoid it, I'd much rather solve puzzles in games from, well, within the game. Generally when I'm looking at a guide it's because I feel the game has failed in guiding me or signposting what it expects from me. For that reason, I can't really say this succeeds as a sequel to the original, which I never ran into that issue with.As for the actual story in the cases, it was nice. Good follow up to the original darkside detective. Good continued building of the setting. Jokes still quite amusing, and the tone of the game bang on to the original, props for all that.All that said, be warned the puzzles in this game are a step down from the first if you are going to get it.

_childDocuments_.review: The introduction of Detective Francis McQueen and his sidekick, Officer Patrick Dooley, in 2017’s comedy horror point-and-click, , was an unexpected delight. The strange and kooky world of Twin Lakes didn’t take the ‘horror’ bit all that seriously; it was much happier indulging obscure film references and finding innuendo .And we were all the better for it.The sequel, , is much the same, only bigger and carried off with a confidence born of its developers knowing they’ve crafted a winning duo, milking it for all it's worth – albeit a little too much at times.There are six cases for McQueen to solve, starting with bringing Dooley back from his entrapment in the eponymous ‘Darkside’ – a ghoulish mirror of Twin Lakes, which is inhabited by a menagerie of monsters and spooks. Some of them are nice, even friendly. Most aren’t.Dooley’s time in the Darkside forms the rough backbone of the narrative, with most of the cases you need to solve in some way related to this endearing and wonderful idiot. In one particularly memorable episode we take a trip to Ireland to visit the Dooley clan, who reside in a magnificent castle (one of a few striking pixely vistas; the game is often very lovely to look at).The cases themselves are of a decent length and do a solid job of poking fun at the illogical logic of the point-and-click, whilst slickly evoking what makes them great – the bizarre thrill of combining items in obscure ways, often without quite understanding  it matters. In this respect I reckon  is more challenging than its predecessor, although there’s the odd silly and inexplicable puzzle that’s difficult to solve in a logical way, even by the game’s standards. But then it wouldn’t be a point-and-click without ‘em, would it?As much as I love the genre, though, it’s not  gameplay that attracts me to it. Much like the first game, Twin Lakes is a wonderful place to spend time in – and such a brilliant locale for point-and-click adventures. It’s full of quirk and character, with every interaction, no matter how small, helping to expand the game’s world into something truly eclectic. Somewhere so far beyond the horizon of supernatural silliness that you can’t help  find pleasure in it.Its immersive qualities owe a great debt not only to the writing, but also Thomas O’Boyle’s stellar soundtrack. He couldn’t have crafted a more ideal set of tunes to go along with McQueen and Dooley’s adventures.It’s been a real kick spending the last few nights in unhinged retirement homes and haunted funfairs (and their Darkside mirrors, ).Which I suppose is weird when I don’t actually find  as funny as most people do. Sure, I always had a smile on my face, but it never quite had me laughing hysterically, which is where I feel I ought to be with its brand of comedy. That may be because it's working overtime to be funny, forever in pursuit of the joke whether there’s one there or not. I think writing-wise that’s a mistake, and it’s something that held the first game back, too. A pause is a valuable tool, but  games aren’t sure where that is, or even which joke or pun is best. So it goes for broke, never quite hitting the highs it wants. It’s a pacing issue.But that smile it elicited never wavered, in part because McQueen and Dooley make for such an enjoyable pair and are the perfect window into Twin Lakes. They charmed me back in 2017 (or whenever it was I played the first…it’s possible it was later, but whatever!) and charm me still. But I think I want them to win my , and the writing will need to find a better balance to do that.With a seventh case to be unlocked at a later date there's still time to do that, and the strengths of  are such that I’m already anticipating the inevitable third game. Spooky Doorway have set themselves no limit on what supernatural shenanigans can manifest in Twin Lakes, and we should be grateful for that.Originally published on .

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is a sequel to The Darkside Detective, being a funny point-and-click mystery game with pixel artstyle. It takes place about a year after the first game, and Det. McQueen is trying to bring his friend Officer Dooley back from the Darkside. Like before, there are 9 cases to solve, actually 11 since case 9 is 3 smaller cases, and each of them pretty longer than the first game. In total, the sequel is almost double its length.Gameplay is identical to the first, and so is the Gravity Falls-like funny mystery in small town vibe. The humor is kinda better, I think they're funnier and more meta, like one time a Bloodwolf tells us to leave a positive review (which of course I did) complete with a *wink wink*. The levels are also bigger, more varied, and also more creative with the events going on, like time travel and digital worlds which makes the cases in the first game feel pretty tame by comparison.If you enjoyed the first game, you'll most likely enjoy The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark more. It's the same, but better and longer yet managed to stay fun and not monotonous. If you're a fan of the genre and looking to play this duology, you should play the first game before this since there are many characters and references to events you won't understand if you skipped straight to the second title.

_childDocuments_.review: A Fumble in the Dark is a solid follow-up to the original Darkside Detective. It’s not so much an iterative sequel as an additional set of cases; it’s the exact same point-and-click mechanics, same art, same characters. Yet I didn’t enjoy it as much as the first one. The developers seem to have upped the difficulty of the puzzles; most are fine, but there are a few that are particularly complex and obtuse, and required me to hit walkthroughs to progress. I also found it less funny; I can’t tell if this is because the jokes aren’t as sharp, or if it’s simply a result of the fact that a sequel is inherently less surprising than the original, and familiarity is the death of comedy.These complaints aside, it’s still an amusing point-and-click, crafted with love, with a nice episodic structure to break things up and free episodes added post-release.

_childDocuments_.review: (AFitD)is the sequel to the excellent  and takes you back to Twin Lakes, the 34th most haunted city in America, and into the role of Detective McQueen. Six more cases will see you solve puzzles in places like a warped funfair, a psychically possessed retirement home and a druid's castle in Ireland. takes place just after the end of the first game and expands on a lot of the characters and themes from it. Thankfully, it doesn't do that stupid sequel trope of re-calling the events or attempting to detail anything from the prequel. It just picks up the baton and runs with it, as all sequels should, in my opinion. This does lead to the game being totally unwelcoming to newcomers. If you have not played the first game, you will have absolutely no clue who anyone is or what's going on.As for the writing, it's still brilliant.  cases go into the finer details on characters and go to strange new places. The dialogue is still sharp and witty and the game uses its large ensemble cast to flesh out the city of Twin Falls really well. We even leave Twin Falls and America in some of the cases, with one taking place in Ireland. Marking one of the few times in gaming that a level set in Ireland has been written by Irish people, this case is easily the best in the series. The main characters of McQueen and Dooley are both given much more backstory imbuing them even more a sense of life than before. Dooley's, in particular, is explored in great depth, and he's fast becoming my favourite character in any game ever. His swings from absurd levels of idiocy to astounding clarity are never jarring and fit perfectly with his goofball side-kick character. His general cluelessness is the basis for a lot of the humour and it's so well done that it never gets old or repetitive. Gameplay is the standard point and click adventure fare. You explore the rooms, pick up items and talk to everyone you can to solve puzzles and progress the story. As with the prequel, there's no moon logic puzzles and most can be solved with a bit of lateral thinking and some time. That said, there are one or two that will have you thinking for a while on the solution, but it's through genuine challenge, and not because you don't happen to think along the same lines as the writer. The main difference between  and its prequel is the length. Where DD could be cleared in around four hours, that would only get you to the end of the third case here. There's still no dying in . While this didn't ruin the game for me, I felt it undermines some of the more dramatic scenes. For example, there's a scene where you're stuck in a box that's filling with water, the music has changed to create a sense of tension, but you've all the time in the world to escape as the water level never rises. It makes no sense to construct a scene to evoke danger, only to erase it right at the start. It didn't ruin any of the scenes for me though, but it did leave me wondering about why that was done.The graphics are the same as in the first game, basic but functional, although a little more effort has gone into making sure that items are more defined than in . The character models are all well done, and the background art sets each scene up nicely. There's much more variety in the backgrounds than in the previous game.The music score is not composed by Ben Prunty as with . The composer here is Thomas O'Boyle, and his score is just as effective. Simple and unique, each track suits the area it's used in perfectly. It doesn't distract from the game and sets the tone nicely. The  which doesn't clash with the comedic elements of the game. The game still lacks voice acting and can get oddly quiet at times due to the lack of any environmental sounds.If you enjoyed , then this is more of what you love. If you didn't enjoy  then this is more of what you disliked.  is a superb second entry in a series I hope runs for a long time. For the most part, it's pretty much identical to the first installment. It does require the player to have played the first game to know what's going on and I'm still convinced the only thing preventing this series from becoming sensational is the lack of a good voice cast.  cements the  series as a staple of every adventure game fan's collection.

This game brought back all the fun characters from the original, introduced even more hilarious dialog and references, and added engaging interactive puzzles; nothing too brain-destroying to make a minimally frustrating experience.Things I liked (in no particular order):- Those chunky, bright-colored pixels - they are positively charming.- The music. _childDocuments_.review: [Early review, will update.]A Fumble in the Dark is excellent. As with the first Darkside Detective game, it's a funny, heartfelt point & click adventure about police work in a moderately-cursed city. The game is structured into self-contained cases, with each case taking about an hour and having its own locations, items, etc., but you'll see plenty of recurrent characters. Puzzles are generally inventory-based, but with some clever set pieces as well, like a devilish telephone switchboard. What separates this game and its predecessor from others in the genre is just how  it is. It's well-written and genuinely funny, without any of the sarcastic edgelord humor that this genre often has. As an adventure game, it hits the right level of difficulty for a fun but thoughtful playthrough: in general, there's little sign-posting about what to do next, but the puzzles are also logical (by the standards of a cursed city, anyway) and you can pretty much always work out what to do next by just thinking through it or paying attention to dialogue. You'll feel very clever but also won't have a migraine.  In comparison to the first game, A Fumble in the Dark doesn't reinvent the wheel but it also doesn't sit still. It's a bit more polished and practiced in a lot of facets. The pixel art's a little more vibrant and eyecatching, the writing's gotten a bit sharper and funnier, and the production values generally seem higher. In sum, it's exactly what I was hoping it would be, and will easily be on my list of top adventure games in 2021.

_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: The only negative I can think of is that I was so excited to play it that I rushed through all six cases and now I have no more Darkside Detective to enjoy... for now.
