_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: – Point-and-click mystery solving and mini games that are fun and not too hard– Lots of humor– An adorable friendship– Cute pixel art– Overall cute and fun, and this one hit me in the feels more than the first!*My actual playtime is about 8 hours. I played this elsewhere but now have a Steam copy too.*This is going to be less of a review and more just me rambling about my feels and specific things I loved. If you’ve already played and loved the first game, all you need to know is that this is just as great, with more of the same gameplay and humor and friendship, and you should play it! If you’re still not convinced, you should know that you also get to see McQueen’s butt (which, let’s be honest, you’re probably a little disappointed that it’s not Dooley’s, but McQueen’s no slouch). 😉 And if you didn’t play the first game yet, you can read my review for that one.There is one potential technical problem, which is my only negative. There seems to be an issue with save data getting deleted. It happened to me multiple times, and I found some other people mention it online too. If it does happen to you, the best workaround I could figure out was to play each case in one sitting and check the Spooky Doorway website FAQ to learn how to unlock all the cases. That way, you can at least move on to the next case even if your previous cases don’t stay marked as “solved.”Now, moving on to my thoughts about the game and story. Warning, there are some spoilers ahead that might ruin some jokes or emotional impact if you haven’t played this sequel yet.There are even some extra jokes if you check out the game settings/options.The launcher I used says I played for 9 hours, though probably half an hour to an hour was spent replaying and trying to fix the save issues.Anyway, another fun game!(May not include everything)– Not accessible for blind / visually impaired players or screen reader users.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Played through! Not as good as the 1st one but still worthy of your time and money. Loads of fun.That said, this overall experience is the best I can get these days... since not a lot of teams are making games in this genre anymore. The last one I enjoyed more than this one is Unavowed. Keep them coming please! Now here is the real stuff↓Pros: - Puzzles are easy enough, if not a bit tedious. - Funny dialogues- Coherent story plotting- Supernatural theme- Slightly dark humorCons:- Font is a little illegible, disrupting the fun of reading the dialogues- Clues for puzzles can be irrelevant sometimes, making it boringI must recommend that either you guys make the game window-able or change the font, because now the fonts are too big yet too pixel-ized, making it hard to read. Also a lot of lines are trying toooooooo hard to be funny, that they are no longer as funny as you wanted them to be.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: A Fumble In The Dark is a perfectly cromulent adventure game, once you turn off the ghastly music.I bought this a while back after not hating the original game. Kept trying to play it, could never make it through more than an episode at a time because the music is literally painful to my ears. Normally I stick with a game's original soundtrack to try respect what the developers intended, but in this case the music just pushes my every button. It's that kind of deliberately dissonant "spooky" style that sounds like someone randomly mashing on a cheap Portasound whose pitch bender got stuck. It's the worst. So I turned it off, cued up something good instead, and suddenly the game got much better.And yet it remains an unremarkable 7/10, same as the first game. The dialog is mildly amusing. The puzzles are absurd, but most of them are signposted well enough. The graphics are what they are, decent enough pixel art. The characters are fine. They're forgettable. And that's the biggest problem with the Darkside Detective series. I don't care about anyone in it. Don't care about their city. Not particularly interested in anything that happens. It's all very wholesome and pleasant, but it never feels like there's any stakes, there's no real conflict, it never feels like anything you do matters. Each episode just comes across as arbitrary set dressing around a handful of puns and puzzles instead of an actual story. If you want some inoffensive point and clicking where you don't need to think or care too much, it's fine, I suppose. Just turn the damn music off.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: They took a great game, and made an even better sequel.Memorable characters, mystifying mysteries, the ghost of Nikola Tesla vowing revenge on a robot pigeon - this game has it all. _childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal adventure game with genuinely funny writing. _childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good sequel. I loved the original, and while this game is longer and more complex it also has less heart, somehow. The biggest drawback is the inability to skip over repeated dialogue. The humor gets really labored really fast when you have to click through multiple dialogue screens over and over again just to see if anyone has anything new to say (which does happen). Still recommended if you enjoyed the first installment, and/or old school games in general.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with a whimsical setting, excellent comedy writing, and decent puzzles. It also solves one of the main problems of the point-and-click genre: moving characters from one point to another. This is usually boring and a waste of time. But here, thanks to the minimalistic and creative screen design, you can fully focus on the story and puzzles without unnecessary movement.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: This is a humorous throw-back to old-school adventure games. You are a detective for a dubious 'Darkside Division'. You are tasked with investigating supernatural crimes with your oblivious partner. The game is delivered in 20-30 minutes episodes, each connected through running gags and characters to the previous. The puzzles are fairly simple, though you may need a walkthrough on occasion. By far, the best part of the game is the humor -- this is not a serious detective game. More like a buddy comedy with puzzles!This series has rekindled my love of old-school adventure games and I can only recommend you buy this along with the first. You won't regret it
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the first game, you'll probably enjoy this because it's more of the funny point and click antics from the first game.If you haven't played the first game you should probably play that first? but also I highly recommend that game to point and click enthusiasts and also enthusiasts of fun.Waited to finish the game to post my review but I don't really know why because it's not like there was any point during my playthrough where I expected this would be anything but positive.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm mixed on this one, but I'm glad I bought it and glad it got me to re-play the original.On the one hand- I absolutely had to go back and play the original again for a solid number of the jokes to land or the plot to make sense. And on top of that, I actually do just feel like the sequel is more guilty of impossible Point-and-Click Puzzle Moon Logic than the original, and that was already the first game's biggest failing.And yet, as I play this game, I keep seeing characters show up again and getting a big stupid smile on my face because I adore them, and I just know that they'll be there for great jokes.This game is still a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ riot, even if I have to spend time looking at guides to get through the cases, finding out that my pixel-hunting skills were off-base, or I didn't remember some weird turn of logic I was supposed to use. Those annoyances are worth it for the jokes. This is a game where you usually have a sidekick or 3 following you from screen to screen, and it's absolutely worth your time to check what they have to say at every step. A more cleanly-designed game might use those points to give you hints to the more challenging puzzles, and I do kinda wish they did, but I also don't want to miss out on all the beautifully stupid dialogue that's gone into this game.I strongly recommend going to the first game and playing its demo first, which is just its first (and best) case. If that seems like your jam, the first game is a riot, and this one follows suit on delivering more Darkside Detective Nonsense, and I means that Oh-so-very affectionately.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I'm a big fan of the point and click genre as well as the first game. I was very excited to play this title when it released, and I'm already loving it. _childDocuments_.review: Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark does not disappoint, it builds off what Darkside Detective 1 was, and continues to be a hilarious game with several puns, meta-jokes, fourth wall breaks, interdimensional portals, bears, embarassing memories, a cladly clothed Dooley, and much, much more. _childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderfully funny adventure game, with entertaining puzzles, charming characters and full of (often quite obscure) in-jokes and references to the adventure game genre and horror/sci fi media. A perfect break for a fan of the Darkside who needs a light break from the heavy stuff and are ready to laugh at beloved tropes and conventions. The game does not solely rely on meta-humor and sci-fi references - don't worry this isn't Rick and Morty - and you can have quite an average IQ to figure out the puzzles, as long as you embrace Adventure Game logic. It does at points reach levels close to "fake-moustache-made-of-cat-hair-and-glued-on-with-honey" (*cough cough* bubblegum *cough cough*) but it's played with a wink and if you ask around enough you should be able to gather enough hints to decipher the moon logic without reaching for a guide. And you don't mind clicking around and trying a bunch of different combinations in this game, because the writing and flavor texts are delightful. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Apart from the same winning dry humor of the original(s), Fumble in the Dark now has 200% more fourth-wall-breaking, and a degree more charm that I don't quite remember being there before: There's still plenty of back-and-forth banter between the duo, but now a sort of budding caramedrie that we get to see as McQueen trusts Dooley with his life at several points, and lets him put the finishing touches on several cases , and Dooley for his part is more generally helpful and friendly, but retains his classic dunderheadedness that gets them into all sorts of misadventures, but naturally in part also due to McQueen's own nerdy, relatable antics.For those new to the series, Darkside Detective is just as advertised, a witty puzzle adventure with not-so-straightforward, ofttimes unearthly solutions to mundane problems, but everything coming together in the end for a satisfying playsession each episode. Certainly worth the price for the playtime you get out of each individual episode (currently there are 8, with a 9th seemingly in the works), plus replayablity in finding all the secrets in each, and who can say no to a weird, winding story with returning references & characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Good sequel. Playing the first two cases took me four hours - that's with talking to everyone and exhausting every dialog option, examining every hotspot and extra backtracking to make sure I didn't miss anything. Your mileage may vary.Still pixel art, somewhat streamlined adventure game but this time you're given more freedom to roam around, backtrack, and wonder what you're supposed to do with a given item.Minor quibble, I did find a minigame involving a map to be unintuitive: you're supposed to examine all locations for certain clues like a phone, but you can't examine a location unless you "cross out" all others first. In a process of elimination, you'd expect the exact reverse.Controller support is good, I was able to alternate seemlessly between the mouse and an Xbox controller, which is always appreciated.I found the writing a bit better, with more jokes landing for me - although I found the fourth-wall-breaking ones to be very hit or miss. However, compared to other titles like Gibbous: A Cthulu Adventure or The Book of Unwritten Tales, there are considerably less custom lines when you try an item on something you're not supposed to. Given the aforementioned games are voiced and this one is not, it's a pity the devs didn't double down on this aspect. It would've given the game a lot more charm.The main characters are parodies but are still likeable, the music is good and the pixel art well done, and you still run into incredibly wacky situations. Verdict: play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This was such a disappointing sequel. If you liked the concept and the demo, play the first game. This sequel only has hints of the old humor and it drags on and on in many ways. They're in stark contrast from each other. Also, I wouldn't be playing a detective/cop game if I wanted to see everyone dog pile on the protagonist for their career. Where's the humor in that? Why would you make a detective game if you hate cops so much? Of course that's not the only thing that's propagandized. So if you don't like smug, condescending as*hats that posture they're the voice, judge, and savior of the people they harm, then I'd say to avoid this game. It becomes more and more apparent with each case the detective takes. The beginnings are palatable, but quickly go downhill.

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside games follow a pretty straightforward path. Weird mystery, goofy jokes, point and click puzzles. Its not aiming to be more than a short fun time and it excels at what it does. Still, the first game struck me as a bit mean-spirited and cynical in its utter disinterest in (even outright distaste for) a wider narrative.That sensibility is still present here, but its more polished and refined. The already tenuous 4th wall completely drops in Fumble in the Dark. Characters bemoan that they don't love the archetype/obstacle they have to be this episode, but push through for the sake of the puzzles. The puzzle designer shows up to get angry at the idea that McQueen would want to skip the puzzle she worked so hard on. So on and so forth. It feels more like actors going through the motions than a goofy world. You'd think it'd get tiring, but it ends up swerving back around to endearing somehow.I think what really makes this work is the shift in McQueen and Dooley's dynamic. They were a classic serious downtrodden protag/goofy sidekick team, with McQueen often the brunt of being treated as a fool and a loser by his "friend" Dooley. Because the 4th wall is almost nonexistent, McQueen and Dooley develop this new dynamic where they both know their roles and thrive in it. The dumb jokes are more for the other's benefit than the audience's. When their usual back-and-forth starts back up, there's more affection to it. Its the Sam and Max dynamic rather than a sadsack hero and his dumb friend. The rare moment the game tries to be sincere, its always focused on McQueen and Dooley's friendship rather than some big threat. It adds a much needed dose of heart to a game series that I enjoyed but found a little hollow. Its just a sweet game about solving puzzles with two goofballs pointing to something weird and going "that's stupid. Let's go make fun of it together."

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game!I bought the first one on a whim, it say in my library for a few months, and when I finally played it I was like 'I HAD A GEM THE WHOLE TIME AND HAD NO IDEA!' _childDocuments_.review: 5/10This game has the good aspects from the original (simple interface, nice pixel art).Unfortunately it has a lot more of the bad aspects too (horrible jokes, many illogical puzzles, absolutely moronic characters).Dooley is totally useless as a partner. Unlike other games where partners provide useful hints or information, Dooley is purely there for comedic relief - making annoying dad jokes and puns. Blind playthrough of the whole game took me about 10 hours, and I cringed at some of the ridiculous puzzles. For example, at one point you need a crank/handle and the solution is to take it out of a painting. And near the end of the game, you have to increase the volume of a speaker by drawing a number higher than its maximum output. WTF."A Fumble in the Dark" is aptly named because a lot of times I felt I was really fumbling around cluelessly, just mindlessly trying inventory objects on everything.

Communism = We must achieve equity in making everyone dirt poor because there is only so much to go around.  (while the elites still live like elites)       Capitalism = We can make, create and produce more guys, and everyone can work their way up.  Even our poorest don't starve. _childDocuments_.review: After having played and hated the first game, my expectations were low for this game. While I can say that this was better than the first, I can't say that it is good. Story-wise, I liked that it actually had some follow-up from the first game and subsequent cases for a while, but after the first three or so, it went downhill. The "action scenes" felt like they were supposed to instill tension but fell flat on its face.Humor-wise, it has even more unfunny references and meta-humor than the last game, which is saying a lot. That said, the few jokes that didn't fall into this category were a lot funnier than the average jokes from the original. But every time I laughed at a good joke, I cringed three times from yet another quip about how they're in a video game.And since I waited until the 9th case to write this review, I gotta say... it was a huge letdown. It was way too easy to solve to feel satisfied. Not to mention it felt rushed, between the constant reuse of characters and other assets (even if you don't count the people in the stands at the baseball game, the number of reused characters far outweigh the original ones) and the spelling and grammar mistakes found throughout, such as one character redundantly using the word "the" twice in a row.Disappoint me once, shame on you. Disappoint me twice, and I won't play whatever third game this series decides to release.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a lot of point and click adventure games. Some of them are good, some of them are bad, and this game is solidly in the latter category.The game is basically a "homage" to the sort of "weird but not necessarily horror" genre - stuff like Twin Peaks. It doesn't do it in a good way though, more of a "Hey, remember Twin Peaks? Huh? Huh?" kind of way. Not to mention that genre's already oversaturated with better games - Thimbleweed Park for one. I played the first of the game's seven cases, and it was just.. bad. It's difficult not from a "this puzzle is actually difficult" perspective, but from one of bad signposting and overall bad game design. There's a puzzle early on where you have to find three things and know where two of them are. You find a mysterious piece of paper with an address on it. It's not hard to figure out the paper has the location of the third thing... only to get the third address as a location, you have to use the paper on a completely unrelated item. I had to look up a guide specifically to figure this out, because I had no idea what the hell the game wanted me to do with it.I grabbed the other two items with relatively little difficulty, and then went to the final puzzle - which involves moving pegs with wires on them to form patterns. This puzzle was where I dropped the game: again, not because it was difficult, but because it was just poorly designed. You see, you can't simply pull the wires out and re-insert them. You have to move them over each other - which is not at all hard to do, just extremely tedious. At that point I felt like I'd had enough and refunded the game.The writing also isn't great. It's trying to be funny, but just.. isn't. At all. I'd say avoid this.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark" is a text adventure game similar to old LucasArts adventure games like The Secret of Monkey Island and Day of the Tentacle but with a kinda lame supernatural detective shtick instead of any kind of interesting topic, leaving us with decades old game-play, pixel-crap "graphics" and an unjustifiably high price tag for the kind of game you can slap together in hours using the Adventure Game Construction Kit (but this is made in Unity, so I guess as well as not knowing how to do computer graphics properly, they also eschew doing things the easy way, having put in a lot of effort to achieve the same thing a construction kit can do). From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  Because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game."The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark" has the far too high price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  For comparison, the $15 asking price for this game could get you games like "Europa Universalis IV", "Grand Theft Auto V" or "Dead by Daylight".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.  There's also thousands of free, superior quality games on Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Edit to add: The developers of this game, Spooky Doorway, are the best.  They just added the first of three planned free bonus cases on Christmas Eve.  I played it as soon as it was available, and it was great fun.  They did the same thing with the first Darkside Detective, adding completely free a series of bonus cases well after initial release.A lot of (sometimes minor) characters from season 1 of The Darkside Detective make return appearances in this second season -- it's cool they keep building out the world like that -- and to refresh my memory I started going back and replaying episodes from the first game while going through this one.  And I enjoyed them so much again that I ended up replaying all of them in random order.  That ended up making me feel as I finished this game up (except the, at this point, unreleased bonus episode) that the second season wasn't quite as good as the first.  But that's a very high bar to try to reach, since I loved the first season.  Main comparative downside for me was that it seemed like they aimed to build out longer episodes with more challenging puzzles, which was a good direction to take a lot of the time, but it was a bit marred by what seemed to me to be some excessively convoluted, directionless puzzles and moon-logicky item combinations that you needed to make and some cases of excessive backtracking through the larger environments trying to find something to interact with.  I don't want to sound down on Fumble in the Dark at all, though.  I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys humorous point and click adventure games.  It's again got top notch writing throughout.  The wrestling case in particular was my favorite from either season.  It's so stupid, but I still crack up every time I remember your antagonist in that episode being called 'The Overgiver.'  That's one minor example of The Darkside Detective games being rare gems in being comedic point and click adventure games that are actually really funny instead of just annoying and even rarer in being games that incorporate parodies of other pop culture that is actually creative instead of just being the usual 'hey remember that thing, this is a reference to that thing you remember, how about that!'  Within the confines of the super crude pixel style, it also looks really good.  Pixel art is often (most of the time probably, actually) just used as an excuse for lazy, crap art and graphics, but Darkside Detective (another example would be the two Last Door games) shows that when developers actually care about what they're doing and put in the effort it doesn't have to be that way at all.  Music and sound is also again excellent, and I suspect that not having voice acting is the right choice.  Bad voice acting is much worse than no voice acting, and indie P&C voice acting is usually bad.[empty edit for Steam awards badge]
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: After enjoying the original Darkside Detective point & click adventure game so much, I was looking forward to this sequel. And it has the same pixel art (crude but nonetheless very expressive), the same funny dialogue interplay between the characters, the same episodic format, and the same mix of achievements for game progression and for odd, easily missed interactions.But... for me, this game was good but somehow not as special and enjoyable as the first game; I've been trying to work out why. Perhaps I played A Fumble in the Dark too soon after the original - certainly I laughed out loud much less in this game. In both games I needed some help from the various excellent guides for the easily missed side achievements, but whereas I worked out nearly all of the puzzle and plot solutions myself in the original game, in this one I found myself stuck much more often; the solutions, when I found (or read) them, often seemed more contrived or "stretched out". This is reflected in my play time - each game had six core cases and three bonus ones, but the first game took me almost exactly half of the time of the second.And that, I think, answers my question about why I preferred the first game - it was more tight and lean, with every action in the game understandable, purposeful and oddly logical (even if weird!), and no sense of "padding". I ended the first one happy and satiated, and hoping for more of the same another time; I ended this game with a slight sense of "job done" and relief.So, in summary, this is a good game, but the first one is extra-special and that is the one I would recommend to anyone trying these kind of point & click games for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: It plays a lot like a mobile game, in that you only need the left mouse button but it's a fun little adventure.The game, like its predecessor, is made up of a bunch of mini adventures or episodes.This means you'll never get stuck for long since every episode only has about a dozen screens.The graphics are great for what they are.There isn't a ton of music, but what there is is good enough that it never gets annoying.And the same goes for the sound effects, the game(s) are a good example of doing a lot with little.The gameplay is fairly standard adventure stuff, grab objects and combine them to solve problems.There are also some fun minigame puzzles, but very few of them.The story/stories are fun and funny and really the whole game has a bunch of jokes in it.Would I recommend it?If you like point and click adventures and don't mind the simplicity of the mobile origins, definitely.The characters, dialogue and story are a lot of fun and it's not too bad with the adventure game logic.Most puzzles have a logical solution and there is often a hint in what the characters are saying.

_childDocuments_.review: Return to the spooky world of Twin Lakes, a city so full of paranormal tomfoolery that it once had its own Spooky Division Police Force. Once again, follow Detective McQueen and his faithful (unofficial sidekick) along their quirky encounters with supernatural forces, from Darkside rescues to Sun restorations to  even escaping the clutches of a crazed clown gameshow. Along the way, encounter the vibrant cast of characters and phenomenon that makes the world of Darkside Detective a whimsical place.Like its predecessor, DD:FD is a point-and-click game spaced out into nine cases. Each case is largely self-contained, with occasional callbacks to previous ones. Most of the charm from the first carries over into the next, with some witty quips and zany antics here and there. I liked the passive worldbuilding and the nonchalant statements of nebulous logic. I especially liked how the last bonus case let us play the game as members of the supporting cast, getting their perspective on the crazy paranormal phenomena plaguing Twin Lakes.However, while I enjoyed the first game, I feel like this one was a step back:- There were multiple times where I was having difficulty following the game's logic, whether it involved where to go next or which items to use to get the next one. I was fine for most of the game, making the few places where I stumbled exceedingly annoying. - The game had an annoying habit of making progress lock out backtracking, making me antsy about missing some flavor dialog or achievements.- They could have toned down the meta commentary humor. Sometimes it felt like they couldn't go more than five sentences without "oh this is so wacky, thank goodness this works somehow" or "Wow, searching trash cans again, so silly". I enjoy third-wall breaking, but there needs to be some restraint.- The last case didn't really feel all that climactic. The first game had a city spanning case, with multiple locations needing to be revisited. No case in this one gave that same grand-ish feeling. That being said, it was still a fun time. I think it's worth the $15. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: I complete the first Darkside Detective so I mostly new what to expect. Despite that it took me a while to get use to the series again. Graphics are intentionally very bad. I don't mind pixel graphics but in DD they are so low resolution it can be hard to pick out what parts of the screen are items that you can interact with.It also took me a while to get used to the humour. The game is funny, assuming you like "out there" humour. Some of the text is funny only because it is absurd. Once I got used to the style of humour again I began to appreciate the game more.The puzzles are mostly reasonable. There are a few "moon logic" puzzles, or more often, puzzles where the simplest solution is just to try every item you have. But mostly the puzzles don't get in the way of my enjoyment of the game.I completed all of the nine cases, including the three bonus cases. Most are fun although I found parts of the final case to be frustrating to play - too much text and the plot was too out there, and that is saying something for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is not only a great point and click adventure game; it's a very good sequel to the first game, now the story. It has been a year since Patrick Dooley was taken and trapped in the darkside, his best friend Francis McQueen desperately searches for him stopping at nothing even when the darkside division have been disbanded.But that will not stop him in finding his best friend, especially when Twin Lakes needs them when in Twin Lakes Spooks are spooking, cultists will be a cultisting and ummm monsters they monstering? Well only these two are capable of stopping the tide of terror with one fumble at time.Okay the likes, the story like the first game is really good with plenty of great twists and turns and plenty of good moments from comical to cool to even badass, all wrapped up in a story that doesn't take itself too seriously. They are also plenty of great callbacks to the previous cases of the first game from the item description to certain returning characters. The story also does a very good job with its commentary taking a lot of jabs at plenty of people, it's not subtle but it is quite enjoyable. The comedy like the first game is very good, quite well written with a good use of puns, innuendos and funny descriptions, some jokes didn't land but there were a lot of other jokes that certainly had me laughing. The characters are still really good and quite interesting even side characters and NPCs both old and new are quite well written with so many people to like, from the main characters like Francis McQueen and his partner Patrick Dooley to side characters like the bloodwolves and Raxa, to new npcs like the Sea Hags. The gameplay is still pretty fun it's your standard point and click game with picking up items and combining them, but there's also plenty of good and well balanced puzzles with a nice sense of exploration. The puzzles are really good and very fair while still quite challenging, just takes a good bit of brain work. The pixel graphic art style is still really good with plenty of great details with a great use of colors, even the more dark and somber colors have a nice sort of brightness to them, it’s all very well detailed and even better than the first game and the first games graphics were really good. The levels are still quite good and very diverse with so many nice little details that make the whole world feel alive; there are also plenty of great call backs to works of horror from the classics to even a few modern ones. The music is very good with plenty of nice tracks to listen too.Okay the dislikes, like the first game I would say this is perfect but there is one or two bugs like there's this one bug in the game where sometimes for some reason in the dialogue box you can't click on any of the different dialogue choices, but that's easily fixed by pausing the game and unpause it. Then there is this one bug, although truth be told it was more from my end, basically if you have a virus protection the game won't completely install no matter how many times you verify, luckily the good team at spooky doors helped me and I made a little tutorial in discussions on how to make sure all the files get downloaded, so future players know what to do.Now that's all done The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is not only a great point and click adventure game; it's a very good sequel to the first game, with a really good story, very good comedy and really good characters. So if you like the first game you're going to love this game I highly, highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: - Visual design is, of course, the same as the first game. Lots of appealing pixel art throughout- I don't know if it's just that I was paying better attention to the music, but it feels much improved this time. There's no real theme or genre to it, but it's all pretty good. The best tracks usually drop when the tension ramps up- Like the first game, the story unfolds as a series of sorta-connected vignettes. Unlike the first game, there's a consistent thread running throughout the narrative that nicely ties everything together. It mostly pertains to what happens in the aftermath of the first game, so be sure you've played the prequel before trying this one out- This is a marked improvement from the first title. My biggest complaint was the lack of a metanarrative to hold the story together, and that's nicely addressed in this game- The humor is still pretty good. This title is maybe a little funnier than the first game, but it's a close contest- As before, the writing/dialogue is superb. I love how well fleshed-out everyone's personality is. You can tell the writers put a lot of effort into this game- It's a point and click adventure game without may innovations on the basic formula. You'll wander around, investigate clues, pick up items, combine those items in humorous and unexpected ways, and inch the story along as you figure out each puzzle- I understand that it's an entrenched genre trope at this point, but I still feel like some of the solutions are really unintuitive sometimes. I wouldn't have naturally figured out to combine decorative bunting and a garden gnome to make a grappling hook. Frustration-induced item combining is more-or-less a prerequisite for plot advancement- Probably not going to return to the game, but only because I 100%ed the achievements. The chapter select menu made this much easier- Except for the graphics (which are basically identical to the the prequel) and the writing (which is still very good), just about every change made in this title is an improvement. It's really nice to see a developer build upon and evolve a series with a simple concept, carefully ironing out the wrinkles and refining their formula- The game ran perfectly on the Steam Deck. Basically just like the first one, but with several improvements. More of a good thing is always a good thing, so buy with confidence if you liked the first title

_childDocuments_.review: Darkside Detective 1 was an unexpected joy - it was an indie adventure that didn't try very hard to impress you with fancy graphics or deep plot. Instead, it just had two very charming characters and spun them off in several episodes to hilarious effect. But the main reason why the first one worked so well was seeing how the friendship between McQueen and Dooley grew. Which is precisely the issue with the 2nd one - their friendship doesn't really grow much anymore. In a bid to franchise this game, they decided to make it closer to a sitcom, but honestly it doesn't quite work. Aside from the lack of progress in their friendship, the jokes are laid way, way, way thicker this time - and the verbosity is honestly overkill. Less is more, and the attempts at jokes in the 2nd one became way more groan-worthy than in the 1st. The addition of some weird moon logic doesn't help. But honestly, one thing they can do is to stop the characters from repeating themselves when you click on them, especially since sometimes the text is multiple pages long (see: verbosity issue). The game still has its charm, but it is clear that less is not more. I'm gonna give this a 6/10 - more like a so-so for me, but not bad enough that I'd give it a thumbs down.

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is everything a sequel should be: bigger, longer, and more ambitious, but still absolutely hilarious.Mechanically, this game is as voluntarily primitive as the first game. Even for a point and click adventure game, it's very no-frills - the character are static in every scene, there are no walk cycle, no voice acting and very few special effects. However, like the first game, that doesn't matter, because it is all about the humour. I was so happy to delve back into this world where everybody is completely loony and weird, but nobody sees it as anything out of the ordinary. It's another absolute riot.Like the first game, A Fumble in the Dark is divided in a number of different, independent cases, like an episodic tv show. However, unlike the first game, these cases are much longer - each one took me at least an hour. This has pros and con. The pros is that the cases are richer, more complex, and more diverse. The cons is that it remove the "bite-sized, play on your break" aspect of the original. It's not a dealbreaker for me, but it could be for you. So yeah, if you want more of one of the funniest point-and-click game ever made, buy this!

_childDocuments_.review: A point and click adventure focussed on jokes, weird occurrences and a detective having to deal with it all, acting as a Sequel to the original The Darkside Detective.The game consists of multiple cases you’ll complete one after the other. Each of them features some spooky occurrence in a unique location, which you’re tasked with resolving. To do this, you can move between different screens making up the location and collect junk, which you’ll then combine in order to solve puzzles. From time to time, the game also throws in a minigame to shake things up. As you work through these cases, you’ll encounter a multitude of characters, who provide you with hints as to what you need to do, while also providing a couple of humours lines of dialogue. Many of these characters are encountered throughout different cases, giving some nice continuity and fleshing out their personalities. Some characters from the first game also return, which I very much enjoyed.You once again play as Francis McQueen, his jokes as dry and self-aware as ever, often joined by his loveable Partner Patrick Dooley, being just as goofy and easily distracted as in the game’s predecessor. These two, along with the other characters, provide a nice mix of light-hearted humour, which kept a smile on my face throughout my time playing the game. Jokes are often self-aware or referential, which works surprisingly well.Each case felt quite distinct to me, providing puzzles that were somewhat obscure, yet not too challenging to solve. The non-grid-aligned pixelated look works well for the game but at points feels too static, with few animations. While certainly rather absurd, the world created by the game feels consistent and scenes feature a convincing atmosphere.All in all, this is a good sequel, which retains the strength of the original, but sadly doesn’t really change things up much. Nevertheless, I still recommend you buy it, along with the first game in the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: Lets talk about how a very simple-looking game can have such a rich world."DsD Fumble in the Dark" and the "Darkside Detective" before it, are consistently well-written; the humor flows naturally, the side characters are treated with backstories making them memorable and fun to interact with. The pixel art is great, the music is appropriately soothing (and vintage) the game interface was very easy, I never "got stuck" due to the lack of cues (nor was I force-fed the cues) and that to me means well-thought game logic and leveled feedback to the player. The Cases are unlocked in a linear manner, complete one to tackle the next. There are 3 bonus cases which players can start, pause to go back to the main story if they want, then return to continue working on the bonus case.  I think that the intended way to experience the story is by playing all the cases as they unlock, then moving on to the bonus area. The linear nature of the cases works for the story narrative, since we get many recurring characters in the series, even from the very first case of "Darkside Detective".Each case is a tongue-in-cheek, fresh and interesting take of a cult reference. They all take place at different city locations so the game can not get repetitive unless intended (bird bones). This brings replay-ability value if you are hunting for achievements and will be revisiting the cases.The game's achievements is actually where my one pain point is, some are a little punishing. It helps that cases are very short to play through once you have solved them once and know what to do. But, you also have a lot of (great but seen) dialogue to click through. All cases can be accessed after completing the main case, that is also a great help, but for example, I missed the Camp Counselor achievement twice because of one rushed click out of the screen. I kept this part for last as it probably doesn't interest most. I was very happy with the good-nature of our characters being evident in the small things. I am a fan of the anti-hero as the next person, however and without spoilers, here is a small example of what I mean here: at some point our Detective discovers an open invitation to a birthday party hidden among some information brochures. After confronting the person stationed at the information booth about it, our detective confirms the employee sneaked their birthday invitation in the brochures, and concludes "We'll be there," and by now we know he means it. These small touches are consistent and bring to life the concept of this open-para-minded small community in the big city, plagued by paranormal havoc and obsurdity but still remember to be human to one another. Definitely give this game (series) a try. It kept me very entertained, for longer than I expected (a good 20 hours according to steam, without achievement hunting). This also includes some long, un-pauses as the game waited patiently while I got distracted, having the background music keeping me company :). Great work!
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Like the first game, the detective cases are creative and blend comedy and the supernatural well. A lot of care is put into the dialogue and interactable objects. The two main characters have a great chemistry that makes a lot of banter found in the game enjoyable. And I also like the simple minigames thrown in so that progression isn't 100% dedicated to just point-and-click. They don't offer much of a challenge but it definitely helps break up monotony and their some of them are pretty creative.Overall this has become my favorite modern point-and-click adventure game series. I really hope a 3rd game is planned for the future.

Treat yourself to a little more fun in Twin Lakes. And I can't wait for another!

_childDocuments_.review: A bigger and better sequel with more cases with more length to them, more puzzles and more comedy.  The very basic pixel art is charming and colourful, the writing is humorous and the challenge feels about right, if a bit on the easy side for adventure game veterans.  The music and settings are good and although quite basic, the full screen puzzles are a nice addition.  There are some truly terrible, groan worthy puns and the 4th wall breaking jokes do get a bit dull after a while, but there’s enough charm, wit and variety to make each case entertaining and a joy to solve.  I found it to be a comfortable and rewarding game which I enjoyed very much.

I highly recommend it!- Tough puzzles that may require help: Guide Link - (guide is not written by me but by XBL Laberbacke)
