_childDocuments_.review: An XCOM-like isometric tactical game set in a dark, gothic, post-apocalyptic world with an interesting visual style. Nightmarish creatures are roaming about and only the Daughters, clones of a great female warrior, can lay those creatures to rest. Aside from the usual XCOM-like features, such as isometric grid movement, action points determining what we can do in a turn, and squad-type missions, Othercide offers some of its own unique features too that spice up the gameplay.The overwatch feature is taken to the next level with a variety of skills acting as interruptions or reactions. Interruptions allow a daughter to counter an enemy attack on an ally in range, while a reaction can cause a daughter to have an additional action, depending on what triggers the reaction (e.g. an enemy coming within melee range getting automatically hit, etc). Daughters come in 3 classes in the beginning (+ a 4th class that becomes available partway through the game), each one with their own strengths and weaknesses. New skills can be unlocked at specific level ups, and at each such instance, we can choose one of two skills to go for, so there's some variety in builds even within the same class.The combat operates on a timeline system, where turns are dynamic. Enemies can be pushed back along the timeline so their turn comes later, and likewise allies can be boosted forward on the timeline to take their turns sooner. Some effects from abilities can also last for a specific duration amount or trigger at certain points on the timeline.Lastly, the game has a recollections system. If we fail at any point during a campaign, we can start over from the beginning with unlocked bonuses, tackling the same challenges with more advantages on our side. Some of these bonuses do allow us to skip past certain eras if we don't wish to replay them, so it's a nice mechanic. Can feel a bit grindy, but adds an interesting twist on the campaign progression.Generally, the game is challenging and we're almost always outnumbered, but there are many ways in which we can tackle these challenges. It's a very rewarding experience. Boss fights are also well-designed and fun. The only part of the game I disliked is the final boss, as it felt like a cheap difficulty spike, intended to force you to grind more.The story is mainly secondary to the gameplay and provides a nice backdrop for the conflict. The grey and red visuals also do great at enhancing the overall experience. There are some really amazing music tracks in places too, such as during the boss fights. But there are also some annoyingly jarring tracks playing during regular missions combat encounters. A great, challenging, tactical turn-based game that shows quality all around with only a few drawbacks. For a more in-depth review and a gameplay video, check here:

_childDocuments_.review: Too frustrating for me, but I'd say give it a shot if it looks good to you.This is not a bad game. The artstyle is nice, you have to be smart about the way you approach everything and the game as a whole feels well thought out.But - you have to be some sort of masochist to play this game, which I am not. And this is coming from someone who played Dark Souls way into NG++. Damage received in battles is permanent and if you want to heal a character, you have to sacrifice one of the same or a higher level. If a character is dead, she is taken to the cemetery where you could theoretically revive her, but the necessary resource can only rarely be obtained. Restarting the game is part of the game cycle and gives you a certain resource you can spend on bonuses, but it also makes all of your characters die. Interesting concepts for sure, but also extremely frustrating, pressuring you into "voluntary setbacks". This game makes me feel like a little more successful Sisyphos. You create characters and level them up only for them to die by the enemies' hand or by yours in order to heal another character. Then you create new characters to fill the gap and everything starts anew...I don't intend to put 50 hours into figuring everything out and leveling a few characters to the max when I could learn everything so much faster if the game was a bit more forgiving.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow...  This is game is seriously different and unique in it's genre class of turn-based games.  The storyline and characters are awesome!  Your character of daughters in this game symbolizes a family of cult fighters with abilities.  The gameplay is striking especially when you're looking at the fluid movements of your characters during combat.  I don't know why people are comparing this to Xcom.  The only thing I can see the two games have in common is they are turn-based.  Xcom is a game about humans fighting space aliens and there are a lot of research involve to make better guns and  ammunition.  Orthercide doesn't have any of these elements and the game is presented pretty much in black and white sort of like the movie Sin City.  The leveling system is very basic and there are only 3 types of classes to have.  But the game is very intriguing to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game!I'm ashamed I rarely play games for long periods of time, but moreso when it comes to this one. It's an absolute gem.The tactical turn based strategy involved is extremely well thought out. The enemy behaviors are phenomenal, to say the least. The roguelike elements make it easier to play through it again and again. The "Daughters" give each playthrough a unique feel, even if you build them the exact same every time. While I have not unlocked all the Daughters, I believe there's 4 classes, you can do most everything with the 3 they give you at the beginning.Shieldbearers - Your bona fide tank. She's got the armor and health to take the hits, while giving you a taunt, knockback, and other skills to keep your other Daughters alive.Blademaster - Could single-handedly massacre the entire enemy force, if it weren't for her complete lack of defense. Don't let the stop you from sending her on her own to take out a small group of annoying enemies, though.Soulslinger - The ranged support you never thought you needed. With interrupt skills as well as escape and crowd control, she's a force to be reckoned with in the right situation. Just, keep her at a distance as she's more fragile than your Blademaster.Even when things feel tough in this game, they still feel winnable. There's not a single scenario I have done where I thought, "Welp, that's it. I'm done for." And there were many times where I was left in awe at my final character getting the job done. However, being a roguelike, it allows you to go in, experience a new enemy, get a bit freaked out, but then go at them anyways because you have all the necessary abilities to take that enemy down.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels actively unpleasant to play. - VOs consist of a sobbing woman repeating the same lines over and over again. Atmospheric? Maybe. Also makes survival missions ridiculously brutal, when a full mission of enemies spawn right on top of the escape zone.- The above also means that you basically have to abandon your run the moment you kill a boss. Which matches the 'all hope is lost' theme, but it also means you don't feel the sense of risk that should come with permadeath.- It lacks QOL features such as viewing enemy-threatened areas.- Complete lack of customization options. There are no options to specialise a character into something, or to remove a trait.

_childDocuments_.review: Othercide is great in theory, but the experience is just awful. The good:Stylistically, the game is pretty nicely themed with that Black, White, and Red style. The Daughters you create are really cool and it's super interesting the way they degrade and such as they battle on. The trait feature with how you randomly gain super powerful buffs depending on what happens in your battles is super cool. The music also gave me like.. heavy early 2000's campy rock tones and I loved it. Also, it's not as difficult as most people say it is. In fact, once one of the classes hits 15 they get a skill that just all-kills the entire board apart from bosses.The Bad:Firstly, You cannot heal your characters without sacrificing one of equal or higher level on the normal difficulty. This kills that character AND changes the trait token you've given to the one being healed through previous sacrifices, which means you're often looking to only sacrifice Blademasters to heal to maintain their damage fragment. Secondly, the only way to revive a dead character is with a credit coin from either A: Restarting from the beginning, or B: Doing a rescue mission. If you do a rescue mission in the final act of the game, the pistol corrupted type enemy will almost always snipe your escortee and fail the mission. This game also massively encourages only 1 style of play to be successful - Ambushing Alpha-Strikes. Since you cannot heal, you often want to keep your character out of the enemies movement bubble so that they have to come to you first, wasting their turn, then pouncing on them and hoping you're able to kill it, otherwise it will be in range and hit you with permanent damage on it's next turn.  So many turns and time is wasted waiting for monsters to tell you they're going to spawn, then spawning, then moving, then you counter. It's a massive waste of time. Also, Boss monsters talk to you during regular missions, often repeating the same voice line over and over again. At one point a boss said "No, No, Memories hurt" 6 times in a row to me with no other lines inbetween.The Ugly: Right away, I'm putting this game as not recommended solely because of the last boss. It's massively overtuned often getting to attack your characters 10-15 (TEN TO FIFTEEN) times between each of your characters attacks. It also can swap places with any of your characters, and then cause them to explode for roughly 20% of their health. He also has a skill that just kills one of your characters. No tactics, no planning, no avoiding, just "Hey, she's dead now." It's definitely a killable boss, but it feels AWFUL and after asking your players to play through the game as many times as needed to be strong enough to get to him, this fight is just terrible. I was often doing one attack and then minimising the game to do something else while the boss took his time doing 6-8 minutes worth of abilities back to back. You don't want your player to be bored in your games climax. So all in all, I would say pass on this game. You're not missing a lot. If you do think you still want to play it get it on sale. I don't think I would ever play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: A rough gem. You should play other games in the genre first (XCOM, Darkest Dungeon, Into the Breach), but Othercide has its own merits and is within a sidestep away from standing against these giants with an expansion or sequel.Pros:- Obviously the art style is incredible. Original and beautiful from concept to execution. This is one of those games that I fell in love with from the title screen.- The gothic, lovecraftian aesthetic is on par with the best. The sense of hopelessness is thick in the air- The tactical complexity is very engaging and rewards smart play. When you understand how enemies and abilities work encounters that seemed impossible can be played through without losing a single HP- The sacrifice mechanic fits very well and forces you to consider every decision carefully- Sisters look bad ass and you will grow to care for them- The audio is top notch. The soundtrack is creepy and tense, the voice acting and sound effects are great. The reaper sounds still make my skin crawlCons:- The game is designed to be played through multiple runs, but it lacks the content to be interesting after one or two. With only 4 classes (3 for half the game) and not that many base enemy archetypes. Also the duration of a single play through is very long and some of the repetitive encounters could be cut down- The UI is buggy and slow to update to input. It often displays wrong information that can be run ending in a game as punishing as this. Do not trust the UI and always double check before committing to an action!- The UI lacks important information. Skill upgrades (memories) are not visible at all in descriptions in game, even though their effect can be as important as the skill itself. Duration of effects like root is not displayed. Character codexes can't be viewed in battle, forcing you to remember that enemy 1 targets lower HP, while visually identical enemy 2 targets higher HP

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really cool tactical turn based game, feels like a hybrid between XCOM and Darkest Dungeon. The music is great, the atmosphere is awesome, and the strategy can be great. I am definitely looking forward to playing more already, but there are a couple things that the developers really need to address to make this game a 10/10.First, there NEEDS to be more level/enemy variety. I had been playing the game for only a half hour when I started a new battle and immediately recognized the same map/enemy location from a battle I had fought earlier. While taking my time in the earlier eras, with 6 hours in so far, I have had ONE mission that was not the generic hunt mission type. I have had to quit and take a break from the game multiple times just to make the fights feel fresh. Even just enabling enemy placement to be random would be a HUGE breath of fresh air. Second, and immediately following point 1, there needs to be some more ability variety for the Daughters. At the moment all of my classes have been built the exact same way in the cookie-cutter pattern I think suits each class best, and the only real variety to each Daughter is what level they are. This is ESPECIALLY bad when paired with point 1, as not only am i fighting the exact same battle again, I am usually clearing it in the exact same ability order I did the first time.Maybe make the ability you get on level up random instead, anything to add a bit more variety.Third (and this is more a Quality of Life) you are able to change the name of a Daughter when they are first "born", but as soon as you pick their class, you can never again change their name. I've had to remove multiple "dead" characters from my graveyard just because they shared the name I wanted, and sacrifice other characters because I didnt like their default name.Fourth, why do ALL of your characters die whenever you reset lol? Getting wiped by a boss, alright maybe, but just resetting to train? Having to completely trash your roster just to go back to the earlier battles to grind kind of defeats the purpose. Either that, or there needs to be a faster way to earn Resurrection tokens. Very early on, you get a perk that allows you ONE Rez token whenever you reset, which means you can essentially carry only ONE character between runs. At this point, I have been playing for over 6 hours, just taking my time and grinding slowly, and I have never gotten a second resurrection token in a run. Maybe they are easier to get in later eras, but then why would you need them when your default un-nameable characters from the start of the run and other new chars are all level 10+?Definitely hurts the "getting attached to your soldiers" concept that we all loved from XCOM, especially in the early game.Let me be clear, I definitely enjoy this game and I do recommend it to anyone who enjoys rougelites and turn based strategy games. I also understand that this is a brand new game and things may be changed around a bit in the coming months. But I really hope that the developers see this review and think about a couple of these changes, while not a developer myself, I cant imagine most of these (such as allowing re-naming or letting enemy placement be random) would be terribly difficult to implement. With just a little bit of polish, this could easily land as one of the top 2020 games of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: More of a 'meh' or 'it's ok' than a real thumbs up. This is really one of those games that makes me wish steam had that option rather than the binary because I don't dislike this game but I also don't love it.The main reason for this is the roguelike format. Now I enjoy roguelikes for the most part but here it really feels like a way to pad out the game more so than anything tied to story or progression. It's as if they decided that four classes and five bosses wasn't enough.The thing is, I think it is enough, or it would be if there were a little more tactical depth to the gameplay. The XCOM reboot games only have 4 classes as well but they make the best of it having mechanics layered over them, like the cover system, the research, the choice of equipment. In Othercide there's just kind of ... nothing.The dynamic timeline system is the only really interesting part to the strategy layer in my opinion, and that's done really well here, but it isn't enough to make up for the fact that each class only has one role to play on the field. Sure you can pick between two abilities at each level milestone, but they are not created equal and some are just plainly more useful then others. So the repeating of sections (thankfully you don't have to repeat the whole game because once you encounter a boss you can skip straight to their section on resetting your playthrough) just became a bit tedious for me and I really felt I'd seen everything by about the 2/3 point. I get what they were going for with the whole 'fight against hopeless odds' thing but I feel like there must have been a less repetitive way to get that feeling across. Add to that the weird 'permadeath but not quite' system where you can bring back high level units between runs but can't heal them without sacrificing an equal or even higher level unit and I found that progress slowed down so much after the halfway point I eventually just lost all motivation to play.Game looks spectacular though and the soundtrack is a standout. I dunno what genre you'd call it, some kind of metal? But it hits different when the lyrics start during the last phase of a boss fight. Would love to see a sequel or successor.

I wanted to enjoy it but I found the game to be too lacking in UI readability and feedback.- The aesthetic is very cool but everything ends up looking very samey and its hard to really understand the battlefield at a glance, having to constantly zoom in and click on things just to remember what they are. Definitely not a good game for people with eye sight trouble.- Lots of information that I would love to know is just not present in the UI for a game of this ilk, like just a number for how far enemies can move.- Speaking of movement, the lack of grid makes it annoying to judge distances, and all you get are weird bubbles on the map to show how far something can go.- Other things in menus are seemingly absent, like the AP cost of your actions when upgrading them.- The timeline is a neat concept but like everything else, hard to gauge, which is a problem since its a core concept. Furthremore, icons on the timeline are sometimes incredibly vague, showing you SOMETHING happens in 30 steps but not what will happen or even who is doing it without clicking on things.Further less significant problems include- Really annoying, pretentious and vague dialogue that happens constantly during a battle. The game really loves its "Plague" theme and wont shut up about it.- Dull music.- Nothing to get you invested in it other than an extremely vague premise and the rogue-like mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: A challenging turn-based tactics game that pulls no punches, but don't let that intimidate you. Othercide's main gimmick is its Initiative timeline. Instead of a static turn order like other turn-based tactics games with set orders, Othercide uses a dynamic timeline where both your army of Daughters and the enemies will move up and down. The further up the initiative you are, the sooner you act. Both Daughters and enemies have abilities that can either pull allies up in the timeline, or push enemies back further down. This will be your saving grace, as manipulation of the timeline is critical to a successful mission, and often means the difference between life and death. Of course, chances are you'll soon find your Daughters defeated and the run over. However, this is not the end; far from it. Whenever you finish a run, you unlock Remembrances; powerful modifiers that can greatly increase your odds of survival. These can include additional damage buffs to specific enemy types, starting with higher level Daughters, or even starting a run with a previous Daughter resurrected from the dead. Every time you fall is another chance to get back up, stronger than before.Othercide's other unique trait is healing: there is none. Not in the traditional sense, at least. The only way to regain health to an injured Daughter is via sacrificing another Daughter of equal or higher level. And as a good amount of abilities cost a small percentage of health, even your Daughters who have never been touched by enemies will soon find themselves on their last legs. This becomes a careful balance of Daughters, managing who keeps around and who must be sacrificed to save another. Those sacrificed also pass on a powerful trait to those they heal, adding another consideration to the mix. For those who find this daunting, you can opt to enable "Dream Mode", which will restore a Daughter's HP at the end of the day instead, allowing for a much more casual approach to the game, with less stress on balancing all your Daughter's HP.Visually, I think Othercide may be among my top prettiest looking game. The monochrome world occasionally interrupted by the splatter of crimson blood and the bright red scarves of your Daughters, which also double as a dynamic HP bar, is captivating. The enemy and boss designs are also equally fascinating and disturbing. The soundtrack also does a wonderful job of bringing the entire game together into a gritty, dark world, where it is up to you and The Red Mother to carry on the last spark of flame in this dying reality.

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings Always!  Today I’ll be reviewing “Othercide” a turn based tactics game with some interesting roguelite mechanics.  I believe this is a first for the tactics genre and along with a very distinctive art style game definitely stands out from the crowd but the question always remains; is it worth your time?  Let’s discuss.Our Journey into Paradise:  Before anything we have to discuss the atmosphere of this game.  Probably one of the most beautifully, high contrast style I’ve seen in a long time.  The only real colors used in the game are black, white (shades of both) and red with some light uses of yellow in the eyes.  Yes, this does create some issues were things tend to blend into the surroundings but it makes the world feel otherworldly and immediately makes the game stand out.  The sound effects and audio lines are all well done, if a bit repetitive and I will say that the music is largely forgettable (except for that pickup on the main song).  The dialog of the story is cryptic and creepy as well as engaging and all of the voice actors did a stellar job; especially the Mother and second boss.  The game also does a great job aesthetically at making the characters attractive without overly sexualizing them; though not opposed to the ‘waifu’ aspect of other games this one keeps the designs attractive without making it the goal to be sexy what you are left with is less Bayonetta and more Sucker Punch.  This was gracefully achieved without making the characters ugly (which seem to be a common thing as of late) but coming off as more stylized than fetishistic.  Although this is where the uniqueness largely ends that doesn’t mean the rest of the game is bad per se.Wait…where’s my Overtwatch:  At the core this game is a tactics game, which means you command a group of characters (your daughters) in a turn based battle against your enemies.  Your daughters level up, gain new abilities but the game also has an interesting trait system where the daughters have a chance of gaining modifies based on how they perform.  If one of them is constantly dying she may get injured or maybe another daughter will see her sister constantly dying and become apathetic to it.  But the gameplay is fairly basic outside of that.  The game is also fairly brutal in regards to taking damage as the only way to heal is sacrificing another daughter and enemies do a considerable amount of damage.  This leaves the game feeling more like a puzzle than a typical tactics game.  The last major part of the game is that you aren’t really meant to clear it in one passing.  At some point you will need to reset the progress; using shards you collected to turn on modifiers for the next game and either train new daughters or resurrect old ones.  Even after beating the game you can continue to reset and try new things; giving the game a high level of replayability.Grind, baby, Grind:  There are a few bugs in the game or at least UI issues from my perspective.  Selecting a target can sometimes be a chore, as the game is missing a lot of the shortcuts that most games of the genre have and I had to deselect and reselect things to get actions to complete.  Managing memories (items) in the game is also tedious and in dire need of a better layout.  You can’t discard or prioritize memories and even the sorting function resets every time you leave it.  The class balance is also off; the sword and gun classes are just so much better than the other two due to their mobility and range.  It also doesn’t help that there really isn’t much difference between multiple daughters of the same class even with the trait system.  Many times they didn’t feel different and when they did never in a good way (mixing up who had which ability).Overall, this is a good game if you like tactics games.  You may find the base gameplay to be a bit basic and once beaten I feel no real drive to keep playing (even though I can) but it is a solid game for the price and the story is enough off the path to be engaging so I’d recommend you grab this if you can.  Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I NEVER THOUGHT THIS GAME WOULD BE SO GOOD!Stylish combos, rocking soundtrack, and one helluva of a feel trip. This game is so close to being an art piece, and even with cheesy boss mechanics and obvious stat-check/DPS rush chokepoints, the game is still awesome.At first it starts slow, you get the hang of taking on small groups of enemies, watch as your daughters die and restart the run because you ♥♥♥♥ up. Then slowly you power through with a small group of your most beloved thralls, as you throw them into the fray. This game has psychological horror woven into every part of its macabre aesthetic, and I loved every bit of it. It gave the dark, gloomy atmosphere of darksouls a run for its own money, with a more coherent storyline hidden in fragments throughout the game.The plot isn't anything home to write about, BUT HELL THE BOSS BATTLES. Most battles drone on with the animations and repetitive soundtrack, but your heart really starts pumping when its boss battle time. The music ramps up beautifully as you get further and further into dangerous territory, and its really a rush when you execute mad combos and exploit the living ♥♥♥♥ outta every single mechanic available to you just to outsmart or outplay the bosses and their gimmicks.I'm not one to shy away from a challenge, but the first few bosses did feel cheap unless you learnt to exploit the reaction mechanic and stack your upgrades, but the battles do get better as the game continues. The deeper in you go, the more complex enemy types and movesets come into the picture, and before long you'll be stacking cheesy combo's off the dynamic timeline and feeling like a boss.I honestly love how they pulled off combat for this. Music and artistic vision really come through as you turn your daughters individual talents into a battlefield blender.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, DID I MENTION I LOVE THIS GAME AND I CANT STOP BINGEING IT? _childDocuments_.review: This game is really well made. It has a great aesthetic and feel that stands out. Also, the combat system is some of the best in this genre. The way all the mechanics work together makes for an extremely rewarding tactical turn based experience. I have played many games in this genre and this one stands out from the rest.Another way this game stands out is that it is actually difficult, and difficult in a really unique way. Basically, as you lose your runs you will get stronger. So the game implicitly challenges you to see how quickly you can beat the game if you want to prove your skill, however, you will get strong enough to beat the game eventually; it is impossible not to get stronger on a lost run (meaning you can't fail so hard you literally lose progress). This is perfectly implemented so that any player can enjoy the game. Part of this difficulty is then when you take damage on your characters it is permanent for that run (except for an extremely costly rare way to heal). I love this feature of the game because again it adds tactical depth. Even taking a single hit in a battle can be costly to your run, however, you can just go on another run when you die. This game perfectly balances the need for perfection and skill with a forgiving way of doing new runs that is something I've never seen pulled off so well before.I'll add that there is 1 drawback to this game that most other games in the genre don't have and that is a lack of unit diversity. There's mostly only the 3 starting classes with 1 hidden class that it's possible to miss unlocking. The classes have 2 options per new skill but often one of those skills is clearly far superior. This means there isn't much variety in how you build out your characters compared to other games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Some excellent turn based boss fights; but meh trash fights that become a grind.It almost feels like the game was designed to be played ironman-style (in which case it does a very good job walking the line of very-hard-but-never-impossible). But then perhaps the devs lost their nerve, and implemented the recollection system.It gives you massive buffs when you lose for the next run. The result of these is to make the trash fights trivial grinds, and it's the weakest bit of the design. The fact as a player you're getting better, and also being handed huge buffs, means the game see-saws almost immediately from hard to way too easy on the 2nd recollection.This isn't helped by the really limited diversity of trash encounters. You will see the exact same spawns and maps so often it becomes a tedious job of repeating the exact same moves over and over to flawlessly clear an area, since there's virtually zero randomness. This is okay on the first recollection - the odd misclick or dodge can still mix things up - but once you're buffed up on the 2nd, it feels like a punitive, trivial grind.I still recommend it as one of the better turn-based games, though it's a '7/10' type game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Verdict - Fans of the genre should buy on-sale.Pros:-Solid customization for your units-some tactical innovations in the form of dynamic turns and boosting-aesthetic and lore are compelling-challenging fights that require a planCons:-a bit on the simple side, most of your decisions will be in limiting your enemy's options, setting up for backstabs and moving just out of reach of enemies-artificial gameplay loop in the form of a not very interesting rogue-like mechanic. can be minimized with the easy mode-some bosses and enemies are very gimmicky-not very many options of units, makes for a predictable setup for your team-not a lot of enemy variety-pretty short game length considering a lot of it will be due to reptition-some levels and modes are incredibly irritating to play through, rescue is a standout annoying mission -- and also the most important mission style in the game.  -massively poor design in terms of inverse difficulty curve.  The first few hours of the game are by far the hardest compared to even the mid game once your characters become stronger-my biggest problem: skills didn't behave predictably, and sometimes wouldn't do anything at all.  modern game design shouldnt require that I read a manual to play the game -- the built-in description should be enough -the boss design is both confusing and unintuitive, with phase changes and % based dynamic interrupting the boss will sometimes just attack 4 times in a row after doing a normal pattern for 3-4 rounds.  There's a middle ground the game is missing where bosses preserve the action economy without getting cheesed by the players.Overall, good for a pick strategic deep-dive, but I don't think the variety is there to keep you coming back. _childDocuments_.review: Laid in black and white with a hint of red, Othercide is a turn-based tactical game developed by indie developer Lightbulb Crew and published by Focus Home Interactive. This title’s most striking quality is its distinct, minimalistic aesthetic. The game has a similarly humble soundtrack to match with subtle ambient and whispers, disturbed by occasional musical track only in the most extraordinary of moments. Impressive both in terms of gameplay and stylistic choices, the title in question is a bittersweet journey about keeping hope amidst despair.Othercide puts the player in charge of a herculean task of mending a literal tear in reality. The quest ahead is to close the latest chapter in the history of wars against immaterial horrors lurking beyond, bent on manifesting themselves in reality. What makes this conflict special is that for the first time the evil has succeeded in coming forth into existence. Laws of physics gave way to temporal loop, ever re-playing the moment the reality broke. The only way out is to defeat the malign influence behind it all.Frankly, Othercide’s story is by far its least tangible aspect. The meat of the game is a steady stream of increasingly more difficult skirmishes where your ever-growing army of daughters, much like light to balance the dark, will face an army of horrors born from nightmares of a suffering child. Conducted over a number of preset maps consisting of square tiles, the player takes turns to carefully engage the enemy, always striding to deal as much damage as possible while also staying out of the harm’s way. Gradually, you will gain experience, increase your daughters’ levels, develop your favourites and eventually watch them die. Only for the cycle to repeat.Simply put, the core gameplay of Othercide is merciless. Perhaps its most telling mechanic is the characters’ lack of ability to heal. Not only every hit taken by a daughter is there to stay – the only way to regenerate a daughter is to sacrifice another one of the same level. Taking into account how challenging the bosses are, heartbreaking as it may be, your most powerful daughters will fall. Furthermore, failure to defeat the boss immediately ends a run. The only thing that remains is to start over. However, you do come back stronger – with game progress the player unlocks global buffs, such as increased starting level or damage, steadily empowering daughters in preparation for the next milestone (and boss) ahead. With ground rules established, let’s take a look at the daughters themselves. Every run begins with 3 warriors at the player’s disposal – blademaster, gunslinger and shieldbearer – each equipped with a dedicated set of skills. Blademaster is a nimble warrior, excelling in mobility and melee damage; gunslinger provides ranged support with both bullets and buffs; shieldbearer’s specialty is protection and disturbing the enemy. Don’t be fooled by her sturdier stature though, there is no tank in a game where every ounce of damage is permanent. To keep things interesting, every class has 4 skills unlockable with level progression. They always come with a choice of 2, allowing for a diversity among the daughters of the same class.Much like the game’s aesthetic, the gameplay loop of Othercide is plain, yet effective. Characters present on the map take turns to traverse a given number of tiles and attack. Each move consumes a set number of Action Points and the amount spent determines the character’s place on the initiative bar. Careful management of initiative is a crucial aspect of the game as untimely overexerted character may end up exposed and killed in a single turn.Once the player gets a firm grip of the basics, the game becomes increasingly nuanced. New enemies are introduced and later replaced by their enhanced versions with a broader moveset. While killing is an inherent part of every mission, the ultimate objective may be different than plain eradication – timed survival, escort or prevention of a dark ritual; each type comes with a tiny spin to further keep things varied and interesting. Daughters in time receive traits that reflect their performance in battle in form of a permanent buff, and you probably get the gist by now. The devil is in the details.For all the joy of creating a seemingly unstoppable force of daughters and excitement that monumental bossfights deliver, one cannot forget that the player is meant to fail by design. Beating the game requires multiple replays and even if this title does everything in its power to smoothen the pill (going so far as to provide easy mode) it is still hard to swallow that what you’ve meticulously built over several hours eventually just falls apart. However, fitting to overarching theme of the game, this design choice will make some of you drop the game long before the credits roll.Charming as Othercide may be, there are some minor concerns that need to be raised. As mentioned, the story of the game is rather difficult to follow. To truly grasp what transpires, one needs to read the codex, especially the memories – droppable bits of lore that second as buffs for daughters’ skills. Memories are assigned to chapters, alas codex pages won’t be complete until the game is beaten. It’s a worthwhile read though, as it covers the protagonist’s past, providing a lot of context to the events unfolding on the screen. It gives depth to the story, completely imperceptible over the regular course of play. A risky design choice to say the least.Second dishonourable mention goes to minor bugs, still present in the game despite multiple updates addressing such issues. Perhaps the most unfortunate one is how a number of reaction skills occasionally don’t work, especially taking into account they cost total health percentage to use. Another vexing example is consistent issues with red markers, representing the area of the enemy’s attack. They almost never respond to skills moving the enemy away, and often linger 1-2 turns past their resolution, introducing confusion and memory game, particularly to otherwise atmospheric bossfights.All things considered, Othercide deserves all of its critical acclaim. This title is a feast for any enthusiast of turn-based, tactical play. As a bright-red cherry on top, the game’s aesthetic is a delightful application of minimalism, coupled with soundtrack evoking pathos where fitting. Minor hiccups I experienced along the way didn’t deter me in any way from greatly enjoying the game. However, one has to remember how difficult Othercide is. The game, by design, is meant to induce pinches of fatigue and hopelessness, alas those looking for light-hearted fun should steer clear away from this title. On the other hand, those who enjoy their gaming a little rough, and especially fans of the genre, can confidently send their daughters to war.

_childDocuments_.review: Othercide is a  fun tactics game that has a lot of strategic depth that will keep you coming back. The closest comparisons I could make would be the X-Com series (but you actually can hit your targets), Turn based combat games like Divinity (with less RPG elements), and toss a bit of spice from something like Amnesia for the astheticThe lore and worldbuilding is captivating and fits well with the minimalist color pallet. If youre a fan of grim, emotional settings you will enjoy this. The visual clarity is on point and there's rarely ever trouble understanding what you're looking at. The boss fights are where this game shines. Difficult encounters that really require you to think carefully before acting. I've wiped a few times against the first three. It has a few problems- Repeating voicelines, sometimes overlaping voicelines (especially at the end of missions)- Occasional bugs in combat including: Permanently getting stuck (must alt F4), Monsters gaining infinite range or otherwise breaking the rules, cutscenes breaking and not completing (must alt f4)- Lack of information in the UI (getting better as of the last update, but still has a ways to go. I would like to be able to see what memories my daughters have equipped mid mission for example) These problems have not been bad enough to stop me in my first 20 hours of this game. Any of the situations that require you to close the game don't lose you too much progress (you return to the start of the mission you were on) All in all, very happy with my purchase. Would highly recommend to anyone who is a fan of difficult strategy games.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very repetitive and super grindy and gets boring very soon.The core mechanic involves failing a campaign, rolling back time at Day 1, and restart with more resources to get stronger. Finishing a campaign requires 4-6 restarts depending on player skills and difficulty level. Consider that1) the maps are NOT randomly generated, there are 2-3 different types, and they are very small.2) enemy position, type, spawn point is always the same.3) you have 3 classes that become 4 lategame, and the viable mechanics to win are a couple at best4) there are 4 diffent types of mission (save hostage, kill everyone, survive x turns, kill the switch after in x turns).5) there are bosses that once you understand how to defeat they play out always the same.Now take these items and repeat them hundred of times and you have your Othercide campaign.Then the stilized and minimalistic art is pleasant, but also very simple, it's a Unity game and I wouldn't be surprised to see a mobile version soon. It's basically a browser game with grindy repetitive mechanics that sells for 40 bucks. Hell no, pick something else or at least wait it to be sold at 5 dollars, wich would be a fair bargain.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - fantastic game that has devs that are still actively listening to the community & working on their game as of this review (9/11/20). worth a buy at full price if u enjoy grid-based combat games & also games with roguelike elements (do NOT expect the variety between runs to be on the same levels as games such as slay the spire) otherwise, consider purchasing at a discount i couldn't recommend this game to most players prior to the most recent patch, while i very much enjoy the game, it served a very niche base of hardcore players, and had some horrible balancing issues with the classes that if utilized properly, could allow you to kill every boss before it even takes its' first action. i also felt like the game still has more of a cookie clicker type progression than a roguelike one because of how brutal the first boss was. the patch hit all of these complaints by toning down the first boss, adding what looks like a really fun casual mode (hadn't tried it yet) and also while the exploit is still possible, it's extremely tedious now and entirely pointless given the new casual mode. the game comes with one of the best game soundtracks i've ever heard in a game, many of the tracks are solid standalone tracks. the art, while lacking a bit in variety due to relatively few layouts you play on, is otherwise a great asset.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent, distinctive turn-based strategy game.  I’d rank it just behind XCOM-2 as one of my favorite-ever tactical games (along with Gears Tactics and Warhammer Mechanicus).Othercide has a lovely and evocative look to it that’s very distinctive. It sounds as good as it looks and ran reliably with no technical issues.  The feeling of making meaningful decisions, sense of mastery as you get a handle on what the different roles can do and how they complement each other, and the overall arc and length of the game were exactly the kinds of things I look for in a turn-based game.  If you think you might like it, don’t hesitate – it’s a very satisfying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun and I recommend it IF you're NOT only getting it for "Turn-based Tactics" combat and IF you're okay with fairly long "roguelite" sessions. It is definitely a unique combination of resource management, RPG and roguelite elements and worth a try.With that said I did not appreciate resource management (health in particular) aspect of the game pushed me towards the only viable strategy in combat (which, by the way, almost guarantees victory).  7/10 (8/10 IF you consciously avoid cheese strategies, which game pushes you into).This game doesn't do any groundbreaking graphics or innovative techniques. It picked a style and it went with it. Literally everything else is something you've likely seen in other games, BUT because of unique style and contrasting colors a lot of it pops out a lot more than in other games.Gameplay is fun unless/until you realize what it takes to win the game makes it a fail as a "tactics" game. That doesn't mean it's not challenging in some ways, but it's is not the core "tactics" gameplay that creates the challenge and I see that as a problem.The reason I gave 2 grades to gameplay is this game has 2 difficulties one of them just makes the problem worse.The reason for that is HEALING and to understand why here's some mechanics for default (nightmare) difficulty:In case  you don't see where this is going, you need to keep your daughters alive, so you really can't afford getting hit. The only way to win the game is to rely on cheese strategies. In most cases you just use first turn or 2 to kill whatever you can kill before it gets close and has a chance to attack. When enemies close in you burn through HP skills that prevent attacks from hitting, because sacrificing 5-15% HP is always cheaper than getting hit and losing 30-60%. Your only real choice is if you want to use more actions and delay your daughters actions by an extra "turn" (it's actually initiative system, not turns).In easier (Dream) difficulty daughters get back 50% of their HP each day (effectively after the fight). This can either be a really good thing or a really bad thing, depending on how you play. On one hand you can now comfortably take a hit, so you're not limited to mostly ranged units and/or HP skill spam. On the other hand you can now do the HP skill spam without really worrying about losing HP...There's a lot more to gameplay elements (mostly to do with progression and resource management), which make the game genuinely good, but in my opinion health management and health skills remove all nuance from combat (core gameplay loop), which brings the entire game down.Sessions are 1-10 hours long (up to 2 hours per boss), which slightly decreases as you unlock buffs. The main problem I found with this, is it's hard to pick up for a roguelite. Like you can't just sit down play a session and not touch it for a year, because if you come back in a year, you'll take a while to remember what's going on or will fail the run in a few turns.Obviously, due to long session time, resetting(or losing) a run feels like a massive loss, which I don't appreciate in most games.There's some permanent progression. Namely you get shards based on how many stages you cleared (total) and you can use those shards in each run to activate buffs you unlocked by hitting certain milestones (dealing damage, killing bosses, etc.). If you play it smart, you also get to resurrect daughters from previous runs on new ones.Temporary progression boils down to The 3 above are fairly well spaced out, so despite not feeling particularly powerful individually, they do give a sense of constant growth... These suffer somewhat from previously mentioned healing mechanic, as you have to keep too many daughters and it's difficult to keep track or even notice progression of individual daughters when you need to switch between 3-4 teams of them.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a very cool and stylish tactics game. I loved the art style and gameplay, I just wish there was more to chew on. But lemme slow things down a bit and start from the top.The story...is confusing. From what I can gather you play as the Red Mother and spawn warriors from her essence that she calls her daughters. You are trying to save a being known as the Child. He is being hurt and hounded from a force known as the Suffering. It takes shape in the forms of monsters and powerful bosses alike. Can you save the Child and defeat Suffering?Confusing story aside, I really like the gameplay. If you play games like XCOM or tactic games like it, you'll fit right in easily. You start with three playable classes, Blademaster, Shieldbearer, and Soulslinger. Each class has their strengths and weaknesses and a set if skills you can learn as you level them up. You can only take 2-4 with you per mission you do and it's important to make them stronger before you face off against the bosses.I like some of the customization that comes with you units. You can alter their looks and weapons. You can gather buffs called memories that you can equip to their skills to give them different effects like bonus damage or shredding armor. The unique thing you'll want to do is to sacrifice them into each other. Upon sacrificing a daughter into another, you heal them and they gain stat increases as well. This is the key to getting stronger as each new run you do, you will get the option to revive previous warriors to use on your new run. You will also gain new passive buffs that you can choose to make your future runs more manageable as well.I absolutely loved the music and look of this game. Very nice use of the black and white with touches of red. The style of this game is very top notch. Really loved how the music would change the longer the stage would go and especially loved the boss battle themes. Those were some of the most epic songs of the OST and made the battles very enjoyable.This game does come with some gripes however. There is only one unlockable class and the leveling up becomes kind of stale after a while. Every few levels you'll have to make the choice between the same two skills over and over. The game starts to lose its luster the more you play unfortunately. I wish there were more classes or more randomized skills they could choose from to keep the game fresh. Maybe some more customizations you could unlock the further you could get in the story, something to just add to the sameness you see. The difficulty spikes pretty fast too when you get further into the game, and with the lack of freshness the further I got into the game, I eventually lost the will to try and finish it which is a shame. The story had me lost as well, so I didn't feel compelled to finish the game and looking at lore videos made my head hurt so it's just a muddy mess.Final verdict? This was a very fun game to sink 10+ hours into. A more hardcore player would probably find more enjoyment out of the mechanics than I did, but I really enjoyed what I played. If you find yourself feeling iffy, I highly recommend grabbing this when it's on sale. It's definitely worth checking out for it's style and aesthetic at the very least. Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Just got done getting achievements to 100%. Othercide can be severely punishing at first, but when you take your time to figure out what to do where and when, get to know the enemy's stats and abilities inside out and build a strong team, you may see yourself conquering seemingly impossible situations, even without a guide. I personally spent hours on some missions, especially boss fights, but a Painslinger/Infested combo and the final boss (he's insane the first time without prior knowledge) were two of the few things that could wipe out my whole team on my first recollection. Also, remembrances make each run a lot easier, and you never lose shards to unlock them with on subsequent recollections. This made my second, full clear recollection a breeze.Gameplay aside, the 1st and 4th boss music is excellent and the protagonist has an interesting backstory you learn more about as you collect "memories" across your missions. It is slightly awkward that we only get "daughters" and there are zero "sons" though, even if it does make sense with the protagonist being female... There's also the noticeable downside of some bugs that ruin gameplay: a moderate amount when the previewed AoE of an enemy's attack stays displayed or becomes displayed wrong when an enemy is pushed (mostly occurs with bosses), and there was one time (and only one, thankfully) that I had a lv14 unit and her traits disappear permanantly into a lv7 unit who couldn't level up anymore in my 2nd recollection.Overall, I really enjoyed Othercide and trying really hard to beat the game in my very first playthrough made me a better tactical RPG gamer.

_childDocuments_.review: Ive not played a lot of Othercide yet, at the time of writing this ive spend 9 Hours with this game.Personally, ive never felt like writing reviews for games, but this one needs an exception.tl;dr: If youre into hard tactical games, enjoy the strong artstyle, or like a story that doesnt tell you all answers from the start, buy this game. and if you dont want to spend money, check it out on youtube, because while not worth your money, it deserves your attention.Gameplay:Othercide is a Rogue Lite, Tactial Game and most would say it is much like XCom, I actually think it has way more similatites to the game Mechanicus, but that game is more under the radar. Othercide is about tough choices and permanence, every point of damage taken, every bad decision is here to stay, this may lead to frustraitio for some and may be a dealbreaker for others, but all failed attempts ontribute to making your next one more succsessful through upgrades that range from stat ups, to the ability to straight up skip bosses.Speaking of the Bosses, ive experienced the first one, and i can allready tell the bosses will be the highpoints of this game, you will need to bing your A-Game, and you will need a strategy that exploits the bosses mechanics. This theme of exploiting machanics is actually taught to you very directly, you can check the AI patterns of all enemies in the in game codex, and adapt your strategies around what you fight. leading to a system that may punish damage hars, but gives you many tools to circumvent it.The only problem ive found is that the gameplay can feel a bit slow, but that isnt even a problem because speeding it up is literally an option in the menu.Art:Othercides defiletly sets its foot forward in the art department, personally i knew this game would be amazing from the title screen and the music that played, the soundtrack, which seems to be either dynamic or very well paced, is nothing short of phenomenal. If youre into Rock or Metal, definetly give this soundtrack a listen, im sure you'll not be dissapointed.the games Black/White/Red colour pallete is nothing short of fantastically exectued. The game feels incredibly alive not despite, but because of this strong art drirection.Story:The story is probably one of the strongest ive seen so far, while the main conflict is pretty straightforward; ie, "white monsters be evil go kill em" what these fights are about and what they actually mean is obsucured form you, but theres enough here to invite and reward you for thinking about what the game is trying to say, it is definetly presenting a story beyond what is happening, i just dont know what yet.I might update this part of the review once i have more context, but this is how i feel about it up until now.In Conclusion:Othercide is a game i that enticed me for its gameplay but made me an instant fan through its Art, Story and Music, and in my opinion, it deserves all attention it can get. While many games shy away from this strong stylization and difficulty, Othercide went all in and succeeded on all fronts. If anythign i just described sounded interessting, and not like the rambling of a fanboy, then go buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: + black / white / bloody styling+ interesting combat system+ various combinations / combos / synergies of individual daughters+ intimate atmosphere+ music- simple and repetitive over time- minor UI shortcomingsOthercide is a turn based roguelite game with a stylized simple story. The player, with his characters of female daughters, fights hordes of cultists and demons to defeat materialized Suffering. The game has 2 difficulties, while one is original and it is not possible to heal your characters other than by sacrificing another. Which is not a particularly bad thing from a long-term perspective, because the character thus healed takes over the time of power from the victim.The player then spins in a series of repeated attempts to conquer the game, while he can, to a very limited extent, revive the characters he has lost and who keep their traits and levels throughout the game.Combat system is interesting and not too complicated, the daughters are 4 types of classes, where each during its development have a choice of a pair of skills. These skills can be modified with memories gained while playing.There are a really large number of combinations of skills, their modifications and combinations of individual characters.The game is really hard at the beginning, but with gradual repetitions, the individual characters become indestructible killing machines, which sweat really only with interesting bosses.Great music is also worth mentioning.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I've pre-ordered in quite some time and I couldn't be happier that I did. I watched the gameplay trailers a few weeks ago which left me immediately intrigued by the semi-monochromatic, gothic aesthetic and the fluid timeline mechanics. I'm 10 hours in now and just passed the first boss... I'm hooked. The game is a near perfect marriage between narrative and gameplay. Let me elaborate a little bit... Othercide is a game about overcoming trauma and each boss is a representation of a specific traumatic instance that the mother (the creator of the Daughters you play as) and the child (the main villain of the story) have endured. You are essentially battling through what is their collective memory of events involving sickness, grief and, of course, suffering. The bosses, just like trauma, are incredibly difficult to overcome and feel like literally insurmountable walls to your progress. The game actively knows you will fail to manage these challenges encounters right away (who can actually manage their trauma head on anyway??) and encourages you to fail in order to see the best ways to grow forward. There is no growth without sacrifice hence literal sacrifice is a crux of the game. I've noticed some reviewers have seen this as a downside since the game requires you to grind a good bit by consistently axes various Daughters in favor of healing others. I haven't felt this to be much of a negative at all and it only strengthens my appreciation for how well the narrative and gameplay come together. Like no pain, no gain right? You may have to sacrifice a Daughter but by doing so you pass on traits and buffs to the Daughter that is being healed. For examples sacrificing a shieldbearer Daughter will buff another with a health and armor boost thus helping with their longevity in future fights. Like in life, you can't see growth without letting things go. So while I knew axing a few Daughters would leave me with less forces... the Daughters I have left would be much better equipped to fight the boss at the end of the week. After my first two attempts on the Surgeon I resorted to preparing to overcome the encounter like I have my own depression and anxiety... I avoided fighting it head on until I felt I had the true resolve and wisdom to actually overcome it. This meant rebooting the recollection a few times without even attempting to fight the boss. This way I gained more access memories and artifacts to buff my Daughters each time I began the recollection again, so by the time my six recollection came around my Daughters were more than prepared to take out the boss. I also haven't found this game as frustratingly difficult or repetitive as some have found it. Each class is easy to get a feel for and you quickly learn what enemy types they are best to match up against. Also don't listen to other reviews that say to avoid the abilities that cost health... those are some of the most unique and, when used right, can actually help you to avoid losing health. For example, the soulslinger has an interrupting move that cost 10% of her health. She will fire at the first enemy that makes an attack on an ally within range. This move has saved my Daughters' collective skins so many times from taking unnecessary damage since the move prevents the enemy from using an attack (if it doesn't outright murder them). I think many players feel funneled into not using them since in many other tactical games damaging a unit is incredibly counterproductive, but in Othercide it is the only way to progress. I also don't find the various systems of the game to be nearly as overwhelming as other tactical games that involve base building and other systems management. In Othercide the Daughters are the stars of the show and everything is pretty much built around their development/survival. I also didn't find myself as frustrating with having to restart the recollection as I did restarting a save on X-Com 2 because half of my units decided to miss Overwatch shots with 80-90% success rate by firing randomly in the f**kin sky. I also found that the timeline system and combos you can create with your Daughters lead to much shorter mission times. Once you get into the rhythm you can easily clear most missions under 20 minutes and that includes the "Impossible" ones. The only cons I have so far are the number of classes available and access to the various game modes. The three classes offered are quite robust and offer a lot of variation in terms of playability. I just personally wish there was another class or two and hope they add a couple with future expansions. I also think that they could definitely introduce the various game modes a lot quicker. For the recollections I've done so far I've almost exclusively been given hunt missions which is only one out of the three types. Survival has come up a couple times and I have yet to see a rescue mission. This is a little annoying since it is obviously nice to have some mission variety and because rescue is the one mode that offers the type of currency you need to resurrect Daughters as a reward. There is one artifact that gives you a resurrection coin at the start of a recollection but other than that I haven't gotten a chance to earn others which is a bummer when you want to run a roster of specific Daughters. Hopefully this can be changed with a future patch to help make the mission variety. All in all this is shaping up to be one of my favorite games of the year. One with a story that is incredibly timely given the circumstances of the world at large right now. Looking forward to overcoming the challenges of Suffering that lie ahead! 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: OVERALL - Not recommended.I cannot recommend this game, unless it is on a big sale and you want to try the tactical combat mechanics (which I think is the only strong point of the game). Otherwise, this game is skippable.STORY - 1/5I really didn't like how the story was presented.   Basically unless you want to read all the codex, the story as presented while playing through the game is almost non-existent.   Chosen Child, Child is corrupted, stop the child, stop the corrupter.   For the most part I just kept asking why do I care at all about these characters.  I read some of the codex, but it didn't peak my interest enough to keep reading.GRAPHICS - 2/5The "gray-scale + red" (red for blood, of course) looks pretty good overall and I enjoyed the intentional style.  But I found it hard to look at and discern details.   I wish all the enemies had a small color added in for each type too.  I think it would have been very helpful visually if cultists, nightmare creatures, and corrupted daughters all had a small amount of different color. COMBAT - 4/5The tactical combat mechanics are quite interesting.  Definitely the strongest part of the game and why I finished it.  I really enjoyed the initiative system and the choice to "burst" or not.   Also, keeping movement and actions all under one action point system was a nice change from most tactical games.  I felt the game had lots of interesting mechanics, but some could have been explored moreOUTSIDE COMBAT - 2/5I felt the outside combat mechanics had some interesting aspects, but almost all of them needed more refinement.   The memories were a mess.  Trying to sort through them was a pain and it felt like most of them weren't very useful.  Also they weren't always clear what they did.   At least a few of the abilities had almost not choice for memories.   The traits were a pain.   Some of them were really good and others were just ok.  Some were even detrimental.  But since they are all random, there was almost nothing you could do about it.  Sacrificing your daughters worked thematically I guess, but overall I didn't like the mechanic.  By the end of the game the vitae(main currency) was pointless.  I also had so many memories it they didn't even feel like a limited resource except for a few of the really rare ones.UI- 2/5I honestly think the UI on this game was ok, but because of the choices with the outside combat buffing it made the flaws in the UI stand out.  The main problem is you just have no good idea how much damage you're going to do.  The UI tries but there's just too many modifiers.Base DmgEnemy Type DamageSkill Memory DamageArmorFlanking/BackstabbingCrit ChanceCrit DamageThere was also quite a few bugs in the UI when using the inspect on enemies.Games I would recommend insteadBanner Saga 1,2,3Into the BreachXCOM 2Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to describe this game is Darkest Dungeon + Xcom/Mutant Year Zero. It's definitely it's own beast and it does some new things that I wasn't for sure was going to work at first. However, I find this game to be very addicting. You will get attached to these girls sometimes and losing them really sucks. Death is permanent however it does offer ways as you progress to keep a couple of your favorite daughters as a dedicated team. It's intimidating as you first start playing and there is a lot of math to take into consideration if you want to take full advantage of the Timeline mechanic. This is the perfect game for guys who love to "Theorycraft" numbers and work out the perfect build/team for defeating your enemies.  However, it's not necessary to play the game. So far I'm really enjoying this game and it is a gem that any Tactical/Strategy Game fan should have in their library.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give it a "meh". I love TRPGs and the aesthetic of this game looked really appealing so i was excited for it. The actual skill trees are pretty bare bones but the gameplay and soundtrack are solid. I actually really enjoyed myself up until the end and then couldn't bring myself to complete it. The game operates in the same fashion as Rogue Legacy or Dead Cells where the game doesn't expect you to complete it on your first try and it gets considerably easier the more times you play through it. Unlike those games, this isn't a roguelite so your gameplay experience is going to be more or less the same on subsequent playthroughs. This is fine in itself until the final boss where the game requires actual grinding. Before this point, bosses can be dealt with by learning the bosses moveset and changing your tactics accordingly on subsequent runs. The final boss just throws a ton of unavoidable damage at you to the point where you have to make sure you have a bunch of adequately leveled characters in your graveyard with good memories. The game at this point becomes a slog.

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing that caught my attention was the artwork. The style of the monsters, characters and color scheme perfectly matches the mood and the music matches the style perfectly. A perfect blend of dark, depressing but yet epic.The story is a bit meh, but interesting enough for you to read the lore and find out what is happening.The one thing that really kept my interest, is the game mechanics. The combat is turn-based tactics, with every character with it's own move. It almost feels like a chess game, but at a whole new level. The combat is also smooth and at some moments pretty epic. One thing that makes the game unique is that you HAVE to die in order to really progress the game. It's very challenging and grindy at first, but as you start over, you get better, smarter and you get certain items and unlockables to help you jump start again, until you reach a point where you are unstoppable and finally beat the game.Overall a pretty solid and addictive game. You do need patience for the grind, but you will be greatly rewarded, especially when you have certain unlockables and maxed out daughters.Graphics: 8/10Gameplay: 8/10Story: 5/10Music: 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: This was the most conflicting hour and a half I've had in a long time. I really wanted to like this game. I have a lot to say because I think this game could have been a masterpiece but, a lot of things are holding it back. I hope that the developers take this criticism constructively and work on either improving this game or making their next game better.The verdict for those who don't want to read: it's not worth the price of admission. Wait until it's on sale or major updates are made to the game.The presentation is top of the line. I love the black, white, and red aesthetic and I think the graphical fidelity of the game deserves praise. The assets are absolutely gorgeous. The models, the animations, the graphical design, the UI, the performance; it's all fantastic. However, the music stands out on its own. It is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ EXCELLENT (it's the reason I bought the game). Clearly there are some talented artists on this team.On the gameplay front, the ideas behind the timeline, the AP/interruption/initiative system are really interesting and I found myself wanting to go back and keep experimenting with the game's battle systems.However... this is where my praise ends.The game has three fundamental problems:* Poor pacing* Confusing gameplay* Abysmal storyAs a whole, the biggest problem with this game is pacing. In the first hour, you will be introduced to so many things you'll eventually ask yourself "why should I care about any of this?" Not only is the game throwing a massive amount of exposition at you, mostly filled with proper nouns like the Chosen One, the Mother, the Daughter, the Veil, the Suffering, etc., but it's also throwing gameplay mechanics at you way too quickly. SLOW DOWN. Let the game breathe! The tutorial doesn't need to introduce every game mechanic in the first thirty minutes. The introduction doesn't need to introduce all of the different elements to the story. Just skip all that ♥♥♥♥! Show me the setting, 1899 or whatever, and go straight to the gameplay! What sucks even more about this is that once you start to understand the systems and its charm, what awaits you is a game that has very little variety. You'll be using the same skills, fighting in the same maps, fighting against the same enemies, all for the goal of reaching the end boss for your run. There's one model for the Daughters (they just have different hairstyles and one of three outfits), and they mostly resemble the Mother, so you'll be seeing the same girls over and over. There simply wasn't enough randomness while I was playing to keep me interested.Then there's the gameplay. Two things are really hurting the game from a gameplay perspective: a UI that values style over substance, and mechanics that are simply too punishing.Firstly on the UI, many of the gameplay terms are vague (like "Remembrance", "Memories", "Inner Void", etc.) Just give it to me straight dude! I'm in a run, I'm going to get upgrades, and I have to manage my party. Secondly, you'll often be wondering what the UI design is supposed to represent. You'll be looking at squares and bars wondering what they mean, what the different shades of color represent on the timeline, how the timeline even works, etc. It won't be until you've permanently lost a couple of Daughters that you'll realize how the game works, which is just frustrating and not fun at all. Also, I had issues understanding what unit was queued up to be moved, how far I had to move to issue certain attacks, and in general the UI just actively worked against me during combat.On the punishing mechanics: this wouldn't be a problem if there was a sense of progression. However while the temporary nature of the game is interesting on paper, in practice it's just frustrating. You'll be killing your own Daughters to heal others. You'll be leveling up other Daughters, just to lose them and then be unable to resurrect them because the game decided to not give you any resurrection tokens.And in general, the early game is way too punishing. It shouldn't be possible for early game mobs to be able to dodge and hit twice. The game should not start with you ZERO resurrection tokens. The game should refund you your memories if your Daughters die. I should always have enough tokens to germinate a new Daughter on the first run. Hell, why did you let me pick the role for my first germination? I would have obviously picked the shield girl had I known she was missing from my team composition. Also, if you're going to design the first run to be impossible, INFORM YOUR PLAYER SO THAT THEY DON'T SUICIDE THEIR ENTIRE SQUAD.And lastly, the story is abysmal. Again, in the span of thirty minutes, you're introduced to the Chosen One, the Veil, the Suffering, the Mother, the Daughters and MORE. Every time a new proper noun was introduced I rolled my eyes. The dialogue was also extremely edgy and cringy. I get it; the game is about a mother's suffering and the evils she has to go through to bring a child into the world when at the end your offspring are the ones who hurt you the most. It doesn't need to be that deep. It's a strategy game. Just stop the exposition, quiet down and show me the game.It also doesn't help that the game pulls a classic Child of Light move, trying to be deep before establishing a cohesive narrative. It just comes across as pretentious. The same comment I made with the gameplay applies here: you don't need to show your entire hand upfront! If you're going to show all of the exposition at the start, make sure it's relevant to the game. None of the exposition changed the gameplay whatsoever. And don't be afraid to give your characters actual names for ♥♥♥♥♥ sake.One of the best moments was seeing the Chosen One holding the Egg, watching the Egg float and grow bigger after every camera cut. I was legitimately impressed by the artistry and it seemed heavily inspired by Berserk. Too bad it was undercut by the horrible dialogue from the Chosen One. I wish I cared enough to keep going to see what the Egg turns out to be.What made this experience even more disappointing for me was the massive missed opportunity. This could have been an excellent game. It almost seems like this game has all of the right ideas but half the execution. Someone on this team knew that the presentation and polish was important, that the gameplay mattered, that a meaningful story mattered, but ultimately no one had the vision to say "this isn't fun" or "this is too far". It's almost like the team was so in love with their product they forgot to put it in front of playtesters. PLAYTEST YOUR GAME. Get opinions outside of your dev team. Next time it will go a long way to making your game truly excellent. I don't believe this game is worth the price tag, and you should probably wait until it's on sale or major updates are made to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I am still very early in the game at the time of this review, but I love the concept and the execution. Roguelite tactical combat gameplay with heavy Claymore vibes that fit perfectly with a Sin City color palette. I don't know how they got the idea to put all that together but the result is great. Now let me explain the description further: Roguelite: Permadeath is a core part of the game. Even if your daughters don't get killed in combat, you will have to sacrifice them sooner or later. The quote unquote "campaign" is short but you will need to start over and upgrade your daughters through multiple playthroughs with persistent unlocks in order to beat it. You will also need to learn how to fight effectively and overcome the difficulty curve, getting better the more you play. In this way Othercide is similar to Dead Cells, Monster Train, Rogue Legacy, and other great games like that with roguelite elements.Tactical combat: Classic turn-based squad combat. Whether you like XCOM, FF Tactics, or Disgaea, you will find something to like in Othercide. So far the gameplay seems to have elements from both western style and Japanese style games. I am only a few unlocks in and the interaction between units can get pretty deep (auras, intercepts, synergy attacks, etc). I can see where this is going and I like it.Claymore vibes: That one is pretty obvious if you know the anime. If you don't and you enjoy this game, you will probably enjoy watching Claymore. But this is not just a similarity in the theme and story. Sacrifice is a big part of the gameplay. This includes incremental sacrifice - giving up a part of yourself to achieve something, or setting off on a path of  no return - and outright offering your life to help another when the time comes. These are core gameplay elements, both during combat and in the campaign meta game.Sin City color palette: What you see in the trailers and screenshots. Goes great with minimal design. Othercide is minimal but not sloppy or unskilled like some indie game graphics are. What is there looks good, it is obviously created with intent, and it all works out great. It also runs on a potato-ish laptop with no real GPU.
