_childDocuments_.review: Positives: This game was an unexpected delight. I am amazed at how deep I got into the game this weekend and I'v only colonized maybe 15% of the surface of Mars. I had dreams this weekend of me obsessing over gathering resources and controlling drone loads. The concept, story, hell even the combat was compelling. I am always interested in how AI might interact with humans in different conditions. And I am still wondering about AMI's future after Mars is a better Earth than Earth is even today. Does she get transferred to Venus? Does she get packaged up and sent on a slower than light ship to prepare another planet for Human's arrival in 100 years? I cant wait for spoilers to come out and I hope there is someway to get an ending where AMI gets her freedom while also peacefully coexisting with humans on Mars.Neutral:1. I wish there were more complex production chains. The game only has "Tier 1" resources (meaning they take two raw or "Tier 0" resources and make a new one). I am so used to games like Anno where you can have something like 5 tiers of resources you need to manage production and consumption. 2. There doesn't seem to be a way to get to resources once they are under water. So, if you start terraforming too soon alot of your easy to get to resources will be under water before they get used up. This provided an interesting mid-game challenge when half my base got flooded but now I have so many resources so close that I just CANT get to.That said...if there was a "wait for a patch or two" review option, then I would select it.The game needs some work. A few examples: 1. There needs to be a way to manage stockpiles of resources. As it stands it seems kinda random where the resources go. Some how...they still get to where they need to be...eventually. But as it stands it is hard to impossible to figure out why factory X is running between 0% and 20% efficiency where as factory Y a few spaces over is running at 100%.2. There needs to be a way to toggle what icons are visible after you zoom out a bit. Too often did I queue up a Hyper Loop and go do something else while it builds, only to forget exactly where I placed it and having to hunt around for it to connect to the Hyper Loop Network.3. The triggers on the dialog need some work. They seem to come out of order more often than not. I'll get dialog triggers and not know what I did to cause them.  Worst, you will get dialog triggers for a quest branch that should no longer be possible to continue on. 4. Maybe I missed it but there seemed to be no way to access your combat squads with hot keys. You have to scroll ALLL the way over to your squads, then scroll ALLL the way over to where the enemies. Squads will merge if they happen to attack the same target and will return home if they dont find anything within 10 feet to attack they will start heading home without orders.I'll be putting this back on the virtual shelf while Cyberpunk consumes my next several weeks. But I hope after a few patches the rough edges will be filed off and this will become a great resource management sim.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like Per Aspera. The UI and visual design is beautiful, with the sleek, geometric style being right up my alley. Playing an AI slowly discovering it's own will was an instant sell for me. This was one of few games that I instantly bought after seeing early gameplay and binged for hours at a time.Unfortunately, it's kind of a wreck. It's not playtested or balanced well at all. The worker AI is atrocious, likely as a result of workers trying to be boxed into specific sectors. There's very little the player can do to control the workers: a prioritize button button that can make a building suck up way too many materials, or controlling each resource's target output tasks with sliders which honestly doesn't seem to do much. It's way too easy to just get stuck in this game, where one can spend all of their starting resources in the beginning playing around or later on when scripted events and random meteor impacts alike can cripple a base beyond recovery without much the player can do about it, and that's even before the military-defense component is introduced. By then, a base can get bogged down so heavily that even if it has a healthy stock of materials and several key resources have redundant extractors and factories, it can be nearly impossible to get the Drone Factory and Towers up in time. That's even assuming it's not your first playthrough, in which you'd have no idea where to build your first Tower(s) for proper defense.As for the story, it's clearly suffered for the lack of playtesting as well. Occasionally AMI, the AI that the player takes the seat of, will chime in to herself to reflect on the current events. Except, due to poor flag tracking, it will often not be the current events at hand. "I wonder if I should use the nuclear warheads on the polar caps?" she muses to herself after the player has already accomplished that. "The sudden base failure, was it a sabotage?" she wonders after the threatening transmission from an unknown entity confirms its presence and influence. It's quite a mess. The nuclear weapons mentioned earlier are framed as a quick method to go through the first terraforming step, Bootstrapping, which involves raising the temperature and pressure enough that all the dry ice at the poles completely sublimates and floods the atmosphere with a boost of CO2. The problem with this framing is that reaching for the nuclear weapons takes far more resources and commitment than a simpler alternative that requires just a handful of techs researched. All in all, I wish Tlön Industries the best. This was clearly an ambitious undertaking, and one that I hope in the future can meet up to industry standards. For now, I must recommend passing on this: it is a rough gem still entombed in stone and wants for far more polishing.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd really like to give Per Aspera a neutral rating if steam allowed it. The fundamental issue is that Per Aspera is a wonderful piece of visual art, but a very weak game. It does the former so well it almost overwhelms all my issues with the later, but not quite. tldr at the bottom.Per Aspera nails the aesthetics of terraforming like nothing else I have ever played. Slowly seeing the Red Planet change as the icecaps melt, your structures expand, and life is introduced to the once barren landscape is a beautiful process. The planet has a sense of majesty and wonder to it that constantly reminded me of the feelings I got reading Kim Stanley Robinson's Mars trilogy (which the devs obviously take a lot of inspiration from). Lots of old science fiction ideas are wonderfully translated into a form that could only really be achieved in a video game. It's a work of art.That's also why it's so painful that the actual gameplay that drives this spectacle is so weak. Per Aspera is a supply chain logistics game where you need to manufacture increasingly complex goods and make sure those goods are delivered to the places they need to be, allowing you to progress the terraforming process. The closest reference point I have is probably the Anno franchise, and despite it's planetary scale Per Aspera does mostly feel and play more like a city builder than anything else. It even has a simple real time tactics mini-game in the same way that Anno does. There are two problems though. First, there's very little complexity to the production chains. You produce basic raw materials, a few tiers of basic refined and manufactured goods, but very little beyond that so there's little serious challenge or escalation to that part of the game. Secondly this is a logistics game where you have no control over the logistics. Goods are moved across the map autonomously by bots who shuffle them from building to building. It's incredibly inefficient and unintutive. You have extremely little control over the flow of items and what control you do have often feels more like an exploit than an intended design feature. Some of this is poorly communicated mechanics, some of it is poor design. This is frustrating in the early game, but excruciating in the late game. There is a late game tech that allows higher volume and distance transport routes, but this felt like something bolted on to stop the system completely grinding to a halt. The lack of control in logistics is also why there are no complex production chains, they would be impossible to produce with any consistency. Choosing to play on hard was a mistake that made this whole process slower and more tedious than it would otherwise have been, but didn't add any meaningful challenge. Finally the game treats Colonists in a very strange way. Colonists are what produces research, more colonists means faster research, and certain techs are gated behind getting to a certain population of colonists. But there's something about the game that makes colonists feel completely superfluous. They produce research, but other than that they play no role in the game. Unlike many similar games I felt no intrinsic satisfaction from growing the population or doing a better job supplying their needs, they were just another currency. Once the research tree is completed you can actually get rid of your colonists, they no longer do anything except place more pressure on your production network. Also overshooting your terraforming goals means nothing. I was expecting the final part of the game to involve balancing the terraforming processes you've set in motion so that temperature or atmospheric pressure don't overshoot and make the planet unlivable again. This doesn't happen, overshooting effects nothing and is not acknowledged by the game in any way. It leaves the simulation feeling hollow at the end.The main campaign is pretty good. It certainly has way more polish than you normally see in city builders, even big budget ones. In particular the voice acting is very good and elevates some of the material. Unfortunately the pacing of the campaign is pretty bad (probably made worse by playing on hard). For example early on you are given the option to nuke the ice caps to accelerate melting them. This is a cool idea, but I never got to use it because the icecaps had entirely melted by the time I had met the requirements to do this. I don't know if I was warming the planet to quickly or reaching this goal to slowly, but either way I don't feel like I could have done much to reach it faster because of how little control of the logistics you get. Later on I would have the opposite problem a number of times, where there would be some story beat that implied urgency, only for the associated mechanical goal to take months or years to be met. It would have been funny if it wasn't so tedious. The main campaign is let down by some weak world building (for example we never learn if it's normal for AI to be self-aware in this world, or if this is a special quality of the terraforming AI you play as, which makes it hard to know where we stand in relation to the rest of the characters). The best writing and world building is in the mini-narratives that can be uncovered through archaeological exploration of older mars missions. These are great, but it's extremely annoying that half of them can be covered by rising water. The DLC supposedly fixes this, but it's a really obvious flaw that should have been addressed in the base game. Really whatever strengths the campaign has are weighed down by the core game play not working as well as it should.tldr: Read Red Mars, it's amazing. Consider Per Aspera if the book grabs you for the beautiful depiction of a changing planet, but keep your expectations for the actual game low. Don't play on hard, it only makes the game more tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: It has some problems, but its still a good choice if you like the concept of Mars, colonizing Mars, changing the surface and all that without becoming too abstract.I mean, its still based on typical production lines like aluminium, water, carbon and all that in typical scifi-esque facilities.The most abstract part is the usage of drones, which is possibly what leads to the three major problems it has:1.) Performance. It can tank quite fast and a lot due to what is going on. A lot of this possibly comes from:2.) Transportation becomes messy and inefficient fast. The priority logic isnt there, you have a ton of untransported goods you need, because your transporter moves stuff it rather shouldnt. Even if you set up your priorities correct, it might be they move stuff they arent allowed or outright bug out and drive in circles, which leads to a massive load on performance after some time.3.) Productionlogic becomes rather confusing after some time. You place down so much stuff and your "base" becomes so big wit ha gigantic and super-messy network due to the roadsystem the game has to create roads automatically. _childDocuments_.review: As it is now, I can't recommend the game, tedious is the only word I can use to describe it.Your worker/hauler units are a big part of that, they have a set lifespan, there's no way to repair them or even see the life they have remaining, and if you don't micromanage them and something else takes your attention away for a while, a large number of them could just poof out of existence while you struggle to bring your workforce back up which is very hard to do while you have such a small number of units because...The priority system is horrible, there are only two priorities to set in a game where you are making dozens of things that depend on each other, not only that, but the priority system is shared between production and building, so if you want to say, prioritize a chain of raw resources to make components to build workers, everything will get done at the same time, workers will go half-way across your colony to extract resources to bring to a solar power plant on the other side of the map and completely neglect your worker factories while you number of workers continues to dwindle.For a story focusing so much on terraforming and bringing life to Mars, the human aspect of the game is entirely overlooked, colonists are a glorified research point generator, you can starve them, get them killed, or treat them the best you ever have and nothing changes aside from a single number, it creates a really damn strong sense of ludonarrative dissonance.There are other things I don't like about the game like the combat, which is entirely without a tutorial (protip, you can move your units by clicking on the number circle) and is more simplistic than even the most basic RTS games so far, enemies blob you and unless you have more than them, you lose, there are no tactics. The performance is not very good, the game is slowing to a crawl and I'm only 5 hours in. Building icons are huge and overlapping, the UI is unresponsive, you can't select multiple buildings at a time.If the game can get some patches to address these issues it could be a lot better, the game has a good bit of potential, but as it is now it's just frustrating to try to play.

_childDocuments_.review: So do you like waiting? Do you like watching numbers tick? Then Per Aspera is the game for you! Now, that's not necessarily purely the fault of the game, being somewhat endemic to city-builders in general. You put down a building, you wait for it to finish. Either that requires time, your peasant to do the work, or in this case, a bunch of robots to gather stuff and pile it into one place to assemble the thing in question. Okay, fair enough.What is somewhat problematic is how *much* the game places an emphasis on the hurry-up-and-wait aspect of the genre. Every step in the process feels like it's elongated for its own sake. A single unit is a full load for a worker, so erecting your factories is dozens of trips. Each factory or resource generator requires someone to take it to storage or another building for it to be consumed. Each worker only takes a load so far before having to hand it off to someone. So you can have resources to build a planet of factories, but it'll take ages simply for the game to shuffle it slowwwlllyyy across your little base before it's built. Were it just that, then eh, maybe that's not so bad, other city-builders might be worse. But as other reviews have noted, there's a research tree and over-arching project to be done: terraforming Mars. Alright, that sounds exciting right? It would be, but much of this ends up being researching something, putting the game on fastforward for a half hour, then starting a project that puts your research into motion. These are for all intents and purposes like watching the progress bar of a large file download. At the latter stages you might have to maybe fine tune a few things, but this is allocating a few buildings to doing a few things repeatedly while you watch the numbers go up. Or down. Very slowly. To a certain extent that's understandable; you're terraforming Mars! It shouldn't even be possible, and it borders on magic. But that's not really compelling game play. You might have a plan on how to melt the polar ice caps. If you have your industrial base built properly, it's literally select a project and wait. Whee. It's probably fun to do the first time, but having beaten it, gotten one of the endings (which is likely a single choice you make 18 hours in), I feel like there's no rush to go back into it and see the rest of it. The story is interesting but the main plot points can fit on an index card and I only kinda felt invested in the outcomes, despite the voice acting doing a very good job of trying to sell the emotional aspect to me. If you're addicted to city builders and like a near-future sci-fi setting, give this a try. You can overlook a lot in that honeymoon period when you first fire up a game, and that might push you to the end through sheer momentum. But I honestly don't see myself returning to this any time soon, and I am a dork who likes it when number go up. Also, shame on Steam for not letting me put in a mixed rating, because not every choice is binary. I'm going to say "recommend" because if you're looking at this you're already in the mindset I imagine, but I'm not going to recommend this to a lot of people in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable title.  There were a few things off with the game but it was mostly fun. The logistics were a bit bizarre, but I got the hang of it. _childDocuments_.review: While I've enjoyed my time playing the early stages of this game, I found way too many frustrating setbacks that stacked up so high that it makes me hesitate to boot it up again.The game is very much city-builder-lite. You're managing the gathering of resources, colonists for the research trees, and long-term goals to eventually terraform Mars. You don't have any sort of budget to keep in mind (aside from building/unit limits) so the most consideration you will have in placing buildings is putting them close enough to other buildings and having the electrical bandwidth to power them all. As someone who's not the best at this kind of genre, this is nice. It's really satisfying seeing my bases expand and potentially build new ones on other parts of the planet.The story itself has been pretty compelling as well! Not to dive into any spoilers but it's a story around an AI (You) building the necessary tools to aid in the mission of terraforming mars and diving into its many mysteries while the AI contemplates their own existence and purpose. Very existential stuff. All voice acted too with great performances which is a plus.My problems arise when you get to a big enough base that keeping track of everything becomes nearly impossible both visually and technically.Hope you have good eyesight, because once your base is big enough, good luck looking for anything specific because the icons representing buildings and what resource they generate when zoomed out are SO TINY that I spent most of my time  at the screen to find the specific resource mines I want to place new factories around or buildings I want to shut off to save power. Some icons are far too similar to each other, how am I supposed to tell the difference between a solar farm and a battery? I can't, they both have the lightning symbol and a background that blends in with the white outlining of icons and roads. Sure I can click a resource from the bottom row to highlight factories and mines that produce/use them, but all that does is create a two thin white lines around those buildings The problem gets exacerbated when you have more than one base. That bottom row of resources also gives you graphs that show you the rise and fall of productivity for each item on a global scale. Overall, this is great for micromanaging what factories and resources to focus on! Number go up and green is good and all that. This immediately falls apart the second you build a second base. Want to know if that second base is being self sufficient? Nope, when you select that bases "district" menu, all you get are flat numbers of its inventory, no graphs. That district has 0 computer chips in its inventory? could that be because they're all being used too quickly to notice? or are they not being produced at all because of some other problem (such as power, another thing that is hard to spot because of its tiny icon over the building)? who knows! Does my second district generate enough food/water to support their colonists long term? Maybe! the first district is inflating the numbers of my global scale that I don't know if district 2 is on the rise or decline.Overall, I see some glaring flaws in this games UI design that it feels too much of a chore to power through to the later stages where I will need to rely on the information the UI gives me to properly manage everything rather than eyeballing it.Dealing with combat and my swarms are the bane of my existence, its like herding cats. For one, it's so annoying switching between swarms when I have to right-click MULTIPLE TIMES before I can select another swarm less I accidentally redirect the course of the currently selected swarm to merge with the other.I hate that as soon as a swarm fully wipes out an enemy swarm, it returns back to base immediately on its own with no regard of other enemies around them. I have to keep a close eye at every encounter to make sure no one leaves the fight early, leaving my buildings wide open for the slow-ass towers.It's also annoying not being able to assign groups of swarms to readily intercept any oncoming swarms, it all needs to be done individually. This then circles back to the frustration that is selecting and deselecting units.It's also frustrating that merged swarms don't split up when returning to base. Each Hive tower holds 100 at the start, but never readjusts themselves when a swarm returns with more than that. Leaving some towers understaffed and underprepared for the next invasion due to the swarm unit limits. This then leaves to more annoying busywork readjusting them yourself.Overall, I feel that this game should have just left out combat all together and focused on its base-building aspects and simulation. It all feels like an afterthought.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting story-sim hybrid game. This isn't a full-blown simulator as it first appears, it's possible to do things that should auto-fail the terraforming but don't seem to have any real effect.  I'd describe it as a cross between Surviving Mars and Civilization VI.Surviving Mars is a more technical, nuanced game that only ends when you close the game, there's no finite ending even after terraforming Mars. However in Per Aspera there's a finite ending, and it's more story focused than a 4Xer or sim style game. If you're looking for a more difficult game with city-building than that would be Surviving Mars. If you want a story/opera style narrative where a few ethical choices can change everything then Per Aspera has that. While the graphics are more polished and the interface is snazzier, the UI is missing some obvious features I would've liked to have to make for easy building navigation. Per Aspera is a fun story game I can recommend if picked up on sale or in a game bundle, though if you are looking for replayability I'd still give it to Surviving Mars.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't the best thing ever, but it is still really nice to play sometimes.- Everything looks nice and makes noises.- It isn't really a complex game where you do crazy production lines, but that doesn't make the game worse.--- The devs did fix some stuff so that the game is actually playable and isn't frustrating, and they seem to be doing content updates as well, so the game can still become better than what it is right now.- Basically, every drone has to know how to navigate all of your base and does all the calculations on the fly, so the game gets very cpu-intensive after midgame or so.- Sometimes they can't move that one resource piece at all even though the building it should go to is prioritized and is literally right next to the resource unit. Just like the framerates, this stuff usually works fine for the most of the game, but gets worse towards the end of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Geez. Last ~8 hours I was basically just waiting for a bar to fill. Generally the art (both visuals and audio) is nice, the gameplay and story are just shallow. I think this game could've been much more but it just didn't work out.The game seems to be logistics/production management but you quickly realize you have no real control over flow of resources. You've got some semi-automated worker drones but only two priorities to control them (default and high priority) so they often do things in their own order. Storage is also problematic.The terraforming aspect is also pretty simple, you just make things that fill some bars (sometimes empty bars). I haven't found any deeper connection between the variables, it was just straightforward mapping like X carbon dioxide -> Y temperature. I hope humans like my 2 bar atmosphere (8% oxygen). Also you have no tools to revert the changes you've made, it's like you get only half of the toolkit because you aren't supposed to need the other half (like you can import nitrogen from some moon but for some reason can't export it).There are more things I could point out but I'm just too tired after finishing the game. If you want to play it better bring a book with you for the latter half of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A good game, fun despite some frustrating quirks that mostly result from worker priorities not always making sense.  The most fun to be had is in the first three phases of terraforming which are satisfying while maintaining a good pace.  The late game, while resulting in more impressive changes to the landscape and much more complex bases, becomes a bit of a slog.  My base was stable and generally effective dozens of years before the terraformation was complete but some of those aforementioned quirks combined with some (intentionally designed) long end-game projects meant more waiting than thinking.  Personally, I gave up on trying to sustain larger populations of colonists for research and instead walked away while Mars finished turning green shortly after 100 years.  My recorded playtime says 30 hours -- 10 of those were inadvertently leaving the title screen up while I was away, 10 were very active and fun, and the last 10 were a combination of slow or hands-off play.I guess it's a testament to the earlier game that I was invested and interested enough to let that happen despite the slog.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, but I understand that it won't be for everyone.I wholeheartedly recommend it if you like high concept games (Last Federation), for example.Don't let it fool you that this game is in city builders, it is closer by a lot to Factorio.There are a number of annoyances that I hope will get addressed in a Quality of Life patch.I would love to be able to upgrade all roads centrally, turn on and off spaceport/elevator projects. reassign hotkeys, have edge scrolling, reorienting the camera.But these are minor annoyances to me, the vision of this game shines through all of it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird game to suggest because it has some really good and really bad elements.The good of it is that its a really nice game to play while doing something else on your other monitor.  The game is mostly about setting systems up and then waiting for them to process through a queue of some sort, so it doesn't require a huge amount of interaction to play this.  That's not a style of game that's for everyone, but I like it since I can "play" it while I work on something else.I wish it gave you a bit more information on how the systems worked, it needs a tier 4/5 logistics building, and the late game balance is a bit wonky.  But at its core it does the whole "set systems up, do something else for bit" genre well.  Also the game itself is beautiful and its really cool to see Mars get visually terraformed.Now for the bad: the plot, which is ironic because that's what the developer seemed to think was the high point of this game (and they tell you not to spoil it, whoops!).You play a hyper advanced AI that was given the personality of a not very intelligent high school girl with some *very* severe mental disorders.  None of this has any impact on the gameplay whatsoever, but you're forced to listen to the AI constantly talk to itself and a few other people.   These conversations are some of the most cringy stuff I've ever heard in a video game - particularly the conversations that you have with the "bad" guy - head of the western hemisphere's Air Force, Lt. Dominguez (yes, that's right, he's a lieutenant).  It really feels like the AI is a self insert for a writer with some severe mental health disorders where the conversations with the bad guy were taken straight from conversations they had upon being involuntarily committed, while the conversations with the "good" guys in the game are how they had wished those conversations had actually gone.I watched a few youtube lets plays on this before buying it and all of the LPer's stopped playing at the exact same part, which is when the conversations transcend from normal cringe to mega-cringe.  So I knew what I was getting into and I enjoyed the gameplay enough to still recommend the game.  But be aware that you're going to have to sit through hours of the AI whining about how it wants to be popular, find someone who understands it, have babies, AND HOW IT IS BEAUTIFUL AND PERFECT JUST THE WAY IT IS AND HAVING A "FRINGE CONSCIOUSNESS" SHOULD BE CELEBRATED, NOT TREATED.Although there also is a sandbox mode that is just the normal mode with the plot removed so you can also play that, but I don't know, it just feels wrong to play that mode when there is a campaign mode available - even if the campaign is just a strictly worse sandbox.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game if you enjoy city builders, it follows a lot of real-world concepts regarding terraforming Mars I was very impressed with the single-player sandbox. I took Mars from a desolate red rock with one lonely landing site to a sprawling connected web of resource generating buildings spanning and entire green and blue planet. To the Devs: One tiny issues with with removing resources from scrapped buildings to preserve building limit. Perhaps add an option to sacrifice the resources to removing the building pad.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Conceptually, I really like Per Aspera; a 4x-like experience with a neat sci-fi story should be right up my alley. Unfortunately, the 4x layer of the game is very shallow (despite appearing quite elaborate) as certain mechanical guardrails make it very difficult for you to 'lose' no matter how inefficiently you lay things out, and so it really only serves as a means for you to kill time in between story beats. If you're looking for a rich sci-fi strategy game, stick with Endless Space 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I was dubious about this game, mainly due to the "mixed" feedback, but was pleasantly surprised. I'm an avid player of resource management/city builder like games, Anno., Factorio cities skylines and the like.The story - This was one of the best parts of the game, really enjoyable to find out the back story, supported by the great voice acting. The game did a great job of drip feeding you with bits of the story to keep you immersed, yet not overwhelmed.Graphics - Simple and lovely. There's an amazing simplicity to the graphics, but with the ability to zoom all the way into minute detail seamlessly from the orbital view.I've heard a lot of complaining about the logistics in this, game, I actually found these worked reasonably well. I seemed to get a recurring issue where my worker factory constantly produced one more worker than I had capacity for, which appeared to happen once I had scrapped a previously built worker hub and then replaced it. Whilst improving the prioritisation feature with logistics wouldn't go a miss, I'd say this is far from broken.The beginning and Mid game are great, supported by the story and resource management of the game, whilst you slowly start expanding. The daisy chaining of worker hubs, did get a little monotonous as you progressed through to the late game. Being totally honest the late game is lacking somewhat and is in definite need of additional content to keep the game from becoming a "fast forward on 16 times" until oxygen drops below 30% affair. The last 30 or so years really dragged as research projects took a very long time, and the story content had all but dried up. The natural disasters never caused a problem, so could do with having more frequent ones of those. I terrafomred Mars, yet the only difference I noted was the melting of water. I would have loved to see grass land, and forests actually visually appear on the planet and I just felt a little cheated that the world did start to pop into life. I think a real wasted opportunity to expand the direction of the game, and introduce gameplay mechanics, like balancing plant and animal life, as you introduce the uncovered cities (which took around 8 years to unlock and then didn't get used as mars was "tarraformed").To conclude - great game, good concept, lovely graphically, engaging story, and despite what the negative comments say, I think well worth the money and totally playable. There needs to be a focus on end game, because after all of that, I felt a little flat when I finally hit year 75 and the credits started rolling!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game but I have to say that it feels unfinished and unbalanced. I would say to wishlist it and keep an eye on it.It certainly has the potential to be a great colony management game, but there are a number of issues with the game design and mechanics that don't feel like challenges as much as poorly implemented mechanics. If I had to give a grade I'd say it's a C+. The game is fun and shows potential but it loses a lot of points for the issues that feel like they were just bad design choices or mechanics poorly implemented; food and nitrogen in the atmosphere are the two biggest offenders here. The major issue with food is that even though we can grow lichens, trees, and animals upon the surface of Mars and were able to melt the polar ice caps  to create oceans upon Mars; we aren't able to cultivate any food crops to sustain a long term colony. Food is made of chemicals and water, both of which are extracted and are finite resources. Water can not be pumped from the seas or rivers in game. A large population of a few thousand colonists can be supported briefly but there is no way they can be maintained indefinitely with finite, non-renewable resources. I look forward to improvements in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I played hours upon hours of this game, always excited to see what would happen in the next stage of terraforming. The hours are not on display since I first tried it out from the account of a friend, for about a day, but sadly, my excitement blinded me and it was after I had paid for it that the mess this game is struck me. I'm studying physics so I've really been looking forward to something that would scratch the itch I got for terraforming Mars, and hopefully with some sense of realism and actual numbers, that a certain other game failed to do.-The monumental let-down is that you terraform a barren planet end up with a beautiful Earth-alike scenery, with forests and a ocean plus some lakes. However comparing that to the first few hours of the game, where you create your first human habitats, you need to supply them with food and water. You collect water by mining for ice deposits, and you process food in a factory that inputs chemicals ( a raw resource you also mine for) and water and produce food. Makes sense when nothing can grow outside of some kind of enclosure. However as you progress, you melt the icecaps, introduce greenhouse gases, you terraform the planet and end up with a temperature of 16 Celsius maybe more, an Earth-like pressure around 1 bar or 1 atmosphere and a very similar concentration of O2, N2 and CO2 to that we have here. AND YET not a SINGLE thing changes about production. You still mine ice. Near the equator, heck there are even ice deposits under the water, and not a single way to filter that to for consumption or any other way. The greenery is also there just for show, you can build "biodomes" that spread radiation resistant lichen and then move on to more complex flora and eventually fauna, but you never grow a single plant to feed your colonists. It's all about getting the chemicals from the mine to the food factory.-The other huge problem is that the logistics are atrocious. You place down a worker hubs, and you produce worker drones ( tracked, not flying) from a worker factory. One worker per hub and roads are auto-generated between buildings when you place them down. Good and simple. However, each worker hub, generates its own 'sector", even if two of them are as physically close as the game allows, they will create a new sector and except for fetching and depositing resources to the immediate neighboring sectors, the drones will never leave their sector. There is absolutely no way to redraw these sectors, or tell the drones where they are needed, or an order of priorities like "1. building materials, 2. production resources 3........"and mind you this is a game about colonising a planet where you eventually are forces to exceed 1000 buildings and driven to expand outwards because raw resource stockpiles/deposits hold finite amounts of the resource. So as the game progresses what starts off a quirky but functional once you learn it, system for a city/planet builder, turns into a cursed mess, with building materials getting stockpiled on some random solar or wind farm, drones maniacally transferring the same unit of carbon up and down between two buildings, on a road, or worse, in a hyperloop connection ( the means of for long range and quick transportation of goods) rendering it completely unusable since only a single unit can be transferred at a time. You end up having to place buildings in opposite sites of the planet, yet the logistics algorithm is borderline functioning when you are confided to 1/30 of the surface. You are the most advanced AI in existence but you cannot tell the drones you supposedly control how to behave.I could go on, but I feel these alone give enough information for anyone reading to stay away. This game is a builder and terraforming sim and it does the first horribly and the second only on a cosmetic level.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Just ignore the positive reviews that has less than 5 hours.I also loved it at first. The storyline interactions are quite well written.Sound actors are very good, and the game gets you, you think you will love it, you think its just your kind of game.Then you get to mid-late game. Here are the problems:1 - Resources: Small patches everywhere, distributed randomly. You have to expand practically all around the planet just to survive. There is no improved mining tech that gives you access to bigger patches of resources or different ways of getting them. Tech helps you mine only faster, thats it. Which is pointless since even the largest patches are mined quite fast.2 - Tech tree: It basically plays with numbers. Completely fails to give you different build options as you progess. You basically build the same tedious base over and over and over.3 - Roads: You cant just connect two of your bases with roads. There is no such option. You always have to grow your base to connect to the other one. No flight connection, no bare road connection. This means if you want to get to that farther mine or research outpost, you have to build all the buildings you have in your main base in a line, so the road doesnt get destroyed by lack of maintenance in 5 turns. This is incredibly annoying. %80 of lategame is about building long lines of bases as road replacements. 4 - Depots: Tech doesnt give you bigger resource depots so you have to build 3-4 depots together. And you have no control over what they collect. Its just random. Drones basically distribute resources anywhere they just randomly like.5 - Logistics: In lategame, drones dumb down. Although you have the superspeed hyperloops and road upgrades, and tons of drones all around your base, some buildings take years to get build. They just refuse to get the resources to that building. You just wait at 16x speed. 6 - Drones & Maintenance: In lategame, somehow drones refuse to supply for drone worker factories and maintenance buildings. This should results in an ALT+F4 almost in every case. Because you end up without any drones to carry stuff, and maintenance stops building maintenance drones, so your base dies in front of you eyes and you feel an excruciating feeling of lack of control. Your base dies in front of you, after a 6 hour playthrough, and there is nothing you can do about it. Overall: Dont BUY. Its very annoying, and even if you play for the well written story, its very likey that you will ALT+F4 and uninstall, and come here for a rant.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: My review for Per Aspera is... that it's alright.The highlights of the game is definitively the story writing and voice acting. I definitively enjoyed playing a more personal version of the typical AI protagonist, and the relationships between the characters are believable enough.Terraforming Mars is definitively also good compared to competition. A lot of details goes into getting temperature, gas composition, and water levels to a certain amount, and there are quite a lot of ways to do it in the game, which gives you a lot of headroom to get everything you need to do just right.HOWEVER - The logistic part of the game is... painful. Let alone the Blue Mars DLC that you somewhat need to access the resources that become flooded in the late game, the AI (the irony isn't lost on me) that handles resource transfers is pretty unoptimized and even dumb at times. The only real way to make things work is to have tons of worker hubs to carry stuff around and use hyperloop to get anything further than 5-7 buildings moving. There's tons of moving parts, which I do appreciate, but it seems things get snagged, goes into a loop, and eventually even had a memory leak for me where the game ran calculations until my PC Crashed.The combat was also evidently an afterthought. You get drones, you send them, numbers vs numbers (and towers underfoot), and eventually it dies out. There's no real strategy or tactics, and even the research tree, while nice, is made so that you can't soft-lock yourself by not doing any military upgrades.All in all, a decent time. I'd play it if you want a chill terraforming mars experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Combat is similar to Nano Wars/Phage Wars, kind of.Infrastructure development similar to that of Settlers 2.The research tree might use some more development.A couple of bugs, but nothing major.The story is nice, love some of the Easter eggs.The graphics are gorgeous, the art style chosen for this type of game fits like a glove. The details when the terraforming really starts are what really adds to the immersion.The sounds are a bit unleveled, and the music can get repetitive, especially if you want to linger on and develop, rather than follow the story.Overall, quite an enjoyable experience, well worth the money.

The visual are impecable, the UI is easy to follow, the concept is appealing, the story is engaging. The game as a product is a pinnacle of perfection in my humble opinion. There is a lot of things the AAA publishers could learn from these guys.10/10I recommend it as a Must Have
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game looking for a Mars terraforming simulator. I'm sorry to say that this game doesn't scratch that itch, although it probably comes closer than any other game (except Terraforming Mars, but that's too abstracted to really count).I suspect that the developers might view this game as being about the narrative, with terraforming Mars as more of a setting. Unfortunately, although the story has some good parts, it's also let down by the fact that it's very easy to trigger parts of the story out of order and have characters act as though certain things either have or haven't happened. I've only had one play-through, but I strongly suspect that there is basically one meaningful choice in the game -- this is very much an on-the-rails experience and not so much choose-your-own-adventure.The gameplay is ultimately pretty rudimentary. I had hoped to dig into logistics and production chains (love Factorio, just to give you a sense of where I'm coming from), but they end up being fairly shallow. I could imagine optimizing the process, but the UI doesn't make it easy and ultimately there just isn't a need because it's so straightforward. I played on medium difficulty, so it's possible that optimization is more crucial on the hard difficulty but honestly that just sounds really tedious.There is a "military" component to the game, but it's even more shallow than the terraforming and the best I can say about it is that the AI is bad enough that you can get through it pretty quickly.I really wanted to like this game. I still do! There is a lot of room for improvement, and the devs have certainly said that they intend to keep working on. Frankly, I'm not sure this game was ready to leave early access -- the core game loop is there, but... it's just not that fun. Hopefully they make enough changes that I can recommend it, but until then save your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera: A worse factorio.Aspera is a very weird game. It hires big name VA's like Troy Baker to prop up the story of asentient AI that is colonising mars. Yet, between the weird simping of Elon Musk and just general vapidness of the story. e.g. every so often,, unprompted and in no way correlative to gameplay you get asked oooo am i alive questions. And its like, i dont know you, i dont really care honestly. If you are going to have a sentient AI, dont just have them question their sentience, do something, make a gameplay purpose, decisions, or at the very least make it interesting. Anyway, very ignorable plot aside (just use sandbox imo). What is the gameplay of Per Aspera. Its kind of like factoro. There are resource nodes around the planet. So you extend your conlony to reach them, with a weird mix of buildings. it says in the tutorial worker hubs are the best bridges (as your colony must be connected by roads). yet after a while it becomes an absolute chore because you need power to your worker hubs, so you build a power building every so often, then they need maintence, so you build a maintenence hub inbetween the two, then you need to protect them from the enemy so you build another military hub, and it just becomes an absolute mess because you have to slosh through the inefficient UI, all to get to a single resource node. But let's say you get through the AI, you have the resource what next? well, the workers take it to a factory where it's processed, and.... that's it. Thats the entire logistics gameplay loop. The only way to improve it is one click improve roads, and the only stoppers are maintenance and enemeies, all a matter of just having the right buildings in the radius. There was never a time when i had to think about any of my placements.  After you realize this, it becomes deadening. There is no solution to logistics. There is no massive transport bus or cool research. There is only one road, and it leads not to Rome but to annoyance. Researching new tech is also kind of a chore. it's based on how many colonists you have. The number of colonists you have is limited by research. So do you either research things that will actually kind of assist (like faster roads, which as aforementioned, are the ONLY logistical improvement) or do you research more colonists for the ability, to do more research? There is no game changer where it's like, you can refine a good twice or thrice to create a better end product. The only research there is is more amount of buildings you can place, yes it is capped, or more colonists. Tl: Dr, Per Aspera has an ignorable story. It has an extremely shallow gameplay loop especially compared to other factory sims, and the progression it has is extremely shallow and never feels rewarding.Buy Dyson Sphere Program, they deserve your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, UI could be a bit better like its annoying having to go into the menu to select each individual mine you want to place, they should make it so you have a centralized "mine" button, having the type automatically switch out depending on which deposit you click as especially once you reach tier 2 mines it just exasperates the problem of just having to change out the selection all the time and its just annoying. You cant even place mines without the deposit at all so there just no reason for the selection to work the way it does, the game kinda tries to play as something its not. Just pretty anti-user in some areas is all like another thing is if your buildings ever die all the way you have to scout find them and press repair on each individual one even if their under a matience bot sector like what was the point of making the things if their not gonna rebuild the gaht dang buildings when a meteor hits them (which is often) and man dont even think about upgradeing your roads it takes years to connect it all, i have no idea why they dont let you drag select all the roads you want upgradedI also just find the Narration a little weak so far with your choices not correctly bouncing off future convos which was sorta one of the main points the game tries to strive for... like i tried picking the options that were "pro nuke the poles" as one could say but then the AI you play as has a whole monolog about "man how am i gonna tell them i dont want to do this" despite the fact i had literally just said i was going to do it like. Mabye it picks up later, im still again just hitting tier 2 afterall but man, thankfully the gameplay satisfies my monkey builder brain greatly and the atmosphere of it all is really nice so its thumbs up worth the time i put into it even if its not perfect

_childDocuments_.review: I would post a more positive review but the drone combat management is pretty bad. _childDocuments_.review: It was a slog, but I managed to finish the game.  It's very much of a grind at times, and then a lot of just waiting for things to happen... even at 16x speed.  There were a lot of interesting and unique concepts, but the gameplay just did not allow them to shine through.  The lack of a proper tutorial was also very frustrating, and I found myself starting over a couple of times because I did not have enough information to make good decisions at the beginning.  The only thing that kept me going was the story, and even that ended up being disappointing.It was a decent effort by the developers, but some poor design decisions pretty much killed the overall enjoyment.Just a side note:  My game took about 93 Mars years to complete which is almost 180 earth years.  During that time only one in-game character aged at all.  She went from a newborn to 20's or 30's.  Also, Mars' light gravity allows rivers to run down one side of a crater (or elevation) and up the other.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a wonderful game in concept but falls incredibly short content wise.Positives? The story is very intriguing and you'll discover more of the story and setting via dialogue and text as you progress the game. The layout and UI are simple and easy to learn and use while the overall colour and design of the game is quite easy on the eyes.Negatives? The game lacks any significant amount of content, with some aspects being very quick and others sluggishly slow, meaning there will be long stretches where you do absolutely nothing! You'll reach build limits quickly and your resources will build up quite quickly which means you'll achieve mission goals very quickly with limited difficulty. Research is incredibly slow and reliant on colonist arrivals, which is also slow, so you're waiting for long stretches of time for research to complete so you have something to do. With 3.5hrs of play time on a single run, nearly an hour of waiting for something to happen occurred, usually in 5-10min blocks. Long wait times isnt a new for long haul strategy games but there is usually some kind of fluff to fill in the space between major events to make the game feel fuller. Sadly this is absent from PA making the game feel very empty and not worth paying full price for. But that being said I did mention it had a good story so if you dont mind the wait its worth picking up when on sale
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite part of the game was the story. Lots of moral questions. Too bad you have to grind your butt off to get there. Most of the game is waiting for things to happen while having the game at 16x speed.As others have mentioned, the stage 4 and stage 5 terraforming takes literally hours. Finding new resources  is watching a bar go up. Doing special projects is "click start project", then wait. Populating new colonies is build it, then wait for people to move in. Getting new people onto mars, is start that special project then... you guessed it, waiting.The systems in the game hide enough information from you that it gets really frustrating to play. Simple things like how your workers decide to do things is mysterious. Let's say you deploy a new base somewhere else on the planet, and want to see how much iron it's producing. Well, you can't do that. The section tool only shows absolute values. So good luck managing that. Ok, later on you get said new base up and running, "oh did I remember to build a steel forge?" time to stare at that section of map and hope I spot it.I could whine more, but this game does have great ideas. I just wished I didn't have to wait for the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game very relaxing. Even the combat was "chill". Which was good, I needed something to relax with when I was tired.The best part of this game was the journey of slowly terminating the dust ball into a green and blue planet.The story was ok.The game does have some problems however.It is very difficult to find your buildings again since you can't really search for them is a big one. So upgrading say colonies to domed cities is annoying.Lastly there is no way to introduce animal life that converts O2 back into CO2. And your humans doesn't do that, so after the game is finished CO2 drops to zero and the planet is actually unsustainable, which was a bit of a let down. Clearly you are meant to stop playing once you finished the campaign.Anyways, I enjoyed it, but there is no reason to play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If I could, I would give this a neutral review.  The story, voice acting, and visuals are all very strong.  The game really endeavors to capture the grandeur and mystery of Mars and it succeeds at that.What holds the game back is the gameplay.  To be frank, for a colony-builder / resource management game, it falls flat.  Sometimes I wonder if the devs playtested the game at all.  Even after several patches, the user interface feels cluttered, and it can be difficult to find relevant information to your tasks.  For example, at the beginning of the game you are limited to a small amount of total colonists.  But you won't know that unless you stumble across it in a tooltip or infer it from a tech tree research option.  If too many colonists show up and you hit the limit, colonists start to leave but the game won't tell you why.  It's that sort of baffling oversight that frustrates me.There's a distinct lack of clear feedback on what you should be doing to between major story beats, and the best ways to avoid resource problems.  The tech tree is a real let-down, as none of the researched options really change your core gameplay loop for most of the experience.  Most of the research boils down to "do what you were doing before, but a little bit better, faster, or deeper, but visually the same."  Big terraforming projects are cool - but they aren't exciting to execute.  You just assign the newly unlocked project to a spaceport and everything happens automatically.There are a number of other gripes and nits I could list that stopped me from fully enjoying the experience.  That's a shame, because the good parts are really exciting and enjoyable.  What tips this review to positive is the heart and effort by the dev team.  They've put a lot into post-launch support and it shows.  I want to see what their next project will be.  But I do hope that next project will strike a better balance between engaging minute-to-minute gameplay and story.
