_childDocuments_.review: The game seems interesting to play, especially in sand box mode. I just began my first campaign mode in easy to get to know the ropes. There is some sort of enemy on the planet that sends out drones to attack. However, the algorithm the programmers put in have it attacking me faster than I can rebuild and faster than I can build my own defense or attack drones. I am spending all of my time defending and rebuilding only to have hundreds more come in before I can even rebuild what I lost in the last battle. If this is the easy mode, then I don't recommend this game for anyone. Easy should give you a chance to feel out the game and not be stressed to losing the entire thing in the first few years. You need to fix that problem or I will continue to not support this and give bad reviews.Part 2 of reviewAnother review on the game. I started a new campaign and go through the issues above. That story line is ridiculous as an AI is not going to forget something like that, but that is all I will see about it. Once I made it past that I then suffered catastrophic failure of all of my buildings at the same time. Part of the story and I get that. I had 146 buildings at the time and every one of them suffered. The problem I have is that it wouldn't build maintenance drones to fix those problems. I had 8 maintenance facilities and put them as priorities, I went 8 years game time at the time of this writing and in all of that time it built me maintenance drones only a handful of times and only 3 at a time. I started losing my worker robots so I took priority off of everything and set my worker factory to priority. My supplies were very high, but I went game time several months before it finally brought me 1 supply of glass to build another worker. Priority evidently doesn't mean anything to the system. Still in easy mode. It appears that the programmers expect you to fail, and if you aren't, they will make you fail. I am still playing to see if there is a way to beat these very obvious programming fails or to see if they will fix them in an update. I like the premise, just not the story the programmers want to tell. I won't change my recommendation until these are fixed and you quit taking the joy away from the game.I had for a moment thought to give this a thumbs up as they supposedly fixed issues. Turns out the core issues are still failing. Either all of the maintenance stops at the same time so you can't repair things for a long time. Or I have tons of energy one month and the next 100 negative and I didn't build anything. I look at the weather and it shows bright hot sun, so it isn't dust storms or sun that is causing the power fluctuations. Then when I look at my research speed, I have 235 people and I have 2 points per month in research being created and another time I have 35 people and 10 points. There is no logic. Unfortunately the research points per month go down just when I have to research the  military stuff, so I can't build enough drones to repel attacks and my place gets destroyed. I think I have played enough hours on this to say, they don't want you to win and will do everything they can to make sure your colony never survives, even in easy mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Actually it would be a 45° thumps up. The game is pretty good and it makes enough fun to play it multiple times for all endings, but there could be improvments.... Short:+ interisting gameplay+ graphic+ really nice storytelling+ while buildung you come to a lot of philosophical question during self-talk as a AI ^^- not a single "endless" mine. Not even in later gameplay..... It gets a little bit anoying to change your infrastructur so much.... - phase 4 of terraforming is not really balanced. You produce O2 and than all building start to burn..... there are only two difficult ways to decrase it...- The O2 producing buildings are really meaningless, because it is more a problem and not something you want....- There could be more buildings in some points or improvements of buildings like a bigger relay station... or monuments as one-time placement or something like this
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is thoroughly unfinished. It's got some depth, but not nearly enough story to justify its playtime. The only reason for the difficulty system presently is to pad incredibly underbaked and unbalanced design overall. I wish I could speak better of this game. Buy on steep sale and to the devs: consider telling people this game is not actually finished, storywise, mechanicwise... anywise. This is pretty damning to your product to not indicate. It is inherently dishonest to call this a 1.0 product. The story just... ends with no resolution to much of anything, no credits roll, and no indication there is anything further beyond the tolerance of the player. I hope you eventually finish the game. As the product stands, wait until they release some form of complete edition, as there's just not enough to work with here for a fully conceived title.POST: My friend Erbkaiser's review is now up as I got him into this game. He made very different choices and got a very different ending to me, one with a credits roll I did not receive. I will update this again if I find out that there is difficulty-locked dialogue as that would just be absurd given how little happens in stages 3 to 5 with the choices I made.. He also took quite a bit longer than I did. I would say do not take any play time for gospel, it can vary drastically. This does not change my lack of recommendation until the devs fix some of that rather glaring issues with pacing. I would like to... but there are too many problems for me to recommend it. This can and possibly will change if the devs address and fix the issues, as I do intend to check it out again when the next major expansion drops in January.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun, but the UI makes the logistics a nightmare. The UI that shows resources, for example, becames completely useless as soon as you get a second settlement, because it only shows you global resources across settlements, not how much is in each settlement. This would be fine, except that there isn't any trade between settlements. So basically, you get a big number that means nothing. Like, I have 500 aluminum rn, so it looks like I'm rich, but one of my settlements is actually out of aluminum and I had no idea because nothing actually shows the local tally.Update: after completing the game, I have to say, I look back on my playthough with great fondness. Once I got over some of the pains of it being an indie game, I found it addictive. The story is great (and has interesting and meaningful choices that make me want to go back and play out the what ifs of going the other way on big decisions), and I loved that you play as a globe spanning AI rather than the typical commander.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended on sale.It's a beautiful game, with fun mechanics and visualizations. The main downside being it drags on too long from the mid game. The first 10-15 hours are a strong recommend, but if you are a completionist you may find it a real slog to finish the campaign - at least I did (and quit before that point).
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Insipid. This game is insipid. The gameplay's thin, the design's clumsy, the scientific gloss flakes off with a mere fingernail's touch, and the writing - God, the writing! - feels like it came out of a mid-tier creative agency staffed exclusively by Reddit. Expect to spend most of your time with Per Aspera daydreaming about what a good colony-building sim with an AI-driven Mars colonisation story might look like while you wait for the game to stumble over its next boring revelation.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I got Per Aspera in a bundle a bit ago and figured I’d give it a shot as it seemed up my alley. Per Aspera is a fairly standard colony simulator except it has a story that is actually pretty interesting. You play as an AI who is tasked with terraforming Mars to make it livable for humans. It’s not the most in-depth story but it kept my interest and does have some interesting twists, which I was not at all excepting from a colony sim. The Story is fully voice acted, which is nice, although at certain parts of the game it can get annoying how frequently voices pop up to talk to you. Additionally, even at 16x speed, there can be times where you just sit there waiting for buildings to complete or tasks to finish. The game is also very poorly optimised. You don’t need tons of frames for this type of game, but it is annoying that I can’t even hold 30 fps when neither my GPU, or my CPU is maxed out. All of my CPU cores seem to be in use, but not a single one is above 70% usage, with most of them being closer to 40% usage.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. It maintains it's pace throughout the entire game with an incredible sci-fi story. If you liked Surviving Mars you will like this.Just finished the game. Oh man it's sooo good. Please play it. To the Developer:Bravo!Make way/road upgrading easier, maybe drag and drop a circle and all roads in that area are improved? Make the space elevator more relevant. I assume it's like a hyperloop but at a global scale. But it's unclear in game. Population a little more relevant. Make me responsible for their happiness. Build parks, hospitals, schools etc to keep them sane. How many different endings are there? Can't wait for a sequel!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The voice acting and story would be superb - if it actually played in a coherent sequence. The campaign is so poorly paced, unbalanced, and full of bugs that it's hard to imagine it was play-tested at all.The overall gameplay is quite fun at first, until the mid-late phase of the game turns your well-thought logistics network into a nightmare web of exhausted mines, inactive factories, and broken-down power generators. The game offers no way to automate or eliminate the micromanaging tasks that become extremely tedious over time, nor any tech options to reduce the sheer quantity of buildings that you have to maintain. The priority system is also extremely basic, and once you have 200+ buildings, it becomes impossible to manually assign priorities, turn buildings on/off, or even remember which facilities are located where. Lots of potential - could even make a neat multiplayer game - if the bugs & usability issues are addressed.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Its fun and I've played a bunch of it.Its a novel and interesting game in many ways - the integration of the narrative elements is probably the most interesting part - the second personality test is fantastic and the high point of the game.As per sci-fi tradition hte final wrap up isn't the strongest, but the rest of the narrative is excellent - i really enjoyed how you can steer the character you are playing as to get their personality to develop in different directions, i still dont understand functionally how that is implemented (and i build these kind of systems for a living) - its just a very interesting system.There are a few annoying characters, and some narrative missteps - i feel like a bunk of plot was awkwardly cut in the handoff between the lab lead and her daughter - in general managing all the loose threads of the open story gets weaker as the game progresses and there are occasional missteps.And it almost starts comically nieve but then deepens as it goes which is quite enjoyable once it gets going i was telling my wife some of the character lines and we couldn't decide if it was satire or not.The actual sim aspect of the game is also interesting and engaging, there are still some quirks in how the drones work (which is the real core of the game) - mainly that I'm not 100% on how long distance resource transfers are scheduled and how they interact with the hyperloops, which has kept me from having great success scaling colony's into the late game, but there are more recent patches and definitely more for me to know.I know one of the newer patches addressed some quirks in how mines worked that would have been my next comment.The only other complaint i would have would be a bit of a lull in the pacing right out of the gate when you are playing on the harder difficulty level - its clearly tuned for normal diff (which makes sense and is fine for this kind of game).All around its fun - I recommend to sim game fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, but there is a lot of waiting involved.Recommend this alongside Terraformers. A bit faster paced game that I played first. I don't think they compete with each other, it just depends on what sort of night you want. Want to terraform Mars in under an hour? Play Terraformers. Want to play a 4x version of terraforming Mars? Per Aspera. This one has way more story too and I appreciate that. Although Terraformers lets you add elephants to Mars, so... Yeah, I recommend both.I'd advise patience with this one, though. It has a VERY slow pace, but is also very grand in scope.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: My friend gifted me this game so we could play it together, we had a blast. Ended up doing like 3 different saves because we realized we (mainly me) goofed up, especially in the realm of "where do we launch or first bases" I highly recommend placing your starting positions relatively near each other (not too close, take the circle that it shows you'll take up, and move at least twice the diameter away from eachother, then connect later, this will give you a great start).ON TO THE REVIEW:I won't be the first to say this game has issues and that Steam needs an 'eh' rating, gonna start with the main pro: pretty cool game overall and you'll have moments of "wow, that's beautiful" that make you briefly forget any issues you've had, the euphoria this game can bring as well as the beauty of it is greatnow for the problems, this list is kinda big but trust me it's not THAT bad, you gotta play it quite a bit for some of these issues to become a problem:- the game can be slowwwwwwwwwwww at times, I would not consider it cheating in this game if one were to use Cheat Engine PURELY to tell the game to run at 4x speed (the game already lets you go to 16x speed but sometimes that's just not good enough, warp drive baby)- the logistics in the game sucks, sometimes saying something has priority will bring 80 robots, 1 per necessary resource, to build the thing instantly. Othertimes it won't do anything because the nearest robot station is rubble or some jazz. I'm not kidding when I say I built a sector up, got pretty far, water started threatening that sector, I removed everything, built a thing that goes next to water, waited 5 years before realizing that it wasn't building because there was 1 resource left (I had 5000 of that resource) and the nearest robot station was broken- seriously, if you want to increase efficiency you pretty much just have to throw down as many robots as you can in the right spots, there's no way for you to be like "alright robot #87 your job is to collect JUST the resources from these mins and put them HERE, ONLY HERE, DO NOT UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES GO ON A 500KM HIKE TO DELIVER THESE RESOURCES YOU DUMB ROBO BOY THANK YOU <3"- if you OPEN the console by accident, no more achievements for you on that save, hopefully you realized that. it's the grave key (you know the ` key with the ~ if you hold shift. Right next to 1. 1-4 being used to set speed control)- if you built in a flood zone, your stuff is probably doomed, there doesn't seem to be a nice way around this- As a guy who likes to mod games to my liking I find this game's modability lackluster and wish they would just compile it normally instead of with il2cpp so I can see the source code and do pretty much whatever I want- oh look at you expanding, you wanna go all the way over there because you've run your mines dry? yeah? that'll ruin your efficiency most of the time until you unlock hyperloops. Building roads is garbo, please let me just paint them. Oh, you built a road through this mine that is now empty? Yeah, sure, delete the miner, see where your road goes. - oh, you thought you'd expand by making another drop pod? that's sweet, good luck connecting those 2 points, you get to play the start of the game again with your new base over there and your 1 robot while your big base ends up having a problem while you were too busy staring at the small base- your fps will suffer in the later game, so many nodes if your base is huge- if you want to make a resource storage that can only hold a particular resource you have to manually set all the other resources to 0, gl with that- seriously, the logistics is a problem- batteries are useless, that is a wasted research node, 3 MWY (3 MWs for a year) is garbo, 1 solar plant, even at the lowest power, beats it - wind power is dumb, I'm fairly certain it never gets better even when the atmosphere gets thicker and I could be wrong but I'm pretty sure thicker atmosphere with more wind = more wind power- as far as I can tell there's no sustainability, the meteors that fall early game should give *something*- if a resource node gets flooded you cannot get those resources ever again. Fun fact: half of Mars is a flood zone (then again like 70% of earth is a flood zone so I guess that's fair)- seriously, there's no research to let you build on water. How can we have a space elevator but not a mining rig that sits atop water- half of the special projects suck- I'm still pissed that there's no way to like build a land wall around a node before the water gets too high, we can pump water from the north to south pole with like 6 pumps, I refuse to believe I don't have an excess of rock that I could take, build up a land bridge, barricade a node with said rock, and pump out the water- eventually you'll be able to build in craters with particular nodes, the craters have to be just right though for it to work, and they have to not flood or whatever you built there is gone, I have a robot army, I should be able to dig my own craters- seriously, let me terraform, you know, landform, form the land, even if it takes a year or something- as far as I can tell, if something gets flooded and you didn't say "scrap this building" before it gets flooded, those resources are gone (meanwhile if you said "scrap this" and then it gets flooded you're fine, the robots will still EVENTUALLY scrap it, I say eventually because my friend and I had a branch that needed destroying before it got flooded, 10 years later and the robot, yes a singular robot, was still working on it)- If you build a building and destroy it you get 100% of the resources back. This is cool BUT if you build a building and realize "whoops, needed to place that a little closer" so you destroy it and build another one RIGHT NEXT TO IT, the robots won't go "oh, I can just move the resources like 50ft and build this in a few seconds" instead they'll USUALLY do something else (usually since I think 1 time they actually did just use those resources to build it)I would still recommend playing the game one time, that's it, just once, there's not a lot of decision making other than which order you want to do your research unless you consider the campaigns options of: "die, kill everyone for some reason, keep going" an option. Your only replayability is going to be "I feel like I understand the game really well, I'm going to try it on hard mode." There are parts where the campaign makes you click a dialogue option but I'm fairly certain those do not change the outcome other than the 1 time as previously listed. Campaign had an interesting story though it really felt like they talked too much at the wrong points and not enough at others. You can mod the game but not really, there's only a few extra assets and if I read the documentation right you're not allowed to bring in your own so you're pretty much limited to just modifying the numbers in the game...Rant over. cool game, just has some issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A resounding YES. Per Aspera is just challenging enough (on the normal difficulty) to not be a push-over, while also generous enough not to be ultra-frustrating. It's not Anno in space, but it does have elements of that game as well, only instead of complex goods chains and satisfying population needs, you basically just produce resource buildings, workers and production facilities that at most need 2 different resources. But you will also manage water, atmosphere, enemy drones, space operations, power and even relationships and ethics. Per Aspera guides the player through a 5 part story, starting out with just your lander and 1 worker and ultimately sprawling out over the entire planet, melting the ice caps, releasing CO2, introducing O2, growing plants and discovering the mysteries of Mars. Without spoiling anything, there are a multitude of research sites you will not all get in your first playthrough, though that isn't necessary. A few interesting ones definitely drive the story forwards and at some points you can make your own decisions and shape the story. Thank god for the 16x speed option though. That one is absolutely necessary. The graphics are nothing to be excited about, but they're functional, just as the HUD is. And thus the high speed is possible without completely breaking the game's animations. It runs perfectly fine and still looks stylish.Now for some criticism:- There are a lot of things the game simply doesn't tell you. Luckily you can find pretty much everything you need in the Steam community hub, but that should NEVER be necessary. Combat for instance, or what certain space projects do. It's great that I can import Ice, but how much am I actually importing? There is no info on that and I never noticed an increase after a delivery. - It's nice that the game features lenses for different things like power distribution, water distribution, worker load, etc., but what it REALLY needs is a filter for buildings. Have fun trying to find a specific building you've built 15 hours ago that you need to get rid of NOW!- The game needs a better prioritization system. I've literally been waiting several in game YEARS for a building to get the last remaining resource to finish construction. And it was prioritized. I had enough resources. I think the game needs to be smarter here. Especially in the later states Hyperloops should make localized production facilities no longer necessary, but it's hard to keep track of the individual worker bots and what they do or don't do.- Generally, the player just needs more info on certain things in the game. Especially in the last stage I was feeling a bit overwhelmed, because I'm not a terraforming expert, so I have no idea how much CO2 the planet still needs. Apparently 0 isn't good. The temperature droppped, flora died, and whatever I did I just could not re-introduce more CO2, despite importing Greenhouse Gases, despite putting up CO2 factories. I'm not sure IF I needed it, but the game said that CO2 should be at 5% or lower. How much lower? Isn't CO2 needed to create a balanced atmosphere in the end?Or how does power work exactly? The game doesn't tell you that it has some kind of day/night cycle (which isn't daily, but rather yearly or sth like that), which means that all your solar power suddenly stops working for a few seconds, which shuts down your entire grid at the beginning.Things I wouldn't mind seeing:- A deeper tech tree with more meaningful options. Quite a few researches are just simple upgrades (that you then have to manually apply to each building). I think it would be better to have upgrades automatically apply with no penalty and instead introduce some more building options. Perhaps new resources even or new space projects.- Worker hubs imho need a redesign or an upgrade option. Why can one hub only house 1 worker? Why does that worker only travel in a certain radius? I think it would be nicer to have LESS worker hubs with MORE workers and a bigger action radius to reduce building clutter and improve worker load.-Even more story beats. Especially for a first time player there could be more missions that guide you and also involve you deeper. Some characters felt flat, because I didn't have the time to properly take care of their missions.- More nuanced combat. Right now it's: Build drone hives, find enemy, send all drones, win. I think the game needs more defensive options and less focus on actual attack with drones. Maybe more upgrades for drones and overall less of them. Maybe even artillery bombardment or some other warfare options.- A next stage end game perhaps. The game has this really cool looking splash art where you see what looks like a giant city from space. Unfortunately, this isn't possibly in the game. The basic gameplay stays the same after you've gotten the military tech tree. Why not have another tech tree for urban development perhaps after terra forming is complete? It "could" transition into a completely new stage after that. Just some musings.I liked the game. Enough to spend almost 20 hours on it, but even though I could make some other choices in my next playthrough I don't really feel it has much replay value. The basic gameplay loop is just too much the same in the end. Unlike Settlers or Anno where each game has unique parameters, Per Aspera can't match that, since you always have the same resources available. The only difference is how quickly you have to expand if you increase the difficulty. However, I cannot share some of the negative reviews' opinions about "just so much waiting". Yes, you WILL play the game at 16x speed at the end. Yes, it WILL take a lot of time to finish stage 4 and 5 in particular, but I've NEVER felt bored, because there was always something to do, always somewhere to expand, some production cycle to improve, some resource to manage, rising water levels requring my buildings to be repositioned, suddenly no longer having access to 5 ice factories, etc., so if there's nothing to do, I dunno, maybe the person is playing with like abundant resources that never run out and just doesn't actually play the game?
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game is definitely interesting for a few hours. The graphics are interesting and the zoom in / zoom out at a planetary level is neat.The core loop is simple and mostly mindless. You put a node on a resource, the roads automatically connect and your drones auto mine it. You place a few of the factory buildings out randomly to provide the next tier of resource, and then after that you put a few of the terraforming buildings out randomly. A large part of the game is waiting on research to uncap your building limit or unlock the next buildiing, so you put it on 16x speed and wait.Something as simple as making you manage the roads / logistics could have probably gone a long way to make the game feel more engaging.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: It was hard to decide what to say... I'd give it 3/5. It is almost more of an interactive story than a game. Everything is extremely easy, except for the tedious stuff. Upgrading things is way too annoying, especially roads, since there is no mass upgrade option. The resources are completely unbalanced, so only a couple kinds of resources are annoying to produce, and you just spam buildings for them. It is hard to call it a city builder when it is just narrative with an unbalanced economy. Since the game is 3 years old, I doubt much will change. I think they'd be better off either focusing more on narrative and getting rid of the complex micromanagement stuff, OR investing much more into the economy and challenges of actually building. The game has a lot of potential and interesting ideas, but it really isn't optimized at all. If it were a major studio, I'd definitely give it a thumbs down. Worth buying on sale if you are interested in AI and sci fi. Not worth it if you just want to build a colony.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: That was fun until unlimited hostile drones appear. Also, lacks some grouping or search functions: I'm desperately trying to find my specific factories to give it priority so I have resources to get some power plants restored and don't have -700 energy consumption while those hordes attack me.Please, get us some QoL updates. The base game is good.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If you are vulnerable, this game'll get ya good with the just-one-more-thing-itis. I typically sleep around 10pm and this game kept me up till 4am last night. Amazing (though frustrating, in a good way) base building gameplay, great map of Mars, and a surprisingly enjoyable narrative with tremendous voice acting. Can't recommend enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game, did not expect it to be really good despite its "simplicity". It's not THAT simple, the complexity is there when talking about the terraforming process, I suppose that's a good thing. The gameplay mechanics involving logistics is very straightforward, although I wish I could place the roads myself. It also puts on a challenge by having a military branch (don't worry, it's very simple to utilize), so the game wouldn't be all too peaceful and bland. One thing I wish that was in this game, though, is being able to settle and terraform other planets/moons as well. I look forward to the progress of this game, I hope I had the money so I could've bought this sooner.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game invokes the wrong expectations in people. For those expecting a Factorio level of logistical neatness, this game is not for you. Its systems have enough meat in them to justify its core gameplay loop, but not enough to make the logistical megalomaniac blush.What it does satisfy is the fantasy of terraforming Mars. The graphs and the systems that track your progress are satisfying to complete, and feel realistic enough to fulfill your fantasy. The story that happens in the background enriches this fantasy by inserting the game in a plausible conflict we may see in the future. Watching Mars slowly grow green as you carefully balance the elements is a treat that satisfies the brain of a very niche type of nerd. If you want that, buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Do not buy--until they fix the software bugs!  Because, right now, here's what you get when you purchase Blue Mars DLC: (1) game-killing lag through all phases of play and (2) a broken tech tree that doesn't let you research water-based capabilities.  The only thing blue about Blue Mars is how you'll feel after playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is unique and brilliant. The core mechanics of colony development are sound, and the story itself is one of the rare good stories where telling it through the video game enhances it even further. For a first playthrough, going blind is best, and while the Blue Mars dlc isn't necessary to win, it is both fun and decreases a lot of resource bottlenecks you can hit starting from midgame.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Decent game. It is stunning and also extremely satisfying to watch the planet transform from being a barren hellscape to being a lush green and blue oasis. The storyline is actually also very compelling and interesting. There are some gripes though, the logistics in the mid-late game are insane, and you have to spam sooo many worker hubs basically just to keep everything working, and the sectors that are drawn and redrawn for the hubs don't make a lot of sense half the time. Some things I think would make this better: allowing players to manually fix hub sectors, and also an upgrade to worker hubs that allow more than one worker....probably up to 5 or so. The deeper mechanics are not explained very well, and honestly I did not even realize that you can look at a list of all of your buildings sorted by name/efficiency/etc until very late in the game. That is something that would have been helpful to know.The military/combat portion of the game feels very bland and not challenging. You can easily walk through the game without taking any upgrades in the military tech tree. And a personal gripe for me is when splitting your drone swarms, the new swarm is the unit that is selected, I feel like it would flow a lot better if the main swarm that is being split off of remained the selected unit. Additionally when having one swarm selected, and clicking another swarm, I feel like it would help gameplay feel if clicking selected the swarm you're clicking on, instead of having the swarm that's currently selected merge with the one you're clicking on. For merging, I think using a modifier key like shift, control, or alt and then clicking would make more sense. Also a longshot, but I would definitely buy an expansion that reworked the military system entirely, like ground combat, more indepth aerial combat, etc, even though I know that's not the focus of the game. Another thing is the weird mid-game where the oceans are constantly rising, but you also need ocean buildings to compensate for all the ice melting. This makes it so that shipyards and piers have to just be built and rebuilt every time to ocean level rises and turns them to rubble. Not sure what a good solution for that is, besides once you get to that point, just rushing as much ice from europa as possible until you're at a comfortable sea level.Anyway, overall, fun game, hyperfixated on it for like 16 hours straight, the little beeping noises that the worker drones make when they complete a run gives me serotoninAnother thing in a similar vein, and I'm not 100% on, but I feel like this is happening. Whenever you start up a new lander site, it spawns a new ice node, no matter what terraforming stage you're at, so then the ice melts and raises the sea level, once again messing up your buildings.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly well done version of the 'colonize mars' type of game. It was a lot more relaxing & forgiving than I was expecting it to be. While the various characters do push you to complete the various stages of the missions, there is no really rush to do so. & the ability to recycle *completely* any resources used in building construction makes it much more forgiving of mistakes or reorganizations.The only time the game actually pushes you is during the periodic attack missions. As the resources used to build anything destroyed during an attack are lost. Though even then it isn't too difficult to turtle up if desired. My only complaint is that during the combat missions, there isn't really a warning of any type if a section of your base gets attacked while you aren't watching. The start of the combat missions is well broadcast, but anything after the first wave simply flies in without any warning at all. Regardless, it is rarely more than a disappointing surprise, not a colony ending disaster.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, very happy with the game as it lets you terraform mars as an AI. Interesting story with a few nice twists. Great to expand your territory and develop your colony. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR - interesting plot (at least what I saw), initially fun, but AI seems to randomly fail to do what needs doing, and even when it is working the late game is slooooooooow.  Also the graphs and management system are often too high level making finding that one problem item/building in the mess painful.  Also, lotsa busy work needed.Main review:I was actually enjoying this game a fair bit in the early stages but once I hit late middle to early end game (Green Mars stage anyway) things just got silly...For starters, everything slows to a crawl as you wait forever for a counter to tick up to finally reach the next milestone.  It also gets fiddly as water consumes things near it and you have to rebuild on and off as it expands.  Unfortunately you need to build things like water treatment plants actually near water, which means they often get wrecked.  Why can't I build a floating or water resistance treatment plant?  Ditto for  other things that must be in or near water.But the real killer (like in Surviving Mars) is the AI just implodes periodically and given this is a hands-off management game that is a real problem.  When I gave up my run  I had a large number of buildings desperately needing resources or waiting to be built but they were not getting resource snot matter what priority I set them to.  Then the game decided (for the second time but I somehow unstuck it the first) that despite the above issue it didn't need worker drones so while I previously had ~80 of the things I suddenly only had 16-18, and none near where they were actually needed!  I also could not get them  to move glass - the core resource most of my stuck or broken buildings needed - even though I had 900 units in stock.  I built hyper loops to try and allow what few drones I had to move them from more distant stockpiles to where they were needed, but they just wouldn't do anything.So I got stuck with a bunch of dead buildings.  Technically I could have actually just left the game running for hours on its own and probably cracked the next stage as my atmospheric mix was (glacially) heading in the right direction and the colony was stable, but man, how boring would that be?  Not fun! Also the graphs and management system are often too high level making finding that one problem item/building in the mess painfulAlso, there is a lot of busy work.  You want to build some new useful buildings or setup a new outpost.  You will need to build all the basic support junk again as you are invariably out of range of the prior infrastructure base.  *Sigh*.All this is a pity, because the plot was looking interesting.  And early on, it does all work ok.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: For AI you have no management options for optimization such as priority resources production and transport. Hyperlenes too slow and no quantity change of rss possible, always 1 per worker no mater the tech. Road upgrades use same worker that do transport, so upgrading roads take forever and holds entire production. No option that a road will spawn or not, upgrading a road that splits and uses part of the other road that has been upgraded will downgrade to upgrade again, or the portion that this does not happen will 'upgrade' at same low pace.I was hoping to see the big upgrades in animation, like space mirrors in action, or aerobreaking a comet trough the atmosphere. Nothing. The only thing I see is a Rocket launch for advanced landing sites and Rocket landings from other places, and a colony space elevator arrival. Go play Terraforming Mars a strategic tabletop and you will have more fun then this so called simulator. Even the events that make you choose your AI views are made up to test if you are going to make your AI paranoid, rebel or something else. That's the only think this game makes right, to make a psychological profile of you.

_childDocuments_.review: Voting No because there isn't a Maybe option on Steam.Per Aspera offers itself as a factory-logistics game wrapped up in sci-fi story of terraforming Mars. To this end you are Artificial Intelligence/Consciousness known as AMI, assigned by ISA space cadets to work the machines on Mars. The story features some interesting premises, and plays to them with a serious weight. I am interested in seeing where it goes, but I have not gotten far past terraforming stage 1.The gameplay of Per Aspera is where the blood is getting drawn.It is problematic in the kindest words to say, and crippling otherwise. The fundamentals of the game are as follows: you setup mines to gather raw resources, your workers then transport these resources to factories. Factories refine the appropriate resource, and workers take as the factory pops it out to wherever they're needed. Simple idea. Per Aspera has a ... bizarre way, of handling this throughput.Every worker needs a 'hub', every hub only has 1 worker. These hubs create 'traffic zones' around themselves automatically, and that hub will only work whatever is in its respective zone. Workers are soft locked to these zones, though they can step outside to do other tasks sometimes. So long as a complete production chain is inside one traffic zone, it will function without issue. When production chains are broken across multiple sectors, it breaks down quickly.Workers will transport materials through their traffic zones, leaving them at the border of another zone for that zone's worker to pick up materials. This 'daisy chain' is how material is moved for the most part throughout your entire planet-scaling base. However, workers must do all their other tasks in that zone, in addition to handling material transport. This can result in supply chains sitting stagnant for literal ingame years as the drones prioritize their zone's production facilities.Additionally, workers suffer from ignorance of how to work with cross-zone functions. Resource storage hubs act as overflow, however only the worker in their zone will feed into them for the most part. They can be neighboring a mining zone of 7 mines and none of the overflow will go into them by either zone's workers. There is no way to setup priority supply routing for central storage or creating 'factory areas', as the daisy chaining effect above simply prevents it. Similarly factories will starve of resources because they are too far from the mining locations and too many work tasks by other drones prevent materials shipping in. Supposedly this is not an issue, given worker load is 40-70%?These fundamental issues have left me a bit flabbergasted. As it stands I cannot really say the game has functional logistics, because it's a simple work queue that goes through its tasks without player intervention. The most you can do is 'higher priority' by one tier a building, where it is pushed to the front of the work queue always. This can cause problems as it greedily gulps down whatever it takes and starves other facilities elsewhere. Increasing drone count is seemingly the answer, but the traffic zones and their fussy behavior make scaling that up rather troublesome. If the zone is too small, drones sit around doing nothing. If it is too big, they are always busy working. If it is just right, they're still busy working in their own space.Perhaps there is some secret sauce I am missing, but even peering down the tech tree, looking at youtube videos, and so forth, I really cannot find it. The logistics model is not intuitive, communicates what it wants/needs poorly, and is hard to come to grips with. I am hopeful these issues will be addressed, for as it stands I am quite miffed at my purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this game is designed very well, The  player assumes an AI role to terraform Mars by developing resources and building bases, etc. The "Base" building aspect is automated mostly in that the player just has to select the building and location, subject to constraining resources, and the interface automates the connections, "roads", etc.  A well thought-out aspect.  The graphics and voice acting are good and overall game play is straightforward. There is much to do with objectives to achieve, a bit of a learning curve as the game advances, options for terraforming, researching and overall management.Interestingly, the game also touches philosophically on issues concerning terraforming Mars and the role of an advanced artificial Intelligence in that task and in interfacing with human colonists offering the player chances to think and make choices related to these issues.

_childDocuments_.review: gave this one a chance despite mixed reviews and actually liked it.its not super deep, but resources are limited and if you don't plan ahead you can totally build yourself into a corner.so there is definitely some challenge here.in some parts progression is quite slow but you can speed up the time to mitigate that.the gameplay also drastically changes 2-3 times when you enter the different terraforming states, which is pretty refreshing and provides new challenges.also the blue mars DLC is pretty much essential, but they added a bunch of other free DLC that also adds a lot of things for free, so i think overall its a fair deal.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on launch because the demo left THAT much of an impression on me. Unfortunately, currently I can't recommend it for the following reasons:1. The logistic web you have to spin sometimes makes it too easy to get yourself caught in a bottleneck where you need X to make Y, but you're waiting on Y to make X better or faster, etc. This isn't so bad in the very beginning when the game is more forgiving so there's more wiggle room, but later on the game tasks you with starting a new base elsewhere in Mars, and you have to begin the whole process over again, but with less leeway. And for some reason you can't send resources from your main base to this offshoot, which was frustrating because my main base had the raw materials to spare.2. YongYea is a voice actor in this. On the realm of "this person is a toxic scumlord AND they don't bring any talent to the table" when it comes to voice acting in video games, this is somewhere between Ronda Rousey as Sonya Blade and whatever Jontron was doing in A Hat in Time. Seriously Tion It looks like there's a decent roadmap of content coming as of the time of me writing this, but how much of it is actually new content and how much of it is quality of life improvements that are sorely needed is a little unclear. _childDocuments_.review: I am very mixed on this recommendation. Overall, I liked the story, the characters were decent, and the voice acting was much better than I expected. The base building is very satisfying to see the end result with a fantastic visual aspect.That said, I am mixed because: the game itself is really wonky. You are ostensibly on Mars to terraform it, however that goal is secondary to your own survival. Most of the time I found progressing through the terraforming requirements wasn't important, and took my time doing it. This ludo-narrative dissonance wouldn't be so bad, except the way you progress in the game is tedious.All resource deposits run out, which means your only survival strategy is to constantly expand. Expanding is critical, as later game projects require too many resources. Setting up secondary bases, and then linking them to your primary base, is all you will do in this game. And the tools for doing that will leave you wanting. You will just power/worker/maintaince/storage walk in a giant line to the base you just slapped down to link them so you can feed your primary base.Each base you create? It will do the exact same bootstrapping process you had done from the beginning. Every single time. Managing production quotas is impossible, though there are plenty of tools for visualizing how your production is failing. Not much you can do to effect change.As the game goes on, performance drops, and the number of resources and robots you needs climbs fast. You need to constantly be expanding to afford all the projects, keep your colonists alive, and more. It becomes a real chore.Here are some improvements that would have a big impact:1) Remote bases are not fun to manage. Starting with more drones on a new base, linking power over greater distances, and having more starting resources on the new base (that don't need buildings) would reduce the repetition. 2) I want to set per-region resource min/max, not per base. Once I had 40 bases or more, I don't want to go through each to manually set resources max, or turning off the steel factory at each base that I needed to get that outpost through the bootstrap phase. Being able to define a "region" of linked bases and setting production quotas would help.3) The grind is too long. You need thousands of carbon, iron, and more resources for various projects. I wasn't even sure the defense network was necessary. The story hinted an attack would come, but once built, the network was never "tested", so it felt pointless. The space elevator was underwhelming for its cost.4) Space ports should be nameable, and clickable through the mission selector. The dropdown is too small.5) Managing pop influx was frustrating. You have a small window to remember to cancel more pop from coming in. You can "cheat" this by turning off the space port, forever freezing the colonist ship in place, and also locking up your space port. Just let me set a max pop or something and have the ship make its own trips, or anything than the current way it works which is frustrating.6) If I have hyperloops, why do colonists take extremely slow airships? Waiting for a colonist ship to spend *months* moving to a new, story required outpost (of which there are many!) is agonizing when I have a globe spanning hyperloop network that can transport water in a few in-game days.7) Upgrading roads is tedious. If I remove a building in between (so as to free up building slots), the upgraded roads are removed.8) Terraforming has no in-game benefit or drawback. It doesn't affect wind or solar output (shouldn't more atmosphere make wind turbines better? Solar worse? Should the mirrors make solar better?). Water on the planet isn't drinkable, apparently. Forests and animals aren't food. By the time you can get open air bases or whatever, the game is past its welcome in terms of grind, and the bases before then can support more pop than I can deliver resources to, let alone generate enough water/food/chemicals.9) Losing pop has no discernible impact on the game. If you starve your people, they just peacefully leave. No impact on the AI whose only job is to...make Mars for humanity. Yes, it makes research slow, but you'll be spending so much time grinding base expansions and other objectives that it doesn't matter. The characters won't even remark on hundreds of pop leaving.10) The only cool tech in the tree are space elevators and hyperloops. Everything else is underwhelming (or just simply required, and thus neutral). Military tech is the least inspiring. 11) New-game plus would be wonderful to experience the other stories. For now, it is too much grind.12) The required amount of sprawl, while obviously carries a strong story component, feels overly forced and annoying. It makes expansion feel necessary only for the story, rather than the stated purpose of your character, which is to terraform. I suppose this ties into the feeling that terraforming is only a goal, and loosely ties into all the events and things happening.I know I had a lot of criticism to provide, and I really did enjoy my time with the game. But I had hoped for more, and these many flaws prevent me from playing it again, rather than spoiling the experience I had.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful city builder/planet terraforming game that unfortunately has glaring issues in logistics and a ton of bugs. This game will, for seemingly arbitrary reasons, sometimes completely cease to function and you'll be forced to just accept it and have to remove and replace buildings from time to time to get things rolling again. There are plenty of features that are just completely broken and should not be used under any circumstances - these include Storage Chests and secondary landing sites. These will 100% break your production and are NEVER worth using under any circumstance. There are other features, like Hyperloops, which will increase productivity overall but require a restart every so often as they tend to get stuck bouncing items back and forth.The campaign has decent writing with good voice acting. I have no complaints on that front (so far at least, I'm at terraforming stage 4 at the time of writing)This game has plenty of potential as terraforming Mars into a habitable planet over time is a really enticing prospect to build your city around. Unfortunately the plenty of issues that are in the game that will frustrate you for hours detract from the interesting premise and makes this a difficult game to enjoy. I got this as part of a Humble Bundle and would not have paid for it normally, and I wouldn't recommend anyone else to do so either, hence the negative review.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a few Mars colonisation games, but with the DLCs, this is by far the best.- The story so far is quite good.- Believable terraforming that is rewarding to complete.- Gameplay is mostly focused on expansion and discovery rather than management.- Base management is very well designed, the player can slip between "broad strokes" management and micromanage when it's (rarely) necessary.The pace is fairly slow (that's a good thing) and the evolving story tied to your exploration keep things fresh.   I found that in the late game the story got very sparse, but that's probably because I wasn't progressing a quickly as I could.I played through with the green mars and blue mars DLCs, and I can't imagine playing without them, so i recommend you buy the bundle.20-25 hours playthrough with the DLCs.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played for 4 hours and I have had a *magical time of it*. The story so far is hauntingly beautiful, and full of self-discovery. It's pretty cerebral, but without being inaccessible. The art style is simplistic, yet I loaded up the game and gasped, as I realised my colony looked like a neural map- the more connections I made, the more Mars begins to look like a living, breathing thing. This game is going to have to *SERIOUSLY* have a terrible ending for me to not consider it one of the best, most engaging games I've ever played.10 hours in, I have to say the background music is simple, but soothing. Could it get old? I'm not really sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If I'm forced to give this either a thumbs up or thumbs down then the scale just barely tips towards thumbs down. On a scale of 1-5, I'd rate this as 2.99.On a Scale of 1-5* Gameplay 4 - I did enjoy it.* Graphics - 2 - Would have been considered state of the hard 10 years ago. Low resolution and not a whole lot to say "wow"* Story line - 1 - plus, there are many numerous bugs which cause the game to crash. * Sandbox mode - 3 - very limited.* User Interface - 2 Very Glitchy, Glitchy and Glitchy!!! Did I say Glitchy? You click on one thing and the nearby thing is selected. Plus the controls are maddenly wonky, they just don't want to behave. I'd say they rushed this before release was ready and didn't do a whole lot of testing. Simple example of this is that when you quit, you can't save the game in the same stroke, you have to save first then quit and then it complains that you'll lose progress. Likewise, there is no way to reload the game without shutting it down completely and waiting for the horrendous load time. Other minor annoyances is a crude file name interface. On the subject of graphics, you would think that 4K would be in the cards. NOPE!!! And while I'm at it, when one zooms out, all of the artifacts get in the way of clicking on the objects underneath. Zooming and scrolling is messy. Plus, you can't look south. The other thing that got old quickly is the lack of icon filters. After more than a few hours of game play, you're looking at a cluttered mess of icons. Last but not least, no manual. I mean really? I guess that's because it's a foreign studio where they don't have English as a first language speaker. All in all, this game studios inexperience in game design shows. I've seen smaller studios produce a much higher quality product.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Much of the time logged was afk, resulting in the one ding I have on this above all else - it feels a bit short lived for the price. There are branching choices that can be made that impact the game that can mostly be realized by creating separate save points rather than needing entirely separate playthroughs. I've had a good time, maybe not enough of a good time to play again. Get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: For someone who is really into autistic 4x games this is one of the better ones I've played. While it technically isn't 4x, the city-building mechanics have significant overlap and the early game feels incredibly intuitive. As you unlock more tech and hit more story beats, more mechanics are added for you to juggle at a steady pace. While the difficulty never "spikes" it does add a constant and daunting difficulty slope that just keeps on ascending and challenging you to keep up. Fortunately there are time controls so you can speed up or slow down the game to match your level of immediacy, regardless of difficulty settings. Everything from the story presentation, music, mechanics and visuals are incredibly polished and high quality. For the asking price I could not recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Props to the studio for making this game free to play for a weekend.  I read the reviews first, which were mixed, about 1/3 to 1/2 said that the basic gameplay loop was some variation on boring/grindy.  I really love the idea of this game, and so decided to check it out. [minor spoilers follow]I picked the second easiest difficulty, and was off to the races.  I didn't read any faqs beforehand, though I have played other basebuilding/"Mars" games in the past.I thought the tutorial was good up to a point, and then left everything to the player to figure out.  Using the journal/notes helps, and I suppose in this day and age the internet faqs are the best bet.The GoodI thought the opening sequence was excellent from a storytelling point of view.  There's a mystic/mythological feel that many classic Mars books talk about, and it became clear eventually that the writers/game designers were generally well read people.  The sounds, voice acting, and the look of a tiny little outpost settling on Mars were very cool.The PotentialReally this game has tremendous potential.  I found combat to be clunky, but not a huge challenge at below-normal difficulty.  A little tweaking here could add a lot.Visually the look of a city spreading across the surface is great.  Having real place names really made it feel like a tour/educational experience of Mars's geography.  The Grind?I play RTS games like Warcraft III quite a bit.  I took it as a challenge to try and 'macro' better.  That worked up to a point, that point being roughly when I got my first colony going.  At that point there were many conflicting directives as the story really got going.  Rapid expansion meant that stuff was just plopped down.  I had to run on x16 speed just so that research would finish in a reasonable timeframe.  It did feel that gameplay fell into a pattern of building the same set of structures over and over again, and there were moments (alluded to in the story) where it felt like this ugly blight was taking over the pristine Martian surface.  The story also felt... odd towards the end of stage 3, where I stopped playing due to the weekend being over.  There were echoes of HAL, and strange culty people.  The history of the past expeditions was also interesting, but maybe could have had a different mechanic?  I found it annoying that the process consisted of a 'rocket launch' followed by the same repetitive process of building a new base, occupying the research site, and waiting.  One of the research sites was underwater, and I couldn't figure out how to access it (and trying to lower the sea level by refreezing the ice caps just seems silly).Overall, I would rate this game about 75%... not quite my cup of tea, but could easily be someone else's
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely insane. I had it on my wish list for a while and was skeptical until now, but now I bought it in the sale and it was worth every single cent.the story, the atmosphere, the gameplay, and the whole way the game is presented is very innovative.if you liked factorio, dyson sphere program and the like, this is your game!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A fun automation game with a great story-line, though the transport network lets it down. With limited transport options and congestion problems the game drags a bit. Terraforming the planet is a delight and a fun challenge to balance, though with care and the guidance of the game I got pretty earth-like conditions on mars with mirrors, greenhouse gases and 20% oxygen / 80% nitrogen.It has really gorgeous and appropriate graphics, good UI and great voice acting. I couldn't stop playing it, it is quite relaxing and addictive. But having reached the end credits there were long periods with little to do. Much of the game is mechanically quite repetitive, building the same structures in a similar pattern but in different places.Most resources are found in shallow mines which cease to function relatively shortly. Most last about 20% of the game. This mechanic makes most of your early structures redundant as the game moves on. While that pushes you to expand to new areas, it is also somewhat tedious.You'll hit the building limit and need to scrap much of your base before you finish the game, clearing out old mines and transporters. Some building sites will get flooded as you melt and introduce water to mars. There are minerals and research sites you might lose access to (due to underwater) if you don't plan well.The game doesn't seem to use multiple CPU cores well. It also doesn't seem to render and simulate in different threads. This means you will experience frame drops as your factory grows into the second half of the game. That gets extreme if you accelerate time.The pacing is indeed lacking at times, fortunately there is a 16x time acceleration which (while running at 3 FPS lategame) helps a lot. I get the feeling that I was too efficient for the story-line, with the military aspect being trivial for me and the whole planet was green well before the end. Even a couple of military upgrades and every part of your base under the umbrella of a defensive drone hive made it a toddle.You will need to take care to stop production of certain items. Specifically Polymers and Parts (they look like cogs) which permanently use up chemicals (needed for food instead), carbon and steel. If you don't turn off Part production early on, you might end up with thousands of useless parts and none of the steel you need to survive. It would be nice if you could set global production targets, with reasonable defaults like 10% of all items (limit of 100 if you have 1000 items, etc). Perhaps all stores should default to a limit of 50 for each item.Terraforming with the bio-domes and their sea eqilivent are poorly explained. Look in the built-in help guide for details. The basic version is that every base should have a couple of these, preferably in the orange/red temperature zone. You'll find getting enough oxygen very easy once the planet has plenty of plantlife.I look forward to see what the developers make next. _childDocuments_.review: I've finished one full game, and I'm unlikely to start a second one. Maybe after a few patches and changes to the mechanics, but that's a stretch. The concept is great, and the AI story/decisions is interesting. However, it's too unpolished in its current state. Lots of projects or items don't have useful descriptions, so you can't always make informed decisions. I won tonight by building something which honestly seemed like a stepping stone to other things. No save, no option to continue. Just....game over. The logistics system is incredibly frustrating, and you mostly poke at limited priority controls and hope that things get to the right places. In practice, your robot workers are stacking random things instead of delivering the things you need.  No controls for managing overproduction of any materials, outside of micromanaging individual factories.Resource spots run out quickly enough that you'll spend most of the game just building out to grab more resources. That's laughable at times, such as when you are scrambling to find ice resources while staring at a giant ocean.Many things on the tech tree are traps, where you really need later techs before you start using the ones you've already unlocked. That's most commonly when converting co2 to oxygen, where you need the nitrogen coming in soon, or some other way to balance co2 and oxygen. It's made worse by many of the space projects being broken - you can't repeat them without saving and restoring the game.Anyway, many aspects of the game just aren't terribly fun in its current state. It feels like early access still. YMMV.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this since launch and it's been really fun watching its progression through development. It's come a long way since then and I'm still having fun with it. I want to say that it's one of those games that's easy to learn but difficult to master but we all know that there's going to be that one guy in the back that expects hand-holding the entire time lol. That said, the game DOES do a great job with easing you into the action, but for alot of it you have to figure things out on your own as you go along. It doesn't tell you what to research/build or when but it does give explanations everywhere in the form of tooltips and an in-game wiki if you need it. In the early beginning it teaches you some of the basics, but after that you're free to play how you see fit. Pure freedom, mostly.Mid to late game you'll find yourself waiting alot, once the water levels start rising...since during that stage of things you'll also find yourself demolishing and rebuilding alot as buildings get submerged (depending on your placement, of course). It doesn't exactly ruin the experience though in my opinion.There's so much more I could say about this game but I prefer to leave out any potential spoilers; however, overall, I highly recommend :) Even all the DLCs are worth owning since they do add definite substance. Personally, I'd easily rate it a solid 8.4 out of 10. I love that this game exists.P.S. Also, yes! It does use actual Mars topography and height maps. I don't know exactly how accurately true-to-life the weather and climate systems are but they're adequate and seem legit. Storms and other random events are well balanced in frequency/intensity as well (there's been alot of changes and tweaks to all of those over the years). They suck, like they should...but they don't rage-inducingly kill the fun :)

_childDocuments_.review: I am really mixed about this game & would say the negative points are more on a subjective level. Played it during its free week.Positive Points:- Absolutely beautiful story for a simulation game. Voice Acting is very nice and the story feels really good. The story is not intertwined mechanically into the game play, but it still doesn't feel out of place. The time that progresses works for both gameplay and story. It was really my main reason to continue this game. That said, it is not something unseen. Feels like a good doctor who episode.- It looks really good (Sadly the looks don't support the gameplay, will comment on that in the negative section)- It is fun for about 2 hours and then again when ressources get scarce. I played it on the recommended mode and the difficulty is on the lower level, but not totally uninteresting, it's definitely a game that you can let your kid play (minus the story).- Traffic System is kinda fun, once you see the logic.- New Game Mechanics unlock at the right time in the game, it was always the moment I was bored that something new got unlocked.- I love the historic stuff they put in there, would be great to get a bit more information on it. I also _love_ the lore they built, their world feels really round (Even though a bit black and white)Neutral Feedback (For me, these things were bad, but some people might enjoy them):-  It is definitely a slow game, I mostly played on the highest speed setting.- No micromanaging possible due to missing informations and options.Now to the negative. None of this is something that can't be improved, but I fear a lot of these are very major things:- My biggest pet peeve: You absolutely can't see what the different buildings are doing, even the icon overlay barely helps. This is something a lot of sci fi simulators have to fight with, and it annoys me a lot. There is no overlay for highlighting certain type buildings (This is _absolutely_ needed and I won't turn my review positive / buy the game until it happens. This is a serious threat!) and in general the UI is not really good. It looks good, every kind of overview/menu misses some information that you need to make a good decision. You also don't have options to e.g. upgrade all streets/ buildings of a certain type once you unlocked the upgrade via your science tree. If your mines are empty, you need to zoom in very closely to see that they are not producing anymore. You never have an overview over why something is missing - Did I just build a bazillion buildings that need this resource, or are all my mines dead? I guess I will just make a few new mines and never find out.Just give me some overview where I see all my buildings and other stuff. Every single other simulation game has this. This is really taking the fun out of optimizing your game.(*I didn't finish the story, which is partly about keeping information from the player, so it would be a great twist if in the end these kind of data are unlocked. But then hint at it more. This way is just frustrating)- Fighting is very basic (which I like!) but kinda unintuitive. Partly due to the reasons mentioned above; I have no idea why sometimes my drone armys combine and sometimes they don't. Still, due to fighting happening only a few times during the story, you're probably either completely overpowered (like I was) or underpowered when it happens.- There should really be side stories / interesting things that you can research or just... do while youre waiting for your ressources to fill up. Just make them textbased or whatever, but right now, research sites that are not relevant to the main plot are absolutely uninteresting, so these would be a great start. Right now, the game is a lot of waiting, and in later stages you are partly waiting for the plot to catch up to you. - Give me more speed. Please, a x32 speed option would be kinda needed. If you only drag out the time your players are playing by limiting their speed, then you really need to think about whether the game you made is actually fun.Right now, I cannot recommend this game. I would love to, I will put it on my wishlist, but until the UI is fixed, it's just not my game. The other issues, especially the speed, are definitely weird game design choices, it almost feels as if the game devs purposefully tried to do things different than in "usual" simulation games. But why tho?

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the kind of busywork logistic games where you set up supply lines and watch them go, but don't like the constant math and optimization that usually comes with the territory, this game is a nice change of pace. _childDocuments_.review: Summary: Amazing narrative, mediocre game mechanics.  78/100 is a fair score.I'm not normally a fan of sandbox/city builder games.  But I had a blast with Frostpunk, and a hard sci-fi Mars terraforming simulator, starring an AI sounded right up my alley.The narrative is AMAZING.  What started as an idealistic mission for the benefit of all humanity, quickly spiraled into a tangled web of secrets and danger.  More than once I stayed up far past my bedtime, eager to see the next twist in the story. Graphics and sound are both great, reminiscent of the excellent show The Expanse.  I'm rather amused that some of the in-game music later on sounds like it belongs in the DOOM series.Unfortunately the game mechanics are mediocre at best, frustrating at worst.  First there's the worker system.  They appear to be massive truck-sized robots that do everything from building & dismantling facilities, working mines, transporting cargo, upgrading roadways.  As your base expands, the load on your workers increases.  But there doesn't seem to be any way to effectively manage or distribute that load.  The game provides zero guidance.  I tried spamming worker hubs, and ended up up with lots of adjacent zones where workers are practically idle.  But there'll be one adjacent worker hub with a backlog of 20+ jobs.  Why???  From the narrative, your AI named AMI cares for those robotic workers.  There could have been a story event, where AMI observes her workers are overloaded, and shows you how to fix that.The UI leaves a lot to be desired.  On my first playthrough, I noticed some mines were turning off seemingly at random.  I kept turning them back on, and after a random time they'd turn off again.  I found out later they had run dry, but the UI doesn't make that readily apparent.  You're not likely to be looking too closely at an individual building, when you've got a huge sprawling base.  Worse: you have the option to turn back on a useless dry mine, and you can even upgrade it!  That makes no sense.  Roads have 2 levels of upgrades, but upgrading is a huge pain.  The worker-hub view shows you which hubs are overloaded, and also which roads have the most congestion.  So you can prioritise those roads right?  Oh wait, you can't upgrade roads from the hub-view.  Also you have to zoom in pretty close to tell what upgrade level a road is.  If you chose the wrong road segment for upgrading, there's no way to un-select, so wasted resources and time.  It seems to me that unlocking and upgrading infrastructure should be where the most fun of a city-builder game is.  Per Aspera turns this aspect into frustrating busy-work.  These are just a couple examples of UI shortcomings.  You can't even load a savegame from within your game!  You have to exit to the main menu first.  What is this, amateur-hour?For all my misgivings, I really enjoyed the game.  But now that I've completed the story campaign, I have zero incentive to replay.  And that's unfortunate.  There is sandbox co-op play which I never tried, but I can't imagine why anyone would care.

_childDocuments_.review: Really wanted to like this game. I played Surviving Mars and didn't really enjoy the fact that it was basically just a city builder with a Mars theme. TLDR its an ok narrative game, but the logistics and science is really eh and sometimes bad. I would suggest people play on easy/story mode. This game poses as a logistics science game with a cool narrative to drive it (AMI the AI). However the logistics/economy of the game just isn't that great. It also trips you up as you go along, with the pacing being wildly all over the place. Water levels started rising and flooded whole areas I'd hoped to mine with little warning - dialogue being somewhat out of step with events - long lulls in story progression with not much to do but wait for the badly designed logistics game to catch up. The story is ok, gets a bit cringe for me at the end and the directions your 'reflections' go are a bit tame/human. But early on it does pose some quite interesting ideas to you. But by the end its lots of A or B questions that deserve much more nuanced answers. I'd kind of recommend it for its story telling and visuals, and I'd like to see something like this again. But with more attention given to the gameplay. I could have AFK'd a third of this game easily. I didn't, but thats not a great sign.

_childDocuments_.review: The game was decent enough till around halfway through (albeit with some weird design/balance issues, like the bio tree raising your colonist cap to levels you could never possibly sustain, extremely easy and unbalanced combat, and resource RNG).  But later on the game really slogs down.  In particular, the poor worker AI often left many of my factories sitting idle because they were waiting on a resource delivery from halfway across the planet instead of the stockpile right next to it.  I had to micromanage prioritizing factories for awhile to actually get the right resources created because without priority, my workers would just never service the factory.  Even with priority, they'd often prioritize overdelivering one resource instead of all necessary resources (later leaving one of my colonies with 200 food and 29 water with more food on the way when I had 300 water in my stockpiles).  On top of that, some later technologies are completely pointless.  Top tier combat drone upgrades only come decades after I wiped out any opposition on the planet.  Bioengineered animals, as far as I can tell, do literally nothing.  They don't even spawn.  But by far the most annoying thing I ran into (even if it was less impactful than the worker AI), is that the south pole is completely bugged.  The game seems to keep the same number of sectors on a line of latitude regardless of how close it is to the pole, and speed (and hyperloop costs) are based on sectors, not geometric distance.  As a result, I spent a bunch of time running hyperloop lines down to run over the pole, only to find that a hyperloop connection that normally costs 20 steel and carbon instead cost 170 of each.  And the connection was a fraction of the speed of what hyperloops normally run.
