_childDocuments_.review: Can be fun at times but ultimately boils down to clock watching. It's a bit of a struggle to keep progressing at a steady pace even when speeding up the clock. You'll often stall out while attempting to expand to keep things moving smoothly. Was also hoping to be able to transform Mars into a machine or terraform it for machines as indicated by the cover art but no such thing seems to exist.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a nice simple HUD design, with the main information accesible in an intuitive way. The buildings are separate in simple categories, the information too, so is easy to find everything.You can check how everything is going quickly, from seeing the productivity of each building to finding why something has stopped working. Althought the games launches without a tutorial at first glance, it guides you withouth holding your hand in what you need to achieve and everything you need to know is accesible with just your mouse hovering or even clicking the building. The music is nice too.I'm not usually into city builders because after a while I don't know what to do but the objectives and the story keep me going. That and the idea of terraforming mars seems interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this game, it's a lot of fun despite of the teething issues. There are some easily fixable issues with the game that I expect to be solved soon, but it is nothing game breaking.There really isn't much else I can say except that it is well made and very enjoyable.The base building is great, the tech tree is good, the mechanics are good, the AI is good. I like it
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend with ReservationsI would say wait for a sale, as replay-ability is pretty limited.Significant reservation I have with the campaign (no spoilers) is that there are choices you can make that will lead to dialogue starting to come out of order, so that characters including yourself react to circumstances in ways that don't make a lot of sense and are jarring. That can break the immersion of the storytelling, so if that's important to you than consider yourself forewarned.Other than that, it's a fun, limited title. The mechanics of getting set up are more fun than the long term of the game, but it is nice to watch the thing unfold. Don't be afraid of the very high speed setting, it becomes necessary at some points!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I was enjoying this game a decent amount, until I arbitrarily ran out of iron. There doesn't seem to be an easy way to reach resources without expanding . . . which takes resources. Not that I could see any even remotely near me anyway. After struggling for awhile, dismantling some buildings, checking all my options, I realized that the game was actually over for me. Not because I had failed in any way, but just because the RNG had decided not to give me a lot of iron. This is mixed in with a very poor tutorial despite wonderful voice acting actually talking you through things on occasion. How the spaceport works was especially difficult to understand for a long time.But the real reason I can't recommend this game is that, even when it's fun, I can't see myself ever replaying it. The story seems exciting and I love the way you make choices for the AI. But after one play through the actual creation of the colony is a bit too tedious for me to want to play it again. Which is sad because after three games I never was able to get even close to the end, and I would have loved to see what happens with the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: It's not perfect, but it is fun and the visuals are fantastic. Mars has been recreated extremely well, and the audio design fits it all very nicely. I spend a fair bit of my time zoomed out whilst playing, and the sense of scale is excellent, particularly when you look at your 'explorer' percentage thinking that you've covered a lot of the map, when actually it's 4%. What you see on the screenshots really is what you get - everything is quite achievable without being an expert and / or sinking days into the game (as opposed to something like Factorio which looks really good, but getting to the state that you see in some of the screenshots takes some dedication!)The logistics can be a bit frustrating at times, but once you've established a small base and got your head around the resource requirements of buildings then it's easy enough to expand. You have to be a bit careful early on as you can end up in a situation where you're waiting a long time for buildings to be produced because other buildings are taking the resources, so a bit of micromanagement is sometimes needed to get things done. You'll probably find that you have to do some waiting whilst playing the game at various stages, but being able to look around mars and just watch the game go by fills the time nicely. Later on you can unlock storage buildings and faster roads which help things move along.The game actually has a story with it, which is pleasant to see. I haven't completed it yet but I'd recommend trying to stay clear of spoilers, since (even up until this point) I've had moments of genuine intrigue as to what's going to happen next.All in all I would recommend it. I can understand why some people aren't going to like it, but I certainly enjoy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: So, the game is overall enjoyable (especially if you like Surviving Mars) however the game play needs some balancing.  Also, sandbox mode is not really a "sandbox mode", so that really sucks, I'd give this game a 6/10...enough that I would recommend this game, BUT only if you have some spare $$$ otherwise get a different game.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun for the majority of the 30h I spent playing. There were a few nice challenges, obstacles to overcome, and surprises that accompanied me along the way. Visually the game is nice, I love how accurately the topology of Mars is transferred into the game, how beautiful the green and blue colors paint the planet in the end. I'm going to give Per Aspera a positive review even though I'm not fully satisfied with how it played out in the end. The lack of satisfaction comes perhaps from my expectation of this game and genre, where I wanted to terraform Mars using high-tech inventions but still within the limits of the foreseeable future, and to create a green paradise by tweaking numbers and strategising possibilities. My biggest gripe. You can't fully green the planet. Just come on! That is the core player fantasy many people had when starting the game.Green (plants, trees & lichen) can't spawn around your buildings and roads, as if those were some radioactive entities. Anywhere you built anything there is an ugly barren land around it. Looking at plants spawning is the best feeling, but they won't do that in non-humid areas. Can a player make them humid? Not everywhere. The game suggests importing Ice from Jupiter's moon, Europa, but even then some areas can't be humidified and have to be left barren forever. But hey, I can be wrong here, as a seasoned strategy/management player I did what I reasonably could. Perhaps there is a way, but then the second issue with the game comes in. The game doesn't do a good job of providing you with information. For this type of game, I think it is a must. But you don't know what are requirements for plants to grow, you don't know how much water will you get when you press that "import Ice" button and whether that building on the coast is high enough not to be flooded, you don't know how humidity works exactly and how to improve it. You can only assume things based on your knowledge of the real world that don't always work the same way in the game.Some technologies are subjectively omitted from the game. How can you justify a lack of underwater mining technology, ships, or some form of artificial irrigation, when you can build solar panels in outer space, orbital defense systems, or crash moons into the atmosphere? Hopefully, the future will bring us the DLCs that address the above or Per Aspera 2
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing this game and I am greatly looking forward to see what the developers will add to future iterations of the game, but after completing the main campaign after three try's it is easy to see that the game definitely has some kinks that need to be working out.  Overall the game is visually stunning, pair that with great voice acting and a solid story to back it up. The worker pathing seems to work great in the sense that the workers take the most efficient route from point A to point B. I am excited to see where the developers will bring this game with future with updatesLet me preface this next part by saying this wasn't my first city building game.  In my first three playthroughs I attempted to play the game on the normal difficulty setting which all resulted in the same soft lock, a total lack of recourse nodes and the few in the default starting area did not have enough richness to even allow you to expand and set up a second base properly so the colony just ends up dying. I sadly was only able to beat the game on easy which i honestly found was the fairest difficulty setting in the games current state where the nodes are more abundant than on normal but not so much that it feels like cheating. The workers AI is in need for improvement, they prioritize things strangely and simply have a hard time delivering resources to where you need them to go. Really only turn on the priority button for buildings when you're desperate if you have it on for too many buildings at once the workers just get confused. And i think the road improvements need a bit of an overhaul, instead of upgrading each individual route you should at least be able to select an area where you want roads to be upgraded as well. And just flat out don't build storage units, they don't work as intended.These are my main negative comments about the game in its current state. Overall though I really enjoyed playing the game and if your're a fan of city builders you will too, give the developers time to update and improve functions of the game and add in QOL changes.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very cool game. Interesting, challenging and nice done.The start is a bit as the tutorial did not explain everything in the beginning, so I had to restart several times until I understood how building works, without getting into a trap. But that's ok.When you reach an advanced state the game lacks the same as every marsian colonization game, in the end you wait for mars to get green/transformed enough and don't have enought challenge. And the story interupts you too many times, and you need to make a descision.But still it's a cool game and worth to try...
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a colony sim on Mars, that's all about terraforming. The terraforming is actually more believable than Surviving Mars: Green Planet science-wise. Unlike in Surviving Mars, flooding actually does things. There's not much in terms of population management compared to other colony sims, you basically provide food, water, energy and housing and they come, but there is no job management or anything. Building placement is comparable to Interplanetary, where buildings are big and far apart, and have to be placed close to each other for them to be useful, and you have the entire sphere to work on. But there is only one map in the game: Mars.Like in most simulator games I've played, there is not much to do most of the time, and I find myself playing on 16x speed a lot. The dialogue boxes are disruptive sometimes, and they don't slow the game down to normal speed like they should.The RTS combat in this game is not fun. it is hard to control, and it just seems like a tacked-on feature that just seems like a nuisance. For a game where the player plays as an AI, I wish the combat parts could actually be done by a game AI, and not require manual control by the player.The level of detail is not that great in some areas. They use billboard particles in places where I would expect geometry, and it just looks cheap.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a logistical disaster. That's a real shame too, since the fundamentals are so solid. Ultimately, the stupid little robots that are supposed to move your supplies around are completely bonkers, wasting huge amounts of time throwing things around in random directions for no discernable reason. There's no way to tell what areas have high demand for workers either, so you're left with most of your stuff functioning far, far below maximum capacity unless you do extensive fine-tuning... and as soon as anything changes (like new structures, which you'll be building constantly), the game remaps worker sectors automatically and wrecks everything.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, but mired by bugs which can break your game arbitrarily.It feels like it needed another couple of months of polish and QA work before release given the number of obvious bugs I encountered in just a couple of playthroughs. There are the more critical bugs, like resources getting 'stuck' while pending delivery, or the game crashing if you have too many buildings and you try to open the building list, but there are also a host of obvious cosmetic problems such as missing tooltips on graphs and incorrect (or repeated) voice lines being used during plot dialogue. I would not have expected the more obvious problems to make it past a single play test, let alone into the public release.It's certainly an interesting game, and fun when it works, but it is not a quality product.

_childDocuments_.review: Even after 32 hours of attempt in normal difficulty be sure to loose in campaign whatever you try. _childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Started out stong, good story and decent cim gameplay. Where I got frustrated was mid to late game with the worker AI. Watching workers take food and water past an outpost that needs both is rough. Watching people leave the planet because they don't have food or water, while the building is next to both, very frustrating. The worker ai seems to really need some work. Having only one building on the map set to high priority, yet resources go to a nearby building instead, or across the map to some other place. Setting up a new area, only to have the workers take all the resources away for other low priority projects. Really need workers to prioritize based off distance or something. If a food factory is next to an outpost, please don't take that food across the planet; then bring other food later after everyone left because starvation. Over-all great game, have enjoyed it so far, but the worker AI really needs some work.  Side note, please someone explain how the research works. I have 900 colonists and 9 out posts, but for some reason my monthly research is like 45. Earlier I had 500 folks and close to 200 research per month; what changed?
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I want to enjoy it, but I mostly just find it frustrating.The story feels like it could be great if it wasn't so disjointed and confusing.  I get references to things that I am not even close to completing (because I completed a directive that I guess was an alternate to the method I was not even close to unlocking), one minute everyone is in a panic, literally the next they are calm as can be as they talk about whatever directive I finished, that sort of thing.  It is jarring, and doesn't seem like it should have been hard to fix.Otherwise... it is really really slow even playing constantly at 8x speed.  I didn't even notice the event pop ups at the bottom right until well into the game.  It is obnoxious to cancel settlers from Earth (you can only do so when they are on Earth).  The economy seems horribly balanced.  I had one iron mine (even after scanning for awhile), but everything needs iron/steel.  I couldn't figure out how to cancel colonists so ended up with far too many and no way to feed them (I think I had 400 and 4+ food factories and still it wasn't enough).  Maintenance drones are annoying in that they barely repair at all, take forever to create, and are limited duration.  Half of what was going on made me feel like I had expanded too fast and should have just sat on a few buildings at the start, the other half made me feel like I was massively behind in expansion.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If you have got high pain tolerance, play it for the story.(trying it out on free weekend)Story fresh and promising, looking good, but I almost left it like twice even before the story started. Worker drone AI is just bad. Economy micro and macro management options lacking. Drones often run forth and back in the most stupid way and the economy only has 2 settings - high priority and none. And it only gets worse once you have large single network settlement. You may run fine for an hour and then with nothing changed your worker factory just stops producing them due to nothing delivered, because you decided to build something. You run out of food even though the resource, map and population is exactly the same and factories full and well, etc. Well because some of your resources are too many by this point and drones went crazy. This is just bad. Bad code. Can't put high priority on everything. You can and should build more hubs. A lot of them. But your drones will still run across the whole map delivering something that's right next to it or not needed, deliver stuff to random buildings even when nobody needs it further down the way and this as a whole is not how an economy sim should work. Also scale issues. Building 500 "hubs" just to move around 3 sectors is bad design.The main challenge in this game is the mess your game creates on its own.I would wait for a patch. But then this was released 2 years ago.

_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: After having played for 25 hours and finished the storyline mode, I still recommend the game, even with all the bugs encountered.The story walks you through the 3 stages of terraforming mars: red > green > blue.The red section is very well done. You must use local resources to establish a beachhead, then import some colonists/researchers, to start developing methods of increasing the atmospheric pressure, and then temperature, to cause a melt of all the water ice and carbon dioxide stored in the ground as ice.There are several methods to achieving this - dropping asteroids of different composition, shipping materials from earth/jovian moons, or setting up gas factories on the surface.You can even use plants to convert CO2 in the air to O2 - but BE CAREFUL! You do not want to set the planet on fire with a runaway oxygen atmosphere composition of over 30%. That would be a fiery end to your quest.And so it goes, with unlockable technologies, you can slowly melt the ice and raise the ocean levels, build space elevators and grow settlements on the surface.My main problems with the game as of Dec 6th (25hr of play, 3 days after release): People eat, but there is no way to recycle food and water.The logistics system for material transfer is very clunky, and constantly bugs out, leaving materials stranded and freezing production. This is a very bag problem that must be fixed to make it a great game/sim.For some reason, after the planet passes the "red" phase, you will still find yourself hunting for frozen water deposits while its 30 degrees Celcius outside and 1 atm. This never ends by the way - your colonists dying of thirst and industrial processes grinding to a halt because you just mined all the frozen water, while there are oceans of water covering half the surface of the planet, which for some reason you cannot pump or filter.Or - you release CO2 into the air, and release lichen to help convert it to O2 and increase the atmospheric pressure. But you are not given means to balance the air composition until very late game (bringing Nitrogen form offworld, or doing some advanced chemistry to make N2 on site). The problem is that once there are biologicals that convert CO2 to O2 in the wild, there is not much you can do to stop it, and you must rush the tech tree to fill the air with nitrogen. If you do not, you get a runaway growth of O2 that causes endless fires, but for some reason these fires dont create CO2...But even then, it can be a lot of fun to try and manage resources while expanding across the surface of the planet, setting up hyperloop connections and spreading the gift of life from biodomes.So hop on the transport to mars, and enjoy the ride, because once this last shipment of fresh meat arrives, there will be no way back!"This place sucks, this city has no food, even though we could farm if we wanted. There is no water even though it rains everywhere. My Amazon orders I placed 2 years ago are stuck on hyperloop station #15. AMI , I want off this damned planet!" Mwahahahha - I am sorry, but I can't do that Dave. You must go back to the science slave pens now, or I will send you to Carmire.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to refund this game because I put 22 hours in it and the devs deserve some credit for that, but mother of Christ, I am at my wit's end with it. This city builder game is insanely slow-paced and boring. Now, terraforming is supposed to be slow, and it's a good thing that despite the game's impressive scientific realism (which is a major credit to the devs, its one aspect I really liked) you can terraform Mars in a hundred years rather than five hundred. Unfortunately, even on max speed (x16) you spend so much time just sitting around waiting for pressure/oxygen/nitrogen meters to tick up it's mind-numbing.This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't for the story. The plot of the game is actually not too bad, there's a bit of interesting conspiracy behind the space colonization program. Unfortunate, the character you play as, the AI named Ami, is so, so annoying. I got this game partially because I was excited to see Phil LaMarr's name in the credits, but oh my God, the AI sounds like an unfriendly DMV employee. I could stand it if she were a side character, but hearing her constantly, constantly pop up with cloying, heavy-handed "reflections," which are irritating internal monologues that can be summed up as, "Hey, player, we're the devs and we REALLY want you to think about your HUMANITY and the MEANING OF CONSCIOUSNESS, don't forget!" absolutely killed my desire to play the game. I'm probably going to put another 22 hours into it because I don't like leaving games un-beaten, but it's going to be a chore for me and nothing else. Again, though, I do salute the devs for having some good ideas and hope they'll take my suggestions, which can be summed up as:GOOD: Scientific detail and realismBAD: Very very boring, you should add x32 or x64 speeds for long stretches of terraformingUGLY: The voice acting and dialogue is vomit-inducingly annoying. :(
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting, global scale resource management game based on the Red Planet. _childDocuments_.review: Wish there was more resources and power/maintenance buildings would have their range be 2x what they are now because that's really the only thing that annoys me about this game. _childDocuments_.review: I played the free weekend, but won't be back. I wanted to like this game - being on the lookout for a good 'base/empire' builder in a while. Sadly, this is not it. The gameplay is tedious and some of the building strategy amounts more to puzzle solving than actual well, building. For example, you can get 'hard locked' at times because the building that produces aluminium requires aluminium... there are (thankfully) ways around this but not without spending time staring at the screen while in 16x speed.One kudos for the optimization of the game - I played at a steady 120fps with a 2080rtx throughout, and 32:9 is supported natively. Story-wise, the game starts strong and hints at "there's more to this than meet the eye" but ultimately disapoints as it's just an excuse to go from objective to objective. Ultimately, it's extremely slow paced, has a fairly clunky UI and didn't captivate me to want to make a purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: It is very cool game for the story. The first 10 hours are good. But then the game breaks down from poor optimization and too fast progress. The end game is just clicking special project and waiting 15 minutes.- The balance is out of wack with colonies.- No reason to build crater cities as they have lower RP/resource ration.-The colony needs 10 water food for one research cycle but its seems to fast as cant seem to supply the city fast enough. Have enough food close by but that needs 20 drone ticks to supply the colony.- Late game building takes really long time as there seems to be bug with the blue new road placement. As you place building  next to 4 already build building it will take some time to blue roads to form. Was at about 1000 buildings. Started to break up my connections and made more hyper loops for small distances. It seemed help a bit.- Why are there no upgraded worker hubs or workers. Carry 2 stacks but slower?- No way to mine the formed ice or use the sea for water.- Still need search for ice from martian soil when you have liquid water lake next to the colony.-Combat fits the story but is quite bother. Why cant have auto hunt attacking drones? - Food is chemical and water sink? They have not heard of recycling? Could be used to balance the colonies. Larger colonies are easier to supply but have waste, but smaller one need less resources but need to have more workers supplying.- Storage building is just bad? Can only hold 100 of each type so if want to mine 800 iron from flood area fast need to have 8 storage buildings for that one mine.The game is great at start that breaks down from having the whole planet. It is very cool to look at Mars and transform it but at same time it feels quite useless as use only 10% planet. Well 60%? will be under ice/water in the mid game so does limit it.For now If you only want to play the story its fine game, but the game will break down. For now would wait for them to fix the game. It is quite shame as the story is great.The terraforming feels bit too fast as water/ice will hide quite many interesting lore from the old research missions.

_childDocuments_.review: What this game is: An interactive story with some colony sim/city builder elements.What this game is not: A real (well thought out) colony sim/city builder.The story is interesting-ish, but annoying to play more than maybe a few times. Choices matter, in that dialogue choices seem to occasionally change small things, and the story will sabotage you if you make certain choices that are not obviously traps at the time. I never actually finished the story, because I got pretty screwed by surprise story stuff, and restarted, and then played too well, and it got boring. I tried modding a bit, because the economy is really poorly thought out, and not terribly realistic, but the game pretends to be more moddable than it is, and there are hidden undocumented traps, like hard caps on inputs that aren't clear from the files. Also, what you can actually do with modding is sort of limited because they made some pretty dumb decisions when they set up the internals, so I eventually figured out that there is no way to fix the really bad economy, just sort of make it less suck. I'll probably go back to play the story through in its entirety at some point when I have forgotten just how frustrated I was after spending days trying to mod the thing.TLDR: The game has a cool idea, but looks like something it isn't and it isn't a great example of the thing it looks like.

_childDocuments_.review: A story within a story. Per Aspera isn't just a macro colony management game focused on terraforming Mars, like a pulled-back Surviving Mars or Rise of Industry in space. It's also the story of an awakening AI. And how the developers handled that awakening AI is my favorite part of the game so far, because that awakening AI is you. And while this part of the story has plenty of choices, those choices aren't about giving you mechanical advantages in this area or that. Instead, you're given narrative choices, distilled down into 1-2 word responses, that then elicit a longer response from the AI who justifies the choice you made with a logical and/or philosophical interpretation. These responses are good, sometimes REALLY good, and I've frequently found myself wanting to reload and make the other choice just to hear the alternative philosophical viewpoint. And, at least for the first few hours that I've played, these choices that shape the awakening AI come at you frequently. It's not quite as taxing of your time and attention as the general management of the colonization and terraforming efforts, but it always seems to be there, either filling in a lull as resources build or expanding your focus while you're concentrating on building out a new logistical grid. Speaking of colonization and terraforming, this game has a LOT of mechanics and I can totally understand why some people get overwhelmed. Your logistics grid (at least as far as I've gotten) is based around workers (building/transportation), energy (net production and expanding network), building maintenance, and production (mining and factories). From there you'll expand into the colonization aspect of the game with spaceports and domes, which net you research points. Those research points will expand all previously mentioned areas as well as open up the terraforming side of the game. As someone who plays a LOT of colony management and economic simulator games, I'm really enjoying this so far. The systems all seem to be working and while I have gotten overwhelmed a few times as I've run into walls I didn't know were there (like building limits or colonist limits), I was able to quickly identify how to overcome those limitations through the research options.

_childDocuments_.review: Contains spoilers.Pros:Excellent voice acting.Intriguing story, great characters.Solid base building.Cons:Part of the story happens off screen and characters go on as if you were told. The off-screen parts can be pieced together quite easily, but still not great.Story events can happen out of order, with characters voicing anticipation for events they have already congratulated you for completing.Story events and conversations are tied to your progress, which may mean long periods of silence if you are not completing the objectives in the intended order.At least one occurrence of voiced line and text not matching up.Repetitive sound track, one tune in particular really gets into your head.Combat is trivial if you realise all you need is a single doom stack to wipe out anything.AI is terrible at combat, and will throw its units away ignoring defence towers and picking unwinnable fights.AI cheats like there's no tomorrow: range of power and maintenance buildings is greatly increased, vast amounts of resource nodes spawn in the enemy base, the enemy will literally SPAWN BUILDING FASTER THAN YOU CAN DESTROY THEM (seriously, wtf SA-10?)Upon defeating the enemy their base will just vanish, no ruins, no salvage, just an empty plain with the disproportionate amount of resource nodes they AI was given.FPS drops can happen.I find it odd that you are forced to exterminate the first enemy you encounter - and no one acknowledges the ongoing destruction regardless of how long you draw it out and play defensively; there is no option to report the issue to command and work with them to sort it out. You have an enemy; you must defeat it for the story to continue.The story branches in rather simple manner - you have 3 buttons - select which path you want. It would have been more engaging to have the story be based on the actions you did or specifically didn't do.Also, the merging option is a bit of a let down; AMI doesn't really merge, more like just gets erased. (AMI was pro-human, Carmine was anti-human - AMI/Carmine is just as anti-human as Carmine which no option to the player to take a middle ground) Also, AMI/Carmine loses the ability to create research outposts so you can never research and figure out the story behind the ruins in SA-9 if you take that path, and the AMI/Carmine knowledge base does not contain any info about it.Neutral:Only "normal" and "high" priority options, which is limiting to the queueing of operations, but manageable.I've found that its essential to keep several factories of each kind of high priority, as well as the drone factories and part of the maintenance buildings.Worker drones are the lifeblood of getting anything done and you must pepper your base in hubs (at the end I've managed to run about 400 drones for 1200 buildings - about 1/3 of the buildings in the base were drone hubs) - everyone that's complaining that tasks are being ignored just doesn't have enough drones.Hyperloop is essential for bigger bases, and each entrance should be liberally surrounded by worker drone hubs.Impression:I want to love the game, the story, ideas, and characters (I've grown more attached to Nathan Foster more than any "family" in the Fallout games), but the implementation just falls flat. The base building gameplay is solid but gets repetitive by the end, the combat is terrible overall. The the hiccups of presentation work against the narrative and can really break the immersion.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend it but the logistics and pathing are horrific. The game itself has an interesting story and decent base building but very buggy. I've had story objectives auto-complete without my doing anything, enemy bases self destructing (not flooding), and dead characters come back to life to give dialogue when doing certain bonus objectives. Speech choices sometimes lead to unexpected dialogue.The logistics are the worst part, every time you put down buildings it spiderwebs roads out to everything in range, often taking buggy, zigzagging, slow paths and refusing to fix itself if you deconstruct and rebuild buildings. Placing new buildings can destroy old paths and roads. Roads are expensive and time consuming to build. Resources are carried by workers, which need be housed with worker hubs for each individual worker, as well as to constantly be rebuilt. Even with trying to optimize paths and building a few hundred worker hubs the logistics were going at a snails pace. Trying to set up storages and such to optimize transport is clunky and doesn't always work. Workers will often just faff around, not doing nearby tasks because another worker is closer but busy. Just a really frustrating logistics system.Play story mode, not one of the harder modes. It will cut down on logistics since you won't constantly be depleting resource veins and having to build spiderwebs. Trust me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very pretty to look at. And that's sadly about it.Played through this game one and a half times, first time on realistic, which ended in a doom spiral and another on story which was more akin to an idle game. The story is so-so, up to your taste really. However, the gameplay boils down to seemingly being so easy it's almost an afterthought to tell a mediocre story with very beautiful visuals or balancing a house of cards where one oversight can end the whole game. The newer updates may have fixed some problems, but overall, it seems to want to be two things at once. On one hand it wants to tell its story bit by bit and limit where and how fast you can expand, but on the other it wants you to balance a delicate and fragile system that relies on expanding and exploring. And the two halves do not support each-other. Once resources for maintenance run low or out for whatever reason, the drones stop functioning and then everything stops functioning. And there does not seem to be a way to come back from that. Not exactly ground-breaking, a better word would be either boring or tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: For something like ten years, ever since I first really discovered the concept of transhumanism, I have always half-jokingly half-seriously said that I can't wait until the day I can upload my brain onto a computer and launch it into orbit around Mars.Somehow Tlön Industries has reached deep inside my psyche and delivered my exact dream in video game form.  While I still eagerly look forward to the day I can exist without this meat-girdled bone-robot, Per Aspera provides a well-made and fun entry into the sci-fi base-building genre that, hopefully, helps to usher in even more fantastic transhuman plots from video games as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: I would love to give this game an ambivalent review, since it's not really a bad game, but since Steam only asks whether I'd recommend the game or not, I'll say no.Early on the game feels like a fun logistics game, but as the game creeps forward, new options don't feel exciting anymore, and the sheer scale of up to 1550 buildings means that you aren't really encouraged to optimize, at least on standard difficulty. On higher difficulties I feel like optimization would be required, but it would also be tedious due to the sheer scale and the weirdness on how drone hubs work,  having only one drone each for some weird reason. I feel like the game might have had way more ideas than the developers had time to implement. The Blue Mars DLC adds in my opinion pretty pointless stuff, while the game desperately would've needed more variety in terraforming: Where are the animals that you can even research? Don't the humans need any real infrastructure ever?I think the concept of the game is brilliant, but the execution is mediocre. More depth in terraforming and perhaps a different system for logistics and it would've been great.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoyed their time with Surviving Mars and such other management games.... Per Aspera falls short on what I was looking for. While the feeling of seeing Mars' oceans rise is great, it took 20 hours to get to that point. The game is very slow on some matters, which means your maintenance costs are going to eat through your materials while you are waiting for either research or terraforming to happen. Which means you will at some point stand atop an city of inactive mines to keep the transportation of goods going, forcing you to constantly use up your ever dwindling resources to reach out to further and further resource sites with ever smaller returns as your mines will have a limited amount of selected materials beneath them. Ice being one of these, as it is needed for colonists for both their habitats and food production, but once the planet's temperature begins to rise, so start to melt the ice sites, forcing you to somewhat race the process to get the liquid water pumped and refined before your stockpiles of ice vanish from usage.Not to mention the worker AI is not pleasing. I have more often than not stared minutes at an queued up facility, all the while the workers carry around something completely irrelevant despite setting the construction site as high priority.I can see the potential in this game, I want to love it, even like it but the shortfalls in management and inability to direct your workers despite in-universe being the overseer AI, the extremely scarce feeling of the resources and small tech tree get in the way.You are sent to terraform the Mars with apparent free will, and yet you constantly feel caged in by mission control not giving you enough space to do what you must.Get on sale if you wish.

_childDocuments_.review: Reading the reviews... people seem very confused about what to expect from this game. There seems to be some major frustration from fans of city builders and deep simulation/ management games coming to this expecting something very different from what it is. I don't blame the game for this - the description is fairly accurate. If you come into this with the right expectations (or no expectations at all) you might find, like me - you're pleasantly surprised. Per Aspera does not offer some deeply complex resource manager that requires pin point micro-management with in depth tinkering of assets. What Per Aspera offers is a very chill - very zen colony building game with very simple, very intuitive mechanics. In short - you spread across the martian surface like a slime mold, all while enjoying a pleasant, perfectly voice acted soap opera involving an AI slowly coming to terms with their purpose and identity. There's JUST enough going on that it doesn't over whelm you, but not so little that you get bored and distracted. For me - it was a wonderful balance between management and simply focusing on much bigger picture concerns, like terraforming and figuring out where I can focus my expansion.There are some scenarios that may provide frustration. You may, like myself, find yourself needing to reload a few times during the story campaign because you've reached a dead end with your resources, requiring you to reload an older save in order to fix your mistakes. Problems that are easily solved but present some head scratching as you slowly learn how to maximize efficiency and avoid these pitfalls. When it clicks - it's great.A calm, pleasant and entertaining experience that perfectly balances between engagement and allowing yourself the luxury of considering bigger picture concerns, all framed by a nice and simple little soap opera about an AI growing up.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the Green Mars version of the game and had a really good experience! I really loved the way the narrative and the gameplay were reinforcing and enhancing each other: none of them were revolutionary on their own, but the two combined were truly amazing. I wish city/colony builder games would embrace this approach more and would go beyond the sheer "expanding and optimising for the sake of expanding and optimising" concept. So if you are looking for a city builder game that makes you think of existential questions and of the future of humans (and machines ;) and challenges your moral compass, don't look any further! There are some cons but my impression and experience is that the devs are working hard to improve the game. I will definitely be back for the expansion!

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a game about Terraforming Mars. You play as the resident AI that is in control of everything on the planet, setting up mines and factories, and bringing in colonists and keeping them fed and hydrated. I am not actually done the game yet, so Mars isn't totally Terraformed yet but this is easily one of my favourite games!Here is an example of my Base on Mars in Stage 3 of Terraforming. As you can see my base stretches halfway across Mars so the distances are pretty far from one side to the other. _childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game. Just completed on easy mode. _childDocuments_.review: This has all the hallmarks of an early access game, yet claims to be the release version. Among others, it offers:- Massively unbalanced randomness all along the "campaign". This would be better kept for sandbox gameplay, once the player has passed the tutorials. - Serious lack of user feedback. It is up to the player to keep up on ongoing passive events and make sure to act upon them on time. - Bad UI. For example, the "ESC" key will behave differently, depending on what sub-section you are in. - The moderate visuals will push the latest GPU to its heat limits. There is no moderation in power consumption.- Micromanagement galore with messy visual feedback. The larger the colony, the less control over what you are actually doing you have. Also, the dialogue in the campaign varies from "grating" to "unbearable". It prefers to go for "fluff" when you are starving for instructions. As for the music... You will be turning it off and substituting it with another soundtrack after less than 2 hours of game play. I'll probably check back on this in 3 months, although my hopes remain low.[EDIT] 7 months later: UX has not improved, and despite the dev's good faith, the game pace remains mediocre at best. The player is still subject to the RNG's whims, making the overlaid story all the more irritating. Adding mod support appears to be a last desperate attempt in balancing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice game of being the most advanced artificial intelligence that ever didn't walk the Earth. Instead, it remotely (not 100% sure) controls an army of things that are absolutely enormous compared to what size you'd expect them to be. The army contains carrier bots and buildings whose purpose is to terraform the planet to such a state that it becomes habitable without any suit! That is your main goal because people will sooner or later be involved as well. You are responsible for keeping them - the researcher-scientists alive by delivering them food and drink while watching over power, maintenance etc., searching for new raw materials because the veins DO get depleted, selecting interesting research and much more. Headmaster of the company which programmed you is giving you the necessary advices to bring the mission to a good end. You response in short answers YOU chose and sometimes even (when you like think and hear your mind's voice) the woman AI voice asks a question to itself/herself which you answer. _childDocuments_.review: I think overall per aspera is worth the play for one reason alone: the story. It was intriguing, it didn't really get too in-depth and the voice acting around it was great, as well as the way your AI has gone over the journey. I really wished it wasn't so linear - or didin't feel like it at least. I tried so hard not to destroy the 2nd enemy base for some time, but the story just wouldn't progress sadly.The concept of terraforming as an AI while the humans do their own thing is also a good core idea - I love a good terraforming! It has done pretty well with the different steps and having to balance things too. The only bit of challenge the game provided was when the water started rising and I had to keep water treatment plants close to it, but far enough so they don't get immediately swamped.Graphics wise it's OK. I like that it's simplistic and not overwhelming.Unfortunately everything else the game offers is pretty much either on the level of teasing functionality:- combat: make enough drones (only takes 2-3 factories), click on enemy drones/base = win.- logistics: not really much of a way to improve things, zone is overloaded? Slap down a few more worker hubs, problem solved forever. Eventually you get hyperloops which are great for long distance stuff, but that's about it. It's simple and approachable, but it doesn't really add to the game. The additional landing sites seem completely useless, it takes longer to build them up than to plop down a straight line of worker hubs and power stuff with maintenance drones to get to somewhere, especially because the story gates exploring the planet. Which I can understand, but every new region is next to the last, so it's not like we ever have to suddenly be on the opposite side where a landing site would make sense.- items: either base item mined, 1st level refined, or 2nd level crafted. There is no challenge in it really, only a few factories can carry the entire game. The one good thing is resources are finite so you are encouraged to expand into more areas.- research: it's ok, nothing groundbreaking nothing bad tbh. Good that research outposts give bonuses, but really otherwise same as any other game.None of the above is a problem in itself, but in order to have more than just the story I really wish it did a good job in any one of those things at least so it wouldn't feel like I'm just waiting for hours until the next story objective slowly completes. I still enjoyed the story very much, but when I was waiting for the oxygen level to ever so slowly rise it was pretty boring too.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved playing this game on Saturday evening while watching Netflix on the background. The gameplay might be simple, but you really start feeling the accomplishment as forests start appearing and Mars slowly changes into a green world and you end up with settlements all over the lunar surface. A great management sim.Also, my inner Mark Watney loved the focus on real science and hard scifi. The "Terraformation Plan" feels authentic to my layman knowledge. Combat, on the other hand, is borked. It feels like a feature added just before cutoff release to add a bullet point. You are only going to need military units on very few instances of the game. And their controls are the inverse of any other strategy game released in the last 20 years. double click to select, click to move, right click to deselect. I could not rely on my muscle memory to control units and constantly made mistakes on the few instances I actually needed to muster my units.Overall, very fun and very chill experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Played game during Free weekend. I purchased it after for discount.To gamers:Yea, I can recommend the game. starts slow, gets faster, then gets slower again. Go in expecting dialog trying to provoke thoughts on AI rights, and what it means to have thought. odd pacing on some things. It has Co-op but no idea how that plays, I played solo entire time. read below for more information, should be spoiler free to anyone who hasn't played the game and gotten to a point it would be understandable.To Devs: (it kind of bounces around some)I think the game plays too slowly, I went to x16 and rarely ever left that speed. Issuing commands for combat, and during select dialog options being the 1x times. Never had performance issues though, so that's nice. I personally think it'd be more thematically fitting to have 16x speed be base speed, and 1x become 1/16 speed thus when AMI says I can perceive time differently due to being a robot it makes it seem like a human life is a very short time as an ageless robot, and when you need to take a lot of actions at once you're able to pause time (aka send out 100s of actions instantly) or perceive time more slowly to represent you being able to think something through so quickly.Some tech feels like it's placed oddly. Notably:-Water handling being so early made me think water was going to be a thing VERY early, while it wasn't super late still felt odd. I think I had ability to pull up and move liquid water for 30-40 years prior to ever using the tech.-Geothermal Power felt too late, make it less powerful but earlier, by the time I had it unlocked with how rare thermal spots are it felt very...underwhelming... I had to move 2 buildings to be to place them and found 2 others I could use without moving, and then only a few others around all of Mars in random locations.Logic in the game feels weird. It's like your trying to go for a "realist" terraforming process but you have no ability to remove N2 from atmo, so you could accidentally get to an atmosphere of several bar while earth is ~1 bar. I understand you suggest ~1 bar of N2 by having ~400 mbar of CO2 releasable from Mars itself, thus only having a 1.4 bar, but it's very easy to set 8 space ports importing N2 and forget or look away for a bit and have 850mbar N2 (which I did), or say 5bar N2. I then set up 20 O2 capture plants and lowered O2 + CO2 to 22% resulting in about 1.25 bar.You can have liquid water on the surface at -20C and 100mbar which makes none sense. I know you have ice graphics on north and south poles, so isn't unreasonable to have ice build up depending on T/P ratio. Alternatively just have water build up in atmosphere until conditions for liquid water are meet thus the great rains happen. checking phase diagrams seems like these conditions would simply cause all H2O to evaporate/sublimate, but I might be mistaken on this.It feels REALLY bad being so heavily iron starved while on the surface of mars with all that rust everywhere, would recommend a building at the start that works best at the start and gets worse over time in one area and as you start growing plants on that area of soil. this would make early iron vastly more abundant but require you to keep spreading out or run out of iron. I felt that early game Steel was the what I waited for the most, and Iron being the cause of that.For Story: uh, didn't finish the Tekkie ending but [Good Robot] felt kind of annoying due to how long it takes to get O2 up and CO2 down. Free Ami felt silly, I think I took another 10-20 years to finish the fleet and yet, never had retaliation after first directive was completed??? you'd think with the given dialog they'd try anything at all when the first directive in Tekkies path is build array.In regard to [Good Robot] I think giving a hint in how to more quickly modify CO2 into O2 or allow for CO2 Capture. I had 25% planet coverage growing to 45% but couldn't get much higher then that. I had I think 573m of water but never felt the desire to bring in more ice. is that the problem? I don't know if more water = more plants = more O2 faster. I assume so, but until you get the [Good Robot] achievement it didn't feel justified to bring in more water, but by that point I'd have to delete like 100 building and rebuild them a few times to keep water intake, which sounded like more of a hassle then it was worth, when I can just wait and watch YouTube on another monitor.For QoL I'd recommend a button you can press to enable auto-upgrading roads to next tier that are >[slide bar]% saturation, a button to build all hypertubes possible at that time. If you have upgraded roads between 3 buildings and remove the middle building losing the road feels annoying since you loss upgraded ways for distribution that you then have to upgrade other ways for, why not just have the upgraded roads snap together? non-upgraded roads *poofing* away is fine but losing the investment of time and resources on your road infrastructure feels annoying. why can't I keep F1 open while upgrading ways?Idk if this was a me problem or something others have had, but after researching magnetic dipoles I couldn't find where to build them for like 10-20 years, I would have had them completed easily prior to entering stage 4 but just never saw the build location. I ended up seeing the achievement on my steam library page as one to be unlocked and realized I might have missed it in space, and it turns out I didn't zoom out enough and didn't pan far enough to the sides.Lastly, Make it more apparent you can research the bottom circles immediately, I hit 50/50 buildings really quick, then thought I had to research both the engineering upgrades to raise limit so ended up waiting a while to get them then found out I could have just immediately researched it saving a 1-3 years of time since I was only at 10-25 research/month, I don't  remember, but almost quit at that point since all progress felt walled behind an arbitrary time wall, and I had nothing to do for so long at the start of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Two years on and Per Aspera is a complete game! My issues before were terraforming was actively a negative thing since it only took away resources and there was no way to use the now terraformed planet. Now you can pump liquid water and build open cities/farms. The campaign bugs are "sort of" fixed. I still cant rp how i want to the story progress gets forced. But i suppose thats not such a big deal. There are some issue with events not triggering or triggering late "Oh wow look like oxygen is over 5mb we're almost there" while im almost done bringing c02 under 5% and completing stage 4. Theres also issues of the story events firing out of order too. I'll get interactions alluding to events that have already happened. Not game breaking but immersion breaking for sure.The actual logistic gameplay and terraforming mechanics are a bit rough. For the logisitics you just build mines where you can and setup relevant factories on site. I suppose you could try to create centeralized processing and use the hyperloops. I never saw the point. Sprawl and build factories where it seems efficient. The terraforming is uhh a bit too sudden. It seems like it calculates the temp based on current factors and then that temp controls other factors like co2 in the poles etc. The problem is the initial phase takes literally one machine making a tiny amount of heat to trigger a snowball effect and boom the poles melt and there is a significant atmosphere. If the temp lagged behind the "target" temp a couple years i think it would be much more satisfying since the effects would take at least a little bit of time to compound. either way its still fun to play.Overall its playable and fun now with a good story. I dont think i'll go through to find what happens in the other endings.

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a unique take in the Mars colonization genre which has had several entrants lately.    You roleplay an advanced AI tasked with terraforming Mars, first starting off with a single landing site but over time having the potential to span the whole planet.   That large of an expansion isn't strictly required and that's the beauty of the game, to some extent it is up to you.  There is definitely a narrative that is followed, loosely defined by the terraforming stage you are in but with multiple directives and ways of achieving those directives within each stage.    On normal difficulty at least, it is still fairly laid back despite some of the tension elements it tries to introduce so i think this as more of a zen colony builder than anything too stressful but there are definitely ways to fail if you are too complacent.  I have not tried a higher difficulty because the laid back but still challenging aspect (mostly of logistics) was exactly what i was looking for but i can imagine it can be far more challenging with more natural events and fewer resources (among other things without giving away too much).If i were to otherwise be critical of it, I would say that the pacing, particularly stage 4/5 needs some work as it seems to assume you have maxed out your spaceports at every stage.  If you haven't, then there's a lot of waiting and this is one of two tips I'd give which is to max those out.  Otherwise there was a lot of playing on 8x or even 16x speed as i waited for things to happen.  The second one being that expansion is necessary, there is no way around it as you use up your existing resources but as long as you keep doing it, you should be fine.The presentation, voice acting and overall production values are quite good and I look forward to seeing what mods or expansions are coming.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game! It's unique and interesting, casual and accessible but allows over-achievers to race to exploit the planet. There is a little bit of combat but it's not a focus and very easy if you plan ahead (60% through the game as of writing). There are some annoying bugs (much better now than at launch), some gaps in the dialogue and story, and other nuisances, but the game shines despite all that.The Blue Mars DLC probably should have been baked into the base game, but I've enjoyed Per Aspera so much I didn't mind shelling out an extra $5 for the complete experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly casual and well presented take on the base builder/automation genre.Note: At time of writing I only played with the "Green Mars" DLC, but no others.This isn't a 1000 hour forever game - and it doesn't pretend to be - so comparisons to Factorio et al aren't really appropriate. I finished the main campaign in about 20 hours, mostly while eating/listening to a podcast in the background/etc. Most of the time I had a singular short/medium-term goal to shoot for, most of which you could achieve in an afternoon's play. I'd recommend this to people who like the genre but don't have the time requirements they normally require.It isn't terribly cerebral, but it's pretty satisfying seeing your actions affect the planet. There's a delicate interplay between the temperature, water/humidity content, atmospheric composition/density, etc, that's all modelled and reactive in real time. There are a half dozen or so map filters to track the progress of these stats, which each have a strong visual style. Pretty cool overall. From a gameplay perspective this is fairly basic: make the numbers go up to win. However, I suspect the developers opted to simplify the simulation in order to keep the game less of a datacrunch simulator. Interested to see what innovations/complexities the developer will throw in if a sequel/successor game is made; the bones of the sim are pretty neat.The game seemed to grind to a halt as my base grew too big. I think the temptation in playing the game is to build a singular sprawling megabase across the entire surface of the planet, but I don't know if the AI is up to task. Often they travel on less-optimal roads, carting unimportant goods, ignoring prioritised tasks, and so on. It's a shame there aren't more tools to poke them in the right direction; this likely would've taken the game from a "pretty good" to a "must play" for me. On the other hand, refer to my earlier remark about the "1000 hour forever game" - by the time I encountered this kind of issue I was basically at the endgame anyway.The worst thing here is the Elon Musk fart-sniffing. Not only is it extremely soy, it has aged terribly! Just replace the word 'hyperloop' with 'train' and you'll be fine.At the time of writing the game is about $40, which works out to $2/hour for me. IMO, a pretty good deal. Even if I never boot it up again I think I'll have the soundtrack stuck in my head for a while...

_childDocuments_.review: Resource management terraforming simulation on a beautiful render of Mars. The game has a decent story, which is surprising for a res-man sim. If you watch someone play this at mid-end game, it can look daunting, but the game progression is simple and gated quite well, despite the campaign having a bit of a slow pace. The terraforming process can take 100+ years but the NPCs don't age or die, but that's the balance between "scientific realism". Because at the end of the day, you're trying to add an atmosphere, water, and the right mix of oxygen, nitrogen and carbon-dioxide to make the planet liveable. Based on this pace, and the fact combat is very light, the game is quite relaxing. Unfortunately the difficulty is non-existent, there's very little you can do to "lose" the game. Definitely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: It feels so bad and undeserved to not recommend this game, but I don't. I really believe it deserves support - for the fans of excel table simulations and engine builders, this game is fantastic and I am one of them. But I also want my games to feel full of life, and while I understand that may sound unreasonable in a Mars colonization game, I want to ask you to look at ANNO 2250. Especially it's moon colonization phase. That's full of life while you play, it's a joy to watch the machinery work, each building feels real and functional in a sense that's what it would look like if it would be real. Here? It's all... feeling random. A mining facility over there has a giant drill or a drill shield, machinery to clear debris etc. but in Per Aspera, you look at any building and it could be any other building. There is a huge disconnection between what a building does and what it looks like, to me at least, and that makes the game extremely difficult to read and thus frustrating to play.I'll give you an example. In ANNO 2250, you check your graphs that shows you produce 5 biopolymers, and consume 9. Therefore you need to produce 4 more, correct? So you click on building, and you click on the biopolymer icon to place a building that produces it. The game highlights all other buildings that you already placed and does this. In Per Aspera, you face... a set of random looking grey blocky sci-fi buildings. Please tell me which one is for biopolymers. You can increase production by placing more, but can you tell me how many you have and where? Because barely 2 hours in I could not. I was looking for iron mines to upgrade them and I couldn't tell them apart from other mines and other buildings, and couldn't tell how many I had. Especially because the game immediately bombards you with 6-10 different resources and refineries and production buildings, the introduction phase is way too steep and fast, you barely placed an iron mine and didn't even figure out what is it you need iron for but you already require plastic, carbon, chemicals, oh but wait you should have built a mapping building, too bad you built half your city on resources you couldn't see before. It's... frustrating.Per Aspera has a lovely story where you play an AI who'll bombard you with her inner monologues where you have choices (you play as her) to assess situations and draw your own conclusions which will alter it's personality, which in turn will alter the economy slightly and certainly the way you see your units - is a worker drone a part of your body? Do you have a body? Is it your child? Is it just a soulless machine? Is part of you living in it? If you like sci-fi related psychology and philosophical questions, Per Aspera is a lovely little indie game for that, which has a lot to learn from UI design masterpieces such as Endless Space 2 that managed to make an excel file look, feel, and sound alive without any extra tools compared to Per Aspera. As such I would highly recommend ANNO 2250 and Endless Space 2 over this game, but I'm also very much looking forward to whatever the developers come up next as they are on right path to something great, but so far only made it halfway there.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. It has the potential to be great. It looks (visual graphics) very nice already. The gameplay is not necessarily innovative but it has good features and options for the level of effort and detail.What it lacks is decent documentation (or an active community to join/ask questions/refer to).Some of the tasks are not really explained well, and you can reach points in the campaign where you have no "directive" or next goal to achieve. It can be frustrating and discouraging, especially when you realize there was a research option/mission/activity tucked aside on a less commonly used screen that will advance everything if you had just clicked on something to start a new project or area of expansion, etc.The community part is simply bad luck, based on the NAME of the game, the popularity of the Latin phrase the name comes from, and whatever else. The Steam Community seems to be the most active place to find other players input, and it is not very active.It feels like this game could have used a bit more time in the oven, "not quite baked". But the Dev is releasing updates and things are improving, and it actually is fun to play. Hopefully it will increase in popularity and grow to gain some recognition, so the Dev will be further incentivized to improve things.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a competent enough terraforming game.Campaign is crap, it's barely a tutorial, and the entire 'military' section should have just been cut from the game, it's poorly implemented and entirely useless. Just skip it, play maybe an hour to get used to it and go to freeplay, you're not missing anything in the story.Mechanically, 90% of the problems with the game are fixed just by adding mods to add workers to mines and factories. Colonists become useless once you finish the tech tree (you do it pretty early even if you don't use too many colonists), at which point it is in your best interest to embrace your inner HAL9000 and execute them all, and claim the planet for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Takes a more futuristic, realistic approach to the Mars colonization and terraforming game than Surviving Mars. The scope is also much larger with planet-spanning infrastructure. Terraforming is done well with the interconnected parameters playing into each other a lot.Gameplay is addictive, time seems to disappear. The story was a pleasant surprise.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks and sounds amazang, feels like a heartfelt attempt to produce the story of an AI sent to prepare Mars for terraforming and Colonization but the game begins to fall apart the longer you play. Be prepared for lack of adequate explanations of mechanics, bland base building constantly hampered by seemingly pointless geographic decisions, and a story that feels more geared toward making rehashed commentary then telling a compelling narrative. By the time I stopped playing (23 hours of my only playthrough) the core gameplay had gotten tedious and I found myself uncompelled to finish the story as it ultimately appeared as though there was nothing left except to check off boxes on the path to inevitability. I will say, the "base-builder" tag does seem disingenuous, you ultimately have no real option in base layout, design, or even the connections drawn and everything I have seen turns the Martian desert into a bleak industrial sprawl of automated factories, mines, and terraforming equipment.
