_childDocuments_.review: No bad for the price. Still needs some balancing but has promise. If you enjoy city builders and/or games about Mars it's worth a try.Late game asteroid mining or something to provide resources would be great. Because eventually you are going to run out of resources and have to stop. But maybe there is something late game, I am only in mid-game.-Very hard to feed and water large numbers of colonists. I hope there is some late game farming tech or something I haven't seen . I want actual Martian cities.*Edit- After 50 hours I still recommend the game. But the end game is bit dull and the tech tree is pretty underwhelming.+ The story and the missions break up the tedium. If it was just you terraforming a whole planet with no missions and no one talking to you, it would get pretty dull. I wish there were more side missions. Missions to give more technology bonuses or something.+ Hyperloops are cool. They should transmit power as well though.-Very few techs offer new buildings or significantly different gameplay. The power techs in particular are very weak. Solar power is very good from the beginning of the game till the end. And the really cool stuff like Fusion is just too far away. The game is long over before you can get it. I almost never used the upgraded mines or factories. You just clog up your roads with resources you can't store. How about some upgrade to workers? Larger batteries? Faster Recharge? Or carrying more than one resource at a time?-Feeding and watering you colonies is a nightmare from beginning of the game to end. I kept the bare minimum to get the tech I wanted because it was such a pain in the neck to always find more chemicals and water to make food. The domed colony looks awesome. But I never built it because I didn't want the hassle of feeding everyone. And Tent City??? What am I running a Mars homeless shelter?-The orbital view seems seriously underused. I thought the space elevator would offer some cool space gameplay. Maybe rare minerals mined on the moon. But there is nothing like that.-Balancing the gas mix in stage 5 terraforming is super dull and time consuming. Maybe realistic, but not fun gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a great many games in this genre and I have to say that none of them have quenched my thirst like this one has. There are many different aspects of the game that are simply built well. the controls are smooth and the graphics are really nice. The real-time terraforming change you see on the planet is a really nice touch. On top of all of this, the story you get to unravel is a really interesting one, one that made me eager for the next chapter. All things considered, well worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera manages to package what a lot of city builders lack into a very special game. There's always a new issue to deal with when progressing in the game, and without going into spoilers, the trials and challenges manage to keep you on your feet for almost the entirety of the game. The only time I achieved critical mass, which is usually the point at which a player has won in all but name for a strategy or city building game, is roughly a few minutes before I actually beat the game, which meant to me that the game was incredibly well paced out. I highly recommend a try to people who enjoy strategy, resource management, and city building.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is purely amazing. It really is. If you like some micro management, seeing your progression in game, great stories and that "high tech" look then this game is made for you. At first i thought "oh well it's gonna be pretty repetitive" but the plot was able to really carry the game foward and made every minute thrilling. You are always pushed to keep expanding, finding new mines, discovering new technologies and making great works of infrastructure to make your base run more efficient. it got just enough challenge and casual play and the story (and twists) really bring that experience foward. The only real downside that I saw was the end. in the last hour or two when your base is really set up, you just "wait for timers to go" which puts a stain on the experience. I didn't take this too badly tho because the other 20 hours of playing were really enjoyable.With beautiful graphics, an amazing story line, some great gameplays and choices that actually impact how you play, this game is a solid 19/20 for me and I would recommend it to everyone who got interested looking at the screenshots. go try it!!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: While there are games with better UI and UX in terms of management, this game comes with a really interesting story which holds your attention and interest as you progress through the game. I'm sure either mods or future updates will improve some of the more lacking aspects of the management gameplay, but the game that's there right now is definitely enjoyable. There are very few city builder/management games with actual characters you'd care about, including your self.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The 'Full release' is hopefully early access. Potential spoilers in review, though your game will likely break too, so I can't really spoil what can't be experienced.Too many bugs - some game breaking to boot! The story that is supposedly a big selling point is rather dry and keeps throwing dialogue out of order. Additionally, my campaign broke and is stuck at 'eliminate enemies in sa-1, while the only thing there is the ocean.Bad game design choices - finite resources and maintenance, limited power building reach, 'worker drones' dying while we have maintenance drones, as well as worker drones being logistics as well as builder bots, boring research tree that doesn't actually unlock sustainability, colonists being the research source FOR AN AI!!! (hello? Wonderful opportunity to make 'cpu blocks' on the surface, have them require power and produce research), food being made from chemicals and water, water only being available in the form of ice, while half the planet is ocean, scientifically incorrect atmospheric requirements, pointless combat that serves only as a story gimmick but doesn't feel good and isn't well explained, completely random resource generation, with over half spawning in eventually unreachable places... I'd write more, but that would be putting in more effort than the game designer.Tedium - The game has a speed up option, which I kept at 16x all the time. I wish there was a 128x option to be honest. The game has 3 hours worth of content stretched into 12 with time gating. Campaigns can also be literally unfinishable due to you running out of water. Literally. You can smash an ice asteroid into the planet, you can make oceans appear out of nothing - water level is based purely on temperature, not on actually extracting underground water or smashing ice comets into mars - but you can run out of water, because the colonists apparently send their excrement to space and only eat ice and chemical food.The music is boring, best turned off after 30 minutes.The UI is stylish and thematic, but poorly explained and lacks many features one would expect in a logistics/management game.The only redeeming feature is that the art overall is very nice.The voice acting is also good, but I honestly couldn't give a rat's ass who you hired to do your voice acting. It's not a selling point in gaming, especially in niche games such as this.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: So I finally got around to giving the game another go with all the patches and the Blue Mars DLC. I started a fresh save. They have fixed most of the issues I mentioned in my original review, I did not experience any out of order story, nor did I have too much trouble with LAND based logistics. My only real gripe was that sometimes the ships would ferry resources rather than much quicker hyperloops being taken.But it was fun and I have got 34 hours out of it, its fairly cheap I would recommend a single play-through for the story which is by far the most compelling aspect of the game.--- Original review below ---TLDR: It becomes a real chore to play and though I would love to know what happens to AMI I simply can't bring myself to grind through the illogical logistics nightmare to keep getting the out of order snippets of storyThis game shows HEAPS of promise at the start...The narrative is engaging.There are mysterious things happening.It is fun to balance the resources needed to ensure your survival and that of the colonists.The Tech tree looks exciting.There are clear goals to reach to terraform the planet.With less than 5 hours in I was enjoying the game much more than say Surviving Mars.However eventually I reached a point where all the good things I listed above turn around in one way or another.The narrative falls apart and you start getting notifications of events out of order, things that your AI character should already have known based on other events. A lot of the responses don't make a lot of sense either.The mysterious things that were happening all just seem to stem from people being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and ignoring long term repurcussions and I eventually got really annoyed with the lead colonist who displayed behaviour unfitting of her position.The logistics management all falls apart later game, you will have colonists needing water and a drone standing next to a full water mine not doing anything. Hyperloops do little to help with this as only 1 resource can pass through them at a time and there is no reliable way to transport resources en mass over distances.The Tech tree becomes kind of boring as you realise all you effort into terraforming mars cant be harnessed. Want to use some of that water on the planet instead of arbitrary water mines? No technology for scooping water out of the sea sorry. Want to grow some plants for food for the colonists? Oh no those plants just convert CO2 to O2 they are not for eating, get back on the chemical and water diet please.The Goals to terraform the planet fall apart towards the end, there are many feedback loops you can get stuck in, flooding the oceans and loosing access to minerals, having the plants and lichen convert too much CO2 to O2.I really wanted to recommend this game and did enjoy it for the first 6 or so hours but it left a sour taste in my mouth as the whole game seems to fall apart later on.

_childDocuments_.review: Great city builder, i fell in love the moment i tried the demo the first time and the full game does not disappoint.Satisfying mechanics of exploring and building up your economy more and more, plus it's on a planetary scale.One specific thing i really love how it turned out is the voice acting and the voicelines of the AI that you play.Still playing the campaign but so far 100% happy with the game despite having been *extremely* hyped by the demo and having had quite high expectations as a result.Con: The autosave is practically nonexistent. _childDocuments_.review: Amazing "city" builder, or rather base builder with well executed terraforming mechanics. Gameplay feels slightly railroaded, so replayability value may be low. _childDocuments_.review: This is a real good and balanced colonization game.  It has repertitive elements like any game of this kind.The complexity increases smoothly and you won't face any nasty surprises.The techtree is straight forward and well balanced.As always one may find it too complex, one other may miss endless ressources. I do neither nor.Let's compare it to other games. The campaign is well narrated and does its best to make the AI setting of the story feel real. There are rare dry spells, but overall the story is omnipresent. This has been done much better than in Surviving Mars. The difficulty and complexity of Surviving Mars can be hard, while Per Aspera plays like clockwork. Is it worth buying?You may check some "how long to beat" sources. I have not regretted it, but would have been very happy if the logistics were more complex and the consequences of planning errors were punished more severely. In the end, though, it's a question of what type of player you are, and I would recommend the game to anyone from beginner to advanced.Cheer, Chaly

_childDocuments_.review: Quick summary of thoughts:I was reserved when approaching this game and chose to wait for a sale because of the number of early negative reviews. I am glad I did so because otherwise I would feel a bit cheated. On the plus side the developer has put a lot of work into workers, districts and, with the new DLC, answered most of the issues with flooding. Whilst those reviews were valid at the time, and they all raised very good points, I feel the developer has done enough for the game to be judged afresh.This is where I am out of nice things to say. I was looking for a game like Factorio, Transport Fever, Project Hospital, OpenTTD, etc. to invest hundreds to thousands of hours into and this isn't it. Yes I am aware it is possible to reroll with my newly gained knowledge and eventually complete the game, yet unlike other games I just do not want to. I just caught myself on a Saturday night starting to answer work emails so after only 15 hours it is time to move on.For:1) I did not run into any bugs during my playthrough.2) The developer has put a lot of work into improving the game and resolved a number of previously identified issues.3) The modelling of Mars is lovely and it does change in real time during terraforming. Someone put a lot of work into this. I really wanted to see the end result.4) Colonists are kept at arms length and really just considered another resource. Unlike Surviving Mars there are no dome buildings requiring individual room design or worries about colonist transportation.Against:1) The game reports as one that rewards a slower playstyle where a playthrough lasts hundreds of hours. This is not the case. The game expects the player to tolerate it running very, very slowly yet a new player is required to make quick decisions in preciously the order the developer wished otherwise just suffer with a soft lock or a miserable gaming experience. Yes, it is possible to reroll or limp on for 10 hours to get Hyperloops, but I just to not have the desire to. Especially considering there are even more new player traps requiring even more rerolls. This is not a Dark Souls or RogueLike game.2) The difficulty of the game comes from these new player traps and not from logistical chains or logistical networks. The player can somewhat control how many roads go to a building and upgrade them for speed yet that is it, the game splits each worker hub into a region and assigns one worker bot.3) Players are reporting the game has a x16 speed for a good reason and not just because they are impatient.4) This is the first game where I would have told myself to avoid the single player campaign and just go sandbox because characters talk, talk and talk some more. To the point where I was pulled out of the game by the constant chatter and pop up dialogue box about a personality test. The bigger challenge was not terraforming the planet but not being pushed to the point where I verbally told the characters to shut up or muted the game entirely. Verbal triggers for events are sometimes minutes behind gameplay.5) Each individual part of the game (such as city building, attacking or terraforming) does not feel complete in itself. I found myself often saying how I wished things were different or was consciously aware I was partaking in a different part of the core game loop, rather than actually taking part in and enjoying the game. For example the game has a defence overlay that shows the range of anti-drone fire from a building yet this is wrong because the outer 5% of this circle is not covered, leaving me questioning why the developer did not make the ring 5% smaller in the first place. I learnt this the fun way during the first attack where the AI quite happily sailed through a fully covered area to the one building I had missed out of hundreds, ganked it in a few seconds and then quite happily sailed out again.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: After several patches the game is in better shape but the one thing that continues to be a sticking point is there is no way to manually intervene in your logistics short of deprioritizing every single building except for the one you need at that moment, a very labor intensive operation when you have hundreds of buildings. I was well into the game, almost done with stage 5 terraforming, with 78 worker hubs humming along, a hyperloop system that circumnavigated the globe, every threat dealt with and a virtual endless supply of raw materials. Suddenly my worker count dropped sharply and (thanks to the advanced lack of warning systems) I caught it when I was 10/78 workers. checking all my worker factories I saw that none of them had parts so I canceled my in progress space pads that had parts stored on them (they were not prioritized, my worker factories were - no idea why they had parts but my worker factories didn't) then waited for the parts they had in stock to be distributed to my worker factories. They never were. I sat there and watched my count go from 10 to 5 to 1 to 0, nearly a hundred parts just sitting there waiting to be used. I could have gone through and deprioritized every one of my important buildings, recovered from the nose dive, then reprioritized them all again but.. why spend the  600+ clicks and all the time hunting the buildings down for that? Why are we given only two levels of priority? Why were parts going to space programs I hadn't marked priority instead of factories I had marked? Why can't I at least declare an emergency and take direct control over a single worker to do a single task if needed? The patches fixed a lot of the issues I was seeing at launch but there is still fundamental, frustrating flaws with this game. At least it's up to feeling like an Early Access game instead of a broken demo.*****OLD review section, some issues still apply*******Decent enough demo, but presented as a completed game. The fact that I had 150 glass, a 12/45 workers and 3 worker factories each needing a single glass to build more workers, all on high priority while my worker count slowly dwindled, my glass simply sitting and doing nothing.. and my only possible solution to manually go through every single high priority building and turn them to normal, then once the situation became normal to go back and re-prioritize all my buildings.. Well, I opted to let my sprawling colony with 5500 colonists die off instead.The game is incredibly incomplete. There is no way to tell your workers to prioritize one thing up until a point, workers evenly spread resources across everything of the same priority instead of finishing one job before moving on to the next, you can't set production goals. There just isn't any way to manage your workers other than marking individual jobs as priority, and if you have too many of those then they get nothing done anyway.Plenty of other unfinished parts of the game drag it down. You can't cancel a road upgrade (and they are pretty pricey!), combat is just a chore, there is no way to improve the game cycle other than roads and upgraded mines/factories (You can't build farms and let humans make their own food, for instance, even once you cover Mars in greenery, your workers will always follow roads and carry a single item each - no upgrading them to carry multiple items or into flying transports or anything, the range of buildings isn't upgradable so building a "branch" to a resource early game is exactly as tedious late game, scanners will scan for resources at the exact same speed the entire game - there is no upgrade possible for them)It doesn't help that half the things in the game happen with no explanation. My biodomes spread forests and lichen across the world. How much is that contributing to the O2 level? No clue. My aquadome spread cynabacteria through an ocean, in ebbs and flows. Why is it ebbing at times? No idea. I built a space elevator after a titan amount of effort (about 1700 resources total!) What is the actual, mechanical benefit? No idea. Coupling that with alerts that are super easy to miss (tiny icon, no noise) and you have a character that is presented as being a data driven entity who literally feels the buildings and workers as part of her body being effectively blind to most of what the colony is doing.The most frustrating part of all of this is Per Aspera is a major update away from being really, really good. Give the players the ability to manage minimum stock, store extra workers for God's sake, make worker break downs random instead of timed (having every worker die off at the same time is basically death for your colony), make the AI smart enough to build dependencies that are missing in a priority chain, have them build things in FIFO queues (or even FILO stacks if you really want.. it'd be weird but whatever, anything but the stupid "evenly distribute resources so nothing ever completes" method).. Do all that, which most of these are related problems, and Per Aspera would feel like a minimum viable complete game.TL;DR - don't buy at any price until it gets some major rework. Currently it isn't a finished game, at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun base-builder, Epic scale, good storyline so far. Some people have been bothered by the resources but not been too bad for me - has made it feel like an achievement to get things up and running.UPDATE:Bit further on and still really enjoying it. It IS a little slow, but that's adding to the epic scale. Would love a bit more range, or at least self-maintaining, on some of the roadside buildings to connect industrial clusters without so much mess in-between, though the way the tendrils expand across the planet is cool. Just worked out how to build lower tech buildings (click the little icon within the build menu) - otherwise the high tech mines cripple your new landings before they can get going, even after dropping two or three of them. Haven't worked out how to separate drone clusters, but its not a real problem. Not sure why so many complaints about the combat - for me it's appropriate, I'm playing this to terraform Mars, not for strategic combat. Using the additional landings to add resources to the map works well (would be nice to have a rationale for why that works - penetrating radar revealing new deposits maybe?). Also, using the scanner to reveal more of interest might be good - the resources are pretty sparse, so you're really just filling in the map otherwise. Would also like the spacing reduced a little so you can build up dense industrial areas, but that's a super minor ♥♥♥♥♥♥.Only real bugbear for me is not being able to get rid of submerged buildings - I did manage to reverse the water level for a bit, which allowed a managed retreat from one area, but left huge tendrils lost underwater I can't salvage - be good to be able to write those off if its impossible/impractical to salvage them, if only to reduce my building count, which at 1200 odd is causing it to take a good 10-15 seconds to generate the building list. Agree with others that a bit more warning that floods are coming would be good, to be fair it does tell you you are building on a flood plain, but you do kinda have to, so having the time and warning for a managed retreat would be nice. Also, to tidy up the map, being able to discard resources you have no intention of exploiting would help keep it clearer.Still playing... :)
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game gives you a beautiful globe of Mars to slowly shape into another green and blue sphere and generally some great tools to do it with. The main loop consists of putting down mines to extract raw resources, building factories to refine some of them, and expanding ever onward. Because most resources aren't actually consumed and refunds give you back all building materials the struggle comes from balancing what you do have and not letting production get too focused on any one end product.As for the terraforming it starts off really strongly and seems to peter out a bit at the end. Early-game terraforming gives you precise readouts of what your actions are doing, a history of changes, and a good number of options to achieve your goals. But mid- and late-game stuff like water and animals offer very little in terms of direct control or understanding, with the former being especially frustrating as you need constant access to water by that point to feed your colonists but any buildings near the water are likely to be flooded unless you decide not to fill the oceans.Overall it's a fun game though, if for no other reason than it has some great systems for terraforming. The story has it's moments but there's always sandbox mode if you don't want to be guided or have certain restrictions placed on you. I would love to see the devs do something with biodiversity and would definitely consider getting a DLC that had a new planet and some new terraforming projects, even if some realism has to be put aside to have an interesting but playable setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Really a fresh take on mars exploration, terraforming and so on. Great voice acting and characters. I really like having a story handed to me in one of these colony management games and not just the blank canvases that most of them are. There are definetly some fine tuning missing, i had some voicelines missing suddenly, and i did encounter some really bad pathing when doing triangles with the hyperloops. Did not stop me from playing it all the way to the end though!!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If you know what you are getting into and are into builder games you most likely will enjoy this game. That being said, after one playthrough it feels more like an interactive novel than something you can fail at. There is a small production chain and you need to make sure to aquire resources but if you ever have played a game like that there is no way to screw up.Positive+ Terraforming Mars is satisfying+ Accurate Mars map and plausible science behind terraforming+ Narration and Story was good enough to not ignore it with apparently multiple way to end+ No bugs, no glitches, no crashes+ Not a f*ing early access titleNegative- Slow pace with no increase in complexity or automation after the first few hours- No challenge other than what you set for your own e.g. terraforming within X years- Some mechanics seem rather unused, e.g. there is a whole combat tree (a quarter of all research) yet I spent at most 30 minutes out of 30 hours or so fighting. Also there are several different housings for colonists but I only every built the first one, and only three of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Frustrating.This game was released too soon. Routing and priority algorithms need to be greatly improved; this includes storehouses. _childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I experienced what many other describe with Per Aspera.The first 5 hours or so are great, really enjoyable and optimistic about what is to come.But then something happens. The game just falls flat. I tried to power through hoping it would get better, but I couldn't do it.At a certain scale, base logistics just fall apart. The system that seemed so clever and worked so well at a small scale just seems to stop functioning at some point. You'll have factories starved of inputs sitting next to mines that are stalled because their output is full, and an idle drone sitting there not moving resources. The only tool you have to work with is flagging things as "priority" but that can cause more problems than it solves since the game doesn't seem to understand second order dependencies.Moving resources at scale also just does not work. Hyperloops (groan) promise to shuttle resources around your base quickly, but if the drones don't actually do their job it doesn't matter much. And there's just no way to transfer resources between landing sites, as far as I can tell? You're an advanced space-colonizing AI, commanding a self-replicating drone army and caretaking the essential needs of thousands of human colonists (that themselves have airships), but you can't fly some machine parts around? None at all?Combat is really quite bad. The controls are bad. The enemies are dumb. There is zero depth, it's just more numbers = better than. The lack of any sort of automation or assistance is bad. It's like a bad, tedious tower defense game.What started out as an exciting experience quickly turned sour, sadly. I really really want to like this game. The overall vibe and theme is good. The base logistics issues feel fixable if given better tools and more sophisticated prioritization. But combat needs a rethink.Obviously micromanagement comes with the territory in a game like Per Aspera, but you end up having to micromanage the wrong things.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game, and like these types of games in general, but there are some bugs that are driving me crazy. For example at the very beginning of the campaign you need to build a solar collector.  The solar collector needs glass.  I have a glass factory and plenty of materials to make glass.  At this point in the game you have 1 robot to move materials around.  I put a priority on the glass factory, tried turning off all the other buildings, and made sure there is no inventory left to move to my main hub, but still my robot wont deliver the silicates to the glass factory so it can produce glass.  I restarted the campaign multiple times and have gotten past this step, but I have no idea why it starts working at some point later.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very good. There's not many games that can make me play for 2+ hours without realising but per aspera strikes a perfect balance between relaxing and challenging. There's always something to do: a big project, a story, or just tinkering. It's more of a resource management game than a city builder, with a focus on terraforming. And the simulation of Mars terrain is excellent. The way it gradually comes to life is inspiring. This is a game I would have loved to have played as a teenager - I'd probably have memorised the entire surface of mars. "Edutainment" sums it up perfectly.However there are a couple of minor issues I'd like to see resolved:"IMMINENT WORKER DEATH" - The death spiral isn't hard to avoid, but there is no notification that's it's happening. Please provide one. Narrative dialogues are often interrupted by research that finishes and prompts you to pick a new one - during the conversation. "Not enough water" is mysterious. My water plant is next to water, what's the issue? Oh, I need to build more. Just say that then.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Only 1hour of 'gameplay' thus this is more of a first impression than a review.And that impression is "is this supposed to be an idle game?" Essentially, 90% of that first hour was spent waiting (on x16 speed, mind you) for workers to move those scarcely produced resources about. Building placement was trivially straight-forward, decision making was mostly non-existant.Sure, the game MIGHT get better at some point, but boring a player to death in the first hour of gameplay doesn't strike me as a very thorough game design concept so I'll rather bail and take my refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game suits me quite well in being a terraforming / city sim where the AI is not the villain. I wish the game didn't pressure me with time-limited quicktime events and combat. I also wish the story was not so linear (if you do things differently or out of order, it gets a bit clunky). But overall the gameplay was an enjoyable experience. Will play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 15 hours in.This game is trying new stuff in the 4X genre and I believe it works. Many of the complaints raised in negative reviews seem to be because they're playing the game wrong, you can't just play this like you'd play any other 4X game. It needs a bit more planning.The story is engaging, which is rare in games as these. The speed is fine, the economy is pretty hands-off so you can speed through parts you don't want.The terraforming part needs a bit more refinement but adds something unique. People I've seen complaining about the terraforming are basically just chucking rocks at the planet, something which you're warned off will have bad results. The combat is simple but reasonably elegant, basically you're just pitting economies at each other. Graphics are fine, the UI is clear (people complaining have not found the building menu I believe). Resources being finite forces you to keep expanding, which I like, most games like these just let you get a god level economy before you go handle tasks. The only thing I'd like was some way to turn buildings you're using into just conductors for energy/roads; I get that it's done this way to force you to keep expanding, but at some point I have like infinite energy because that's what you build to get places. So maybe that after 10 years of use you can just turn buildings into husks or something.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Loving it so far. You play as this AI who is in charge of terraforming Mars. You gotta balance resources (natural, power, workers etc)It's equal amounts cool and cute. Zoom out to space/rotate around Mars, then zoom into a 'crashed before I arrived' rover from the year 2021.It's deep and complex too,  one of the main reasons I play sims like elite,  or sim management games like Planet zoo/coaster.  You feel like you're learning and progressing for ages with a nice high skill ceiling and complexity done right.  Per Aspera does this.

_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Story - Plays as the tutorial for the sandbox game, but the story as told through voice and text that occurs around AMI is actually pretty interesting and makes learning the actual game play mechanics enjoyable.Gameplay - Is mostly logistic simulation. While making sure you push the terraforming process forward or you will run out of resources and lose. Its mostly a relaxing experience with minimal stress. Many factors of the gameplay are nuanced, they may mean nothing to some players and a lot for others. A greater variety of structures would create some replay ability because as is there really is no reason to play again. A great upgrade to the game would be attempting to terraform other real planets. Even though it wouldn't be feasible it would make an interesting challenge.UI - Is sometimes limited in giving relevant information, but they have improved it.Music - Needs more tracks.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera absolutely captures the energy of working on an enormous generations-long project and the patience necessary to see it through. The game takes place on Mars, and as such, it uses the topographical map of Mars that you would find in an astronomy textbook. It also marks the landing sites of mars missions that actually happened, as well as other missions that are yet to come. When the game would start to slow down and become a little dry, it introduces political intrigue and side quests to spice things up.Excellent, absolutely would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Played it during a free weekend recently, and had a lot of fun! The main campaign of the game had more facets to it than I had originally imagined, and made for a pretty solid experience managing resources and prioritizing certain goals over others. In this way it kind of reminded me of the more guided experience you would get from Frostpunk, rather then the pure sandbox nature of like Cities: Skylines. There is of course a sandbox mode in the game, but I can only speak to my experience with the campaign. One criticism I would levy towards the experience would be the time it takes between certain major milestones feels a little too lengthy. There was more then once that I had set my colony on a positive trajectory, with all of my resources properly managed for the long-term, then I simply had to wait as the atmosphere slowly began to normalize, with very little change to the moment to moment gameplay. It felt like I was just kind of expected to stand up and walk away as the game ran itself for awhile, even with playing at the fastest possible game speed constantly.I'm surprised I hadn't heard of this game before the free weekend, all-in-all, I'd say its a worthwhile experience if you enjoy other games in this genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool to start with, but the story just seems to stop and some of the terraforming actions(comets and asteroids and the like) seem to do nothing at all. Cannot seem to unlock most of the map. A bit of google suggests the story is bugged and the whole thing buggy. Feedback for player actions is so bad it is hard to tell what is and is not working. Excellent game early on, could be awesome, but fundamentally flawed and depressing I cannot progress after 20 odd hours(including one restart). It is not a finished project, it is not cheap and I would avoid it.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike most city-building games, Per Aspera has an engaging story about AMI, a lady (masquerading as an artificial intelligence) setting up a Mars Colony with emotionally-driven colonists. After mismanaging the colony for several years resulting in a tragic drone accident, her cover was blown when the Space Agency board members accused her of being schizophrenia. Her handler was deposed and she started to question her purpose on Mars. (In case you don't realize by now, it is my satirical recount of the story)Defining moment: the first time you connect a series of hyperloops, how easy the game would have been if we had this technology from the start.+ Clean and futuristic aesthetics+ Beautiful Red Planet which will gradually change to blue+ Unique and engaging game play+ Great Story-line for a city-building game- Steep learning curve, expect to "discover as you play" and it is a long game - Can be draggy at times- Combat control and interface quite finicky and not intuitive- Go easy on the Eastern Coalition narrative, naming a colony "fire dragon" really lacks imagination, especially when planet-nuking is involved =)
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: THE GOOD* Very solid, mostly scientific model of martian terraforming. It's the first game I've played that made terraforming mars feel like... well... terraforming mars.* Pretty good UI, easy to navigate and well-polished.* Cool graphics. Not terrific, but good. Watching Mars change as terraforming continues is really fun. Also, no spoilers, but one of the aerobraking animations is pretty dang epic.THE MEH* The worker / boat systems. They make sense, but a lot of the game involves painstakingly placing infrastructure hubs to give enough support for transportation. This eases in the late game, but the early game can be a PITA. Boats are actually easier to deal with.* Future history stuff. Mostly well-written and cool, but some of it makes no sense - e.g. you'll find the ruins of a colony described primarily as "successful". Also, many entries refer to incidents about ground transportation... even if the research site is currently underwater.* Campaign story. Pretty good, but it didn't engage me enough to finish. Ended up playing about 2/3 of the way through and then going to sandbox mode.* The music. It's okay, but I really wasn't impressed and ended up turning it off after a while.THE BAD* Endgame is pretty boring, it turns into spamming farms and open colonies while accruing research bonuses you can't use because you already researched everything.* Food production. Crater farms don't produce nearly enough to justify their costs. Fisheries are pretty broken - as long as you have enough ships, it's just tons of food with no resource cost. Open farms are pretty cool though. Also, the abstraction behind the "food factories", where "chemicals" and ice get combined into rations is pretty gross IMO.* Zero import/export. Other than importing people and greenhouse gases from Earth, you don't hear a peep from them. Surviving Mars did a much better job simulating the political relationships.* Slim replayability. There are obvious optimal strategies and no real alternatives to them. IMO, the higher difficulty settings don't make the game more challenging, only more tedious.Summary: An interesting experiment with unique aesthetics and a mostly scientific view of Martian terraforming. Worth buying on sale and, for most I'd say, worth playing through campaign and sandbox mode once each. Not a worthwhile buy at full price due to lack of replayability and its rather niche hard sci-fi approach to the genre. All in all, curious to see what this developer will come up with next.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings new life to city building type games. You may have to restart your game until you get a better understanding of what to do or how to play. There is a learning option to play that speeds up this learning process. It's still easier to learn than a lot of other similar games out there, that in my opinion, are far too taxing to enjoy. This game is a real pleasure. Once you get the hang of it you may want to download the rest of DLC's. That's what I did. This is a great game and I'll get lots of hours in this. I totally recommend Per Aspera to any city builder lover, and to all those that lost their interest in city building simulation games. You won't regret this purchase. PEACE!!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of this genre and had a couple of hours really good fun with Per Aspera, but beginning with the mid game I was more and more disappointed.The Good:- AI Story and SF Setting- Voiceacting- "Hard Science"- Combination of planet and orbital layer- Inclusion of historic mars missionsThe Bad:- Terrible Pacing (a lot of waiting time until the next terraforming milestone is reached)- Micromanagement (spamming always the same building and structures gets tedious)- Readability (yes there a Icons, but try to find all your not-upgraded food fabrics...)- Controlling units in the real-time fights is contraintuitive and ignores all standards- Campaign objectives are not always clear (which location should I explore and where was it?)It's not a terrible game by far, but in this genre you have better choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Got just over 5 hours into the game, just expanding into the 4th section of land and it was going really well, then something broke with the robot AI and it started completely ignored all priority settings for buildings, causing a cascading failure of the repair systems and the bot replacement factories. By the time I realised what was happening I was down to only a handful of bots left and nowhere near enough to prevent the failure of my entire base. Given how severe this bug is I can't recommend this game at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is far from perfect, but it's the only mars colony sim that I actually played to completion and would still recommend coming out the other end of it. That is worth something, I think. There is a certain kind of joy that comes from seeing this detailed model of a planet change directly from your actions that just isn't available in any other game I've played, and that little shot of happiness that comes from seeing your first cloud is honestly worth buying the game for. Check it out, just know that the gameplay is very slow, and not entirely polished.With every update the devs drop, the game gets better and better, and I'm excited to see where their hard work takes this
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through and somehow barely terraforming mars to have so much oxygen in its atmosphere that one match would set the planet ablaze, i can say it was quite a fun experience. Good Stuff: - The Gameplay loop is decent, with the game keeping it simple with 5 resources you can harvest and about 10 things you can turn that into. - The story and voice acting are stellar, troy baker knocked it out of the part and the AI you play as truly does feel like she is slowly coming aware of everything with the choices you make. Especially since there are characters that evolve with you, or even are born because of your actions, like the colonists. - For it's current price, i think it was worth what I paid for. The game is a solid B-B+ for me. Bad:- So I don't know if it's something I did wrong, as sometimes the game didn't tell you how to actually control things, but once I got water on mars the boats would NOT take apart anything in the water. As soon as you start to switch to planning for building in the ocean, you have to take apart your base in the flood zone or else lose the resources you put into making them. Shipyards and Ports SHOULD NOT be a separate thing. I understand the game makers probably wanted it to be how the land workers worked, but once you finally get to where your coastlines are set, sometimes that is NOT enough space. - Ocean Gameplay really was my issue I guess, because the HYPERLANES SHOULD BE ALLOWED TO BE BUILT ON THE WATER!?!?! If it is a underground system like how oil rigs can dig down into, why can't hyper lane towers be the same thing?! I had to eventually only have one lane between an island area and the mainland which killed production and logistics until I covered the island in ports. Either Boats need an overhaul (Which the DLC did not fix) or there needs to be more research with them to allow for more boats per harbor. - Towards the end of trying to cover the planet 50% in foliage and the 50k pop goal, the game REALLY started to chug fps wise, but I did have almost half the planet covered in buildings and over 700 boats running around the oceans. I don't know if the replayability was a strong factor for me. This is a game that you come back to every once in a while to either have a better run, or complete the campaign with different choices given the multiple endings. It's a great podcast/youtube game to have running on multiple screens and zone out.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Good fun game if you like city builders. Ok, this is at a bigger scale but just the same. Graphics are not what you would expect from an 2020 release but considering the size of the game I guess you cannot expect more. The building interface is simple and you will feel at home within minutes but on a negative side once the base gets bigger and bigger eventually the whole planet (I'm not there yet) it will get difficult to keep track of the mines and factories and when you will want to upgrade them it will a bit of a pain to go over each and every one. If there is an upgrade all option I've not found it yet. After Surviving Mars this game offers whole new take on how we could do it and the Campaign so far was pretty good and fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I pushed through to the end of terraformation, and I don't have statisfaction.The ressource movement betwen mine, factory, construction is severly broken once you have a few hundred building.I had to wait years in game simulation for a ressource to arrive destination when it was available in a stockpile 2 building away.Factories that lack ressource, and mine fullstack that don't see a robot to move them, while every sector are green, i had up to 400 robot. _childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game essentially feels like a "hardcore" version of Surviving Mars - however, the incredible high death probability and failure modes, which make it "hardcore" only serve to overshadow the fact that the game is incredibly shallow. The game is tedious, often boring and requires an insance and unwanted amount of micro-management.MechanicsThe game follows a simple resource / worker mechanic. However, resources are finite and thus you always need to expand. Since every building requires constant maintenance (and thus consumes resources), you have to do an incredible amount of micro management at all times. Especially in the late game, the constant building of new bases, claiming of new resources is tedious at best and boringly repetitive at worst.The mechanics themselves are incredibly shallow. And while the game offers many tools for fine tuning (ultra micro management), it fails to convey basic aspects (how to solve bottlenecks? how much resources do I really need).Death SpiralsOne of the main issues with the game is the large amount of death spirals, which can occur even late into the game and force you to abandon ten hours of gameplay. This can be the terraforming process, an attack damaging a core factory line, which in turn prevents maintenance, which in turn prevents the factory line from producing the resources for mainteance... you get the gist. Especially since the game does a very poor job of explaining what is happening and why.StoryIt is ok. The voice acting is excellent. The scripts sometimes feel unrelated and strangely out of place if you complete the game at your own pace. The philosophical questions are nice, but have become trivial by now. The outcome is ok-ish. As is the end.GraphicsQuite nice. Taxes the GPU far too much. Since you're not going to look close-up anyway (you need to manage multiple areas accross Mars, remember?), there should be a low-GPU mode whenever you scroll out, but the fans from my (somewhat older) GPU did not indicate this was the case.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: While the game at first is fun and neat, seeing the red planet slowly turn blue, then green. It lack in content and worst of all, it is very easy to soft-lock the game if you don't rapidly expand the base as resources run dry. The story that runs along side the game is neat and good, but has major problems with it. First off, it expects you to have read all of the lore presented in a small box in the top of your screen to understand a lot of it. but the worst part of it, is that due to the way you can progress the game, the story jumps back and fourth, as it will talk about things that has yet to happen in the past tense and talk about things that happened 5 years ago as if it just happened today. The UI looks clean and elegant, but it controls terribly. There are no ways to undo a building construction, let alone cancel it outside tearing the whole thing down. Also, guess what, there is combat in your mars colonization, teraforming game. Why is it there? don't know, but its terrible. It completely takes away from the experience in attempts to add unneeded drama into the underlining plot line, and on top of that, it too to unresponsive and terrible to control. Over all 4.8/10. Very fun, and strong start which quickly turns sour, even with multiple play-thoughs
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: For anybody with even just a normal level of interest in topics such as Mars, Terraforming, Hard Science Fiction this game is a delight. I love the accuracy of the planetary surface. I love being able to make a red Mars green. It's a game that plays right into the hands of those who love reading Kim Stanley Robinson - or his little brother Andy Weir :)
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Game is seems to be too raw, or just unbalanced. Game speed. Game is super slow, it's nearly impossible to play on x1,x2,x4 speeds. I have started to use x16 speed, and realized that only at this speed level game proceeds fast enough.The game process. It's too long, and this is not a long campaign, but super boring steps to next step in the game. Sometimes i just setted the game on x16 speed and went to make a tea. Sometimes you must complete same step multiple times, to finish some project, like space elevator. It will take you 30 to 60 mins on x16 speed without any gameplay, just watching it slowly completing.Logistics. There is something weird with logistics, extending your base takes years in game for some drone to decide to move resource to building place instead of endlessly unloading some silicon or carbon to the storage. Game really needs priority system.Bugs. There was some crashes. One was on load of game, the other one was during automatic save. Game just crashes without any message. Not cool.Balance and mechanics. I was always not getting enough water, chemicals and food for your colonists, at 80 year of colonization there were very few water deposit reserves. Looks like colonists just annihilates matter. And for some reason, you cant take water from martian seas, and cant grow plants by yourself, or collect them from mars surface when it is terraformed.Researching. Researching are too long. You need thousands of colonists to study technologies. It takes me about 30 minutes to research one last level technology at x16 speed with 2000 population. I'd happily created more research bases, colonies and bases, but i was very limited at available resources. At the same time, some technologies are useless, I can't imagine situation where i need to discover all military tech tree.Some of technologies are just created to make your game longer, like magnetic shield satellite, called an old technology requires 50k research points, and and the same time space elevator requires 10 times less.Anyway, game music is perfect. Protagonist as artificial intelligence, which is trying to realize itself, and always reflects about anything is really good and interesting idea.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Yes BUT!I recommend this game as I have enjoyed while playing. But first I want to point out fixable issues and then tackle the good part.However, game suffers from lacking multiple Quality of Life improvements and it is noticeable in mid to late game stage. All this can be easily sorted primarily with modifying certain aspects of UI and adding button or two for search/filter functionality. Those which are in top of the screen are bare bones and later it would be good to find a specific spaceport/space elevator. Or filter specific resource by type and tier. Combat interaction is really bad and needs improvement. Lack of underwater structures is strange (as game is set in future where humanity is creating powerful AI and colonizing Mars can't make underwater structures?It's enjoyable experience where player takes a role of a brand new honest AI built by humans to terraform Mars. Player as AI makes not only production decisions but also tackles evolution of it's own personality, uncovers the mystery that happened on Mars before the mission starts. Player takes responsibility of the production chains and terraforming process as well as take care of research trough human colonists who arrive on Mars. Depending on the player choices, certain stages can take longer and there is a bit of a learning curve. As I have mentioned, game could have more QoL improvements to make this easier. It is quite enjoyable to watch Mars slowly transform into a blue-green planet as game progress. Also game supports mods (personally haven't played with mods but kudos for the support).
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game shows great promise but there are a few bugs that makes it almost unplayable.Even if you have plenty of workers, using the priority feature does nothing. Resources to build are often stuck at hubs or hyperloops or storage and will not move to the building unless you upgrade the road or turn the building off and then on again. You cannot select which resources are stored in storage centers so you workers will just fill them all up with junk across the map. This ends up starving industry and your workers are constantly busy not building. Sandbox mode asteroids keep raining down even after 300mb atmosphere is established - destroying workers and building faster than can be replaced.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of Kim Stanley Robinson's book "Red Mars" this game's story was really enjoyable. While there isn't as much depth between the factions and interests in this game compared to the book, I am up to a point in the story where there 3 different forks that presumably determine the future fate of Mars. This isn't really even the main story though which seems to be about AMI's character development and her internal monologue and reflections are really interesting as a story telling device and allow you to get insight into her thoughts. One issue with the game though is that the story triggers seem to be associated with different actions you perform but do not have any sense of dependency or knowledge of previous interactions, this can lead to a lot of dialogue talking about plot arcs that either haven't happened yet or have already happened and been resolved.The main attraction for the game for me was the terraforming aspects which take an appropriately long time and proceed in stages. Options are afforded to the player to control temperature, atmospheric composition and basic lifeforms (at least where I am at the moment). There are some cool interactions here with increasing the temperature at the poles with space mirrors which allowed my algae colonies to spread to a larger area in the northern ocean I had created. You can end up completing multiple terraforming stages this way as they are associated with certain atmospheric goals which seems a bit weird gameplay wise but is nice as an option to the player.At points in the game you will need to make smaller bases that require you to remember the build order from the beginning, which becomes a bit boring after you have done it >5 times already. It would be nice if you could deploy smaller bases with more resources to speed this up later in the game. It's possible that this is something you can access later but I had not seen anything after ~12 hours into the campaign and around halfway through the tech tree. After setting up these bases it is very satisfying to connect them up to the main base however.I'm not certain how much this is an intentional design choice, but as the game progresses you will become increasingly starved for water which requires you to expand across the surface in search of it to sustain your colonies and terraforming processes. The game balance seems a little bit off, but resources being scarce does push the gameplay forward and allow you to disassemble older structures that become obsolete for resources. This plays quite well which making sure that your production facilities are close to raw resources to minimise traffic.The combat is very underwhelming but I was more interested in the base building and terraforming aspects of the game. It seems to be there more in service of the narrative than as something that a lot of game development time was spent on.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I originally rated this game negatively at launch, as it had a great many problems. It was a very good concept, and the early game was great, but the endgame was a tedious, unfun chore and there were multiple, plot-breaking bugs throughout the game.I decided to give it another chance, and I will say that the Developers really put a lot of work into this. Most of the issues I had raised at the beginning (poor worker AI, absolute slogs of projects, scarcity of resources) have been resolved. The endgame still tends to drag a little longer than it should (at least for me), wherein in the early to mid game, you're getting plot points and messages every 15-20 minutes, and then you're looking at hours between them as the late game terraforming and space projects take FOREVER. But it is better.It's a good game, it's not perfect, but there's a lot here to like as a large-scale planet building game, and I'm a sucker for anything that lets me terraform Mars. The developers have clearly put in a lot of time and effort to improve the game post-launch, and I don' regret having played it again to have given it that final chance to make a new impression. If you like the resource chain management city builder genre of games, it's a thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the game, i definetly do not reccomend playing this on hard or normal.the resources get even more scarce, you're pushed to expand even more hastily because of a maintenance mechanic that does not fit a game with finite resources.Maybe dont let asteroids destroy buildings without being able to reclaim any resources from the rubble. because you've made them finite.maybe let people defecate and urinate? people dont destroy water on the atomic level you know, that whole planet you see there, that's a closed loop you troglodyte. that means let people reuse resources for gods sakes or here's a hint DONT MAKE THEM FINITE.the whole maintenance bot dying mechanic is way too unstable, after the first major story events mine all died and put me in a maintenance hole for hours on end. maybe let me recycle the dead bots??? or dont make the resources finite..combat isn't explained at all, i presumed it was a tower defence type combat at first because i saw no indications otherwise. seeing hostile troops fly over my towers seriously wasn't fun because they wrecked my already crippled maintenance supplies. maybe fix that or let me recycle destroyed buildings?So i decided to hold off on terraforming for a while to fix my resources by getting at a huge area of resources that were placed at a low height map, this game spawns more stuff the lower you go. so in that directions players like me will go.Except it then punishes those very players by destroying those buildings the second water appears. thanks for telling me to go somewhere with mechanics and then punishing me for it.long story short this game suffers from the biggest oversight a planet wide game like this can have: it's not treating it like a closed loop system on the recycling/destruction/combat/maintenance/projects side whilst its definetly treating it like that on the mining side of things. how the ♥♥♥♥ can a PLANET run out of SAND IRON or WATER when that constitutes the overwhelming majority of the planets mass, surface AND deep. FIX THIS.aside from those glaring issues the story is okay, it can get wildly out of order though and at some points AMI's dialogue didn't even have audio.. it's okay in the first 2.5hrs after that it's a 4/10Implement Steam workshop, fix this whole "i can't get at the water because the water is on the water" debacle, the  conflicting design choices for finite un-recyclable resources and the infinite maintenance costs that scale worse the more you build and then I'll look at it again..Tip for players don't expand your colonies, keep as little people as you can. even if the research is a snails pace at least you won't be without water or food within the year because those colonists have the most insane bladders and constipation the universe will ever see.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, Per Aspera is an automation/building game which is abstracted to nodes and workers. At first it looks very basic, but I'd say it grows on you as you create large networks. The mechanics are relaxed, as far as I can tell there is very little chance to get to a fail state and most of the game will be a slow wait as you grow towards various objectives. The audio and visuals support the chill vibe, while the story themes are also largely contemplative and existentialist.Indeed, the catch is that this is a story driven builder game.  It's good news for underserved fans of hard sci-fi, as the narrative is relatively grounded, and explores terraforming with the aid of a possibly conscious AI. Not wholly groundbreaking per se, but it does hold a good amount of mystery and intrigue. I also thought that it was a nice touch that it starts from real life lore surrounding Mars exploration missions, and then expands them into a fictional future. My criticism here is that the voice acting can be uneven, ranging from good to melodramatic, and often feels too chatty to the point it overstays its welcome. Meanwhile, at times the dialogue/monologue can become a tad redundant when it circles round into existential AI territory. I found the story started strong and ended a bit shakily, and while it suffered from second half pacing issues, I'd say that overall it was enjoyable. About a 6-7 out of 10 as far as SF goes for me, and considering how rare decent hard SF is, I'd say that's not too bad.Overall I'll give it a thumbs up because it was a pretty different experience, though I'd caution you to only try it if you're armed with patience and prepared to be quite generous to a small game which is rough around the edges.

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a logistics and resource management game.It has a similar flavor to games like Factorio and Satisfactory with this game being much more chill.The Story mode of this game took me about 20 hours  / 104 in game years to complete on Easy mode without researching all the technologies.I recommend playing Story mode for at least a few hours as it does a good job of introducing you to how some of the game mechanics and play works.The core game mechanics and concept of the game is solid!The games does need a few tweaks and improvements to the documentation/tutorial as it needs to do a better job of explaining to a new player how to move your military drones around.-Lessons learned during my first play through.-Building more factories does not solve the issues of production.Your factories should run around 80% efficiency. Other then food production, you may end up only needing one or two factories for the whole game.A good indicator of when you might need a second factory is to look at potential production and potential demand. As long as the potential production is 20% higher then potential demand then do not consider building another factory.For every one factory, you need at least 2-3 worker hubs connected to just that factory.If you are having issues with the factory efficiency, look at the connections between it and the raw resources. You don't want resources stacking up at your worker hubs.If you see a lot of resources stacking up on your main highways connecting your bases you may need additional worker hubs/hyperloops installed. Raw resources really only need one worker hub and it is ok if resources stack up.Over building raw resource production is not a bad thing.Scanners are your friends. During my play through I only managed to scan about 49% of the whole planet.A mix of solar and wind power is important to mitigate power dips caused by the environment.Adding a battery for every 3rd or 4th   power generation may not be a bad idea.There will be often times where you build out a path to a resource then later remove all buildings to recover your building count and is part of the game mechanics.As soon as possible build more then one space port, with at least one being dedicated to importing people and the others for special projects.Research outposts make a world of difference and I would prioritize those over building additional colonies. Late game research takes a long time, and each outpost contributes a bonus to the research projects.In regards to lander sites: this is something I need to dig deeper into. I had more then one, but then ended up connecting them all together. This review was written for the 1.3 version.In conclusion I hope the devs for this game create a new game based on Europa or some other moon/planet of the Sol system. If they do, I will be buying and playing that game!

_childDocuments_.review: Fairly effective Martian terraforming simulator. Not a fan of the campaign, particularly the combat and the whole rogue AI thing that I imagine it will eventually lead to, but thankfully there's a sandbox mode which removes the strange plot and immersion breaking combat. The game is at it's strongest when you're working on maintaining your production capacity and terraforming efforts, and can pretty effectively simulate a systems collapse if you mess up. Failure and repetition are a big part of this, you learn and you move on. I wouldn't pay too much notice to people who claim the game is too slow or that they didn't understand that there was more than one tech tree; the buttons to remedy these are pretty obvious. The only thing that's somewhat obtuse is the resource system, which can be hard to manage due to indistinct icons and a lack of proper warnings and overlays.Overall, if you want to terraform Mars and deal with the logistics of what that entails, this is the game for you. It's not SimCity, it's not Surviving Mars.

_childDocuments_.review: In a setting with strong AI, and planetary terraforming the most fantastical element is the idea that the hyperloop will be viewed as a transformative technology. Hilariously, even in the future it still Isn't useful for long distance transportation. The central theme of this game is the FOLLY OF THOSE WHO HAVE SPURNED THE TRAIN.All of the mechanics of resource gathering/ production technically work, but the gameplay involved in resource management is totally flat. there isn't much to consider aside from building more mines/factories when you need more of a particular resource. there are 3 non-productive buildings that need to cover your entire network which you need to tediously build with every expansion. Resources often appear in patches but without TRAINS you can't really centralize or strategically plan production aside from building factories roughly in the middle of the two patches that it uses. As mines are depleted you simply scrap them and move on so you never get the sense that you're building a permanent settlement, or specializing different areas in a meaningful way. Compared to Surviving Mars the depth of the resource management is like playing cookie-clicker.As alluded to above: the Hyperpoop you get access to in the midgame does not have the range to connect the colonies that the game prompts you to settle without building intermediate stations which must be connected to one of your colony networks, so it really does not let you bridge significant gaps. Not a replacement for rails on any planet!Now that I've started comparing it to Surviving Mars, I really can't stop. managing colonists really doesn't exist aside from providing them food/water. Terraforming happens fast with little actual investment, and has little effect on gameplay aside form rising water levels denying access to resource nodes. Somehow the combat system is worse compared to a game that doesn't really have a combat system?The story is decent, but it really undermines my suspension of disbelief that a supposed strong AI can't figure out that it should build a train.To be fair Surviving Mars doesn't have trains, but it does have pipes which is the trains of fluid transportation.In conclusion: A proprietary road system is no basis for interplanetary colonization. Mark my words: Only the train can tame Mars for humanity. The best thing this game does is remind me to play Surviving Mars. The pinnacle of Mars colonization games will not be reached until someone puts a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ train on Mars.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR  Recommended if you want a casual one play-through builder and can put up with some logistics issues.  This isn't a game to replay for hundreds of hours, and you can't build your roads and cities square by square as in some other games.  I respect that they tried to do something different with Per Aspera as compared to a typical colony builder, but this isn't going to work for some players, so be warned.  Expect 40-50 hours for a playthrough and all endings.I would conditionally recommend Per Aspera, only to very patient players, who aren't taking the game too seriously and just want to do one play-through.  As others have said, the story, visuals and sound are first-rate.  The voice acting in particular is very well done.The worker drone and resource allocation systems however are so finicky that you really can only play one way in order not to fail into a death spiral.  You have to keep a watch on your worker drones all the time, because if their numbers drop off, it will take forever to rebuild, as there won't be enough drones left to move the resources needed to build more drones.  As well, since everything is done by drones and AI, if you need even one resource in a certain facility, there is literally no way for you to drag and drop that resource yourself, you have to set the allocation sliders and priority markers on your buildings and resources and then hope for the best.That being said, there is a lot to like here.  Exploring the different sectors and finding abandoned sites to research is quite interesting. As well the story allows for three endings, which branch near to the end of the game.  You can easily save before this point and play through each of the endings, which take only about 2-3 hours each on top speed.  Watching the planet slowly change is rewarding if you are a casual player like me who wants a fairly easy-going terraforming game.  This process is slow, even on top speeds, so again I would not recommend Per Aspera to someone who wants a very action-heavy base builder.As for the building system, for each new facility you build, if it is not located right next to an existing facility, you basically have to build it ist own worker hub, power supply and maintenance facility.  If it's far away from anything, you might have to build a chain of these thress types of resources to even get to the place whwere you want to build the new facility.  To my knowledge you have to select each one on the menu as you go, instead of dropping a line of them, so the process can get tedious.  It didn't bother me too much but I can see some people getting fed up.A mixed review in all, as I mostly enjoyed it, but I can't necessarily recommend it to others without a lot of warnings.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played lots of city builders over the years but not one with the precise logistical mechanic here.  The logistic system consists of a graph with edges connecting nodes; a worker stationed at each node can go get an item from a connected node and take it somewhere it needs to go, or put it at its node to be passed down the line.Most of the gameplay consists of building and expanding one (or more) of these graphs for maximum efficiency.  It's often clumsy, frustrating, and very, very slow.  However, at the same time it's very easy, to the point where this could be considered a Casual game.By complete coincidence, after I finished this game I played another one with the exact same logistics mechanic.  I didn't know that going in.  That other game is structurally very similar to this one but far more fun, interesting, challenging, and focused.  Go play The Colonists instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Don’t. I mean the story is very nice, haven’t done all the possible branches yet, but this should be a visual novel. And it would be a good one. But the gameplay elements range from OK to slopy or even bad. At best it’s a nice pre-release but it’s not marked as one so …So just find a game movie on YT, I know I will to see the other endings and not have to deal with the gameplay again.The building part starts fine but is limited and quickly repetitive, tech system is contrived and poor (at some point someone must have said “building game need tech tree” so slap one on top), combat system is downright bad (“hey, game gets repetitive, let’s add a combat system, pew pew”), oh and UI is hard (allowing to set your own controls if you don’t have an azerty keyboard or just don’t like them is a no go, and to give an idea of the general states of control and UI, even the save name text bow is a mess).Just why. The combat system that's slapped on top of this is unnecessary and incredibly bad. It doesn’t bring anything, it isn’t fun, it isn’t tactical (saying you can use tactic in dialogs doesn’t count you know). The system boils down to the following: can you produce a lot of military points (I mean the one single generic type of drone) and then deals with the infuriating controls to try to hurl those points at the enemy. Oh, and the system actively prevents you from being tactical:•	cannot queue orders •	drones spawn where the heck they want if you build more than one turret•	can’t rally point them•	they sometimes merge on their own during combat•	you can’t split them, you can’t selection box•	they auto target whatever they want•	the select/move click gets you 1/5 times which is aggravating because you can’t box select•	the autotargeting is a random number generator•	they leave on their own when the autotargeting can’t figure what to target next•	they leave on their if you mess the select/move click•	you have to play where’s waldo to find your units•	staying put appears to be the most complex command those drones can deal with•	if your building is attacked by 10 enemy drones, your 100 drones parked 1 meter away will happily let it get destroyed •	there is only one type of unit, you can only research a stat increase for attack/defense/speed (and you don’t even know by how much or if the enemy upgraded theirs)•	barely any warning to find where you are attackedAnd that is just about the combat system, which admittedly, is the worst part. Maybe some of the points can be done but I don’t feel like it was ever hinted or explained, and there’s just too much to deal with, combat was the cherry on top, I’ve ran out of good will at this point.Minor spoiler warning maybe I guess, the last battle is the **insert 5 harsh words** worst. Things can just downright spawn from nothingness and with the combat system it takes forever and you just can’t have to deal with that and drop anything else you are doing, which I guess was nothing more than setting up your n-th outpost and sending stuff to your spaceport.I’ll maybe give another go at the last combat to say that I completed at least on branch, bust as things stand, I think I’ll just go watch the game movie on YT.
