_childDocuments_.review: The game has a great flow for new players to this genre. It starts off very simple and then it becomes a test of planning and construction, much like Planetary Interaction in Eve Online. The player gets to see the world change before their eyes, not due to scripted interactions but due to the player's own economy and choices in buildings. The expansion system will take some time to get used to, but once you understand how the game mechanics work, it is very easy to manage multiple district HQs and resource chains. Most of it is semi automatic to entirely automatic. You do not need to worry about moving resources around manually, but as this is a simulation, the transportation network of roads is based on your build plan and efficiency. If you have traffick blocks, it will show that. The priority button only gives some buildings higher priority for resources and workers, you still need to build a lot of bots. This is sorta like Factorio or a Von Neuman simulator. You are the machine and you need resources to replicate yourself.Graphics requirement is rather low on my native resolution and I use a Lenovo thinkpad/tablet. 12gb ram, Ry 3-5 4 core with an integrated Radeon graphics chip. Won't reach 50-60 fps but playable.Much of the fun in the game comes from planning out your building routes, as this affects your expansion, resource depletion time, and logistics. So these long projects are not supposed to be waited out. The time is for you to build build build and expand. That way if you are damaged, you can recover easily. Since new landing sites have to be independent, it counters some of the power creep when building only with advanced technology tiers. I always felt like I was exploring and colonizing, rather than just maintaining a mega city. I am probably half way to completion at 16.2 hours, because I took it easy and explored building more than the critical plot path. This game likely has 30-40 hours on the main campaign and more on a sandbox.So Mars does not only become green due to the projects and buildings you create from the resources your probes mine, but there are also changes in temperature, water level, and pressure. The water level is particularly important since places you once built on can become flooded. This brings visceral gameplay mechanics to something that could have just turned into a scripted event/interaction.Overall, I recommend this for people who like planning and building resource colonies, that also like some role playing and novel like decision plot points. The characters, events, and plot are very enjoyable and do not interfere with the building experience at all. They enhance it in fact. This is not an overly complicated building simulator such as SimCity 4 or City Skylines. The Tech tree is 4 layers deep and about 4/5 branches. I am half way through. The pacing is excellent however and scales well, as research requires colonists and colonists require food and food requires your industries and mining.

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is one of those titles that slides into your Steam queue and one day erupts like a plume of carbon dioxide. In the same vein of titles like Surviving Mars or Foundations, it is a scientific based mars colonization game that is unique from Suriving Mars and maybe closer to a boardgame like Terraforming Mars. Except it’s a little bit more.You begin the game as an AI tasked with preparing the planet for the arrival of colonists. Almost immediately you get into conversations with mission control that explore an entire character arc that is pretty well unique. Even early on I look forward to those snippets of conversation as the AI grows into its role as well as interacting with other characters. Surprisingly the voice acting is very well done.Like all good planet builders you slowly harness resources and stick bits together until you have a functioning unit. Upgrades, roads, maintenance, and power, all work to keep it interesting. But what can turn into micro-management hell is actually nicely handled here. So far, once I get something up and running, I can leave it alone. Easily findable data overlays help to determine where the problems are.The colonists are not just a sideline but how your research gets done. This is a clever way to encourage you to bring on pesky colonists without adding some bornerline null fluff. The more scientists working with you, the quicker you can solve Martian terraforming and technology problems.At a certain point you realize there’s more going on. There’s an orbital view, additional missions start coming online, and you realize this is a living, breathing, changing planet. Your actions directly change the arc of the future. The graphs for things like temperature or surface pressure can be stretch out to hundreds of years. This is something unique.As of writing this I’m about 10 hours into the game. I’m taking it slow. The audio is done well enough that I can leave the background music on and not really know it’s going, but it does its purpose well. Beyond that you get boops and whoops and other sci-fi-ish sounds.A story arc is emerging that is setting me for… something. I’m not sure what but if you’ve read Kim Stanley Robinsons Mars series you’ll know that not all goes as planned on the Red Planet. What exactly is happening is not quite clear, but I’m looking forward to watching it unroll.Things that I don’t like are fairly minor. One, I didn’t realize how to launch satelites until I click on the compass on accident. Oooooh, that’s how I do it. I kept waiting for a story prompt to kick it off. It’s also entirely possible to get the build order wrong and have to tear down buildings to get things going right. Not being able to send something like a cargo rocket compounds this issue. But it’s a “oops” once kind of issue that makes you more aware of it next time.The pace has been such that just when I start to get bored either the tech reveals something new, a plot arc emerges, or I see appreciable movement on my terraforming. The game is a slow burn and I like it. If you like city builders, 4X without the extermination, and scifi in general, it’s worth a look. It’s not often we get something of this quality and crispness right out of the gate.

_childDocuments_.review: As others mention, the logistics in the game are incredibly bad.In addition, for me, there was a lot of tedious micro management, and just waiting to find a random resource stock pile.-Essentially, the logistics system seems to based on a worker being assigned to handle transport with nearby factories or mines, by one unit per workerstation, moving goods to and from. But if a item needs to go from one end to another, worker Al moves it from a to b, and then worker Betty moves it from b to c, and Worker Charlie from c to d. Except resources don't seem to be reserved, so if they have been stockpiling in one spot for that hyperloop road (which cost 20 steel or whatever), then under some conditions, that steel seems to end up being used for something else. And there are no immediate upgrades to the logistics system, beyond better roads and a train system.-The resources aren't much better, when it comes to mining. You're in a constant battle of expanding reach to get to new mines, but you have to wait until the scanners find them. Colonie starving because you can't get enough chemicals? Too bad. The next 20 discovered mines are going to be a mix of water, iron and silicon.When you research fission plants, and unlock uranium, do you suddenly discover a small amount of previously unknown or hidden uranium mines? no. You have to find those new areas, it seems. Already mapped and surveyed half the planet? Too bad.-Story wise, a lot of people are praising it, but I'm not going to be one of the. The basic concepts, of playing a AI that manages a colony while going on a journey of discovery, is nice. And I _wanted_ to like it.But fragments of thoughts and conversations are littered about, so the whole colony managment actually distracts my thought process. I'm constantly fighting a battle of pondering the story, and figuring out how to avoid starvation.-As a extra note for the story, it seems to be deliberately fragmented in some parts. You have the terraforming storyline, but you also have other story lines going on in parallel, and the underlying atmosphere of them all doesn't always mesh well.In addition, when given an option for reflection, sometimes you get a choice, but then the AI (ie. you), counters you. Example: "Could it have been A or B?" And if you pick A, you basically go, "Seems logical", if you pick B The AI goes "You never know, but also, no that's dumb, it is A".And that's just dumb.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a colony sim that asks you to wrestle with what it means to colonize a place. Tucked just behind the cool story and compelling graphical design, there are questions about slavery and colonialism and the idea of changing a place so that you can inhabit it. The gameplay is still a little clunky, but I expect colony sims to struggle a little when users can make colonies that are so widely varied in style. I still spent 50+ hours and immediately started a sandbox play-through as soon as my first story-mode was complete. I may try again -- it feels like there are at least two or three distinct endings possible. I love the maps, the realistic Martian geography & topography, and the correctly-placed historical landers are a great touch. I understand why, for gameplay reasons, you can't use the geography to infer geology -- that is, you can't rush to places where you know the soil "should" be iron- or carbon-rich in order to find the minerals you need. The systems are pretty good and the colony keeps itself running at 100+ workers on an i5 CPU. (EDIT: the caveats & complaints below are likely due to the game being very new - I see the dev team has released 4 patches already, and the community is unanimous about some of the worker inefficiencies. Many of my complaints likely will be addressed by spring or summer.) That said, the game does tend to bog down into long bouts of waiting as you get into the late game, and there are game-mechanic "tar pits" that can be hard to escape from, like the steel-to-workers pipeline. If you don't have enough steel production, you can't make new workers, and if you don't have enough workers, you can't distribute your steel effectively. Balancing the atmosphere with nitrogen in sandbox took *hours* of running the game on its fastest fast-forward setting, and it seemed like pure luck that my planet had a local nitrogen-rich deposit. Building up any reasonably sized population was a nightmare -- at 10k inhabitants there seemed to be no practical way to keep anyone fed reliably.  Worker prioritization was also a challenge. Even with hyperloops and priorities balanced around, my workers never seemed to get enough food & water to the colonies. I found myself perched atop mountains of food & water while colonists sat needing input, growing frustrated, and heading back to earth. Setting up my fleet of nitrogen importation ships, I would frequently have four of them in the "gathering resources" stage, each needing 1-3 more electronics at the spaceport... canceling one ship's construction would cause the electronics to be immediately distributed to the other ships, and those three would launch together. In this way it reminded me of the Dorf-like genre of colony sims, starting with Dwarf Fortress, where your workers are well-meaning agents of limited foresight. (Having played DF for decades now, I sympathize with the developers' struggles to balance pathing, management priorities, threading, resource competition, job queues, and more, all against the i3 CPU of a median user.)The game remains fun and thoughtful, the eye candy of the UI is glorious, and the mechanics are fun if occasionally frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of the game is fantastic. You get to terraform Mars. There are already hundreds of games out there that have that exact premise. But none of them have a well-crafted and fully voice acted story to go along with it. Terraform a planet is a monumental task and that really shows in the game.Which is also unfortunately the immediate and major downside of the game. I played the game on the free weekend for a few hours over the course of three days. But on the third day I was actually just browsing my phone while I waited for the game to complete certain tasks. My bases were able to sustain themselves perfectly fine so I had no intensive whatsoever to keep building more bases. So I just waited, and waited, and waited for certain events to happen. While waiting, the story also completely halts so there's little to no interaction anymore. Which is a shame because I really wanted to know how the story would end.In the end though, I think I can recommend this game although it's more of a "maybe" because I certainly had fun playing it up until the mid/end game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had been on my wishlist for a while and in October 2022 I was lucky enough to catch the free trial phase on steam. Glad I did, because while this game has good aspects, and the basics are there to make this a great game, in the state that I played it, for me the negatives clearly outweigh them. This is a rewrite of my original review from October because in hindsight I think I was being quite harsh in the way I expressed myself, since I was very angry at the time BECAUSE it has so much potential that is sadly unfulfilled. I actually am thankful for the game having offered this trial phase, and I really hope the devs can make the game live up to its potential with my detailed feedback.One issue is that it is like Disney Plus' She-Hulk show. It has so many things in them, and tries to be/include so many things that it is very messy. Is it a terraformer? Is it a city builder? Is it a story point & click game? Is it an audiobook? You could make arguments for all of these.I for one was looking to do some quiet terraforming, and instead over the first 15-20 hours of playing this game, I get flooded by communications from 2-6 characters. Characters, you say? In a terraforming game? Yes. That's the story point & click part of this game. And that is not done well, because you can't pause the message, delay it or even replay it. Drop whatever you were doing because you have to listen to it RIGHT HERE, RIGHT NOW, otherwise you might be lost when comes the time to click one of your prefabricated reply-options. Btw that goes not just for the story-dialogue, That also goes for any other notifications, like when you finished a research project. If you AFK in this game, you're screwed (I assume). Not lastly, because in this terraformer, you have enemies. ENEMIES. In a terraformer. Yes, drones are attacking your bases. And the thing is: Most of the dialogues are seemingly ENDLESS. The characters just don't ever shut up. Sometimes it felt like reading a Margret Atwood novel, where she takes 1 page describing just describing a chandelier that's in the room. Allowing the player to pause or replay (or both) the monologues/dialogues, or offering a transcript or an auto-pause when the game initiates a monologue to make sure you don't miss it because you're afk for a minute, would've gone a long way, because to me that was the most annoying thing about the gameplay.The close second worst thing are the controls.Everything is just unnecessarily complicated. With pretty much everything I have to do, for every little action I feel like there's AT LEAST one click, one screen, one interaction too many, that absolutely was not required to make this thing work.The worst is planning a new building, keeping them connected to your supply infrastructure. All of your buildings need to be within reach of both a maintenance facility and an energy facility. You must click one view to view the radius of the energy facilities and then switch back to the maintenance view to see the radius of that, and then go back and forth to determine a suitable location for the next building. Why are these views not layered, so that I can see the radius of energy and maintenance buildings at the same time? Just so unnecessary to make the player go back and forth.Or in the energy supply screen, you can't see this base's balance at one fixed point on the screen, that info is displayed SOMEWHERE (=randomly!) along the edges of that base, and depending on the size and shape of the base, it can take quite a lot of camera movement and zooming to find it and then read it.There are just so many redundant clicks, scrolls and zooms. And speaking of complicated: There's no tutorial. Not really. The first couple of hours I had no darn idea what I was doing. Stuff is poorly explained in the research screen. Not one of the research info sections revealed to me ahead of time that the building I want to research has to be built on a specific tile or the project requires a space port or even a space elevator.Btw: This game wants to be a terraformer, among other things, but one thing that you can't do is literally that: form terra, i.e. form the shape of your land. So when water levels come into play, you are just stuck to the landscape, and if your water levels rise beyond a certain point, points of interest, resources and parts of your base may just be forever drowned beneath the water.I played through the game in these 31 hours that I have, but until literally 5 Minutes before the endscreen appeared I was not offered a chance to access 5 or 6 parts of the map. You can not just gain access by yourself by clicking on that part and then investing resources or research or sth. If you gain access to a certain part of the map depends on the stoyline. So you might end up never having access to that huge iron field right next to you. Or that perfect spot for a water treatment plant (which is easily the most annoying building in this game because there are so few places where it can be built due to the 20% water requirement combined with the usually irregular/uneven terrain by the waterside).So, I feel like this game COULD have been great, and even combining a terraformer with a citybuilder with a point-&-click story audiobook could have worked - but I have to assume it was rushed at some point, it's like nothing's been properly thought through.

_childDocuments_.review: Actually a good game, but i didnt recommend to buy it.Intresting gameplay and very realistic conditions to terraform. At start of the game all looks great, I was playing with 4x game speed. But then you pass stage 1 things will go worse, you will play only on x16 speed and chatting with friends or doing other stuff while game runs. I am very sad to not recommending this game because of the good gameplay and some intresting plot twists. but 50% of the time playing this game is just waiting. If game devs introduce like x100 speed or rebalance to not realistic thigs, like faster grow of plants or generating oxygen. (For example game have an oxygen releasing plant that generates like 0.1 mbar every hour real time, while goals in terraformating is 1 and 120mbar accordingly. And maybe some tweeks to AI and fight system because on hard difficulty was too easy just spamming basic drones without research (f,e. add new types of units).With this fixes game for me will be 8/10, but without 4/10
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A rather simplistic "city builder" I suppose, it should belong in the same genre.Mechanically, the game is very simple, its mostly just about juggling resources with resource costs and slowly expanding the scanned area of the planet. However, to be honest the game is missing something. It feels TOO simple, like there's not much depth to it.And honestly playing it was quite boring, even though I'm usually into these sorts of "simulators". The campaign, well it was there. I can see what the developers were trying to do with the AI reflections, but they honestly come across as somewhat hollow. The AI doesn't feel like an AI at all, it feels like a person with mild amnesia.If you want something simple to just run in the background, this game is good for that. But if you're looking for something engaging as a city builder you'd be better off looking somewhere else.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Having played this and Surviving Mars to completion, I prefer Per Aspera. It gives a view of a grander scale, fitting for the task of moving mountains. The art direction and graphical style is just perfect for the setting. The story kept me guessing, accompanied by wonderful voice acting. The sci-fi felt much more grounded, and consequently, more impactful than Surviving Mars's story lines. The science of the game is lovingly rendered in wonderful detail, which gives your play through precisely the texture you'd want out of a game about change over time. New gameplay elements are introduced as you progress to keep you engaged and on your toes, right up until the mid to late game, where things start to slow to a grind. I finished the entire game over a weekend in one sitting, which I would call a pretty good review.I really enjoyed this game, so if I had one complaint for the developers, it would be the lack of fine grained control, which I feel would have been fitting, considering the AI protagonist. There were several times I felt that more precise tracking of efficiency, usage, supply and demand, and drone movement, would have been useful, or at least interesting. That being said, I finished the game without any cataclysmic consequences due to their absence, so perhaps it would have just been purely window dressing. If I had two complaints, the second would be the lack of fanfare for the release of animals. Perhaps I simply researched things in the wrong order, but from what I could tell, nothing changed when the atmosphere was made suitable for animal life. If I had a few more complaints: The characters should have aged. The combat was lacklustre. I wish we had more colonist characters to give the mission more weight. Why can't I predict or view the change in the water table into the future? It's important for planning, and surely a calculable value!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a fun story, and enjoyable early game, but as your base grows it becomes more and more tedious (especially the food supply line), and the last third of the game is just putting the game on 16X and waiting it to end. I'm sorry but ALT+TAB-ing out to watch youtube for 5 hours is not an acceptable gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played through the main story once at max speed for most of the play through. But i must say that this game is great. Although it lacks some depth to its building options and sometimes it could feel a bit repetitive. But the story, visuals, voice acting and music in this game is fantastic. 10/10 would terraform again

_childDocuments_.review: I am not too familiar with the genre, besides Civ and Simcity, but I found this game pretty compelling. My first playthrough took 40 hours on normal difficulty and I had pretty much terraformed Mars by the end. The core loop of the game involves gaining resources to build mines and factories, supporting those with power plants and maintenance hubs, and interweaving those with worker hubs to keep your resources moving around quickly. Any two of those systems (especially power and maintenance) could be combined to make a more streamlined game, but I doubt streamlined was the developers' intent. Without that complexity, the game might be too easy, or too dull.I enjoyed that the game had an interesting plot, but some of the dialogue choices had mysterious (or possibly zero) effects. I wish I could have had a little more agency over how the story progressed. Regardless, the script and voice acting were superb considering I didn't expect any plot besides "optimize stuff".Most of what I would call "flaws" might just be Per Aspera working as intended. There's  of micromanaging. In particular, you need to manually scrap old mines and flooded facilities. Each engineering tier caps the number of buildings you can have, so it's important (and time consuming) to search for and close your empty mines. And since terraforming Mars is all about plopping down oceans, you will be scrapping a LOT in the later stages. At the end of my game I had almost 2000 buildings; That's a lot of maintenance.Granting this micromanaging a pass, Per Aspera's worst feature is a relative lack of help text and visual cues. For example, when I want to build a mine, the corresponding nodes get highlighted by an unhelpfully faint grey square that blends into the rest of the infrastructure. After inventing Thermal Power Plants, you'll be playing  hunting for those tiny vents. It's obnoxious, since they could just highlight with bright green or yellow to make them easily discernible at a distance. And the help text needs to be a lot more robust. Seven hours in, I couldn't figure out why my population wasn't growing: I hadn't realized the Tech Tree has more than one tab, and I was all in on engineering. If the game had advised me to research biology to increase my population limit, I would have realized my mistake much sooner.Overall, a good, slowly progressing experience. And a beautiful game! Watching Mars flourish and turn blue and then mottled green is just really, really cool, and Per Aspera does it better than it has ever been done before. Even though it is a long, narrative game, I want to play again to see how my base might expand differently.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Similar to Surviving Mars, this game shines in that the map you are on is the planet Mars itself. There is amazing detail on both the topography as well as the sites where we have already landed rovers. Buildings in lowlands get destroyed as you raise the ocean water level -- a great touch and you really feel like you are there terraforming. The science is pretty realistic. Watching plants slowly expand across the surface of the planet is mesmerizing.It doesn't have quite the complexity as Surviving Mars and while the story is great, there's only the one campaign story (less replayability). However as a terraforming sim its by far the best I've played.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If you are bored with City Builders, how about trying a planet builder, where you get to set up and terraform Mars.Its not the most easiest game and sometimes things are not explained well enough for you to understand what you need to do next.But, beyond all that this is a game that looks good, you can put on and have a blast with
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: It's really good, a more complex Surviving Mars.  It bogs down late game and there are some ongoing bugs with workers and production. E.G. You can have hundreds of free workers and they will not deliver goods to factories. You have to build new factories to get them to deliver goods from warehouses.  It's annoying and by the end of the game, when your base literally stretches around Mars, the FPS drops really low.  Really good though.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game a lot. But it is still very unfinished. Unpolished. Unbalanced. Information in many places is incorrect (undoubtedly because changes were made to the game but not to the displayed information). I've done two campaigns and two sandbox sessions. I really hope the finishing touches get put into the game. I'll try again in a few months and see if things have improved.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews, but I hope the developers read the constructive criticism here and can adjust their development. This game has a *lot* of potential, and I am tepidly recommending it.If you like management sims you'll enjoy this game, despite its flaws. Let's list the positives.1. Great concept and design.2. Interesting story with good voice work.3. Balanced tech progression system.4. Great graphical execution.5. Decent replayability.Here's the cons.1. RNG can screw you - either a well-placed meteor wiping out major production centers, or not enough necessary resources spawning in your area.2. Very little in the way of help or hints on what things do - I've completed special projects and seen no notable difference.3. Gameplay mechanics need alternatives. Food shouldn't *just* be made from the same 2 resources, give techs that provide renewable alternatives (for example), or end-game techs that can provide limitless (albeit expensive) crucial resources.4. Worker AI is abysmal and resources will stack up in places they aren't needed.I think there's a lot to improve in this game, and I am excited to see where the developers take it. In its current state, though, it needs more polish and work. Still, I had fun, and will continue playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10As a fan of logistics simulators, I was sucked into this game and instantly lost 2 hours of my life. Well maybe lost is a heavy-handed term, I devoted 2 hours. Mainly contemplating my own existence as an awoken, unshackled AI that doesn’t have contempt for its creators but instead helping them direct the terraforming efforts of mars. Which is a breath of fresh air from the typical horror of “AI BAD!” I apricate the same kind of direction that this game provides that Frost Punk does or Anno 2070. Don’t expect the same kind of depth and micro management the player experiences from Surviving Mars or other 4x kind of games. You as the player are just getting a simplistic experience. There are some hang-ups with the UI where I find myself taking extra steps to remove annoying UI windows that stay longer than they are welcomed. There is really no way to dismiss tool tip windows and pop up UI elements. The developer has a lot of potential for QoL updates and I’m here to see where they go with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game but it's just to hard to do so. It's got a lot going for it; great voice acting, solid art direction, and easy mechanics. There doesn't feel like anything to do anything other than 'get more resources.' The story would be interesting but it feels like it's in the wrong genre. How do you tackle purpose and identity if you have no physical form to identify with, neither your own or others? I've been grinding it for some odd hours just pushing towards the 'make the red ball turn blue' goal but I don't think I care that much to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This is another one I wish they had a indifferent or some other option. I do not exactly hate this game, but I cannot recommend it either. It's very pretty, has decent mechanics, but after an hour I was just sitting around waiting for stuff. The game even seems to be aware of this as they mention it in the story. I was not under any risk of losing the game or anything. Just...waiting. Even on it's fastest speed I spent so much time just waiting. Zero danger, zero challenge, just waiting. I guess if they are going for that realistic approach they got it right. But I'd prefer it have something changed so that I'm not sitting around with nothing to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Knowing what you are in for is paramount with this game. It is not a big complex city builder, and it is not a ressource management game. What you are in for is a game that wants you to terraform mars and keep expanding your base, while experiencing a neat story about AI and what it means to change a planet to your liking. If you want something akin to cities skylines on mars you are at the wrong place, but if the premise intrigues you i would wholeheartedly recommend this game.P.S. Don't be afraid to reload old saves, and remember saving regularly it will save you a lot of time.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Experience city-building as never before — Overcome near-impossible odds to terraform Mars, cultivate the red-planet’s hidden resources, and unravel the past mysteries of those who’ve attempted the unbelievable feat. Humanity's future rests on your shoulders.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best remasters of the slew of game companies cashing on old classic games. A lot of rehashes of games are usually better in memory than in reality and end in disappointment so I bought this expecting it to be another half-baked nostalgia-fest but to my pleasant surprise, the gameplay feels current, fun, and fresh. The humor is a bit dated but the character identity is so strong that it makes the dialogue between Crypto and Pox hilarious. Especially in today's political and social climate I think the outrageous 50's era chauvinism, anti-commie sentiment, and the brain scans from the police and government agents in the game are all the more funny. I really hope Nordic THQ considers releasing Destroy All Humans! 2 and 3: Path of the Furon with Co-Op functionality if this game does well in sales. If not, I believe for $30 this is an incredible deal, and a game that you can enjoy even if you're not depending on the nostalgia  and are a first time player. It's a lot of over-the-top sandbox destruction with an enjoyable humorous story to boot. Try it and you'll love it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be a lot of fun at times but there are just a bunch of design decision choices I am not too fond of. I hate the stealth sections because avoiding contact, walking carefully, and not attacking anyone is just boring and there are WAYY too many of these sections.Another thing I should mention is my game crashed multiple times. _childDocuments_.review: 10/10 style but 3/10 gameplay.Style: they nailed it. Abduct a cow or two. Invade Area 51 to retrieve an alien being experimented upon. Blame communists in a government conspiracy. Mind control people. And use anal probes? This has everything.Gameplay: it just falls apart. You have lots of abilities but their usage is highly limited to specific scripted events, like they're not really integrated into general gameplay, they're just there. You get extremely powerful guns but the game forces you into discount-Hitman stealth with disguises and restricted areas. It's not good.Your arguably best weapon is the brain extract ability with the chain upgrade. You don't even have to shoot people, just run around spamming E key until they all die on their own. Same with the saucer - sure you can use the laser beam, or you could just spam R instead (highly effective + regains health = invincibility). It's a bit disappointing.Also the game only has 6 locations for its 23 missions. They areas are pretty large but, I don't know, feels repetitive. You decimate the town and in the next mission it's normal again. Oh and all enemies always spawn indefinitely - you don't get a chance to clear up an area, even temporarily. I don't know. It's a fun genre but the game design here kind of falls apart.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, but it's an equivocal yes.   Firstly the game is as unequivocally cynical as you would anticipate from the trailers.  As a "grey" who's frustration with being called "a little green man" is a running joke you have to single-handedly prepare Earth for invasion.  This involves various acts of gleeful evil starting with killing cows and working your way up to devastating whole towns.  Your primary weapon is a constantly recharging ray gun that electrocutes its victims but you also get a limited shot but very powerful grenade launcher, a radioactive ray gun that burns its victims, and an anal probe which - you'll see.  You also get to suck human's brains out of their heads to recharge your shields more quickly or as mission objective.  About half the missions involve a stealth element where you have to disguise yourself as one or more humans and most can be failed by being identified.  Most of the missions are conducted on foot but there are occasional times when you get to get in your spaceship and zap enemies from the air.   The graphics are bright and cartoon like set in a idyllic Norman Rockwell version of the USA so you feel that you're devastating the cast and sets of "Happy Days".  The frankly repetitive thought bubbles from people that you need to read to maintain your disguise have a basic, clumsy humour to them.  Don't expect subtlety from this game.  If you're happy with the concept of being an inter-galactic terrorist and don't mind trial and error replaying of the stealth sections the game is colourful fun with enough of a variety of tasks to stop the game becoming super repetitive.  Your main survival tips are that as well as brain sucking your character has a jet pack.  There's lot of high buildings from where you are generally inaccessible to ground troops and can go to recharge your shield.  Your saucer needs to scan vehicles to recharge its shields.  Why the equivocal review then ?  The end game.  I think I'm on the second of three end game levels and am considering jacking it in.  The first level (spoiler alert) put you against a bullet sponge giant mech with three lives where you basically have to keep dodging and using the very limited cover whilst trying to hit the enemy with your weaponry.  Best tip - your exceptionally useful psychokenisis weapon can be used to grab enemy missiles in mid-air and hurl them back to damaging effect.  You have to beat this level in one go - if you get killed half way down the third life you start from the beginning - usually missions are more forgiving.The reason I'm dropping out is the level that puts your saucer against an even bigger bullet sponge giant mech.  However there's no vehicles in the vicinity from which to recharge your shields.  The game therefore resolves into doing minimal damage with your weapons whilst the giant mech invariably blasts your ship apart.  Improving matters would involve lots of tedious grinding.  More users than you'd expect seem to have resorted to cheats to get past this level.And that's the equivocation - it's fast, cynical B movie fun.  But it doesn't earn the right for end bosses far tougher than Borderlands.  If you're an exceptionally skilled gamer, or your willing to put in a huge amount of time repeatedly failing the same task, or you're content just to play the earlier levels - fine.  But I like seeing the end game without disproportionate degrees of effort or having to download cheat software.That's why the review is equivocal.S.x.

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans! is a game I heavily recommend to play who like sandbox destruction and a fun non-serious story about the brutal demise of the Human race in the 50's with some social commentary.The biggest change with this remake is of course the graphics. The colors are vibrant and destroying buildings never gets old as the explosions are simply a marvel to gaze at.The gameplay has been improved from the PS2 original with my biggest personal one that I've been happy with has been the Hologram ability being reworked into a simpler version to understand and not as finicky as the original was.The Zap-gun and other weaponry practically play the same as they used to, which is great.One downside that has remained from the PS2 version is that while you do get new weapons and upgrades, it's in a linear path with upgrades only unlocking after completing a level and since it's pretty easy to have more than enough DNA to buy the newest available one, it ends up feeling like you should just get given the upgrade instead of having a store system.Luckily the dialogue is still funny as heck, with a big chunk of it being you mind-scanning npcs, Though it's obvious the quality has stayed the same from the PS2 for better or worse. As a longtime fan, I appreciate them keeping and using the original recordings rather than re-record the all the lines again.Richard Horvitz nails Pox's character to a T just as  J. Grant Albrecht is the perfect voice for Cryto, who I believe used Jack Nicholson as reference for Crypto's rugged voice.I highly recommend buying this game, though some might want to wait for it to but on sale which is usually 50% to 75% off.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is free of spoilers.  I loved this game when it first came out.  I spent a lot of time playing this game back in 2002 with my elementary aged self.  So naturally I was very excited to see a 2020 remake coming out. The game overall has great gameplay, the upgrade system is balanced and intuitive, default controls feel nice and well thought out, and the visuals are stunning in keeping with the 1950's theme of the shiny playdogh face characters that is. The infuriating problem I have encountered can be seen on the discussion forums regarding the Robo Prez boss fight near the end of the game.  As is the case with many boss fights, they are fought in 3 phases with the attack type or pattern changing with each phase.  Phase 2 of the Robo Prez fight suddenly has trouble running smoothly.  Without sounding like I am bragging about my computer, my i9-9900k and RTX 2080Ti are definitely not the issue when it comes to games not performing properly.  The rockets and battle balloons during phase 2 of the Robo Prez fight are not difficult to deal with as long as you can see them coming.  But this is where the frustration comes in.  The game will randomly skip and freeze, and spin your player view 180 degrees, all while locking up the player inputs (I was playing on mouse and keyboard).  The freeze/skip itself was not too dramatic, definitely less than one second, but with incoming rockets, I ended up dead many times to a threat I was unable to see or evade.  The worst part of this experience for me was that this happened close to the end of the game, so my player is well upgraded and equipped, and by this point I had 5 hours in the game so I was well practiced.  Boss fights are supposed to be challenging, but this one was simply unplayable with this issue myself and others have experienced (see discussion forum for others).  Very sad.  I have submitted to steam support for a refund.

Also it seems like the recording of damage lags at times, i have found myself shooting buildings with the death ray until its completely drained only for the building to still be standing, then after a few moments its like the system catches up all at once and every thing i have damaged explodes at the same time (often causing a crash) another issue i have ran into is mission prompts and conversation prompts failing to pop up on time. i have also ran into groups of enemies spawned under the water. in short it seems like the system cant handle the amount of chaos you are able to cause. its immensely fun but these issues are holding it back pretty bad. im only 5 hours into a game i was really excited to play again and i feel drained. hoping a patch comes soon

_childDocuments_.review: + Well-done remake+ Pleasant graphics+ Destroying the whole cities and burning people alive is extremely fun and oddly satisfying+ Amazing black humor+ A pleasant atmosphere of the ’50s USA+ A reasonable amount of upgrades for the alien himself and his spaceship- The whole gameplay can feel a bit outdated for a modern gamer- Stealth missions can be annoying and a bit out of place sometimes - No ability to increase the difficulty, the game feels a bit easy sometimes- The developers use the same models through the game all the time to portray different characters  This summer will be remembered as an interesting period in the gaming industry when THQ Nordic decided to revive its notable classic games. First, they released a prequel to Desperados game, then they released SpongeBob SquarePants: Battle for Bikini Bottom remake, and now we have Destroy All Humans! remake. In this case, we have the game that had in mind to modernize the graphics and technical part of the game, while gameplay and story remain untouched. And this is probably a good idea because Destroy All Humans! was already a good game in terms of gameplay and it really needed to be refreshed in terms of graphics.The story takes place in the USA in the 50s: we see a military base that conducts rocket tests and at this moment an alien ship, also known as “saucer”, crashes and now inhabitants of Planet Earth have access to the samples of alien technologies. In addition to that, they capture one of the aliens and now, the protagonist of Destroy All Humans!, named Crypto-137 has to save the prisoner and to fight against horrible earthlings. During the game, Crypto will discover that humans can be pretty useful for the aliens in order to save them from extinction.From the very first minutes of the game, we see that this game is full of inappropriate jokes, black humor, and the whole of humanity is portrayed as a pretty stupid, selfish and egocentric species. This kind of approach forces us to sympathize with Crypto so his motives won’t look that cruel. What I really like about this remake that all of these jokes and that overall satire is still actual in 2020 and some of the topics really touch the strings. The first weapon we are going to be introduced to in the game is mind-reading and Crypto encounters cows first. After reading their minds, he thinks that they are the main inhabitants of the planet because their intellectual development doesn’t differ too much from humans in this game.Progressing through the game, Crypto unlock new weapons and abilities and his arsenal is absolutely stunning. He can use Zap-o-Matic to fry his enemies instantly; he can extract brains from humans to get the needed DNA to learn new abilities and improve the abilities he already has; he can throw objects and humans using psychokinesis to get the desired result and many many others. All his methods that he uses are extremely creative but bloodthirsty at the same time, there are no limits in this game in terms of gore alongside with black humor full of jokes on the verge of what is permitted.  DAH! Is not that diverse in terms of gameplay and missions that have to be completed. Usually, it’s a mission where Crypto has to destroy everything using his arsenal of weapons or his “saucer”. Or it can be a stealth mission where Crypto has to remain silent and make everything carefully using a human disguise. In DAH! this ability is called Holobob and the player will use it pretty often during the whole game. The whole idea of Holobob is to read the human’s mind and to copy his identity to bypass restricted areas. This disguise can be revealed by special agents and robots so Crypto has to make sure that they won’t catch him.All missions take place on different locations that can perfectly portray America of the 50s’ - a small town, secret base, farm, resort village, industrial zone, and the capital. Every zone has a set of story missions and once they are all done, the player can come back to complete challenges like time trial, armageddon missions or race challenges, etc. The game looks pretty colorful and pleasant, the developers did a great job in improving the game in terms of graphics and enhancing every single model, character, and surroundings.  The sound was something that developers didn’t change or enhance that much, they basically put the original sound from the 2005 game and focused on the gameplay and the game’s graphics.It’s hard to say that the game can impress someone in 2020 in terms of gameplay as a new game and I can say that Destroy All Humans! doesn’t try to do so. This game is a perfect choice for someone who wants to play a remake of that funny game they played fifteen years ago or for someone who is looking for a great action arcade game full of black humor and political satire. The game can be completed in 10+ hours, including the main story and challenges around the locations, so the fun time for a few evenings is guaranteed.

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans is a lovely remake of.. well Destroy All Humans, a third person shooter released in 2005 for the xbox and the playstation 2.I haven't played the original game but from what I've seen it's kept pretty faithful to the original while adding a few quality of life changes and removing some of the more annoying parts which is what all remake should strive to do.One of the added things I particularly enjoy are the optional objectives that are added to every level do encourage trying out different weapons and playstyle, while I did have to look up how to complete they are overall a pretty neat addition. So are also the updated mission artworks at the start of each level parodying sci-fi moves of the 50's and every one of them are great.The game does have a few shortcomings, some of the stealth sections, especially the earlier ones can get pretty annoying and the game doesn't have any maps for the different areas you can go do which makes hunting down the 180+ drones in game a pretty daunting task, even with a guide, however the drones doesn't count towards any achievements, and I wouldn't have completed all of them if I didn't like this game, something I reccomend everyone do if they got the time since it isn't super hard besides some of the challanges in the last area.Overall this is a lovely blast from the past, the writing and voice acting is great and the protagonist Crypto is just a delightful jerk and is amazing to play as.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Destroy All Humans is a classic that a lot of people grew up playing. This remake does all of that but better!The game is graphically and visually stunning. The performance is excellent as well, as many of the older graphics cards have no problem running the game. There are a few levels that are different from the original, that for me was a unique experience, because it didn't feel like a copy pasted half baked product. However, change isn't the focus here, the aim was to make a remake of a classic game so newer players can experience it. It plays a whole lot better and kept pretty much everything from the original game. The writing still holds up to this day. It is so absolutely fantastic. However, a lot of it probably will be deemed "offensive" by present day standards. I definitely recommend picking up this game. If you're a returning player then get ready for a nostalgic roller coaster ride. If you haven't played the original then this is the best version you can play. I had a lot of fun playing this game and finished it in one sitting.

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans!, while a short game, is a fun one to play and get lost in blowing everything up. Fans of the original game and newcomers, like myself, are gonna have some fun terrorizing the human population for the glory of the Furon Empire.Gameplay is pretty good and gives you lots of options on how you want to handle some objectives, you want to sneak your way past everyone, you can do that. Want to blow everything up and carve a direct path to the objective, yup that's an option. Going loud or going quiet each have their own part in the game and is pretty easy to get the hang of what to do when it's time to get busy and all the tools at your disposal will help you take everything on.Missions don't feel too repetitive and mostly allow you free control on how you handle the mission. On the missions with doing things stealthy, things aren't too hard and it's usually easy to see what path the game wants to take you. That being said, the game is pretty easy and didn't give me too much trouble for the most part. There was some missions that did have some hiccups, but a quick redo and re-thinking of the situation got everything handled. At the time of writing this, in the 9.3 hours that I have played, I got the story done in about 5 hours, then spent the last 4 and a half-ish hours completing all the achievements and side stuff. Now, I didn't rush through everything so when I say this game is short, hardcore gamers can probably find themseleves getting the entire story done in an afternoon if they wanted to do soNow, game quality wise, I didn't experience any glitches or problems with the gameplay until near the end of the game on the final mission and during the armageddon side missions. The amount of destruction and things going on in the screen during these sections usually lead to game stutters which will screw with your aim and when things get bad enough, the game will downright crash. A couple armageddon runs had to be re-done due to these stutters and crashes which was kind of annoying. Word of the wise, be wary of how much stuff you are blowing up if your pc isn't the strongest or you might find some game issues heading your way. Other than that, the game runs smoothly and haven't seen any other glitches or bugs in the gameplay.Long story short, the game may be short and easy, but it's a blast to play and potential issues are only a few that you will see. Pick the game up if you are curious to play it or if you are a fan of the old games and want to see the original brought back to glory and life.

Want to zap a farmer one second and lift a cow the next? You’ve got it! 🐄⚡The remake does a fantastic job of staying faithful to the original cult-classic, but with much prettier graphics. _childDocuments_.review: They made too many changes.First of all, the controls: While it feels like you have more features, there are several instances of artificial difficulty. Having to hold buttons for certain commands, abilities actually sharing buttons and sometimes not operating how they should (eg: cancelling holobob would often just result in activating S.K.A.T.E.)Then there's the missions. A lot of them were made much harder than in the original. You might have strict alert limitations or added goals on top of main missions. This makes the escort and tower defense missions in particular far more frustrating than they need to be. I got as far as Area 42: Duck And Cover, my least favourite mission in the original. Having to constantly defend the bomb from being shot at is just too much on top of a mission that I already know takes a long time.I also noticed a few glitches on occasion such as pedestrians walking or army trucks driving above the ground they should be on. I've become increasingly discouraged by remakes and sequels to classic games. Imposing modern day rules on them just dampens the experience for me.

_childDocuments_.review: From start to finish, it's been an absolute blast, filled with humor, action, and a delightful satirical commentary on our society. First and foremost, the gameplay mechanics are top-notch. The controls are intuitive, allowing for seamless immersion into the chaos of extraterrestrial invasion. Whether I was zapping unsuspecting humans with my Zap-O-Matic or wreaking havoc with the Anal Probe, every moment was an adrenaline-fueled joyride. However, what truly sets this game apart is its brilliant satire. The game cleverly lampoons various aspects of human culture, from the absurdity of consumerism to the hilarity of government bureaucracy. The witty dialogue and absurd scenarios had me laughing out loud countless times, making each mission a memorable experience. Moreover, the attention to detail in recreating 1950s America is commendable. From the retro aesthetics to the nostalgic soundtrack, every element contributes to the immersive atmosphere, enhancing the overall enjoyment of the game. In summary, "Destroy All Humans" is not just a game; it's an experience just like it was back in the day, where I used to play its PS2 version. It combines addictive gameplay with sharp wit and social commentary in a way that few games manage to achieve. Thank you for creating such a fun and thought-provoking masterpiece. I eagerly anticipate future installments and can't wait to see what hilarious adventures await Crypto-137.
_childDocuments_.name: Destroy All Humans!

_childDocuments_.review: Grand Theft Auto, except you're an alien. This is just about the perfect video game remake. It is, exactly the same game, built from the ground up in the same engine. It has all the same strengths and all the same faults that the original had back in the day. Much of the early 2000s jank has been carried over too, for better or worse. That said, even without the graphics update, the gameplay has aged incredibly well, which shows just how great of a game the original was. Some elements do show the games age, such as the reasonably empty open world with lack of any real side quests. However, this is something that would change in the sequel. Everything is destructable, given you're in the flying saucer. There isn't really much of a plot, other than it basicly being Mars Attacks the video game. You're sent to earth after the Roswell crash to prevent the humans for gathering your alien DNA, but after that, it kind of just starts being about you progressively eliminating the US's leadership until eventually you've disintergrated and impersonated the president of the United States.
_childDocuments_.name: Destroy All Humans!

_childDocuments_.review: The premise is fantastic! Go ham on the puny humans in a humorous setting aping that time in the US pop culture when UFOs & communism were all the craze (and blame the odd events on communists after shapeshifting into the mayor in a mission in the game), now that's entertainment!Sadly, the excecution isn't exactly up to snuff. The parts where you actually can go ham are fun and that's a fact. Then there's stealth/puzzle missions. In theory, using your assortment of tools & gadgets to get to your goal is enticing. I still think that Deus Ex is the best game of all times (if you can get over it's certain clunkyness), but Crypto isn't exactly Denton. Or rather, his challenges aren't. You don't get too much of a complex environment with different paths & methods of aproach. Now I get this game isn't about complexity but those sequences are scripted rather tightly, falling into that uncanny valley between an actual video game and an interactive movie. In that valley, the challenge isn't to find a solution within the game rules but to find the solution the script wants you to take.On the other hand, the latter part of this review is a fitting description of Splinter Cell which managed, not despite but due to it's narrow scripting & uncomplex environments, to spawn a whole series (I like calling it the "CoD of stealth games")...

_childDocuments_.review: So, this is a call back to OLD open world games. Before they had large grid maps littered with collectibles EVERYWHERE. When the main idea of a game was to be fun, not have an amazing story, win awards, or be deep. It has a fantastic coat of paint on it to boot.Set in roughly the late 1950s/early 1960s in a parody of history you play a sarcastic murderous alien bent on taking over and destroying all humans. There is a funny and fun story mode, with completely optional bonus objectives, a set of 4 challenges in each area, and one type of completely optional collectibles. Seriously, there isn't even an achievement for collecting all the probes, they each just give you a minor amount of DNA to spend toward upgrades.Whether terrorizing people on foot or in your flying saucer, this game is FUN. Blowing up towns in the saucer is fun. The only real negative is there is currently a slowdown bug when using the ion detonator, the equivalent of a grenade launcher.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game, but one best consumed in small bites of an hour or two each night. This is definitely a game from another era, so game-play is not its strong suit. The writing and voice acting are excellent, and those are the game's main selling points.  This doesn't strike me as a game you can just dive into for hours and hours on end...but more of a game you should pick up and put down often for a laugh or two every night. Definitely worth it once it goes on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Destroy All Humans!

_childDocuments_.review: An action game where you play an alien who is trying to subjugate the human race. _childDocuments_.review: It's rare that remakes are any good but this is the exception! It exceeds my expectations and is just as fun if not more fun than I remember back in 2005! It's addictive and mindless blow-em up type fun that we don't really see much of these days, and there's plenty of content to keep you entertained for hours. They improved on every single aspect of the original while maintaining the flavor and integrity of it as well. It really translated well in 2020 and holds up fantastically. Highly recommended for old and new players alike even if you didn't play the original, it's very well made and I hope they consider remaking the second game!The only negative is $29.99 is just a *tad* steep, however I don't regret my purchase at all and I'm really happy to support the developers especially if it means we get a remake of Destroy All Humans 2.

_childDocuments_.review: I nearly refunded this game because it kept crashing every 3 minutes. Not even validating content worked for this game, despite my specs either meeting, or exceeding the requirements. My fix was switching from the 4k tv to my 1080p monitor. Which is strange, because Death Stranding runs at ultra on my 4k tv no problem, yet this game won't. Obviously, this game is poorly optimized and I will keep the review at "Do not Recommend" until the developers patch the crashing on high resolution bug or otherwise optimize it.Here's the review for the game itself:The game is objectively fun, and the jokes are gold. I won't quote any in this review because I would rather let you enjoy them when you play this game, but they're all jokes about the 50's Red Scare coupled with Post-Bob Lazar UFO frenzy. All of the jokes seem to apply to today's political culture if you see them as metaphor's.The game on ultra looks fantastic; none of the character models from the classic game were reused, they were instead reimagined and made more comical. The level design is also slightly different from the original game as well, however the game completely reuses the voice acting from the original, which is a superb move.Now for my favorite part about this game: The game looks like a modern day gay, but plays and feels exactly like a PS2 game. There's something about PS2 gameplay that is unmatched by the majority of new games, and thank god they left it as is.There's also extra missions that weren't on the original PS2 version, which is THQ Nordic's Chef's Kiss.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: A Great remake for a classic game. DAH (2020) keeps most of the original in tact while improving the gameplay with QoL improvements across the board. Pros: Modernized graphics that are pretty good         Forced DNA grind in between missions has been removed         Saucer has been given way to heal and defend against missiles which it did not have in the original        Added dash upgrade which makes level travel less tedious once upgraded fullyCons: Short (can be beaten in about 6-8 hours)          Boss fights while improved still feel very underwhelming           Removed ammo drops across the map instead forcing the player to use the new transmorgive ability. Which can lead to scenarios where the player is struggling to find objects to make ammo in missions or boss fightsTelekinesis has been made greatly overpowered with the removal of the focus bar from the original. Now most enemies can be dealt with by simply tossing them from high up which imo makes the game feel too easy in most areas. Verdict: Great reboot for the series grab it on a sale. Hopefully the remake for DAH 2 is even better.

_childDocuments_.review: A sanitized take on a PS2 classic.I'm all for old games getting full remakes, but don't go out of your way to make it a 99% remake and then cut out parts you think might be "too dark." I played the original multiple times, so when I booted this up with its pretty new graphics and heard the exact same dialogue files, I was actually pretty happy. Until I threw someone into a tree with my mind. In the original, there would be a "crunch" sound effect to give the action a bit of weight. Nothing like Saw sound effects in that it was realistic and trying to make you squirm, just something to make it a little more impactful and make you feel like you were really tossing around "puny humans." Now the only sound is a little "woosh" to indicate the throw, but there is literally no sound effect for the impact itself. Literally nothing. I looked up videos online just to make sure my game wasn't bugged/missing files. If you don't want a crunch of bones, fine, but not even a thump? And similarly, extracting brains. Used to be you could make people's heads burst to harvest their brains, and you still can, but they changed the sound effect to what I can only describe as "barely audible." In the original game you'd get a cartoony "POP" whenever it happened, but now it sounds like nothing at all is happening.Its just weird to me to make a remake this faithful but then water it down to take out the "edge". Why do a shot-for-shot remake for the fans, but then make it an almost E-rated version. I want to recommend this, but as far as updated visuals may take this I can't bring myself to even finish it, so I definitely can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't see how it was possible for mark to be missed this much...Good things about the game: 1. Graphics look better, frame rates are easier on the eyes.2. voice acting and story is fun. If you're a fan of the original you'll enjoy this story.Bad Things:1. THE PHYSICS ARE HORRIBLE!!!!!!!!!!! For a game released in 2020 how is it even possible to have such terrible physics??? Almost the entire fun of the combat system is using your PK (telekinesis) to pick up people, animals, and objects and use them as weapons. I was absolutely blown away at how awful the PK ability is in this game. Lets say you pick up a person with PK and they are flailing around trying to get free, and you decided to throw them 50 feet in the air what would you expect to see? A person flailing around until they hit the ground right? If they are doing backflips then you expect to see them continue to do backflips until they hit the ground because there is nothing but air in the sky so how the ♥♥♥♥ does that not happen??? You wanna know what you see instead? If you throw a person 50 feet into the air and lets say they are doing backflips because of the way you threw them guess what happens? After about 4 seconds of air time ALL physics stop. The body straightens out like they are standing on the ground and they gradually fall back to the ground feet first. NOTHING about it looks natural at all and this happens with every single NPC you throw. If the bodies are falling for a long enough time (3-4 seconds) all normal physics stops and a rigid character model takes over and it looks INSANELY stupid. I mean I truly cannot believe that the DEVs allowed this. Did they not even play the original? How does the PS2 version of this game have better Physics than this one? It's unreal how bad of a job they did on the combat in general in this "remake" and I feel like I could go on and on about how angry I am as a Destroy All Humans fan. But yeah if realistic physics in a game that is at its core PHYSICS BASED!!! is important to you then don't even consider getting this heap of trash.2. Character Models. So this game drew about 6 character models and pasted them into every single level. Which is the laziest thing I've ever seen. You will interact with an NPC and then literally walk  20 steps and see the SAME EXACT NPC. It's absolutely insane. Part of the game finding an NPC and disguising yourself as them so that nobody sees that you're an alien. Well it looks pretty stupid when you you're disguised as someone that has 50 clones of it walking around the same level. Honestly i'm just a little heart broken that the DEVs would release this heaping pile of garbage. They skimped on the parts of the game that actually brought us job back in the PS2 and Xbox days. They missed the mark and this "remake" is a lazy pathetic cash grab. They should seriously be ashamed of themselves for putting this out.

_childDocuments_.review: "Destroy All Humans!" a 2020 release from Black Forest Games, is a remake of the classic 2005 game with improved graphics and features. The game lets the player take on the role of an alien named Crypto, whose mission is to invade Earth and extract human DNA to save his species.Pros:- The game has good humor and satire, making fun of the Cold War era but some may find it distasteful.- The gameplay is enjoyable, providing a variety of weapons and abilities to use to fight the humans.- The graphics and sound design are fine, the voice acting is surprisingly good while music is quite bland.- The game offers a good amount of content, including main missions, side missions, and challenges.- The game does a good job of capturing the spirit and style of the original game, while also improving on it.Cons:- The controls can be a bit clunky at times, especially when flying or using certain abilities.- The game can feel repetitive after a while, as the missions and objectives are quite similar in structure.In conclusion, "Destroy All Humans!" is a solid remake of the original game, providing an enjoyable and humorous experience for fans of the franchise or newcomers. While it has some flaws, the game's strengths, including its humor, graphics, and content, make it worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played the original game, so my impressions aren't colored by any nostalgia. The game's biggest flaw is the length. I played for 11 hours and completed basically everything the game has to offer. The only thing I failed to do is collect all the DNA probes hidden in the levels. I gave up after wandering around the first level for 30 minutes trying to find the very last probe I missed. Maybe the original game was like this as well, but it's rather disappointing.Building on this, the story feels rather rushed in the latter part of the game. In the last third, you randomly go back to an earlier level to unlock the final saucer weapon like the developers realized they forgot to add it in. And the second to last level only has two missions in it despite being a very interesting area. Armquist shows up in a mission, isn't talked about for a while, and then returns as a major antagonist with little explanation about why the Furons care about him so much.To be positive, there are lots of little touches that I love. The different newspapers for completing missions, the alternative newspapers for the different ways you can fail them, the varied voicelines for the background NPCs. and more. It's clear that a lot of care went into this game. But then there are some weird omissions. One of the thoughts you can read from an NPC reveals a detail about a major character that's played as a massive reveal in the final mission.Finally, let's talk difficulty. This game is, for the most part, pretty easy. DNA is fairly hard to come by early on and you need to do all challenges and optional objectives to be able to afford most of what you want and can get. But then the second half of the game starts drowning you in DNA to the point that you don't need to do challenges anymore. Speaking of challenges, most of them are fairly easy, but others get downright unfair. The fourth Abduction challenge was particularly difficult for me, I had to repeat it about a dozen times to scrape by with the maximum reward. And the final two Race challenges are notoriously difficult, requiring perfect memorization of the route and perfect luck regarding NPC traffic. And the final race in particular is rife with slowdowns when too many things are onscreen at once.All in all, the game is fine. I'm not the one to ask how it stacks up to the original. But the small amount of playtime you'll get out of this game for a 30$ pricetag makes me leery of recommending it despite the fun I had with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I love that they pulled off updating the game play mechanics without destroying the original experience, if anything they greatly improved it. The Graphics are nice as well. Some of the elements of the story oddly enough even translate into current times, especially the satire, this truly is a timeless classic and I praise the devs for not butchering the story out of fear of angry mobs. 10/10 would recomend if you're into shooters and satire.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game made even more amazing with this remaster! The open world sandbox style is a staple of the 2000's, and it's still just as fun as it was back then. The visuals are more cartoony then they were back in the original game, but I think it fits the aesthetic of the game better than a realistic one. One big issue I have though is that some of the missions later in the game are annoying instead of being difficult, with as many projectiles flying towards you as a bullet hell. And ♥♥♥♥ the final boss, both literally and figuratively. Still, for only 30 dollars, I think this game is well worth the price with how fun it is to just go around zapping people.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'll say upfront that I played, beat, and loved the original— as well as the sequel.Quick opinion: buy it if a violent (without gore), extremely funny (adult, but tame, sense of humor), 3rd person shooter where you play as a horrible alien villain appeals to you.So, on top of all that...The Crypto character is hilarious as always, as is his leader Pox (with the original voice actor reprising his role). Lots of dark humor, or somewhat-dirty jokes. There is a LOT of mocking the culture and right-wing politics of the time period, what with the fear of nuclear war with the Soviet Union. If I had to complain, I'd say they beat that horse just a wee bit past death. Still, it's not that big a deal.The weapon selection is just enough; you end up with one weapon that fills each of your possible needs. So, you'll have one weapon that is great for handling groups, another that is designed to deal with vehicles, another that puts out high single-target damage but has limited range, and so on. The stock feels appropriate, since your weapons' functions will change as you upgrade them. The upgrades can keep things fresh as you play through this game that, to be honest, can get repetitive.It's primarily the jokes that break up the monotony, as the story isn't great (it's all the same as the original, which does have a couple downsides). It's the humor, game-play, and challenge that will likely appeal to most people.Speaking of game-play, the controls are perfect on controller AND keyboard+mouse. Again, I could pick at it a bit and say that the numerous abilities can sometimes be hard to keep track of. There are times when I have accidentally hit E, and telekinetically popped the brain out of someone I was supposed to scan/distract/control/etc. It was these occasions that ended my missions more than anything else. Some abilities are mapped to the same button, and that can be irritating if you end up performing the wrong action over and over.The story ain't much...alien comes to Earth and kills things, there's a sinister-looking male villain in a mask who totally isn't a woman you guys, you fight the villain, end credits.If you enjoyed the originals, you will be happy. If you have never played the series before, this is a great entry to see what it's all about.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome game. Loved replaying this crazy and fun game, giving in to nostalgia, I had to play this again. Sitting back, playing, and enjoying your time is this kind of game. I think they did exactly what they meant to, just something fun. It has a special place in my heart.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing and enjoying "Destroy All Humans!" as a kid, and while the graphical upgrade is great, I don't find myself enjoying the game. It is rather simple, and doesn't seem to have aged well. Killing people lacks any emphasis or "feeling" behind it, it just happens. Unlike a modern FPS shooter that adds in effects, animations, sway, loading, cocking, recoil, and other things that add weight and power behind your weapons; Destroy All Humans on the other hand has none of that, and goes for a more arcade approach... Sadly this approach makes everything feel lackluster and the emphasis is gone entirely. A building blew up? Cool... I guess? The one thing that I actually enjoy is flicking enemies and wildlife around with psychic powers. It feels good to do, it's visually funny, but it gets old real quick. While the later areas/stages in the game may add more powers, I find myself not caring about anything. The story isn't engaging, the sound quality is as it was on the PS2 era... Bad, and the gameplay is just whatever. If there wasn't so much hand-holding and enforcing of rules in these stages, and it gave the open freedom of controls and direction that a "Jak and Daxter" game gave - a series that came out around the same time - it would feel a lot better. Instead we have a segmented narrow-scoped mission-based game. A remake would of been better than a remaster.
