_childDocuments_.review: So many bugsSo many hidden cheat statsSo many bad or plain wrong descriptionsSo many bland gamedesign choices over the last two yearsI was a fan from the first hour of early access but now I can´t even bring myself to care to grind. It´s not bad, it´s just boring.I would give this game a 65% sure, its not bad at all, but there are things that are not expressed in a number and what I have to express is: Disappointment.I played this game first getting a code from their marketing efforts back in early 2018. And back then in its pre/early alpha state I actually really enjoyed what the game had to offer for what it was. Meaning that I was seeing a really fun baseline for great development. And then I played it again back in mid 2019, which was still fun but I really wanted to not burn myself out and wait for the actual final product.Now we have it almost May 2020...and I wonder what even happened? What happened in all that development time? I can barely tell if there was any changes made to over a year ago. Maybe there was some tweaks being made...but infact I actually had to look up videos to see what even was done with all of that development time?And yes there are things here and there that got improved, but the baseline is: I have LESS fun with the game now, than I did back in its unpolished version of 2018.What this game constantly gets compared to is Darkest Dungeon, but I really felt this was doing a disservice to this games idea, it was literally just the looks. But now? I don´t know.And I do want to harp on one exact point here: The game feels bland. When in 2018-2019 they had minion parts actually give the buffs like luck stats or health, even special interactions that are now only achieveable from items. WHY DID YOU CHANGE THAT?? Now the only thing you get from rarer minion parts are more statpoints. That might equate to the same thing, but makes ALL minions that can get created feel so bland and worthless to build. Every minion that you can build is the same because at most you get to spend a few more statpoints THAT ARE EVEN LOCKING AWAY CERTAIN IMPROVEMENTS AFTER A POINT. So what is the point in grinding for items?Beforehand the game had this very unique feeling, that if what I hoped for they would build this game up from, they would really have something special going. Instead they made the system more limiting, bland and even less sophisticated. WHY WOULD YOU DO THAT?? It was your one big selling point that put you really apart from DD. What happened in those last two years of development?What I imagined they´d do, would make it so that they add even more stats and unique effects to random part finds, that way every run would be different and it would have been super fun to grind the game and luck out and for example get 3 or even all monster parts for one of your minions to make it into a real unique beast, make it a oneshot monster or give it tons of evasion, the way you want to play it IF you luck out and find the right parts, or get creative if you don´t, exploring new synergies out of necessity, but also the way that only you can build it, because you lucked out finding great minion parts. What happened instead? Every minion part now gives 2/6/14 stat points, that´s it, there is no difference to that. There is a clear endgoal of what is best to use, 4 legendary components. Everyone wants to build the same thing. There is no uniqueness at all, just a clear cut endpoint. And the items that you can give your minions? There is like 1 unique kind of item for each minion, that are super easy to get. And those are really bad, they are not making the experience unique at all. Every minion that you can build is the same. And I thought that was the big difference between this and DD, that here I could actually create real monsters the way I want to, form them up from the ground...what´s the point if I literally grind for the same thing every single run?What´s the fun in it if every one of them is the same? So yeah, I really hoped that Iratus would build up on the great ideas it seemed to had 2 years ago, I defended it lots against the almost inevitable "that looks like a Darkest Dungeon clone"...but in 2 years time none of my hopes for this game came true and yeah, it really just is another DD clone, it works different, its not unfun for a while...but the features that could make this an actually amazing game are all still there, they have just all been reduced to shadows of what they used to be or could have been. The graveyard is fun, if you didn´t make it a useless grind everytime, equipping artefacts to Iratus is amazing...if there was maybe more than 40?...you´ll find all of them in no time and have a clear best one to go for. The alchemy table is still an amazing feature but holds nothing of great interest, its just "throw stuff at it and hope the 10% chance works out" and like said, the monster components give statpoints now...and that´s all they do. They don´t change how minions work, how they look, how they can be made something unique, its just "get the best components and put them in blindly, it doesn´t make a difference anyways, they´ll all come out the same" and the only thing that makes minions different somewhat is their unique items you can give them of which there is like 10 in the whole game and even then its just basically a difference of: "I have 10% more resistance now". And the dungeons give only the promise of different paths, in reality they are all the same, just left/right/middle. It´s not like you can avoid fights, it´s always every second step is fighting, there is no big choices, it gets stale after the second dungeon already. The bosses have hidden stats that are not explained and not all minions work against them so if you have a favourite you´ll lose without anything you can do because the gameplay dictates you use the correct strategy. And the ability descriptions have misleading wording often, or alternatively the game completely doesn´t tell you. Like hidden hitchecks for example, or bossmechanics. There is also tons of bugs still.  So yeah, everything is balanced correctly now, you won´t get stuck, but you won´t overpower either. There is perfect builds and there is correct and there is wrong compositions. You just don´t get a choice in that anymore as a player. You either play the game as it was intended to be played, or you don´t.It was just developed to be bland. A real shame. It could have been so much more, it was already on its way there, it just abandoned mission halfway through.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Darkest Dungeon, you'll probably like this. If you have a thing for necromancy and playing the bad guys and like turn-based combat, you'll probably also like this.This game draws obvious inspiration from Darkest Dungeon and doesn't try to hide it. The premise is basically Darkest Dungeon but you are the evil necromancer and instead of having to manage stress for your own party, it is YOU who can deal both physical damage and stress damage in order to defeat your enemies.The game doesn't quite have as much polish or depth as Darkest Dungeon, however. One example would be how the abilities for your minions develop. All abilities for each minion is already unlocked, but each can be upgraded in two different exclusive ways. On the surface this is an interesting idea, as you must choose between two roughly equally good upgrades. In practice, however, the upgrades mostly change stat values instead of offering any unique gameplay mechanics.The progress system does feel a bit weird, you have to essentially accomplish in-game challenges (trigger insanity 80 times, deal 750 damage to your own minions, etc) to unlock new minion types, but once you have them, they are unlocked for all future runs you do.  It effectively means you should just play through the game on the tutorial difficulty and unlock all the minions you can before starting a "real" campaign where you have access to everything. Part of me wishes there was a per-run progression needed to unlock each minion type each campaign.Overall I really enjoy the game and I'm a sucker for any game that lets me be a necromancer.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this game sits in a weird spot for me. Darkest Dungeon introduced me to this genre, and maybe it set my expectations too high for the rest of them. I enjoyed this game, it was fun, I played around with a handful of the characters, and I liked that there were set goals to unlock all of the different units. I didn't find a need for 80% of the units, I found a layout that worked for me and it carried me through the game and I only ever lost 1 major minion. I was able to immediately replace that minion thanks to the OVERWHELMING forgiveness of the starter difficulty. But that leads to the downfall of the game for me. I enjoyed the content, it took me 10 hours to beat the game, and it was 10 hours of relaxed enjoyment. So I sat through the rather disappointing end and started again on the normal difficulty. Despite having access to 1/4 or maybe even 1/5 of the items and resources I was able to clear the first area and am halfway through the 2nd area in 2 hours. I've experimented with different units and more volatile setups, but I quickly came to a rather disappointing realization.I was bored. The difficulty doesn't effect the types of enemies you come across, or their move sets. So even though I had less to work with, I only had to manage units better instead of strong-arming with the same 4 units. I saw everything before already, so I knew what to anticipate, how to counter, and how I wanted to build troops. There isn't enough left for me to explore in the game to make me want to spend more time beating the exact same thing again, and so I won't.So I've grown bored after 12 hours, which is more time than dollars I spent on the game, which makes it worth buying on sale, but I honestly think I would have been disappointed had I paid full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus has a lot of promise. It really does. The game actually learnt lessons from Darkest Dungeon, the map generation means there's interesting decisions to make as you work your way to the boss, there's a graveyard that provides incrementally more useful assistance (and more critically, it takes time to build up so you're never quite able to steamroll the game simply by putting more slots into the mortuary to recycle your units). The idea of "parts" providing stat benefits is good (albeit the benefits provide for the investment you need to put in is abysmal), the artifacts you can equip on Iratus offering conditional benefits is well thought out.So there's lots of good. But then you play the game and go "Oh dear".The developers clearly thought what makes a good Darkest Dungeon is difficulty, as opposed to challenge. Challenge is where you're tested on your knowledge of systems and your ability to come up with good strategies that counter steadily evolving enemy compositions. Difficulty tends to be stat and gear checks. In this case we have mobs with anywhere up to 70% crit chance (lolwut), mobs that will chew through your squishies regardless of position (so positional play seems to not help you out here), mobs that will stack block/ward and then AE the everliving hell out of your entire team. All of the mobs are tuned to what appears to be endgame compositions, and this is in the first floor, and that doesn't count the game tossing in "elite" versions of their normal brethren who can and will annihilate your entire team single-handed.Mobs that crit your units for well over two thirds of your units health (if not one shotting them) before you have time to take action, and it should be noted that none of your starting units really have the defensive facilities to withstand this kind of punishment. Again, this is on the first floor. The information the game provides is not helpful in planning for what comes ahead, you get a portrait of what is possibly the lead unit in the enemy team but that doesn’t tell you if the enemy team has elites in, or if it has “specials” like the golem which require magical damage to really make a dent into. (The Golem, by the way, has low accuracy, but can very easily one shot just about everything you have).The units level up their skills but their abilities and raw stats do not improve with them in anything more than a token sense, so the sense of power gain is limited, the parts can be upgraded similarly, but until you get to rank 3 (purple) or possibly higher, again, the gain is very limited. This makes for a game where losses are absurdly punishing and a team loss on the first floor is grounds to wipe the save and start over. It’s a shame because the art, the sound design, everything else is right there. But with the balance so far out of whack and enemies being designed for what I can only term as “Russian” difficulty, this is a game that will only appeal to people willing to bash their heads against a wall constantly in the hope that the RNG will offer them a good set of rolls. Playing this as a game of skill is not an option because it only needs one good team comp by the AI and you’ll lose your entire team and there is *nothing* you can do to mitigate this.Oh, and a retreat button that kills your whole team?Who thought that was a good idea.Difficulty is not "Make your opponents so uber that they can hulksmash the player in one go if they score a crit", that's not difficulty, that's just saying "HARR HARR I AM DEV AND I CAN CRUSH YOU", you want to make difficult, you make the game full of interesting decisions. Right up to combat, you've got that -nailed-. The player choices -in- combat are there too, but your enemies need *work* and need major retuning for this to be the game it could be.Not the game it is right now. Wait.EDIT: In response to the dev message - this is *after* the first balance patch, and no, that's not made any significant difference. By balancing, I mean you're going to have to do some major rethinking of how Iratus' forces level up, and how enemy forces are structured (right now there's very little interplay between enemy forces, instead they just tend to be stupidly powerful to make up for the lack of team comp).EDIT 2: Further bashing my skull on this game has yielded progress. Amusingly it turns out that the tools you need to get further in the game are locked behind achievement gates. See, you only start with six classes available to you, of which I'd say three (Dark Knight, Zombie, Bride) are absolutely useful, with Banshee being useful in specific cases, and the Shade only helpful if you can set up a stress team (more on that another time). The Skeleton is a pile of toss and should be ignored at all costs.Thing is, once you unlock the mummy or if you're going for a magic/stress build, the Lich, suddenly your options open up. This is particularly true of the mummy who can stack a debuff which decreases luck and essentially robs your opponents of the ability to crit you, whilst at the same time INCREASING your chance to crit.Long story short. The starting classes aren't great, once you unlock a few, you can improve your starting team and the first floor isn't such a teeth clenching horror.That does _not_ say good things about the design though.EDIT 3 : It's been brought to my attention the game has now had a major content and balance pass, the Skeleton got *some* much needed attention but I laid out a much more thorough proposal as to how to fix old bony. This only seems to be a baby step.I'll give the game a second blast to see if it merits a re-review.

_childDocuments_.review: I really cannot recommend this game in any fashion. Anything it does, Darkest Dungeon does better. While one of the reviews I read is true to an extent, in that this game mitigates some of the RNG associated with Darkest Dungeon's gameplay, it instead replaces it with stacked enemies as the compromise. Enemies towards the later stages of the game start having 3x as much HP, damage, or other stats than you. I cannot fathom playing this game on harder difficulties as it's already arbitrary in nature with "challenge" as it is.The only way of protecting your units from getting absolutely chunked at the last floor is a mechanic called Block or Ward which negate a physical or magic attack entirely. The thing is, the enemy also gets access to this mechanic, they're just too stupid to actually capitalize on it properly. Alternatives to not getting absolutely melted is stacking Evasion, but this is just praying RNG is in your favor until it's not and you lose some high ranking unit to a crit.Unlike Darkest Dungeon there is nothing really to explore build or unit wise. Each unit comes with all abilities unlocked, there are no perks or negative traits to make things diffierent or unique, there are no items that offer any real difference to play. It all just falls flat. The equivalent of your "town" in this game also doesn't really offer much, and the only real 2 buildings you'll find yourself bothering with are the Arena(passive XP gain) and Mausoleum(so units can heal).If I wanted to be nitpicky and keep going, one minor gripe as well is that some of the units don't even feel good thematically. The Zombie shoots a giant cannon for example. As an aside the artwork in this game isn't even charming like the 2D sprite work of Darkest Dungeon, looking like a Flash game from newgrounds.I hate to be a debby downer, but Christ...There's also no Workshop support, so it isn't even like you can spice up gameplay for a second playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this was a pleasant surprise. It's like Darkest Dungeon, but - by and large - fairer and more streamlined. Better grouping and presentation of information, for instance. Accuracy is tracked per combatant rather than per individual ability, so estimating enemy hit chances involves far less guesswork or wiki-delving.Also, you play as a sinister, conquering necromancer voiced by the delightful Stephan Weyte, whom greybeards like myself may recall as the voice of Caleb in Blood, or Nathaniel Claw from Captain Claw. The necromancer himself takes the place of the Ancestor from D.D. in providing narration during combat and otherwise. Instead of a hamlet, you restore a graveyard; instead of expeditions to dungeons with random encounters, you choose your own path through a smaller number of larger, Slay The Spire-style branching dungeons, fighting varied groups of highly questionable 'good guys' as you go.There is a large selection of minions, most of which are made available as you progress, and which then stay unlocked for subsequent playthroughs; each has its strengths and weaknesses, as well as variable growth potential; some minions can gain a lot of single-attack-nullifying Blocks and Wards, while others are focused toward permanent (albeit debuffable and bypassable) damage reduction or simply soaking up damage with high health and then recovering it. Still others are dodge-based.Enemies are much the same - the design is compassionate in that there are relatively few enemies who are simply powerful in every way. Rather, an enemy may have very high magical damage reduction, but no physical defence at all - or vice versa. Thus, with the foresight of examining the enemy types on the map before battle, and selecting minions suited to obliterating each of them while effectively defending against their attacks, you can often triumph handily.Similar to Darkest Dungeon, there is also a "stress" bar in addition to the health bar, which dictates whether someone will go insane (receiving a random impairing effect for the rest of the battle) or, eventually, die of a heart attack, regardless of their current health. Unlike Darkest Dungeon, in Iratus,  get to be the creepy undead bastards freaking enemies out and giving them heart attacks! Your own minions are, thankfully, not susceptible to stress. It all makes a nice change from the much-aforementioned game, and offers another avenue of attack which comes in very handy against many types of enemy, when compared to brute force physical or magical assault.The graphics are lovely, too; sure, "deliberately rough strokes" and "big black blotch over the eyes" and so forth are valid stylistic choices, but Iratus is  While still being quite gruesome and horrifying when it means to be. No reason not to look good while you're slaying the fools who oppose you, right? And they get to look good dying.Between the morally bankrupt opposition and the wonderful array of fearsome undead minions on offer here... not to mention all the spells! ...There are plentiful opportunities for maniacal laughter as you cleverly destroy one troublesome opponent after another. It's a game that is fun. Yes, some of the bosses pile on the BS rather high, but there are ways to defeat them as well, can confirm this even up to the expansion episode's finale at the third and final remotely sensible difficulty setting (though that took some doing, let me tell you)... but the game is, overall, fun. And that's something more games these days could stand to be.Heartily recommended to anyone who thinks it might be their cup of tea!

_childDocuments_.review: As it stands right now, I just can't recommend this game as it is way too frustrating to play. I've sunk hundreds of hours into Darkest Dungeon and can appreciate the inspiration from the game by the developpers, but some aspects of the game are just way out of balance.While the roster looks cool, you'll soon see that most of the available units are unreliable because the mecanics themselves are unreliable. You're gonna miss 90% chances 2 out of 3 times while the ennemies will double crit you on a 2% chance, you can't know for sure what you're gonna encounter in your next fight, some ennemies are just so brutal it's not even funny. The more you play this game, the less confidence you'll have in any action you take because the deck is so heavily stacked against you that winning is almost impossible. So what do people do? They find cheese strats or wonder comps that use "meta strats" to spam in every fights, because you just can't beat the game with legit casual play.And you know what? All of that is fine to some degree if your ressources weren't finite and losing your current run because you ran out of these ressources wasn't a thing.You're playing a game that tells you outright that your minions are replaceable but losing minions punishes you heavily. You're playing a game that takes inspiration from the greatest dungeon crawlers but also removes all forms of farming while still having the difficulty curve of a normal dungeon crawler.So many things are wrong with all of this and thank god the game is in early access and can be improved. Because it needs improving quite badly. The atmosphere is cool, the art is great, some gameplay mecanics are great and the bosses are challenging... but the core gameplay is frustrating, unfun, and not worthy of a good game.I'm not giving up on you, Iratus. But you're gonna need to work on a lot of things to make me go back.

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus LOTD is a turn-based, troop-management roguelike RPG where you lead undead minions from the depths of your subterranean prison to the world above. For a roguelike RPG, Iratus is more RPG and less roguelike which I personally like. The core of the game is leveling your units and going to battle against scores of baddies (or in this case, "goodies"). Unit build customization is in between average and complex. You can select their stats, skill types and accessories. Other mechanics include base upgrades, alchemy, talent tree and artifact customization for Iratus (you).PROS+ Deep RPG elements and unit build customization.+ Lots of accessories that change the way a unit plays.+ Good variety of units. Large variety of enemies.+ Spell effects are very nice and impactful.+ Lovely art style. Some forgivable anatomy issues.+ The dialogue and voice overs are fantastic!!!+ You can name your units. Very important because...CONS- Units only have 1 skin!!! Unless you buy the DLCs.- UI seems floaty and non-interactive sometimes.- The "wait" command for units didn't work for me.- In-battle dialogue causes unnecessary delay in actions.- And the biggest CON: Replacing high-level units is a little too easy. When your unit dies, there's a good chance that a "brain" will drop after you win the battle. The brain will have a level at or close to the level of the unit that died. So if my dead unit was lv 35, the brain drop will be lv 35. I can create a new lv 1 unit, plug the lv 35 brain into him/her, and now I have a new lv 35 unit. Often, the dead unit drops some of its upgrades and OP accessories which help rebuild the new unit almost identically. Further, in your battles, brains would randomly drop matching the high level of the enemies. So I just stockpile brains and never have to fear losing a unit. It makes me feel less attached to a unit and feel less bad when they're gone. Granted, I played at the second to the hardest difficulty. Maybe I will change my tune at the hardest game mode.Don't let these cons deter you from buying the game. They are easily overlooked with the fun I had. Iratus gets an 8.5 from me. Very good addition to my library which I see my self replaying. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Remarkable game, enjoying it far more than Darkest Dungeon, and that is high praise.The only problem is lack of content, which is to be expected of an early access game. Haven't ran into bugs or glitches whatsoever, completed the game three times with no team wipes apart from one time when I killed my entire team because I found a Dhampir that I wanted to recruit but only had physical damage dealers.I love the quests you find along the way and the multiple ways to approach each problem but it feels bad every time the quest says that you need to have a specific type of undead in your team to get a reward and most of the time I don't have that one in the group.  I know it'd be too easy if you outright told what units you should have in your team for the best outcome but it's still a buzzkill.I feel like there should be more ways to upgrade your units, 7 levels max feels very low and there's only so much you can do with 2 equipment slots and the body parts. A unit  at level 7 with all purples still feels very weak and the changes are very marginal, ranging from 2-10 extra damage, 10-30 extra health or 2-4 armor/resist.The UI is intuitive, easy to learn and fast to use, but there are some minor complaints, for example, the alchemy lab is pretty clunky, the left side where you have the recipes, you could have smaller quick tabs to each of the devices in the table ( distillation, extraction, transmutation )Graveyard also has certain clumsiness to it when trying to upgrade the buildings, I always try to drag units on top of the green icons, it should work that way instead of having to open the extra window.The icons on the top left in the main room never see use because its far easier to remember and navigate from the stylized icons themselves.Apart from that, there is very little to complain, the game is so damn enjoyable, playing the bad guys is a great twist, the variety of undead can be forever be expanded upon, now all we need is more units, expand the spell book for Iratus, have a way of making use of artifacts that just lie in the inventory unused, expand the graveyard, expand unit customization, maybe have an option for map sizes, the current ones are so easy to breeze through, if there was infinite scaling for units we could also have an infinite adventure to dwell deeper on a series of dungeons.Can't wait for further updates, keep up the good work.Almost forgot to mention: The voice actor for Iratus is incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: It is inspired in Darkest Dungeon, but I wouldn't compare them directly. This game is far less frustrating due to the nature of the game itself: - Here you're the Lord of the Dead and command hordes of undead units, not some guy in some town trying to be a hero in the darkest of times. - In Iratus, you craft your minions out of human limbs and they don't ask questions, they simply obey. In Darkest Dungeon you have a hard time convincing folks to fight incredible odds to ultimately die. - Your undead minions in Iratus don't panic, they fear nothing, they feel nothing, and would certainly won't bother dying again. When you start playing, go on for the Cakewalk difficulty (the 1st of 4 difficulties)  to learn the basics, then jump to the 2nd  to unlock units. The right way to play this game is on the 3rd difficulty, that is where the real hardcore tactical roguelike takes place. You'll enjoy figuring out how units work and how they do synergy together. There are specific units to counter specific enemies, you'll learn how to counter them. You won't get frustrated if one of your minions die, they were already dead anyway! You'll build new units to replace them.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright we already know this game is a lot like Darkest Dungeon on a core level. What you're probably asking yourself is "what can I do in this that I can't in Darkest Dungeon already?", so I'll summarize it for you.-Play as the Darkest Dungeon itself with your goal being to piss on the Hamlet instead of trying to rebuild it.-Have the stress system on your side where the enemy is the one trying to roll against afflictions at 100 stress and dying to heart attacks instead of you (and yes, stress builds are a thing and are perfectly viable depending on the enemy).-Assume direct control in combat with a mana system that lets you personally blast the enemy with cheap magic spells from the safety of your home. (There's even a wine skeleton spell for stressing everyone on the enemy team)-Manage the health of your monsters because they don't heal between fights by either sending them to the morgue for their version of a relaxing vacation, or performing dark alchemy by taking whatever organs, bones, or trash you have laying around your house and distilling them into funny zombie beer.-Control an army of undead who are both willing to play as a team and step right the hell over one another in a desperate power-struggle for your affection, such as the ghoul who can cannibalize her own team for health, or the Bone Golem who is willing to explode and die for your sins at a moments notice.-Equip items like burning blood and cannibals jaw to a Lich to create a miniboss that will have the enemy screaming in eldritch horror as they are single handedly wiped out by a funny floating skeleton who gets absurd stat bonuses for being alone on the field and whenever an ally dies.-Cry when your favorite monster gets nuked because there's no death's door mechanic, only suffering, but sigh in relief as you're able to get a new one up and running so long as you have an appropriately leveled brain you can place into it.-The zombie has a gun.If any of that sounds interesting, then you should give this game a whirl. It's really good. Flawed in some aspects, like enemy variety is kinda shallow and there's currently no workshop, but I'd say it's still a really fun experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Balance all but dies after the first dungeon. The devs have made one crucial mistake: the block and ward are too strong. It seems like the guy designing player units figured that out, you get no abilities of the sort from units within the first two dungeons. Near the end I got a lost soul unit, which is able to offer a block+ward (buffed ability) at the cost of the unit doing less damage for two turns. The guy who designed the enemies didn't know this.So what makes this ability so strong? It completely nullifies an attack. No damage, no CC, nothing. Any unit with this buff becomes a difficult battle.The elite dwarves seem to have some sort of superinitiative, they all went for a single unit on my team and killed him before I even had a chance to act. A level 7 skeleton dies without a chance.I went up against a dwarf with 2 golden axes, when he went berserk he does 80 damage+ enough to do 2/3rds of my tanks hp and enough to oneshot most units on my team.I would have killed him from his berserk state, but to my surprise he couldn't be hurt. He was in the third slot on enemy team, only reachable by 1 unit on my team, he was repeatedly buffed by a potion user who gave him a block and ward every turn and ended up mopping my team.I went back in, and to my surprise the stacking shields remained on the dwarf and to top it off, he quickly went berserk and I ended up in a similar state. I managed to win the fight with 3 units on my team dying. Technically 4 units died if you count the skeleton my wraith summoned.And that was a singular fight.I checked out what spells would be most ideal and found one that gifted me vampires from fleeing opponents.i now have about 7 vampires since I keep getting them from fleeing enemies, they're all I seem to have left now that all my units keep ending up dead.When you get close to the end of the second dungeon, there's a dwarf that can offer a 4 unit buff on both shield and ward, meaning they can block attacks from my team of 4 units. And those wards will not go away until I hit them. The developer who came up with that dwarf is crazier than the man you're playing as.This rng fest featuring wards all over the place make it impossible to enjoy the gameplay. I'll keep going in the hopes of seeing something fun, but honestly? I doubt it'll improve. I thought there were serious balance issues with darkest dungeon, but this game makes it look like easy game. At least when I attacked enemies in DD, it did damage. Here II have to plan my party out on AoE and multiattack on single target.I expect a complete and full balanced game, devs, you're not in early access anymore. I see complaints, a year old, on similar issues that have not been taken care of. There's waaaay too much RNG, unbalanced abilities on enemies and weak abilities on units. Also, it would have been nice to let players know they can unlock units and carry over that unit unlock from easy to harder difficulties in the tutorial. If you plan a difficulty based on the player unlocking units, don't tell them they can exit and play a higher difficulty, your game is not balanced around that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an IMMENSELY satisfying itch to my crave for a Darkest Dungeon-esque game. Gameplay: This game really excels in tying a vast amount of systems together. You can focus on magic, minion empowerment and enemy downgrading. You can customize your individual minions creation process, item equips and abilities. There was clearly a lot of thought put into how each team can synchronize together to make a team that focuses on causing the enemy to flee or eradicating all foes. In case people are wondering - just because you are evil does NOT mean your minions are expendable. They feel expendable, which is fantastic to the feeling of the game, but each one performs unique capabilities that can be further enhanced. That skeleton you started with? You can make him into a dedicated tank or frontline DPS with ability customization alone.The enemies descriptions, abilities and unique-ness all keep the game interesting. 2 hours in and I have fought at least 6 unique enemies that each have 6 abilities, keeping me on my toes for how I want to react. Narrative: I personally love games where you play as the villain, and this one does it exceedingly well with a chilling opening scene and voice acting. Some of the lines are a bit cheesy but you really get a feel for being a Necromancer crafting your minions, building your Mausoleum and empowering yourself with evergrowing spells. Sound: Chilling, grave and depressing. Hit an enemy with stress? Hear the doldrums of defeat. Hack an enemy? Feel the bite of metal. Good work here, it does the job and does it well. My only issue with the game at the moment is moving throughout the dungeon. This game clearly is imitating Darkest Dungeon, so I will use it as a comparison. Moving your team through the dungeons and interacting really created an atmosphere that this game lacks. It's a major system that I believe really adds immersion. If the developers decide to innovate in this direction I believe it could really enhance the game. VERDICT:: Purchase NOW and support these developers, as they have clearly put a lot of thought and love into this game. If there was more I could purchase I would, I truly love this style of game and the thought process they have put into it. BLUF / TLDR: 8/10 --> future updates WILL make this a 9 or even 10/10 for this style of game.

_childDocuments_.review: Finishing the game/run on the second of the four difficulties (normal I guess), I think its time to leave a "short-ish" review :)Iratus is a roguelike. You built a team of undead and fight your way to the surface. There is some resource management regarding the parts you collect, in order to create/replenish your undead minions. Mana, and money. It is one of the slow paced roguelikes, a run can take up to 20hrs I guess, if you are taking it slow like me. Especially if you are not familiar with the many minion types and their skills. It can be overwhelming in the beginning with all the choices and the combinations of minions you can pick for you 4-minion party. On top of that, every one of the 6 minion skills has two upgraded versions that most of the times change the skill in a significant way. That said, I think you can play the game casually for sure, especially on the easy/normal difficulty. But the analysis-paralysis from the many choices you have can dishearten you I guess. I loved the fact you can change your team before every fight, in order to counter the enemy team. You are not locked in a serious disadvantaged fight, because you drafted the wrong team, that gets countered by the particular enemy. In my opinion Iratus is an honest game. What it tries to do, it does well. You can try so many team combinations that it is crazy, and the minions feel very well ballanced. Yes there are stronger team combinations, but there are so many of them that it does not feel unfair or broken, just rewarding. You can tell how many hours where spent on ballancing and mixing up the abilities. It is very well done. And that is the main fun part of the game, trying different team comps. In my opinion there are no poor game design choices in Iratus, everything feels fitting and well ballanced.If you like a slow paced roguelike, with great tactics, and nice strategy layers you should definetely give it a try.Awesome game devs!

_childDocuments_.review: Overview:In Iratus:LotD you assume the role of a necromancer up to no good. You will assemble a roster of undead, selecting from roughly a dozen or so (more with unlocks and DLC) undead creature types. From this roster, you select 4 creatures (possibly including duplicate creature types), and engage in 4v4 battle turn-based battle ala Darkest Dungeon (i.e. battle position matters). Your roster will level up, allowing the allocation of stats (with options differing by creature type) and the selection of enhanced abilities, from your core of 6 per creature. Each creature may hold two items, which may not be removed once placed. Similarly Iratus (i.e. you) may equip 5 items, though these may be swapped in and out. There is also a tech tree for Iratus, allowing the casting of spells (one per round) and the accumulation of battle passives. There is also a minor base building aspect. The game is a rouge-like taking place over 5 levels. Each level is comprised of various branching nodes (think Slay the Spire) but each level is much larger.Your individual creatures may permanently die, though exact replicates may more-or-less be created using "brains" you acquire, which basically let you create a creature from scratch and level it to the specified level (often higher than the creatures you have been leveling the entire game).Summary: For full disclosure, I played only once, on the 'cakewalk' difficulty, and it was unsurprisingly super-easy. I still found the mechanics (battles, creature creation, base building) mildly engaging for a time, but sadly grew bored with the gameplay about 60% through. Not necessarily because the game was on easy difficulty, but mostly because I just got bored with the fighting. Though I can't comment too fully since I didn't play on a proper difficulty level, the fact that you could lose a high-level monster to permadeath, and then create a better one immediately soured me somewhat. I think some of the enjoyment is to be derived from team-building, but this aspect just wasn't enough to keep me engaged. I also thought each run was much longer than it needed to be.You should be able to get this for under $10. It isn't quite like DD (nor is it as good), but if you like that kind of turn-based fighting you may give it try. Overall, I must say I was disappointed, and was hoping that I could get more playtime out of this title. But on the whole I don't regret by purchase or time invested.Overall: 6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10 - good and engaging yet somewhat redundantWhile the inspiration behind the game is obvious, Iratus, as the Lord of the Dead he is, manages to be different enough from The Darkest Dungeon to warrant its own existence. Sady, the comparisons are inevitable and most of them are not in favor of Iratus.GAMEPLAYThe battle is basically The Darkest Dungeon but less engaging visually and minor differences are irrelevant. When battling enemies, you may very well be playing less RNG-based and more forgiving TDD. However, base management and RPG elements are quite nice and gathering resources feels a little bit more rewarding since most of collected trinkets and parts can be used in multple ways.Some components feel unnecessary or underdeveloped. The economy hardly exists despite there being some components of it. You don't really need to manage everything but the game allows you to so it very well may exist.SOUNDMusic here is repetitive and not as atmospheric as I would like. The variety of lines uttered by the narrator here is lacking. The voiceover is done nicely but it feels so desperate to copy what TDD achieved that at some point the overacting of the narrator starts feeling too much. VISUALSUninspired. Quality work here in the visual department. Characters are distinctly different visually, animations are good. To avoid bing just as redundant as the game in question, I will abstain from saying anything else about how it looks and what it tries to mimic.STORYThe story is fine. The lore here is shallow and vapid as you basically play through the whole world-building. An all-powerful necromancer returns once again to slaughter the heroes, conquer the world, reduce all life to dust, and bla-bla-bla.The issue here is that this short story is all there is to the lore. Yes, there are detailed descriptions of minions and enemies, but they hardly matter and nothing of importance is revealed while you make your way through ancient catacombs. The story is sufficient and tight (maybe overly so) but nothing else.OVERALLIratus: Lord of the Dead is a good game. If you played TDD, you will most certainly like it. But! If you want the same teeth-grinding experience and the feeling of desperation while you crawl deeper and deeper into madness, you should wait for TDD2 or replay TDD.For TDD fans, Iratus is just something "casual" and fun to scratch that TDD itch as we all wait for the sequel. For people who found TDD too unfair or hard, Iratus is a really good alternative that is lighter in all possible ways from gameplay to graphics and sound.Not as good as I hoped, but certainly deserves its right to live. The overall quality of assets and polishing warrants the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus isn't exactly a great game but is still worth a recommmandation.It is very obviously inspired by Darkest Dungeon to the point where it could almost be called a rip-off except you're playing as the baddies in a mission to conquer the world. This notably means that the stress meter taken straight from DD (including the death by cardiac arrest if a hero becomes too stressed) is your ally in this game and I have to admit that turning your enemies mad with terror before killing them is very fun and satisfying.Aside from that, the character progression is pretty well-made with many ways to upgrade your minions or yourself and making for an engaging evolution as you and your undead warriors progressively grow stronger. I would have liked for it to go even more in the mad scientist direction, with the ability to take parts of your monsters and graft them on others to give them some of their abilities, or even fuse them all together into one massive undead abomination, but what we have was fun enough to keep me entertained for the whole run and the unlocking of new characters adds a nice side-challenge. I don't know if it will have enough replayability to keep that charm on multiple runs though, as I fear they might end up all feeling a bit too similar...I also want to salute the balancing as each minion felt pretty useful and there wasn't a single completly dominant strategy among those I tried (although some comps are obviously better than others and might become mandatory on higher difficulties).Still, there are some issues with this game, notably when it comes to the presentation. While the design is detailed and intricate (although dreadfully unoriginal, the dwarf warriors are taken straight out of the LotR movie and the berzerkers staight out of Warhammer to give a few examples...), this doesn't translate well to animation. The game looks fine still, but terrible in motion and that translate to the battles feeling stiff and awkward, even compared to DD which had barely six frames to work with. As the combat is turn-based, this doesn't affect gameplay but it makes fights unappealing to look at and you'll be looking at them for most of your run.Soundwise, while the music and sound design felt pretty unremarkable, the narrator (because of course there is one) was pretty grating and his line cheesy, not in the good kind of way but the annoying one. Now, some might disagree with me on that but personally, it took me barely an hour to be unable to stand it and mute him.Finally, one last criticism for me had to do with the difficulty. As of now, I did one run of the game on standard difficulty which took me roughly six hours. I went through all stages basically steamrolling every opponent without barely losing any of my guys. But, as I thought I just had put the difficulty too low and should try on hard, I reached the final boss and got crushed. Now, I'm not complaining that the boss is too hard. I was unprepared and so I lost, I'm not owed a victory. What I didn't like is that the game did nothing to communicate to me I was doing something wrong as I had no trouble during any other fight prior to that point, meaning I had no way to know my team wouldn't be able to take him on.This is especially grating since this happened at the end of a six hour run, which is pretty long by rogulike standard, If I had wiped on the first boss I wouldn't complain, but this sudden difficuly spike at the end really left a sour taste in my mouth. I will still try a new run and finish it now that I'm more familiar with the mechanics, maybe even another one on a harder difficulty, but this experience certainly dampened my enthusiasm. Now, once again, I'm not saying the final boss should have been a free win, I expected a tough battle, but if I went through the level preceding it without losing a unit or needing to heal outside of battle, it should mean I have the means to win against the boss at the end.Conclusion/TL;DRIratus is a pretty unoriginal game that shamelessly copied other titles like Darkest Dungeon and other roguelikes, it also suffers from an at best mediocre presentation. That being said, it still has interesting mechanics and a well-fleshed battle system and progression path that makes it worth playing if you like the genre. Although if you haven't played Darkest Dungeon yet, go play it first, this isn't as good.

_childDocuments_.review: In this game you play the villain as a necromancer hellbent on ruling/destroying the world. You raise a team of undead minions and use them to destroy your enemies throughout various dungeons. The dungeon contains multiple paths containg various events culmunating in a boss fight which you have to route for yourself depending on your priorities not unlike slay the spire. The minions in this game have each 6 abilities (of which at least one an "ultimate" move). Depending on the position of the minion in the formation, the minion can use a subset of these abilities. You can customise these abilities as you progress throughout the game. Addtionally each minion has a specific spread of base stats and a set of which you can upgrade them with a different cost. Finally you can accessorize with items which give them an extra bonus. This make each minion unique , gives them a role(s) and even some synercy and anti-synergy. However they are not inflexible at all. How a minion plays can change drastically even during the same playthrough. Finally You can customize the necromancer as well with perks and artifacts which either gives you spells to use in combat or passive bonusses to complete your formation.The combat is very fun, the enemies are quite distinct with unique roles. They are dangerous enough that if you are not carefull can wipe out your team. That said most have them an element of counterplay to them. This means that with the right minion choice and good tactics, you can shut them down. This also applies to the bosses as well. They are more powerfull sure but they are not without weakness which you can exploit.If you however make a mistake and lose a minion it is not the end of the world; the game puts in a mechanic that allows you to recreate a minion and train it up instanously. So you don't need to grind up a supbar minion. They are not disposable though these instant level ups are not limitless and you still lose some of the rare resources (like items or special parts) you invested in the minion. the game strikes a good balance in that regard. So all in all, it is a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’ve been looking for something that does the unthinkable by taking inspiration from titles like FTL and Darkest Dungeon while offering a comparable, if not superior experience, Iratus: Lord of the Dead may be the next big hit for you. It combines large-scale party management, branching advancement paths, and a dark setting to create something that’s quite familiar, but also fresh in many ways, that stands out from the many clones that seem to have flooded the market in recent years.Iratus: Lord of the Dead has you taking on the role of the revived necromancer himself as some unfortunate miners happened to dig just a little too deep. As you grow in power and push ever upward in your struggle to reclaim the world as your own undead playground, you’ll travel through locations like the mines and the catacombs as you encounter a plethora of not-so-do-gooder foes that will attempt to subdue your growing power and influence.Though you’ll start off facing off against less impressive foes like slave miners and simple stone golems, you’ll eventually be facing off against powerful heroes that just won’t quit. Lucky for you, you have a variety of tools for the job and whether you slay them all with brute force or terrify them to the point that their heart gives out makes no difference. The enemy variety is truly impressive, and I’ll leave the rest of that for you to encounter on your own without spoilers.Although you begin with rather modest capabilities in the form of low-level minions, as you progress, they will gain experience and improve. They’ll gain stat points that can be used to improve everything from their damage output (physical and magical) to their dread (stress damage) to their evasion, durability, and health. They’ll also be able to upgrade each of their six basic starter abilities into one of two superior options.Many of these offer significantly different specialization and grant plenty of customization opportunities for tailoring your minions for specific tactics. For example, one of the minion types that you start with access to, the skeleton, has a move that allows them to take a defensive stance to reduce incoming damage. When upgraded, this move can either reduce even more damage or it can cause any that attack it to suffer a retaliation that deals a noticeable amount of stress damage. This system allows you to build each minion in a different way, sometimes even changing up their role entirely in some of the more extreme situations.The number of minions available to you is impressive considering that each can already be specialized into differing roles. You’ll only be able to create a select few at first, though the others will unlock as you reach certain milestones. New creatures aren’t recruited in the old-fashioned sense either; they’ll have to be created through the use of body parts collects from your fallen foes, such as bones, hearts, and flesh. Each minion requires four specific pats, though differing tiers of rarity for these offers attribute bonuses that make them far more powerful.This means that they with a selection of all purple, ultra-rare parts, a new level one monster will begin with as many stat points as if they’d achieved level twenty-five! Fortunately, parts can be replaced and destroyed so you are able to upgrade your long-standing minions that have survived as opposed to creating new ones entirely, though death is a part of the game so don’t grow too attached to them all the same! New parts are always coming along, and the second deaths of your servants aren’t disasters, only inconveniences that need to be corrected.Iratus joins in on the party by gaining experience as well. Though he never enters the battle directly, his levels grant many spells that can be used in battle as well as abilities that grant passive benefits whether you’re in combat or not. These abilities are divided into four skill trees that can be built upon: alchemy, magic, ire, and destruction. Alchemy focuses mostly on improving your out-of-control capabilities by increasing the number of body parts that drop as well as making their usage more potent and efficient.Magic tends to be a mixed bag of spells, some aiding you while others complicate matters for your foes. Ire offers buffs for your minions by improving their capabilities in a variety of way, assisting in them bringing the hurt to your enemies for you. Finally, destruction is what you’re probably expecting; it specializes in directly slapping around your foes with significant damage potential. All of these paths are balanced well and which trees you choose are likely to differ based on your playstyle.Combat is incredibly fulfilling in Iratus: Lord of the Dead. Every battle feels fairly unique as the combinations and synergies, even among your enemies, is impressive. I never really found myself to be bored at any point, and on several occasions I found myself losing track of time and playing for over four hours in one sitting. For those who have played Darkest Dungeon, it will feel familiar in many ways, but there are several differences that make it stand out. The most game-changing of these is the stress mechanic that attacks the minds of your foes instead of their bodies.In Darkest Dungeon, your characters suffered stress while the enemy did not. In Iratus, this is reversed as you’re the monsters this time around. Other than that, you have a wide variety of minions with plenty of abilities to synergize with and countless foes that will force you to swap up your go-to strategies to overcome them. Don’t send in a party specialized in causing fear when your enemy’s party is composed mostly of constructs, for example.Iratus: Lord of the Dead is an excellent title and one that I highly recommend to any who enjoy the rogue-lite feel of those who have come before it, especially Darkest Dungeon. I’ve been keeping my eyes open for something that could truly compete with Darkest Dungeon instead of simply copying certain aspects of it, and Iratus has exceeded my expectations in nearly every way. Although I struggle with making a strong claim on either of these games on which is the superior experience, I believe that Iratus: Lord of the Dead may be the one that has finally dethroned Darkest Dungeon and that’s no small feat to be sure; it really is a must-play title for those who enjoy the genre. I can’t praise the game enough for having an excellent variety in both wicked minions and pesky living foes that will keep you engaged and playing long after many of its competitors would have you shutting down to play something else. Give it a try and I doubt you’ll be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: A definite improvement on the Darkest Dungeon formula, cutting away the obnoxious grind and making it a more "proper" rogue-lite.The game is very forgiving; it refunds half the ingredients and equipment for every unit you lose, and even if you retreat or get wiped out, all non-boss enemies retain the damage you inflicted on them. Play the hardest difficulty available despite the game's insistence that you try "normal" first, lest you fall asleep.The later unit designs will baffle you the first time you look at them. They all have major drawbacks and complications and don't appear to improve on anything the basic units do, but the tactical options they add will start to make sense when more challenging enemies begin appearing. It's a very elegant and flavorful design philosophy.Plot and characterization are a bit on the thin side, but it works, with the fully voice-acted protagonist growing on you over time.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's a good game - probably the best darkest dungeon clone I've played. However there are some issues that make it hard for me to recommend currently. For 45 bucks total w/ the dlc, it's a hard sell. But if you can grab it for 20 bucks or so then it's definitely a must get.  The DLC definitely feels required to get the most out of the game, as it adds more enemy and boss variety which the base game is sorely lacking. The true ending is locked behind the DLC as well, which really really grinds my gears. It's a bit of a pet peeve of mine when companies (indie or not) add DLC that really, really should of been a free update to the base game. Hardest difficulties are just not that fun, and this is coming from someone whose done a few blood moon runs on DD. A lot of the minions just aren't good on harder difficulties and the way they scaled the difficulty just isn't fun to go through. Certain mechanics just don't scale well on the harder difficulties. You're also basically forced to focus on one squad of minions as well. All this combined leaves a meta where you have very few ways to go about playing and your options are very limited. I'll finished up my Good Always Wins run and I'm putting the game down until there's some more significant balance and QoL changes

_childDocuments_.review: is a villain-centric  clone that does enough things right. Will it knock your socks off? No. Is it better than ? No. Is it challenging…diverse and interesting…replayable…make you really  about how to win? Yes. I’m 100% sure you will find things to be disappointed in, but the devs invested enough in the right areas to make it worth my time.It’s inescapable.  looks, plays, and feels exactly like a  for  If you’re tired and frustrated with reading review after review comparing this to  I’m sorry.  did it first, and did it better. I didn’t find anything……to make me say you should play  over  so I am just going to focus on how  is different.All that said, a good clone can be a breath of fresh air while keeping the gameplay, mechanics, and atmosphere that you fell in love with.  definitely does that.Things that  does well includes diverse units to build your team. I have only finished two complete runs and found good uses for most of the units. That said, unit balance feels like a bit of an issue. Some units are clear favorites…and others are like…well, would you ever really take a ghoul over a werewolf for your elite squad of undead hitmen? No, you don’t need to know anything else to answer that question.I also really enjoyed how  took the concept of sanity and turned it on its ear. Instead of another way for your dudes to die, it’s a completely different way for you to approach combat. All units have some physical and sanity-based uses, but it is pretty clear each unit will do much better in a team that focuses on one type of damage. You  be rewarded for a grab-bag of physical and sanity based attacks. Enemies only die when you deplete their health  sanity. Having separate physical and sanity-based teams will be very useful.As you move through the dungeons, you will know exactly what you are up against next. AND you can change which team goes into the next fight. Instead of being rewarded for building a balanced team that can handle the entire dungeon, you are rewarded for having multiple focused team comps. Your total team size is very limited, though. You do need to think through your builds and options when you add/remove units from your team, and you need options that are useful against the enemies in your current dungeon.One thing I did not like was the “meta” progression. More than half your units don’t unlock until after you have “driven 50 enemies insane.” While I understand that from a “learn the game in steps” perspective, it feels too limiting. You can’t even build a strong sanity damage team until after you have unlocked everyone…which more or less requires you to successfully complete a run. So, half the game isn’t even there until you complete the arbitrary meta-challenge.Voice acting is pretty good, but writing and world building is was not. It goes beyond cringeworthy. Reading unit descriptions, I can tell the writers were trying to tell a joke…but it comes off as a tired, poorly executed trope that just makes you turn off the TV.Finally, there isn’t much diversity in gameplay. Once you have completed the game, you know exactly what to expect. The challenge won’t be in “how to beat the enemy”…the challenge will be in building a new team from a different set of units to finish the game…or just do better. I read another review that discussed how they tried a team made up of 4 Specters.  An interesting idea, and turns out it worked pretty well.So, if you enjoy playing around with unit/party compositions, and trying to min/max the game,  has some decent offerings. If things outside of immediate gameplay are important, this will not likely be a game for you. Even all that said, I can’t imagine myself playing  for more than 100-200 hours before I will wake up in the middle of the night, cold sweat, screaming “why didn’t I just play more ”

_childDocuments_.review: I have been loving this game and though it still needs work I would recommend it to people who enjoy roguelikes. That said the main reason I am writting a review is because I saw in another review that the devs read these (major kudos for that) and respond and there are a few things I would like to point out as someone who has played the game for a while now and give my two cents.Though I acknowledge the need for the lich cloud changes I think the way it was addressed was wrong, you could have a similar results by halfing the amount of stress damage done and kept the fun of the shuffling strategy which was far far more fun to use than any other strategy I have tried out so far, the strength of roguelikes is that it is single player and that can allow for insane combos and one of the two biggest distinctive features of iratus is traps (and stances) so you should have some strategies that showcase these.On the subject of strategies I have also been trying to make other comps work and the ignision comp has been specifically hard to make work. The fact there is no decent position 4 ignition minion coupled with 2 of the bosses being effectively immune to this makes it hard to make a decent ignision comp. Focusing your ignite effects on one target with brides makes the guy die to the direct damage far before the burn damage matters and spreading it with zombies makes it obvious how underwhelming stoke the flames (one of the few spells that is made to compliment this comp) is for only affecting one target rather than everyone.The scarcity of healing makes the 75 wrath healing talent mandatory to have and rush for all comps and discourages using your wrath abilities unless it either ends the battle or cost less than 25 so you're still over the 75 threshold if you had 100 at the start of the round. I understand the concept of the game is supposed to be that the minions are replaceable but with the high costs of making a good team at the moment plus the trinkets being lost you cannot win if you lose members of your A team to a couple of crits. On that front I would suggest you get back their parts after they die but them being damaged and costing a few parts of the same type to repair (saving costs on getting purple parts to remake your minions makes it less impactful if they die which was the original theme) and if you did win the fight to be able to retrieve the trinkets since you usually don't have too many of them and many have effects you just cannot use and are only there for the flat bonus. I understand that this makes it harder to get a game over but as is you hardly ever get a game over as is, you have a bunch of level 1 minions with only gray parts in buildings and sending them to die would be a waste of time so you would usually just delete the save once you're out of brains so it's more complex than what it seems.On the subject of the map I would like to be able to see the enemy comp without having to go there and sacrifice a minion so I can choose my path based on which elite I am hunting for my humanorium collection, I have done 7 runs just trying to get the elite trader, defensive pylon and elite bard and they have either never showed up or just refuse to drop their token (looking at you defensive pylon).Finally I would like to ask the devs how do I get the infected and the different minion models since I have bought the bundle with the dlc but I don't have these and I would like to ask the fans if anyone is doing an ainz ooal gown model for iratus and making the nazaric guardians as minions, I cannot be the only one who thought of that while playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: well completed tutorial and more pain difficulty  (2-4). I can say it's worth the money, and pretty well done especially for a new company. I personally think a couple minions needs some buffs as they are just lack luster to me. but with soooo many different compositions of minions it's possible i just didn't find the "right" one to maximize their play style or it just didn't match my own.        If you like games like darkest dungeon this is definitely one you will enjoy.  22 unlock-able minions with no limit to how many of each you can use. all having their own unique skills, and special passives, along with a 1 out of 2 choice to upgrade every skill. Upgrades for base stats of damage, dread, armor, accuracy, crit, dodge, ect. alot more customization to each minion available which is very nice. Items for your minions along with items for yourself, unlockable spells, and passives.        I can say i did lose a few of my minions even in the more pain difficulty. but not enough to make it really difficult, which is good for a lower difficulty. So having two extra difficulties will definitely add a challenge and test your strategy. I it's re-playable if you are the type that want to try and run a completely different group(s) a second time or want to up the difficulty and complete the game again.  I would say eventually you will run into redundancy of the game play.  but since there are 6 "maps" to conquer with completely different enemies in each. the game does space it out enough that i think you could get a good 70+ hours of playing before you'd have to worry about that at all.       All in all there wasn't really anything wrong with the game. i didn't run into any bugs personally or anything that i felt was done badly. it's a good game and refreshing to see it's less money than what lots of games are going for. glad to bought and will still be playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Great first impression for this. I liked DD a lot, and this is scratching that itch while waiting for a sequel. This is also the first game I've picked up in quite a while that I am actually finding enjoyable (have hit lots of duds lately).It has a sleek look to it and offers a large set of minions to choose from. I like how you can find instant upgrades along the way to get newly acquired minions up to a usable level.Only complaint so far is there is a overly limited way to explore the dungeon. Once you select a path on a fork, you cannot backtrack or even take that path when it comes up deeper in the dungeon. It would be nice if the game provided some sort of mechanic like food from DD that at least gives you the chance to further explore areas.Overall, definitely a recommend if you enjoy turn-base strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems to be based on the premise of darkest dungeon, but from the other side (i.e. the bad guy perspective). In general, I find this game more fun than darkest dungeon (and its not even fully released yet). It is hard, and people who say that losing monsters can snowball into making the game impossible to win are correct (i.e. you would have to  start over), at the same time however, there is some strategy here and as i have played, i wipe (lose monsters) far less than i initially did. The gameplay is fun, in part because you can inflict stress dmg (to eventually drive enemy insane, whereby they may dmg each other or do other crazy stuff) or damage their health bar. If the stress bar is at zero, further stress attacks have a chance to kill the enemy. Each of your minions has its own role (some are not really apparent until you get further into the game), but i have found each unit i have used to be interesting, and the upgrade path (through xp your minion levels) allow you to make choices that determine how you will play the match with that unit (i.e. a bit more health or dmg or accuracy etc, you only have a choice of 2 options for each power your minion has but it still changes things up. all in all i like the art, sound, gameplay and general feel of the game. it is enjoyable even in its early stages. Although it is fairly hard, you can choose an easy mode (i played that first to learn the game) now i am on the harder mode and it is a lot more difficult to chain wins and not lose minions. I think this game would benefit from some buffs to some of your units and or include more options for players..i.e. handicap/buff slider for when you start a game (so you can further make the game harder/easier depending on your preferences). Also i think this game could benefit from a general game mode where you can pick 4 minions for a team and get to choose which enemies you would play (it would not be part of the campaign) so you could learn new strategies against various enemies without having to start a new campaign. I think it would be fun and allow people to decide which gameplay style worked for them. Overall though this game is more fun than darkest dungeon, has great art and is enjoyable to play. if you are on the fence i would still buy it at this point, its that good!
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: It would be easy to write off Iratus as a Darkest Dungeon clone. In many ways it is; a hand drawn dungeon crawler using a customized party of 4 with permadeath and a haunting aesthetic.But in many ways I prefer it to Darkest Dungeon. First, it eliminates the need to grind as there are a fixed number of encounters in the game. Second, it offers multiple difficulty levels to ease people into what can be a very difficult game. Third, characters can be customized in both ability customization and stat distribution. The quirky "quirks" system is gone from Iratus. Lastly, instead of being victims of insanity, you can inflict psychic damage on your foes.The story, art direction, and voice acting are probably better in Darkest Dungeon, but these are all still good here. Most importantly, there's plenty of gameplay depth in customizing your minions, the artifacts they equip, the spells you take into battle, and global artifacts you can use. The DLC is also a great purchase.I liked Darkest Dungeon, but this is a pretty damn good clone.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: The comparisons to Darkest Dungeon are apt, but don't mistake this for a cheap imitation for even a moment.Iratus: Lord of the Dead, admittedly, lacks the same polish of Darkest Dungeon's sound, art and narrative design, and in its current state is distinctly incomplete. It's a little sparse in content right now (notably with only 3/5 Acts available at the time of this review, very little narrative outside of textboxes and few bosses), and there's the occasional spelling error or game mechanic that's not fully intuitive. It also lacks the certain 'character' of Darkest Dungeon, where you find yourself strongly invested in your best heroes that you've dedicated so much time and effort into developing - but then, you wouldn't quite expect that same investment in your undead hordes, either.However, with all of that said, the core mechanics of Iratus are ; quite probably better than Darkest Dungeon in many core facets. Each 'class' is extremely distinct, mechanically deep and with ample customisation options. The game is designed to encourage you to keep changing which creatures you field on a battle-by-battle basis, ever trying new lineups with new synergies and new interactions to try. In my experience, battles in Iratus are more strategically deep and difficult than almost any in vanilla Darkest Dungeon; but there is a certain forgiving element that you can keep trying the same battle over and over again (as long as you have the troops to throw at the problem) and the ability to have your own troops retreat is pretty generous and player-friendly.In brief; Iratus is a take on a Darkest-Dungeon like genre, only focused on providing an excellent, mechanically deep and challenging combat-centric experience at, perhaps, the expense of its main competitor's polish and charm. Personally, I find it an easy, strong recommendation for how well-crafted the core gameplay loop is, and how varied and satisfying the myriad 'class' designs are.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game, Iratus has an interesting sense of humor and the art style will probably grow on you.Its a early access game so these things may be improved on. At the moment however the game is just unbalanced beyond belief. You can really see that the devs put the effort in to make the characters kits work together, and integrate the magic system into the combat. However in practice the game does not deliver on balance. As you go up in floors, your damage increases due to better parts marginally, however the enemies become much stronger. In damage, defenses, resistances and most importantly evasion. Enemies that get much tankier should not scale upwards in evasion simultaneously as this just causes situations where a miss will cost you dearly and RNG will be allowed to skew the results of any particular run. The game has a very intuitive interface, but its rather confusing at first because it requires interaction with the art presented rather than just menus.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty sure this is the first time I've ever posted a negative review, but this game has earned it.I love strategy rogue likes and rogue lites. But to call this a game of strategy would be to stretch the word beyond reason. It's all about swingy dice rolls. If you lose, it's unsatisfying because you know that it wasn't clearly due to your mistakes. If you win, it's just as unsatisfying, because you know it was just dumb luck.Sure, there's some strategy that can go into how you compose your team, but when you get to the boss fights the number of teams that have any real chance of winning are vanishingly small, and even then it comes down to dumb luck.Nope. Would not recommend that you waste your money on this one, even on a fire sale. After 51 hours (I'm stubborn, and really wanted to like the game.) I have to say this is a failure.Perhaps if they massively re-balance and allow for a great deal more real strategy it'll be a good game some day. For now my advice would be look elsewhere.
