_childDocuments_.review: It might be early access, but this is EA done right. The devs, you cheeky bses you are so smart I will give you that. You took the two most played games of a similar genre at this time - Darkest Dungeon and Slay the Spire, and added your own twist into the mixture - playing as the bad guy. Well played, you clever people, well played.TL;DR. Am I endorsing this game? You can bet your ass that I am. I always write reviews either to tell people that they got good stuff on their hands or to stay away from it. And I can tell you, this is the good ****.So let's start. What's good about the game?1. Involvement.I ragequitted so many times in Darkest Dungeon (DD for short) when I lost a char I loved so much. Even the chance to get it back later on didn't entice me. In this case, we have undead (granted, you can involve yourself, or invest yourself in them by changing their names), but it was so much easy for me. I don't care if they die, or something happens to them, I just keep going on.In this game we get exactly what we got in Slay the Spire. Barebones, but good barebones, so much so to get invested.2. Depth.The game is as deep as the ocean. You can mix and match characters + builds + items + level ups. The options are so much it's insane. It foregoes the stale DD improvement and lets you customize as much as you like, down to the items themselves, while DD was simple % increases. Kudos to the devs, DD 2 needs to learn from them to keep us sufficienty interested and invested in it.3. Gameplay.Quick and fulfilling. The game is prettier than DD and plays as fast as DD and Slay the Spire (STS for short). There is plenty for you to do, and plenty of hours to invest to get good in this game. Even the barebones material now is decent, just as STS was when it launched.The game in and of itself is interesting and involving. It plays the way you expect, snappy. You pick your route, you stick with it and you overcome dangers with what you are given. Based on your way of playing, you can make it easier on yourself, tougher on yourself or steamroll the game if you are really good at it. As things stand, I already see lineups that can beat the game as easily as a snap of a finger.What's bad about this game then?1. As things stand in this early access build, the option menus are stale, boring and bare-bones as heck. You have as much to tweak as in a flash game.2. Lots of content needs to be added in. Meaningful campaign, challenges, sandbox mode, etc. However, I am positive that the devs are aiming high, and that this is coming.3. Tough as nails. Cakewalk??? The devs really need to add a few more difficulties, and change their names. Whoever thinks the cakewalk difficulty is a cakewalk are sorely mistaken. I had top soldiers and still LOST!!!4. The devs are hard pressed to deliver. They have the base, but they also have a challenge to overcome. I can already see builds that will totally trash the game. They have a lot of tweaking and balancing to do.Conclusion.Buy it. Just do it. even in its barebones state, I can see myself dumping multiples of hours in this game. People who have followed my reviews know that I expect a good return on my money. In this EA build, I can see myself getting at least 4 times the amount without getting bored. That, along with the pleasing graphics, the great gameplay and the horrendous challenge I am up against, is enough to merit a purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game. And they'll remain high hopes until the official release. In theory it has all the aspects of a dungeon crawler that have been missing from the genre. You play the bad guys, with a replaceable army of henchmen that you smash into enemies until they fall over or have a heart attack. Unfortunately in its current state, it's in dire need of balancing. I like a difficult game from time to time, but right now this is a step beyond difficult. It's downright punishing, and on certain run throughs impossible. But first lets start with what this game is doing right. :A variety of minionsA fairly unique creation system for the genreFun abilities and tactics to be employedA solid variation of enemiesencounters that really make you think your way around them.Proper use of a disposable army. Solid artwork(though it's debated. I like it).Great soundtrack to fit the atmosphereand RNG that can make or break you (this is a plus for me)Now the things that the game is missing or that just don't work in current state:Overly punishing enemies(One of the first floor boss fights has 3 of each block, 300+health and 300+ sanity, AND he summons 3 minions regularly that he will buff to do extreme damage. on cakewalk, easy, mode)The minion selection is barren at first and requires a lot of time spent to unlock anything worthwhile. Of the starting minions, creating a solid team that will get you to the first floor boss on the "More Pain" difficulty is near impossible.Building rarer monster parts is a waste due to how often youll lose monsters, even higher leveled with buffed parts and items.The game while geared to losing monsters, punishes you terribly for losing monsters. Leaving it in a limbo of whether you want a solid team or an endless assault of fresh recruitsIf you do go for an endless team, without some luck and everything spent on the graveyard building, you'll run out of monster parts long before you can wave assault.Boss fights are the only fights that reset health(Even though waves of monsters appears to be what the devs had in mind). All in all, the game clearly has some balancing issues to address. Like I said, I still have high hopes for the game, since it comes from a unique angle for the genre its in. It does a lot of things well but the balancing in it desperately needs revamped. I'll updated my review once it's been out for a while. But for now, i'm going to say, proceed with caution.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:  Think of LotD as Darkest Dungeon, designed by a Euro company that puts out detailed city sims or RPGs with tons of complexity-by-design.  It is simular enough to be picked up rather quickly by a DD fan, but it is definitely different enough that you won't feel like it's just an extension of DD.  I find it enjoyable, but there is a bit of a learning curve that I think on hour 7 i'm just starting to realize what I'm missing...forget about actually playing well.DD has this game beat on style, story, mood, art, and a bunch of nebulous characteristics that I would call "cool".  But...this is still pretty good in those categories.  Looking at a video should give you all you need to know if you want to try it.  I definitely think if you like DD then this game does things differently enough that they don't cannabalize each other, and having both is enjoyable.So anyway, as to LotD itself?  The differences as I see it are "fiddley bits".  Like the difference between a German game and an American game.  There are lots more to fiddle with; town development is more complex, character levelling is more complex, combat is more complex, and there is the added difference from DD in that you as the master of your party can cast spells and carry your own items...you're not actually IN the battle, but you can affect it.This game puts a lot of focus on using fear/insanity effects, so you can either kill an enemy, or make them run.  Buffing is also a much more complicated process here; every class and every monster has a number of buffs...for themselves and their party.  It makes the puzzle aspect of the game more complex.One thing I wasn't a big fan of; I played this game a few hours when I first bought it, but skidded a bit a few levels in because I felt the added complexity didn't really add anything.  I returned to the game and the more I play it, the more I appreciate all the interrelated buffs and debuffs and counter-buffs and the multiple layers of combat, damage/avoidance/mental state, etc.What I didn't see is a tutorial.  I have done a cursory glance through the menus and it looks like after the first tutorial, you can't go back and do it again...not so cool  if you haven't played in a while.  There are also a lot of "oh, I didn't see that thing over there to click on it, it really affects the game".  It's almost as if the came has a search and click aspect with regards to the interface.  I still have a lot of questions on the interface (where do I see % to hit?) which I'm sure I'll get answers to in forums.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: This game is already excellent for an Early Access title, and I'm really looking forward to its ongoing development.What I like:-Proud Darkest Dungeon inspiration with enough tweaks to make it new and interesting.-Beautiful art and voice and sound design-Slay the Spire-like dungeon maps and progression-Unlocks for Minion types that persist between playthroughs-Enemies you kill/damage stay dead even if you lose - Making it satisfying to send wave after wave of weaker undead at difficult enemies to slowly whittle them down.-Driving enemies insane and being the one that CAUSES a heart-attack chain for a change.-Brain and body-part swapping/upgrading to buff your minions up.What I hope for:- Better comeback mechanics - it feels bad to lose your A squad, dooming the run to a slow death long before you inevitably lose your last weak minion.  Something like a resurrect spell or more undead-themed recovery mechanics would be nice.- More persistent unlocks across playthroughs, like artifacts or talents or just something that makes subsequent runs feel less like starting over from scratch.- Maybe better/cheaper Graveyard buildings? I built a couple of these that seemed fairly essential, like the Mortuary, but after awhile it didn't feel worth it to expend my precious limited minions on constructing them.- Little more Balance - There were a couple of enemies I ran across that could just one-shot my minions on their own without giving me a chance to react, especially if I was unfortunate enough to give them the Berserk or All that's Left insanity debuffs.  This would honestly be fine if the game had better comeback mechanics, but on the topic of balance, overall I think I'd just like the incoming damage curve to be smoothed out a bit more.IMHO this game is worth buying now, but if the devs keep at it, I consider it a must-buy for anyone who loves to play as the bad guy.  :)

_childDocuments_.review: Alright.Iratus.Another "Darkest Dungeon but you're the bad guys' game.The fact I can say "another" both pleases and confuses me.Anyway, the core Idea, the aesthetics and world is great and the voice acting and humor made me want to keep playing.Customization is just fantastic as well and I love the many ideas for minions and their flavor, iratus himself helps this a lot.It also tries to, like most of the othet games of this caliber, to build it's own gameplay loop.But alas, just like the others this is where it also falls off.To me this kind of game needs a really solid base loop to keep me caring and engaged.But this also has this puzzle-ish feeling.Instead of fighting weaker enemies you still shouldn't underestimate as one bad move could turn things around, these are hulking behemoths.The second you leave the mines the game just turns up to overdrive and turns from fun challenge to not too fun and frustrating.Xcom, Darkest dungeon and so on.They have one thing in common, while they can feel unfair, it adds to tension instead of actually taking away.You spend time with your people and once you inevitably lose them you usually blame yourself (and the bad rng).But you know you COULD have done better.That's where this game turns frustrating.It baits you into thinking you can do as you wish and to have fun, customizing your squads and trying out wacky combos, but as soon as you do it stabs you in the face and kicks you while you're down.The way missions work and the forced pace don't do it any favors here, but I suppose it didn't want to copy darkest dungeon too much.Take the one man army build.It is fantastic, funny and works amazingly if you use the right minion and get the item.But then suddenly the game says "nay" and just robs you of the core on the next floor and spits in your face.You have a stress build? Here are berserkers they will now one-shot your entire team instantly.I get it.It's this odd puzzle-ish keep your team mixed up idea.But why.You allow me to customize and do as I like really, so why make enemies hard-shut down a ton of playstyles.It really, really limits replayability and variety, sadly.In a way I wish they'd have went heavier on the darkest dungeon but you are the monster side of things, but all these games seem kind of scared to really do it. Instead they all try to force as much as they can this "heroes are broken, try your best to not die by hard countering them" approach which ends up playing like a chore and making me not want to come back while darkest dungeon is a game I still install every other month for wacky adventures.Freedom in your stupidity with these games is key and you need to have choices to make what happens really feel something, but the choices in iratus just end up short in too many aspects sadly.I think there are a lot of people who might enjoy it, but in the end it just misses the mark, keeping me mainly interested with the top notch presentation instead of the mediocre gameplay.Disappointing because I feel that it could have been darkest dungeon but with a mighty fine twist to make it unique and interesting if it wanted to be, instead choosing an oddly overpopulated niche and ending up feeling suprisingly uninspired gameplay.I just don't recommend it because I feel that it just won't be fun to a lot of people as it's not what you expect it to be.But if you do enjoy the gameplay I do actually whole heartedly recommend this, as iratus is most likely the by far best in it's weird niche.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge Darkest Dungeon fan, and I love this game too.  I would say that I am bias, but at least honest about it.  A lot of people have been complaining about bad RNG, I agree.  I am on my first playthrough within the first 2-3 hours had three unavoidable deaths due to RNG.  There is absolutely nothing you can do to defend against the instant deaths.  Some examples:#1)  This executioner "regular enemy" can just pull anyone to the front line and immediately one-shot kill them from full HP.  I literally have no idea how to stop this RNG from instantly killing my guys.  It's just a fact of the game.  You will lose those hard earned minioins.  (NOTE: If you know how to 100% stop this type of death, then give me a hint.  Like it's possible to live?)#2)  If you are unsure of the enemy's abilities, then there are some enemy's that can one-shot your toughest tanks from full HP to dead.  Some "common" enemies unchecked can one-shot kill your entire party.  However, seeing them a second time, you learn how to avoid the instant death attacks.There is no point in leveling up your favorite minion.  There is no point in giving all the best items to one minion.  THEY WILL DIE.  It's best to spread out the power ups to several backups.  You are better off building up two teams equally.  Replacing the dead will take time, and the second team will give you the time needed to restore lost members.  I assume the game is designed to kill your minions, because it is LITERALLY stated at the introduction of the game.7/31/2019 Edit:  After playing the game for less than 19 hours (I was afk through most of it.  I'd say around 15 hours of game content).  I have completed the first three dungeons (all of the released content) on the easiest difficulty mode.Everything was a super cake walk, except for the Boss of the 3rd dungeon.  The game is planning on releasing two more dungeons and I assume they will make the 3rd boss easier.  There is far too much RNG luck required to beat the 3rd boss.  I assume this game will contain at least 25 hours of easy mode content.  Min-maxing to beat the other difficulties doesn't appeal to me at all.  Anyways, I had a ton of fun (because I didn't lose a single battle till the 3rd boss).

_childDocuments_.review: Good technical strategy game, I've beaten it on normal and hard settings, haven't played the 'very hard' mode yet.  I'm playing the base game which has 4 floors with the a unique boss at the end of each and might take 20 hours to finish the game depending your speed. (not sure what the expansions offer)RNG is reasonable.  It's above average in giving you relevant information to make your decisions (it's not one of those ridiculous games that says 'this talent increases damage' leaving out the fact that it could be 1% or 50%)The normal mode is questionable, I found a good group compositions and geared them up about 1/3 of the way through the game and their gear and stats didn't change much through the entire rest of the game which felt very lack luster.  I almost quit at that point then figured it's probably meant for a harder setting where it takes the entire game to max your characters out to have an enjoyable progression.  Hard mode was more enjoyable, my minions died multiple times, forcing me to try different strategies.I enjoyed it, the reason I'll stop playing is the extreme learning curve to be really good at it, which includes the amount of time I have to spend thinking of possibilities.  There are too many possibilities...  21 different types of minions in a group of 4 (or you can have a group with just 1, or 2 or 3 to get more buffs) and you can have a team of all one type.  That's 1,000 possibilities for group comps and each minion has 6 abilities with all 6 abilities that have two options for an upgrade.   I love being challenged and coming up with ideas, but this has gone too far, I spent about an hour just sitting and reading all the abilities trying to match up possibilities for group comps, it's exhausting to think about.  When your playing on hard you have to mana/rage/hp/evasion/debuff removal/block removal/burst to delete one enemy quickly/interrupt ability.... and it goes on.My main conclusion is that this game is wanting you to not 'max out' a group or minion but create different groups based on who your fighting (BTW means you have to know all the enemies abilities before engaging to actually counter them)   I feel there is less enjoyment progressing games with multiple minions, which is the reason many games have a hero you play or a core group so you can focus feeling good about always progressing a single character every fight.   You can cast one additional spell from a list every round, and they turned this into your 'main character' but he has no physical presence and his leveling abilities are helpful but you can't gear him up or min/max him.  Just feels like somethings missing.Good game, you should try it, try to get past the normal setting and play on hard for a better experience.

If you enjoy games like Darkest Dungeon or Dead In Vinland you will love this.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Darkest Dungeon, you are probably here thinking if this is similar, but in reverse.And the answer is, yes..kind of. I'll be comparing the two games, so if you haven't played DD some of the comparisons may not make sense. Sorry about that.The style of combat is a very similar 4v4 where position determines which skills are accessible (but less punishing than DD). You face heroes that you can kill either with stress or pure damage. The enemy and, more importantly, your units, variety is really (really) good. There is less RNG in combat, and both good tactics and team composition are equally important. Team composition might be even more important thatn DD as sometimes you need to deal with enemy buffs, debuffs or dangerous stances. Oh, and no need to bring your Vestal :)In short the combat is awesome, more plz.The only complaint is that it does not have you at the edge of your seat due to less RNG but also no death's door.Units are upgradable in two ways, both available after leveling up. One is improving the stats, the other is picking a special upgrade of their core abilities which may now work very differently than before.You get your units by using parts (like skulls, bone) that you get from enemies. However your units always start at lvl 1 which is a problem when your current highest level unit is 40. Thankfully, you have another limited resource called brains, which essentially levels up the unit to keep pace. Personally, I don't like this mechanic at all. If you lose a unit in combat you need to give it a brain and then spent 40+ attribute points again to spec. Redoing this is the most painful part of your units dying.Your main character also levels up, giving access to some perks and spells, but you can cast only once per round so meh. There are also "town" upgrades, which give you some higher chance of getting loot, or more exp but really nothing exciting.The game is far less grindy than DD (thankfully). Units are more easier replaced, but it's also more possible to reach a dead end due to level difference (although unlikely). HOWEVER, the game takes quite a while to beat. The levels are huge and you have multiples of them. I would have preferred much shorter levels to have more time to experiment with different team compositions.I feel that the first difficulty after the tutorial is too easy once you learn the game, and the next one is just right (with more to be unlocked). However, the issue is that some units are locked and take time to acess. You may only get to use them in a different playthrough so starting right away with the harder one would make it even more difficult.All in all, a pretty good game. It does have some DD vibes but without the exciting moments (will my hero panic or become virtuous? will he survive the next hit on death's door or die). But it's also without the grind. It's tactical and there are many ways to make your team composition. My biggest grief is that a single run takes way too long to beat.Overall, if you liked DD, you'll likely like Iratus. If you haven't played DD but like tactical games, it's still a great pick up!One last thing: The "real" ending is locked behind an expensive DLC. That alone would normally bring a review down to negative, but the story does not really matter here making the DLC just more added content. However, if you really need closure even to an essentially non-existent story, just be warned that the base game does not provide it.

_childDocuments_.review: High fantasy setting along with „hero saves the day” trope is easily one of the most prevalent archetypes of storytelling across video games as a whole. Having seen it milled 100 times over, with a varying degree of success, I always find it refreshing when a game tries to twist this formula. This particular dungeon isn’t your ordinary adventurer’s piggy bank. Here the evil is on the offensive, this unassuming set of caverns is but a staging ground for an undead invasion that will sweep over the mortal world. The player is granted the mantle of Iratus, a master necromancer and the mind behind the nascent undead horde. Create yourself a team of 4 minions and have them carve the way to the surface, one turn-based engagement at the time.To address the elephant in the room – Iratus is overall a decent game, provided you enjoy turn-based combat or have fond experience with Darkest Dungeon, you can hop straight into this title without much hesitation. , one may be tempted to ask. That really takes the long answer, for now keep in mind that Iratus involves several design choices working to its own detriment.Before we can move on to the game’s issues, it’s vital to establish what Iratus: LotD is in the first place. The in-game disclaimer fittingly describes the title as a “hardcore tactical rougelike”. Tactical aspect of the game is twofold. First being the turn-based combat with a core principle of dealing the most damage possible at the least own cost. To further this goal, the player may choose from an astounding variety of 19 minion types, each with a unique set of 6 abilities. Most minions are unlocked through fulfilling specific requirements (e.g. deal X physical damage or slay bosses), both encouraging the player to build a team composition with meeting these objectives in mind and as a way to reward game progression.Every minion also has a dedicated set of stats which can be upgraded as they gain experience. While skill tree does leave room for minor tailoring, each minion type has a single specific role to fill. Said loosely-defined classes revolve around one of 3 types of damage present in Iratus – physical, magical and stress. While the first two deliver severe case of being dead, stress damage is often able to circumvent the enemy’s defences to make them rout or get a heart attack. Take note that while morale is not a factor for your undead horde, when minion’s health hits 0 they are gone forever.Second tactical aspect is the resource management. Frankly, the amount of options available may seem overwhelming at first. Minion creation, base building, Iratus’ own skill tree, alchemy and a comprehensive tutorial to allow player to take all of that in. However, once you start the game proper, it soon becomes apparent that factual management is extremely basic and boils down mostly to order in which you will build new facilities. Time spent in Iratus’ chambers is primarily means to add diversity to combat-heavy gameplay and is at best a second fiddle to managing the minions themselves.The rougelike piece of the game is conducted in genre’s most classical take. Game is divided into 5 areas, each being a set of meandering corridors with pre-determined set of encounters. The player may use an occasional crossroads to alter the chosen path but this is about all one can do to adapt to the current state of your undead army. Hopefully this robust introduction conveys well what makes Iratus: LotD tick. Alas, it’s time to move on to less rosy aspects of the game. You might have noticed how I didn’t bring up the game’s story. This is because the game doesn’t have one, it has Stephen Weyte voicing Iratus instead. Frankly, stellar voiceacting is the only thing that gives the character of Iratus a personality, while also being the driving force behind the game’s slightly dark tone. Otherwise, the game’s lore can be summarised by “world domination”. To make matters worse, this title’s writing ranges from uninspired to miserable – skeleton’s only shtick is being bullied for how unremarkable it is, while some of the enemy lore entries are downright painful to read. On the note of overarching tone of the game, reception of Iratus: LotD artstyle is a matter of taste, however a damned soul sporting a pair of voluptuous breasts feels out of place. Sure, sexy and undead both have their appeal but in this case, game appears to actively contradict its own darker tone for the sake of .Another major issue of Iratus: LotD is the game’s seeming infatuation with Darkest Dungeon. The ever-present narrator with a profound voice, the entire stress mechanic and aspiration to be both extremely difficult and replayable title, seem a little familiar. It has to be stated that Iratus: LotD has more than enough of its own ideas to not be a copycat, which makes this heavy-handed take on inspiration all the more baffling. Especially the game’s pursuit of “hardcore”, almost encouraging a degree of association with Darkest Dungeon, which to me works foremost to undermine the game’s own ideas.This flaw is worked into the core of how Iratus handles game progression. The game clearly is intended to be replayed as the player needs to beat the game on medium difficulty to unlock higher one. Make no mistake, it is a perfectly reasonable design choice, allowing the player to properly learn the game and unlock all the minions first. Initial run of Iratus is a surprisingly forgiving experience. Save and floor restart features provide all the safety net in the world, thus you can experiment without restraint to develop a strategy that suits you most.Having beaten the game once, the player finally can move onto the “hardcore” proper. One may finally gather all the knowledge accumulated throughout the first playthrough and throw it out of the window. Difficulty spike between normal and hard is staggering. With saves gone and enemy damage upped to eleven, rather than capitalise on gathered experience, you are forced to completely revise your approach to the game. Alas, not only your minions drop like flies, easily half of the roster is no longer viable. Playing on hard becomes tedious relatively quickly, especially as you realise that after beating the game once you really have seen everything it had to offer. Is that truly the pinnacle experience Iratus was building towards? Many reviews cite the forgiving nature as the game’s defining positive quality. Further giving credence to the notion, that most players are satisfied with beating the game once and don’t ever bother delving into hard difficulty,  if we were to follow the “hardcore” angle. Perhaps Iratus would be much better off if the developers instead saved the limelight for the laid-back fun it can deliver, especially as it seems to be better suited to showcase the aspects that make the game stand out.Iratus: LotD is one of these games that really makes me wish for a mixed rating to still be available. All in all, it is a legitimately decent title – one I was able to enjoy despite its mild identity crisis. The game can be easily recommended to fans of turn-based combat, if they are not deterred by aforementioned red flags. Iratus’ greatest vice is completely overselling its high difficulty level, which mostly falls flat in comparison to the freedom of the first playthrough. Ultimately, I decided that the game’s reception could benefit from a little of a contrarian viewpoint.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely a challenge, but it is written in capital letters at the very beginning, and yes, you will be losing your minions periodically, especially at higher levels of difficulty and/or while experimenting with the party composition, or just due to bad luck and huge crit.To be successful, you need to think about tactics first: what minions complement each other based on their abilities (some can buff other minions in a specific way and/or debuff enemies), position during a fight, rotation (usage of some abilities moves the minion thus changing the position(s) of other(s)), the main type of damage (physical or stress), in what way to level up the minions (2 alternatives to choose from), not to mention that you have mana (spells are opened through research and artifacts/items), rage, mixtures (opened by mixing ingredients), items/clothes that you can wear, your personal develepment tree (4 talent tabs) which affects minions/spell power, etc. You are forced to win on lower difficulty levels to make the higher ones available. Thus you can understand the mechanics, open new minions and learn the bosses (abilities, stages, etc) to increase survivability of the party. Or you can read the illustrated strategy guide written by the devs, but only if you own the supporter pack (if nothing has changed).The game had bugs when I played it, but what game does not today?! While I myself did not face with any game breaking bugs, some small issues still happened, and I'd like to note the way in which the customer support team works. You won't hear advices like restart your PC, update all possible drivers or change the internet provider, but, on the contrary, will get all necessary directions how to settle the issue. They can ask you to send them a specific file from the game directory so they could check and correct it. Getting it back and replacing the old one, will fix the problem.If you are a fan of the genre, the game is worth trying!

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, it is too short for the moment. After watching some gameplay videos and researching the wiki, I rushed though the game on Cakewalk difficulty with ease. If I minus the time spent thinking about tactics, the actual gameplay time should be around 5 hours as of this moment. Considering the current roadmap, the creators should have much more in store for the future.For Darkest Dungeons players, if you are comparing this to Iratus, here are my insights:- Iratus has a forgiving difficulty dedicated to beginners: Cakewalk. Not like Darkest Dungeon which is hard regardless of difficulty.- Battles seem to be longer, critical hits occur somewhat more often.- It's less focused on RNG mechanics. Targets are guaranteed to suffer from effects like DOT and moving if they get hit.- Stress mechanic is quite interesting, it is reversed and you can inflict insanity on foes.- If you are veteran DD player and consider that you research tactics, party combos,... carefully, you should have a much easier time with Iratus.- The map is currently quite bland from my view. Instead of a large map parchment, you could replace it with a circular tank that gives Iratus an aerial view on the actual human world and use that as a map instead. The map then should have a more lively look. A paper map is a bit outdated idea in my opinion, so you should have something more mystical.- Easy-to-approach modding mechanics. A game lives long when it has a modding community that constantly makes custom modifications to give it a newer look. Since Iratus is an unfinished game for the moment, I believe this is not your top priority right now. But in the far future when Iratus has received enough attention, making the game easily moddable might be a good move.- Make it possible to fight all battles and interact with points of interest. This should prolong the gameplay and give undead armies more time to gain experience, training and more resources.- Give the option for minions to move themselves rather than relying on spells and the different effectiveness when they move (1,2 or 3 positions). - I don't know if you intend to implement more skins for minions and even humans later, but giving the game a new look isn't bad at all.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as i'm aware this is the first Darkest Dungeon-like game that has seen any amount of success (aside from the original of course). I hope this becomes a trend because the combat system has the potential to work quite well in all sorts of settings. Iratus adds new mechanics to the now familiar Darkest Dungeon style combat such as making your enemies go insane, single time use shields that block all damage from a certain type of attack, and spell casting that can be used once per round on any of your minion's turns.The out of combat management is expanded on somewhat from what is available in Darkest Dungeon. You create your minions from all sorts of different parts of varying quality; the higher quality the parts the more stat points you get to allocate into your minions various attribute fields. Iratus also implements a version of the hamlet from Darkest Dungeon by giving you Iratus' tomb to build out with different structures. These structures  give various bonuses such as healing a minion after combat if they're placed inside, or improving how much mana Iratus recovers after combat.The evil-side spin on the concept is certainly refreshing Iratus himself giving his musings about what's happening both in and out of combat is quite charming. The undead minions, despite being undead, all have personalities and little quips they send out during combat.It's clear that the developers saw Darkest Dungeon and didn't just want to make a carbon copy of it. I think this game really tries to stand on it's own two feet. Ultimately I can definitely say I had quite a bit of fun with Iradus: Lord of the Dead, but if I had pick out the most glaring flaw with the game it would be that it gets to be a bit repetitive towards the end.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun twist on the "Darkest Dungeon" style game, where you play as the bad guy.  I like that your minions don't just show up out of the blue, but you have to actually construct and reanimate them from the pieces of your defeated enemies.  I also like that you have to unlock most of them through various achievements, all of which are thematic to the individual minion type.  The graphics are a nice digitally painted style, but it sometimes feels like some of the designs were left over from an Artifex Mundi game, if you know what I mean.  The music does it's job, giving a fitting atmosphere to each of the areas.  The main character's voice work was nicely done, and it sounds like they really had fun making him an over-the-top villain, both in performance and in script content.  As a side note, the "Wrath of the Necromancer" DLC feels like it's necessary for full enjoyment of the game, adding new minion types and a variety of features - like potion brewing - which I found to be fairly indispensable.  The "Supporter pack" DLC is totally optional, but I bought it anyway to support the devs.  When this game goes on sale, you can pick up the total package for around $10, and it is absolutely worth it if you like this kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: A great and shameless copy of Darkest Dungeon, but not quite as unforgiving. Perhaps even a bit easy, on 'normal' difficulty, but a pleasant learning curve nonetheless. It also feels as though the choice of party (minion) members is not quite as rock/paper/scissors as one would expect, but there is still plenty of variety to build different teams with different strengths and weaknesses. By comparison with DD: - most minions are quite capable on every spot and have something to hit every opposing spot on the field as well; most minions have several damage types at their disposal and each also capable of hitting multiple spots; synergy comes from rhythm and correct sequence of abilities, more so than the individual abilities themselves. The game really does a great job at it all though; it looks and sounds good, it plays smoothly and without annoying wait times or long ending or opening sequences. Its something you can pick up and play for a few battles, and put back down.... but I didn't manage to all that quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very tepid recommend. Iratus steals a lot of good ideas and has some problems, but overall I enjoyed it for a while.Iratus is a turn-based dungeon crawl almost rogue-like. It isn't a true rogue-like, runs can take 10 hours or more, and the number of meta unlockables is very small, so it feels more like a permadeath run with little, or no, reward for failure than it does a rogue-like.This game borrows HEAVILY from darkest dungeon. As result I am going to say it right now, if you have not played Darkest Dungeon play that first and don't assume because you liked Darkest Dungeon you will like this. Iratus is not as polished and creative as darkest dungeon so the experience just is not as good (normally I would't compare two games like this but Iratus forces the comparison by taking so much from the prior).Gameplay wise the bones of the game are good. You have a dungeon you go through room by room, fighting enemies in 4 v 4 turn based battles, with lots of mechanics and resources to use and balance. All the interesting stuff, like the stress mechanic, sending your minions to town to rest, having to get used to losing characters often, is pretty much all taken from Darkest Dungeon. It all works and it can be pretty fun to plan your battles and then play them out.Art and atmosphere wise the game is fine. I found the production values to be pretty cheap but passable. Again they try to ape Darkest Dungeon by having a narrator comment on things going on but the voice acting and writing is nowhere near as good.I personally found the difficulty curve and the meta progression to be pretty bad and resulting in me quitting so early. After the tutorial I jumped into the highest difficulty it allowed me to. While the beginning was a bit of a struggle, it actually started to turn into a cakewalk by the end where I was drowning in resources that I didn't need. By the end of my very first run I had unlocked almost everything. I then played a new run maybe 10 minutes to quickly unlock the remainder. Then I start a run on a higher difficulty I had just unlocked. Those first few floors were great, probably the most fun I had in the game, but then I hit a difficult boss and I realized that maybe I had made a mistake in how I got here. 10 hours into a run where I was not going to unlock anything I realized that maybe I should have done things differently and should start over. No thanks. Without the incentive to unlock more there really was nothing keeping me around after needing to restart.Bottomline, I got 1 and 1/2 good runs out of my 20+ hours play time, had some fun, but ultimately I do think the game borrows too much Darkest Dungeon and really messes up its meta progression.

_childDocuments_.review: Ahhhh, yeah, it's pretty good. It's BASICALLY Darkest Dungeon, but you control the bad guys, though it isn't one-to-one. You can cast spells that affect the fights (think Dungeon Keeper) in addition to giving orders. There's also a little more animation to it (though Darkest's art style is more.... enthralling?). There aren't as many unit types here as Darkest, but there're a lot of cool minions to bust out. I'm particularly fond of the Ghoul and Dark Knight.You have to unlock enemies, as well, which I guess is a trade-off for being able to create whomever you want (so long as you have the parts). You only have to do it the one time; I've started eight or nine new games and the minions never become re-locked, which is nice. I was actually surprised that the expansion's units were available right off the bat. Grateful, too; unlocking a few of those guys really sucked.Uhh.... Your dudes level up over time and you spend points in their stats, and pick an upgraded form of their moves every so many levels. YOU also level up over time, as well, and get access to more spells and passives. It's a pretty subdued system; your units take a much greater precedence than do any of your abilities as a necromancer.I played the Hell out of this in EA, and you could beat the three available floors there in a few hours, but the levels are much longer now. It's pretty fun, overall, but for some reason, despite how similar they are, this can't hold me like Darkest can. Don't get me wrong; I can't play DD for more than five or six hours straight, because it's so stressful, but this...? I dunno; I LIKE it, but it just can't hold my interest as long.I DID just beat it for the first time since its release (fitting; Halloween and all that), and I think I can honestly say, I will never bother beating it again. I'll almost certainly PLAY it, but I was SHOCKED at how much the final zone made the game completely un-fun. Between enemies that hit like runaway freight trains (and it didn't matter what stats I beefed or how high of a level I made my minions; even twenty levels above the area's enemies, which you can do by inserting brains into your minions, didn't matter. Didn't matter if I leveled evasion or defense or armor or block or HP, the Monk enemies would kill level-50-and-change tank units in four hits, and there was nothing I could do to stop them) and enemies that can full-restore the entire enemy party, it was a COMPLETE slog. The secret turned out to be Stress-builds, which, fine, I guess, but it was very irritating to have half of the tactics of the game just be obviated by enemies that felt fake difficult.Plus, I'm pretty sure more than once an enemy bugged out and made the fight basically unwinnable.Obviously, one time through the game doesn't make me an inside-and-outside master, but it took quite a while and gave me a lot of time to experiment with tactics, which didn't appear to make much of a difference.I dunno. This one's fine, particularly if you can get it on sale. I like its concept, and had area 5 been the last one, I'd probably be a LITTLE more breathless in my recommendation, but the endgame area really took the wind out of my sales.I don't mind difficult (I've posted bona-fides in a buncha reviews already, and I'm going to stop), but I hate it when it feels cheap.

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically Darkest Dungeon where you play as the bad guys in a type of Slay the Spire scenario. I think the game is fun, but the difficulty settings feel so out of place. This isn't the type of game that should have difficulty options. You also have to beat the game one time before you can play the hardest difficulty. They should have just gotten rid of the difficulty settings, placed us in the hardest one and let us go crazy.They also allow you to start over combat as many times as you want. I dislike that too. I am not a fan of roguelikes that allow you to reload. It sort of defeats the purpose of being a roguelike.Also a lot of the semantics are slightly off in the way the game explains some things. For example: there is a debuff that says "you take twice as much damage". But that is not exactly how it works. What is ACTUALLY happening is the incoming potency of the enemies attacks is doubled. So if you have 5 armor that blocks 5 damage and an enemy hits you with an attack with a base of 10 potency, you will take 15 damage instead of 10. The incoming potency is doubled from 10 to 20 instead of the damage you receive being doubled from 5 to 10. Fixing the first 2 things would change this review to a highly recommend from a no recommend. It is quite fun, but it requires too much of an open mind for me to recommend it to anyone. I also could never recommend a game that locks the hardest difficulty setting for your first playthrough under any circumstance. That mechanic is video game cancer.

_childDocuments_.review: edit: im changing the review to positive because I want this game to succeed and love the concept but im keeping my original one below ----vedit edit: THEY DID IT! Blocks/wards now affect crits! They listened! ahahahaThis is why you give games a chance boysOriginal review: ---vi really, really enjoyed this game and thought it was the game i was looking for until you get to higher difficulties.when you play on the game mode "good always wins" deaths seem to not root from mistakes anymore but instead getting your minions instantly destroyed by RNG, and then it inevitably snowballs out of the control because you have to play the rest of the fight from a disadvantage, or in cases like the Inventor (second boss) on good always wins, your entire team can get two-shot all at the same time by ONE of his attacks (not even counting his pylon which mimics the same attack) within under a minute. The only possible counterplay you think you can do other than hoping that the crits don't happen, is creating "blocks" or "wards" which flat-out prevent the next attack from damaging them, but guess what? Crits flat out IGNORE this feature so your team will be inevitably blasted to pieces regardless of whether you prepare ahead or not, and one of the solutions I can think of this would be crits being REDUCED to a normal hit while still consuming a block/ward, that way they would still be punishing but not to the point where your team all dies instantly within 2 turns in certain fights regardless of preparation. On the difficulty "more pain", lots of fights kept me on my toes and it was enjoyable and sometimes I didn't know if I was going to make it out alive, and none of it was because of random crits instantly slaughtering my team, for example lots of times it came where I had one minion left and I still managed to pull a victory out. I think this is the state the game should be in and it's actually enjoyable. But bumping up the difficulty doesn't really feel like it adds anything or any new attacks but just, bumps up the random crit chance and the game instantly becomes based on whether the dice rolled in your favorite or not and if it didn't WELP say goodbye and have fun restarting.It's sad to give a negative review because I really like the concept of this game and have been waiting for another hardcore turn-based game like Darkest Dungeon but the sheer amount of RNG that determines your fate and lack of skill and planning requirement on higher difficulties is just too infuriating and feels like throwing yourself at a brick wall over and over until the RNG gods bash you through. I'm sorry developers but something needs to change, like maybe add more tactical and different attacks and attack patterns enemies can do or make their AI smarter, or even just give them more health/damage rather than make it all based on random crits.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfrozen’s  is one of the greatest tactical rogue-likes one can enjoy right now; one that surpasses the titles it pays homage to in almost every way. The road to getting rid of anything that breaths with your necromancer is filled with a series of challenging battles, with an enormous amount of depth in the mechanics on offer, and with a heavy dose of resource management thrown in as well. _childDocuments_.review: Didn't get it for free, but got it through Humble BundleThis game is not a Darkest Dungeon clone, I want to get that out of the way now. There is a lot that is borrowed from that game, but the two are distinct experiences. The whole 'reverse' dungeon crawler plays into this, your monsters don't get stressed but your enemies do. But that's mostly superficial, the positioning of your units isn't nearly as important. All of your units will be effective at pretty much every position, barely any enemies are able to move your units in fact you have to mana to move your characters around (though it does not take up a turn). In a way it feels like a simplified Darkest Dungeon, which is still pretty good. resource management is much different in this game. You don't have buildings to upgrade your units, though you build some to generate mana, heal minions and train them. Though the game says they're not expendable your minions do feel like that some time. Your characters are likely to be very easily killed by some really, really annoying enemies. If they do die you can instantly level them up to a useful level if you have certain items. Beyond that the resource management comes from having enough materials to make your minions. There are alternate ways to recruit, but you must fulfill certain requirements which may not be practical.If you're choosing between this game and Darkest Dungeon I would recommend Darkest Dungeon. Not only is Darkest Dungeon cheaper, but it also has more depth and I personally find it more fun. However, if you want something similar to Darkest Dungeon but still different enough to be unique, then this game is perfect for you. Though I think the price is a little steep, so you may want to wait for a sale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like Darkest Dungeon, there are differences of course. But out of all the games that are like Darkest Dungeon, this one is it the most, and that's not a bad thing, but let the comparisons commence.The battles are extremely similar with the positioning of your troops and uses of buffs/debuffs playing way more importance than any other game of this kind. The one big difference between the two games in this regard would be the lack of corpses in this game, so killing an enemy will always bring them all forwards towards your position.There are more classes for you to use in your party but there seems to be a bit less variety when it comes to enemies and bosses instead.The city section is also quite similar but I found it a bit less useful here and mostly used the menus for crafting and creature customization.The map is a bit more like in Slay the Spire with a straight road with some branching paths rather than the usually also kinda linear, but occasionally labyrinthian levels of Darkest Dungeon.The artstyle is very nice, while not as striking as in DD at a glance, it all looks very good. Although it could have done with some more animations since while the characters all look good while idle or attacking, when they die they just turn into embers or something rather than having a real death animation, there's also no frames for blocking or such.At launch you have two out of four difficulty settings to play with, apparently you unlock at least the third one just by playing the tutorial but I dove into the second one which seems to be a medium difficulty setting. Right from the start I was feeling the game to be a fair bit easier than its predecessor and in the end I got the achievement for losing my first battle with a complete party wipe while facing off against the final boss (pre-DLC, since I don't own that yet.) I also had my second party wipe against said boss and then had to give up. The difficulty spike was pretty big, makes sense since it was the end boss, but while I did have some setbacks during the other parts of the game, even there the blows are made much softer because since you play a necromancer you constantly get body parts that can be used to instantly level up new soldiers, sometimes all the way up to where your fallen ones were at.TL;DRI think the game is pretty great but a little flawed.

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line, Iratus does the best job of any pseudo-Darkest Dungeon clone of scratching that itch if you're looking for more Darkest Dungeon (1, to be clear).  There is a variety of monsters for different group builds (more than you can hold in the main roster at once, in fact), some clever ideas with the economy (you build your monsters out of parts that you get from enemies, use those monsters to upgrade buildings, and can repurpose parts for alchemy, although I do think the Diggers Souls currency needs something else to do once buildings are upgraded), and some good production value with the voice acting.It is held back by some very rough edges with the UX.  Some have already pointed out that the subtitles for a voiceover overlap the x button on a lot of windows, and there's a lot of clunk with what you can do, where.  You can store buildings in a training and health recovery building, for example, but can't set up your party without first going to a particular screen and dragging them back into the roster.  If you open up the character screen AT that particular screen, you can't see items you can equip or upgrade your monster with.  And you can't open up the character screen at all from the dungeon map screen as you try to decide where to go and who should go there.  Your main roster is at the bottom of the screen, and is divided into several different groups so you could have different cohesive parties, but since you only use one at once, and take everyone with you, this seemed like a needless feature when there are so many other QOL issues that get annoying after awhile.The animation is another thing holding Iratus back, for me.  It's paperdoll based, though obviously a high production version.  But it lagged the sound design and I never felt like the animations brought much impact.Finally, I think the non-combat gameplay will be in an uncanny valley between a more simple roguelike and a true campaign.  The dungeon map is really a Slay the Spire style branching path; you can't go back, you can't return.  You don't make any choices about which dungeon to attack next and have no goal other than getting to the end, and if you meet an encounter that proves difficult, there's nothing to do but keep sending monsters at the exact same encounter until you either win or run out of resources to make more.This can work, and is the vogue for a lot of game design these days, but a single "run" in this game can still take 20+ hours.  At that length, I think implementing a more fleshed-out strategy layer would have been a proper choice (I've also said the same with games that are more obviously built around the rogue-like experience, like Legend of the Keepers, but the game time there is such where you could see the rationale behind the choice).  Giving players a choice about whether to attack the dwarves or the mercenaries next, maybe to hunt for specific parts for specific projects or party build ideas, with specific objectives that could be achieved in a shorter play session, I think would have made the back side of the gameplay loop more engaging.But far as the combat system goes, there isn't a truer replication of Darkest Dungeon out there (that I've played anyway).  All characters have different attacks from different positions, monsters start with the base version of all abilities unlocked (with a choice between two different upgrades available for each), and, if you have the resources (including brains, which determine the monsters level) you can have fun building different compositions as you like without needing to grind them up (although since grinding isn't really an option, this could be considered silver lining).  Others have pointed that the game does really incentivize just leveling a few monsters to stay ahead of the difficulty curve, and I agree. This seems like an oversight rather than a conscious design decision, and could be remediated by either tweaking how monsters level or, again, adding a strategic layer that allows you to return to lower level opponents to try out new builds and level monsters that have fallen behind.  But this wouldn't even be an issue if a run in this game was only designed to last an hour or so and then start again like a proper roguelike, because then you could just try a different build.Got off track there, but returning to the combat, of course this has you play as the monsters.  You don't preserve sanity, you attack it (which if you decide to really focus on it, can be a lot of fun).  And other than the above, most of the changes will either be to your taste or not: whereas DD has a cartoony art style and a dark mood, Iratus has a style that looks more middle school "dark and edgy", masking a sense of humor to match.   It's a good game, not great.  Gets in its own way in a lot of ways, but if you're looking for what it's offering, it's worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game. But hardcore. So let me explain before you pick this game up and then rage in a review.This game is designed to make you fail. Okay? The units you can make in game? Most are locked and require a certain number of in-game achievements to unlock. And you're not going to get them any time soon. And basic units probably aren't going to cut it.So again - if you can't handle failure, don't buy this game. You'll just end up frustrated and write a crappy review. Don't do that. The game is fine, it's just a hardcore genre. It's okay not to like it, doesn't make the game bad.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun, and I don't know why it's not more popular.It's like Darkest Dungeon, except better.It obviously took a lot of of inspiration from Darkest Dungeon, but there's a little bit of inspiration from Slay the Spire as well. But that's a GOOD thing. Both are great games. No harm done.The graphics are amazing, the music is amazing, but the gameplay is even better.Unlike Darkest Dungeon, you can't just keep grinding.Unlike Darkest Dungeon, your high level units can keep doing content and you don't have to bench them unless they're injured.Unlike Darkest Dungeon, the final dungeon isn't stupid (well, the final one in it so far; more are coming in the future).They took everything from Darkest Dungeon and made it BETTER.Like Slay the Spire, you can chose the path you want and see what's there as you go. No going back. No grinding. But, the battles take longer than in Slay the Spire and you can go to your base between EVERY battle. So it's basically Slay the Spire with more depth and less RNG (well, except it's totally different, but...not really?).Play it. It's fun. You won't regret it.Iratus: Lord of the Dead is just as polished in EA as Slay the Spire was. No reason not to try it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Great Game. Never played Darkest Dungeon, but wow I really like gameplay of Iratus. Love the Graphics, Love the interface and how all the buildings physically are place in relationship to each other. It was honestly a little confusing how the mechanics worked at first for me but once your figured out the basics it's quite addicting. My first wonder was how do I heal my minions? Well, there are several ways, e.g. hitting a point on the map to heal, or building up a specific building in the graveyard, artifacts, or probably even easiest is having multiple sets of minions because they heal if they are inactive for that battle. So, you can just swap them out. I love the story in the game about necromancy and all the body parts, collecting them and using alchemy, etc it's quite fun and silly. I didn't think I'd like this game so much but the aesthetics, game play, story, and how things nicely, intuitively and seamlessly come together make this so much fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: The review, so far: "Do you recommend it?" Absolutely!Was keeping an eye for this one and it did not faulter my expectations. The only thing I have to tell about it is that I wish to explore the entire dungeons instead of having to choose determined paths thus being unable to retrace missed enemies, boons and free minions, yet this makes it interesting and different. You do need to think carefully :cell:There's a fair amount of characters to unlock, each one with different stress and fighting abilities (i use the Werewolf in every run, love it!); you can enhance their skills, stats and equip them with better items. Also, there are useful tree Talents that you will be able to choose by gaining levels with Iratus, some with stats and others with spells that can aid you in battle as well. Similar to Darkest, you have a few buildings you can make and level up, by earning and spending Diggers' Souls and sacrifice a minion type. These buildings can grant exp (Arena), heal (Mortuary) and find parts and items for your minions (Excavation and Dead Lake), for example. Library is a must have. Obelisk will give you a few more Diggers' Souls.Darkest made me like these type of RNG game and Iratus is both refreshing and somewhat a bit alike but not quite. You should definitely check it out >:3
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: An outstanding combination of (reversed) Darkest Dungeon and villain protagonist game. The mechanics are refreshing and the combat fairly challenging (though on normal difficulty "More pain" I did expect it to be a bit harder). Overall it does feel like you are a necromancer when you harvest body parts from defeated enemies to build your minions. Overall I would recommend the game. Though I would not go beyond "More pain" before you finish the game at least once. Even though later in the game it might be a bit easy on this difficulty, trying to tackle the more challenging fights without having more minions unlocked than just the starting few will severely limit the available tactics. Played with Wrath of the Necromancer DLC that I also very much recommend. All in all a very good game for its price.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not far in but I have to say this game has some nice features that darkest dungeons doesn't have. Way more emphasis on resource management and you can power up very quickly. You can choose to spec into spell damage or increase resource generation there is a lot of cool choices. Minion (Your party) variety is pretty awesome and have satisfying abilities. One minion has a spell that does damage based on his armour and another unit can buff an ally with armour so you can get sweet little synergies like that. Darkest Dungeon + Slay the Spire - done pretty well!
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game because it was similar to other turn-based strategy games that I have enjoyed.  This game is very fun to play.  The characters are diverse with many different types of abilities.  The story line is good.  The graphics are great, as are the sound effects.   This is a game I will play again and again for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: The game still has a long way to go, but it's already lots of fun. It doesn't feel like a Darkest Dungeon rip-off as the game manages to establish its own feel with a nice premise. What I like the most so far is the crafting and enhancing the minions which opens up LOTS of ways to play further complemented by a nice set of spells dependent on the skill tree and artifacts. What I feel could use some more love is the graveyard, which is not bad, but in comparison to other features of the game it's kinda bland to just "put a minion here to receive sth after battle". I cannot think of some serious bad things in the game so far, but of course at the moment of the review I have only 5.5 hours played.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending this because the game was put into early access and released in a timely manner.  Balancing and resource management was fine in EA, will revise if that's changed on release.  The game was challenging if not difficult, but not punishing for the sake of ekeing out more playtime due to a lack of content (like other titles in its field).  It also was not a grindfest.  If anything, the balancing and progression was done well enough that I, as a player, am not qualified to judge.Solid entry and great example of how to release a game.  A fun game at that.After playing through the game, I have revised this review to do not recommend.Game hangs at the end of combat constantly, not registering victory.  Currently unable to finish the game on the last boss.  Last boss is killed, game hangs allowing no input except to exit to main menu or load last checkpoint.  Loaded last checkpoint, have to restart the entire last dungeon again.  Game is fun, but I take back my statements about "doing EA right".
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a successor to Darkest Dungeon and I've got to say - I enjoyed this experience a lot more. Three major changes to the formula1. You are progressing your way into the world, this means you feel progression through a story faster and you're not just leveling up characters for the sake of making them strong enough to try the final dungeon.2. The sanity system is flipped, you can kill your foes with damage or stress and insanity checks occur on your foes. Much less infuriating and lets you build teams around a damage type instead of trying to heal stress3. Healing is sparce. Your team likely won't have a healer because what little healing options there are come with large drawbacks. Being the villain is great.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: This game is almost good, but it has couple really horrible design decisions, that makes it really bad and boring.First time I was playing I completed the tutorial and started playing on hardest difficulty that was available, I made few major mistakes and lost pretty quick. After that I figured out I give a try on easier difficulty called "more pain".I got 1 single artifact that gave my units 6 armor, this caused most of my units to take any damage during combat and made the game way too easy, I used this item till 3rd dungeon. And it was just boring grind, not a challenging experience at all and game got really boring really fast.After this I figured out I change my strategy to use heart attacks against my enemies. This made the game little bit more interesting trying different builds for a time, but in the end everything I tried just worked and there was no challenge at all.All the combat was starting to feel really same and I started to wonder how long does it take me to finish my run.I ended up spending like 7 hours in fights that proved no challenge and was just a grind. The final boss fight was way too easy also, I just used my same group of undead that I had been using for long time and beat the boss on first try.I don't understand why game designers made it so that the dungeons are so long, instead they should have only like 3-6 fights before boss and more optional events with more interesting mechnanics.I feel this game would be much more fun if the runs would take only maximum of 1 hour and would only have 1 difficulty where the game would be balanced around it. I will probably give game another try on harder difficulty, but knowing that it will take ~7 hours to complete my run and losing all my resources will cause me to start from beginning...Also the mechanic of unlocking stuff is really stupid, I would have wanted to start expanding my graveyard more, but I didnt have specific units unlocked so I cannot still do everything if I start on the harder difficulty now.Everything should get unlocked after playing the tutorial.Looking at steam achievement stats, only 3% of the players have achievement "I'll Be Back!", that means player has lost a run, seems like most people probably got bored in the grind and stopped playing after finishing 1st or 2nd dungeon.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: So far have enjoyed the game a lot. Its basically like darkest dungeon, but from the point of view of the monsters instead which is pretty interesting and different once you start playing it. The game is pretty hard, so if your not someone that gets frustrated easily with hard games you might want to take a step back. A lot of angry reviews were people that cant beat the game on the lowest difficulty. In darkest dungeon you couldnt really "lose" a run, you just get set back. In this game you can actually lose so with that brings frustration to some people.I would by lying if I said the game was perfect, its early access and has problems, but the devs have already fixed some of the problem even though its only been a few days after launch. So far they have responded very quickly and have made good changes so im pretty hopeful that they will keep up the good work.Overall even with its problems is a solid game and im excited for more development on it. I would give it something like a 7/10 at the moment for its genre type with decent chance of it going up once improvements and more content are added. I would say if you like these types of games and dont mind a challenge to give it a try. Its really quite fun once you start learning it.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Okey, this game has lots of potential, BUT, suffers from terrible design failures. 1. someone wrote a terrible RNG,Honestly, 118% accuracy vs 25% dodge will miss 4 turns continuously, 50% redirect will trigger 7 times continuously...so on and so forth. The RNG distribution is just terrible, in such a game, make a better distribution okey? The game actually knows about how bad its RNG works, so it offers a free "restart" battle option by quit current session and continue. well...if u KNOW how terrible the RNG is, u FIX the RNG, u don't waste the plyers time by restart every 10 minutes just because low percentage ♥♥♥♥ keeps happening. 2. horrible, horrible enemy design.It's okey u want every enemy to do sth different, and pose a different challenge. BUT, let's look at this random battle: barbarian, have to push it all the way back or it stuns your frontlines constantly.bard, have to kill her quickly otherwise it will just heal everyone back with no sweat.elven archer, u have to interrupt its stance, BUT it can also one-shot you if it decides not to use stance. so u have to kill it quickly. swordsman, this dude protects and also slowly gains damage buff, need to kill it before it grwos too strong. So in a word, the enemy design is simply that, "you have to kill this one first" on every enemy. Don't get me wrong, in "good always win", u can build your critter bride or whatever and quickly go through it. BUT, the design flaw makes the endless mode simply BS. Because EVERY ENEMY needs to be prioritized, i mean seriously, design some filler enemy that DOESN"T need to be killed in turn 1 or 2, so i can get my priorities proper. I worked in game industry for years and i know this pattern, it's called "ambitious deisgner". This is because the designer is afraid of designing something mediocre and unimpressive, so he made everything as impactful as possible. After some time when he gets better at game designing, he'll realise that, the game has to be composed by things that's impactful and things that's not. That's the healthy environment and a much better experience.3. monster talent pointsThis is very personal, but i have to be honest i like the previous iteration. Like we made a system, and then reading some feedbacks saying it's stiff. Instead of fixing it, we decided to simply turn everything into currency and let the player directly tune numbers. C'mon man, do more events/encounters, let player customize his minions through gameplay, don't let them customize by pouring currency(body parts) and tweaking numbers by "literally tweaking numbers". All in all, the game has potential, BUT terrible rng combined with "ambitious designer" makes the user experience awful. And then with certain systems i really don't like, my conclusion is a "not recommended".

_childDocuments_.review: It's alright, it doesn't really stand out to me. I played 53 hours and got to Eternal Havest 5 which makes it the mobs harder and the player weaker, but that's about it, I don't see myself playing more. 8 difficulty levels, 1 ending, 5 levels(maps?tilesets?zones?), hardest zone is the first one because you start from 0, but once you get going it becomes a breeze. It seems like it has alot to offer at first however the Talents are very narrow in scope so even tho there is player choice, it's false choice since most of the play-throughs will look the same(at least for me).Not much variation hapening on the levels either, so you wont get mobs from level 5 appear on level 1, they all stay in their zone.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: I find the negative reviews regarding balance rather annoying, as most of the people giving negative reviews say they like/love the game but that it needs to be better balanced.  FFS people, it just released into early access and is very playable and fun. Of course it has balance and gameplay issues. Giving a game negative reviews because of something that's inherent in early access is only hurting the game and developers. Seriously, if you aren't up for playtesting the game in its early form just don't buy the thing. It's not complicated.As to my take, I love this game despite it's early access flaws. Obviously it is punishing, and needs work in terms of balance. That said, the core here is better than Darkest Dungeon imo. Not having to rely on RNG to build the groups you want to use is a huge improvement as are many of the "meta" level strategic elements that DD doesn't have (yes DD is a better game right now, I'm only talking about the foundation elements). Overall, right now, if you liked DD and have patience for a game in early access, this is a can't miss purchase. If you are expecting a finished product on the first day of early access, it's probably best to just wait. And please don't review bomb the game if you do buy it and discover that, yes, it's not polished or fully finished yet. Jeez.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Great game to challenge yourself if you like turn-based combat.Positive+ Plenty of mechanics to discover, items to acquire and build your own army of the dead+ Quite a bit of depth with combinations to try and explore+ Difficulty is controllable, and the first level is doable by everyoneNegative- I wish that moving in dungeons had more control and options. _childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: After coming back to this game after it's been released and a few patches after that even.  I can't recommend the game.  There are some glaring mechanics issues, and balance issues.  The game seems like it's not finished.  There hasn't been too much changed in terms of play since early access just more minions added, level lengths increased, and a few bad design choices later we have another unfinished game.The bad: The price is a bit high for the game in it's current state (still broken).  The different monsters aren't balanced well as specific combos will wreck you (still broken)The game isn't balanced well level to level as there are spikes and complete cakewalks (still).The bosses are harsher than they need be (fixed but almost too easy). There are some very annoying enemy actions that bypass wards completely (kinda fixed).The voice acting is repetitive and needs more variety (still broken).The music needs more variety, and there needs to be more variety in the quests (still broken).  There is not much happening in your main chamber just dude staring at you, which gets old dude needs some other positions to chill in, and maybe have some animated actions happen. (still bad).Now that the game is out of early access it's clear it was rushed to it's current state.  I played a few hours on cakewalk, just to get my feet wet.  Switched to normal, and found that the game still needs a lot of work.  I'd say if you can get it for 50% off then it's a good time waster.  Just be prepared to be frustrated by mechanics that are still in the works.  Don't expect the devs to listen to feedback as clearly all my issues were suggested in discussion forums during early access, and on their discord server.  Don't expect this game to be polished enough for you to beat it on anything but the easiest mode.  I haven't heard or seen anything about updates coming since April, but doubt anything will roll out anytime soon.  Will check back in a few months to see if anything has changed for the better to see if my review needs to change.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: It may be very similar to Darkest Dungeon but in "Iratus" the other side of the story is being told (necromancer). Different from the DD, you (the necromancer) may have some impact on the battles by casting spells or with some passive bonuses.Another difference is that you have limited resources and a fixed path, which is fine by me as I like to complete things not to do them again and again.In conclusion, this is a very good alternative game to Darkest Dungeon (especially if you are tired of diseases, sicknesses, grinding, etc.) and hopefully will be better at the full release.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite fun and a little different from Darkest Dungeon. The refreshment lies not only in its PoV, but also the base management and minion creation, as well as the protagonist's direct impact on an encounter in the way of MMH, like global spells, buffs from equipments. Its not surprising that the devs were from behind the Disciple series. Right now, i just hope it will have an endless mode.Recommended for people who like turn-based tactics, team management, dark fantasy and being a bad bad guy.
