_childDocuments_.review: Everyone can tell by looking how gorgeous the game is, can tell from the trailer how atmospheric the music is. So let's talk gameplay.Animal Well is one of those rare gems that trusts the player to try and figure it out. Trusts that you have a working brain and eyes and thoughts of your own. The gameplay revolves around a handful of items you find and the special actions they perform that are mostly straightforward at first glance but have an impressive depth that allows for extremely varied techniques. The game is mostly platforming and puzzle solving, and each item has not only its primary role in either aspect, almost all of them cross-pollinate those roles, giving the player patient enough to master those tools incredible mobility and adaptability. The game is open ended in when and how you find those tools, and if a player is dedicated they can beat the game with a surprisingly limited loadout so long as they really know their stuff. And the average player probably will know their stuff, as the game actually takes a very patient hand in at least presenting the multi-faceted capabilities of each tool in very subtle and innocuous tutorial rooms that allow the player as much time as they need to come to grips with the finer aspects of the tools and their uses.Animal well is beautiful, interesting, intelligent, and most of all it's humble. Amazing game.
_childDocuments_.name: ANIMAL WELL

_childDocuments_.review: So it's a Metroidvania. Fine, fair enough. It looks and sounds good in that charmingly retro sense- in the "intentionally retro, not because the guy who made it can't do anything better" way. But that's nothing that hasn't been done before. You need to go further to realize what makes this game great.So I did my first clear. Found many eggs, did the main story progression, all of that. Also find a weird [redacted by Logstar] by [redacted by Logstar] which raises some questions. Then there are all of the background features that get you thinking...that has to mean something.The thing that makes this game interesting is that it all does. Or at least I think. I'm not sure at this point. People talk about the layers. There's layer 1, which is what people will do for a completion, layer 2, which is the formal 100% layer, layer 3, which is a level where some truly strange, obscure puzzles come up that are a community effort and only for true completionists...and then there's layer 4. That's the thing. I can't say too much without spoiling but it feels like this game keeps going deeper. There's a solid Metroidvania that feels good including the 100% stuff. Then you go deeper and there are these obscure puzzles that it took a community to find. And the amazing part is it doesn't feel like we're done yet.In a certain sense that's both what's great and what's awful about Animal Well. The third layer is done. There is this sense of FOMO from when the community was solving these brutal puzzles since we won't be able to recreate that unless there are groups of many people going in blind together. The fourth layer may or may not be done...and that's what does it. Few games go this deep and still give the feeling that there's more we haven't found. I hope we haven't. I hope I didn't miss it.And no matter what you think of this specific game it feels like this is going to be a huge influence on the future of the genre. This is the beginning. It feels like, in the future, other developers, even big-budget ones, will start adding these deeper layers. I think this is the beginning of a new generation of Metroidvanias and that generation will do spectacular things.
_childDocuments_.name: ANIMAL WELL

_childDocuments_.review: Animal well is a very unique and fun puzzle/exploration game with lots of charm. It’s quite a simple game, although quite a bit of complexity is hiding in this simplicity. My first go at the game I had a good time exploring and interacting with all the environment and its animals using the quirky, funny items it has to offer.Everywhere you go there this charming cozy-ness to be found driving you forward to see more, get more, do more. There a puzzle and a secret every step you take yet they still surprise you in their inventiveness. “huh this is a fun new puzzle”, “wow cool concept”, “wow I had no idea this was here!” over and over again until you reach the enda nd its pride itself on you figuring this stuff out by yourself. The game will tell you absolutely nothing while simultaneously showing you everything, although a lot of the puzzles will be so clear and cleverly designed to the point of becoming trivial, at least the ones relevent for completion. Yet they are very often still fun to do and hard enough to be interesting.The ending was satisfying enough for me, even though its hard for anything to have a bigger impact when lacking any larger context for anything.The second go around was still good, getting the last eggs to be found is still fun because really you’re just doing more of the same, however at least to me its design started to get in the way a bit more here. It tells you so little that at some point I didn’t even know where to look anymore and even if I had seen some of the important stuff before it was often still not clear how it was important, or when, making you go back just to see if it’s important yet. A lot of it becomes easy to overlook. In the end getting the last couple eggs started feeling more like I was just going through every room desperately trying every item you can think of to find that hidden wall that I missed. Looking up at least the location of the last eggs made it doable but also way less satisfying.Needless to say I do not feel the need to dive deeper into its well of secret upon secret however I have a huge respect for the dev for going this far with it while still keeping the main experience very curated. And if you at all enjoy finding secret then you will LOVE animal well. The cute animals are a nice bonus.
_childDocuments_.name: ANIMAL WELL

_childDocuments_.review: Animal Well is an I've played lots of Metroidvania games over the years, and have always been hooked on that "Explore to Level-up" feeling of those games. Finding new things makes you stronger, gives you new ways to interact with the world, and make old challenges feel trivial. By the end of the game, you're blasting through areas you used to find difficult, sometimes bypassing old puzzles with the power of your new tools. That's what it felt like to beat Axiom Verge, Shadow Complex, Guacamelee, and Ori and the Blind Forest. Animal Well is not one of those games. Every time I found a new item in the Well I didn't feel stronger or faster, bigger or better equipped. My sense of dominance over the world didn't change. The old challenges remained challenging. New tools  new challenges. A layer of the Onion peeled away. And layer after layer, the peels fell away and Animal Well became deeper, more interconnected, and more mysterious. If you love peeling away the layers of an onion, unravelling an expanding mystery, then you'll absolutely love Animal Well. It's truly intricate and contains more discovery than you'd think possible in such a small, tightly-packed game.I found all the eggs, opened all the doors, and uncovered as much of the game as is reasonable, and... I'm not sure I really I'd recommend it to the other gamers in my life. I felt frustrated more than I felt triumphant. Puzzles in Animal Well come in two varieties: "Obvious and hard to execute," and "Invisible, Esoteric, and hard to execute." One of the first big rooms you encounter is a perfect example. There's a room full of bubbles, being blown by fish below. You already have the bubble-gun at this point. As soon as you see the bubbles you know what to do: jump on them to cross the big room. Actually executing the jumps is half-way infuriating, and executing the jumps while enduring a screen transition is all the way infuriating. A lot of the game felt like that to me. I would either breeze through a new room as if I'd done it a dozen times before because the solution was obvious, or I would grind through executing the solution that was obvious. I agree with the Game Developer wisdom that good puzzles are hard to solve, easy to execute. The exception is, as I mentioned, the second category of puzzle: the invisible and esoteric. There were things that I eventually uncovered that felt really cool to discover, as they had previously been invisible. The elements that it took to find and solve those puzzles were complex and unexpected. But I don't think the average gamer in my life would have the inclination to carefully turn over every rock to find the best parts of what this game is. Animal Well is not for people who don't like onions.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an exceptionally good game, to the point where I'm actually kind of shocked at how much I enjoyed playing it. To put things in perspective, I don't generally vibe with metroidvanias or strict puzzle games all that much but despite that, Animal Well is currently my pick for game of the year.(Granted, that's mostly because Shadow of the Erdtree was a DLC and not a full game but I digress.)The pixel art is undeniably gorgeous and complimented beautifully by peaceful nature ambiance, making the world an absolute joy to explore, and man is it worth it to explore every tiny corner of this game. The puzzles and secrets are incredibly satisfying to figure out, and that's to say nothing of the larger community wide puzzles and ARG elements, which I hear are amazing!The game also fully embraces creative solutions. There were so many moments in my playthrough where I found a secret using a bizarre method and then found the "intended" solution after the fact. You're encouraged to play the game however you see fit, and I love that!Honestly I don't want to get into that much more detail because the less you know about this game, the more fun you're likely to have with it. As such, I highly recommend avoiding spoilers or walkthroughs. Just sit down and immerse yourself into the world. Even if this style of game doesn't look like your thing, you should really give it a try anyway! I genuinely think just about anyone would get something special out of this experience.
_childDocuments_.name: ANIMAL WELL

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I haven't had this kind of fun since i played Fez or Tunic which I thoroughly enjoyed and which Animal Well feels very similar to in aspects such as exploration, secret collecting, and puzzles. The art is cool, the world design and atmosphere is pretty and wacky, the platforming and level design is very fun, and most of all the puzzles are hard yet very satisfying. Discovering secrets, environments, and tools feels really good and every tool has multiple uses that you're forced to get creative with. I've beaten the game at 8.8 hours (pretty slow cause I'm stupid) and I know there is so much more to see and discover. I've gotten lost more than once, I've felt directionless more than once and, I've gotten stuck on the puzzles hundreds of times, but I think it was worth it. Although, I don't think the average person would want it for $25. Wait for a big sale. Read the negative reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game with great visual and audio ambience. The movement is enjoyable and some tricks can require pretty high mechanical skill. Every 5 minutes I find myself amazed and my entire perspective of the game renewed, because I discover by complete accident a new mechanic, a new item or the use of an object I've been seeing everywhere on the map.The gameplay is really fun and rewards skill, problem solving, exploration and experimentation very handsomely.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10 puzzle platformer. Fun, clever, nice movement, plenty to explore. Appreciate that the dev wrote his own engine and actually kept the content size to a few MB. Short for the price -- got the credits in under 8 hours without rushing, and with ~45/64 eggs iirc. Would recommend purchasing at $10 or less.Critique:- Maybe 5 mechanically challenging screens in the game? Bosses, timed puzzles, etc. A bit disappointed that the skill floor didn't feel like it increased over time / I didn't feel pushed to improve very much- I appreciate the  for the movement tech you can discover as a player and was hoping to see more items like this. Most items do more than one thing, which is nice to discover, but are little more than glorified keys. There's no reason that as a player I use the , , , , or  (and possibly more -- I'm missing 2 currently) except because the puzzle is  to require that item, and it's usually a pretty straightforward interaction once you see it. That's kind of frustrating by contrast to the  and  (and to some extent the ), which represent paradigm shifts in how I can move and interact with the world. In general I hope and expect that items will do that, rather than being pure metroidvania progression-gates.- On the topic of progression, it gets less and less impactful as time goes on, which feels disappointing -- later items, especially post-credits, become more about walking through the  map again looking for what you unlocked or missed (as opposed to beelining to known roadblocks and being able to progress immediately). I'm thinking about  and  especially. Probably not going to try to 100% for this reason.

_childDocuments_.review: Animal Well is the kind of game that makes you say "with the frisbee maybe I'll be able to hit the gecko in the eye and move forward," and that's a reasonable thing to think and one of the many fun things to try in this game.After getting all the items, 35/64 eggs, and viewing the credits, I still feel like Animal Well has a whole lot left to show me after 10 hours of binge gameplay.Considering a pizza, wings, and a drink costs more than £30-40 and can be eaten in 15 minutes, £20 for a game I will probably sink another 10 hours into is totally worth the money. Without any dialogue, relying on art and sound design alone, Animal Well always feels intuitive without giving the game away when it comes to its puzzles.It oozes atmosphere, and even after replying the same sequences multiple times through dying, I never felt that it lost its charm or became stale. Time and again, the game incentivises you to think about your tools, and even after having items throughout the playthrough, I continued to discover new quirks in an inventory I thought I knew.Great game, worth your time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: ANIMAL WELL

_childDocuments_.review: I really like puzzle games and metroidvania's, so both should be great and they usually mesh with each other pretty well and makes for a lot of aha! moments which makes you feel smart for figuring it out. Animal well does not do that. There have been two instances now of the game just forcing me to guess how to progress. I was stuck in a dead end loop for way longer than I should have cause the game wanted me to do something its never even hinted at being possible. I get they want you to experiment and see what works, but the solution was just dumb. I didn't feel good figuring it out, I triggered it on accident and I'm glad I did because there was no way I was going to purposely do what I did. It's entirely possible I missed a clue on how to do it and wasn't very observant in a room I was supposed to be, but it was definitely a "how was I supposed to know I could do that" moment.The world is very interesting and I want to explore all of it, however traversing the map get tedious with the amount of backtracking there is and they lock fast travel behind finding secrets. Find enough secrets and you unlock a hub for fast travel. Why is this locked behind an optional objective? Some of those secrets are really hard to find too. I guess they figure you'll stumble upon enough of them to unlock it since you don't need very many, but still, its such a basic gameplay mechanic.I do really like the items in this game, they offer some fun traversal skills and you can do some pretty cool tech with them and get into areas early. That is a big plus though I do wish the first item you get could be set up easier to use to make traveling faster, but its very satisfying in rooms that allow for it.Overall its an okay metroidvania, the progression pushes you into a really specific way of going, so its not very metroidvania-y, but still fun. Ultimately I decided to switch my review to recommended because the rest was great, just a few really annoying things like community secrets that you are not ever going to figure out by yourself, but if you don't care about that, fire away.
_childDocuments_.name: ANIMAL WELL

_childDocuments_.review: Came across this game while browsing the store and was immediately captured by it's pretty scenes of nature and stylized animation plus the dreamy music that accompanied it.This was the first game in a long time that I've purchased and played without having first heard about it online, and it was worth every penny. The soundtrack is surreal, and the music during exciting moments is top notch. I love the contrast of light and dark. The abilities are incredibly unique, each time I got a new item my expectations were subverted from that of generic movement in any other Metroidvania.10/10 Loved it!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not typically big on platformers. This one I've played for 8 hours almost straight, and I think I'll try to 100% the map. It's stunning visually and has brilliant sound design. In some ways it reminds me of exploring in Hollow Knight. I always feel like there'll be something surprising, beautiful, dangerous, or all three waiting in the next room - if I can just get to it. Every creature design is unique.The platforming is challenging and even punishing in parts. In typical metroidvania fashion, your access to various areas of the map is limited by the tools you have to traverse with, but these tools aren't only used for movement: you'll have to play around with them to figure out what else they can do.If you've just started the game and don't know what to do or where to go:Wander around. Poke at everything. Pretty early on you'll find a map that you fill in as you go along, which shows you room passages you haven't used yet. _childDocuments_.review: (SOME SPOILERS, also this is based on first playthrough where I only went to the first ending, I'll update this review once I dig deeper into the game if my thoughts change.) I've seen a lot of people who absolutely love this game, and the only the actual criticism I've seen directed at it is either people with huge skill issues, or people just complaining about the keyboard controls. I really enjoyed this game, but I don't think it's a masterpiece like many claim, at least not for me at this moment.The core metroidvania approach here is great, as it's main feature is the way that it foregoes combat, instead focusing entirely on it's exploration and puzzles to avoid and traverse around enemies. Out of all the metroidvania's I've played, this one reminds me the most of Super Metroid, and as great as that game is, I'd definetly argue that SM's combat is probably it's weakest element. So to take a similar approach but without combat is something that works quite well for this game. I got stuck a couple times and got a little bit frustrated, but that's the metroid formula at it's core, unless you really strip down the sense of exploration like with a game like Metroid Dread, it's inevitable that you'll get lost. I think this game is clearly well-designed enough that getting lost isn't a problem as I generally was able to figure out what to do after each pick-up or door unlocked, and the map is pretty easy to traverse through once you discover each area, so backtracking isn't tedious. Visually, the game is obviously very beautiful, such a sharp aesthetic with the scan lines which really help it feel unique and retro. However, something that might be controversial to say is that I wish the game had more visual variety. From what I played, I feel as if a lot of the areas look very similar, without too much distinction between them. There are some different shades of blue in different areas which is nice, but it dosen't have the same visual variety that a game like Hollow Knight, or even Super Metroid. For me, part of the fun of those games is the actual discovery of each area, and seeing the new theme and aesthetic of each new location. This game dosen't really have that, as the very most you'll see is a new shade of blue for each room and maybe a couple new background elements, for how much this game's visuals and exploration has been praised, It's weird to me I haven't seen more people talk about this. To summarize, the game has a timeless, memorable aesthetic, and the things in the areas like the puzzles and animals are memorable but the actual environments themselves just aren't memorable visually.Really, that right there is honestly my biggest criticism of the game, which shows just how good it is. The other closest thing I have to criticism is how the game's soundtrack is pretty limited, but It's very clear that the lack of music and the focus on the great sound design is a core design principle, so well I did sorta miss something like the masterpiece soundtrack of a game like Super Metroid, In this case, the game is fine with out it. That's pretty much my main thoughts on the game. I don't quite love it yet like many other seem to, as from what I played, it felt like a fun game that pays homage to a more classic style of game design. I think i'll be back though, as I imagine this game has so much more to offer through secrets, as the abrupt ending alongside cryptic final areas gives me a feeling that there's much more to see outside the main game. I've made a lot of comparisons to Super Metroid in this review, and that because not only are they very comparble, but Super Metroid is just straight up one of my favorite games of all time, and a big part of that game was that it literally got better on each playthrough for me, so who knows, maybe this game will work the same way for me.The last thing to note of is the price. Now for what this game offers, I think it's a very reasonable price, however in comparison to games like Hollow Knight or Terraria, it's on the pricer side of sprite-based indies. Really that's not because this game is overpriced, it's because those games are just so underpriced. If you've got the money, play this game. If you've already played those other games, play this game. However, if you are very strapped for cash and haven't played some of the other heavy-hitting indies, I would be lying if I said I wouldn't reccomend waiting for a bigger sale. TL;DR Great Game, worth the price, but dosen't feel like a masterpiece to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Score w/o Context: 60/64 EggsThe Context:I have a deep respect for movies that minimize their dialogue, leaving a lot of the narrative up to the director. A quickly exchanged look can convey just as much info as a monologue in a fraction of the time if done well. Similarly, leaving a player to their own devices in a game world and designing it in such a way as to be decipherable and explorable with minimal help can be mystifying. I think Animal Well largely succeeds at this goal, creating an easily navigated world with intuitive designs around every corner. Being a combat-less metroidvania lends an air of familiarity to the environments you are dropped into, but also a bit of helplessness. It isn't a danger-free game after all, you just can't really fight back. These two tones mix well together, with the pull of unexplored biomes contrasting with the fear of the unknown constantly during my 12 hour jaunt. It was always worth it to push through however, if only to find the next gorgeously animated creature or flexible puzzle solver (aka item).These items almost all had multiple uses throughout the journey, and all were unique in their form and function, controllable yo-yo being my personal favorite. The puzzles I mentioned before were vastly solvable with clever thinking or usage of your inventory, minus a couple beats near the end that I found a bit more unintuitive and esoteric. Exploration and backtracking also mostly hits the mark of this genre, with each journey back getting quicker and easier with practice. Good thing too, as this game has layers to its world rivalling only Tunic that I can remember recently, and you'll find yourself going back and forth a lot. This brings my to my final standout of the game, the map! It's incredibly helpful with gaps and highlighting possible new avenues to probe. Without it, I would've been lost many more times. Still, I never got tired of digging for new secrets, and that's a triumph of design.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard game to describe. It’s a Metroidvana with a focus on puzzles. The puzzles are the best part of the game. A bunch of times I went “Man! That was so cool!” when I figured out how to do it. So many little hints and ideas. Even after 100% (all eggs, items, achievements and the true ending) there’s a lot of secrets to find. One I found (cause of a Reddit post I passed) had a room with grass. The grass was in binary and if you played that number using the other secret code you open a room with a cool looking thing. Another one I actually found was a bone fish boss. Nothing feels cheap or stupid. I can see why people were calling this a game of the year. There is no other game I’ve seen or played just like this. No dialogue at all. No 5 minute cutscene before you can move. You just start. I like how it is all gameplay. This game was really fun and a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: Remember Fez and how it had layers of meta puzzles that used each-other as stepping stones? Remember how La Mulana took it a step too far and made it even harder and more esoteric? This game reigns in the meta elements of games like this, and successfully confuses you without you even knowing how and why you are. Every nook and cranny of this game has some form of secret. Every item you collect has some use the game never tells you about. The map itself plays with you and misdirects you on how to move forwards in a way that still lets you feel like you discovered how to do so.Environment Station Alpha is the closes game to this one in both truly meta puzzles and progression. You feel totally powerless and lost for most of the experience in a way no other game does. You don't defeat bosses, you outsmart them. The game has "stages" where the deeper you dig, the more details you have to find and contextualize. The eggs you find everywhere are its own ending, but also form part of another ending, which is of itself part of another ending. Counting a secret dev message, there's talk that there is at least 4 layers of secrets, with a theorized 5th layer that requires glitches the developers hint at occasionally. That's how deep the rabbit hole goes. Think easier than Noita's puzzles, but without the game difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: So the biggest question you should ask yourself is: Do you enjoy platforming? And medium-to-hard, somewhat traditional metroidvania mechanics, that over time diverge from tradition to create a helluva lot more than your typical metroidvania experience would have? Do you not mind occasional setbacks in pursuit of a goal? If so, you'll probably enjoy this.I happen to be built out of Skill Issues and as such it's not the game for me, but is one that I find intriguing nonetheless, and one which I recommend those with Bad-At-Platforming-Itus consider watching a blind playthrough of rather than calling it "bad" for being harder than you expected. I've heard this described as the metroidvania-ey equivalent of Outer Wilds, which imo is *the* greatest game of all time, from people who have played Outer Wilds but don't have the Skill Issues i do. And I can see how and why they came to that conclusion - but remember, in a metroidvania you have to EARN it. If you are up to that challenge, give it a go.If you aren't at least moderately good at platforming and resilient in the face of setbacks, you may not get far enough to truly appreciate what lurks under the surface of this title. I still highly recommend this even though I personally am too much of a klutz to sink the time needed into it to overcome my lack of dexterity.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings on the game.  I like the aesthetic, and the animal theme reminds me of Kero Blaster, which is a beloved game for me.  However, the obtuse game design, pixel-perfect speedrunning platform sections in the mid-late game, and punishing backtracking when you mistime a jump or fail to move quickly enough in certain sections detract from the game.My overall complaint for the game is that it does not respect the player's time, and with no story, no music, no combat, etc., the punishing backtracking and archaic map system, it makes me question why I should waste my time on searching for eggs or other post game content when I can just watch a video of it (if I wanted to) instead and save my time, and honestly there were several times before I beat the game where I stopped because the game felt like a fruitless waste of time.  There's very little payoff.Now I don't want to be all negative, there are elements of a very good game in there, and there are compelling moments.  But the game didn't live up to my expectations. _childDocuments_.review: This is a metroidvania that's nearly exclusively puzzles and platforming. If you're attacking an enemy it's just to scare it off, and more frequently you're running from them. Many puzzles have multiple solutions and the upgrades are unique and novel for the genre. Beating the game will probably take about 4 hours with postgame tripling that or more.Puzzles are generally solved by putting together various techniques you've gathered and those techniques interacting in certain ways. Nothing outside of bonus collectibles requires things like ciphers, math (beyond addition), or musical knowledge, with the exception of one puzzle that requires knowing technical definitions of certain words but that can be googled, and I don't believe there's an ARG within the game.There's one puzzle that can't be solved alone that you'll need to find information online for, but the rest is theoretically doable without any guides or outside knowledge -- though finding the final ones yourself would be extremely difficult.As for the game's weaknesses, there isn't good hinting for where unfound collectibles are, so without a guide you'll have to scour the map repeatedly. There's also two early game items that enable you to have infinite height with certain techniques, which is never required to solve any puzzle but players encounter puzzles aimed for later game items that can be solved with the infinite height techniques that then lead them to believe it's an intended mechanic. Some items also have quite limited use.Overall pretty enjoyable for about 8 hours and then quite a bit of mindless wandering and searching.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually review games, so I'll admit I'm doing it for the Steam Awards gamification rewards.With that out of the way. I'm voting Animal Well for GOTY, Innovative Gameplay and Best Game on Deck. Of these three categories, the one that describes it the best is Innovative Gameplay.Lots of "innovative" games nowadays mix two genres or come up with one original mechanic and call it a day. Animal Well becomes its own thing by rejecting all the typical moves you get in a Metroidvania like Double Jump and Dash. Instead, the game gives you several tools, each one with little tricks to learn and tons of situations to take advantage of them. All the tools come with their own original mechanics. As an extra touch, they are all based on toys, which really fits in the context of it being a game.Everything the game has, it's been honed to perfection. I'm sure there are, but I can't find any flaws with the game. I could argue is perfect on every aspect.I'm not a huge fan of Metroidvanias, but this game had me hooked from start to end.Get it, full price or sale, it will be worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: Will try to minimize spoilers, play this game! Puzzle-focused metroidvanias are an interesting twist on what metroidvania fans think of when they hear "exploration focused gameplay". Usually, the more combat focused games like Metroid and Castlevania are what draw me to the genre, but a puzzle focused one with good mechanics and gameplay can make for a really unique experience. I am really glad Animal Well delivered on this idea in style. Even though it strays from the titles we have come to know and love, it still gives nods to other games ().The game tosses you right in, and you are left to figure out the mechanics through experience and the subtle cues the game gives throughout. It can take some time to grasp what the game expects of you with certain mechanics, but usually it becomes evident when right path is forward, and you're left to think on a puzzle for a bit. The game has a pretty engaging learning curve, and you get choices, especially once you play around with items. The one annoyance I had was that the locked doors that require keys are the same colour as the closed gates that you unlock with buttons. From far away on the TV, it took me time to realize I could progress because I thought a key door was a button gate. Similarly, some areas look very cluttered with detail, so it can be hard to pick out platforms in some areas, but the detail is always stunning and it doesn't hinder gameplay much.The item names themselves don't sound like anything crazy, but in practice, the puzzles have a lot of variety and lead to some of the coolest "aha" moments I have ever seen in a game (). Encounters can sometimes feel "boss like", but the game is never setting the expectation of bosses, so the simple setups of some of them didn't bother me. Even the regular enemy encounters are often immersive, because the game's environment is more subtle and quiet, until animals break the silence and even jumpscare a little. It's cute, yet unsettling, and a sense of massive relief comes when the game finishes, because in each room, you question what's safe.This is probably the only puzzle focused metroidvania I can recommend right now, at least for a first play through () it's excellent and pushes the boundaries in a lot of ways with it's gameplay and vibes.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves the Metroidvania genre, I struggle to find enjoyment out of one so obtuse in its level and puzzle design that I quit before completing it.I found myself lost and annoyed way too often, struggling to understand what I was doing wrong in many portions of the map just to find out I either didn't have the right item locked away in a portion of the map or that I just wasn't using it exactly how the single developer intended it to be used. Which I understand is the case for a lot of Metroidvanias, I just feel others have done this medium more justice by not tossing the player into the fire or treating them like a dumbass for not immediately understanding the game's processes.Building the entire game's progression on finding "secret eggs,' hidden around the map seems cool at first but becomes irritating the closer you get to the 64 that are scattered around. Since the map doesn't mark down the areas of the ones you found, an online guide is almost certainly a must.I didn't find the sound or music all that compelling which is a shame because games like these can be carried a lot by a killer soundtrack and sound design.Some positives: The visuals are incredible. It feels like playing through a zoo full of neon lights and many of the individual animal areas are quite unique. There is still stuff to enjoy here, I just myself cannot recommend it as I don't hate anyone enough for that.Overall, an alright first go for a developer with a lot of potential, that I personally struggle to gel with. I'm definitely in the minority here haha. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Metroidvania with interesting movement tech. 8/10. Unfortunately, I can only recommend the game with hestitation, due to how sucky the lategame is.You beat the final challenge. Credits roll -- but it doesn't feel satisfying. You walk through an ending area that screams: "There's more to find! You're not done!!!"If only I were done. What comes next is a sludgefest of rubbing multiple different metal detectors over the entire map, one pixel at a time. This journey is accompanied by ARG-style puzzles. Some of these puzzles are good. Some have the design sensibilities of NotPron, requiring a player to brute force 120 reasonable interpretations of a clue. At least one is literally impossible to solve without buying 100+ copies of the game. If you're stuck on a puzzle, there is no way to tell which of these is the case. I imagine this was fun for the players collaborating on the Discord 24 hours after release, and that's beautiful. But it's not fun for me to solve on my own.I would happily ignore all this if the game had any satisfying ending. But the developer clearly wanted to tantalize players into diving into the ARG sludge. And that leaves a sour taste in my mouth.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing through the metroidvania part, I would recommend that to any fans of the genre or just platformers in general. The atmosphere is great. Loads of care and love was put into it and I think the developer was amazing making this. It's expensive for a 5 hour game but its not bad. My issue with it is that most of its intended content is a puzzle game, and not an exploration based puzzle platformer like I thought. The whole idea is that its a mystery that the player works out (and a very difficult one at that). So the game is placed in the same kind of genre as Outer Wilds, or other games I haven't played for reasons that I hope will be clear. You are told nothing and have to work out the game by yourself or with the community, and every space in the map is a room. The whole world is a big puzzle that you have to solve. The issue is that its a puzzle, not a mystery. There's no emotional hook, there's no sign of reward, there's nothing I wanted an answer to. There's not really exploration, you've seen all the areas once you finish the metroidvania, its not like Dark Souls where there is an amazing and spectacular area hidden away. The whole world is a puzzle but there is no mystery to the whole world. I love intriguing worlds like Dark Souls or Rain World where information has to be earned and you have to think about it. I love narrative games with difficult puzzles like Signalis because in these games the puzzles give weight to the narrative and I have a reason to solve them. I love Outer Wilds because it doesn't feel like you're solving puzzles, it feels like you're solving the mystery. I love problem solving under pressure where there are stakes, or science problem solving. I hate all puzzle games. Except for maybe Portal as the exception. There's no satisfaction for me in doing these boring problem solving tasks where there is no reward other than the satisfaction of solving that task. There's no world to uncover here, there is no lore or characters or anything other than repeated mechanical tasks on small scales and big scales. It's boring and not fun and I am deeply disappointed. Call me schizo but puzzle games scare me because of how clinical and soulless they are. This is a really good horror game if nothing else.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably my favorite game of 2024 so far.  I absolutely loved how it dropped me into this mysterious world without telling me a single thing, and left it up to me to experiment and explore, and figure everything out.  Unlike most games, Animal Well treats you like you have a functioning brain, and as a result it feels VERY rewarding to solve its many puzzles.  Most metroidvanias tend to have little hand-holding, but I feel Animal Well takes it to the next level.  It'll also test your dexterity at times, too, though nothing on par with something like Super Meat Boy or Celeste.  More puzzly than platformy, though there is ONE moment that might have your palms sweating.The art style is also beautiful, especially on a OLED screen, and the audio design is stellar.  I love how most of the game doesn't have music, but what's there fits the game perfectly.  The quietness of the soundtrack allows you to focus on all the fantastic ambient audio, which coupled with the groovy colors of the art design and atmospheric environments can at times be rather peaceful.And all this made almost entirely by one person, optimized down to just 40MB of storage.  Yes, that's right: megabytes, not gigabytes.  I had to do a double-take, myself.If I had ONE gripe (and only one), it's that at least one of the later puzzles I've run into (after beating the game) required the entire gaming community to solve.  You simply couldn't do it on your own, unless you no life the game which would require MANY MANY playthroughs and would be an absolute chore.  I just don't find this kind of puzzle appealing.  All puzzles in a singleplayer game should be solvable by the one person playing it.  And of course the game doesn't tell you that it's impossible for you to do it alone, and I'm pretty stubborn, so I spent a good while trying to figure it out without Googling.  So I was a tad disgruntled when I discovered that I was wasting my time.Other than that, I had a blast with Animal Well, and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys puzzle platformers and metroidvanias.  It's among the best.  Play it on a OLED panel if you can.

_childDocuments_.review: To say near anything will spoil the joy. _childDocuments_.review: You may have seen multiple reviews stating this game has several layers. That’s true, and you’ll need to decide how far you want to go.The first layer is simply completing the game without focusing much on collectibles, just to see the basic ending. It’s fun, and the visuals are a real treat for the eyes (I’d even say it’s one of the most beautiful pixel art styles ever). Playing with all the instruments feels amazing. For most people, this is where you should stop, admire the game, and move on to something else.The second layer is finding all the  and witnessing the . At this point, the game might start to irritate you. With each new instrument, you’ll be forced to backtrack — A LOT. You may revisit almost every area 2, 3, or even 5 times, just to see if your latest tool reveals new secrets or collectibles. If you really want to continue here, I recommend using a guide or map to minimize aimless backtracking.The next layers are where I think you should stop unless you were absolutely thrilled by the previous two. This is where the hardest challenges lie, and they WILL take an enormous amount of your time, even with guides. The community collectively solved many of these puzzles, so the chances of figuring them out on your own are slim. If you’re still curious, I’d suggest watching some YouTube videos of the hardcore players who spent countless hours unlocking these "rewards."TL;DR: The game is amazing, but you should suppress your inner completionist.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic example of what a game should be. A pinnacle of game design. Complex puzzles with great eureka moments! A vast world to explore that has so much depth and character and feels very much alive. Several times, during my playthrough to the end credits I found myself saying "this guy is a f***ing genius!" Plenty of "oh sh*t", "wtf", and panic inducing moments that caught me off guard and copious amounts of satisfaction from overcoming those challenges makes this game a clear GOTY so far for me. Easily sitting in my top 10 games of all time.A game that once finished still has so much to offer, and I find myself thinking about stuff I have missed or having ideas on how I can approach stuff whilst I'm not even playing, itching to get back to it with any amount of spare time I have. Props to Billy Basso for an incredible feat in gaming and BigMode on their first published game! An easy 10/10, for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't mean to gate keep with this comment but, this game is not for everyone.I don't know if its even for me. I've had some moments of pure frustration being stuck on a puzzle for longer than i would think the average person would be, rage quitting then coming back a few hours later to solve it. I've been debating myself if it was just bad game design or if i'm just bad at puzzles.Maybe I went into it with the wrong mind set of oh it'll be a casual fun kids game, its not, the description of "metroid-brainia" is very fair.When things don't click I feel stupid which sucks but when things do click it really is an ah-ha moment.Lets move to less about my feelings and more from a technical side, from a programming stand point Billy did a crazy good job, the particle fluid simulations are beautiful, the pixel art is beautiful, the soundscapes are beautiful, music is rarely used mostly conserved for "safe rooms" and more tense sequences, its very effective for setting the mood; all in a nice compact 35-ish Megabytes.At the start you're not locked into one path so you are free to explore a rather large part of the map before being item restricted from progressing.The inter-connectivity of the map is great, I think it's brilliantly designed there is a lot of "oh how do i get there, lemme make a note of that for later" and there's some crazy secrets, secret areas, secrets within secrets.At the time of writing this I've completed the main line for the game and now I'm working on side content. _childDocuments_.review: Disclamer for this review: I am currently on the 3/4th layer of depth this game has to offer and currently working with friends/the community to figure out what exactly we need to do next. I've gotten all the collectibles we know of so far.It should also be mentioned that if you stumbled across this review or one of the ones that ACTUALLY TALKS ABOUT THE GAME please understand those are the truest reviews here, I've heard many people are hesitant to check out this game because of all the """funny""" joke reviews. This is a genuinely great game that deserves your time, not an epic wacky wahoo youtuber moment. Remember that Dunkey is the publisher that helped fund/get eyes on the game, not Billy Basso; the dev who made 100% of everything himself.Animal is a puzzle-focused metroidvania with little to no "direct combat". Rather than approach the game as a sort of action-combat platformer animal well is primarily focused on its collectibles post game content as well as its main first ending. Its hard to go into detail about either of this without spoiling much of the game itself.This is a game that treats the player with a ton of respect, never outright telling you how an item or mechanic works but rather being forgiving enough (in most cases) for the player to figure it out themselves. Some instances of collectibles or pathways in this game often require the player to figure out a new clever way to use an item, often in combination with another at the same time Link's Awakening style.At the time of writing this I've completed the first ending and I'm not sure how much more is deeper below, I've got a current goal in mind in finding the remaining items + collectibles but I know there's much more to be found besides that, this gaming having so much packed into it and only being 34 MB is genuinely a feat of programming and game design as a whole. Overall? This is one of the best metroidvanias/games in general I've played in quite some time, it treats the player with a great deal of respect and trusts that they're smart enough to figure out even the wildest puzzles, alongside giving you mapping tools and markers the game is incredibly accessible no matter what level of completionist you may be.

_childDocuments_.review: The Classic Marathon (originally released in 1994) that just released (for free) on Steam is 66 megabytes. This game released in 2024 is f*cking 40 megabytes. How? No, seriously... how??? The lighting, the sound design, the pixel art, the v i b e s. The cat alone feels like it should be 40 mb worth of visuals and code data and yet this entire game is 40 megabytes. I have no reason to ever uninstall it. Steamdeck users have no reason to ever uninstall it.Thankfully, the game that you have no excuse for ever uninstalling is also fantastic, like "blew me away" fantastic not just good. Not the cat, though, the cat was an assh*le. I am quite well known by my friends and community as someone that rather strongly dislikes Metroidvanias. I liked Hollow Knight, Rain World was cool, Ori was pretty nice, but the rest of them? Ehhhhh, not for me. Animal Well is definitely a metroidvania, and it also has a ton of puzzles which I also typically don't like, but thats because Billy Basso doesn't make the puzzles in every game I play, he just made the puzzles in this game and damn if they aren't smart as hell. There's no tutorializing, much like Rain World you just kinda figure stuff out because of really strong map design and puzzle design that leads to you intuitively trying the correct thing. I took my time puttering around in the 5 hours I have so far (1/4 of the big goals collected... f*cking cat...) and I have yet to truly encounter something that completely stumps me. It always makes sense and I don't think thats just me and the game vibing, I think thats just what happens when someone as clever and talented as Billy Basso makes a video game. I really appreciate a lot of little stuff about Animal Well, this stuff is mostly personal taste but still. The deaths when they happen are quick and without fanfare, you get a zero delay respawn and then back to it. The saves are in great spots and most platforming or really any kind of challenge the game lays out doesn't bend for you to beat it but it does place significant amounts of shortcuts and tools for you to get back to that challenge quickly if you fail it. One of the things that drives me nuts about Metroidvanias as a genre is going reaaaally far in one direction, trying to find a save so you can explore more comfortably and then dying and seeing that you're like 7 miles away from where you died when you respawn. That? That makes me not want to play these games. Animal Well doesn't suffer from that. The map is laid out in such a manner that no matter where you might die you are almost always only a few rooms away from getting back there. Its just... its so well made. The visuals: I am not qualified to describe in detail about *why* it looks so good and still only takes up 40 mb of space BUT I do know that the lighting and the VFX are gorgeous. This game can run on a f*cking sentient potato and it looks and sounds this good, actual black magic. The only reason I'm reviewing this game before I've finished it is because I want it to sell more, I want Bigmode to succeed more, I want Billy Basso to be able to hole away and work on as much cool stuff as he wants or just retire, I want creative people to be able to do creative things and Bigmode/Dunkey's marketing working and setting an example for how to lift up cool weird indie games like Animal Well is such a massive win for the industry. Discoverability is the biggest hurdle for most indies and yet here we are, Animal Well being the #1 top seller on day 1 of its launch. I made a video talking about why this is such a huge thing for the indie industry if you're interested, and if you'd like to read more reviews my curator page is linked at the top of my profile. Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: ANIMAL WELL has a breathtaking aesthetic, satisfying puzzles, and tight platforming. I really love how it has a hidden layer of extremely complex and ARG-like puzzles. Even if you choose not to pursue solving them, they contribute to this horror atmosphere the game has of foreboding complexity and obscured depths. If you're looking for a comparison, it's like a cross between FEZ's puzzles and Super Metroid's overall structure and alien horror.  But make no mistake, just like Super Metroid, you will find yourself wandering around areas you've already been to if you intend to find all of those secrets. If there's one gripe I had with the game, it's that the real difficulty of finding the secret eggs really wasn't the small puzzles that guarded the various eggs' treasure chests, but instead stumbling around the large map aimlessly, retreading the same platforming puzzles hoping to find some nook or cranny I had overlooked that might have an egg inside. There is something you can find to make this search very slightly easier, but I only personally found it after I had 59/64 eggs. I already knew where the remaining ones were, too, but I didn't have an item I needed to get to them. Eventually I needed to look up a hint, since I had spent hours searching after I realized the egg-hunting item wasn't the item I was looking for. Well, it turned out that the last item I needed was gated behind finding the secret of using five hidden "keys". Except, I already figured out the puzzle of using the keys, I just hadn't stumbled upon the remaining two keys after hours of wandering around. My problem was that I wasn't sure if I needed the item to find the keys or if I needed to explore around more for the keys to find the item. Really, that kind of dilemma is always looming in a puzzle-heavy Metroidvania. Are you just stumped by the solution to the puzzle, or are you lacking some critical item to solve it? Even if you're convinced it's the latter, how much backtracking can you take before you decide to look up a guide? These are problems endemic to the genre, so if you know this part of Metroidvanias really bothers you ANIMAL WELL might not be your cup of tea. That all having been said, I still think overall this game does a great job communicating wordlessly that you might not have a tool you need to solve its puzzles, and that one trip up wasn't nearly enough to sour my experience. If you like Metroidvanias or are curious about the genre or this game's aesthetic, I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Animal Well is fun and mystical for the first few hours. Reaching the ending of the game will leave you satisfied if you are content with only finishing the game. However, if you are someone that finds thrill in uncovering all the deep mysteries of a game and feeling truly rewarded for your hard work and ingenuity - this game is not for you.I've personally 100% Animal Well. This is not a proclamation for achievement, but I hope some will understand I went the distance to give this game an earnest try by seeing all it had to offer.In Animal Well, you will find the graphical beauty, cutesy fantastical vibe, and the creative mind that went into this game. You will not view yourself creative though. Every puzzle will be a challenge which may or may not come naturally to you, and that's okay. The beauty of playing the game to its end is wrapping your head around what nonsense was intended versus what you actually concocted. This remains true until the end of the game. Once the credits roll and players begin their hunt for the game's remaining secrets, the critique begins to manifest.There is a sincere lack of mobility, so back tracking will be a slog on a map so large. This may give you the opportunity to uncover secrets you had previously missed, or fill you with frustration that you are again trekking back where you just came from. Puzzles are narrowed down to a single intended solution and your tools will appear niche. You will receive a treasure and discover it's applicable uses can be counted on one hand. If you track the furthest layer of secrets, you will see that you aren't meant to solve some puzzles alone and will require online help, a physical printer, or even complete an ARG. These solutions have been discovered and posted online already, but if you are expecting to complete this game 100%, you can not do so alone. It is impossible. There is not a hint of dialogue or a guiding hand past the main game.If you are to enjoy the main game for the cute puzzles it presents on the surface or tackle the senseless secrets that become further obscured and frustrating as you get deeper down, this game is for you. If you were hoping for something more or a sensation of reward, please save your time and money. This is a neutral-positive recommendation. I just don't believe being frustrating is a valid reason to not recommend a game.

Basically every single room has some puzzle elements, which makes the backtracking excruciating slow and boring. I've already solved the puzzles, I don't want to do them again and again every time I want to go to a different part of the map.I'm at a point in the game where I have a new item but not sure what to do next, and it's completely sapped my enthusiasm to figure it out because I really don't want to comb through the entire map all over again and do everything all over a second or even a third + times. _childDocuments_.review: A delightful metroidvania with a focus on exploration rather than combat. Instead of traditional upgrades, you collect various items that can be used to help traverse the world and solve puzzles. The ways in which these items interact with the environment are very clever and satisfying. As you play through Animal Well, you will continue to discover new use cases for your items. There were multiple occasions where I crossed an obstacle or discovered a secret in a way that made me question whether or not I did it the "intended" way.For me, this is where Animal Well really shines. The game is relatively non-linear and chock full of secrets, so playing around with your items and finding your own ways to get around comes naturally. Speaking of secrets, the mysteries of Animal Well are appropriately deep. There are multiple layers of hidden extras after beating the "main" game, so if you're someone who enjoys going down a rabbit hole of puzzles, Animal Well might be up your alley. But even if you're not, the game's strong overall mechanics and gameplay are still worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Short but a pretty novel game. The powerups are pretty creative for the genre (no double jumps as far as I can tell). The puzzles were satisfying to solve. The backtracking is pretty repetitive and it was wearing me out towards the end, but I did get to the credits. I would recommend playing the game in multiple sittings very casually. Don't bother pushing through the game. There is a postgame, I do not know what its about nor care to do it.I think its a bit expensive for the experience, but I don't regret buying it. _childDocuments_.review: Animal Well is a unique game that combines aspects of various different genres to create something special. This game takes the metroidvania style but uses it as a base for the main focus of secret-hunting, similar to FEZ. The game just throws you into it, as the player awakens from their pod and is set to venture into the different biomes of the well. As they explore, they find various different tools to use, different animals living within the well, and many, many secrets to find.I enjoyed my playthrough of the game thoroughly, as I loved the organic nature of learning the mechanics of the game. I'd get a new tool, mess with it a bit to understand it on the surface, and then use it in a new way accidentally hours later. While that may not be nice for some people, it fits the vision of this game perfectly. As a puzzle game, I also really appreciated the different "layers" of the well. It makes the game more accessible to people who aren't as keen on the puzzle-solving aspect, allowing them to choose how deep into the well they want to go. The spritework done for the game is very pleasing to look at, really giving off the proper vibes that each area of the well is trying to present, especially when working in tandem with the lighting engine. Overall, Animal Well is a great game, and if you enjoy solving puzzles with some light platforming, you'll probably enjoy it as well!

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Halo 2 meets Halo 32024/05/16 edit:Animal Well has been a great surprise for me.I usually do not like Metroidvanias because I think the tight gameplay makes the experience very frustrating for me, like when you lose progress because you fell on the last jump.But with Animal Well I just get so immersed into the game that I do not realise I have been stuck on the same screen, or, since the game is clearly "open-world", I think I just don't have the tools right now and go somewhere else.The graphics are stunning, there is something about the aesthetic of the game that, I didn't really like that much at the beginning but now I absolutely love it.The puzzles blow my mind, like, how come a single guy come up with so many different ideas? It feels like when I first played Mario Oddisey, in both games I was constantly impressed by the number of mechanics that keep coming even though when you feel like your toolbox is complete.I honestly bought this game just for the memes but I was blown my socks off. I understand why this was the publisher's first release, because this is a powerful way of coming out to the world. I expect both the publisher and the developer give us more of this because I am loving it!

_childDocuments_.review: Much more compelling game design than Metroid Dread (AKA The last metroidvania I played), in terms of both level design and the versatility of the upgrades you receive. The open-ended nature makes me want to start a new game seeing how far I can get with only one item, then another with a different one. Lots of replay value. Tight controls. The somewhat lack of an OST actually fits the atmosphere of the game (what else do you expect to hear trapped in a well?) and aurally, this game's strength is in its sound design - not music.Another thing worth mentioning is that this world is DENSE. It requires a mind in overdrive to create a large open world that doesn't waste its own space.Inevitably every metroidvania enthusiast will compare the brand new metroidvania to Hollow Knight, here are my takeaways:- Gameplay and design are by far in Animal Well's favor- This game is not as beautiful as Hollow Knight and it shouldn't be. This is one guy using Aseprite and (if I saw the end credits correctly), Reaper, a free DAW. - This is actually not the same offshoot of metroidvania as HK. HK's gameplay is mostly action-oriented, this may have a sprinkle of it but it's almost nothing but puzzle solving and platforming.- The secrets in this game are not as formulaic as HK. The 'grubs' exist in the form of eggs, but after my first playthrough I have things in my inventory that I'm yet to even fathom how to use. What the hell is a pencil for? I have half of a medallion? For what?

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems like it ought to be right up my alley. I love metroidvanias and I love brainy games. Unfortunately, it really rubbed me the wrong way. I found myself feeling vaguely annoyed the whole time I was playing it through. It felt like there were design decisions that make the user experience just a little more user hostile in almost every area.* Enemies who ambush you and kill you the first time you enter a room.* Knowing how to solve a puzzle, but having to navigate a finicky platforming challenge to finish it.* The map is awkward to use, and the tools you have to mark it are way too limited for the number of curiosities you will want to flag.* When looking for secrets I would often find myself poring over the map for the tiniest gap in boundaries. It's so tiny, though, that it's really hard to look at.* Some of the late game items open up new pathways, but until you get them you don't even have a clear sign that those pathways exist. If you don't notice them, you won't think to mark them on your map, which means you basically have to re explore the whole map again and again each time you gain a new item.* It doesn't pause the game when you pull up the map, which makes the chase sequences even more frustrating.* Switching items is super awkward for a game that requires so much of it. A radial menu would have been handy. Some of the items are passives, but you need to have them as your active item for them to be active. It would be nice if you could toggle them and still use other items while they're active.* The visual contrast is really bad. Even if you know something is there, it can be really hard to parse out what it is, even with the contrast way up.* And, while beautiful, the visual style is oddly inconsistent. Different animals are rendered with varying degrees of fidelity. Some are beautifully shaded and rendered and others are vague blobby representations.Probably my biggest complaint, though, is that so much of the game is nigh impossible to solve without external resources. I don't mind a couple of things that I have to look up, but it seems like probably at least a third of the content is too obscure to figure out without a hint. I could have solved more of it if I were willing to spend a dozen more hours scouring every inch of the well. That's not puzzle solving, though, it's just scut work.This kind of game could be a lot of fun if you're part of the initial rush to figure everything out, discussing it with everybody else playing it. But beyond that point, you're basically stuck having a guide up for a good chunk of the game, which really takes the satisfaction out of the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I have completed the game, including all of the achievements.  The following is my fair assessment of the game's strengths and weaknesses, and I trend towards the technical, especially when it comes to nitpicks.Short version: If you aren't a One Piece fan, you might want to give this one a miss.  Enjoyment of this game is extremely dependent on this factor.As a JRPG, this game is extremely laid back.  You will not find any real challenge until the very end, and then essentially only with the optional content outside of the story.  This was definitely one of my main gripes with the game.  But I eventually realized that this was done in order to keep the gameplay loop from interfering with the story progression.  By and large, the game is balanced so that as long as you defeat every map enemy you see exactly once, you're set.  Balanced both in terms of enemy difficulty and tolerable enjoyment.  By that I mean this game doesn't inspire a desire to grind for levels, nor does it require this from the player.The story is exactly what you would expect: A contrivance is conjured to provide an excuse for the Strawhats to relive the events of the story, just as generally occurs in the Pirate Warriors games.  There is a LOT of dialogue from just about everyone in the anime.  Enough to fill a season.  This helps considerably in selling the idea that you're taking part in the anime.The combat has a surprisingly functional gimmick that perpetually inspires the player to do more than hit attack—fights simply take too long to finish if one is literally that lazy.  And here is where the game's biggest strength shines: The character animations for various attacks are extremely well done.  Easily the highest tier of competence in the game was lavished right here.  This turns out to be important, since fighting ends up being about half of what they player does in this game.The music is serviceable with the occasional shining moment.  It's certainly not completely forgettable, but also not something you'd add to your playlist.  It's about as good as, say, the average Sakuraba OST—this is not praise, but not a condemnation.  It would have been surprising if the soundtrack had been amazing, but I wasn't expecting it to be.  As is tradition with anime-turned-game, there are ZERO references to the anime's music, front to back.Sound effects are about on par here.  Just like with the music, even when there were definitely certain sounds that are always used in the anime for certain moments—such as Sanji's air hop, or the sound of Law's Room ability—the game doesn't tap those sounds and instead just comes up with something of its own.  Disappointing, but entirely within precedent.This game uses an accessory system that has no meaningful balance.  In a game where difficulty simply does not come into play, it could be argued that a lack of balance doesn't matter.  Indeed, I just about ignored the accessories until I reached the end of the game and began grinding out the remainder of the levels, at which point I went about as ham as I could with making my characters overpowered... because the endgame/post-game is the only time when the content is actually truly balanced against those accessories.  This feels like the correct way to approach the accessory topic: Don't pay much attention to them until you reach the end, and then go crazy.  It's satisfying that the game DOES give the player a reason to grind out some powerful accessories, if only at the very end.Exploration is there, but not much rewarded.  Things are only rarely cleverly hidden.  Luffy gets a haki detection ability that's intended to find hidden items, but actually discovering anything with said ability is extremely rare and, if you will pardon the mild spoiler, almost entirely limited to moments when you've fought a new boss—you almost invariably locate their codex entry if you do a search.  Since there are no rewards or achievements tied to this, the only incentive is headcanon completionism.  The same thing goes for finding hidden items that only Sanji and Nami can see: They're there, at least, but you get nothing unique out of it, the game doesn't reward you, and it's all headcanon.  The exception to this is Robin, whose hidden items are required if one is interested in finishing the game's list of tasks.Small nitpick: This is the kind of game that will inexplicably hide food items and ingredients in chests.  Meaning you'd better be prepared not to treat this game as something immersive.  Treasure chests tucked away in dungeons for who knows how long will very frequently contain MEALS.  Meals which SHOULD have been something only Sanji could prepare for you.The graphics are better than I expected them to be.  With a 3080, the game can be played at a flat 4K 60fps from start to finish, and the only hiccups I ever saw were in the "strange place", possibly because the room is very busy and shows every crew member simultaneously.  Unfortunately, because the engine is UE4, one has very little choice but to use temporal anti-aliasing, which always causes afterimages on objects moving in contrast with the background.  Comically, the pre-rendered cutscenes, which always play at 30fps, were very clearly rendered in UE4 themselves, as they ALSO reveal the artifacting characteristic of TAA.My recommendation of this game is a bit like how I might recommend a One Piece movie: It's a spinoff, but it treats the property with respect and care, it uses the real voice cast fair and square, and it has a pretty high production value.  Fans of the anime are the target audience.  Pure JRPG fans should probably stay away unless you're out of options and need that blank filled.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I love One Piece to death, and i preordered the deluxe edition as there were many, many positive thoughts on the game and there still is, everybody is talking about the positives. Here are my thoughts so far.The game is, in my opinion, the best looking one piece game there is, all the artistic details can not go unnoticed. The sand, for example, has the style of a straw basket, making it look torn from the manga, with various other impressive visual details to boot.But to be frank, that's about where my praise ends. The combat has a very interesting idea, with multiple small battles happening at once in a turn based style. However i find the execution was rather poor, as for all the interesting ideas implemented, its really just using the best attack repeatedly. the auto battle shows this best, as even the AI simply uses the same attack over and over again. The fact that there is an auto battle system should show you already how repetitive the game can get, along with a speed multiplier which seems like it was ripped out of a mobile game. Continuing with the combat segments, where during game-play you spend most of your time, the UI is extremely cumbersome, with blinking lights everywhere, making it very hard to tell who you are targeting. One last thing for this section is the actual encounters. All random encounters seem to have three possible variations, randomly picked, and as such you can have the same fight multiple times in a row, making me personally at least avoid random encounters at all costs, as they just feel repetitive.Leaving combat, the other thing you are doing most is walking around. seeing all the characters in a three dimensional space is very fun, but the walking animations for most of them seem very static, after looking at each of them for a while, Zoro and Luffy just felt incomplete. for Luffy, the one you are likely to walk around with the most, while his general walking animation is decent, his main use is to zip to a point, not unlike the latest SpiderMan game, however there is little fluidity or  realistic momentum, and the second he get to where you "zip" to, all momentum is lost and he falls strait down. Continuing on, however, the story to the point i am, which i assume is little more than half way through the Alabasta arc, is consistently fetch quest after fetch quest. for example, a bird wants ten nuts, which all happen to be in birds nests throughout the town. however Luffy cant knock them down, even though they are all within reach of him, so to have the player use more characters, in this case Ussop, who is used to shoot them down. The world itself is also extremely linear, not allowing you to leave the path essentially ever, and from a game called "Odyssey" that is somewhat disheartening. there are invisible walls everywhere not allowing Luffy to jump down from the pillar hes on without first being dropped to the vines below. (said vines are on almost everything climbable as well) and if you attempt to jump down or walk off the edge of anything Luffy says the same line on repeat with absolutely no variation.For the final section id just like to point out the level system... during the first area of game-play, one fight is able to get you three or so levels at a time, with the stats each character has skyrocket. At the end of each fight, your characters will say something along the lines of, it wasn't my blades, it was me (not a direct quote), which can happen even after Zoro one shots the entire group of enemy's. in general, i love the idea of the game, but there are too many issues with the actual gamplay and story for me to recommend this to anybody, as playing this for any amount of time leaves me drained looking for the next checkpoint so i can quit. It seems I'm alone in this however, as all I've seen online has just been nothing besides praise. Either way, that's all I have to say.
