_childDocuments_.review: Hokko Life is an Animal Crossing clone arriving on Steam Early Access the June 2nd. This is a title that clearly tries to exploit the absence of Animal Crossing on the PC gaming landscape, similarly to how Temtem used the absence of a Pokémon game. But Hokko Life doesn’t only try to copy the mechanics of the brand, adding instead interesting feature that will please a lot of Animal Crossing’s fans!Sleeping on a TrainHokko Life makes a very short introduction on how we got the little dusty city in the middle of nowhere that we will call home: we overslept on the train and ended up there! And, how! How unfortunate! The next train will take days to come! Luckily, the little bar that we find ourselves in is filled with two very kind gentlemen (can an elephant be a gentleman?) that offer us a place to stay for a few nights. Obviously, in order to repay them, we will offer our help to make this little forgotten town a little bit more welcoming to new visitors!This quick introduction, while not particularly original, allows us to put our hands on the game immediately, without the need to wait for long dialogues that could’ve been boring. After that, we start off immediately with a place to sleep and our trusty axe: the latter will be particularly useful in the first two hours of the game, since most of the quests will involve gathering wood to build a bunch of items. In these first two hours we are also introduced to new characters, all different animals following Animal Crossing’s tradition, and complete a bunch of quests for them, culminating in the building of the first home for a new citizen.As for its current state, the very first hours of the game leave little freedom to the player in terms of activities: we will in fact work for the various NPCs that inhabit the village, gathering resource, crafting items and placing them, all according to their requests. In terms of gameplay, this quickly becomes a checklist of things to do: – go to Oma to get the quest – gather x resources – go to Moss to deliver them – Moss crafts something and asks us to place it wherever we want. I certainly would’ve appreciated to have more choices during this first part, in order to break the otherwise serrated rhythm of the initial quests.After the first bunch of quests, you’ll get access to the more advanced features that Hokko Life offers to its players: besides having items to craft, like in Animal Crossing, you will also have the possibility to design completely new items. This is done by starting from smaller, craftable parts, like a wooden leg of a chair or a plank of wood: by using for leg and one plank, for example, we could create a small table to decorate our home or, if we are willing to share, also the entire village by putting it outside. This system gives an incredible degree of freedom to the players, allowing them to create incredible items to display in their villages, with some limitations: the first one is that complex objects will obviously use more items to craft, plus the designed object must fit inside a bounding box that limits the size of the final result. In this case, bigger objects can designed by talking to Sallie, the carpenter, who sells both bigger bounding boxes and new item pieces to merge together.Obviously all this freedom in the hand of the internet could be a little dangerous, and I honestly expect to see tons of peni… tentiaries filling a lot of players’ villages. Luckily though, since this a game that will also be played by little kids, Hokko Life will only be singleplayer, with no plans for multiplayer or cooperative sessions: the only way to visit other player’s villages will be via the screenshots on Steam I fear.Similarly to Animal Crossing, we won’t have an entire house at our disposal from the very beginning, which means that we will have to work hard to earn one. After that, we will have complete liberty and customize it however we want. The customization of our home allows players to create really nice interiors, given that they have the right items to decorate them, and this can also be seen from the start by looking at the cozy little houses where the first few NPCs live in.Speaking of NPCs, we will start with just a couple of them, randomized at the start. On my second savegame (the first got corrupted after an update, something that the developer said won’t happen during the EA period) I started playing with a really rude dog called Oleander and a cute pink elephant called Mei. While the villagers are initially random, once you expand your town you will get new ones, eventually gathering them all to your friendly neighbourhood: in total there are 24 of them, with the possibility that more will be added during the Early Access period.Hokko Life is an interesting Animal Crossing clone: while it doesn’t add new groundbreaking features, it also puts the foundations for a title that could potentially be the one filling the void in the PC gaming landscape, similarly to what Temtem did for Pokémon games. Unfortunately, seasoned Animal Crossing players won’t find a whole lot of new stuff in the game, but PC players that never experienced this kind of title could be in for a surprise!

_childDocuments_.review: As you can see from my playtime, I gave this one more than just an honest shot.Nothing about this really works. The big "You can design things"-feature they advertise with is so janky, you'll just find yourself enduring pain whenever you play around with it. Just designing a bridge (and let's be clear here - you HAVE to, there's no premade blueprints you can opt for to ease the pain) is a pain in the behind.The NPCs are soulless. Not necessarily a dealbreaker from a game that's very Animal Crossing-esque - only they somehow managed to make them even less fun to talk to. The gameplay loop grows old. Even if you're the type to jump back into things and just go with the flow, you'll find yourself bored of the grind, uninterested in the perspective of progress and overall just shrugging the whole thing off.If you're into Animal Crossing, play that or Dinkum. If you're into farming sims or crafting games, play literally ANYTHING else.This game offers nothing other than a very bad attempt at cloning a game whose charm comes from the fact that Nintendo know wtf they're doing.The dev was too ambitious and by now it's abandonware - without the promised QoL-update ever happening.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is something special! Yes, at first it might look like another Animal Crossing clone...but what makes this game really cool is that there is an awesome community mechanic to it! You're given a huge variety of pieces (think building blocks) which you can resize, color, rotate, and basically use to make just about ANYTHING! From chairs, to lights, to storage, to any kind of furniture you can imagine! And once or twice a month, there is a contest with a theme for you to create something and submit it, and the community votes on it, along with what the next theme will be!Now here's the most awesome part! You can upload your item you create to your "shop," where others can see it and download the item into their world! For totally free! And there are some REALLY creative people out there who make some AMAZING stuff!So that's what I believe is the main selling point of this game...and the discord community is AWESOME! There's also the rest of the game: farming, fishing, moving NPCs in to your town, butterfly collecting, resource collecting, etc. It's really like what Animal Crossing SHOULD be. Your tools don't wear out, items stack pretty much infinitely, and there's a fast travel system. Time flows at its own pace (it's not real time), but it doesn't seem rushed, like other games like Stardew Valley, Garden Paws, etc. It's just right! Also, there's no stamina system! Bottom line, THIS GAME IS PERFECT!
_childDocuments_.name: Hokko Life

_childDocuments_.review: I've played just about every life sim out there. Life-long Animal Crossing stan. This game holds up among the best.  If you like games like that (and Cozy Grove, Stardew Valley, etc) you will like this. It has a great balance overall with resources and money that it never feels like a grind.Pros:- The building feature is so much fun. I'm not as talented as some others, but it's extremely fun- Piggybacking off the last point, being able to download things other creators have made FOR FREE- The freedom to move villagers in and out and move houses around at will- Like Animal Crossing, you can design your own wallpaper, flooring and clothes, but there's more option in the clothing such as shoes and hats- This has the best fishing minigame of all similar games I've played.  It's not as difficult to pick up as Stardew nor as simple as Cozy Grove or Animal Crossing. Cozy Grove has way better aiming though, something similar here would been great. I don't even mind that the shadow doesn't change per type of fish.- Great loading times- Adorable and interesting villagers- Fun Archeological minigame (the ones with the blue gemstone shovel are probably the most difficult part of the game)- Resources don't ever feel too constraining/hard to have enough of. Not grindy, especially with errands and the villager donation box that can be unlocked pretty easilyCons:- Limited house exterior/roof options- Depending on which hairstyle, the hats look sort of off/cuts into hair at weird spots.- Flooring is pretty difficult to make nice with the way the pattern repeats- Repetitive, but easy requests from villagers- Stores don't refresh daily, more like every other day- You can accidentally waste water in the watering can. Should have been like when you try and plant something without a hole dug or sow seeds without an open tilled soil spot/overtop already sowed seeds. Pretty frustrating until you get the unlimited watering can (which I still don't have yet at 70hrs in)Pick it up, you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is in early access so some bugs here and there are inevitable, but the team is responsive and helpful and the updates and patches are plentiful. It's REALLY CUTE, there's many items in the game, it's not too grindy, the villagers are sweet. The crafting is very open ended but that just means i end up spending way too much time making absolutely eye-searing furniture. A dealbreaker for me in games like this is the day cycle - which in my opinion is great here. You don't drop dead in the middle of the caves at a random hour, you don't have to manage stamina, and you can take naps to advance time or skip to the next day. It has a gameplay cycle that keeps me hooked without ever being frustrating or tedious. From posts in the forums I understand item management was a big problem before the storage update, but I started after it and while sometimes I DO run out of space, i haven't hit stack limits on anything which is really important to make inventory management alright and not a chore. All in all, a lovely little game.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Review edited to reflect recent updates - several of my problems were fixed!It's early days still and there is a lot of bug-squashing and such to do, but Hokko Life is already a lot of fun. However, only buy it in early access if you're prepared to deal with bugs and unfinished bits - otherwise, wait till it's finished.Check out my first 15 days in the game with commentary: Also, although the game is clearly influenced by Animal Crossing, it is NOT a clone of the game and there are significant differences. If you come into it expecting "Animal Crossing on PC" you might be disappointed. Great Stuff:+Beautiful graphics and sound+Cute characters+Design system lets you make unique furniture and art which you can then share online with others+All controls are rebindable+Slow-paced with no pressure, but not linked to real time, so you don't need to wait real life days for progress+Devs are listening to feedback and making changes/updates just about every dayNeeds Work (These things may be fixed during early access):-Fishing minigame is tedious and complex for no real reward-Gamepad support is still only partial-When you interact with someone/something while holding a tool, it puts your tool away (minor annoyance)-Limited stamina for running which seems very out of place in a game like this (annoying)-Can't manually reorganize inventory-Only one save file and it can't be deleted without finding the folder on your hard drive and deleting it-Design editor is still fairly clumsy to use and in particular, there are issues making functional bridges and ramps (often takes several tries to get a design that works and is placeable)-General bugs typical of early access (prompts and graphics not showing correctly, NPCs glitching through the landscape, and rarely, save-breaking bugs that require you to start over)Overall, I found Hokko Life worth playing and I will continue playing it through early access, but you should only get it now if you are okay with unfinished bits and bugs.

The villagers here in Hokko are better written but the variation is smaller, The graphics are more uncanny valley than animal crossing too.I only know since I played this on my switch but it wasn't very optimized on the switch: the furniture design. THIS is where the game shines but you're not going to be getting to it in under three hours. The pacing is a bit slow in the beginning that way.TL;DR: I think this is a cheap way to fill an animal crossing hole, if thats what you need. If you like decoration and furniture making, it can be a good time if you can get past the slightly uncanny valley Graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: Update 2024-06-16:After two years I finally came back to try the full release. For a single developer this is an impressive project. It captures a lot of the look and feel of Animal Crossing. Compared to a $60 AAA game from a massive studio, this is a good effort. I can appreciate the work that went into this.However it is not a good game. The story and characters are underwhelming. That has been my biggest gripe since the beginning, and I'm sad to say that there was never any real improvement here. I agree with the other reviewers who say that the progression is weird. Just for one example, some of the milestones require sprinting for some thousands of seconds. Given that you can sprint for only a few seconds at a time before needing to wait to recharge, this takes forever. You could spend in-game weeks doing nothing but sprinting, recharging, and repeating to unlock those milestones.Most of the game feels better when played on a Steam Deck (or otherwise with a controller). Keyboard and mouse just feel clunky for lots of activities. The game doesn't support ultrawide resolutions and the graphics aren't anything special anyway, so a small "average" resolution screen is all you need to enjoy the game. The only thing that feels very, very bad with a controller is the designer/workbench system. Building furniture is a chore with a mouse, and it is miserable with a controller.It's a real shame that the dev clearly put so much time and effort into the furniture design system. In an otherwise good game it would be the cherry on the cake to make the game unforgettable, but here it just makes for another source of clunkiness.I'm out of room to write but I want to leave my old reviews here for the benefit of anyone who wants to read them.Update 2022-04-16:Well, I tried it again a few updates later and I'm pretty impressed with the progress. This is still very much an early access game mind you, but it feels much better than when I last played. Not all of my concerns are addressed (yet), and several (most) of the changes could still be better (like the dialogue) but in my opinion the developer is taking the game in the right direction. I hope they continue refining what's already here before adding new stuff.Don't buy if you're expecting a finished or even mostly finished game. I'm hoping that I can update this review in another few months with some more positive comments, but it could just as easily regress in the other direction. For now, keep up the good work, dev.Update 2021-11-09:Despite the addition of features and the fixing of bugs, the game feels worse off now. The economy "exploit" allowing you to sell minimalist furniture for big bucks was the only way to really get money, at least early on. Now you have to fish and catch bugs non-stop while hoping that your villagers have requests that you can actually complete so that you can progress.The crafting system has always been finicky when it comes to bridges/ramps, but now it feels worse off than before. I had to spend half an hour iterating on bridge designs until I got one that would finally allow me to cross the river without myself or the bridge getting stuck. What ought to be one of the most fun systems of the game feels like an absolute chore thanks to the sheer number of materials required, especially for customization. I don't like the customization kits in AC:NH and I really don't like the paints here.Fishing is one of my least favorite activities in AC, and I like it even less here too. Forget pressing a button quickly after the fish bites (but not when it fakes you out with a nibble), now you have to spend another 15 or so seconds trying to reel the fish in. I would go the other way: automatically reel in the fish as soon as it bites. Bug catching is easy; fishing shouldn't be so much more difficult in a relaxing game. Taking the time to cast accurately and wait for a fish is enough work for the player. Make it a setting if you must: allow players to decide whether they want the easy fishing mode, the AC medium fishing mode, or the HL hard fishing mode. Even reward players who choose to play on one of the harder modes. But don't make the game feel like a chore with no alternatives.The deviation from the real-life time system of AC is proving to be more of a drawback than a benefit here. There isn't enough to do each day, especially in the first week or so, and the player will spend much of their time running to the inn to sleep, sleeping, and then running back to the meadow. I would very much be down for a real-life time system; that way I would have incentive to check in for a half-hour or so each day like AC. Otherwise there need to be some systems changes. Allow waiting outside. Have plants grow in (in-game) hours instead of days. Come up with additional ways to deviate from the AC formula so that the game feels like it's meant to be played for hours at a time instead of a short time each day.The interactive world space needs work. The player can dig holes and plant trees inside of the cliffs bordering the map. Objects placed in the north-most part of the town area will clip into the ground due to the slope. As mentioned earlier, bridges/ramps are really wonky. The item-placement camera system is an improvement over AC's push/pull system for manually relocating items, but even they have added a more top-down free-form design system for positioning things. It's not perfect, but it could definitely be imitated and improved upon in HL.Speaking of camera, why do we need to be stuck with a camera that always faces one way? The older AC games did what they could with the hardware that was available (hence the camera chunk-snapping in the original and the "rolling-log" technique in Wild World) but there's no need to stick with that formula now. Let us look around more freely.I am glad that the inventory system is more free than in AC games, but there are still artificially-imposed limitations that do nothing but add frustration. There's no need for backpack size limitations at all. It's great that items stack indefinitely (including bugs and fish) but restricting the number of stacks we can carry makes no sense when I can haul around tons of like materials. If a carry-weight mechanic was part of the game this would be different, but as far as I can tell we have a magical backpack that can hold enough materials to construct an entire village. Why can't I hold one more type of fish or flower?My original criticism of the game still stands. The writing lacks consistency and charm. It is jarring to have characters seemingly switch dialects, sometimes speaking in older English and other times in more modern slang. And if I fell asleep on the train and am now stuck in Hokko, how are other people coming and going so freely? At the end of the day, the story and characters are what will make or break this game. AC has memorable characters, Stardew Valley has memorable characters, and if no-one in HL is memorable then players simply won't get invested.I'd still like to believe that there is a great game in the works here, but at this time I do not recommend it. Hold off on buying until future updates are released.Original Review, 2021-06-02:This shows a lot of promise but also needs a lot of work. I'm rating it positively in good faith that the developer will continue their work and deliver a finished product, though my opinion may change in the future.My biggest suggestion to the developer thus far would be to hire an author for the story and characters. Distinct personalities and dialogue are what make this game's inspiration so great, and while it is apparent that they have tried to capture that charm, it comes off as forced and inconsistent. Additionally the "I fell asleep on the train and now I'm stuck here forever" plot doesn't work for me. It lacks the excitement of optimistically starting a new life.

_childDocuments_.review: Thanks to other reviews I didn't expect much of this game, and honestly, I was pleasantly surprised. I wouldn't have bought it for full price, but on sale for £3.19, it's well worth a gander. Think of it as a knock-off junior Animal Crossing game, with more creative elements. It's slow to start, and monotonous and repetitive in a way that - for my autistic brain at least - is quite soothing. I think for kids particularly this would be a good start to the life sim genre, especially if they lean artistic. You can design your own 3D objects and furniture in the game, as well as paintings and designs later, with the ability to upload those for others to download and use too. I'm very grateful to the community of this game for their excellent designs, they've decorated my little town far better than I could alone. There's a few things that aren't so straight-forward that I had to google, like how you fish up treasure () and where to obtain chalk (), but for the most part you follow the 'Mayor Merits' to unlock things as you go. Like Animal Crossing, there's no energy limit or need to sleep unless you want to, you can just potter about. It's not nearly as filled out as AC, but it's still being updated, and for under £4, I'm willing to forgive it quite a lot. It's a solid 6/10 and a good game to mindlessly wind down with.

_childDocuments_.review: Current pro's and con's for this game:Pro's:-design and characters are cute and vibrant-soundtrack is really chill-has animal crossing elements such as crafting, animal npc's, planting flowers, etc.Con's:-characters feel a bit static, lack of facial animation-lack of direction on how to get things done-lack of reason/desire to keep exploring and progress the game further-technical issue for having multiple screens on my end, but there wasn't a way to be able to make it have borders enabled nor switch to a different screenFeedback/Thoughts/Opinion/Critique:(to clarify, just providing ideas that could help make the game a bit better followed by my own thoughts and questions when playing this game)-have a clear objective or direction to get from point a to point b in order to keep progressing further-having temporary events, other places to explore and/or side quests may help-ability to make the game have a border option rather than only full screen and borderless option.-depending on the overall game direction itself, could have more exploration towards crafting/survival/farming to help provide purpose to selling items to earn more money or tasks to earn rewards-For day time/night time settings, since it's not matching to current time IRL, is there a purpose to it, or is it there just to be there? -Is there a specific purpose to using the futon to sleep to gain more activities/quests later onward, or something else?There's still potential to this game itself and I'm really looking forward to see further updates in the near future, it's just as of now there's some errors that can to be improved.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to "update" my review as it has been a few months since this game first came out as early access.I still recommend the game as early access. About:The game is very similar to animal crossing except there is a focus on crafting. And if you like animal crossing, I think you will like this game too. Villagers are interesting and I feel like, their dialog is pretty varied. They don't really sound like broken records to me.The game does start slow but once you get past a certain point, it is better. It does however, have a sandbox feel to it.Crafting:The game has a crafting system that allows alot of freedom. You can also share those creations with other players. I feel like the crafting system is the main part of the game. You create whatever for yourself, the map, and your villagers. Villagers may request supplies, fish, bugs, or for you to build something for them. Beyond that, there isn't much for quests. Oma in the Inn has some food related ones after you get so far in the farming however.The crafting process can take getting use too. There is alot of adjusting, and saving to make sure things are the correct measurements for the blueprint or appropriate size compared to characters. Having more detailed measurements and more ghosted character models during the crafting would be helpful. Since I have gotten my copy of the game, more ghosted models have appeared to assist in making stairs or whatever.Bugs:I personally have not came across too many bugs. I think the worst ones I have came across (and they are being worked on, but it is taking time I am not gonna lie) are the cherry blossom and fruit crafting bug that makes your crafted item look like a hot mess of colors, and the other one is losing your items in your storage to the void. Until it gets fixed, I would avoid crafting with those items and avoid putting things in storage. Or wait/take a break from the game. I am sure they will eventually get fixed however the storage bug does feel like it is taking longer than it should considering this is the kind of game you are going to store alot of stuff with all the crafting and creation sharing going on. There has been lots of bug patching since early access release.There have been some polishing of graphics as well. Villagers have also been readjusted to be more proportionate and cuter (shorter and heads are a little larger. maybe some villagers are more round now too?) We have had the farm update and the clothing update which added a little more content and player creative outlets. The Dev has been attentive which is a huge plus. I do think this game will be a great game when it is completed :)

_childDocuments_.review: As a short tl;dr, this game on paper should be better than Animal Crossing but isn't in actual execution.This game has many advantages to the average player of this type of game when compared to Animal Crossing. I will say first off there is way more you can do in terms of customization in this game, so if that is your thing you might possibly like it better than a game like Animal Crossing. Some ideas such as the quick travel between map areas, as well as some of the upgrades you can obtain are really cool quality of life ideas that would make Animal Crossing so much better if implemented. The timing in game is accelerated and broken down into seasons, making the game easier to grind or progress forward if that is your style of play (I feel like that is the majority of people who play animal crossing.) I feel like at times however the progression for the upgrades come at bad points, and is counter productive to the faster pace gameplay the game is trying to achieve. And for better or for worse, a lot of the things you do in game don't feel as rewarding as they would in animal crossing, coming from someone who put in 200+ hours on Animal Crossing without time skipping. Obviously the quality of the game is nowhere near on par which is the main reason I would prefer Animal Crossing if given a choice in this type of game. Certainly not a replacement, but you can get a lot out of for 20 bucks. Also easy 100% on the achievement front in a good 20-25 hours if you're focused on that goal going into it. Took me 35 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Today I want to tell you about a miraculous week...Actually, it was not planned, but after I fell asleep on a train trip and landed in a remote village, I had to spend there willy-nilly a few nights until the next train goes home. During this time I got to know and love the place and the people and now I don't want to leave but build a new life there.During a long train ride I unfortunately fell asleep and woke up again in a strange city. Since it was the end of the line, I got off and made my way to the small town that sits on the edge of a forest.Arriving at the town square, I went to the resident hotel and got a place to sleep from the nice manager, Oma. That evening I also met Moss, the manager of the market in this little town.I went to my room and fell asleep immediately, even though it was only a transitional room.I set out to explore the city a bit. Since the train wouldn't be leaving for a few days anyway, I figured I might as well get to know the city a little better. I met Sally, who was in charge of repairs and new purchases in town. Sally showed me around the workshop. It is called crafting when you make something new from materials. We repaired two benches for the town and then I got to put them wherever I wanted. I also got to meet a few residents and did a small job for them right away. For that I got a great shirt as a gift which I wear until today.I got an axe from Moss to chop wood and to prove myself at the crafting table. I built a bridge and got access to another part of the city that I couldn't reach before because of the river. I immediately beautified the city by sowing flowers. They will surely blossom soon, I'm looking forward to it.I explored the beach and received a fishing rod from a resident. We are now fishing together. If I catch a big or rare fish, I even get a reward.Today I bought a pickaxe in Moss's store. Since there are so many stones standing around everywhere, I thought I should clean up a bit. I'm sure I can use the stones I've collected at the crafting table.This day was also special because Sally introduced me to designing new objects. For this you use the design board in the workshop and can create your own objects based on blueprints or edit existing objects.In the evening, when I wanted to go to my room, Oma had a visitor and introduced me to Rosa, who wants to open a new store in town. The construction is supposed to start tomorrow.Today I built a ramp to get over the ledge in town and into the mountains. It didn't work right at first, but after a bit of trial and error, I managed to build a suitable ramp. I explored the mountains and saw that another bridge was needed here to get further. In the other direction was something like a mine shaft. However, it was blocked by rocks that I could not carry away.Back in town I bought a landing net and started catching butterflies. Of course I didn't want to hurt them, but they looked so beautiful that I wanted to see them up close.The flowers I had sown had now blossomed and I was able to pick some to make flower pots on them for the city. Now the marketplace looks even more beautiful.I took a bridge for the mountain path today. It worked right away and I was happy to discover a pond behind the next corner. I fished a little bit and caught a tadpole.Rosa's store opened today, I wonder what it's all about? I went right in and we talked a bit. It looks like I can build houses now. I wonder if I can build one for myself. In the evening I met again someone in the hotel who wants to open a business. I am already very excited about it.After this week I realized that I don't want to go back to my old life at all. I want to stay in this city and help my new friends crafting, building houses and beautifying the city. Next I will try to uncover the mine and build my own house.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this game for around a year and while there are a number of bugs and graphical glitches, it's being actively worked on, the Discord is active and helpful and the game is playable. It's Early Access, bugs and hiccups are to be expected, and they don't take away from the charm of the game. It's cute, the music is chill, the designing tool, while tricky at first, is fun and new. _childDocuments_.review: I bought this game in early access because I wanted a cozy Animal Crossing-style game for PC. I think I played for about an hour trying to like it, but it never did capture my attention. I gave it the benefit of the doubt and decided I would come back when the game released.It's a rainy autumn day, and I was missing Animal Crossing after I sold my Switch. I was really excited to try out this game on the Steam Deck now that it's out of early access. So I did, and my feelings about the game are exactly the same. It wasn't terrible; it was mostly just boring. Everything feels shallow.You show up at an inn with no backstory. The people there are friendly, but perhaps overly-friendly. They pressure you to move in. As a result of your move, you are suddenly tasked with town upkeep and building a ton of houses to attract other people to the town. As you do things, you get 'mayor rewards'. While I was playing, I couldn't help but think this sounded a little cultish, lol.The NPCs are very bland. They have no real quirks to make them interesting or fun to interact with. The conversations have no sustenance. I liked Moss' personality, but that's about it.The layout of your town feels cramped. This made things like positioning the bridge look and feel awkward. You cross your bridge and there's a whole open area with hardly anything in it. The beach was the same way.The game ran well on Deck aside from the dropdown menus in settings, but that's all fine. The graphics looked very unpolished though. My character's face was more pixelated than the rest of the game, which bugged me a little. There were random sparkles that I found very distracting. None of this would have mattered that much if the game itself was good, but unfortunately it isn't. I really wanted to like Hokko Life, and I might come back to it in the future, but for now it just isn't worth my time.

_childDocuments_.review: At its heart, Hokko Life is a casual, easygoing game, and that works much in its favor. What it lacks in challenge, polish, and complexity, it more than makes up for with unimaginable freedom, ease of use, and intuitive creative features. While obvious influences are drawn from games like Animal Crossing, Hokko Life has a unique enough combination of features to stand on its own. Though not without its flaws, it is still a solid, engaging experience that has so far consistently surprised and delighted me. When I start playing it, I find it hard to stop, the gameplay is that addicting! (And I can only play Animal Crossing for a few hours at a time!)

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to like this one. PC gamers have been begging for an Animal Crossing game for years. Hokko Life had been on my wishlist for some time so I was quite excited to see it appear in a Humble Monthly offering. Sadly Hokko feels like a classic example of a developer copying a game whilst not understanding what made the that game popular in the first place. A bland and shallow homage to Animal Crossing with none of that title's charm or polish. The characters and town are lifeless, the controls are clunky and the soundtrack lands with a thud. In the nearly two hours I played I've made about as much progress as I would have in 15 or so minutes of playing AC. I've encountered several bugs and issues in my short time playing that simply should not exist given how tiny the starting map is. Resources that are dropped by felled trees only to land in an inaccessible area, trees that can't be walked behind nor cut down even though they block access to other resources. Even the opening scene was not free of issues as several other reviewers have pointed out. Your character will walk into a shop and be told to have a seat. You'll then have to figure out how to take that seat, fight the awkward controls to actually do so and you'll likely end up repeatedly interacting with the friendly NPC, who keeps cheerful requesting you take a seat as you stumble your way about their inn. The hunt for Animal Crossing on PC continues.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like Hokko Life! I really want to play game that is so cozy, slow, and relaxing but also affordable. I've tried Stardew Valley (paid) and other (free) farming games, that of course, in the end it don't feel quite relaxing because of the pace, events, selling, and farming etc. But Hokko Life is really relaxing! It is so laid back and slow. I understand that the "slowness" of Hokko Life make some people impatient, but this is not the case for me. It is a perfect game if you want to have a simulation of "slow living". Also the graphics are nice. It's very simple, the animals are cute, the music are relaxing, the controls are simple, I know that we mostly can just interact with chair to "sit", but that what makes the game really simple! Although, there are still some "complex" aspect of the game, too, like building a custom furniture. By the time I write this review, I "just" playing it for 7 hours, but I feel like it's been ages! It even include me dozing off at a beach for half an hour enjoying the music, ambience, and scenery. Hokko Life is simple yet still very much interesting, as you will find some progress with time, so it is relaxing but at the same time interesting. However, if you want some "stimulating" games, just don't play this. I know many people put negative reviews to this game just because the slowness and its simplicity, and compare this so much with Animals Crossing. BUT this is indeed a different game and if you wish to play AC, you can just... Go with it? Why bother play another "similar" game if you already have AC? Look, I don't have Nintendo Switch for money reason. Please also consider that not everyone have some means to purchase a relaxing game with fancy price tag. At first I was hesitated to purchase this because of the negative and/or mixed review. But turns out, for the price, I find Hokko Life really nails it!
_childDocuments_.name: Hokko Life

_childDocuments_.review: Honest question: Did you AI generate the character designs? They look like programmer art that never got replaced. I mean, it's either that, or you hired a FNAF fan artist and told them to draw Animal Crossing characters without any further context because I can't imagine a world where someone puts down a tablet pen, looks at this aesthetic, and says "Yeah, that's fine" without being pressured by a fast-approaching deadline or just baked out of their mind. I really hope whoever made those models for you wasn't paid too much but honestly, any price for that would be a ripoff.Anyway, here's the pros and cons, hideous character art notwithstanding:PROS:-UI is very readable. As someone with eyesight problems (that this game's art made worse) I really appreciate large text and clear menus that make everything very snappy and easy to find.-The game is full of direction on how to progress and learn the mechanics without overwhelming you.-There's plenty of time in a day to get things done.-The fishing is a proper minigame and not just a boring "click A", and all the people complaining about this just have skill issues.-You can make any furniture you like, and have a lot of freedom so long as you have the materials.-The environmental art is actually quite nice and was clearly made by a competent artist.CONS:-The furniture making UI is not as precise as it could be, and it can be difficult to line things up properly.-Early game is a bit slow before it takes the reigns off.-Character customization is a little limited/it's hard to get something that looks good (but when the NPCs look like abominations, I guess that's a given.)-There are seasonal events tied to real-world time that turn the game into a pseudo service model.-There isn't a lot to the game and Early Access barely received content updates, masked conveniently by flooding the news section with community challenges. (Which also made it hard to follow development...)Overall, there are better games like this. Its one major selling point is furniture creation, but in every other way, other games in the genre do a better job at everything else. I think if it were still in Early Access, I would consider it to have more potential, but now that it's left Early Access, it feels pretty middling when compared with its peers.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a review... it's just something for you to consider while you read the reviews and comments around here.Hokko Life is:An  Animal Crossing-Like. If you can accept that, consider this: Animal Crossing is made by a team of around 90 developers. Each with their own job, and their own specialty. They have a nearly infinite budget thrown at them by the board of directors, and it shows in the amount of polish that game has as a series, overall. , we tend to collectively criticize everything we don't like within a given entry of the series, as a community. Go to any AC forum, you're going to find a 50/50 split of players who are just there to have a good time, and players who are there to complain...Compared to: Hokko Life, a passion project by a one-man development team. One person, with a very limited budget (not just by comparison) working on a game and picked up by Team 17. I'm not suggesting that we should ignore problems the game has, or that we should give a game a pass because it's from a very small dev team. I'm merely suggesting that measuring this game with the same metric you would use to judge Animal Crossing is more imperfect than this game could ever be. if there was a halfway thumb, that's what I would give this game, because I think it's really going to come down to the mindset of the individual giving it a try. Recommended because it's definitely not a negative experience, imo (and hey, it's not like you can't refund if it isn't your jam).

_childDocuments_.review: Hokko Life unfortunately feels very directionless. You have wonderful freedom in what you do with your time, and compared to Stardew Valley it doesn't feel like every second or minute is vitally important. However it also feels like you've finished most of the content within the first month/season and for the rest you have to make your own fun. Again with Team17 publishing it feels like they got an idea, smoothed it out, but never fleshed out and finished an actual game.On the other hand, in regards to making your own fun.. Hokko Life gives the player wonderful freedom, with the first player-made content system I've personally seen since APB Reloaded. You can make and detail your own furniture and clothing. While the system isn't the most convenient to use, you and others can make fantastic items in game, share them, place them. It would be nice if it was a little easier to encounter other peoples items, and if the game's built in selection was wider and more readily available for those that don't want the extra hassle, but it is still great to see players being enabled to express their creativity in such a way.Just remember to grow an orange tree in the first season or you'll be waiting a year for any farming related upgrades ever.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an updated review. The original review is at the bottom.=======================================================================So. Version 1.0, eh?Well, point to the devs: they did fix the bugs I encountered during my previous attempt to play, so there's that.It's not completely without its charm, either. There's some interesting ideas, and a vague sense of a specific direction. However, it feels very hollow.I have been playing for a solid 6 hours now, and I have not once stopped to think, "Oh, that's such a cool touch!"Furniture doesn't do anything — a TV can't have a screen to turn on, even with like three still animations. There's no music played by radios. You can't sit at a table with a bench unless it's designed specifically as a chair — things that are tables only let you put stuff on them.It's interesting you can design your own furniture, but it's pretty limiting. You need a lot of resources for each item, as every board of wood costs an actual plank from your inventory — so your creativity is very limited at the start. You also need to purchase crafting recipes, and can't go straight to painting in a color you like without growing the plants necessary to make the dye. This causes a single furniture item to be a multi-day affair. However, it *does* allow for crafting multiple items at a time, and it doesn't make you wait for multiple bars to complete the job.The character designs remind me of the old Teddy Ruxpin dolls. They're fine, but I can't say they look particularly endearing. They also don't have particularly interesting, or charming, dialogue. From what I've looked into it, it also sounds like there's a very small selection of possible villagers, and they have unlock requirements.There are perks you can unlock by doing normal activities. This is a neat idea. Unfortunately, none of the perks (that I've come into so far, at least) are particularly polished. The mini-map is designed with a color scheme that reminds me of sitting in an elementary school room with everyone's houses pinned on it. Still, it is functional, and as a bonus it does show where the villagers are.You can redesign the interior of a house. This was a unique concept at the time the Early Access started, and had ACNH not launched their sole DLC, it would have no comparison on that front. However, having played both, there's just no way for that feature to carry the game even close to the amount of cool stuff possible in that expansion.There's butterflies to catch and fish to fish up. I didn't manage to find a way to unlock fishing in the six hours I played. When you catch them, it adds them to a scrapbook page in your menu. The menu art isn't particularly stunning, but it does represent the butterflies adequately. Additionally, the butterflies can clip through trees and rocks indiscriminately. It's unclear exactly how to best aim the net — it seemed somewhat random if a swing would work or not at any given distance.On top of that, there are some UX choices that were annoying — the top of my list being that pressing A will simply skip to the next panel instead of speeding up the current one. It didn't really matter since most of the text was pretty drab, but it doesn't make sense to skip text that scrolls so incredibly slowly. Other small things cropped up as well — using a controller to design items is a slow process, placing bridges is finicky at best, and there's a lot of back and forth involved in mining at first (since you must place your own lighting, which requires materials from within the mine, and it's not close to town and there's seemingly no way to fast travel).It's... fine. Absolutely fine. However, between ACNH and Disney Dreamlight Valley, I can't see a reason to recommend this game over the others. One is way more polished and has a massive amount of content beyond what this can provide, while the other has various Disney IP at a bare minimum.The timing is rough. If this game had come out before DDV, or been a bit more robust (or polished), my recommendation might be different.=======================================================================Original Review=======================================================================This is a mess still. While it's expected Early Access would have unimplemented sections of code, this is a bit beyond that. I'm not expecting a perfectly polished statue at this point... but whatever pebbles exist should not look like chunks of asphalt. The new character creation screen isn't even polished, and that's first impressions type stuff.It was too immersion breaking to bother with. I'll probably come back to this later, but I would highly recommend waiting on it for now.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing nearly 20 hours I feel like I've only just stuck my toe  into this game. Its really fun to play and I'm obsessed with catching butterflies and fish, and checking out player shops for decorations and furniture.  I hope the community for this game continues to grow and that the devs will continue to innovate.If I can critique anything at all, I'd say the animal folks should eventually get animation updates. When they talk and move they look kinda robotic, especially around the neck area.Edit and Update: February 6 2023. I have to admit that since the game has come out of early access, I'm not as impressed by this game as I used to be.  But there is no middle "maybe/try it" option. And I don't dislike it enough to switch to "not recommended".To be clear, I still enjoy the game. But I debate if some of that is due to coping with the time sink and hoping the game will get better.  While it was in EA I expected some more substantial changes. It may seem shallow but most of my complaint comes from the writing and character design. The human character is fine, they animate nicely. (I wish the villagers also animated nicely, I swear its like they were created by two separate people.) Just wish I could have some more hair and face options.I'd love to have eye shape options. I have to be honest, the npc designs are kinda hideous. There are a few cute ones but the issue is the eyes. (yeah for some reason I'm obsessed with their eyes) They are freaky and soulless with 0 capacity for emoting. And I remember when I first bought this game, the previous eye designs looked a lot better (though still kinda 'eh'). I was hoping for a variety of eye shapes to give the villagers more personality but that didn't happen, it somehow got worse.  Also they all still move rather stiffly and robotically. I'd forgive almost everything if they had better animation. A lot can be done to improve presentation.I wish there were more in game events taking place. Fishing contest and the bug survey are okay but is that really it? I don't count the meta of the furniture making contests for the players because the villagers don't seem to care about it at all, it is completely disconnected from them. I'd add in some dialogue where they are aware of the big custom furniture making craze to make it feel more natural. Example: Some villagers will mention a contest going on in the city, so players know a contest is happening without having to go to the steam group to find out.I'd like to see some festivals or special event days. Nothing deep, it can be shallow af, just as long as its something to shake up monotony. Maybe have events in the city, npcs in the city with quests would be really good. Maybe have an apartment there too. An apartment you have to actually pay rent for seasonally to give me a reason to keep earning money. Have the npcs doing things besides mindlessly walking around like zombies. Example, you might see them sitting at tables you set out, eating or talking, or sitting on a blanket having a picnic, walking in the rain wearing umbrella hats, picking flowers etc.Oh and some kind of aquarium/ bug collection area. That would require making 3d models for the fish but I don't think that is beyond the dev's capabilities. And bugs other than butterflies....So tl;dr. Its an okay game but can be better.  This game has so much potential though so I'm still rooting for it.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has logged more hours than I count to share on Animal Crossing for Nintendo Switch, I bought this game with low expectations and tried to enjoy it for what it obviously is -- an attempt to find success by copying a popular console exclusive game and bringing it to PC, albiet a few months after the hype for it's source material has all but died out.After putting some time in, I went through the motions of doing what I knew was expected of my character in the game -- chopping, mining, crafting, building and whatever it took to help grow this strange town full of Five Nights-looking animals who don't seem to have any child labor laws on the books. But I felt no joy at all as I did with Animal Crossing. But I couldn't peg exactly why.It wasn't the weird way the story begins, with your obviously adolescent character waking up in this weird place after falling asleep on a train, immediately accepting the weirdness of it without reaction and accepts his new life that begins in a closet-sized room with a futon, clothes basket and side table. Instead of, you know, freaking the heck out and wondering if he will ever see his family or anything he knows again, he just carries out any order creepy animal barks at him.It wasn't the system you must use to design your own furniture including bridges and the whatnots needed to continue to other areas, although it is clunky, unpleasant to use and in taller pieces, useless because the camera can't be zoomed out enough for you to see what you are placing. And the most infuriating part is when your design doesn't meet size specifications to continue, but instead of showing you specifically where or even giving you a hint, you're given numbered measurements as guidelines there's not a number to be found on the building grid.It's not even that the fishing "mini-game" is awful (my pet peeve with nearly every game like this I've played). Although, if you're going to copy a successful game series, why not copy that particular game mechanic along with everything else? Any game that ever tries to introduce any kind of sliding bars or thumbstick tugs in strategic directions have failed in making fishing more fun in a game. Plus, I live in a town built on fishing tourism, I've actually fished and it's not remotely as complicated as it seems in games like this.Though it should have, I found that it didn't even bother me that much that the only store in town carries only your basic beginner tools, some oft -used ingredients they likely included because they couldn't figure out a sensible way to make you craft them and then a slightly changing selection of flower seeds to plant, plus a few furniture items and wallpaper/flooring that alternates out every day. Or is supposed to I assume, although sometimes it doesn't.Now, I will say that I moved from disappointed to perturbed when I found out the new computer system in the store wasn't for access to a larger selection of what you'd see there, but instead a user-generated content portal which if done correctly would be awesome, especially if you were over designing your own stuff about three items in. But aside from the featured items you see on the home screen, you'll need a creator code to see literally anything else. You can't search for items at all. Instead, you'll try scouring the internet for codes to find what you need, and this day in age, a game shouldn't be forcing you to set it down for a second in order to find what you need, because many won't bother picking it back up again.No, the thing that bothered me most and where this game really failed to copy one of the most important parts of Animal Crossing lies in the animal characters that eventually become the citizens of the town you're single-handedly growing, and therefore the ones handing off banal, simple tasks to you so they can resume their day walking around aimlessly dead behind their eyes as if they've are all products of taxidermy. They either don't have any personality to speak of throughout or they come off as jerks when they ask you to take an item to another character you literally interrupted their conversation with or when they ask you to build them furniture to fit some vague specification and after fumbling with the horrid design engine, tell you that your piece looks unfinished and could use some more time. There is no likeable one in the bunch, even your own character, who rudely greets the shopkeeper with "Buy my stuff!" when you're selling off everything not tied down to make money. I think a large portion of the budget should be redirected into writing, to include the half-attempt at a storyline but mainly, to give the NPCs personalities -- likeable ones, and give you a reason to want to stop and talk to them. Even in AC, the athletic personality types are immediately grating to me because of their one-track minds, but they still manage to come across as warm, caring and most of the time, act as if they are your biggest fan. When a character on that game asks to leave the island the first time, you almost feel sad about it. As for the characters in this game, in one of their own words after receiving free housing and furniture "This seems unfinished. More time needs to be spent on it, I reckon."

_childDocuments_.review: 8 hours in and it doesn't reeeaaally feel like the game has "started" yet. What's odd is that this game might be close to being fantastic, but its various systems are in conflict with each other.- Full range of customization for building objects is a really cool concept for a town sim, but the controls and UI for doing so are really, really bad. It's an incredible chore to make anything that looks good, and the game will happily let you continue building something that falls outside of accepted parameters, only to tell you that you can't finalize the build -after- you press confirm. - Having a wide variety of activities, like mining and farming and decorating and fabricating, means that you could theoretically spend days just meandering from spot to spot doing different things, but the incredibly limited inventory space and immediate dearth of materials ensures that you're either constantly using multiple storage units (where are you even fitting those?) or resign yourself to only focusing on one or activities at a time for multiple in-game days, and heaven help you if a bug flies by that you want to catch.- Randomly-generated quests ensure that there's usually something to do that'll feel like "progress", but the map only ever shows you your immediate surroundings, NPCs wander around all over, and again the limited inventory means you might not have room to work towards whatever particular item or build type the quest demands.It feels like too many ideas and not enough editing. This could be a pretty stellar AC-clone, but it needs to actually decide what it's about and build its systems in support of that, rather than designing a bunch of fluff and then hoping it all sticks together magically.

_childDocuments_.review: I just wouldn't recommend this game FOR NOW. It's extremely impressive that it was done by one person and you can tell that the potential is there, but I wouldn't dish out the $20 unless you have the extra cash laying around. it's a very cute and relaxing game, but my biggest gripe is honestly with the crafting system. I tried it both on mouse and keyboard along with controller and it feels a little wonky both ways. I honestly would much prefer purchasing furniture to decorate new resident homes as apposed to using the base crafting system with very generic looks. I totally understand that this is meant to be a nice build up with new colors/materials you may unlock, but I find no pleasure in a new resident moving in with a generic wooden plank of a bed that I created myself (that and I also lack creativity). This is why the crafting system in Animal Crossing was so well received because you just had to worry about materials as apposed to the full on craft. I also understand that it's in early access, but it's very confusing to figure out what you're supposed to do. The tutorial was cute because the NPCs would explain base mechanics, but the second you pass that point, it's not very clear of what the expectations of the game are. I'd like to think that this is just an oversight with it being early access, but I definitely think it'd be more beneficial to guide players better instead of making it somewhat of a guessing and experimental game. BUT YEAH, I'm looking forward to the growth of this game and I do truly hope it becomes a solid game for future gamers!

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly I want to say the game has great potential. It bears similar markings to social simulator games but is actually a dressed up crafting game. Also it seems like a simple game but it's actually fairly complex.Good graphics, and nice simple story for a living world. You can go fishing, mine, catch butterflies, build items for villagers, and design your own clothing.  You can even share items you make in the game with other players even though you cannot visit them to play together. That I can live with, some things still need to change though. You cannot turn off the snap grid and the pieces snap to each other of their own will in the crafting station. The fashion design station is still new so the bugs with that are forgivable, just do not click the undo button whatever you do, or else all that hard work will have been for nothing because your design will be ruined. My review may change when the bugs are fixed or when it's out of early access but we'll just have to wait and see.

_childDocuments_.review: I really thought about refunding, but since I paid $15 I'll keep it in hopes that it gets better before/at release. I'm not going to do a long-winded review, just some bullet points:CONS.Don't like the art design, looks like one of those off-brand 90's kids' shows..So much clipping!!!.Some of the harvesting animations feel oddly 25fps..Start of the game is soooo slow. .Dialog choices that aren't even choices. Sometimes there's only one. .Barely there controller support. wth?PROS.Cool designer features, honestly the ONLY selling point..Nice choices in player customization..No Stamina!!.Really nice lighting/shadow system for a game that looks like it does.But yeah, this is SUCH a crowded market, if you want to do a Farm/Life Sim, especially one with Animals doing some Crossing, you have to step up your game. _childDocuments_.review:
Hokko Life is a cosy, creativity filled community sim game.

Step off the train into the town of Hokko and get settled into your new home! This quiet village needs your help to turn it into the charming rural town everyone loves. With hammer and paints in hand it's up to you to design, build and decorate homes for all of your new friends!

Busy yourself away in the dusty old workshop and let your creativity flow! Craft materials and combine them in whatever way you desire to create new and wonderful furniture and items for your town. Collect flowers, mix paints and use them to design wallpapers, flooring and even clothing!

Will you design an urban-industrial furniture collection or maybe a bright flowery wallpaper set? With all of the workshop at your disposal, you'll have complete freedom to design a town your villagers will absolutely love.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of this writing, SD Gundam Battle Alliance is currently at the mixed rating. I believe this might not change, and I will also echo the sentiment that Steam should have a middle of the ground option...especially for a game like this.I initially saw the game as promising, as earlier in the year, I had decided to dive deep into the Gundam franchise, and at the time around the game released, I had seen almost all of the source material that was used in this game, excluding the DLC (a different matter altogether). I usually never pre-order, but I bit the bullet. Well, there's a good reason why I don't pre-order...The biggest thing about this game that may be surprising to most people is how hard it can be at times, and not in a way that is gradual, unfortunately. This is especially the case if you play solo, which is how I have played it at the time of this review. As many people have echoed, the Mobile Armor fights are the worst in this regard, while the devs have nerfed the health of early MA bosses, they are still not all that fun to fight, and this ties into an aspect ingrained into the game.Another aspect that is perhaps unexpected is the feeling of playing a Souls-like. I don't want to be that guy, but supposedly to pull off a counter, it is harder than even doing it in those games! I have no experience to speak of for this, but unless you're really good at seeing pixel perfect frames, you will no doubt have a hard time mitigating damage if you aren't already using a part that has Auto-Guard on it. Speaking of parts, this is something I don't see many people bring up. The game has parts that are equippable on your Mobile Suits, and the acquisition of parts that have good effects beyond the base stat can be random, as the rarity of parts do not guarantee higher or even better stats of desired parts, other than they will have a higher base stat and sale rate. Regarding getting Counters, there are parts that give 0.01-0.02 seconds of a window for it, which might not sound like much, but it was the difference between me never getting a counter and getting one half the times. Tying into MA fights, sometimes MAs will drop chips that have very good stats tied to it, but again, this is random. This feeling of little concreteness, is a feeling that is echoed in the frankly underwhelming story. I really didn't know what to expect out of a Gundam game story like this, but all I really got out of it was how creatively bankrupt Seed Destiny was with the many times the game pointed out, "Wow, this is just like how it was in Zeta!" for the 50th time. It's more of a fanservice fare, and that can be reflected in the pre-mission banter between pilots that can occur if you put two of them with some kind of similarities together, some of which may not be obvious (McGillis from IBO and Loran from Turn A for example, talk about unearthed Mobile Suits, which impressed me since it went beyond surface level stuff like, oh they're both part of the Feddies, Zeon, etc.). However, it can be weird to see who has dialogue with who, and like the game itself, especially if you do Hard mode after, can feel like a slog.I would have put this review up earlier but I decided to do Hard mode even without achievements tied to it. I'm glad the achievements don't make people do Hard all the way, as it's just inflated numbers and hunting for higher parts that might give more benefits. They also allow you to uncap past MS level 40, and pilot level 40 as well, I believe. I have not used the Hard mode unlockable MS, but I doubt they are worth it that much. (Actually, the unlockable GM can be pretty fun to use) Don't even bother trying to do EX missions solo, as the AI teammates cannot handle that kind of broken, and excessive subweapon spamming from the bosses. Oh yeah, the AI teammates suck. They can sometimes pull a reversal or block ranged shots! But will still try to revive you even if they are the focus of the enemy attack, often spiralling the mission into failure if you do not have any repair kits left. Also, the skill to get more repair kits from doing Role Actions is  the Hard mode run. How ironic that I was surviving more in Hard than in some regular Normal missions because of this...The lineup of MS is also rather weird. I understand Wing was not that popular in Gundam's place of origin, but they have more Wing songs in the game than MS. Not all the series featured will have a story mission tied to it, and that is both a good (ZZ, Victory) and bad thing (X, Turn A). DLC suits are also really weird picks overall, but at least I understand the SD and Moon Gundam lore now? Every suit is unique though, which is really the only real incentive to play this game...to collect suits and make them stronger.That being said, I will still say I had more positive than negative experiences with this game, even if it does not feel like it and with how EX solo really grinded my gears. If all you want to do is collect some recognisable Gundams and beat things up with it, then really it's good enough for that. I highly recommend doing it with people to mitigate your frustrations, as playing solo will lay bare the problems of this game full. Get it on a sale, and if this game gets a sequel...I hope they learn their mistakes from this. With some polish, this could be a lot better.

_childDocuments_.review: unless you're a massive, and I mean *massive* fan of gundam, I don't think this game is going to be for youit has a massive roster, yes, but unfortunately the progression system works completely contrary to itselfyou can unlock an absurd amount of gundams, but unless you want to grind for ages, you only get to focus on one or two.This is because not only do you need to pay credits to upgrade a mech, you need to "unlock" mechs with certain parts, dropped in missions or found in cratessounds good, right? wrong. Because every time you unlock a mech, you need to drop more credits to max out its level again.I'm pretty sure the amount to max out a gundam's level, at the 2nd unlock point, is around 1 million credits, probably more. I did like it until about the 6th ring, but that's when the grind finally got to me and I had to bail. because at that point the levels went from easy 10 minute affairs to complex 30 minute affairs with branching paths and multiple bosses, all of which you'll have to gun down if you want all the drops. I did like how in the beginning it was pretty simple, you play the mission, you get 1-2 parts, and you need 4-ish parts per gundam. I was still on board a few missions in where you needed multiple types of parts to finish a gundam, like type I dropped from one mission, and type II dropped from another, but usually they didn't bother and had both parts drop from the same enemy.It only gets worse when you consider chaos missions, which require an item to accessyou get one from every chaos mission you beat, and there's a rotating roster of free chaos missions you can complete. But it takes 2-3 keys to enter a missions that isn't free, and that starts to add up quick when you might need to beat a missions 5 times to unlock it's associated gundam.tl;dr, I thought I could handle the grind, but nope.

_childDocuments_.review: When this game was initially announced I hoped for months that it would come out and actually be good, as unfortunately not all Gundam Games are created equal. Since the release I've been dying to finish the campaign of this game so that I can write a review with a clear picture as to the entirety of the game. SD Gundam Battle Alliance may quite possibly be the best Gundam PC Game I've played to date. Currently there's a lot of vitriol being spewed upon the review section of this game, regarding things such as the game not being SD Gundam Online 2, not being a Gundam Battle Game continuation by ARTDINK (last release was in 2012 on the PSP), and also related to the lock-on system which can be disabled in the menu. Before buying this game, please be fully aware that this game is NOT a sequel to SDGO nor is it a continuation of the Gundam Battle series and has never advertised itself to be either of these things. Also be aware that it is an ACTION RPG experience with long grinding.Combat - There's a vast arsenal of mobile suits at your disposal, with differing combat styles and weapons available to them which can vary combat quite a bit. In my current 51 hours of playing the game I've yet to play two mobile suits which feel similar, with even ranged mobile suits having distinct differences to their playstyles which fit their actual designation and actual in-lore arsenals.Unit Design & Animations - You can clearly tell that the animations and design of these mobile suits were done with love. There's a staggering amount of detail put into the tiny SD Mobile Suits, from their weapons to their animations with things such as the Wrench Mace for Barbatos looking masterfully weathered. Attack animations sometimes will have callbacks to obscure instances within either manga or spinoff anime's. ARTDINK's team has really done their homework, and it shows.Map Design - The maps are truly designed to feel like they're properly at scale for the mobile suits, making it to where it seems as though the SD's are truly just meant to portray shrunken versions of the full-size mobile suits. Traversal of these maps is easy, with quite a lot of detail for not being the center of attention, and with how quickly the players zip around it makes it so that even missions which you're farming for parts don't feel tedious. Class and Mobile Suit Variety - This game truly does have something for everyone. There's 74(?) mobile suits available with extremely diversified movesets and playstyles, as well as three individual unique class types for mobile suits which have specializations.Built with Co-op in mind - This may be a negative for some people, but it is extremely obvious that this game has been built from the ground up with Cooperative Gameplay in mind. None of Bandai's proprietary online account based stuff is required, this game just allows you to start it up and join up with friends easily with no issues whatsoever. Latency doesn't seem to effect the game much as well, which makes it much easier to swap hosts to anyone within a friend group.Story - The Story is interesting at times, but has your somewhat familiar SRW style story. Unfortunately as well, there's a lot of the storyline which I'm missing as if you play Co-op with people it doesn't give you the Visual Novel styled storyline information, only giving you quick summarizations whilst in a mission.Unit Selection - Whilst this may seem to contradict what I'd said regarding Class and Mobile Suit Variety, this isn't what I'm trying to imply. From a gameplay perspective the variety of classes and mobile suits is incredible, but the unit choices are... Meh? There's a lot of iconic mobile suits and their variations missing from the game, as well as mobile suits which are just built into the game with their own playstyles being missing from the roster such as Gato's Gelgoog, or Ramba Ral's Gouf. Whilst I don't hate the selection, I truly wish they'd done more and given us more grunt suits as well.I-Fields - I've played many Gundam games where I-fields are present, and the way they're presented in this game is probably the worst iteration I've ever seen, as they actively dissuade you from playing anything but Physical Suits. If you're playing Co-op and you're the only person using beam weapons it is particularly awful, as you'll be stuck doing nothing against mobile armors with them for 80% of the fight. There are better ways they could've been handled, such as damage degradation based off of I-Field charge percentage, but it's just the laziest way for them to be handled.A Lack of Multiplayer Modes - Whilst I don't necessarily mean a PvP mode, I'd like to see some stuff related to large-scale arena style boss fights, or boss rushes themed around specific factions. This game definitely feels like it would work well with such, so it's a bit of a shame that they don't exist.No Rare Drop Listings - There is virtually no rare drop listing available for this game be it online, in-game, or otherwise. I'm not talking about unit drops however, but rather rare chips as they remain a mystery unless you or your friends happen to randomly find one and mention it. This wouldn't necessarily be an issue if they weren't the BEST in the specific category they cover, but that is unfortunately the case.-Overall Score: 8.5/10. An incredibly fun Co-op experience for Gundam fans and newcomers alike. Worth $59.99? Honestly, if you have two other friends you're able to pile in together with that can also get the game, I'd say yes. I've thoroughly enjoyed all my time spent playing this game.Closing Thoughts: Currently I've played 55 hours of this game, and I STILL keep finding new things to obtain or tinker with, and not to mention the additional content that will be added for free as time goes on. Hopefully they'll address the unit choice issues and capital earning rates in time so that it's a better experience for first-time players as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid single and multi-player mission based action RPG. The game centers around grinding missions for parts and upgrading your roster. Customization is on the limited side - each MS only has a few option slots. Fortunately, the entire roster seems quite big. Plot is serviceable but nothing incredibly special. The environments, lighting and animation are where this game shines - the mobile suits look beautiful. Worth it as a Gundam fan! But if you are looking for the next genre-breaking mech sim or action game (or even RPG) look elsewhere.
