short_description: A quirky 3D puzzle game about three musicians forming a band and trying to score their breakout hit.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Nope, but it is a polished puzzle game. Reach the level exit with your musicians that look like an instrument, which isn't so easy because those instruments are bulky. So you have to turn and twist to reach the desired point. Can be quite funny, especially combined with the background story of the three musicians trying make it big. You even have optional side missions. Great visuals (for a puzzle game), cool soundtrack, gamepad support. A rather charming puzzler recommended to all fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: fun cast of characters, you can tell the production spent a lot of time making this work and it's a labour of love.Personally, puzzles ranged from well-thought-out where I can see 4-moves-til-checkmate solutions to bumbling around until somehow you make it there.but the bad...only 1 save slot. Classic.poor controls:Only 1 key to cycle through the characters/limbs. There's no toggle limb for the character nor is there a forward-cycle/back-cycle. You're locked to cycling in one direction if you stay on a keyboard. Mouse controls aren't much better as you have to be very precise in clicking the limb you want. Why not make the mouse click a limb-toggle, if that character is already highlighted?poor controls 2:if you accidentally click the reset button (or hit R, or was it Z, or was it X, or was it F?), there's no way of undoing that. Hope you weren't close to the solution.poor interface:even though you have a free camera, you're locked to orthogonal views. I get that up-down-left-right has to be in relation to the view, but so much is always obscured. Maybe make the foreground obstacles alpha translucent or something so you're not rotating constantly and obstacles keep swinging in and out of view.poor interface 2:In order to access the overall menu to check on options or control mapping or such you have to exit the puzzle you're in and endure the transitory animations. Animations are great don't get me wrong, but it eventually can add up to be too self-indulgent and over-flaired. Oh, and if you made any progress in your puzzle, you can forget about taking a break and jumping to another before coming back and returning to that state because the level resets when you leave.poor gameplay music(yeah, I'm saying it): there are reasons why puzzle games have very ambient music and not upbeat or swing; it melts into the background and lets puzzle solving take center stage (topical!). When you spend say over 10+ minutes on a puzzle, there just isn't enough variation in the bg music here to keep it from getting repetitive and grating. Whereas ambient music takes a backseat to the puzzle solving, the music in this game has _too_ much character to let it meld into the background, but _not enough_ character/variation to keep the same riff you hear over and over from wearing down your nerves.Love Gwen Frey's contributions to games such as flame and the flood and bioshock infinite. Her video tuts talking about animation sequences and the attention to detail in how to make the wolves or Scout's movement more fluid to fit the set of frames in TFatF are topnotch and show someone who's really thought a lot about polishing up a product. Love sokoban games such as fidel's dungeon rescue and cosmic express and steven's sausage roll. Love big-band style music. Been following this game for years, literally. Bought it as soon as I could upon release (I never do this for any game: case in point I'm waiting for the reviews on Manifold Garden, another puzzle game, to roll in). But I just couldn't love this game. Wish I could get a refund. I'm terribly sad about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: The most important part of a puzzle game are the puzzles, and that is where this game falls short. Every puzzle seemed to be about fiddling until stumbling on the solution, rather than requiring deep thinking and planning. Games like Stephen's Sausage Roll, or Baba is You, or The Golem all feature "eureka" moments that are the result of pausing and thinking, and in my opinion those are the most rewarding puzzles. But in Kine there were no eureka discoveries, and there wasn't a single puzzle where I could plan and see the solution in advance. Looking at let's play videos online, it seems most other people play the game that same way -- somewhat randomly trying all possible paths until happening on the solution, rather than thinking through each move. In my opinion, that is not good puzzle design, and is not rewarding to solve.Aside from the puzzles, the graphics and animations are great. The storyline is surprisingly decent for a puzzle game. The controls are a bit annoying, having to repeatedly cycle through each character sometimes hundreds of time within a single puzzle. Made lots of keystroke mistakes with that. The puzzle mechanic itself is fresh and interesting, sort of like rolling six-sided dies, except with weird appendages that change how they roll.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: It doesn't feel like you are really solving anything, it just feels like you are randomly moving through an abstract maze and brute forcing your way to the end.The aesthetic and style of the game are top notch. I just found the "puzzle" gameplay very unsatisfying. I only made it maybe 20% through the game, but I can imagine it only gets worse so I'm just stopping now.Here's some other puzzle games I have enjoyed and would recommend instead.Baba is You (Best puzzle game ever)BraidClosureDeleveledFEZFidel Dungeon RescueKeenPortal 1&2Steal Bastard DeluxeStealth Inc 2The SwapperThe Talos Principle
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Kine is a charming and unique puzzle game. Really lean design, beautiful polished art and a really ambitious (successful!) attempt to marry narrative and puzzle gameplay. I am firmly in the "narrative often gets in the way" camp, but it somehow manages to never feel tacked on or intrusive. Kine does a good job of wrestling with some tricky design problems - for example, the number and variety of inputs make it tricky to internalize movement, get comfortable with the controls, and plan several moves ahead. Thankfully, it does a good job of guiding you to the solution (or at least toward forward progress) by not giving you an overwhelming amount of choices at any point. If you make a mistake or take a wrong turn, the game lets you know quickly. Also, there are accessibility options like input remapping that'll surely be of crucial help to some players.All in all, Kine stands tall and confident among the great puzzle games, and will likely feel distinct among them for a long time. Play it! And on a personal note, tell your friends about good puzzle games so there'll be more of them! <3
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Think Stephen's Sausage Roll but with more story and less unrelenting difficulty. Kine is an extremely clever and charming puzzle game that, while clocking in at around 6-10 hours depending on your puzzle skills, manages to use that short time wisely. The puzzles are never too hard, but what really makes the game stand out are the characters, their dialogue that often relates and matches with the puzzle at hand, and the outstanding presentation.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Clever game, with fabulous music.It is creative to set musical instruments as protagonists. They each can change shape, which is also the highlight. Regular steps in a level involve rotate, stand, change shape, repeat those steps magically, the protagonist reaches the destination. Games are very challenging, and sometimes I need to switch cameras to see better. I bought this game out of curiosity, I probably would stop for the first 30 mins if not for the fab music (not for it is not fun but for it is too difficult).2 hours I am doing maths... I had to keep trying and not exactly know making any progress. The game reaches the utmost difficulty when a level contains all 3 band members, I stack them one on the other, then move the lowest one as an elevator. It's crazy, I really believe the devs are geniuses, and whoever beat the level are potential International Mathematical Olympiad champions.I give up after finishing a few levels containing all band members. I aim to finish all the main quests but really cannot, I get confused even watching a solution walkthrough. Kine is a great game, though, I had fun and the music (again) is unbelievably wonderful.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: The game has some of the most satisfying puzzles i have done in a long time and a really cute and charming story. once you start switching between the characters at the same time is where the game really shines and gets you to think outside of the box, and the entire time during the puzzle the characters talk to each other, the story is really simple but the way its done is extremely cute. if you don't care about story it never gets in the way or anything, just speech bubbles that pop up a few times per level and you can focus all on the puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely and cute and rather brilliant. Kine has a delicious charisma and some of the nicest contained puzzles I ever saw. Contrary to most puzzle games out there, which get harder by simply increasing the game area, Kine keeps its tiles to a minimum (at least in the first couple hours I played) and tricks you with small changes: a thing I love and respect very much.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Hard thinky puzzle game; solid graphics, good music, cute story.The difficulty ramped up at a nice pace, sortof the classic "the first few levels are automatic and then it starts getting into the game." I guess I'd describe it as a medium difficulty curve. I got flummoxed on a number of the puzzles and had to come back the next day.The puzzle mechanics were novel for me, rolling oddly shaped characters around a blocky world.The story is just little bits of text and whatnot around the beginning/end of levels, you could easily ignore it, but it's a fun little story.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun and interesting concept for a puzzle game. The controls can be a bit awkward (playing with keyboard and mouse) and certain series of levels can feel grindy and repetetive. The difficulty is pretty nice for my liking, its not super insane difficult but just enough to make you feel satisfied after solving a puzzle.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: I play a lot of puzzle games and Kine is very well made one. It focuses on rotating anthropomorphic, cube like musical instruments and manipulating limbs to navigate to the destination of a level. The mechanics are simple and intuitive but the puzzles can get quite challenging.The game also focuses on music and the accompanying sound track is excellent as well. The music slowly builds up as you progress in the levels.The thing that stuck out to me the most about Kine is that for most puzzle games, I can work back from the solution and solve the puzzle. Most puzzles from other games only have one obvious solution and because of this, deducing the possible paths to that solution is usually simple. Some of the harder puzzles in Kine manage to hide this very well so you have to rely on educated guesses. It managed to give me a satisfactory challenge.The game also introduces new and interesting mechanics at a decent rate. The game should take around 6 hours or more to complete. I recommend this game for fans of puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favourite puzzle games of all time Beautiful story, beautiful music, and most importantly of all, beautiful design.The way all the mechanics fit together is magical, by the halfway point I was finishing every level with a smile on my face and in awe of the puzzle design. What an incredible game!
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Kine is a fun movement-based puzzle game. With great art and music to accompany you in solving the puzzles.The puzzles are fun to try, and since it is movement-based, certain characters and map have their own complexity to be solved, which makes it challenging, yet fun.The variety of the puzzles are also great, with some focused according to your character movement, some on the environment, and the later levels combining both.Small gripe I have with the game are mostly on the controls. I played exclusively using my keyboard only.Whenever you control a character in the game, it works just fine in cycling movement and moving the character itself.But when it comes down to controlling more than 1 character, selecting parts and cycling it can be annoying to play.And also there are no way to access the option menu when you are in a level, so you have to quit the level to access the options to adjust volume and other stuffs.But other than that, Kine is a solid puzzle game that is Fun.If you are looking for a simple short game to rack your brain, I personally recommend this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: This is the one game at PAX East 2020 that I played and instantly fell in love with and bought a key on the spot for the Epic Games store.The core puzzle element is to move a rolling block from a start position to and end position. Kine elevates this by creating a world where each character is a unique rolling block. The game start off by introducing each character separately and then introduces puzzles that build upon each character's unique element.There is a nice story to go along with everything as all the characters come together. The artwork is visually refreshing, and the upbeat jazz music really lends itself to the world these characters live in. Like the puzzles themselves, the music also builds upon itself once you progress further through the game. The soundtrack alone was a big draw for me too as well.All in all, this is a really great take on the classic rolling block puzzle.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Kine easily earns its thumb up for its excellent puzzle design.Built on amusing mechanics, great effort was put in crafting them, making them tricky with satisfying solutions.Difficult enough. A couple of levels gave me a terrific amount of trouble.The main flaw is suboptimal visibility.In particular, the fact that rotation, while smooth, is limited to 4 angles, kept bugging me throughout, Quite irritating that, when you rotate to an ideal angle, it doesn't stop there but keeps moving on its own to an inconvenient 90 degrees position.In those 4 preset angles, things often obfuscate the playground and hinder your planning.In rare instances, it's difficult to notice that a tile is a moving piece.Finally, I'm never sure which character is currently selected. I could have done with more highlight or outline or any form of emphasis.A minor flaw pertains to the music: As invigorating as it is, it's also repetitive, due to very short loops, and so can be slightly irritating at times.A surprising fact, considering how central music is to the story.The gamepad interface is simple and rather intuitive, with convenient undo and redo buttons (extremely useful to me since I keep moving the wrong piece, thinking it's the selected one.)I never fully mastered the trombone, especially the crippled one.Sometimes it made a solution easier to figure out than to implement.However I do enjoy a dose of chaos in games, even in puzzles, and some of my progress was chaotic indeed, lacking in elegance but not in entertainment.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: This game does what any great puzzle game should--it makes your mind move in unusual ways, keeps things constrained enough that there are a finite number of player options so players don't feel overwhelmed, and leaves enough freedom that players feel smart for solving puzzles (even if it's well enough bounded that they were, well, "bound" to get there eventually). Three playable characters and a later spin on each of them, combined with some fun environmental objects like the rolling "Dance" tables and river boat, make for a great amount of variety that keeps the game feeling fresh throughout.All that, plus great music and a cute narrative arc? Nothing not to love. Get the game already!
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice puzzle game.The gameplay revolves around maneuvering one or more slightly-shapeshifting-robots throughout the level. Most levels are quite short so you usually spend a few minutes at most on one of them, so it's easy to jump into the game for a quick break to solve some puzzles.Music and graphics are extremely pleasant. The music changes and builds up as you progress throughout the levels and each character has i's own variation of the theme. There are also nice little touches like characters dancing to the rhythm when idle. The art and graphics fit very well with the theme of the game in a comic-book style.If I had to point out some "bad" things about the game I would say that the game is . However I don't mean that the game has some obtuse mechanics or some bs out-of-the-box solutions. Actually, the mechanics are very straightforward and rarely are there completely new mechanics that you have to learn from ground up. 2nd half of the game basically revolves around rotating 3d objects on a flat surface and this isn't something easy or immediately intuitive. Imagine having a 6-sided die on a grid and trying to figure out the sequence of moves to get a particular face up an a specific square on the grid. It's not that obvious right away how to do it without physically doing an experiment and that's basically the criticism founf in other reviews - that you have play around with the moves in the level to figure out the solution. And some people may find it rather discouraging.However, at the same time this real-world application of rotation mechanics is a very nice way of practicing your understanding of how this stuff works and getting a better grasp on 3d rotations.Perhaps another flaw is that it's sometimes hard to correctly jusge height and distance in the game.Nevertheless, I would still recommend playing this game, even if for the sole purpose of practicing your imagination.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun and quirky puzzler. The characters in the game are weird musical instruments cobbled together with random pieces. They are silly and charming and the interactions between them are fun. The story, despite being minimal, was appreciated.Other than that, it's a standard grid based puzzler where space is at a premium and movement is limited. There are not a ton of levels, so the game doesn't have enough time to get stale or become oppressively complicated.  Most of the levels are fairly straight forward, but a few had me scratching my head and I needed a few hints. For these levels, I realized that if you don't make certain moves early on, you can lock yourself out of possible solutions do to movement and space limitations. I found that to be a bit frustrating, and maybe I'm wrong about that but if I'm right, a this can no longer be completed warning would have been appreciated. Perhaps it is possible to revert the characters to correct orientations in the instances that I'm talking about, but I was unable to do so at times.I also ran into some difficulty where the game would lock itself up when I made a move that was impossible. This primarily happened with the trombone. I would slide into some position that was impossible, and the game would freeze. Not actually, the music would keep playing, and the animations would continue, but I could not undo, reset, or access the menu. I had to alt-F4 out of it each time, which was frustrating.This game took me about 8 hours with a few hints. I had difficulty unlocking the no machine left behind achievement, but I redid the solutions a few times and it worked. The game seems to go on a generous sale often enough. Despite the issues I mentioned, it's definitely worth picking up if you like these type of grid-based puzzlers.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Putting a backstory in a level-based puzzle game is not an easy task... except for Kine! I absolutely LOVED how well interconnected and fitting the story is on the various level sets and also how it follows the evolution and the variations on the main puzzle mechanism. The jazzy, funky style of both the art and (of course) the music are the perfect complement for this gem of a game.The only thing I found a bit annoying is how you switch among characters... it can get tricky, especially when you have the full trio, with the trombone having two moving parts... maybe it's just me, but I couldn't get used to it!The overall game is fantastic, anyway, a must have for all puzzle lovers out there!
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: kine's gameplay doesn't look like music composing, but it's characters interactions and the game overall narrative, combined with the level design makes it feel like you are actually doing what the characters are doing, which may be trying to get along with each other, paying the bills, etc, but always through those lens of music.not yet a masterpiece to my eyes but an easy recommendation to puzzle lovers.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Very charming game! It's got a strong, polished style, with characters that develop their own stories that mesh well with the gameplay, and relationships that progress throughout. The puzzles start out very simple and feel like you're just mashing your way through, but soon enough the difficulty ramps up a fair bit and you have to carefully consider your approach. It never gets toooo hard (I'm looking at you, stephen's sausage roll), but I did have to step away from the game for a few puzzles and come back to them later, and look up a couple of solutions for ones I just did not get.My only criticisms are:a) the music can get a little repetitive and distracting, and the option to turn it down is a few menus away from the puzzles, andb) the controls to select and interact with each of the instruments and their "limbs" could be better.Honestly, the fact that this cute as hell game isn't better known seems somewhat criminal!
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing. I saw it and it looked cute. Decided to try the demo and was captivated by it. It is a funny and challenging game. And the soundtrack is just amazing. It kept me going! Some puzzles were quite tough but doing then while listening to the music was justt pure fun. BUY IT! Also get the soundtrack!!
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: The most impressive thing for me about this game is the visuals. The comic book art-style is lovely. The music stands out, too, which isn't surprising in a game where you play as anthropomorphic musical instruments aspiring to be musicians. I did find it a bit too lively and upbeat at times, though, which can be a bit distracting when you're doing puzzles that require patience and focus to solve, but this is pretty much a nitpick, easily remedied by turning the volume down a bit. On top of that, this is a relatively narrative-driven puzzle game, where the story is told via dialogue by the characters in the form of speech bubbles. There are three characters altogether, and they each have their own personalities! There's no voice acting in the game, but that is probably too much to expect from an indie puzzle game where a lot of effort has already been put into the visuals and music.As for the gameplay, I found it pretty solid. The puzzles aren't too difficult, but I found them a bit trickier than most 'casual' puzzle games. I found the mechanics of each character being able to change their shape in different ways refreshing, though not ground-breaking. My only complaint is that the control scheme can get a bit annoying, and I definitely recommend you play the game with a controller. Apart from four movement keys, you also have a button to change the shape of your character, and another to cycle between characters, and on top of that, there's one particular instrument with two separate moving parts, so you need to press another button to cycle between the two parts, as each part would change that character's shape in different ways. This is especially tedious when playing levels where all three characters are present, and I can't even say that I fully mastered the controls by the end of the game, as I was still making plenty of mistakes towards the end haha. With that said, the controls are required to be this way due to the game mechanics, and since this is a turn-based puzzle game with no timing-based challenges, they aren't really a deal-breaker, and you can always undo the mistake. Apart from that, the game has a redo button, which can be pretty helpful at times. The reset button requires you to hold the button for 1-2 seconds, which is a design to prevent you from accidentally resetting the level, which is quite possible when playing with a gamepad.All in all, this is a solid puzzle game with great presentation. There is a free demo available, so I recommend you check that out to get a feel for the game and see if it's to your liking or not.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: A really unique puzzle game. The movement of Roo, Quat, and Euler is very unique and unlike anything else I have ever seen. This makes for really unique and fun puzzles. I really love the music too. The controls take a little getting used to and I often forget how each character moves but that's not a huge problem.After about 45 minutes, the puzzles start to get really fun and challenging with multiple characters and moving platforms. Worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked Kine. It's a fun puzzle game about moving one or more of three musical instrument characters around what looks like a simple block oriented course. Each puzzle only takes a few moves but it's not as simple as it sounds because it involves rotating the character and extending their 'limbs' to help movement. Movement from one position to another is very slick and its just as easy to revert a move so the game encourages a try and see if it works approach. The music is fun and there is a story which ties it all together.Highly recommended if you like puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Kine is a one-of-a-kind puzzle game with an awesome style.You solve short stages by moving (up to) three characters around. It is a lot harder than it sounds, as each character moves in their own, very distinct and weird way. Controlling the characters is a bit unintuitive at first which can be a little frustrating, but if you play the game with the right mindset it is really satisfying to figure out their quirks and solve the puzzles.Many of the levels can be played out of order so if you are stuck on something you can easily switch to another puzzle for a change. However there is a well designed difficulty curve.The game is polished. It controls nice and the animations are great. There is also a simple story that progresses as you solve puzzles, but it doesn't get in the way of anything. In fact, the game is at its best when the story and 'puzzle feel' align.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated puzzle game. Self-aware writing that is breaking the fourth wall in funny ways. Charming characters, great jazz soundtrack. Gameplay is challenging, levels are brain twisters. Game feels like a product of love, attention to detail just screams "I had this cool idea in my head and want to do it", well the idea was great and is executed perfectly.Not sure why this isn't known more.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: In this video I take a look at Kine, a musical puzzle game. This is an extremely well made puzzle game. Different musicians posses different movement abilities and need to work together to get to the end of the block path. It is a very high quality product should be worth the time of any music game or puzzle fan, take a look.Watch the video to see what the game is like...Check'n Games Video Curation, providing you with as many Let's Play's as we can.Thanks for watching. Please like comment and subscribe.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: charming puzzle game! i played and finished the demo and i loved it! soundtrack is very good (sorta big band style), the music builds up adding more layers onto it as you progress thru the puzzlesit's a game where you literally 'play musical instruments' by taking advantages of their shape and size , which also determines each instrument's movement.it's also an indie game with a small dev team, so if you're a fan of the genre, play the demo first, then go and buy!
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the demo I was so excited for to get the full game, and so far it has not disappointed! Clever puzzles abound, and though as of right now I haven't reached the endgame, there are hints of what's to come, (plus you can see some things in the trailer!), and they're sure to be a delight. The graphics, soundtrack and sound design, humour, and characters all work to help Kine stand out as a puzzle game absolutely worth checking out. A true gem that any puzzle enthusiast should check out!
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Already falling in love with the charm of this game after about half an hour of play.The characters are super charming, the music is delightful (not to mention dynamic based on the selected character) and the puzzles have all been quite engaging in regards to spacial reasoning. The multi character stages are especially interesting due to the differing movement mechanics for each character and how the interplay with each other.Excited to see what else is in store for me as I continue playing~
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

_childDocuments_.review: Kine is a 3D puzzle game about three whimsical machines that aspire to be musicians. Embark across a theatrically rendered cityscape by solving increasingly difficult 3D puzzles. Guide Euler, Quat, and Roo as they struggle to form a band and find their big break.
_childDocuments_.name: Kine

name: HROT
detailed_description: HROT is a single-player retro FPS set in a small socialist country neighboring Soviet Union (Czechoslovakia) after an unspecified disaster in 1986. Those times were dark and terrifying and so is the game. You start in a civil defense shelter deep under a Prague Metro station. As a proud holder of the military readiness badge you know what your duty is: put on a non-functioning gas mask, load the vz. 52 pistol and protect the peace and your socialist homeland from the strange intruders. The classic gameplay and vibe of romeric shooters from 1990s including a fitting brown retro aesthetic. You'll find a shotgun, a vz. 13 SMG, a rocket launcher and even some secret experimental Soviet battery-powered weapon. If you run out of ammo, you might find the hammer and sickle coming in handy. Handcrafted levels inspired by real locations with an emphasis on historical details. Every level contains socialist paraphernalia which nowadays can only be found in museums or your grandma's attic (Eastern Bloc only). Flushable toilets, destructible light bulbs and horses with gas/latex masks. In short, conservative values that never disappoint. A custom engine written in Pascal imitating 1990s software-style rendering with unfiltered textures and polygon jitter.
about_the_game: HROT is a single-player retro FPS set in a small socialist country neighboring Soviet Union (Czechoslovakia) after an unspecified disaster in 1986. Those times were dark and terrifying and so is the game. You start in a civil defense shelter deep under a Prague Metro station. As a proud holder of the military readiness badge you know what your duty is: put on a non-functioning gas mask, load the vz. 52 pistol and protect the peace and your socialist homeland from the strange intruders. The classic gameplay and vibe of romeric shooters from 1990s including a fitting brown retro aesthetic. You'll find a shotgun, a vz. 13 SMG, a rocket launcher and even some secret experimental Soviet battery-powered weapon. If you run out of ammo, you might find the hammer and sickle coming in handy. Handcrafted levels inspired by real locations with an emphasis on historical details. Every level contains socialist paraphernalia which nowadays can only be found in museums or your grandma's attic (Eastern Bloc only). Flushable toilets, destructible light bulbs and horses with gas/latex masks. In short, conservative values that never disappoint. A custom engine written in Pascal imitating 1990s software-style rendering with unfiltered textures and polygon jitter.
short_description: HROT is a single-player retro FPS set in a small socialist country neighboring Soviet Union (Czechoslovakia) after an unspecified disaster in 1986. Those times were dark and terrifying and so is the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful fever dream.Overall a fantastic retro FPS heavily inspired by Quake (basically if you liked Quake this will be up your alley), packed to the brim with clever nods to the times of the Soviet Union. Each level has a lot of bits and pieces that will be instantly familiar to anyone who grew up in a post-communist country.I found all of the levels fun to play, both visaully and gameplay wise - there is always something new around the corner, levels can be finished quickly but the abundance of secrets and Soviet era details encourage exploration. On Very Hard I felt that the game's challenge was just right, with some tougher moments, but never hard enough to be considered unfair.Weapons were also fun to use and the ammo placement was great - it was abundant enough that I could use my favorite weapons but it did encourage me to swap from time to time to avoid running dry.Music is used sparingly but when it's there it hits the spot - fits the tone and accentuates the combat when necessary. On the other hand, the weapon sounds could use work since they lacked the 'unf' that would make them much more satisfying.If you're not sure - I say just buy it and you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: HROT is another one of these boomer shooters but it's honestly one of the best in its genre. The quickest way to sum it up is that it's a goofy slavic take on Dusk or Quake. There are three episodes each with 8 levels that you can finish it in around 7 or so hours. Of course you can get many more hours out of it if you're looking for all the secrets on higher difficulties, but I was satisfied with halfheartedly looking for these on normal.The story doesn't really matter: you're some guy in the Soviet controlled Czech Republic and you have to kill a bunch of guys wearing gasmasks across very brown and depressing looking Eastern Bloc locales. It's got a good variety of weapons and a bunch of interesting enemies. The levels are definitely old school with their designs and key finding but rarely did I feel lost or unsure of where to go. It's just long enough to where you want more from it.There are a TON of historical references, figures, tidbits, and jokes that will be lost on the average Westerner. I had no clue what most of this stuff was referencing but it all came across as amusing and gives the game a fun, unique atmosphere somewhat reminiscent of STALKER and other 'Eurojank' games. There are two great Steam guides ("a guide to Symbolism in HROT (SPOILERS!!!)" and "Lost in Translation") that explains most of this stuff if you are interested.Even though it's kind of short for it's price I still had a great time with it. I got this from a Humble Bundle a while ago along with Ion Fury and more so I'm very happy with what I paid. $20 full price is kind of steep if you're the kind of person to one-and-done games, but it seems to hit $13.99 regularly on the big sales. It's a very well-done, competent, and funny old school throwback that I would wholeheartedly recommend to anyone who enjoys these kind of modern boomer shooters.
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: The true beauty of HROT is not in its weapons or movement, but its levels and the depth and love that each one is shown as gamified recreations of Czech landmarks. This game fills a dull and bleak color scheme of brown and beige full of historic character scored by a moody ambient soundtrack. There are plenty of small details and even more references, and by the end I felt I had actually learned something about a country and its history.Yet as a boomer shooter, HROT does not hold anything particularly impressive for the average fan. Your jump is a stiff hop and you lack the ability to slide, crouch, or bunny hop, but most combat takes place in close quarters and the movement is extremely responsive otherwise.The guns are mostly standard fare, going so far as to include a super shotgun and a BFG equivalent, but even without an alt fire or flashy abilities I never found them coming up short (except for the land mines, but I've always found such weapons at odd with fast-paced gameplay). You can run people over with a motorbike too, but that only features in a handful of levels. You CAN get wine drunk in most others, though!But what HROT lacks in mobility and its arsenal, it more than makes up for in enemy variety and number of bosses with a staggering 51 entries in the game's bestiary. Most wear masks and carry a gun, but there are some stranger invaders threatening the homeland, too. There are some problem enemies (I will never underestimate wheelchair users again) while others could stand to take a bullet or two more, but they are thankfully rare among an otherwise mostly fairly-balanced cast.The game is split into three episodes, with episode 1 having you meet the most common enemies throughout the rest of the game. Episodes 2 and 3 are where HROT really comes into its own, and that includes a sprinkle of Eastern European humor throughout. I won't talk about what each episode is about (and would have trouble doing so with how loosely the game connects itself) because I feel each surprise has the most impact when done totally blind. And by my memory, only two secrets can be made impossible to get by progressing through a level, so no need to fear if you're a secret-hunter.Overall?Grab your hammer and sickle and go save the homeland! It's full of charm and lovingly made, and I think that makes it more than just a decent boomer shooter.EDIT: words, no major changes

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start this review, a quick caveat; this is being posted during the early-access period of this game's release, at a point where approximately one-and-a-half of the game's three episodes have been released. Some stuff might be subject to change.This game manages to perfectly capture the feel of mid-'90s early-3D shooters, to the degree that - if I wasn't aware of the fact that this was A. a new game and B. in early access (at time of writing) - I would honestly think it really was one. Add to this a plot communicated almost entirely through environmental storytelling, as well as an entire dumptruck of pure, unbridled  and you've got an instant classic.The weapons and enemies are very interesting; while the former is the standard retro-FPS weapon-structure (melee, pistol, shotgun, super-shotgun, some kind of rapid-fire gun, explosive-launcher, a lightning gun, some form of powerful projectile-based weapon, a BFG-knockoff and a set of grenades), it manages to do most of them in interesting ways. My favourite example of this is the relationship between the aforementioned explosive-launching weapon and grenades; while the latter can be thrown at any time with the right mouse button (this game has no secondary-fire weapons) and explode at a set interval, they can also be launched further and detonated on impact with the former's primary-fire.Meanwhile, the enemies are disturbing, and a good example of the environmental storytelling I mentioned earlier. The most basic ones can commonly be seen vomiting when encountered, the horse-like Semik wear humanlike gas-masks (as opposed to horse-specific ones), and one of the enemies is essentially a smaller and weaker version of Quake's Ogres.When the game fully releases, I will probably post another review, although I may have forgotten by then.
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic classic FPS in most regards. The artistic direction is especially well done. The ambient is comprised of dark and oppressive music and sounds. The entirety of the game is brown and bleak, which works well in this weird communist zombie dystopia.The level design is simple enough that I didn't get lost, and it also features a few gimmicks to keep things fresh. Weapons are the best part. Here's a breakdown of the weapons I found:Pistol - Nothing fancy, generally well made but I don't understand why it has to reload. It's the only weapon in the game that has to do that.Single-barrel shotgun - Well paced and balanced weapon, although it becomes less useful after you get the super shotgunSuper shotgun - double-barreled boomstick - it seems like this weapon is better in every respect when compared to the previous shotgun, since it does double damage and shells are rarely scarceSMG - The fast-firing, ammo dump of this game. Works well against lower health enemies, like soldiersGrenade launcher - uses your grenades as ammo and deals more damage than just throwing them(I think?), but even if it doesn't, it's still very useful because the grenade thrown by it explode on impact and fly in a straight like.Mines - Almost never used them. They can be useful if you know where an enemy will come from. The one great use for them is in the last current level(E2M6), where a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ snakes appear out of the walls. I'll have to talk about the snakes too.Crossbow - Not bad, but I don't really see the point of it. It's kind of like a sniper, in the sense that it's great for killing enemies at a distance. Kind of like the rifle in Dusk. The problem is, Dusk has larger spaces, whereas in Hrot, 95% of the game is close quarters.Energy gun - This one's a secret which can be found on many maps - does a lot of damage and burns through ammo at the speed of light. Can be recharged by opening electric panels while holding it, though that damages you. Great at fighting bosses.I think there is at least one secret weapon that I haven't found. Something like the BFG from Doom.Enemies:Most enemies are fair, in my opinion. You start with soldiers, who run around and shoot one bullet at a time. They're easy, and a good first enemy.Then you get the biohazard shotgun dudes, who are kind of hard to deal with at first, because they require two shotgun blasts and they are also using shotguns.I think it's best that potential players find out the rest by themselves. It's quite a good roster of enemies... except one:The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ snakes in E2M6 - They deal a ton of damage and they're the most resilient enemy, I think. They don't die from a grenade launcher shot. It takes one grenade and two super-shotgun blasts. What is this? Why can a snake survive a grenade or a shotgun blast? I don't understand what the purpose of this enemy is, besides frustrating players. Hopefully the get taken down a peg or two in the future.Overall, a great ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game which I will gladly revisit when more episodes get added. Great job guys, you nailed it.

_childDocuments_.review: *Turns on HROT, ready to gib some monsters and sickle up some ravenous rats******Immediately gets stuck for 20 mins on the wikipedia entry for 'Klement Gottwald'*****A truly underrated title, HROT delivers and it delivers BIG. Like so many others, I learned about this gem from Civvie 11 and took the leap while it was still in Early Access. Not because I wanted to play early, but because I wanted to support the dev while they were in the most difficult part of indie game development. Where work is being done regularly but little to no pay is coming in until it gets finished. HROT is a retro FPS in the vein of OG Quake as so many have mentioned and yet still has just the right amount of the modern trappings you would expect of an FPS title made in THIS decade. The reviews weren't kidding either, so many call-backs / references to classic Quake! As someone born in 1987 and who literally spent THOUSANDS of hours inside original Quake and Duke Nukem 3D as a kid on our family Windows 95 PC, this game was such a welcome breath of fresh air, albeit with a very Czech influence of course! ☑ Level design is masterfully constructed and environments varied enough to never be stale☑ Weapon selection and response (feedback, recoil, audio and audio sync, etc) feels amazing ☑ Enemy and Boss design, AI, and enemy variance is top notch and widely varied☑ Level of attention to detail and sheer amount of small details is unparalleled. Very obvious this was a labor of love☑ Incredible value for the quantity and quality. This game could be double the price and it would still be worth it!Wtf are you waiting for? All you're doing by not picking this game up is screwing yourself ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: a dark and surprisingly funny nightmare simultaneously mundane (positive), muddy and industrial, unrepentant in its highly surreal and disgusting corpus and world, filled to the brim with czech and soviet historical and cultural references (as well as most locations being recreations of real or fabled czech locations) that are delightful, clever, and way beyond skin deep. among hrot's finer qualities is that looks and feels like a roy andersson movie if one of the characters just started Killing Peopleit slots real nice into the larger realm of soviet aestheticisation, as well as the microscopic gaming realm shared by games like You Are Empty-but it most interestingly feels (to me at least) shockingly coherent/fitting as an entry into or homage to the far more amorphous sphere of dark? soviet art ranging everywhere from nazim tulyahodzhayev's adaptations of ray bradbury stories to beksinski paintings with their brown oppressive haze, throw in tarkovsky's stalker for good measure. although with orders of magnitude more beer and farts than any mentioned above.as im not czech i couldnt tell if the Beer And Farts aspect of the humour has any basis in anything specific or is something the developer brought to the table themselves, but its appreciated and makes the game stand out, and doesnt get in the way of the tension or unsettling moodthere is a niche of brown, slimy, droning soviet grime i've had a life long obsession with whose itch is not left unscratched by this game, and it's the only game i can think of that's gone this deep and this hard into this nicheyou run around concrete, filth, and filthy concrete, scraping along rust, eating cans of blood and fat, picking up underwear and wifebeaters for armour, in environments that are exclusively brown from start to finish as the ambient music drones in the darkest pits of the human hearing range, enemies clad in gp-5 gas masks and hazmat suits will throw up as they lay eyes on you, and with guttural grunts will shamble towards you, this game is in a league of its own, and the indulgence is amazinggoing from factory to streets to countryside to mines to churches to megastructures, the game is pleasantly varied and creative, taking you indoors and outdoors evoking as many moods and settings as can possibly fit within the grimy soviet aesthetic, be it oppressive brutalism, creepy liminality in the mundane, or scarfing down liberty caps in the fertile grounds of a graveyard. hrot is consistently scaring, challenging, and intriguing the player at every turn, relying on extremely fascinating and evocative architecture and atmosphere/ambience outlining the whole experience, hosting a huge array of consistently creative, creepy, and gross enemies, ensuring no two places feel the same, and always keeping the player on their toes giving them new puzzles, encounters, secrets, and playstyles throughout it feels like the whole game is dripping and seeping and rotting, admirably made for a very select and insular demographic, and i think it's all the better for it. i'd also consider it a technical feat because the game is on a custom built engine that runs criminally well with no bugs in my playtime from first early-access release to now, and it does not use modern hardware as a crutch.absolutely worth the price of admission and every second spent if anything at all about it strikes your fancy

_childDocuments_.review: I really like how minimalist HROT is. While many other retro shooters are going for a sort of maximal ism to justify the older graphics HROT sees fit to strip away things. The pallet never goes beyond a navy green, the weapons are so basic that they may even be called dull at times (which doesn't matter to me since the shooting is really good and snappy) and the levels are mostly small winding spaces. Hrot focuses on what it wants to be and meets that goal fantastically. The atmosphere is constantly oppressive and at the same time alienating. Plus, the game is filled with toys and bobbles for you to interact with. As someone who plays a ton of these retro shooters HROT felt like a real pallet cleanser bringing the games back to the main things that made them great. Despite episode 3 feeling a bit weaker than the first two episodes (and honestly which retro shooter doesnt have a weak third epsiode?) I would heartily recommend HROT.

_childDocuments_.review: HROT is yet another in the seemingly endless line of modern retro FPS games. Made by a single developer it takes you on a monochromatic journey through Czechoslovakia where an "unspecified" disaster populated the area with hostiles, including flying Lenin heads and horses with gasmasks. And no, those are not the weirdest enemies in the game.If you've played any other game like that then you know what to expect. Neatly designed levels inspired by the classics, lots of secrets, lots of shooting and blowing things up, end-level stats and toilets. It's a little bit of Quake1 (visuals), a little bit of Dusk (combat), a little bit of Rise of the Triad (ludicrousness). Not a bad mix, if you ask me.A while ago I played Prodeus and I still maintain that in terms of combat and the overall gameplay flow it's the best modern retro shooter out there. However what Prodeus lacked was immersion. Levels comprised almost entirely of industrial facilities and caves and I didn't get a very strong sense of place there. HROT is kind of the opposite. The combat is just sort of there - it's not bad, it's not amazing. But the environments feel a lot more immersive. I don't want to say "realistic" because that's not the right word for this game. But the places you visit feel like they're actual places rather than some semi-abstract gameplay areas. The atmosphere is surprisingly strong.Of course a big part of that is the interactivity and all the random stuff you can do. I really appreciate the fact that the developer of HROT has spent time working on all those seemingly pointless little details and interactions that do not affect the gameplay at all but make the game world feel more immersive. I won't spoil them because part of the fun is discovering all those fun optional things but they're all cool and endearing. They certainly add a lot of personality to the game. And there are A LOT of them.The same goes for a number of features that are unique to certain levels. Some things only appear once in the entire game which not only makes them more interesting but also shows the developer's commitment. It takes time and effort to create something that only shows up once and not all devs would bother to do that. I mean, this game has a fully functional astronomical clock simulator that exists just because. I think that settles it.HROT is also unique amongst all the other retro shooters in that it runs on a completely custom engine. There's just something special about that fact, even if you could probably achieve the same effect using Unity or Unreal. And on that note, I want to commend the author for sticking to his guns and keeping the game's monochromatic look. I mean sure, HROT is brown. All brown all day every day. But that's fine. It's fine to sometimes have a game with a very limited color palette.So what's bad about this game? Well, there are some things to nitpick. Most people probably agree that the sounds, especially gun sounds are kind of unremarkable (to say the least). Many secrets rely on pixel hunting, like finding a wall that's literally one pixel deeper than the others. You have probably the lowest jump I've ever seen in an FPS. There's absolutely no story... and I know that this is not that important in a retro shooter but even Quake had a background story. It'd be nice to have some sort of context other than "something happened, kill the bad guys". I mean, the game gives you recipes at the end of each episode, instead of anything related to the game, come on. It's kinda funny... but still. The higher difficulty levels feel rather unbalanced. They're playable but not very fun.However I have very much enjoyed my time with HROT. It's endearing, clunky, campy and silly while maintaining the depressing atmosphere. Very much a labour of love and that alone makes it worth playing. If you don't mind the monochromatic look and can forgive the weak sound design, that is.

_childDocuments_.review: HROT is an excellent retro fps in the vein of Quake, Blood and Dusk that already has grabbed my attention in a genre that is truly saturated with incredible titles. If you've enjoyed games like Dusk, Ion Fury or Doom 64 then this is the next game to wait on. There's only one act finished out of three, but there's a fun endless mode that you can mess around with if you've got the urge to return but don't want to replay the first act. Also, the reward for finishing the current game is truly delicious. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favourite games to come out of the boomer shooter revival. The reason being that most new games in the genre tend to feel over-designed, having lots of fancy mechanics that create bloat without really stepping out of their predecessor's shadow. Hrot is a simple game with simple visuals, making it a very convincing throwback, and it's better for it. Despite looking like Quake, its gameplay has more in common with Doom, given the lack of vertical movement and abundance of traps. The levels are often cramped, which makes combat tense and exciting. Unlike Doom, however, the game is actually scary.From what I've played so far it doesn't seem to do anything groundbreaking, and there are some flaws, but what's there is really fun.
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: HROT's main selling point is its unique post-apocalyptic and post-Soviet setting full of strange monsters and remnants from the past that may just as well help you as try to kill you. From the very moment you boot up the game the atmosphere is very much palpable. From the brownish colour palette, to the hollow industrial soundscape full of eerie howling and muted geiger counters, the setting is elevated to its fullest potential. But what would a setting be without great level design and, luckily, HROT delivers in spades. Not only is there great variety with everything from dilapidated castles to run-down industrial and apartment complexes but the levels are all teeming with secrets both friendly and hostile. But what really helps tie it all together is the fast-paced gameplay coupled with great gun-variety with a sprinkle of dark humour on top which seasoned old-school FPS players will feel right at home with.If my love for this game isn't evident yet I would also like to highlight how, despite its impressive 17 levels, the developer is also working on a third and final chapter which will be added to the game completely free of charge at a later date!
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: HROT has easily become one of my favourite shooters. Unlike many other retro throwback FPS, it's not bombastic but rather bleak and even serene at times. It runs on a custom engine to achieve the rendering style it precisely wants and also has quite the pleasing filesize of under 200 MB. Developer is active on the Steam discussions and has implemented many small requests like keybinds, adding last weapon switch function and arachnophobia mode.
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: HROT is a very fun game. I think it would be fair to call this a "DOOMlike", which I find exciting given how most shooters operate these days. You wake up in a Soviet Replublic (I believe Czechoslovakia) and your mission is to start killing the invaders in your country. But really your mission is to kill whatever you find and get through the level. The setting and aesthetic are both very cool, and the gameplay is on par if not better than classic DOOM games, although I'm not sure it has the same enemy variety DOOM2. I've really enjoyed my time in the game and there's not really much more to say.8/10 Best beef stroganoff recipe I could find.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty dang awesome!  If Doom were set in Silent Hill, and if Silent Hill was located in some Soviet puppet regime in Eastern Europe, THIS would be that game!  I mean that in the best possible way.  Not really a horror game so much a throw-back retro FPS with an unsettling atmosphere and a few moments that constitute jump scares, usually baddies busting through walls to surprise you or opening a door to find a monsters waiting to shoot you.  And some genuinely unnerving bosses based off of communist motifs.You are a nameless citizen of some Commie Despotism or another.  With no clear motivation except to lock horns with the monsters.  The main bad-guys look like a cross between diesel-punk soldiers and Silent Hill's Order cultists of Silent Hill: Homecoming.  Uniformed goons with gas masks who shoot you on sight.  Later variants can teleport away from you at will and try to ambush you.  Giant floating heads that bear a striking resemblance to Valdmir Lenin fire projectiles at you.  Occasionally Hind attack choppers of Rambo 3 fame show up but somehow seem to bleed when you shoot them with shotguns (which are the best weapon against them).  And it wouldn't be that creepy without giant spindly spiders, so they're in it too.My favorite part is at the end where the final boss is a four-legged Joseph Stalin!  I have been a staunch anti-communist since freshmen year of High School when I read The Red Scarf Girl (highly recommended for anyone who actually THINKS communism is a good idea...lol) .  Even on normal difficulty it can be pretty unforgiving but very gratifying.Hats off to another indie developer who has managed to succeed where triple A developers often fail!  Here's hoping the developers keep at updating it and maybe give us some exposition.  But even as it is it's still a pretty darn good game.

_childDocuments_.review: HROT is a first-person shooter that pays homage to iconic shooters like Doom (id Tech 1 engine) and Quake (Quake engine) (1990s), blending retro aesthetics with modern gameplay mechanics. Set in a dystopian version of Czechoslovakia during the late 1980s, players navigate through meticulously crafted environments that evoke a sense of nostalgia while delivering fresh challenges. The game features an array of weapons, each with distinct characteristics, allowing for varied combat strategies. The movement feels sharp ,fluid (running bunnyhopping) and responsive.The visual style of HROT is strikingly unique, utilizing pixel art graphics that capture the essence of early 3D games. The environments are richly detailed and secrets cleverly hidden all the plenty.   The levels, filled with atmospheric lighting and textures that enhance immersion. The game’s art direction effectively conveys a sense of decay and desolation, immersing players in its eerie world. Additionally, the sound design complements the visuals perfectly; ambient noises and retro-inspired soundtracks create an engaging auditory experience that heightens tension during gameplay.While HROT primarily focuses on action-packed gameplay, it also weaves a narrative that reflects themes of oppression and societal decay. Players encounter various enemies that symbolize the oppressive regime of the time, adding depth to the otherwise straightforward shooting mechanics.Overall, HROT stands out as a compelling tribute to retro FPS games while carving its own identity through innovative design choices and thematic depth. It successfully balances nostalgia with modern gaming sensibilities, making it an enjoyable experience for both veteran gamers and newcomers alike.Highly recommend this game 10/10 , thank u for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: Had HROT in my game library for quite some time. Can't remember when I bought it, it was definitely during it's first "phase" of being in Early Access when it was basically just a demo/proof of concept. Ignored it because usually even if I am extremely excited for a game and even buy it in Early Access to support the devs, I usually wait for it to completely finish before giving it a go. Still even after it was fully released, I didn't really bothered with it because it felt like a "cheap" attempt to copy Quake but in a Soviet Setting. After trying it, I admit I was completely wrong judging the game so superficially. Under the layers upon layers of brown, lies one of them most fun FPS games I've played in a while. Shooting feels great (maybe the only exception being the SMG which feels way too under powered for how ammo hungry it is), exploring each level is fun without being overwhelming or confusing (impressive given how every single level is colored using the same shade of brown), the visuals despite their brownness are appealing and atmospheric. I was also pleasantly surprised that despite being basically a "boomer shooter" the game also is filled with creepy moments, it enjoys playing with your head and it manages to build tension without feeling cheap. The random references and memes also felt like I was playing an interactive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which also elevated the weird atmosphere the game had. Overall, an extremely fun experience.

Each of them have their own strengths and weakness but you'll find that an up close shotgun blast pretty much takes care of any enemy.*Ammo is pretty scarce so you'll have to be accurate and plan your route.*The level design so far is intuitive enough to where you wont need to use your map, which is good to keep the flow of the game constant.*The enemy projectile speed is just fast enough that you can dodge it and be able to see it. *The sounds are satisfying and the music is done very well, its more ambient dark than anything else.*Game is more sedated in its presentation compared to dusk but will mess you up something awful if you think cero miedo was challenging. _childDocuments_.review: HROT (or Slavic Quake as it's know in retro FPS circles) is an excellent little Quake style shooter. Running on it's on engine (written in Pascal which couldn't have been fun), it nails the atmosphere, visual artefacts and general vibe of the engine John Carmack wrote back in 1996 down to a tee. Unlike retro shooters before HROT that used shaders to make Unity look old, this is the real deal. It's hard to convey just how beautifully old this feels, you just need to play it.The movement in HROT however is a little weak. Walking around is okay but the jumping is pretty clunky and hard to pull off. There's one secret that I just couldn't reach because of the weak jumping which felt a little unfair to me. I also felt that the game was a little too easy on Normal which admittedly can be remedied by picking a higher difficulty but at the moment I feel it could still challenge new players a little more. The enemies are great I feel! Their designs are fantastic and utterly inspired! The humanoid enemies walk around with their Soviet gas masks and trench coats and leave you wondering if they're even alive in there. The enemies telegraph their attacks well and communicate damage well. Nothing to complain about there!My last gripe is the weapons. They feel fine and as long as you ration your ammo, you should be good on that front. But the weapon sounds and introductions are the weakest link in this whole game. They sound far too delicate and weak, some more oomf in their sound would be excellent! As for the introductions, I felt that at the moment I got a new weapon, it wasn't too bad... but later on I'd forget I even had some very powerful weapons and I feel that stronger and more memorable introductions could fix this. However, If this is just me being dumb and everyone else got on hunky dory then I guess I'll just shut up :PHROT is a little short for the price but that will change! Its in early access and has more chapters coming! So I'd 100% recommend you buy this! You won't regret it!
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome little retro shooter with a unique setting.While there isn't much content as of writing this review, what is here is soaking with a dreary soviet era atmosphere and i absolutely adore it.Ambience and music for the most part is really good and helps add tension, just like in Quake.Levels are nicely compact and are pretty well designed with plenty of secrets to find, and enemies to shoot.And if you love games like Quake, Dusk, Chasm, you'll feel right at home.The only serious negative i would say the game currently has, is the sound effects for a lot of the weapons themselves outside of maybe the rocket launcher sound a bit weak, and ofc, being an early access game, there isn't much to offer outside of 8 levels, a horde mode, and an interesting "NG+" mode (which randomizes the enemies and weapons, but you'll still be playing the same 8 levels again)But with time, i'm sure this'll be one of the top throwback shooters out there!If you are willing to support a single man dev team, and love these kind of games, definitely consider picking it up now! Otherwise, check back in a couple months once there is more content.

_childDocuments_.review: (Follow  for more reviews like this)Absolutely amazing, probably my favorite of the new wave of retro FPS. At the start, I expected it to be just your average Quake/Dusk style neo-retro shooter in drab brutalist concrete jungles, but it kept throwing surprises at me and never stopped delivering. Excellent game, a masterclass in level design and pacing.Episode 1 is a solid romp through communist-era Prague, with several recognizable landmarks and depressing brutalist architecture. Episode 2 moves on to the countryside with equal parts medieval Czech castles and industrial facilities. There are a couple of jumpscares here (two, to be exact) that add an unexpected horror element. Episode 3 is where HROT goes all out with creativity - while it's mostly brutalist structures again, the game keeps throwing weird and unexpected things at you. It's oftentimes hilarious, always connected to Czech culture in some way, and feels delightfully surreal.Level design and pacing are excellent. Even though the visuals are consistently brown, every level looks different because of the lovingly crafted architecture. Be it brutalist commie buildings or traditional medieval architecture, every edifice in this game has a recognizable shape and style. You go from streets to open plazas to sewers to hallways... the game constantly throws you into different environments and mixes up the action so it never feels repetitive.The core shooting gameplay is great, too. While the pistols and SMG sound a little weak (and lack a little punch), the shotguns are effective and feel satisfying to use, the grenade launcher and crossbow can deal massive damage, and the lightning gun is extremely powerful (but there's not much ammo for it). Every weapon in this game is useful and I found myself using the entire arsenal... except for the landmines, which you place straight down and then lure enemies into. They're the only weapon that's very situational and I only used a few times; everything else is always useful.The game doesn't really have a story, instead it focuses on delivering an atmosphere, and it does that excellently. When you explore abandoned brutalist architecture from the communist era, that's exactly what HROT looks and feels like.Excellent game, 100% recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wondered what would it be like if DUSK was set in a soviet republic? If the answer is “no”, this is perfectly understandable. To all 3 of you for whom the answer is “yes”, this is an oddly specific request but you are bound to love what comes next! HROT may not belong to New Blood brand of modern boomer-shooters, however it sure as hell looks, feels and plays like it could. This Quake-inspired piece of action is work of a single Prague-based developer by the nickname Spytihněv.Set in a post-apocalyptic depiction of Czechoslovakia, this title blends a smooth, old-school gunplay, references to communism, copious amounts of brown and a peculiar sense of humour to deliver a premiere retro experience.No matter whether it is  or the new wave – if old-school shooters ring true at all, you will soon recognise that HROT comes from a place of deep understanding of what makes such games tick. All of the components you would come to expect from a title like this are in place: a level-based structure divided into episodes, memorable setpieces, a key-based pacing and a secret behind a cracked wall in need of explosives. Thus, not only the game manages to check all of the retro boxes, (even nods to the classics are there) it does all of these things really well.Possibly the best example to highlight that the smooth flow of the game is hardly a coincidence, is how well it handles enemies’ visibility. One of the more distinct facets of HROT is that out of 100 colours used in the game about 90 of them are various shades of brown. With this in mind, it is quite amazing that the opposition never truly blends with the surroundings despite chaos often ensuing on the screen. Through careful application of contrasting pieces of equipment or something as mundane as red eyes of a rat, threats remain easy to follow across well over 40 bestiary entries.Now, it needs to be stated that while HROT definitely dedicates due attention to roots of its chosen genre, it would be a disservice to imply that the game merely follows the footsteps of its predecessors. Beyond a shadow of a doubt, this title has an identity of its own – it is a mix of extreme soviet brutalism, Czech references and dank memes. I would venture the end result may impair your ability to drive.Simply put, the setting of HROT is utterly bizarre and what I can imagine to be one of the game’s most polarizing aspects. On one hand, the player traverses an oppressively bleak world of gas masks, ticking away to the rhythm Geiger’s counter. On the other, an animate bulldozer springs to life to fill the role of a minor Boss and one of the levels has a dance party worked into progression route. If you prefer your dystopia morose with a gravel aftertaste, I can imagine “Dank stuff” tab in the main menu is going to be a letdown.For better or worse, this title doesn’t take itself particularly seriously and to be fair, I find the absurdity to be working in the game’s favour. Taking into account how deeply entrenched in soviet-era Czechoslovakia HROT is, a sardonic spin on the setting goes a long way. Especially in a game which is ultimately about gunning down lots of dudes with extreme prejudice.Speaking of the devil, HROT’s rouges gallery fits well with the game’s peculiar sense of humour. Most prevalent enemy types consist of faceless invading army, suited with full environmental suits – they seem to help little though, as soldiers are often seen throwing up through the filters of their masks. Once bunkers and cityscape give way to castle-themed levels, meat for the grinder follows suit to include hooded maniacs, leaping at the player with axe in hand. Harsh and gritty. However, it wouldn’t be HROT if things were to remain this subdued – an enemy called “Konfident” is a large flying head of Lenin, which shoots vision-impairing bullets. There are also mutated chickens, Nazi Newts and hostile inanimate objects, which prompt concern for protagonist’s mental state.No less interesting level filling is a myriad of curious little details scattered across the game. Random interactable items provide a fun change of pace from action-packed gameplay, rewarding the player for sparing a while to take in their surroundings. Some of them are simple distractions, such as a grinding washing machine or a fully interactive keyboard; while others can be a fully-fledged minigame or have an achievement tied to them. One may be tempted to write-off dedicating attention to seemingly pointless items, nevertheless to me this is a chef’s kiss, making HROT’s world vivid despite its bleak colour palette.Worth a separate mention is the level design itself. For the most part, the game maintains a steady flow, with progression route looping nicely as new areas become available. Crossing certain sections of the level multiple times is often used to provide smart visual clues regarding the way forward. In spite of all that, I did get stuck in HROT on several occasions, as the game at times considers finding the correct path as a sort of environmental puzzle. In few instances, I scolded myself for missing a passage that seemed obvious when I finally found it, in others, extra hoops left an aftertaste of mild frustration.Having reached the nitpicking part, if HROT has a single genuine caveat, it is the uninspired arsenal. Overwhelming majority of guns available you have seen in every shooter, especially a retro one. The few exotic pieces being a lightning gun pulled straight from Quake and my personal favourite - Veltlínske zelené, a bottle of healing wine which doubles as a Molotov. Using tried and tested guns isn’t terrible in itself, they also have distinct quirks making certain weapons more fitting to a given combat scenario. Unfortunately, the player often will be shooting whatever currently has ammo left as HROT seems to be optimized towards giving the player “just enough” ammo to get by, somewhat undermining the nuance of gun performance. With all that in mind, I need to stress this is nitpicking rather than a true issue with the game.Ultimately, HROT’s Steam rating of “Overwhelmingly Positive” seems fully deserved. While I am tempted to call this game niche, with boomer-shooter genre becoming increasingly more popular over the years, I believe it reaches out to a sensibly wide audience. I especially recommend the game to inhabitants of former Warsaw Pact countries, as all the soviet references will hit harder, particularly the mature players who experienced the reality of communism on their own skin. In both content and gameplay, HROT is a proper blast from the past, delivering a true morsel for all fans of retro FPS.
