_childDocuments_.review: As a preface, I am inexperienced with Iron Harvest, but not with RTS or TBS games as a whole.  TLDR; if your not a beast at micro, you probably won't enjoy the gameplay. Still looks nice though.To start with the pros: The Aesthetic is fantastic, and honestly if you like mechs, the hard industrial aesthetic, or WW1 vibes this game will look amazing, every bit as amazing in fact as the trailers. The game runs wonderfully, even my decade old laptop can run it smoothly and still look nice from the bird's eye view.The setting feels immersive right from the start, its an alternative history with a cool set of altered European powers and every moment genuinely feels like that. The also have a cool setting which causes each character to speak the native language of the real nation that their fictional one is based on.Now regrettably onto the cons:The only real one is the gameplay. The controls feel clunky and badly polished, or even outright badly designed. It features a cover mechanic, but squads are often too big to fit behind any one piece of cover causing them to spread out oddly, which would be okay as it does feature a system which automatically causes them to spread out along nearby cover on the same side you selected (if you ordered your forces to take cover against an enemy to the west then the squad will only take cover on the east side of objects)  however there often simply isnt enough, leading your troops to simply get mowed down because their friends occupied every other spot. Additionally if you have more than one squad selected, you no longer get to see where each soldier will stand, and instead just get a single small dot to roughly indicate where the squad will end up.On the topic of squads, you can assign them to number groups just like in other games, but doing so is weirdly difficult as if you simply click on a squad and hit ctrl+the group number you want, it will not add the unit to the group, but either do nothing, or remove all other units from the group. Additionally shift+ click on your units in the hotbar at the bottom doesn't seem to select all units between the two you clicked, only the units you specifically clicked on, forcing you to click on every single unit manually, slowing you down in a fast paced game.The damage values feel inconsistent, in that weapons are HYPER specialized. Rifles are mediocre at absolute best, cannons shred tanks but can't hit infantry, Machine guns and flamethrowers mop away infantry but do nothing to armor. This makes sense, however it is to such a degree that on the micro level it feels less like playing a strategy game and more like playing a game of rock, paper, mech.The only reason I would say that this is a problem, is that this game is clearly built with micro in mind, between the cover mechanics and the unique cooldown abilities of hero and almost all specialist units. Ultimately it feels like the game's complexity is fighting itself, as it is trying to be a fast paced micro game, but the mechanics don't allow for skill expression in micro and the game is too fast for the slower paced macro style of strategic play that the unit specificity suggests. While I'm certain that the game is enormously fun for those with the time, patience, and skill to master it, I don't find it particularly enjoyable otherwise, nor do I think will others. If you are good at micro, love this sort of aesthetic, and don't mind some jank you'll probably love the game. Otherwise stick to watching it streamed.

_childDocuments_.review: A thin recommendation. Just finished damn near marathoning it over a weekend and did all of the campaigns. The setting and premise are great - very dieselpunk, the factions are fairly interesting, and the campaign story is a 7/10 that shines through having some characters you love to hate.Gameplay-wise, the campaign is probably a 6/10 at its low points and a 8/10 at its high points. Several missions, especially plenty in the Saxony, Ursonia, and Rusviet Revolution campaigns, are absolute slogs that take way longer than they should. Mechanically, it's a Company of Heroes-type, where you have a 'base' with three buildings and have to capture and hold resource generating sites elsewhere in the map. Many of the campaign missions give you hero units, and they're generally overpowered, but it's fun to use them as force multipliers. Something else to mention is how damned slow every unit is - even aircraft - and I ran into pathing issues every so often given how large some of the mechs can get.Certainly worth about $40 if you get the all inclusive release. Hope they do a sequel!

_childDocuments_.review: Love the concept and have been hyped for a while. But honestly outside of settings and graphics this game does not have much going for it. Gameplay is bad. Giving a unit orders is painful. I have had times were I order a squad to a far off area and half of the squad split off and walked though the enemy to reach that point. Thinking that the game's firing arcs and redeploying times were an invitation to out micro a field gun with infantry was a mistake. The squad did no damage shooting the back of the field gun and twice got hit while standing fully out of the guns arc.Also lets talk about unit counters because units that feel like they should be anti armor are incredibly good against infantry. anti mech infantry go trade 1 for 1 against standard infantry?!?!? an anti mech field gun can take out 3 squads of infantry unsupported?!?! Anti mech infantry cant take out a mech with only anti mech guns without fully encircling them?!?! Speaking of mechs they seem to have no counter except other mechs. I am definitely a noob but i cant see a reason to build infantry when mechs of any type shred infantry while infantry struggles to deal any damage. On the topic of infantry, each country's infantry is basically the same. Zero thought seems to have been put into infantry gameplay which hurts the already low unit variety and faction identity in this game. For example, each of the three factions standard infantry use a different weapon type but outside of animations this doesn't have an impact. The only interesting variety is in the limited number of mechs. Might as well have left out infantry entirely.  Also the AI does not seem to understand how to play the game. I just did a skirmish where I, a noob, mega stomped a "difficult" ai. they don't even try to use the counter system and will try capturing a point while machine guns kill them. Funny thing was that even though I had a 10 - 0 kd for units they got almost the same combat score. Campaign story is fine but I hate how I must play through every campaign linearly when 3 different national campaigns would have been the perfect opportunity for convergent storytelling. Also I am thinking I am trying to play a strategy game when the best strategy seems to be create a mech clump and steamroll every mission. While some of the mission ideas seem fun they are poorly executed. Escorting a railway artillery piece-fun! The railway artillery has a range comparable to a sniper and will leave gunning mode at the slightest misclick- not fun. Finally I find it strange how tech tiers are gated by engineer veterancy. I spent a game spam building with 1 engineer and could not even get them to veteran. And then what? You lose the unit and you get to start the grind over again? Unless they are aiming for a glacial game pace this is not a good system.I really hope the devs improve this game and address the issues I currently have.

_childDocuments_.review: A breath of fresh air to the dying RTS genre.Really fun units diesel punk aesthetic is really enjoyable and new to many.Combat feels impactful and the story was not tossed to the side for the sake of skirmish or multiplayer its actually really good and enjoyable.The 3 factions so far feel very different from eachother and play differently but neither feels to be stronger than the other balancing seems to be done well at the moment. (who knows if a patch will mess that up)Now for the cons:The AI is REALLY dumb.You will be playing it on easy at first to try it out in skirmish and then find yourself going all the way up to hard and only feel very slight increases in tactics and ability, and then you'll try insane thinking its going to be very difficult but if you just have a baseline idea how to play your faction you are going to steamroll them as well, which then brings us to the things that are supposed to make the AI more difficult or challenging the modifiers.There are 3 modifiers for an increase in challenge.1. Time limit on completion of the skirmish2. Unit loss cap3. Unit max health decreaseThese are great to have and feel really nice when doing them, but they shouldn't be the thing that makes the game worth playing against AI because not everyone wants to play against other players. The AI is not very advanced at all and needs a serious rework in order to be reasonable. There is no reason that I should be able to ROFLSTOMP the insane AI after just playing the game for 30 min. (I am not a good RTS players just an avid RTS player I could only get to silver in Star Craft 2)Other than that I can definitely recommend the game as a buy for sure. _childDocuments_.review: This is a no-brainer buy for me. Althought far from perfect it is great fun.The gameplay harkens back to a time of classic DoW, WC3, CoH and those of the time with some quirks of it's own. You have to pay a lot of attention to what your units are up to at almost ALL times and they usually don't move so fast. That makes the gameplay feel intense but slow at times, given the more powerful the unit the slower it moves, pretty much. But that only makes positioning and having the right reserves at the ready very important. Backup can take a long time and the *retreat* command takes units all the way back to base, so again the game falls into micromanaging the manual retreat of a unit if you choose to do so. And giving a command to attack will make your unit hunt the target to the ends of the Earth, so be careful.That said, I really enjoy these features. To me they make the combat a lot more meaningful and more rewarding than most RTSs around these days.

_childDocuments_.review: A Company of Heroes variant RTS, which swaps tanks for mechs. Set in Eastern Europe, game explores the power struggles of 3 nations and a plotting secret society trying to dominate the world. The story campaign has a linear narrative, tons of well made cinematics to further the story, and its fairly lengthy. Apart from the main campaign, the game also features a variety of world maps which you have to dominate in a turn based mini game, Total War style (albeit very rudimentary). All in all the single player experience has been fleshed out entirely, which makes the game very replayable. Game also has multiplayer which I haven't tried yet, but people claim its pretty solid, although matches can run a bit slow because of the slow moving mechs. Overal a very decent purchase, grab it on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on December 2020 during the winter sale. I'll summarize it here very easily, after nearly 300 hours of play.I have been looking to replace CoH 1/2 from my library and was looking for something 'fresh'. This is it. - , simple. It plays similarly to CoH, but is different enough not to make it a 'copy'. Don't expect what you know in CoH can as easily transfer here, though it does help.-  is great and teaches you the basics, strengths, and weaknesses of each faction.- . There's a lore section for those invested. - . The official IH discord is where you will find most of us. We run in-house matches and tournaments, as well as training new players and give them tips on how to play their favorite faction. Tournaments are also sponsored by the devs, so there's prizes (like the limited edition Eisenhans statue). Probably the  online community I've met to date.- , twice a month regularly. Although at the time I'm writing this, the devs are focused on releasing the new faction before moving to further balance adjustment and adding new mechanics/abilities. -  is atrocious. Even on 'insane', they're still quite easy to beat. -  is slow, though this . Weekends is usually the best time to find one. Though if it's taking too long, there's always the community in discord to find someone to play with. - , a bit wonky. Though this just takes getting used to. It's not outright imbalanced to the point it's broken. Some units counter one unit or another and each faction has something that counters another. As they say, you can adjust numbers, but you can't adjust experience and skill. - , moderately high. Though the game is easy to pickup, it can be quite difficult to master. IH is a game where the 3As  (Assessment, Assembly, Action) happen in split-second. Throwing units to the wall only lead to miserable consequences and smell of inexperience. When things fail, improvise. Should you get it? Definitely. You may want to hold on for just a bit after Usonia is released and the coming balance patches comes out. Do grab it when it's on sale and come find us in the discord. See you on the battlefield.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy the game.  My rts experience is Warcraft games, Age of empires games, some Total War and a LOT of Starcraft 2.  This is the first RTS I've played and really liked since SC2.  Granted, I wasn't tainted by what I hear is the amazing Company of Heroes games.  People complain about the price, but I feel like I get more content than I got from Starcraft 2 when it came out.  I got the Terran campaign and had to purchase subsequent faction campaigns.  Mostly I enjoyed SC2 for multiplayer.  My biggest complaint of this game is that it's hard to find a match.  Maybe it's a matchmaking problem, a cross platform problem, or a lack of player base.  People complain about clunkiness/pathfinding.  I don't find it to be too big an issue.  The other complaints is lack of tech tree and base building.  It's certainly a more streamlined approach but I find it more focused on battle strategy rather than building/teching strategy.  And the final most repeated complaint I hear is that it wasn't really complete.  With this, I totally agree. I think they spent much time and care in the campaigns (which I think are very well done) and left the multiplayer on the back burner.  I think this was a big mistake by them, being that it's an RTS and competitive multiplayer is where the most fun lies.  With all that said, it runs smoothly, the graphics are great, destruction is awesome and it's a lot of fun.  So, my summary is that it's worth the price, so get it and hop on so I have some people to wipe the floor with me in multiplayer! :)

_childDocuments_.review: Iron Harvest is a good RTS starter from a profoundly passionate small dev team. It's not your COH, C&C, or AoE, but it isn't bad. I enjoyed the game's setting; WW1 with mechs is an interesting concept. The art style, the quality/quantity of the map, and the character design are really nice. For me, this game runs great and is visually appealing for an RTS. There is some lovely destruction physics. The music slaps, especially Saxony. I enjoyed the campaigns and the continuation of the story from each nation's perspective. Each and every character is memorable, and I would remember pretty much everything and everyone if a sequel was made. Pretty much, play for the campaign, but don't expect Multiplayer to be the selling point. The more you play, the more repetitive and grindy it becomes, to the point that it gets boring. I think the game was trying to save itself by incorporating its own season pass rewards system and a RISK-style game mode, but it gets too easy and boring at times. Achievements are short and not all that memorable. The game is not perfect, but I wouldn't regret 100% it, and I wouldn't oppose a sequel. 8/10

To what I can see for how that most of the Iron Harvest game been inspired by Jakub Rozalski mech art, I find that its a fair solid game I can enjoy. Most of the gameplay works to what I can tell seem to be a CoH with some changes here n there. In that idea it dose make most of the game familiar  to play from the get go. Though I'm sure there are a few bits that have some fantasy element in it to make a compelling story. As the game suggests its very mech focused. Dose have infantry, though of course they get chewed like gummies if not properly equipped. Curious enough the game dose let you swap out weapons and gear for infantry making it so ya can save some materials by telling the engineers to pick up the MGs. To what I've exp it dose have a good story to keep ya going even if the missions get hard after some time. Playing defense doesn't seem to pay out so well in this game being how that mechs or artillery can quickly over run your lines. There is also the rate of resources that seem to be rather low even with the upgraded mines and pumps for how expensive mechs can be.For a RTS game I add this one to the library if you're a fan.

_childDocuments_.review: Iron Harvest is a fun and uniquely atmospheric game with creative world building and design choicesPlay through any of three engaging campaigns in a steampunk alternate early 20th century. The voice acting is a tad over the top but...........eh it is what it is, each campaign is still an immersive experience you won't find anywhere else. The missions are all interconnected but unique with different settings and objectives. as well as differing degrees of available resources and strategies. However the actual game play is at times clunky and the AI isn't great. It's still playable but if you were expecting Men of War with Mechs, this isn't that. That being said, even by the developers own admission this game is still in Beta. What bugs it has now are being put up against a wall and shot daily with every new update. Diversity in factions and units are impressive, you have the basic cannon fodder grunts, engineers, machine gunners, artillery, and of course mechs. And these mechs aren't just skinned differently from faction to faction but mechanically different as well while still being similarly balanced. (the cheapest scouting mech for Polania holds a comedically large bolt action anti tank rifle and shoots it like a large metal man..... the cheapest scouting mech for the Rusviets flings Grenades)Multiplayer is fun and more to the point. You have  a base, they have a base................ you know how this goes. Overall while still undeniably in beta there's no where to go but up7/10

_childDocuments_.review: My review concerns the singleplayer experience, which I bought this for in high, high hopes. TLDR; Sadly, it's a seriously flawed let-down and I can't recommend it despite very much wanting to.I managed to get about two thirds into the campaign, finding some good fun here and there. The story is nothing unique, but plays out well, the setting is interesting and playing around with gritty smoke-spewing steel behemoths is always metric tons of cool. The many hero-centered adventure missions also work just fine. The rest of it, though... I'm not going to bother slogging through to the ending.Unfortunately, gameplay is besides clunky and buggy, which might in itself be excusable, but also as my number one  put-off - made difficult in all the wrong ways. I love me some intelligently challenging games, but here there really is almost no AI at all and instead the challenge is built around scripted, massive, endless blobs of troops the enemy gets for free and that often spawn out of thin air right on top of you. The last mission I finished was utterly horrible. I was presented with a big map full of resource nodes, chokepoints, variable terrain and cover... A great setting for some fine tactics. After some minutes of grabbing resource nodes without any meaningful resistance, I was abruptly assaulted by dozens of enemy squads and mechs from all sides every minute or so. I realized, I had no way of fighting it out fairly. Instead, I simply marched my two nearly invincible hero units into the enemy base and ended the travesty there. Refusing to dance to the tune, there was no challenge to speak of afterall. I then tried out a couple skirmish battles to see if the AI might step up. Well, again it hardly  anything. In a 1v1, I quickly bulldozed through a couple infantry squads after which I got to destroy an empty base with no resistance. In a 2v2, my ally AI sent all their troops to sit in the middle of a destroyed enemy base while the remaining enemy slowly destroyed theirs unopposed. I marched over the enemy and gave up on the game.Varied other, less serious offences:- Slow UI. There is a small delay between selecting a control group and being able to issue a command. As a result, rapidly clicking through orders for your army results in some of them not going through.- A 20 m tall mech can't fire onto a ridge 5 m high - what? Instead, I have to walk my units around to a ramp while a mortar rains fire on me.- Useless and obscure cover system.- Lack of variety in infantry units between factions. Although, infantry is mostly pointless anyway.- Base-building. Three structures with one upgrade for two of them? With close-to-zero tech tree, why even bother? Might as well just order in units as off-map reinforcements. As is, bases just drag games on, being very slow to tear down.- Bugs. Graphical issues. Sometimes explosions from cannon shots don't seem to connect or the audio doesn't play. Instead, a unit just quietly stops living. For me, the game also always crashes when quitting.- Pathing really is kind of bad, though I personally haven't found it that much of an issue.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Company of Heroes, C&C, AOE2, and Starcraft 2 player I just could not enjoy playing this game. I would describe Iron Harvest as a failed steampunk copy of the Company of Heroes franchise. It has infantry squads, infantry cover mechanics, unit retreating, armor facing, and capturing resource territories. All of the listed can already be found in the 2007 Company of Heroes and believe it or not, all these mechanics work better in that game which was released 14 years ago! I'm going to list just a few problems and my PERSONAL observations below. Remember this review is based on MY EXPERIENCE. If you enjoyed the game I'm happy for you.Firstly, I do must say that the game has good graphics and the overall art style is amazing. The unit design looks unique and every faction has its aesthetic. There are three nations with their campaign and unit roster. Saxony is a german nation with, with emphasis on technological supremacy and superior firepower. Rusviet units are robust and rely on brute force to win. Polania favors mobility and long-range fighting. The newly added Usonia relies on air supremacy to win the day. In any case, every faction feels unique and plays a little bit differently.  The story however is dull.  Back to the gameplay: Unit control feels so unresponsive and the pathfinding is terrible, units turn and move too slow, they have a problem navigating tight corners and narrow paths. These problems are most visible on a skirmish map called "Dark Forest" (overall a terrible map IMO, because it just consists of linear paths). On the topic of movement: Why is retreating soo slow? It feels like they are walking back to base. Some units like the Field Gun retreat so slow that it is not even worth it. Next up: Cover! Only green cover exists and even that is on certain maps scarce. Destroyed buildings and mechs can't be used as cover. Again, something that a certain 14-year-old game had.Base Building: This game is tagged on Steam as "Base Building RTS". Comparing this game's "bAsE bUiLdInG" to games like Age of Empires 2, Starcraft, Command and Conquer, Supreme Commander, Act of Aggression, and Rise of Nations is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ joke. In Iron Harvest, you can only build TWO BASE STRUCTURES (no, the fortifications don't count), and even those two, like in COH, can only be built around preplaced Headquarters. There is also no technology to research (upgrading 2 base structures in my book isn't research). Please remove the tag on steam because you don't deserve it.Overall I can't recommend this game at the moment. The developers are working hard to add new content and fix the existing issues, but this game is a sinking ship. It doesn't bring anything new to the RTS genre other than the setting and there are way better strategy games on the market than this. If there are any plans for a sequel I hope the developers at least learned some valuable lessons from the community and will make a kickass RTS in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: As cool as the setting is, sadly it's incredibly clunky to play and feels very unresponsive. Units are slugs - not just the mechs, but the soldiers too. Pathfinding is very basic. You use a unit ability and it takes ages for it to go off, if at all. Makes microing multiple battles difficult, because you can't fire-and-forget abilities, because you need to be constantly worried about whether the units do what you tell them and not something stupid. It's very difficult to get them to line up behind walls (on the correct side), especially if you have multiple squads grouped.Well, at least the game is very slow paced, so that kinda smooths things out a bit, but it's annoying to have to worry about your units doing something dumb. It's a shame too, because the unit abilities are fairly impactful, so microing them would be otherwise enjoyable (well placed grenade could blow up half a squad), but it's too unresponsive for that. If you send a squad into a building, you can't re-select them by pressing their control group, even though it shows their number above the house. You have to click the house... why?! Garrisoned houses seem to be bugged too. I can't really tell the units inside to focus any specific enemy. They just shoot whatever.The default control scheme is moronic too. Who tf thought camera controls were important enough to be put on WASD?!!??!?! Guys, this is a strategy game, helloooooo?! The unit hotkeys are like in Starcraft (personally am a fan of the DoTA standard)... Yeah, I pretty much rebound everything.Beyond that, this RTS just has a lot of mechanics I dislike (coming from C&C), starting with the unit cap. Base building is limited, there's no upgrade branching (as far as I'm aware).You can pick up new weapons with your soldiers from crates or take from enemies. This is really neat, but that's all there is in terms of upgrades. They feel more like side-grades, depending on what you need (machine-gun vs. soldiers, launchers vs. mechs, engineer for building/repair, medic for heals etc.). This just doesn't cut it for me.I suppose if you liked Company of Heroes you'll like this... maybe?

_childDocuments_.review: Iron Harvest is a game that takes a lot from the most modern evolution of Real-Time Strategy: Company of Heroes. Which sounds like an unexpected, but very welcome gift from heavens.Sadly, it does so quite poorly. Pathfinding is questionable, animations are all over the place, performance is very sluggish and frame drops get insane in bigger battles.It looks very good, but... on screenshots. In movement, with jerky physics and animations, it isn't half as nice. Horrible performace could have been salvaged... or at least suffered through - if everything else was on point. But sadly combat feels loose and weird, there's no metal-meets-metal in a game with mechs, not in sound, not animation, not in overall feeling. Voiceover and sound design is pretty bleak in general. Also, if they copied COH so much, why not take all the good parts? This game *seems* to have a cover system, yet there's no clear indicator if unit's in cover and does it even help, there's veterancy, but I have no idea what it does, and so on. Perhaps it's all hidden somewhere in UI but if it's not apparent and easily player-readable, then it's as good as not there. COH had annoyingly vague descriptions about what veterancy does; Iron Harvest seemed to skip this whatsoever.That's sad, because ambition of this game is breathtaking, just that in every nook and cranny, it's visible that there wasn't enough budget, people or skill to implement it. I don't think it's worth full price. I'm sure there'll be a lot of patching in the future and heavy cult following despite problems - because there's no sadder gamer than RTS lover in 2020 - and i'm one of them, but at current performance nad overall package, I cannot recommend Iron Harvest.

_childDocuments_.review: I like big mechs and cannot lie, you other brothas can't deny.Iron Harvest, based on the alternate history world of 1920+ by polish artist Jakub Różalski, features some great RTS gameplay. While the base building mechanics are lacking (you build about 2 buildings each game) and the tech tree is non-existant (again, you can research two upgrades to your two buildings), the RTS mechanics are great. Each faction plays to its strengths and weaknesses, your losses matter - it is cheaper to retreat your units and reinforce or repair them than building new ones. The cover system for infantry units is also great and quite comprehensive.One of the major downsides, however, is that Iron Harvest is slow. Very slow. Your units move very slowly, especially the mechs. Do not expect quick matches.Overall I'd highly recommend this game for any RTS fan.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this? I will do more than just recommend it, I'll recommend they make a sequel. Now, I'm gonna preface this by saying that I have not played the DLCs so this review is exclusive to the base game. First, the setting. It is alternate 1920. World War One doesn't happen, however, the three main factions mirror those of Germany, Russia, and Poland. Their differences are laid out in vivid detail and you feel like you understand where each faction stands. Second, Units. The game does a really good job of balancing units of the main three and making it so you have to change up play styles for each faction. One is very defensive, another more offensive, and the third is the middle ground. All three play amazingly well and offer enough differences in even some of their common units to force players to consider their options carefully. Third, the story. The story, more than anything is why I want a sequel. It was very well written, few things feel like they were just randomly stuck there and those that did were clarified later. The end of the game feels like the end of the first act and that it is only going to get more insane before it gets better. Overall? I give this game 10/5, yes, I'm breaking the scale for it. It is that good!

_childDocuments_.review: This is so on the fence to being a recommend.The Good:- Story is somewhat interesting.- The setting is interesting.- Big old time mechs are objectively cool.- The mechs are responsive and handle well and tons of creativity. - Big Booms.- Has a high ceiling for skillThe Bad:- doesn't really play all too well. Wants to be CoH but cant really get too tactical with it as mechs just sorta roll over everything. What i mean is: Infantry is clunky. As with most tactical games, moving infantry isn't as responsive as say Starcraft. But it makes up for it by rewarding the player that their moving will get them in good attacking/defensive positions and using their units abilities can change the flow of battle. In Iron Harvest, getting your infantry to do anything is.... like herding cats. Especially considering cover is more or less worthless with mechs that can walk over everything, destroy cover, and don't really take bullet damage. And even the anti-vehicle infantry get destroyed by mechs, making them worthless. And your infantry have.... 1 to 2 abilities maybe. From my experience in the campaign its just- a bunch of mechs running at each other, engineers are the only infantry that matter because they repair mechs but this leads into my next point.- Resources gather too quickly. Sure, you can repair your mechs with engineers. But you gain SO many resources it doesn't matter to lose them and instantly rebuild your army. - battles of attrition. Every fight has just been: "Throw enough units at one another until one wins." Tactics go out the window when it comes down to when you can build your own units and fights are just so tug of war. Its so close to being a recommend. I just wish units were more lethal. Infantry actually had a bigger role in the game and could kill other squads faster. Mechs need to just cost more but be juggernauts when you get them. More infantry abilities. It feels like there is a game here, but it does feel unfinished. I hope we see some development and i can switch this.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this game is a hard pass if you don't have it. I am playing through the campaign with a bud and we are noticing glaring issues just with the basic mechanics of the game. Its more of grabbing action figures and smashing them together than a RTS. Don't go in expecting Starcraft level micromanagement, AI pathing, resource management, upgrading units, building upgrades, etc. all non existent. This is a very basic RTS. There are only three main buildings, headquarters, barracks, and a workshop. The barracks and the workshop can be upgraded to "advance" versions of themselves but that only allows for certain units to be built. The stationary bunker, pillbox, sentry, whatever you want to call the building you put units into to defend has two upgrades. A auto gun then later a auto cannon. Great idea except the base bunker already cost unit supply which is very limited already. Certain units will not attack even when fired upon just because YOU the player HAVE to tell them to fire back. One particular unit HAS to level up just to siege and THEN it will attack on its own. This is intentional and frankly dumb. The unit rolled off the factory line with the capability to siege but because the crew hasn't seen combat they can't siege. Keep in mind each one HAS to level so if you have 4 or 5 of them they ALL need to see combat and YOU the player HAVE to tell them to fire at the enemy in front of them. Might as well have built a different unit then ADVANCE the workshop just to build a siege unit to then micromanage it just so it can siege and fire back. Starcraft got rid of that siege upgrade for the Siege Tank for a reason. The Siege Tank just comes with it now. NEVER use the retreat command, "r" key. You can't cancel the order so if the units get ambushed while retreating they won't fire back and you cant tell them too. Pair that with bad pathing and your units will just be running into one another incapable to retreat because the pathing is just having them smash into each other and YOU the player can't stop them because they are retreating. Apparently in every military once the order to retreat is sent ALL units just turn off their radio and receive no further commands till they are back at home. Just WHY? Let me be a commander, if I issue a retreat command and change my mind let me change the command! THAT is literally what a commander does! They command the troops! LET me the PLAYER decided what commands to issue and what commands stay and what commands change. Let me cancel a retreat! It's almost hard to recommend playing just for the story because even with bad game mechanics the story is still good. Nothing new but worth playing the game for if you don't mind losing your hair to bad mechanics. My recommendation is a hard pass. Wait for the second one or a spiritual successor. It's mechanics are too unrefined. Unit pathing needs to be fixed! We are talking original starcraft pathing. Even then the original starcraft had better pathing! A game from the 90's has better pathing than this game.Edit: Just finished the campaign. Just wow, a bug ridden ending with a story ending that spits in the face of its players, that is not an ending. If you have played Starcraft 2 epilogue its pretty much that level of bad.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love Iron Harvest. It has a lot of qualities that I love and dearly miss from RTS games of the 2000s including base building, control point / resource capturing, but the game is utterly spoiled by a tremendous flaw with the AI.The AI are stupid, and a really special kind of stupid that I have not encountered in any RTS I've ever played (and I've played a lot of them since the 1990s). The AI will only attack a specific unit that you command them to attack. So the second you defeat that unit, they just stand there doing nothing. They get shot at, take damage etc and DO NOTHING?! What's worse, you cannot set an attack stance, so they can defend themselves or pursue enemies, or guard an area etc. Why is this not a feature? Instead you must micromanage absolutely every unit individually. This also goes for your engineers and medics. Want you're engineers to repair your army? Or want your medics to heal units? You must click every single unit one by one for them to bother to repair. This becomes a real pain and challenge when you have a number of units all the the same small area. You must try ti select your engineer / medic unit but it is so easy to accidentally click the wrong unit and try again in a clicking frenzy. All of this is happening while your army is just standing there taking damage from any attacker and not responding.For these tremendous flaws, I cannot recommend Iron Harvest. I was glad I was able to play it in a Steam free weekend. Saved myself throwing money away. It's really a shame as the multiplayer is fun, the story is great and the concept is excellent, but the retarded AI breaks the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very enjoyable once you realise that it's more of a Real-Time Tactics then a Real-Time Strategy game, which means that positioning and planing ahead are just as important as finding the right counter to the enemy troops and deciding when to attack.That said, the issues other people are listing are still present. I don't care much for Coop or Multiplayer, so these don't effect me personally. What does effect me is the bad pathfinding, which regulary sends your soldiers to the wrong side of a freaking wall because for some reason the side you're on doesn't count as cover. And your troops also blindly follow retreating enemies they were ordered to fire upon and get slaughtered in the process. The game is also far from pretty, the soundtrack is forgettable at best and there are some anoying bugs, for example I wasn't able to complete a secondary objective in the second campaign mission because the enemies where invincible.The campaign so far is solid, although I really wish you could choose in which order to play the campaigns. They force you to play Polania fitst, which is the faction thats the least interesting to me. The writing is also rather inconsistent. The cutscenes are well done and follow interesting characters, but the in-mission writing is horrible and obnoxious at times.The reason why I ultimately decided to give the game a recommendation despite all it's flaws is that the core gameplay is fun, and most of the issues can and probably will be fixed with patches in the near future. But if the price tag is a bit heavy for you, you might want to wait a month or so until you buy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game, even less so for the AAA price tag it has. Maybe during a big sale it's nice to get, but don't expect a polished game.EDIT: Regarding the sale, that's where I got the game myself. Just wanted to point out I wouldn't recommend buying for full price. Since you actually care about comments (and that's commendable because most devs don't), let me be a bit more specific about the issues I have, what I consider from most to least important:1. There are a lot of bugs. Solely playing the campaign, there have been plenty black screens that got me stuck where I had to Alt F4 out. There are also many instances where things disappear or fade out for no reason, such as the enemy mech boss disappearing during the cutscene after the 3rd wave in that defense mission, or some units' attacks don't even work, like the shotgun ability in the gorilla mech hero. This is my main reason to say the game isn't really polished.2. There are a lot of problems with the controls, even when I rebind the keys, the final result is a mess. If I opt for a grid-keys-based layout, buttons don't make sense as the QWER line uses all main commands when it should use special actions and viceversa. When I try to adapt it to a real, usable layout (A: Attack, S: Stop, QWER: Abilities, etc.) there's still no way to adapt the visuals to match the layout, resulting in the next problem, which I swear I don't understand why no RTS has ever thought that this is a big deal, when I think it's pretty much necessary and should have happened out of raw evolution of the genre, which is even more obvious when you look at MOBAs and they all use the same layout. Then again, even if you set keys perfectly and forget about the UI, whenever you want to build something o train a unit it suddenly becomes even more tedious as keys just seem to be randomized. This is also a big deal for me, and wouldn't disregard in an RTS from late 2019.3. During the course of the game, there's a lot of emphasis on using cover. When playing skirmish normal matches this works fine, and maps seem to have been designed with that in mind, but my experience after 10 hours in campaign mode is that most buildings can't be garrisoned, there's barely no cover at all, and the little pieces I've found are just positioned for enemy squads. This is just a problem for campaign mode of course, but still relevant.4. I can't get stable 60FPS in lowest settings with a 6 core CPU @4700MHz and a 1070. And I'm not even talking about massive battles, just 2 squads on screen shooting each other and it already dips.5. Sometimes the units don't feel responsive. moving a squad to a point, the squad goes somewhere else. Takes the wrong cover direction even when manually appointed to do so, some mechs also like to facebump each other and block themselves, and sometimes I've killed and lost mechs because they refuse to turn around and fight whomever is shooting them, and they just idle there and die. Not saying units should be super smart, but there's a minimum I would expect.I've noted all this in your Discord at one point or another, and also submitted some screenshots whenever I found a bug with a description of how to pop it up. I understand you are still working in fixing a lot of stuff, but so far my perception of the game has to be negative. If all these things are fixed in the future I'll change the review.Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: The moment I saw the art for this game, I was immediately reminded of Scythe—and for good reason, too. It is set in the same universe as Scythe, designed by artist Jakub Różalski. An alternate 1920s, right after the aftermath of World War I. There is once again another war brewing in Europe, seen through the eyes of the Polania Republic, the Rusviet Union, and the Saxony Empire (Poland, the Soviet Union, and Germany). The campaign you play through will span through these three nations, each with their separate story arcs and hero units. Iron Harvest is an RTS that maintains a stunning but gritty atmosphere through its dieselpunk mechs clashing against Great War era battlefields.The RTS genre is one where it’s difficult to innovate in, and Iron Harvest realizes this; the gameplay feels just like the classic RTS games of yore. In a typical skirmish match, your objective is clear: destroy the enemy headquarters at all costs. You start with your own headquarters on a different part of the map from your opponent. You have a basic infantry unit and an engineer, but to expand, you need resources. Iron and oil are the two resources needed to construct anything, with oil being the primary limiting factor for the powerful mechs.While your headquarters will passively generate resources, you will need to increase your production rate by capturing iron mines and oil pumps scattered across the map. Skirmishes essentially end up being a ceaseless tug of war game between resource buildings and strategic positions all while staging attacks against the enemy HQ and defending your own base of operations. In the case that it becomes far too difficult to destroy the enemy’s base, you can opt for a victory by victory points, obtained by capturing strategic positions around the playing field.The infantry units are what you will rely on for much of your games. Each faction’s soldiers all look unique and dressed to suit their class. Most of the specialized infantry are identical in stats and equipment, but the standard infantry differ in that they are equipped with either rifles, shotguns, or machine pistols for the troops of Polania, Rusviet, and Saxony, respectively. Up close, Rusviet infantry will prevail with their shotguns, but at range, the Polania hold the advantage with their accurate bolt actions.The specialized troops will cover the needs your rank and file cannot, from anti-infantry for light or heavy troops, to more specialized needs such as healing for a medic or constructing fortification and repairing mechs for engineers. And if you ever feel like changing a unit’s class, you can do so without spending resources by finding a fallen unit’s weapon kit and equipping it. You can have a standard infantry unit and upgrade straight to a grenadier by killing an enemy grenadier unit and taking their weapon kit.But infantry isn’t what you’re playing this game for, right? There’s mechs! Unlike infantry, the mechs of the three factions are much more varied. Some are melee-focused, some are designed to mow down swaths of enemies, some are mech busters made to take out enemy mechs, and some are created to just be unstoppable gigantic machines of death. In exchange for offering the most firepower and being able to take on an onslaught of bullets, they are expensive to make and tend to be very slow-moving. Still, not only do they change the state of the battlefield, but they just look cool.Iron Harvest’s campaign missions are more complex than a skirmish match. You have many more objectives to consider, from defending against waves of enemies to freeing your captive comrades-in-arms to capturing and holding a specific location. And you’re not just given objectives without further explanation: there is a story that is told through cutscenes and in-game sequences that occur during the missions. Indeed, many missions don’t play out entirely like a typical RTS match and don’t rely on an enemy headquarters’ destruction to end.Every faction’s heroes are all characters in the campaign. They are your most important units in your missions as they come with special abilities (both passive and active). For instance, Anna Kos of the Polania faction uses a bolt action rifle that can shoot through multiple troops in a straight line with her active. As for her passive, she has a bear as a companion. Yep. You can control who he decides to attack and reign him in if he gets too far from you. As a bonus, he can heal any friendly infantry units that are near him, including Anna.In terms of story, it’s about what you would expect from an RTS. It’s not bad, and is honestly quite interesting since it provides lore about the war and how the mechs came to be; it’s just not something to write home about. But the missions themselves are well-designed with different paths you can take to accomplish your objective. A mission where you have to escort a train won’t force you to take a single railroad track: you can switch tracks to take a different route to avoid one set of enemies in favor of another set.Admittedly, I did notice some flaws that are important to note. For one, the graphics aren’t always palpable. Now, I know for a game of this genre it shouldn’t matter much, but because you will see cutscenes frequently in the campaign, you will most definitely notice some glaring issues with the visuals. If you were to compare a mech and Anna’s bear, you will notice the mech looks great while the bear’s face isn’t properly textured. This isn’t something that is detrimental to your experience per se, but it’s something you will definitely notice.It also bugged me that when you zoomed in on a character model, a depth of field effect occurs where the face of the unit is blurred. I’m a fan of the Total War games and part of what makes them feel amazing for me is how there is a cinematic mode you can turn on, with mods you can install for a free camera with adjustable heights. Unfortunately, Iron Harvest doesn’t support either of those things. There is a button to turn off the HUD, but it doesn’t remove the cursor nor does it stop highlighting units. I get that it wouldn’t make much sense to have a free camera mode in a RTS, but there’s so many moments in the game where you could think it would make a great screenshot that you would at least wish you could adjust the camera better to get the right angle for the picture.In addition, the pathfinding is… well, it works most of the time. However, sometimes you will see an enemy unit get stuck on a rock for a few moments, or perhaps you will direct your unit to move to a location but decides to take a long route to their destination. Or perhaps, you want to move your units into cover, but for some reason, they decide to clump up on a single spot at the sandbags you placed instead of lining up across the whole row. Or maybe you will attempt to use a sniping ability at someone while you are in cover, but you end up shooting that sniper shot at your own cover, forcing you to wait for the ability to cooldown. It’s almost impossible to have flawless pathfinding, I know, but I feel something could be done to improve it, especially since this is a game where you are going to command multiple gigantic mechs at a time. [...]

_childDocuments_.review: Iron harvest has an amazing theme, great visual design, good audio... But the game itself is a bit of a mess, best described as "We have Company of Heroes at home". The infantry combat feels alright, with a cover system, flanking, a suppression mechanic that rarely comes into play, though cover gets destroyed easily and there aren't any craters left behind by ground pounding for them to hide in. There's also a discount retreat mechanic, though it doesn't help much.The mechs, the centrepiece of the game? Clunky, buggy garbage. Their pathfinding is awful and they get stuck on terrain, most of them are slow as molasses, and bringing their firepower to bear is an exercise in frustration. Sometimes they mess up for no reason, e.g. using Lech Kos's gorilla mech in the campaign, it started twitching and slowly sliding whenever I told him to slap a building. The mechs just feel bad to use, and this robs the game of its spectacle and leaves you wondering what the game would be like if it was more polished.

_childDocuments_.review: So, best reference I can give is Company of Heroes 2. If you liked Company of Heroes 2, you will find a lot of the same mechanics and aspects. Which is good because its very familiar and those mechanics work such as:-The cover mechanic when moving units (green circle, yellow circle, etc.)-Positioning buildings and units by holding the right mouse click-Rock, paper, scissor unit strengths, instead of tank vs. infantry, it goes by armor level (unarmored, light, medium, heavy)-Multiplayer matches earning in-game currency to spend on cosmeticsSome of those mechanics just don't work as well as they do in CoH 2, but its not game breaking. Three campaigns, decent story, good graphics. The time period and steampunk-ish unit flavor is new and cool to see. The combat is not as fast as I would like it to be, it falls short when compared to CoH 2. It also lacks a lot of diversity in units between factions. No upgrades, many of the units with one faction will been very similar to the same unit type in another faction. Once you have unlocked the top tier mech, thats it. Thats all you will see after that. That is the one downside. The game has alot, but once you get to a certain point, there is not much left to explore. The campaign level designs try to make up for this by creating unique objectives that are superior to CoH 2 in my opinion because of the usage of hero units. So its kinda like the original Starcraft RTS in that regard. All in all, its a good game. I do recommend it. If you liked CoH 2 you will like this.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'll be blunt, if you are familiar with any other RTS that has ever been made: Company of heroes, Halo Wars, Universe at War, Dawn of War, etc, you're probably going to be unsatisfied / disappointed with Iron Harvest.The biggest thing for me was that the campaign was simply not fun, as the objectives were tedious at best most the time. Made worse by the fact the enemy ai is very basic. It's simply a wave based enemy unit spawner set on a timer, with no reliance on supplies, so crippling the enemy structures is pointless. You're just playing a war game with a bot that isn't smart enough to respond to anything you do or any unit you use. One moment the enemy has a few soldiers, the next they spawn the next wave all at once to throw at you, and guess what the next wave is going to be the exact same. Also the balance between units is rather non-existent. You'll end up finding the one unit for each faction that is good and just spam in order to survive in the campaign. Though before you say don't spam that unit then. Trust me, the campaign isn't well made, the story is fine.But welcome to 2020 folks, as you all know since 2014 games have progressively gotten worse and not better despite all the new technology and tools out there for game developers.

_childDocuments_.review: **Kickstarter Backer Review**Greetings!  Today I’ll be reviewing Iron Harvest; a spiritual successor of games in the vein of Company of Heroes (and DOW) which I played heavily and have returned to over the years.  Iron Harvest’s goals seem to be to implement an amazing new world into an RTS and in that regard it does very well.  It’s just the RTS in question feels like a beta for COH and not a reimagining of it.  Let’s discuss.Atmospheric Brilliance:  I want to start on one of the best qualities of this game, the atmosphere.  I include in this the overall inspiration of the setting, graphics, sound and animation. The premise (if you can’t tell) is WWI with gasoline powered mechs and thanks to the source material (mainly artwork and some short stories) this is done very well.  The world feels very lived in and believable as the only real ‘lie’ is that they now have mechs; everything else is easy because it leans so heavily on the real tragedy and war of WWI.  The details of the story itself are kind of forgettable but that just leans to the charm of it: it may be forgettable but it feels real.Imitation and Flattery:  The game starts out very strong with its heavy (very heavy) inspiration of the COH games; one might even mistake it as a mod.  If you like COH you will probably enjoy Iron Harvest’s core gameplay loop; though nowhere near as polished.  Infantry want to hug cover and capture locations and the death of a unit is a much bigger blow to the army than other RTS.  There is also a much less focus on base building and more on the slow grind of a tug of war style of gameplay.  Mechs take the place of tanks / vehicles and this causes some very satisfying changes like a mech walking through buildings or melee mechs fighting like Kaiju’s.  Alas, this is the beginning of the problems.Let them Fight:  The matches tends to quickly devolve into mech battles; I heard someone say ‘you basically build the biggest thing you can and march it to the enemy until you win’ and I feel this is very accurate overall.  I’m sure the game is very different at the high end of competition but I’m unashamedly a casual player who just happens to play RTS a lot.  Some units just feel a step above what they should (the infantry manned artillery are an example) and any weapon that is ‘anti-armor’ is basically anti-infantry as well; which makes sense and COH had a very elegant solution to this, accuracy and cover.  Neither of which seem to really be impactful on Iron Harvest.  This game uses armor grades: Unarmored, Light, Medium and Heavy.  But the sad thing is that it just doesn’t work; the power dynamics are just too extreme.  Light Arms tend to do too much damage to Medium and Light armor making many of these mechs less valuable but immediately upon building the end game big mechs everything else is washed away.  Ironically the issues with armor leaves this odd issue where smaller mechs feel useless, larger feel godlike and infantry quickly loose favor.War is hell…so is this game:  Okay, let’s talk about the unforgivable… Many of the levels are extremely frustrating, focusing around ‘gotcha mechanics’ designed (in my view) to cause a restart.  One mission has a massive army appear behind the lines without any form of notice and was well into my base before I could even get to them.  This may be a decent add for many faster RTS but this game is intentionally paced slowly and focuses on individual units.  The campaign forgets it is an RTS and tries to be a Stealth ARPG in some levels and set pieces that should just be a cutscene are turned into a mission and vice-versa.  This leaves the victory screen feeling exhausted and not accomplished.  The game also doesn’t seem to want you to learn anything; new unit unlocked?  No time to learn your base is being attacked right now and you have 5 minutes to capture the main objective.  It’s not necessarily hard…just frustrating.  The level design is just bad on the campaign, I tend to point to StarCraft 2 as having the best level design in the industry especially if you are trying to tell a good story.  Add to this the silly control changes and numerous bugs (invisible buildings, crashes, keyboard lighting issues, etc) the game just needs a lot of work to feel complete.Overall, like a mech with one leg broken and no ammo it’s not a bad game…just an incomplete one that needs a bit of repairs.  Mainly I can’t recommend a game that feels like an early access / beta game at full retail.  This game probably should have retailed for about ½ of what it is.   I don’t think the community will last and the single player has its moments but is too full of frustrating and un-fun missions just have little replay value.  I am a proud Kickstarter Backer for this game and would do so over again, the game has potential it just isn’t there yet.  There are achievements and unlocks and such but none of feels ready or gives a real reason to keep playing.  Regardless, as always; enoy!

_childDocuments_.review: When Iron Harvest blipped onto my radar, I was eager to dip my toes back into the RTS genre. It had been AGES since I last played one, and this weird alternate history take on the 1920s seemed like a perfect reentry point.  In some ways, Iron Harvest succeeded in filling the RTS-shaped hole in my heart. However, it also revealed that I had rose-tinted glasses when looking at that hole. Um that was a weird metaphor... Let's move on. I spent most of my playtime with the single player campaign. Similar to some older RTS games, the campaign is split into multiple acts with each act following one of the three playable factions: Polania, Rusviet, and Saxony. The plot itself is riddled with tropes and frequently cheesy (a flavor not everyone enjoys). On the flip side, I found the core cast of characters to be an endearing bunch. Despite the weak overarching story, these characters do an excellent job grounding the emotional and narrative stakes for each mission. Also, several of the hero characters have an animal companion. I'm not sure why the devs did this, but I'm a fan of this decision. I'm also a fan of Iron Harvest's individual mission designs. Missions tend to change and evolve as you play through them. You may initially be asked to destroy an enemy base, only to shift to defending that same base from waves of enemies. Or a mission may start with a focus on stealth and ultimately become an escort mission. This is nothing groundbreaking of course, but Iron Harvest used a wide variety of mission components to keep me on my toes and engaged throughout. I was raised on games like Starcraft and Age of Mythology, so I was expecting the core gameplay of Iron Harvest to feel pretty similar. However, instead of letting me relive my childhood gaming memories, this game shattered my nostalgia by revealing that… I actually sort of suck at RTS games. The minute-to-minute gameplay was the same: moving units around a map and ordering them to shoot at things. But it turns out that I had developed some very bad habits as a younger gamer, and Iron Harvest is not very forgiving. I was surprised to find myself struggling to get through some of the early missions. Before calling it quits, I decided to take some time to practice and internalize Iron Harvest's mechanics. And from there, the game really opened up to me. Engagements began to feel more tactical and less like a meat grinder. It shouldn't have come as a surprise that I needed to use strategy in a strategy game, but I wanted to bring this up just in case others encounter similar difficulties. You can definitely brute force your way through the campaign like I initially did, but I can't see anyone truly having a fun time playing that way. One difference from other RTS games worth noting is that… Iron Harvest is SLOW. Most of the mechs are lumbering with glacial movement and attack speeds. This is thematically appropriate, but I can see it frustrating some players. On the one hand, as a person with very low APM (actions per minute) having more time to direct my troops is a godsend. On the other hand, waiting 9 seconds between a heavy mech's attacks feels like an eternity. This design decision seems very deliberate, and I personally don't hate it. However, some will likely be turned off by how unresponsive the units are. This last point doesn't have any gameplay significance, but I'd be remiss if I didn't give a shoutout to the best part of Iron Harvest's world: it's got WAY better mechs than the real 1920s. In setting, these monstrous war machines are absolute terrors that revolutionized the face of warfare forever. From the outside looking in… they are wonderfully silly chonkers, and I love them to bits. There's just something about the obvious inefficiency of the mech designs that I can't help but find incredibly charming. But I'm strange, so your milage may vary. Overall, I enjoyed Iron Harvest quite a bit. It's a little rough around the edges, and demanded more from me than other games in the genre. However, I found it surprisingly refreshing that the game forced me to become a better player to get through its campaign. I'm not one for multiplayer, but if more campaign DLC is released, I would definitely pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game come down to one single question : '' Is it worth the price ? " . If you have no patience , very casual , just want some fleeting fun , not care about single player campaign , easy to get mad at unbalance things , have unrealistic demands for a uber super perfect game but willing to pay a lot for those lack luster triple A games full of Gacha and paid DLC . Or you just don't have enough money right now , it is not the game for you . For those who said Yes , these are main reasons : + A great campaign that not only tell the story of hero but also tell a story of moral gray and war PTSD . +Mech : These mighty beast of war are beautifully crafted and animated , ooze with personality , they all play differently in according to the strength of the faction. Mechs are the strong point of this game , infantry need to be more diverse though .+A CoH style gameplay : So yes , the game did take inspiration on CoH , but there are differences , for starter the pace is slower since mech usually not fast  , cover ( not building though ) are useful early game as your infantry will stick to it and not move away to shoot someone , unless someone destroy those cover . The big mech can easily walk through the entire building block and create new attack path .+ Dev always watching : Dev very active on this game and always collect data , expect patch every week to address balance and changes . +New contents coming up : I was one of those people who said the game need to be delayed to polish more , unfortunately , the Covid pandemic along with Deep Silver not help it , so any ways , the dev have road map for new contents , most importantly free DLC campaign and even new Factions , free of charge .

_childDocuments_.review: I like it, especially being a fan of the Scythe boardgame helps. It's a fairly straightforward RTS with cool mechs that could have been made much more of. I've seen it for under £3 at times, and for that, it's a steal. The bits I struggle with:  I find the main characters voice like fingers down a blackboard after a while. I won't be sorry to not hear 'whatcha need?' again. In general, the in game voices don't really fit with the tone, and break immersion. Overall, it feels like the game doesn't really know what tone to hit. In this kind of game, I'd say the bleaker the better, but it seems like a lot of concessions were made here, I'm assuming for the mainstream crowd (which didn't arrive until it was abandonware).

Maybe in the future there will be improvements but I won't part with my money just yet.

_childDocuments_.review: For $15 this is a no-brainer. If you like Company of Heroes and steampunk you will dig this. _childDocuments_.review: Iron Harvest is a fun RTS with an amazing setting. The Mechs are really the selling point and they are wonderful. When fire their guns, blow through buildings, and explode its such an awesome sight. The developers have been working hard over beta to take feedback and tweak the game to be the best it can be.I understand why some people may not like this game. I can say that at launch it is lacking features. Few maps, heroes, and buildings makes the game feel light. However, the developers have already said they are going to be adding tothe game with free updates.When Iron Harvest is at its best, it is a unique and wonderful experience. I think if they keep adding and taking community feedback this will be a real gem of a RTS.As of now, I am having a blast in single player. The story is fun and the combat is a blast. I played a lot of 1v1 matches in beta and vastly enjoyed it. When you are fighting for ground, when mechs charge through terrain, and when heroes join the fight - Iron Harvest is a great RTS with the best setting imaginable.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Harvest

_childDocuments_.review: From what I've played so far, Iron Harvest has the potential to be a fantastic RTS.From environment destruction to unit variety and factions, everything looks and feels polished. However, the game in its current state seems to be missing much of what was promised in the Kickstarter campaign, and thus the game in its current state feels like a promising exclusive backer demo or early access.For £46.99 at time of writing I cannot justify recommending this game to my friends in its current state. I've also had problems with seemingly random crashes, about 4 at time of writing.I can only assume the devs will continue to work on the game until it has reached a finished state at which point I will change my recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend Iron Harvest. the campaign is good for an RTS (not starcraft 2 level of story) but compared with more recent RTS' it's up there and not just a tutorial for multiplayer. gameplay is similar to the Company of Heroes if you like that style, there are four factions (1 dlc faction) to play as, with the mechs I think being a game highlight with unique designs, styles and gameplay for their factions. voice work is good with an option for a 'native' language rather than overriding polish, russian and german characters under one language. infantry and airships are universally shared between every faction and are the same, it would be nice if the devs added like a upgrade building/system for units so even if they are shared, each faction could have a unique flavor of that unit with different abilties/passive upgrades making them fit into their gameplay role (anti-mech, medic, support team, etc) with a faction twist, the mechs do this perfectly as they fit in a role but are visually and mechanically different between each faction. multiplayer is kinda dead with low numbers of players, i wish the devs added vs a.i. into quickplay matchmaking as to boost the player number and reduce wait time for those who want to play cooperative online.

_childDocuments_.review: Played for just over an hour during the free weekend. My review is only reflective of the single player campaign, as that's all I touched.GAMEPLAY:The gameplay is super basic and generic. Everything I saw in my first hour of play has already been done before, multiple times over, and this game certainly doesn't do any of it better than prior games. It has basic RTS mechanics with environmental cover systems which are immediately annoying and clunky to get your units into, especially when controlling more than one unit.STORY:Again very generic. The game takes place in an alternate/fictional history where "Polania" is at war with "Sovruski" (or something like that). You play a young girl, so OF COURSE you're a super-soldier who is a better shot, more brave, and a better strategist than the grown men around you. And, at the same time, you're also morally superior because you apologize to the enemy soldiers while you're killing them, and even chastise your own men for "getting good" at killing the enemy. I only got an hour into the game and can already tell where this story is going, and it's nowhere good.Maybe the game shines in multiplayer, but from what I saw of the gameplay and story in the campaign, I kind of doubt it. I cannot recommend the game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid alternative to Company of Heroes (which it cribs from routinely).  The alternative setting with unique units is interesting, even if the plot of the campaign is sometimes contrived.It doesn't have the same kind of in between mission downtime or unit upgrade that StarCraft 2 has in its campaign (which would have been to its benefit, to flesh out the unique world), and a major frustration in the game is the limited line of sight ... I mean, in CoH it makes some sense as you're dealing with infantry and such, with aircraft being call ins ... but in IH you have multi-story walking war machines that should be able to see halfway across most of these maps (and the fog of war has no 'object permenance' so an enemy base vanishes as soon as it's out of Los).Hoping for an IH2.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game, quite a few thing to go over to make a quick review:Campaign: The campaign lasts quite a while, it starts slowly with something not really interesting, it will go through each faction of the game, Polonia, Rusviets and Saxons, in that order, I felt that the story was really getting strong near the end of the rusviet chapter, and during the saxon one even so, the final boss is extremely cheesy, you kill it using the power of friendship basically and it literally cheats to create a sense of urgency while remaining simple as ♥♥♥♥.I started out expecting to take part in an alternate version of the First World War, the game even sells us the conflict with several cutscenes but the only times you play during this war will be through flashbacks during the Saxons chapter, instead two thirds of the campaign is a goose chase across Eastern Europe with a political conspiracy plot. But Gunter is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gigachad so that's worth everything.The difficulty is reasonable I would say, I played the game on average and the moments where I suffered the most was the last rusviet mission, this mission is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mess, the "Gunter night infiltration mission" so I don't spoil anything, very poorly thought out, the game forces your hero to retreat if you advance too quickly towards the secondary objectives instead of simply assigning them to you when you can actually do them, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sense, and finally the penultimate mission where the ally's AI does nothing except constantly ask you for help and even after helping him he won't do anything.Overall 7/10, just wished it didn't ended on a cliffhanger.As for multiplayer, it's ok, can't really say since I'm really trash at it, but I'm having fun so it must be good, just wished there was a couple more maps especially for 6 players, since I really like playing with a ton of AIs.The strange things that I noticed however are the following: often on the road to defeat I no longer have any units yet the game still counts me 5 each time, the structures and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mines (no kidding) also count towards the unit limit, I think it also includes equipment like cannons and machine guns but I'm not sure.There is also a world campaign, a strange mix of risk and galactic conquest of Battlefront 2, it could be very good but for the moment it is extremely limited, particularly on the size of the 3 maps offered and the fact of not being able to play it with a friend like a board game, or straight up Battlefront 2.Otherwise, good graphics, good ambience, etc, the package is very nicely done, and the immersive setting for audio is a great addition.Really good game for anyone who enjoys strategy honestly.

_childDocuments_.review: can't recommend because the performance is atrocious. Most people say to just play windowed with small resolution but I'm not interested. I tried to play on 30 FPS but it just looks bad. I don't expect to have 60 fps with everything turned up but 1080p with settings on low should be attainable on an RTS without having a NASA computer. It's not like the graphics are mind blowing anyway.The controls are clunky. Sometimes I can't tell if the game accepts my orders. There's no feedback of any kind on clicking and sometimes units don't respond in any way so it's a mystery if my command went through or not. In CoH you can order a unit to move to the position it's already on and it will shuffle around a bit or move a pixel so you know your order was accepted, but nothing like that happens in the game. Unit pathing is very strange and sometimes units are just chasing fleeing enemies down even though I redirected them to attack a new target. I really like the world map mode. It's basically risk+RTS but too bad the performance and gameplay are lacking too much and I feel like time is better spent elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR If you like the sound of Dieselpunk Euro-Slav Mecha, and can accept a perfectly serviceable if micro-intensive RTS system on the side - grab it and go. Firm 8.5/10As far as RTS' go, this is pretty standard fare - very similar, mechanically, to the Company of Heroes series. There's destructible terrain, Most units benefit from a veterancy system - many units require it to unlock better abilities or building options. There's a built in cover system. Units can pick up equipment left by friendly or enemy units once they're dead, you can harvest resources from destroyed mechs, there are luggable machine guns and anti-tank cannons, your resources are brought in by capture points scattered across the map - it's exactly what you'd expect from a standard squad-based real time. There are a lot of ways you can play Iron Harvest, too! It has a fully voice acted campaign with a fine, if a little thin, plotline that takes you through each faction (and a built in video player, letting you pause the narrative out-of-game-enginge cutscenes! Which is frankly, outstanding!).It has a world-map style campaign ala Dawn of War, and standard skirmish games. The gamemodes are usual - tickets, domination, what you'd expect. Though, if you're looking for multiplayer, I may suggest trying to find a friend to play with you rather than looking for a match online.All in all, it's a perfectly normal game, with common-sense mechanics and plenty of options for any player.But let's be real. You're not here for the "this is a solid RTS" chat.You're here because of the Mechs.And to be honest, they're dumb fun to play with - each faction has their own unique approach to how their Mechs want to play (This *does* have some balance issues), and considerably different designs and aesthetic faction to faction. Noble Polania has a gamut of close and long range with the can like Smialy and stompy quadrapedal supports, Rusviet Mechs are thick and blocky, with flamethrowers, massive scythes, and light rocket batteries. The Saxons have effectively stapled legs onto any tank they could repurpose into a densely armoured crawler, and sent them on their howitzer-toting way.Outside the looks and themes, though, all the Mechs require an amount of finesse to see truly meaningful results in the field. Keeping them pointed Forward to prevent getting flanked is vital. Proper application of their weaponry to intended targets is necessary, or you'll see little effect. Micro-management and unit-countering is often the difference between a crushing assault or an abysmal rout.Speaking of - get ready to micro your wrists off.Unit selection is standard - assignable control groups, double-click a unit for all of it's type, and a "select all on screen / all on map" option if you're a SC2 zerg player who fell in love with the F2 button. But in the heat of battle, hitting control-group buttons often isn't enough - you'll need to quickly select through multiple different units, activate abilities, move to better angles, affect repairs - the front line is a busy and hectic place.Line of Sight and effective weapon LoS isn't always clear when selecting a target - sometimes, you're a little *too* far up hill to see or shoot at the enemy, and you'll need to reposition to a cleaner lane of fire. Artillery will need spotters, and will need to move up repeatedly to keep pressure on the front lines.Infantry need frequent repositioning for cover, which is often destroyed by any medium or heavy mech stomping around, friendly or otherwise. Generally speaking individual unit AI is quite plain - most units, when attacked, will stand in place, enduring whatever enemy fire there is, waiting for units to get inside their own weapons range.You'll need to be quick on the draw, efficient in a crisis, and ready to outmaneuver your opponent at every turn to make sure you're getting the best out of your army.With all that said, I have nothing but praise for this game. Folks are down on things that yes, *could* use a little polish, but nothing makes it unplayable, or un-fun. Let yourself fall in love with the setting, and allow some lenience for a game made with love for the setting it's built on.
