_childDocuments_.review: Our story opens on a mysterious train ride to somewhere. The protagonist reads a letter from his lover begging for help and a rescue. Through the train’s window, you’re greeted by beautiful vistas of the Welsh countryside circa the 1890s. Before long you arrive at the village of Sker’s train station. As you exit the mostly mundane train, you begin to feel dread slithering up inside of you. Suddenly, there’s nothing mundane about where you’re standing now. The world is still beautiful, but something is off. As you make your way toward Sker Hotel (the train disappearing behind a bend in the woods) you gaze upon signs of faded glory, ghosts of what this place once was, now choked to death by overgrown vegetation and the ever-present indifference of nature. Up the dirt path you go, pushing past the decrepit gate of Sker Hotel, toward your endangered lover. You feel it now. Somewhere, hiding beneath this faded, horror-masking glamour, there’s something that wants to kill you.  The tragedy of Maid of Sker has little to do with its town, hotel, or even its titular maid. No, the real tragedy is that you’ve already experienced the best the game has to offer. Glorious exposition, coupled with incredibly deft sound design and beautifully realized visuals, eventually gives way to a tedious game of hide and seek that lacks all the fun of the children’s game. The threat of something coming, and the anticipation of what that might be, it turns out, is infinitely more anxiety-inducing than anything you’re going to be dealing with at the hotel. Our monsters are the hotel’s “guests,” transformed by something plot (and spoiler) related. They’re all more or less blind (more) and mindless horrors (less), stalking the halls searching for a victim. In order to navigate the hotel, you must circumvent its inhabitants. If they hear you, they will chase you. And the game’s systems talk to each other well in that regard. If you move, you’ll make noise, if you make noise, they will hear, and if they hear, you’ll want to run—which makes noise. And that’s the lion’s share of the entire experience. The problem is, there’s absolutely no reason to hurry. So, actually, the question becomes whether or not you’re willing to be bored enough to play the game effectively. Are you willing to sit and wait for something that resembles a blind 90 year old man (they’re all men; I guess the women took one look at the gate and went to the Holiday Inn) to lurk by so you can quietly, and simply, move past undetected? And trust me, you will do that. Over and over. It’s Pac-Man except no one gets eaten. That would be too scary or something. Instead these evil granddad creatures just want to, well, punch you. That’s really it. If they find you, they just want to smack you around a little. Which only seems like a mildly inconvenient punishment for whatever has them so upset. So if the enemy isn’t intimidating, and the results of being captured aren’t frightening, how is Maid of Sker actually supposed to scare you? The game suffers an identity crisis trying to manufacture something that might actually horrify the player. Occasionally spikes will shoot through a bed, or a mutilated corpse may lie incinerated in a bathtub, or a trap door may send you down a deep, dark tunnel. And even, God forbid, a Jack-in-the-Box might spring! But none of it amounts to anything particularly scary because most of it lacks compelling context. It just exists.Obviously these elements taken by themselves have the characteristics of something scary. No one is denying that. Which is what makes the entire endeavor of Maid of Sker so damn odd. The creators have a good handle on horror aesthetics, as those aesthetics are all over the game, but they just don’t know how to manage them. In pictures, Maid of Sker is indeed horrifying because it’s loaded with beautiful, malevolent imagery that works wonders. The issue is that there’s nothing adequately frightening holding this malevolence together. It’s just a haunted house. Not a real one; the pop-up ones that you venture through on Halloween. The ones that employ scary things like vampires, mummies, and fat men with fake chainsaws. But why would a vampire, a mummy, and a corpulent chainsaw wielder be hanging out together? No one ever asks that, do they? Maid of Sker should have. The game needs a narrative that joins all of its scary imagery into a context that means something important. And, in the early parts, it does a decent job of delivering that.But the narrative undoes itself. The main culprit for this is in the way the game delivers its dialogue. Maid of Sker allows the player to choose which lines of dialogue to say, but oddly never gives the main character, Thomas, the agency of asking anything sensical. Besides, they’re not really options anyway. They only provide an illusion of choice, playing at being dynamic based on your selections. It’s downright infuriating that there are no choices to actually ask something, I don’t know, logical? Questions like, “Why, if you love me, did you invite me to a place where I am most likely going to die?” Thomas, to the contrary, treats everything happening like it’s an entirely normal inconvenience. As if, at some point in all our lives, we’re going to walk into a haunted hotel. As you do. You just gotta accept it and deal with it. He’s a bit of a buffoon.A video game caring about its plot, while admirable, doesn’t mean that its plot is good by default. In fact, it may actually make the game worse by unnecessarily drawing attention to its weaknesses. I never questioned the silly puzzles in the original Resident Evil, but then again, it never asked me to.Thomas is also a goofy guy mechanically! In order to not make noise, Thomas can place his hand over his mouth to avoid breathing (why does he breathe so loud?) so you can sneak past enemies. If Thomas stands too close to a fire (by close I mean several feet away), he coughs, which makes noise and alerts your foes. If there’s too much dust in the air, same thing. I didn’t learn much about Thomas, but I did learn that the man will cough if he doesn’t cover his mouth. And running? Forget about it. A short dash has Thomas sucking air like he just ran a marathon.  It’s the creator’s  job to make mechanics that add strategy and tension, but Maid of Sker does it at a high cost to the game’s verisimilitude. Is this guy asthmatic? Does he have TB or something? That could actually have been an interesting device in a game where breathing makes you vulnerable. As is, it’s entirely too (in)convenient that the very thing that Thomas needs to be—quiet—is the very thing he sucks at. This chronic hypoxia must explain why he can’t jump. Too much air required. Because if Thomas could simply jump (or step) over a couple of three-foot-high boxes, he’d have saved the day in half the time. But instead of jumping, Thomas would rather take unnecessary detours past things that want to kill him (and punch him!). Thomas is either incompetent or the least athletic person in Wales. Or both.The game isn't a total waste. It is, as mentioned, stunning to look at. Even if I’m not entertained by its content, the game’s visual and audio fidelity command attention. But it just isn’t scary. Which is a problem because it's a horror game. And based on that, perhaps solely, I can’t recommend it.(This game was received for free)
_childDocuments_.name: Maid of Sker

_childDocuments_.review: This rather classy stealth-horror has an interesting mechanic: covering your mouth to stop yourself from coughing, from things such as dust particles floating in a basement or smoke wafting from a nearby fire. This is especially relevant in a game where all the enemies stalking you are ! (You can also do fun stuff like ring hotel bells to attract enemies to specific areas; and you eventually get a nifty, limited-use item that also aids you on an aural level...)   Fittingly enough, the sound design and music in this game are truly excellent - no end of spooky creaks and dramatic melodic "stabs"! - as are the graphics, for that matter. The atmosphere, overall, is about as good as it gets, even if it never reaches the fever-pitch terror of a game like Outlast, for instance (this certainly isn't one of the "scarier" horror games on the market).    A slight flaw: your character frequently comes across items that could - and thereby probably should! - be picked up as weapons. Take the proliferation of pickaxes in a certain mine-like area, for instance...why not grab one, just to be safe? Presumably your character is some kind of stubborn pacifist; I just don't remember that being mentioned anywhere in the story! Oh well...   There's also a slight lack of manual save points (phonograms, 'natch) in some portions of the game, so be sure to save as often as possible, and be willing to go back and re-use save points whenever you're able (unless you're especially fond of repeating the last ten minutes or so of gameplay that you've already conquered)! Aside from that, this isn't a particularly hard stealth-horror game as the sub-genre goes - at least not on Normal difficulty, which is the only one I've braved thus far - so it may even be a decent place for newbies to find their feet. As someone who's beaten Alien: Isolation on "Nightmare" difficulty I won't lie and say this was a tremendous challenge...but it  a very worthwhile experience, with an interesting tale to tell, and its fair share of memorable "moments". (Those of us who enjoy exploring Resident Evil-style mansions should get an especially big buzz!)   Oh, and don't get too duped by all the guns you see in the trailers and screenshots: they're only in some reasonably fun "challenge" modes you can play, not the main storyline. But evidently a nice bonus, just the same, as is the fact that you can use your final Continue in the menu to backtrack slightly and get the good ending if you got the bad one the first time (or vice versa)!Verdict: 9/10.(PS If you enjoyed this review, feel free to check out my two Curator pages: Cheers!)

_childDocuments_.review: Quite good horror game, tho it's really just soft horror and a lot of times it feels more than a stealth game instead of a horror game. Story is ok. The game looks quite good, voice acting is all right. Tho it's really strange that just one character is voiced, Elizabeth, but not the playable character even tho you often talk to her. That's really a missed opportunity.The stealth is mostly fine. Enemies are blind, they can only hear you. You can hold your breath for some time to avoid them hearing you when close. It just doesn't feel very consistent when you don't hold your breath. Sometimes they can then hear you even tho they really shouldn't. And like most stealth games it's mostly just about patience which can definitly be something to dislike. At some point you also get a "weapon" to stun enemies with very limited ammo which I barely used but just because I didn't need it.The game definitly has some similarities to survival horror games, i.e. you explore the hotel, finding keys, (music key, crown key, yes, hello Resident Evil) to open previously locked doors, opening shortcuts, puzzles, limited ressources in form of health items and ammo for the stun "weapon" and manual saves at phonograhs and saves are even limited on highest difficulty. So yeah, I guess the game is like a Resident Evil game, but instead of fighting you avoid enemies by sneaking around them. It definitly has it's charm tho I would definitly have preferred if you could actually fight enemies, so that the game would be an actual survival horror game.I guess devs also knew that, because they later added a challenge mode to the game which is basically mercenaries from RE8. So in this one you walk through a different (but linear) path through the hotel, but this time you can actually fight the enemies with 4 different weapons: axe, revolver, shotgun and (sniper) rifle. And you can play this mode in 4 different difficulties. This mode is definitly fun and challanging, at least on the highest difficulty. Even tho it's quite short. It's really just a bonus.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I’m big on horror, I’ve been running through an unlucky string of subpar titles that have disappointed me lately. I’m always on the lookout for a new Outlast (1 or 2), Resident Evil 7, or The Cat Lady, though it seems that they’re in short supply these days. If anyone has any good recommendations for me, I’m all ears!Maid of Sker is the latest in my quest to find the next great horror game. While I can’t say that it’s an instant classic that immediately carved out a place in my heart, I can say that it’s good overall and easily one of the better titles in the genre in the last couple of years.Maid of Sker begins with you arriving at the Sker Hotel after receiving a letter of distress from that special lady in your life. Odd events seem to have transpired though, as everything is in disrepair, everyone that you meet seems to be insane and inflicted by some kind of supernatural blindness, and your girlfriend has tucker herself away into a safe hiding spot in the attic that is surprisingly inconvenient to get to. You’ll have to use your head if you’re going to make it out of the other side of this nightmare with it still attached to your shoulders.Progression requires you to explore a variety of locations while avoiding plenty of hazards and solving puzzles as you do. Hazards are more often than not the masked and brainwashed residents of the hotel. Although their inability to see can be used to your advantage, they’re highly sensitive to sound and you’ll need to keep that in mind or you’ll be spending plenty of time running away from them. Sneaking around is important to avoid their attention and keeping an eye out for noisy items that can be stepped on or bumped into is a must; there’s plenty of opportunities for the environment to mess up your near-perfectly executed ninja maneuvering, some of which is mandatory to move forward. TThese triggers can include anything from powering up machinery to dusty air that will make you cough if you happen to take in a lungful. For the former, always have an exit strategy helps, especially since there are no quick hiding spots, like lockers or under desks from other games. For the latter, the ability to hold your breath offers more advantages than you would think.Maid of Sker’s greatest strength is its atmosphere. There’s usually a sense of tension as you explore, though it does tend to dissipate once you’re passing through areas that you’ve scouted out before. Enemies mostly follow predetermined routes that make them easy to avoid once you’ve had an eye on them for a few moments. Once you’ve gotten a hang of the controls, you’ll likely be navigating like a pro, only alerting the enemies when you get a little too arrogant and happen to run into one that’s been added in or had its route changed thanks to your progression. To top this off, you end up with a weapon that can be used against these masked lunatics that overwhelms their senses and makes them no threat whatsoever for noticeably longer than it would take you to escape. It uses ammo that you could quickly burn through if you were using it all the time, but the combination of healing tonics and easily avoided enemies tends to mean that you’ve got plenty to spare as long as you’re playing it safe.The environment itself is impressive. It’s not only enjoyable to see as you explore, but it captures the era of the setting near-perfectly. The architecture, decorations, and technology really pushed it to the point of feeling much different from many of its horror peers. Even the short conversations that you have with your lady friend skillfully brought the setting to the forefront.Puzzles are frequent and tend to be fairly straightforward. I only ended up stuck for more than a few seconds a couple of times throughout my playthrough. I don’t get much of a thrill of being bogged down when I want to be experiencing the tension of horror so I’d rather puzzles were too simple rather than too complex, though puzzle fanatics will likely not find themselves pushed anywhere near their limits here. I’d classify this as a horror adventure rather than a horror puzzler, for sure.As far as recent horror releases go, Maid of Sker is easily one of the better ones. I enjoyed the atmosphere and the narrative, though the gameplay was a bit on the lighter side. I felt a continual sense of curiosity throughout, though the apprehension and dread that I was hoping for never really hit me as hard as I would’ve liked. It’s a middle ground between walking simulator, action/stealth, and puzzle varieties of horror, though it succeeds in performing admirably in each category.All in all, Wales Interactive put together a solid experience that I could see most horror fans enjoying, even if it may not be the next great classic that defines the genre for years. I’m glad that I played it and recommend it to those who are looking for enjoyable titles in a genre that needs more reliably good titles. Just be aware that it can be beaten in three to four hours on your first go.

_childDocuments_.review: Maid of Sker is an atmospheric, anxiety-inducing horror game with some good jump scares. It's a stealth based game, so those looking for an action based horror might be disappointed as there are no weapons or combat here. Gameplay consists of finding things (keys, music sheets, collectables etc.) inside a huge mansion, whilst remaining undetected by the monsters that inhabit the place. Silence is key here, so sneaking around and holding your breath is required much of the time. As you work your way through the story, there are some nice puzzles too. The music and sounds make the atmosphere really spooky, it can feel pretty claustrophobic at times, building the sense of dread which is great. The story is basic, it's nothing new and doesn't have a great deal of depth but it does the job. My total playthrough was about 5 hours, but I didn't hunt all of the achievements. I recommend playing this game if you're interested in a few hours of intense, atmospheric, stealth horror.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start off by saying that Maid of Sker has used a fair amount of influences from other games that players know and love in the genre. Immediate fans will link the exploration of a spooky mansion to the older games in the Resident Evil franchise. It's hard to create something original now without someone looking at it and saying this is just that with a different coat of paint. Despite having influences from survival horror games this still stands proud as a different game to scratch that itch of getting to experience instead of playing through silent hill or resident evil 2 for the hundreth time. The main thing this game has going for it is the sound design and environment. Sneaking around the mansion really makes you feel like something can happen at any moment and it makes the jump scares that happen that much more exciting on your first play through. There are three difficulties to play the game on which mainly effects how sensitive the AI is to noise such as you breathing, taking that final breath in before you hold your breath, coughing because of dust, and bumping into various objects. You're only real defense given in the game is either your sneaking abilities or a sound ball given to the player about half way through. The story is decent enough with some solid voice work but what is cool about it is how you are rewarded by doing a bit of exploration with a second ending. I also really enjoyed the songs in this game. This game had some bad AI to start out with from what I've heard. I got here after a few patches to the AI and it doesn't seem as bad but it is still pretty easy to get around once you get used to it regardless of the difficulty. It becomes more of an aggravation of waiting for enemies to shamble down the hallway rather than fear of them finding you. Perhaps this AI gripe goes hand in hand with the return of diminishing effects mentality. The other thing that bothered me about the AI is their attention to specific noises. They'll jump at you for most noises but than ignore noises such as ringing bells, switches, and telephones you leave ringing. As I mentioned the story is decent enough but knowing that some of the writers behind this were also behind SOMA it just felt a bit underwhelming. Most of the story is found in notes as lore filler but it feels like it the main story could have had more interaction and conversation going on to build up more.So you don't have the pure adrenaline fueled fear like in Alien Isolation. You don't have the super smart AI like in F.E.A.R.. You have some heavily inspired influences right down to Mr. X. like in resident evil. With all this it still manages to be a pretty competent stand alone title. The first play through will probably take you around 6 hours and it will only get quicker from there if you replay for achievements. I'd say grab this one during a bit deeper of a sale but it's still worth the experience. 𝕀𝕗 𝕐𝕠𝕦 𝔼𝕟𝕛𝕠𝕪 𝕋𝕙𝕚𝕤 𝕋𝕣𝕪

_childDocuments_.review: I must say this game was extremely dull. I was very excited to explore the hotel, but the design is really lacking. You could tell what was going on already in the first hour of the game, making the storytelling kind of useless from that point on. The enemies...are completely useless, they just roam the corridors super slowly, and they just get in the way of your exploration. Basically 99% of the time you will just be crawling behind them waiting for them to get the f*** out of the way so you can go on with what you wanted to do. The AI is horrible...if for some unknown reason they acknowledge your presence, you are done, because there is nowhere to hide and they will not get tired of chasing unless you basically change map or go in a no limit area for them so good luck with that. It's just tedious, not challenging. For this reason it is probably better to play the game in story mode (no enemies, just puzzles and story).Sound compartment is also not very well executed. Enemy steps can sound right next to you even though they are maybe 3 rooms further. The sense of distance is completely absent. Closed doors or walls don't muffle the sounds. Whatever in game sound (when solving puzzles, for instance) no matter how loud, you never know if it will trigger the enemies or not (mostly not, unless it's scripted in the game for one big puzzle). Very disappointing and breaks immersion totally, coupled with the bad AI.The additional challenges give you weapons in your hand. Yes, for the very first seconds it was fun finally being able to shoot those idiots in the head...but then again, it gets extremely repetitive very shortly. Kill guys, find key, use key, kill guys, go on (and this in the same corridors and rooms that you saw until that moment for the whole game).I mean it's fine if you want to play it, it is still decent...but too many things make this game totally skippable.

_childDocuments_.review: Maid of Sker had a few jump scares here and there, but it was the tension and curiosity of the unknown that kept me invested in moving forward. After the first hour or so of my playthrough, it stopped being quite as scary, and had me hooked into the narrative, struggling to piece together what was real. Like the beautifully haunting siren’s song that persists throughout Maid of Sker, I was lulled into a trance, needing to see Thomas’s journey through to the end. There are few games that have captured my attention as much as Maid of Sker, and I think for any fan of the horror genre, especially those that love to explore, it would be an absolute disservice not to give this game a try if not for the story alone.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a letdown, It started so good, having very good visuals and audio while including an intriguing story line and borrowing some basic mechanics from games like the resident evil series. But where the game fall apart is the horror factor, I just didn't find it very scary due to the game only having one main enemy type while the others are just variations of it. So playing the game it doesn't take long to figure out exactly how the enemies react and how to avoid them, and when you do get caught it turns from scary to frustrating fast, and whenever a horror game gets frustrating it looses all of it's scare factor. If the game had different enemy variations and game mechanics it would have made the game so much better. My feelings are more mixed then negative as there are some good aspects, but as it stands I would only recommend getting it if it is on a good sale and you can't find anything else worth getting.

_childDocuments_.review: You have been summoned to a long-abandoned hotel called Sker, by your girlfriend Elizabeth. She states that she is trapped there, and she is being hunted by malicious men, known as The Quiet Ones, who are combing every nook and cranny to find her. Playing as her boyfriend, Thomas Evans, you set out to save Elizabeth; despite the fact that you're seemingly asthmatic and severely allergic to dust, as you cough every time particles are in the air. Though you do end up getting more than you bargained for, as the mystery of the Maid of Sker unravels while you quietly slink along forgotten corridors of the hotel, searching for phonograph cylinders, keys, and music sheets to bring the ensuing nightmare to an end. It should be noted that the plot of this title has nothing to do with the 1872 three-volume British novel of the same name, but rather much of the inspiration comes from Welsh origins.Maid of Sker is pretty much your run-of-the-mill stealth horror game. You sneak around and avoid enemies while finding key progression items, as well as occasionally solve very easy puzzles. The whole premise is to find a handful of phonograph cylinders, and most of the puzzles are the same; find two levers to open a gate, or ring bells/pull levers in a certain order. The content doesn't feel very engaging or stimulating, especially since half of the mechanics intended for fending off the enemies don't actually do anything in the long run; with the exception of a gadget you get at the halfway point, which overwhelms their senses and stuns them for a short duration. Additionally, there's zero suspense in the stealth sections that encompass nearly the entire campaign, which is something that really makes hide-and-seek games both fun and terrifying; looking at Alien: Isolation is a great example of how suspense in stealth horror can completely push a game to a whole new level.That said, some players may find the popping and creaking of the old hotel unsettling. There's also a slight inability to distinguish your own footsteps from those of The Quiet Ones, which forces you to actually stop and second guess if there is or isn't someone lurking around the bend. The sound design is actually one of the few upsides to this game, but without a proper atmosphere, set of working mechanics, or decent enemy design, it largely goes to waste.The foes themselves are among some of the worst that've been encountered in any modern horror game. Although Wales Interactive released an update not long after the title launched, it did little to fix the core issues. Prior to the hotfix, the enemies were bypassed easily, as nothing less than bumping straight into them triggered any sort of response from them. Post-patch, they seem to be proximity-based, which is odd for bad guys that are purportedly sound-based according to the developers. They almost feel like they rely on their sense of smell to sniff you out rather than anything else, and quite often they'll just keep casually walking toward you and smack you, even though you didn't actually trigger a response from them. Thomas has a mechanic to hold his breath so that enemies cannot hear him when his asthma and dust allergies start acting up, and this mechanic now does absolutely nothing to absolve a foe's interest in the player. You can be silent, holding your breath, and simply too close to an enemy and they will saunter up and whack you for no reason.There is something terribly wrong with the graphics. They look as though they should be extremely crisp and modern, but for whatever reason they have an awful foggy, blurriness to them that can't be circumvented even by cranking the anti-aliasing and shutting off optional settings like motion blur and chromatic aberration. Worse still, the colors look totally muted and washed out. The default brightness and gamma is far too dark, but even after fiddling with it for ten minutes it's impossible to get a ratio that makes the game actually look good. If you leave it as-is, you'll end up being unable to see most of the enemies until you're face-to-face with them. This is a problem that somehow gets worse the further into the campaign that you get.At the end of the day, Maid of Sker doesn't have much going for it. For a game that's supposed to have writers from masterpieces SOMA and Don't Knock Twice, it sure is lacking an interesting plot; it's close to a Bioshock Infinite rip-off, and even Elizabeth looks reminiscent to the very Elizabeth from that game as well. The core stealth mechanics don't even work properly; holding your breath does nothing, and you either have to reset your save point or run very far away to even get enemies to reset. The campaign also features a Resident Evil 2, Mr. X clone. Even the graphics have a ton of problems, but at least the game is well optimized. There are simply no original ideas here, very few scares, little atmosphere, and overall Maid of Sker could've used another few months of development before being kicked out of the nest.The Horror Network  |  Click for Gore

_childDocuments_.review: This is what horror games on steam should be like.  I've played too many horribly made indie horror games in the past few months.  All of which are always lacking in the following...1. controller support2. invert y axis for mouse/controller3. proper optimization4. good voice acting5. great pc performance6. intense scripted scenesThis game has all of the above so far.  I have the settings cranked to ultra, playing in 4K resolution and am getting a solid 60 fps on a 2080Ti + i7 8700.  Other indie developers definitely should be taking notes here, as many of the indie horror games have terrible performance in 4K due to not being optimized.  Optimization in Maid of Sker is fantastic.  I haven't played too much of it yet, as this will be one of those games I play with my brother on a 55 inch 4K gaming tv while drinking some beers and smoking some green in a dark spooky room.Props to Wales Interactive!  Definitely keep making more first person survival horror games!  I would love to see a Resident Evil VII + Silent Hills combination type game in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: The Quiet Ones, eh? Maid Of Sker' blind enemies weren't given that name ironically because they go tromping around making a huge racket. They're quiet, them Quiet Ones. Vewwy, vewwy quiet.But they're not hunting wascally wabbits. They're hunting you by sound. Your footsteps on the floor, the ragged gasping for air after prolonged running, or coughs as you inhale smoke and dust. So what are you gonna do about it? Uh, well....it's a stealth horror game, so what you're gonna do about it is...um, be stealthy. Be stealthy a lot.Have nerves of steel as you crabwalk around a corner, and you can hear the phlegmy slurping noises a Quiet One makes, or them sobbing to themselves. Backpedalling as you try to avoid their patrol route, and still it keeps moving forward.Your back is against the wall, and there's nowhere else to go. It stops, mere inches from your face. Eyes watering from the fetid stench of its breath, trying not to flinch or cry out in disgust as its rancid spittle hits your skin.A hand madly gripping your mouth to keep yourself from breaking. Lungs burning for fresh new air. The creature shrieks, but still you manage to subdue the terror. It turns and shuffles away.Your head throbs, and your vision turns red. Uncontrollably you suck in desperately needed oxygen. The Quiet One stops.You poo yourself. Did....it.....hear.....me? Or was it that canned animation they do where they briefly hesitate and search around, in an attempt to get you needlessly bricking yourself that you were rumbled?And the answer to that question, as it spins around and comes hurtling at you, before smashing your head in like an egg, is yes. Yes it did hear you. And you died.This is pure stealth: there's no distracting them by throwing things, or cracking them on the back of the head with a billy club. You either don't get caught, or you generally get dead. You can run away, but they wil pursue you fairly thoroughly and it's much harder to hold your breath after the physical exertion. If one comes searching for you it will be trickier to evade them, though thankfully not impossible once alerted.Beyond patiently creeping about enemies you have one means of defence, and it only briefly incapacitates them and is limited in its ammo. Essentially it's the slow methodical stealth of Amnesia, meets the chase sequences of Outlast, meets a bit of Resident Evil 2, as there is a supertough enemy who hunts you down more persistently than the others and can one hit kill you. If you are the type of person who, like me, inhabits these games fully and is immersed in every tense second of the cat and mouse experience, then you should enjoy this. But if you're the kind of person who wants to be able to turn around to enemies, whip out a rocket launcher and say"say heh-lo to my leedle freend" then, uh, yeah - nope. Not for you....Maid Of Sker is nerve wracking, scary and exciting, but it is also built around a gameplay mechanic it never deviates from. It does have chase sequences, but again: running like mad is your only option, and there's only 3 or so of these events. Some puzzles and a few other trippy sequences round it out some more, but the main emphasis here is on being powerless and patient in a life and death game of hide and seek.As a fan of games like Thief / Alien Isolation / Apsulov / SOMA etc I have thoroughly enjoyed the 10 hours this game has taken so far. The visuals aren't topnotch, but do enough to make it quite atmospheric. With heavy shadows, and dim environments obscured by clouds of dust particles hanging in the illuminated areas, you'll be frantically peering into the gloom for signs of movement. Effective audio adds to the tension, as you hear the soft shuffle of approaching feet and wet rasping breaths, or the sharp stab of violin as you blunder into an enemy and for a second wonder if you made enough noise to make it aware of you.Whilst the graphics are only reasonable it does run well generally. There is a section taking place outdoors at night that struggles a bit, but otherwise its pretty smooth and doesn't have to load often. The story and voice acting are well done, and on the hard difficulty level it gets pretty oldskool, in that you're only given 10 saves. Jump scares are effectively done, and infrequent enough to not be overplayed. The AI is basic, yet it works as intended and does just enough to be a challenging foe, without being infuriatingly persistent or overly dozy.  It ticks all the boxes I look for in a game like this, and gets a very enthusiastic thumbs up!If you liked this review, and want to see more about the genre, then check out my curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: Maid of Sker is a hauntingly rich tale that will send chills up your spine like the voices that whisper your name in the night. Will you succumb to the lure of the spider's web, or will you be able to harden your senses into adamantium and brave the hallowed halls of Sker?Firstly, allow me to get out of the way that there is a small divide within the community over whether the game is more like Bioshock or Resident Evil or not at all. As a person who is mostly neutral on the whole thing(and has played both), I saw things that reminded me of them both. But only in the very beginning when you enter the grand hall of the hotel. Everything was set up for the grand re-opening day but was clearly all put to a sudden end by some sort of tragedy. The nautical theme and dive helmets immediately made me nostalgic for Bioshock, but the entryway reminded me more of one of the early rooms in the first RE where you meet in a large foyer with a staircase much like the one in this game.The verdict? Freudian. Sometimes a cigar is just a cigar and people are reading way too much into things. I feel like maybe the team at Bioshock was inspired by the legend of Sker house which was constructed nearly 900 years ago originally as an abby. Later on, the story of the ghost of Elizabeth was brought to public light by author R.D. Blackmore in his 1872 novel 'The Maid of Sker'. Definitely worth looking into. History! It's good stuff. Beyond all of this hullabulloo(congratulations if you read all that and you're still with me) aside, the game does a very good job of making its own identity. It stands completely apart. Let go of any and all preconceived notions of what other games this may remind people of, relax, and enjoy the effing game. :P Brass tacks time, friends. I'm going to get into my problems first. Blurry, blurry, blurry. I had to turn off 90% of the camera effects to be able to see clearly. Yes, I understand that certain elements of horror are poor vision, but this went beyond  poor vision and straight into feeling legally blind. - Luckily the Devs have been hard at work releasing hotfixes and tweaks because they are aware that many people are having a hard time visually. Yay! It's *mostly* fixed and I was able to see well enough to complete the game. The mob AI is fickle as f*ck. Sometimes they're dumb as a box of rocks, other times they have super hearing and super speed. I found myself frequently being camped inside the save rooms, which was incredibly frustrating. **Pro-tip** I have found a way to do a soft reset of the AI by saving and reloading in the room. This was invaluable to me 'shaking' them off if they were being stubborn. - The Devs have been working on this too. After a couple patches, I wasn't stuck being trapped in rooms and I was able to outrun the higher level mobs. I feel like it could still use a little more tweaking, but I'm happy with the changes so far. The game time feels a little padded with all the sneaking you need to do. That being said, the actual playtime and length of the story(sneak-padding taken into consideration) was still satisfying. I didn't feel like it was too short or too long. I liked it. Now onto the stuff I loved. It's a big spooky house with locked doors and collectibles, which is almost always enough to sell me on a game. I'm an explorer, a discoverer of secrets, a seeker of lore. This tickled me pink. <3 While it's kind of a bummer that many of the achievements are able to be missed, it adds a good amount of replay value to a game. As a little bit of an achievement wh*re, I appreciate this a lot. I like to get a lot of bang(giggity) for my buck. The artwork and atmosphere were absolutely tantalizing. A creeping void brought to life by a long lost lullaby. It permeates, consumes you, and it isn't long before you start to understand the house. It wants you to find all it has to offer in every hidden nook and crevice. Finally the music was simply breathtaking. My compliments to the folks who put the musical score together. I was misty-eyed at the end. Bravo.After all that, do I recommend this? A velvet box wrapped with a satin bow, darlings. All the yeses. Grab this game for sure. If you're still skeptical, wait for a sale. <3

_childDocuments_.review: Maid of Sker is a worthy experience for any horror fan willing to discover its unique creepiness and intriguing story exploring Welsh folklore in a macabre way. The plot was very clear and progressed at a perfect pace to keep the player in a constant state of interest. I loved the fact that almost everything in the game was sound-based varying from puzzles to enemies, even to collectibles! I really took in the marvelous atmosphere of the Sker hotel, topped off with beautiful graphics and amazing sound design.This game requires patience and nerves to complete, for the enemies roam about the area pretty freely. The monsters’ behavior seems to be quite inconsistent and there are some unfinished game mechanics, which is why I understand the criticism. I didn’t like the fact that I’d have to visit a certain location to manually save while having to deal with a multitude of monsters, therefore I opted for the safe mode first. I will update my review once I finish the original mode.But judging from the reviews I’ve read and the videos I’ve watched, Maid of Sker might be even better on safe mode as it removes the most frustrating encounters and lets you focus on the game itself that works just fine without all the sneaking. _childDocuments_.review: I will admit to being legitimately torn as I begin writing this on whether to hit thumbs up or thumbs down. One one hand, I didn't hate the game, and am reluctant to tear the work of a small but competent studio to shreds, on the other hand, I somewhat struggle to recommend it. Whichever I eventually press, this is only because Valve (Peace be upon their name) have not yet seen fit to give us an option for a thumb wavering halfway.Anyway, on to the game. Maid of Sker is a visually gorgeous and beautifully scored mess that's one part Resident Evil and one Part Amnesia. I would say without the strengths of either, but I have yet to finish Resident Evil 1 as I honestly don't much care for it, although will probably get around to it eventually. I must iterate though, the game is honestly one of the nicest looking games that I have played. The visuals are near photorealistic at times, although having spent a few days in Northern Wales I think the game sells the setting a little short by only being set in one small hotel and the grounds of. The lighting is low and atmospheric, and a few scenes, especially those under red light look absolutely incredible. The soundtrack is also gorgeous, and the vocal performance given by Tia Kalmaru (No I don't know who that is either) is simply stunning. There is one section fairly early on, where you come up a path lined with bear traps, to find a red lit cage overlooking the ocean as the song "Calon Lun" plays, and it is simply breathtaking, equal parts mournful, haunting and beautiful and will stick with me long after finishing the game. Sadly, as this and the Order 1886 showed us, you can spend literally years making the game beautiful, and this won't necessarily equate to a good game, but credit is deserved here, as a very large amount of effort has gone into it.So, biggest issue out of the way first. The game is barely scary. The core mechanic is that the monsters, of whom there are somewhere between 10 and 20 in the hotel are blind due to a bad case of the strange welsh illness known as "sack on head", and will only respond to sound or the dolt with a camera for a face walking into them. You can sneak to avoid them, and hold your breath when one comes near. This sounds good in theory, but falls apart in execution, primarily as the sack also appears to be muffling a lot of their hearing, and the implied oxygen deprivation may also be hitting hard at their brains and resulting in powers of memory that would make the average goldfish look like your mother in law. You will very rarely need to breath in, as the monsters have to be very close to even be aware of your presence, and a lot of the times that I used it I was attacked regardless. Very few noises will actually alert the enemies, and they will forget almost immediately in the rare event that they are. If you get injured, your character will make little terrified blubbering noises, which is a nice touch, and serves to make the game slightly harder if you are injured. Unfortunately the monsters can run faster than you can, so in almost every occasion I was detected I was bludgeoned to death. This was used to good effect in the the final section however, but this can be given the further counterpoint that you are in almost no danger in this section this is not much of a caveat. There is also very little in the way of interactivity in the environment. One would think when the enemies hunt based upon noise, that the developers would make good use of the building interior, having creaking floorboards, easily knocked over piles of books and the like, but there is almost none of this. Even the act of opening a door could have been made tense, and was early in the game, until you realise just how little danger you actually are in. There is one point where this is used, where a model train set will let out a toot, but the toot is so low that I was actually killed because I didn't realise that they had been alerted. The model train had also been running around the track the entire time I had been on that floor and had not been smashed, so I have no idea why a small toot barely audible over the sound of the train and all the monsters struggling for breath under their sacks would have upset all of them so much. The game is also somewhat confused in it's environmental design. The first few areas are solid, with the player conversing with their fiance over the telephone, and getting drawn deeper into the hotel as the creepy factor is gradually ramped up. I'll actually say that the earlier sections are the highlight, as they are properly scripted. They are heavily linear, but that ensures good control over the pacing. The issues arise as you begin to get back towards the house. The game loves to lock you in these open areas with three or four sackheads roaming about, trying to find switches to open the door or stealth around a few of them. The last garden area will even play sudden loud piano chords at random (As most games, including this one, will do when you are detected) in an attempt to cause you to panic. It's here that the issues begin to show, as the sack men seem to have very little interest in actually finding or hunting you. They just dander about breathing heavily, and that is it. Upon returning to the house, the game becomes somewhat more open, allowing you to roam around the hotel. (Albeit, you still have to do every puzzle and set piece in order, so all this setting actually serves to do is sacrifice control of the the pacing in favour of copying resident evil) Sadly, this is quite a small building, and it is chock full of the same enemies wandering about doing nothing in particular. Very quickly you will stop fearing them, and they become simply an obstacle to slip around, an annoyance at the very best.  The atmosphere is still decent, but the game looses it's scare factor very quickly as a result. I honestly feel that it would have made more sense to keep the rest of the game scripted like the earlier sections, and keeping it well paced, but the game looses a lot of it's charm in the fact that the greatest part of it's length is spent stealthing easily around the same enemies and backtracking around the same building, trying to find the one way that you are meant to go forward. Finally, the safe rooms that you can hide in and save in are far too frequent and easy to hide in. The game also has a story, which is ok. To a seasoned horror game player like myself it was pretty predictable, and threw it's plot elements around far too freely to create much sense of mystery. Elements like a cult or a creature from a certain popular mythology are just dumped on the player early on with very little fanfare, and after you piece together mystery, which is not hard, nothing remains but to follow on and be drip fed information which we already have.  This is, excepting the final twist, which comes out of absolutely nowhere. If you do somehow manage to see it coming (Or used a walkthrough) the surprise villain will literally be too busy giving a monologue right next to you to stop you from foiling their plan. Finally, the game has a few technical issues. Load times are obnoxiously long, and the game crashed to desktop almost every time I died, and a few times during loading screens as well. Frame rate stutters were annoyingly common also. Now I finish, I realise that, as it pains me to say, I can't recommend. A lot of effort has gone into it, but it was misdirected. I would rather have a scary game with mediocre graphics and a good story than a gorgeous game with weak gameplay and an undisciplined mess of a story. As I seem to say so often in horror reviews, go play "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" instead. It's a perfect showcase of how to create a wonderful horror game on a small budget. Perhaps get this on sale, but I doubt you are going to get more than 5 hours out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: “Old stories often turn out to be true” - Arthur MachenI had a good time with this. It's a stealth-horror experience not miles away from Alien Isolation in terms of gameplay. You aren't really able to defend yourself from your foes - the middle section of the game gives you a gadget to stun enemies temporarily but you don't keep it forever. The interesting twist is that most enemies cannot see you at all, so you can be standing right next to them and they'll have no idea that you're there unless you make some noise. If you're a clumsy oaf and keep running around, banging into furniture and having coughing fits (our man coughs like he has tuberculosis every time he gets even a whiff of particles in the air) then things escalate quickly and you'll find yourself being chased around the hotel like a Welsh Benny Hill; if you take your time and hold your breath when needed you can ghost around the place almost completely unmolested. The setting is quite unique, with events taking place in an isolated location on the Welsh Coast and a new take on an ancient Greek myth providing the impetus driving events; these combine to create a folk horror atmosphere that is further facilitated by some nice character designs and decent graphics. I have to praise Wales Interactive for embracing and representing their locality; Wales is a little-used setting but as a fan of Arthur Machen I certainly appreciated the decision. The game actually reminded me of Machen in some ways - he wasn't one for action as such, but the modern-man-meets-mythology, science-and-commerce-vs-supernatural themes and the brooding Celtic setting certainly created a resonance for me. There are only a couple of jump scares, with the build-up and release of tension from evading the enemies favoured over loud noises and sudden startles. Though I've seen several complaints about bugs and performance issues I didn't encounter any myself. It's not a particularly long experience and you could complete it in 3 hours if you didn't care about missing detail or about 5 hours if you're very thorough, which for me was just about the right amount of time. Like horror fiction, I tend to think that horror games are best executed in short story or novella format, with any further increases in length risking overfamiliarity with the antagonist and a dilution of the horror. Some might complain about the price vs length ratio but from my perspective I did feel it was worth the money I spent buying a key on sale from the Humble Store - you can get it absurdly cheap if you're willing to be patient. Rounding off the package is the challenge mode, a later addition to the game in which you're given a bundle of firearms and have to escape the hotel by hunting keys and killing enemies. I didn't much care for it as I felt it drifted too far from what the core game stood for, but if you want to blow off some steam after all that sneaking it's certainly not horribly executed. I would recommend that you only play it after finishing the story as it might spoil some areas for you and from a gameplay perspective it'll benefit you to be familiar with the floorplan. Overall, I found it to be a competent and unusual sneaky horror experience that unites Soma-like gameplay with folk horror, mythology, and the careful exploration of A Quiet Place.

_childDocuments_.review: Maid of Sker is like diving headfirst into this Victorian-flavored horror tale set on a remote island off the Welsh coast. You're Thomas Evans, on a mission to save your damsel in distress, Elizabeth Williams, from her creepy family holed up in this spooky hotel.Now, don't get me wrong, the world they've built here is pretty intriguing. But story-wise, it's a bit like predicting the ending of a rom-com. You pretty much clock where it's heading within the first hour. It's entertaining, sure, but not exactly groundbreaking.Visually, though, it's a treat. The environments look like they're straight out of a Gothic painting. But here's the kicker - it's not exactly a horror game. Nope, it's more like a stealth game trying to wear a scary mask. The enemies? They're blind as a bat but have ears like a fox. Sneak around them, hold your breath, rinse and repeat. Gets old real quick, trust me.And don't even get me started on the gameplay mechanics. It's like they threw you in a maze with a broken compass. You're constantly tiptoeing around, trying not to get caught, but guess what? You're gonna get caught. A lot. And the only way out is to run like you're being chased by a pack of rabid dogs.Sure, it's got its moments. The graphics are pretty, the music sets the mood, and the story's got potential. But when it comes down to it, Maid of Sker is like a haunted house with all the scares turned off. If you're looking for a real fright fest, stick to the classics like Outlast or Alien: Isolation. They know how to deliver the goods without leaving you feeling like you've been tricked into a game of hide-and-seek with blindfolded toddlers.

_childDocuments_.review: Maid of Sker is overall pretty uninteresting. The voice acting isn't terrible, but the dialogue only kills time in the game. The characters attempt to voice their roles in their horrific setting, but have nothing of interest or importance to speak of. The game's story doesn't really make too much sense. Ideally, if the game wanted to trail the story along the lines of British Folklore, it wouldn't have too many elaborate mechanisms. Having telephones and other people surviving around the situation kind of kills the immersion of "being isolated with the killers." The controls are pretty limited and it feels very sluggish, leaving little room for versatility. It implements use of a map as well as general objective in order to attempt to direct you in a linear direction. The game doesn't provide a map legend that would allow the player to understand their progress as well as other things they would need to eventually backtrack to, which is disorienting to the chronology of what objectives to complete. So to summarize the issue, the game lacks fluidity.It's a game that has enemies that are supposed to pursue and track while putting pressure on the player's navigation through the environment. If a player is not of the cautious variety, the player will test boundaries on the enemies. After testing the boundaries, this game didn't really have a decent scale of difficulty. Furthermore, the enemies and the atmosphere aren't really unsettling or scary.The sound design is the strongest element of the game, but it is abused for the sake of attempting to create an atmosphere that is unsettling. After several sound cues that were played at distasteful or moments where the player is just walking around, I found the strongest element of the game became an annoying factor in gameplay.I played through one-third of the story in less than an hour, so it isn't a long game.If you are open to a story and have an extremely good attention span, I would wait till it's like 5 dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, the new s... Gotta love 'em, right? When I was a kid, we rarely had sequels. Every new game was a surprise. We never knew what to expect from it. And it was, like, part of the fun. I mean, there's nothing wrong with the people who play  or  (or whatever else there is) every day and feel content. As long as they're happy, that's perfectly fine with me. But personally, I can't help but feel that the current generation of players is missing something really great. It's just people nowadays know  what to expect from a game long before they start playing it. Every single  title comes with tons of gameplay footage long before the release and it's not like there's a lot of space for expectations. I mean, seriously. What new could you expect from yet another  or ? Sure, there are always indies, but... you know how it is about those. Those are great, but sometimes you just want something fresh that also looks cool on your big . Something that comes with both something new  a competitive picture. Even if we're talking about the  level. A game that you pick up just because you liked the title and ended up being surprised in a good way. I totally miss such stuff. That's why I always feel thankful for games like . But I'm getting ahead of myself. Let's start from the beginning.What is  exactly?  is a first-person horror adventure with action and stealth elements. Technically, there are quite a lot of “walking sim” elements, but... I can't call it like that. Personally, I'm a  hater of “walking sims” (always end up bored to death). And even though  does incorporate quite a lot of those “walk and watch” mechanics, it does it totally right. All those walks and movie-like sequences are used to create the atmosphere. To make you feel scared. In the best way possible (strange sounds, blinking light, that kind of stuff). Remember the old adventure game called ? That's pretty much what I'm talking about. I'm not trying to compare the gameplay, of course, these two are totally different games, I'm talking about the fact that there aren't many things to interact with. Most of the time you'll be just walking around and looking for things. . Unlike our usual “walking sims”,  includes quite a lot of proper gameplay mechanics. In other words, you'll never  walk around. There'll always be something.First of all, there's stealth. See, in this game? There are no weapons. Well, technically there's a special  mode that offers you some basic shooting fun, but that's a different story. In the main game there are no weapons and that's it. And the funniest thing is – your enemies won't see you. Remember  movies? The ones with the evil aliens who tracked people by sound? That's exactly what we've got here. You run, you bump into the furniture – they'll hear you. And when they'll hear you... let's just say you won't want that. And to make things worse – the game takes place in the old mansion (technically – a hotel, but whatever), where there's a lot of dust in the air. And when there'll be dust, your character will sneeze.  So, what do you do? First of all – you move slowly and you listen. And when there are enemies nearby, you move even slower and you hold your breath (right trigger on your gamepad). You can also use the environment to trick the enemies. Make a distraction and while enemies will look for the source of the sound, use that time to run away. Finally, in the second half of the game you'll get a handy device that'll be able to stun enemies (remember  from  and their main weakness?),  every use will require a special cartridge and those'll be pretty hard to find, so-o-o... Yeah. Walk slowly and don't make any sounds. .Another thing about  is -like level design. Well, the old mansion (I know, I know, it's a hotel), keys, some basic puzzles that involve looking for certain items... you know. The  stuff. When it's about level design and exploration, you can call this game “ Lite”. Especially since  started to do first-person stuff since its seventh main installment too. Thankfully, its own unique mechanics prevent this game from getting “ rip-off” aftertaste. And another one of such things is... multiple endings. Technically, there's nothing new about those. At the end of the story, the game just determines how good you did and gives you one of the two endings. Good or bad, that's pretty much it. Again, pretty -like, but the way this game wants us to unlock the good ending... Let's just say it fits. To finish this game, you'll need to collect four brass cylinders. But to get the good ending, you'll also need to collect four music sheets. Which means one thing – more exploration. Sounds boring, but with pretty much every room in this game presenting a certain kind of challenge (traps, puzzles, locked doors, stealth, every room in this game feels different) and some actions will even have consequences... Like I said, such an approach fits perfectly. Even though there isn't much stuff here ( is a pretty short game that can be finished in only four hours as long as you know exactly what to do), everything here has a purpose. It's one of those games that have that certain handmade aftertaste and it feels really,  good.Looks solid too. It's far from being a  experience, but still, backgrounds here look pretty charming. The story isn't that great, though. Can't argue with that. It's yet another one of those stories, in which the guy comes to a spooky mansion (don't... say anything,  it's a hotel, lol) to save his beloved one. There's nothing else here. Just that. And it's probably the worst thing about this game. Seriously, getting something like that in ? Feels like a sad joke. , , ... Don't know 'bout you, guys, but personally, I'm totally tired of such stuff and was really disappointed to get exactly that in . On the other hand, though, the deep atmosphere that incorporates a lot of elements from classic horror novels sure compensates for that.  cult, family secrets, th century, real influences (the game is somewhat inspired by 's  novel of the same name, and even though technically, it's a totally different story with different characters and motif, you can see where that family stuff came from), nods to folklore (even though the game takes place in a fictional place, it's a direct nod to  in  and local folklore)... All that sure helps you to make peace with the lack of complicated story.So... yeah.  is a totally underrated title. The one that deserves way,  more attention. It's not the next big thing, it's not a groundbreaking experience and it sure needs better story, but if you want a good horror? Here it is. Here's a very good horror for you. With competitive  visuals, deep atmosphere and juicy gameplay mechanics. And they only ask  for it. Not only I enjoyed this game, it's one of those rare cases, in which I can say that the game is worth buying for its full price. In other words, I totally recommend it to all horror fans. Pretty nice surprise, huh? , I love it when such things happen. Dixi.

_childDocuments_.review: This is pretty close to a lower budget Resident Evil 7 or 8 where you replace the combat with stealth and surprisingly it's a pretty decent experience.After you disable motion blur and turn off TAA there are actually pretty nice looking visuals here. Also when you add the sound design to the mix, the atmosphere is easily one of the strong suits of this game while exploring the Sker hotel.Sadly the stealth itself is kinda wishy-washy and it feels very forgiving which sadly lowers the effectiveness of the scares. _childDocuments_.review: Alright...so this is going to sound super harsh, but there are really great redeeming elements, just not for an overall rounded experience. Pros- Phenomenal voice acting. Honestly, I've heard worse voice over work in triple A titles. There wasn't a moment that I thought "this sounds pretty good for an indie game" it was just a great expressive job especially on Elisabeth's part. - Sound design is done pretty well. It's nothing that REALLY jumps out at you, but there's subtle sounds that are solid. The coughing, breathing, your character does is done well and the sounds of the floor creaking is one of my favorite horror game sounds. Just adds the illusion of tension especially in a game about sound attracting the horror elements. - Story is great! Well okay so there's a lot of parts that are  fact a lot of it is, but the story itself is pretty neat and I was interesting in playing it all out. If it wasn't for the story, I honestly would've quit the game a long time ago. Cons- Horror is nonexistent here. I mean REALLY non-existent. I may be a bit hardened by the trauma of horror games, but this one is very predictable and the enemies don't really add tension to the horror elements. Evading them is simple enough, more tedious than anything else. I played it on normal and the only times I felt a little jumpy is when I turned the corner and there was someone I nearly ran into. - The puzzles are few & far and literally some of the worst/easiest puzzles ever. I know that sounds super harsh and I'm really sorry, BUT I'm like one of the worst people at solving puzzles or problems...or life problems, anyhow, there's moments where I'm not even sure why a "puzzle" exists. Maybe the game didn't intend for it to be a puzzle, but you know what it is if not a puzzle? A literal set of step by step directions to make a moment in the game tedious. Small spoiler for one puzzle, but if you couldn't get this...I don't know what to tell you. There's a point where there's three bells and a locked gate. There's a giant compass that literally points to the bell you are to ring in the right order. In plain view. There's no enemies around. You just do what the arrow tells you. That was met with a very heavy sigh. - I know in 2020 it's hard not to be derivative of other games, but this game borrows a LOT from the Resident Evil series in terms of minor plot devices, design, and light game mechanics. - Small complaint that may be my own fault, but in the beginning of the game, you use a little grate to traverse rooms. Later, you see more grates, but it appears you aren't able to use them? They're not damaged or anything, but then when a threat appears, they become available again? Inconsistent mechanics like that are a little annoying as my brain thinks "oh okay, can't do that anymore" and then out of necessity or by accident I try it again and notice it works. Seems odd. TLDR; (too late) overall, this game lacks any horror elements, is derivative of other games, is incredibly predictable, and isn't particularly challenging as a puzzle game or "stealth" horror evasion game. However, the story and voice acting are compelling and were enough to let me finish the game. Overall, I give this a very strong okay. I was real on the fence with this one, but the cons outweighed the pros (as you can see)

_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable and atmospheric game. Soundtrack and graphics are awesome, story isn't complex but ok for a horror game, the game mechanics are simple and fun. sound and voice acting are amazing. Has a lot of sneeking, which is in most cases very simple. The AI isn't broken, like some others wrote: you don't just have to walk slowly to not get heard. You have to crouch and sneek, then it's very easy to not get heard by them blind ememies. You can walk a metre behind them and they won't get it - this comes from a person who is not very patient with time wasting sneeking mechanics, that just want to lengthen your gaming time. As to expect, it doesn't come without a little backtracking inside of a house, but they never overdid it. Saving points are very fair in this one - don't let someone tell you about sneeking for 20 minutes without the possibility to save. All in all it's an easy game, if you stay concentrated and don't forget to hold your breath at the right - clearly visible - points, or to crouch-sneek. After finishing the game offers you four little challenges (to get an A - rank you have to make it in 15 minutes), in which you can fight the enemies and have to complete some goals. Also a nice alternation after the sneeking-stuff in the main game. I played it with controller, which worked very fine and without the Resident Evil-like clunkyness. All very smooth and enemies are not the RE-like bulletsponges. All in all very recommendable game.

_childDocuments_.review: Maid of Sker is a first-person horror game taking place on a remote island off the Welsh coast. You play as Thomas Evans, and are tasked by his lover, Elizabeth Williams, to travel to the hotel located on the island and rescue her from her family who are holding her captive. Despite having a Victorian setting, it's very much a fantasy world, with the hotels inhabitants becoming shells of what they once were. They are now twisted monsters who lack the ability to see, meaning they rely on sound to navigate their surroundings. Because of this, stealth is the game's main focus.Story-wise, it's interesting to say the least. I really enjoyed delving into the worldbuilding, and I greatly appreciated how well it ties with the main story. As far as the main narrative is concerned, however, it's just okay. It's fairly predictable, I pretty much had it figured out about an hour in, but it's still entertaining.The visuals are what impressed me the most. The environments look stunning, especially the opening area. The atmosphere isn't always there though, and this is where the game begins to completely fall apart. Maid of Sker is not a scary game. Barely even remotely, and this becomes apparent when you meet the enemies for the first time.  Every single encounter you have with an enemy goes nearly the exact same way. Crouch around them, hold your breath if they get too close, then continue moving away. The game makes barely any effort to deviate from this. What you experience the first time you meet them is what you'll essentially get for the rest of the game. It's a shame because, conceptually, Maid of Sker has a lot of merit. It just fumbles the ball on its execution.If you would like to see a slightly more detailed version of this review, as well as reviews for other free to play indie games, be sure to check out my video for them here:

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun horror game for those who enjoy the genre! The story is interesting, the atmosphere very well done, and everything was just very pretty! (Minus the dead bodies and gore, of course)I played through on the normal difficulty which honestly was probably the best choice for a first playthrough. The enemies have a predictable reaction to most things (which I imagine scales with difficulty) so once you get an idea how they work, it becomes quite easy to navigate around them (be that a good thing or bad thing is up to you). The manual save feature is a bit tedious, but being that the map shows where the save rooms are, it isn't too hard to finagle your way over. (However, actually remembering to save after you've done 45 minutes worth of progress is another story lmao)I think my biggest complaint is being that the monsters are sound based and are ABSOLUTELY EVERYWHERE, you basically spend the whole game crouching. Thomas' poor knees!! And for some reason, just the act of standing makes them freak out. They can't hear you open and close this huge creaking metal door, but they can hear your clothes rustle as you teabag four rooms over. I can only imagine how that works at the higher difficulties. All that considered, though, the game is still very enjoyable as a horror experience. Especially with Abraham and his sick techno beat footsteps.

_childDocuments_.review: Very weak horror game, story is kind of ok.The horror game consists of stealth and only stealth, which is funnily enough can be solved by simply running through "scary" monsters. Literally it is just you memorising their movement patterns and then crawling through an expected-to-be free pathway. All of that is to find audio recordings of the story or get phone calls from a person in-trouble. No other methods to communicate the story were used. The setting is a house, four medium-sized floors and one garden. You run through the same corridors because you found some key that unlocks something on the first floor. In the corridors there are monsters, through which you need to use stealth. Despite there being maybe 40 monsters, you remember the monster-you-are-about-to-meet movement. For those who like puzzles, there are none, as long as you can solve lever -> door mechanic. Maybe other cool mechanics? No. There are only three mechanics: pull levers (through stealth) to activate doors, insert a key in the door, and one cool thing in the end that lasted maybe 7 minutes. If you remember the first horror games ever created, where the mechanic was "find 10 items to escape", here is absolutely the same thing. A very absurd thing is that in the end, there is a minigame, where you run with guns (which are not in the main game), kill all monsters and then escape. The gun mechanic is atrocious, which may be why it wasn't added, but the fact that they had an idea on how to improve it but decided to make the never-ending non-scary stealth is fascinating.The story. It is weird. The origin of the horrific story was interesting, but how it continued seemed a bit underdeveloped. Imagine if Harry Potter franchise went like "there was once a boy, who secretly was a wizard, but didn't know about it, and then Hagrid came and they all lived happily. the end". There is no "Hogwarts" in the game.Atmosphere is very weak. I mean, graphics are great, but the eeriness is manifested solely through (1) disorganised non-bloody non-absurd non-scary furniture (2) the same type of monster appearing a billion times. So, you know, you stare at a (relatively) very highly detailed candle, but get no sense of fear at all. The only scary part was not to die, just because the saving was a long time ago.Finally, the ending. It was kind of ok too, the main character is given a choice. The twist could be hypothesised throughout the game, but at the end it became apparent when the main character is given a choice, and to unlock one unexpected choice, the main character needs to do something. Very not suspicious. The ending is just a video, whose content was nothing but ok. There was no "wow" effect. So overall a very weak game. I wanted to close it at the start but decided to give it another chance just because it became just a bit more interesting. Yet, there was nothing worth playing. Conceptually, the game was a good try, but to be frank, who wants to stealth through same graphics and same calculable monsters for 8 hours without proper mechanics or just even a story. For the price of 25 euros it is just absurd. The game definitely caught much attention from graphic designers, programmers, I don't know, but the product just turned out to be unsatisfactorily. Price-wise it seems like the game wishes to position itself along other games like RE, outlast, the evil within, etc, but really comes on the shelf of "find 10 items to escape Slenderman".

The enemy behavior is largely the same throughout the entire game. They path around incredibly slowly and consistently block doors and pathways you need to take. _childDocuments_.review: As an avid horror game fan, I initially received this as a gift from someone else. Admittedly I was confusing this game with another that was released at roughly the same time and my expectations were completely bare when I realised the difference.Overall, I'd say the game does a fairly good job at presenting a Resident-Evil style mixture between Puzzles and Horror - the story is interesting, though fairly simple - but easy to follow. The environments despite being hinged around a single relative environment are fairly diverse but not too dense to be confusing (as aided by a map). Further, the level design itself is fairly high class.However - to the horror.(as a preamble) - I define Horror and Terror as two separate intents for delivering a scary 'thing' - you can consider a jumpscare to be an element of 'terror' in that it was not expected, delivers its payload of scary and then the 'terror' wears off immediately after. While 'horror' I value as the FEELING that a jumpscare could appear at any point, or an enemy or something - but in fact it never does.Both are critical in scary video games, terror keeps you on your toes and horror holds you there until you take a risk. Some games that apply these well include Alien: Isolation, Amnesia: The Dark Descent and so on.Some games only apply 'terror' in the hopes that it generates 'horror' without the extra effort - Layers of Fear, Five Nights at Freddies, etc.For Maid of Sker, both are utilised fairly well and with enough creativity that the jumpscares are the reward for the work of terror and the horror is represented in the purposefully slow trudging around the levels clutched mouth as the enemies walk mere inches away from your face and you're aware the screen is getting darker and darker.In that regard, Maid of Sker is already recommendable for making the effort to use both Horror and Terror. It's only failing for me (and this will not be the case in general I wager) - is that the game looks and feels small (though polished in that regard). This means that the enemies lack a lot of variety in functionality and simply become something to chase you down (endlessly until you run to a save room or vent) and beat you with the 'ol one-two punches. Further the 'combat' isn't combat as I had anticipated reading the tooltips about 'ammo' but instead a single ball with limited ammo that 'indeterminably' delays the enemies from giving chase. It does a good job of making the hotel a combination of 'Escape-Room' scenarios with enemies patrolling the area enough to prevent people from simply running around and ignoring the horror, but the enemies otherwise pose no real threat or creativity to be threatening after the first encounter. I look forward to the next game from Wales Interactive, because as far as a 'scary game' goes. This ticked a lot of boxes that studios with 4x the budget and experience fail to get.

_childDocuments_.review: "Maid of Sker is the perfect game for anyone who's ever wanted to spend hours wandering around a spooky mansion, getting lost in endless hallways, and being scared out of their mind by creepy music.The game takes place in a haunted hotel where the staff has been replaced by killer mannequins, which is probably not a great sign for the hotel's Yelp reviews. Your job is to explore the hotel, solve puzzles, and try not to become the next victim of the deadly mannequins.The game's sound design is especially impressive, with chilling music and realistic sound effects that will make you feel like you're really in a haunted hotel. I had to turn off the game several times because I was convinced that someone was knocking on my door or whispering my name.But the real highlight of Maid of Sker is the maid herself. She's the star of the game and the reason why I kept playing even when I was scared out of my mind. Her delightful accent and charming personality made me forget about the killer mannequins for a few precious moments – until they started chasing me again.Overall, Maid of Sker is a great game for anyone who loves a good scare, a good puzzle, or a good maid. Just be prepared to sleep with the lights on for a few nights afterward."
