_childDocuments_.review: If one of those “games like XCOM” videos lead you to this game, don’t get it just play XCOM 2 or Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within. At least those games try to be subtle about the “get bent” situations you may find yourself in. First, some things this game gets right. The equipment the player can obtain looks really cool. The Phoenix weapons and armor specifically strike a nice balance of sci-fi and believable practically that’s over all visually pleasing. I like how the player has the option to bring in vehicles to combat missions, though this is not without flaws. Now, the negatives. You are not allowed to roll over the small-medium sized enemies with your ground vehicles. If you try to, the game will either grey out the path you are trying to take, or it will redirect you through some trees and concrete barriers to go around the enemy. Why is it not an option to plow over enemies with the vehicle at the cost of vehicle health? Balancing reasons I assume, but at that point why bother having these vehicles in combat in the first place. The ideologies of the factions make no sense. Synedrion’s approach is most absurd, “we’re faced with a natural force that is actively hunting humanity to extinction, so let’s try to find a way to coexist with it” .... what? Imagine this happening with the Flood in Halo, if the UNSC and The Covenant instead of joining forces to exterminate the threat, just sent The Arbiter and Johnson to The Gravemind to say “Can’t we all just get along?” Then there’s the Disciples of Anu, they seem to think that if they convert themselves into Pandoran-Human hybrids the encroaching threat will leave them alone. Even though this is clearly not the case because the Pandorans continue to attack and destroy Anu havens. New Jericho makes the most sense, but given their competition this isn’t saying much. Jericho rallied behind a resolute commander to fight back against the Pandoran threat. How do they do this? Well, they created a special unit you see, a unit with big mechanical arms… that… is a healer. It goes around, applying med kits to wounded soldiers and and repair kits for soldiers with augments. A faction whose goal is to beat back an enemy force with military might had a healer for a special unit instead of say, oh I don’t know, tanks?! Or even a flame thrower unit makes more sense. I know this doesn't affect the game play that much, but it is difficult to get invested in the story when your "allies" are not very smart.The UI is overall a mess. When in the manufacturing tab, sometimes the class filters for items won’t change colors to indicate whether that filter is active or not. Also, when scrolling to view the items to craft it won’t show the bottom 2 slots until you scroll ~3/4 of the way down, then they will re-appear. The sight line indicator for when previewing a soldier’s movement can sometimes be a lie. Move to a square to get an angle on an enemy only to make the move and not be able to target said enemy. This is partially an issue with Snipers and Heavies, since they have limited movement they can execute before they lose the ability to take a shot that round. Speaking of shots, once Pandorans get their guns, your soldiers are basically done. Even if they do not die, it only takes one bullet of the six round burst to incapacitate one of your soldier’s arms, making them unable to use their rifles. To add insult to injury, enemies simply DO NOT MISS. Half cover, full cover, does not matter, your soldier is taking damage along with a bleed or a disabled limb, generally both in my experience. It does not help there seems to be no way to increase the accuracy of your soldiers outside of getting closer. There are perks and helmets that give “+perception” and “+accuracy” but these boosts do not translate clearly into the gameplay (assuming they actually affect anything and are not bugged). Unless your soldier is in an adjacent tile to whatever they are shooting at, the percentage to hit does not seem to rise above 40%.The operative extraction and objective defense missions are the ultimate “get bent” to the player. Both are pretty straight forward: go in, escort target out, or defend structures from enemy attacks. The catch is you will spawn 2-3 turns away from the already active enemies. So, by the time you do get to where the action is, your objective is either already dead or is about to die. For example, a mission where you need to clear out a base with Pandorans inside and keep structural integrity from hitting zero. You load in and the enemies already have the key structures surrounded. Those 2-3 turns to get to the enemies is enough to allow the enemies to attack and destroy as much upwards of 90% of all structural integrity. My worst case of this was when I had 11% left by the time my soldiers saw the first enemies, and the slowest unit had 17/20 speed. The final straw that broke the camel's back for me was this last extraction mission. I was tasked by an independent haven to find and escort a VIP out of a Disciple of Anu haven. Again, my soldiers spawn 2-3 turns away from being able to engage the enemy. Meanwhile the VIP is already active, surrounded by 6 soldiers, unable to defend himself, and with nowhere to hide. Mind you this was the third mission of a fresh play through. I cannot tell whether this is intentional or was an over site during development that never got fixed. This is not just a small issue, these rescue missions given to you by factions can determine how your relationship with said faction develops. If the VIP dies, the relationship can sour, causing that faction to hate you and not trade resources or research with you. These faction relationships can also influence which ending you get from what I understand. Meaning, you have a chance to get locked out of one of the potential ending to the game because of an unlucky (or potentially bugged) designed mission.In summary, this game gives off the impression of not being finished and will never get finished. It has an interesting premise for a story but fails to make it compelling in the beginning. The Epic Games store should have kept this for itself.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game - it's got a lot going for it. But I just can't.It's got depth, a sort of less RNG physical bullet system which allows you to sometimes pull off some cool shots in manual fire mode where, say, XCom would just say "nah, you don't have line of sight" (while you clearly do), and the body part targeting is great.However, it is also still insanely crash prone, after all these years - it's absolutely infuriating when after the hardest of missions it simply decides to crash while loading back into the geoscape. Almost as infuriating are the sometimes quite BS ways your team gets sniped from across the map, or some of the very tedious, endlessly repeated missions - looking at you, Legacy of the Ancients missions (I kinda gave up on getting those weapons just because I couldn't stand to do another one of those maps, not because they're hard, but because they're a black hole sucking out all of the fun). Speaking of repetitiveness, a lot of the depth turns out to be bloat: 90% of research is somewhat useless, as are a lot of the weapons. The classes on the other hand are just flat undercooked and bland, each having only one line of skill with the only choice in there being what secondary class you choose (which is fun, but doesn't quite make up for the lack of options). Most of the skills in those trees are also pretty meh, with a few others that are absolutely gamebreaking. Oh, and the maps are relatively small if you're used to other games, which is both disappointing and also not the worst thing, as moving in this game is generally very slow.So, as someone who enjoys a bit of self-flagellation, I will try to get through the game - it's not NOT entertaining when it's good. But I can't in good conscience give a flat recommendation. It's still too undercooked, poorly balanced, and crash prone to be fun for everyone. If you're like me, and it's on sale, go for it. But only if you've already played through XCom or Chaos Gate.

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Point has a bunch of great ideas, but there is two major problems with the game. Both if which are relates to the enemy turns in the game.  The performance during those turns is slow, it drags the game to a crawl especially on maps with high enemy density.  There needs to be a fast forward option of some sort, because it sucks taking all your units turns in two minutes and then waiting 10 while the enemy goes.  The other problem with this is you can't do anything during that time, you can ESC and load up a save or anything else.  If a mission goes terribly wrong and I want to reload my game, i should have to wait for 14 enemy units to take 45 seconds each to move to be able to access a menu. Also the game needs some serious optimization, I run an i7 with a 3090 and 32GB of ram and there are times this game stutters, again on enemy turns mostly.  The other minor pet peeve I have is with the UI layout.  Over the top of your action buttons is a place where the UI puts enemies spoted, and if your mousing over that to get to the buttons you get moved to where the enemy is and have to scroll back, it's really weird and inconvenient place to put that. If you can get past those things, the rest of the game is pretty solid, if they cleaned those issues up it would be near the top of the genre.  Right now after putting 30+ hours into the complete version (plus time in early builds as a KS backer)  I'd be hopeful for a Phoenix Point 2, but I probably won't slog through this much more.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated Review @ 297 hours of game playMy early initial feeling of being transported back almost 30 years to the original X-Com was pretty close.  Phoenix Point is what I had hoped the X-Com reboot would be.  It was a rare combination of nostalgia and new at the same time.  Game play felt extremely familiar, but in a good way, not the feeling of 'this again?’  There are enough new gameplay elements to prevent it from seeming like you have already played the game, and the story is only similar on the surface.The one part of the original X-Com that I missed, UFO interception, is already planned for the next DLC (which is free).Even at normal/standard game play level, the game is challenging (sometimes boarding on frustrating).  It took multiple play troughs in order for me to win a game.  And unless you like restarting battles and having lots of saves, expect to lose people.  Much like the original X-Com, it takes very little to cause the death of your troops.  If you hate troop loss this is probably not the game for you.Review @ 4.3 hours of game playThis game feels much more like the successor of the original X-COM series than the X-COM reboot.  I still have not experienced much of the game but what I have is good.  If you are a fan of the original X-COM (from the 90's) then chances are that you will like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you ever get annoyed while playing X-COM then take a break and play this for a few hours. Nothing will make you happier with all X-COM's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like this game. It's almost a meditative experience looking at a blank wall or miscellaneous object that you should be able to shoot around but find that you cannot while you contemplate the merits of re installing X-COM. The anger of missing a 98% chance hit in X-COM evaporates when your PP Character on overwatch simply ignores movement in its sight. You almost miss the stun batons, and Chryssalids when you watch these weird water creatures beat your character senseless even though you watched it move and it attacked three times already. The overly large maps of X-COM don't seem so bad when your running through the same exact map for the tenth time and again spawn on the opposite end of a wall that you cannot climb, blow up, or get around without expending three turns.In all seriousness Phoenix point isn't a bad game. I want to like it more than I do. I'm not particularly good at these games, though I love them for some reason. This game however makes itself hard to love. It doesn't work, at its core. Yeah we all missed a 98% shot before but you would never need to twist X-COM's arm into working. I feel like 90% of PP is just getting ♥♥♥♥ to work. Placing characters in good defensive positions isn't enough, you need to make sure that these defensive positions also work with the leaning around corners, overwatch, and explosives, and because the game is jank it never does. Its a miracle when your sniper you set up to provide cover fire can see and take shots, its a miracle when you can move fluidly through a stage and not get angry at a door closing lines of sight, or wondering why the enemy just doesn't take any damage that round.I got this game through humble bundle and I am glad I didn't spend more than a few dollars on it when the dlc went on sale. I think if you like X-COM but are like me and either want more, or something different you probably will like the game to an extent. How much you like the game really will boil down to how much your willing to finagle with the mechanics. Some people have a ton more patience for stuff like this than me. Some people will tell you if you play a certain way you don't have to worry as much. For my part I think a game's core mechanic should function most of the time. I mean you might make fun of Bethesda games for being buggy but I guarantee you don't complain that dust particles or firefly's block your sword swings. I hope if you decide to give this game a shot you like it. I don't want to overly dissuade anyone really. Its not so bad it cannot be played or likely beaten, its just...X-COM exists, and if you had to put time and money into a game why not get the good one.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I get into the detailed reasons why I’m going to answer the three most important questions I have when buying a game. Q: Should you buy this game? A: Yes. Q: Is it worth the money? Yes especially if you buy it now while it’s discounted on steam. Q: Will you still be playing it a few years from now? A: Yes I’m pretty sure I will as it has a lot of  replayability built into it. Now to the details. I was one of the game’s original backers, but I opted to wait until the steam release when it went Epic exclusive (yes I was pretty annoyed about it at the time) and so it’s pretty much a brand new game from my perspective. Nearly 50 hours in and I have not encountered a single bug either major or minor and it seems completely stable at least on my system. The graphics are not as pretty and the production values not as high as its nearest direct comparison XCOM2, but it does a lot of things that game failed to do. I’ve heard the bullet mechanics described by one streamer as “gimmicky” but actually I think they work really well. Shoot your enemies from behind walls & destroy buildings and cover with your heavies. Target specific body parts and more. No more misses at point blank range as most of the time you are almost guaranteed at least a partial hit with a spray of bullets. Overall the combat feels quite meaty as opposed to the cartoonish feel of XCOM2. It also has quite a deep back story too with a whole range of novellas tied to the main storyline. Essentially the game a big sandbox with a lot of randomization in terms of starting points and the resources available to you so every time you start a new game you will have a slightly different experience.  I love the way that the game allows you to pursue so many different strategies and paths to victory, giving you maximum versatility in how develop your troops. Right now the biggest issues remaining from my point of view are the uneven jumps in difficulty during the campaign and some minor balancing issues that still need to be resolved. Still to those sitting on the fence I would definitely say buy it, no ifs or buts.

_childDocuments_.review: First; TL, DR. I've played every tactical TBS on the market since OG X-COM. I love the suspense of the unknown, technological advancements that turn your early cannon fodder into BA killing machines, and I love sci-fi lore when it comes from a place of fantasy while remaining believable. This game has all of that. What I really like the most is that it has a more old school feel than XCOM 2 while simultaneously implementing some very sweet QoL improvements to the the same feeling combat system, such as return fire, getting rid of the percentage to hit dice rolls, and the new scope perspective is just great. It really pulls you in to a much more immersive understanding of what the aliens are like, face to face.Graphically I have absolutely nothing bad to say. The Geoscape, tactical maps, character models and special effects really are satisfying to the eyes. Especially if you're running a decent machine, I really think the optimization is spot on for more updated machines. I've yet to encounter a bug or crash.Sound may be my only complaint but it gets the job done. Some of the voice over talent really had me shaking my head. The music is dark and occasionally suspenseful enough to draw your into that zone of concern and excitement. Weapons sound typical for the genre. The story, lore, and characters are all very interesting to me, but again, I'm a sucker for that type of thing. I really enjoyed the way lore research is backed up with some very high quality artwork and cut scenes. I don't do spoilers so you'll just have to see for yourself.Lastly, there is just enough customization of your troops to give you meaningful decisions to make regarding their specialization. It's really worth it to plan ahead when making these types of selections and the game doesn't really give you enough information or explanation as to what some of the quirks actually will work like in the field. Live and learn though, most of the quirks are game changing, but never game breaking.I have not played this game prior to it's release on Steam and I got it at the introduction price,  $30 USD. It's been well worth it so far and I'm really looking forward to continuing my experience with Phoenix Point. Don't listen to the fan boy crying babies that don't actually provide you with a helpful review. It's an excellent game and you'll surely enjoy it too.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not want to give this a thumbs down for the brilliant innovations it brings but... oh boy... it is not a smooth ride.The highlights:->This game has the best concept/implementation for "aiming" in a turn-based game that I have seen. Every weapon you want to fire shows you a "crosshair" that consists of two concentric circles (instead of a to-hit-chance) and all shots (if there are more than one, with a shotgun in particular) land within the outermost circle and >50% land within the inner circle. The closer you are the more of an enemy is within the circle(s). Different weapons have differently sized circles (sniper rifles have very small ones, of course). Line of sight and positioning are paramount. This works extremely well.->This game has an excellent overwatch system. You can define a 3D cone (starting at your soldiers weapon) in which your soldier will activate overwatch. This sounds simple but you can set up the cone in such a way that they shoot after the enemy leaves cover (among other things) which also works really well.Aside from its brilliant aspects it just has all-around solid game design in some areas (those that can be implemented on a budget):-> The strategic layer is quite interesting and works very well even for people who are new to a geoscape. The flow in the strategic layer is very nicely balanced.-> The game is quite good at gripping you to go for one more technology or one more mission.That being said, aside from a nasty bug (reloading the game in an alien environment/base means the game thinks all your soldiers have used all of their skills already) there are so many problems with this game...-> The main point: the game uses WAY to much randomness. Example: you finish a mission and get the second mission in that sub-story line - the problem is that the position of this second mission on the globe is almost completely random and not related to its predecessor. Which means it can take you forever to get there (>10 hours of real time, you are limited by the range of your planes and the number of your bases) and by then you have forgotten why you even wanted to be there. This is true for basically all of the story missions. It would have been a vastly superior experience if the campaign was set-up to work properly and afterwards, you get random placements if you want to play the game again (knowing what all the missions actually mean and so on.).-> The missions are VERY similar. There are different mission types but once you are able to reliably win a certain type of mission they are just a bother (the enemies get stronger but that is inconsequential). This means the game takes about 35 hours longer than it should (depending on the difficulty).-> You can hardly control which technologies you get. Almost everything is locked behind loyalty levels at the factions AND depends on them researching what you want (there are two ways to mitigate the first point but not the second). Connected to this: you have almost no control over which faction you gain loyalty with - this is connected to random missions and is not a choice made by the player.-> There is a massive list of weapons and armor and no way to easily compare them.-> Most weapons are outperformed by others and whole weapon classes are useless (in comparison).-> Practically all armor items are useless.-> You are told how far an enemy can move but there is no visual indicator so you need to count squares for some enemies you cannot kill fast enough (at least up until mid-game).-> There is no reliable way to play defensively. You need to be hyper aggressive (for a game of this kind), which is a major reason armor is useless.-> The story is ok (the short stories that were published as e-books are excellent) but later on complete nonsense happens so that the game state changes.-> They use mechanics implemented by/for XCOM and some work well while others do not. The camera jumps around after you move a soldier without being prompted to do so. If you aim, the camera jumps to a third person view (mentioned above as a strength) centered on the soldiers which makes it quite hard to see which enemie you are looking at. You cannot opt out of this if you just want to shoot a trivial shot that needs no manual aiming.-> There is no option to skip animations altogether so you need to watch you soldiers sprint around a lot.-> Overwatch quickly becomes obsolete. Aiming becomes obsolete 15 hours later. After that, combat is completely trivial/tedious and the main innovations of the game are irrelevant.-> Most of the interesting technologies become available when the game is already in a state where the player has won.-> During missions, you cannot see which temporary buffs/debuffs are active for each of your soldiers - and there are quite a few of those effects. You are shown tiny symbols for each effect but you cannot see what those mean and not all of them are self-explanatory (the debuffs caused by the enemies in particular).There is LOTS more to say about the game both pros and cons but I think you get the gist. Play it if you want to see the work of one of the best game designers in gaming-history who had too small of a budget and too few people on his level to talk to during development. For me, Phoenix Point is good enough but barely so.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not X-Com, this is what x-com could have been. Depending on DLC the game loop differs somewhat. I for one don’t like Festering Skies, I didn’t like air fight or submarine fights in the old xcom games, and I don’t like air fights in festering skies. The world map is good with a lot of interesting side missions, places to explore and bases to build. It can feel a bit overwhelming at first. You will alter between building bases, level up troops, doing research, defending fraction bases, defend you bases, gather resources, doing missions and attack hives.Missions are divided between kill, gather, and protect, with random mobs that gets harder after a while. Some might feel that the game gets too hard in late-game, but by then you should know the different classes strength so there is no big problem on normal. Yes some bosses can be hard, but if you have the Ancient DLC your new weapons will tip the scale, no problem. With the possibility to augment you soldiers whit tec or mutations you can create new good squads very fast so there is no problem if one of your soldiers die, even if I hate when they do.  To manage your squads and bases you need resources and most of them you can get easy from buying and selling with other fractions. There is only really one type of resources that is a bit hard to get and that is the one for building ancient weapons. Well it is not hard, but it is a RNG where they spawn.The different fractions you can support and to replay ability, thou synedrion is the best from my position, and there infiltrator class with spider drones is a given in any group. And yes you can mix different classes to create super soldiers. If you are new to the game google some tips on what class to mix.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Point

_childDocuments_.review: I love the idea of this game, but I already have some concerns regarding simple things that become big problems. First, I have had 3 crashes on the same mission. This wouldn't be so bad but the load times for this game seems to be excessive to say the least. In the same mission I discovered that the soldiers don't change facing even when they are in overwatch. That doesn't seem to be a big deal...however, my most experienced soldier was attacked from behind two turns in a row through her overwatch cone. This after she spent the whole time on her turn "bashing" her original attacker...who was behind her; she never turned around! So on the second turn she got attacked from behind again even though it was through her overwatch cone! There should be a way to "face" the soldiers, but it doesn't seem to exist. Seemingly simple problems (and just as simple solutions) that cause a great deal of frustration. This needs some reworking. I can't recommend this game right now.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Point

_childDocuments_.review: It is a exceptionally good turn-based strategy game with one unpleasant flaw: even the early game could turn into a quick massacre of your squad as there is no real strategy against such an overpower where each enemy has 3 times more hit/shield points (some of them has 10x more), and your team is already outnumbered by 5 to 1 anyway. you will be on the edge of the seat by simply focusing on evacuating the squad alive from turn 0, without having a slim chance to complete the current mission and save humanity.so, this game is really not for the faint-hearted gamers, you really need to be sharp all the time while playing it and you will find yourself more focused to achieve victory than you'd do in your real life, so basically when you finish gaming for the day, you will be relieved that your current life in the middle of a real pandemic is less stressful than this game.totally recommend as it gives you a new perspective of appreciating little successes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best tactic game at the moment.It wasn’t love at first sight. Quite to the contrary – accustomed to the glamor and glitter of X-Com 2, at first I was disappointed year ago and regretted that I donated (initially it looked worse than now). But I gave the game a chance – and that was the best I could do.The game revealed itself gradually. Every difference from X-Com 2 was a revelation. The most serious Sci-fi story. Independent factions with their own havens to build relationships with. Many classes, but not only that - the ability to combine them, so that you can create anyone, even a berserk-sniper. An unprecedented variety of enemies. Realistic ballistics and a very complex firing system - each bullet does its own damage. Destructability of everything - if you wish, you can raze the entire map to the ground. The ability to disable the enemy as you wish – there’s no necessity to kill him. Tons of weapons with any damaging factor. Transport. Battle beasts. Mutations! Augmentation! ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ FLAMETHROWER!!! I haven’t never seen anything similar. The king of tactics and X-Com 3 was hiding behind an unprepossessing signboard. After playing Phoenix Point, I tried to play X-Com 2 and was surprised - it was so boring. It was like missing a lot of vital things that I'm already accustomed in Phoenix Point. And if you also consider that the next DLC will contain air battles...Several responses to particularly frequently encountered points of criticism."Raw game". I don't even quite understand what that means. However, I must say that the game is more "baked" than X-Com 2 has ever been: there is not even a part in it of the features that Phoenix have."Bugs". I do not know in what mode and for how long the game was tested by those who say about "a tons of bugs". In 260 hours of playing, I saw 3 bugs that have already been fixed."The game does not have that one, the other, the third...". All who say so forget one (the most important thing) - this is not an AAA class game, but INDY. Created with donations. However, such criticism is even good – It shows that the game is perceived as AAA.So, Phoenix Point has set new standards for tactical games and is the undisputed leader in the genre today.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Point

_childDocuments_.review: To call it a X-COM re-skin does not do it justice. Yes this game is headed by the same people, and those that play X-COM will feel right at home with its tactics and sight, having an easy transition over because of many of the mirrored styles and mechanics, but this game manages to grow from X-COM in such a innovative and interesting way with improved mechanics that feel way more immersive (the way weapons/armor are stocked and the free aim feature). It's what the new Star Wars Trilogy should've been, nice and familiar, with enough new content to not seem like its trying to rip off its predecessors.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Point

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game but I can't recommend it until they fix a few things that make the game incredibly frustrating to play. As many other reviewers have said the enemy turns take ages. During the several minute enemy turns you can not pause, or access the menu. You can lose the mission and still have to wait 20 minutes to do anything at all. You can spend several minutes looking at nothing while enemies you may never actually see do things that you will never know about. and that's every single turn. EVERY SINGLE TURN! All of the things I love about this game fall out the window when I find myself Alt-F4ing out of the game because I've gotten tired of waiting forever to take my 30 second turn. The Balancing is also terrible. You can spawn with a creature that spawns 6 bad guys every turn and one of those bad guys can be a bad guy that spawns 6 bad guys every turn. What?! The real aiming combat is a great advancement over x-com but don't be fooled into thinking it will eliminate point blank misses, if so much as a pixel of your reticle falls outside of the hit box there s a 99.9% chance you are missing that shot. I enjoy this game 95% of the time but 5% of the game is so painful I'd say, wait until it's patched.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is taken from a point of view of someone who recently bought the game (April 2021) and from someone looking for something to scratch the XCom itch.Like XCom, the game consists of both a strategic layer - or Geoscape - and the tactical layer. I will cover both and then mention some overall game play elements.The strategic game is, in my opinion, superior to the recent XCom reboots in every way. It is not simply and random RNG excuse for supplies or a few story mission placements but there is actual game play value in the layer. Later in the game, it can take a bit of getting used to since so many things are going on, but I feel the game did a very good job on this aspect of the game.The tactical layer, however, is where the game finds itself lacking a bit. First off, the maps are very limited and not randomly generated. As the game is much longer than an XCom play through, this can make things a bit tedious and feeling representative as you go through the missions. I do like that the aliens are spread over the map, active since the beginning of the mission and not sitting around in 'pods' waiting for you to discover and pick apart at your whim.Overall though, the game lacks any kind of progression curve like you find in XCom. Most of the research is rather useless and makes no sense for many items (why do I need to research an alien to unlock shotguns in the year 2047?). Furthermore, there really is no progression tech wise. Most weapons are similar in the game with slight variation in their stats (one offers higher damage and range, while one may offer lower damage, shorter range and armor penetration but neither is necessarily better than the other). The lack of progression in weapons is rather peculiar considering all the aliens in the game have a progression as the game goes on (most aliens progressing through five levels). This does keep the game a challenge throughout, but I feel they could have had some kind of progression to at least keep up with the alien progression throughout the game.I do like that the game has a bit more complexity than XCom but some of it is there for the sake of being there. For example, in 2021, there is really no need in a tactical game of soldiers to have to manage ammo inventory. It adds nothing to the game and is nothing more than a tedious step for the sake of being there. In a RPG fine, but not a game where you are managing 12-24 soldiers.To conclude, the game does offer an alternative XCom experience, though with many enough difference you should not play like XCom. Is the game bad? No. Like all games, including XCom, it has it's places it does well and others that could use improvement and therefore, if what I mentioned above would be okay with you in a game, than I would recommend purchasing it.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game itself is ok, the amount of  micromanagment sucks. Every few minutes you have to go over your entire list of soldiers and choose their next skills. Every hour or so you need to redo their equipment. If you deploy one soldier to the wrong base, screw you, because now you need to manually send a taxi to pick them up and move them around. Tactical mode is a repetitive and biring drag which can't be turned off or set to auto-battle.And because it's like XCOM, they absolutely had to put in a whopping 80% miss chance on air fights. Who designs games like that??The game balancing is horrible. Having a backlog of 20 research projects, and one dozen soldiers without any equipment is apparently completely normal. Events progress at light speed while your own research and production is as slow as a snail. Recruitment is faster than research and both are faster than production, which leads to ridiculous situations like above.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Point

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just like the original XCOM from 1994 - Ambitious, complex, with fascinating new mechanics and fresh ideas. And just like the original XCOM it is a buggy, half-finished mess. Its UI is cluttered and poorly designed, its gameplay requires careful tedious control and constant fiddling to behave correctly, and its enemies are extremely challenging, often cheating outright to present a strong enough challenge. There is little story, little polish, and few efforts put towards the player's QoL. The buggy tedium outweighs how much potential is still locked up in this game. It starts strong, and becomes stagnant quickly - likely to be a game you play some but never finish. But it sure is fascinating to see so many cool ideas brought together almost 30 years later, iterating on XCOM. Can't wait for a 2K and Firaxis remake.

_childDocuments_.review: For me, the enemies progress too much too quickly, and your soldiers reach a plateau in development pretty fast, leaving your soldiers emptying magazines to humungus mind-controlling, smoke-producing beasts who will look at them with contempt before crushing them in two turns. The soldiers need means to develop more.Second, the resource management is bad, like the trading mechanics are work and you never get nearly enough of them, like just replenish those hard earned magazines will deplete your treasury like a corrupt government.Please make those vehicles more useful, either reload, more ammo or less space in the aircraft.Tech is hard to acquire and is not good enough to fight high level monsters. Like cavemen fighting SWATS.Those things enter your base like taking a walk to the park, and they come back over and over for a second round! Is like Like Ezra Miller going to Hawaii! Why not make some form of self defense for the base? Or some stationary soldiers or something.Finally, the factions hate each other and do nothing but attacking each other, how about you could influence that?So basically the disparity between your progress and enemy progress is huge.A mod has helped with that but please fix the game difficulty, it could be a great game! It just needs a bit of tuning.

_childDocuments_.review: Early backer, glad it is finally on Steam after one year. It is an OK game with tactic innovation, but overall it does not come anywhere close to XCOM 2 or WOTC. Cons:Graphics and music are inferior. Soldier customization option is even less than XCOM 1. Strategy side is far less interesting. Story is also boring, despite a great background.Soldier perks are few, so tactic options are far limited than XCOM.Tactic maps are roughly 1/4 of XCOM 2 maps......bland and less diversity.And most importantly no mod & workshop support yet to enrich the game. This is a huge letdown, I keep on going back to XCOM 2 largely bc of the mods (LWOTC).Pro:That said, the most refreshing part of the game is the tactic system. Free aiming, better overwatch, more realistic cover system. (This complex system is fun but paced really slow, I guess that is why PP's map is so small)Overall:IMO this game still worth play or grab at a discounted price.But don't expect the same replayability or game immersion like XCOM 2.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Good foundation. Mostly lacking in content and polish. Would recommend.I've played all of the reboot XCOMs extensively. I've also played a bit of the OGs, but I never completed them.Phoenix Point comes along as a kind of middle-ground between the old and the new. Where the new (reboot XCOM) focuses mainly on tactical combat with a brief strategy layer getting you between battles and old is mostly about having the right number of men with the right gear in the right place at the right time, Phoenix Point straddles a fine middle line. Whether or not it does so successfully is up to the player. In my opinion it does well enough.The good:The mediocre:Some criticisms:

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy this game. Greatly looking forward to it getting modding support, as I have quite a few tweaks in mind.Sure, it has some warts:- The UI could definitely do with some streamlining, such as separating weapons and consumables in the inventory sorting categories, and letting you manufacture medkits in the loadout screen even if you're in a base defense and you're fresh out of medkits; Currently you can only produce more of an item you already have at least 1 of in the squad you're bringing, unless you exit out of the loadout screen to enter the manufacturing screen. But doing that during a base defense mission results in instantly losing the base, so that's no bueno.- The Legacy of the Ancients DLC has both super overpowered enemies *and* super overpowered rewards that trivialize a lot of the endgame if you save scum your way through the overpowered enemies as early as possible.- There are some nasty bugs, such as being unable to use Overwatch after reloading a save, or certain localization keys showing instead of showing the actual localization.- Some balancing decisions make no sense. Why does a REPAIR KIT (No idea why its name is in ALL CAPS, but it is) cost more than 10 medkits when it heals for only half as much and only on augmented soldiers? Why are the ammo types for the spider drones, grenade launcher and rocket launcher so prohibitively expensive?- Pandoran Nests can get a bit stale in the end-game.But I still like the actual gameplay a whole lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Point

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people did not like XCOM: Apocalypse. I actually enjoyed it quite a lot. Why does that matter? Because I feel like this game was the unfinished business left over from XCOM: Apocalypse and then some. This game is pretty tough, and much like XCOM of old your first play through is going to be humbling. I definitely recommend turning off all the DLC and attempting just the vanilla game on your first couple of attempts to get the core mechanics down, otherwise you will be overwhelmed and frustrated. It doesn't have the replayability of the XCOM series but there is still plenty of ground to uncover before you'll be done. The mechanics are good. The combat is good if at times frustrating. The story isn't going to win awards but it is interesting enough to pay attention to it. One area I think it suffers a lot when compared to XCOM is in the research and weaponry. The focus is largely on tactics and less on growth; by growth I mean researching upgrades or improving tech. There is some of this, but nothing like there was/is in other games. "Upgrades" aren't really an upgrade but just another avenue of attack, or a hard counter to a specific tactic/creature. The growth applies to soliders as well. They will never be on the same footing as the enemy. The enemy is always stronger, faster, more skilled, etc etc etc. Veteran's have access to more skills and there are certainly ways to cheese them but they don't grow like XCOM soldiers did. They just unlock a skill... but never actually improve at anything. All being said though... this isn't XCOM. This is Phoenix Point and it is good. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Feel more like what XCOM should be than XCOM The lore is pretty interesting The gameplay is ho hum, not bad, its like a hotdog with the works Not a 5 star meal by any means, but can hit the spotThe music is forgettable and the voice acting is passableOverall, is it fun?YaNothing that will stand the test of time, I doubt you'll see a 10th anniversary edition down the line, but its funNot a game for zoomers who need their handheldThis game can be challenging, nothing that will tax you, when it comes to thinking up tactics or doing resource management, its akin to ramping up from a relaxed walk to a brisk power walkYou'll see reviews with people crying about your squad needing silly things like ammo and needing to reload *gasp*, or voting the game down because they didn't win a mission just by showing upYa, so if you want a game where you insta win after hitting new game, this ain't for youIf you like a light challenge and want to scratch that tactical squad combat itch, then give this a goHeres hoping for a sequel that ignores that haters

_childDocuments_.review: This game is essentially the original X-COM games, the ones that came back in the 90', this brings some things I wish stayed back in those days, like managing ammo for e v e r y s i n g l e g u nI am not kidding when I say that, there is no standardisation in this game, as much as I understand from a lore perspective, as you won't use the same ammo in a laser weapon as a magnetic rifle, and that's fine, but I do wish ammo was something you didn't have to build at all unless you didn't have the tech for it yet, maybe a one time purchase and you get infinite quantities of that ammo but you still have to take mags for missionsOne of the things that jumps out real quick from the reboot X-COM games is the aiming, yes, you actually have to *aim* you guns, line of sight and cover do a lot in this game, which I like and hate, if you miss, well, you should have taken a better position, which is good, flanking makes shotting at enemies easier, but it's also the game's biggest downfall, you can individually target bodyparts of your enemies, except a good chunk of the enemies simply have far too much health on their bodyparts or regenerate the limb (even if disabled, aka red) ON THE START OF THEIR TURN, not the END OF IT, this makes shooting at a good chunk of enemies not about disabling their most dangerous aspects, but more trying to kill them in one turn before they just shrug off that damage like it never existedThe factions feel... Fine, they are stupid, but they can hold their own half the time without your help, they might even attack enemy bases at times, though it seems really rare... And they feel different but are all so up their own ideology they don't even try to work together for anything, even when the situation is dire as all hellAnd the enemies are... Well, they are either made to make you suffer or to be fodder, there is no in between here, ♥♥♥♥ like mind control is plenty on some of the tankiest non-massive units (Multi-tile enemies) or just excessive pain afflicting, especially with some of the DLCAnd the biggest gripe I have with the game is just the lack of people you can use, like, your soldiers are not replaceable at all, and vehicles don't help much in that regard, for they take 3-4 slots in your dropships, like in the old X-COMs, but unlike the old X-COMs, your dropships don't have 14 spaces for people, so taking a vehicle is like halving your squad size for something either useless or dedicated to supporting your groupOh and the weapons aren't even all that different between the factions, it's still just "Synedrian assault rifle" and "New Jerico assault rifle" and it's just a flavour of scifi you wish to take, between lasers or mags respectivelyThough, even will all of this negative I put forward, this game DOES have a lot of potential, and it just doesn't use it to it's fullest and seems to be rushed a fair bit

_childDocuments_.review: --- At a glance ---Phoenix Point is very much the spiritual successor to the original (1994 – 1997) X-COM series that Julian Gollop set out to make. While it takes a few cues from the Firaxis/2K reboot in its tactical / mission mode, its overview or ‘geoscape’ mode and accompanying strategic elements have at first glance been plucked right out of the 1994 original.In many ways the game seems to walk the fine line of avoiding to infringe upon the IP trademarks and copyrights that are now held by the current owner of Mr Gollop’s brainchild. 	That which 2K/Firaxis incorporated into the reboot was left mostly untouched, while that which was left behind was picked up and brought back to life in Phoenix Point. It’s an impressive feat: design a new game that doesn’t infringe on the creator’s lost IP by creating a new backstory, threat and tactical setup that still leaves plenty of room to give fans what they would expect from a spiritual successor to the 1994 classic – and to do so both believably and entertainingly.A few things that were reintroduced and enhanced in Phoenix Point;(that were sorely missed in the X-COM reboot):- free aiming (1): shoot at anything at any time to create a path- free aiming (2): aim for specific body parts to maximise damage and avoid armour.- multiple bases: multiple actual bases – with staff and facilities, not just aircraft hangars.- ranged stun weaponsApart from that, the game features additional tactical layers (and accompanying difficulties / points of frustration) – such as destructible weapons and ‘active’ factions.Destructible weapons are a double edged sword... Players can target specific enemy body parts in the hopes of incapacitating them, effectively leaving an enemy defenceless. The same also holds true in reverse – get shot or touched (or sometimes it seems even looked at the wrong way) by an enemy and find your weapon destroyed. While the War of the Chosen DLC in 2016’s XCOM 2 features a number of factions, they are anything but active and seem to purely exist passively at the behest of the player. In Phoenix Point however factions are akin to 1997’s X-COM Apocalypse. They will either assist or actively seek conflict with the player as well as other factions – depending on both the players actions as well as the procedural elements in the game. Graphically I would put the game between Xenonauts and the 2012 reboot of X-COM. It is certainly a lot more polished than Xenonauts (including the upcoming Xenonauts 2 sequel) – but lacks the X-COM reboots deluxe camera effects, zoom levels, special effects and cutscenes - despite having superior textures and artwork. 2016’s X-COM 2 however graphically trumps Phoenix Point in every possible way despite being 3 years older. The difference in development budget can clearly be seen on this front.All in all – Phoenix Point is a great game and a worthy spiritual successor to the X-COM family of games. Potential players must realise though that Phoenix Point is not affiliated with the X-COM franchise in any way whatsoever. It is not a sequel, it shares none of the lore and backstory and thus should not be confused with X-COM in any way. It is a standalone game in the spirit of the original X-COM series as it was from 1994 to 1997 – made by its original creator in such a way as to provide a compelling experience without infringing on the intellectual property of the continued X-COM franchise as per its 2012 reboot.I recommend getting the game and playing it – as I also recommend getting and playing 2012’s  X-COM and 2016’s X-COM 2 as well. There is great fun to be had on both playing fields.On a personal note however I will add that I am sorely disappointed in Mr. Gollop for having dropped Linux support – which was originally promised. This was later revised to ‘not at launch time’ due to the strain it put on Snapshot’s small development team – but would be revisited later. Here we are a year later and no Linux support in sight. Now that Mr. Gollop’s company has been purchased by Embracer Group through it’s Saber Interactive division, it is unlikely to ever happen. Snapshot should have pushed harder for Linux support.	It was difficult for me to accept the choice of Unity and C# for Phoenix Point’s development, but I could look past it. I mourned the choice to have Phoenix Point be an Epic Game Store exclusive for a year – but I understood the financial aid it would bring to a small developer. But dropping Linux support altogether – that I find an unacceptable blemish on all of this. As a long term fan of Mr. Gollop’s work I still decided to purchase and play Phoenix Point – but not without some bitterness tainting my palate in what should otherwise be a thoroughly enjoyable dish.✔ enhanced tactical depth (in-mission)✔ enhanced tactical depth (global overview)✔ interesting lore✗ lacklustre graphics – comic book style cutscenes✗ simplistic, repetitive and sometimes flat-out bad voice acting (mission mode)--- In-Depth Review ---Note: In-depth review will have to be a little more limited than initially planned due to the length of the ‘at a glance’ section.• GameplayMechanically the campaign / global elements of Phoenix Point function like a hybridisation of the original 1994 X-COM game and modern iterations of the Civilization franchise. Game-changing choices are put before the player in the form of questionnaires, while base management and map navigation are near-identical to the original X-COM.In-mission mechanics draw heavily upon the X-COM franchise reboot – save the addition of melee combat for any and all characters (i.e. striking with the stock of a rifle) as well as the reinvigorated ‘free aiming system’ which allows players to shoot anything at any time. Aside from creating a path and tactically selecting which body part to focus on when shooting, it satisfyingly ‘proves’ to the player that there is no line of sight – thus no way to make the shot.Combat depth has further been increased by the very real risk of shooting team mates by accident. Overview is now a specific conical field of vision as opposed to 360 degree ‘awareness’ - with anything and everything being shot in the view cone. Team mates are sure to be hit by stray bullets if they’re standing between a unit and an enemy in the view cone. Lastly – ranged stun weapons are back – which is great.• NarrativeThe technological development of humanity has come at a cost far greater than we ever could have imagined. Our development and industry changed the face of the earth – as we unwittingly opened the proverbial ‘Pandora’s Box’.	We worried about rising temperatures and sea levels as the polar and arctic ice was melting away – never realising what we were releasing onto the world, buried deep within the ice. A virus like no other; insidious and pervasive – merging with everything in its path, depositing its hateful nature into whatever it can grasp - before releasing it into the wild. Waiting, watching, learning. Adapting, honing and experimenting. It will not come all at once, it has patience. It wants to be thorough – humanity must end.• AtmosphereCreepy, organic – almost dirty and infectious if it wasn’t offset by clean industrial design. What remains of humanity is marred by self-righteous platitudes – the results ultimately no different from that which the enemy is trying to force upon us. As time moves on - it is becoming more difficult to say which is the more infectious, or insidious. • Graphics / VisualsWell put together – but lacklustre. The developer did what they could with the budget they had. Cutscenes are similar to those found in X-COM Chimera Squad, while gameplay looks polished – but somewhat shallow in its presentation (not its gameplay). Zoom levels are limited as are camera effects – but design and artwork are glorious.CONTINUED IN COMMENT SECTION

_childDocuments_.review: A really good game. Good concept, mechanics, and storyline. As someone who had played XCOM series before, I found this game to be excitingly challenging to play. Aiming mechanic makes me felt more justified when it come to missed shots. Increased in management such as ammunitions and base (both personnel, construction, and defense) also makes the game more challenging, making you to think more carefully of what to do and spend on.Although, I would admit that this game still had some flaws, such as the lack of mission rewards, adaptive difficulty seemed to develop too quick, and little to no passive generation of resources. Late game can turn into a struggle if things did not goes well in the middle. DLC contents requires these resources and extra time to explore, time with the campaign will not provide more since there is no mechanics to buy more time and the adaptive difficulty. Soundtrack, while it is atmospheric for the geoscope part, it isn't in combat, perhaps makes the combat tad too dreadful and stressful.

_childDocuments_.review: I love XCOM and really wanted to love this game. Revised - For sure, do not buy the DLC - it turns an already incredibly difficult game into certain defeat. It would have been nice to not have a really tough pitched battle and then win, but then to read the hints and realize "oh well, you did not bring the right classes and weapons."PRO - the free aim is the best part. CONS - the interface for sorting your inventory and manufacturing is appalling. Half the time the class buttons did not work. Sorting by weapon type would have been helpful. I want to see what grenades I can make - hmm.. no sort by name or weapon. Scroll up /down/up down there it is.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: there are better games out there.I bought it 50 % off and i regret that purchase a little bit. The game starts of promising and isn`t bad per se, but there are many things to throw a spanner in the works.To get the positive out first. I had one moment, that sticks with me. I had to defend an outpost on extreme difficulty the first time. Never had been to a citadel either. So i spawned in a little villiage full of fog. Than i moved my squad a few fight and saw IT for the first time. My jaw dropped and i regretted the life choices of my boys and girls in the field. Great moment.A few of the bad things:1. The game doesn`T explain many of its mechanics in game. You`ll start with no real idea, what to do and how to win. You can reconstruct outposts, but the game doesn`t explain to you, why you should do that. And you get no feedback that you are overextending, which might bite you in the behind hours in the game, since you need an aircraft to get an tradeloop going and generate resources without waiting for outposts of the factions to get attacked. There a a few damage types you can use, but if the enemy isn`t shooting you with damage type X, the game won`t tell, what it does. You can dual-class, but the screen won`T show you the ability of the dual class. With the DLC you can explore archiological sites, but you will be confused as what to do, if you get one, since the game doesn`t tell you, that you`ll need 2 of them in specific pairs. The list goes on.2. The combat system is not that fun. The game doesn`t tell you when you are going to be spotted. (Its a skill check perception vs stealth). So you can get spotted across the map in round 1 and get bombed by artillery you can`t see and that doesn`t see you but hits you dead center.  Mind control enemies cross half the map, and have enough points to MC your soldier and get back into cover. So you can set your soldiers up, but you can`t really prepare for anything. In a bad way.The game also talks about the realistic bullet physics. "No hit percentages!" True, but you might be suprised how often your soldiers will just shoot at the pixel of air that your free aim didn`t cover, while the enemy gets headshots across the map.Not to mention, you can`t move soldiers at the same time.The worst part for me, the classes just don`t feel that good. In X-Com, you got that feeling for each class and their abilites. The dual classes in PP are necessary but take away from that. The abilities also are often forgettable.3. Just 2 % of the player-base have finished the campaign. I can see why you wouldn`t.Endgame ist boring. Just boring. About halfway through a campaign, you`ll just sit there, waiting for research, while you play the same defense mission in the same map over and over or attack the same 3 lairs over and over for the next hours. Its not fun. The only time the difficulty ramps up is the last mission, and at least for the Anu-faction, its quite balls to the walls. The enemy will pin you down and bomb you away shooting perfectly over a huge wall. I`m tired of writing about it, so just play XCom, JA2 or even Gears of War (at least the combat is faster and the plot isn`t worse).

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Point at first glance does not seem to have recognizable similarities to XCOM,  you have to give it a chance.  The story line is based on the fall of XCOM, the reactivation of XCOM Bases and man kinds struggle to survive.  I do like the game but liked it better when you could train operatives in skills you needed, not random selection as it is.  Training adds points to a pool that allows activation of a skill as well as character development.  I also liked being able to select a starting Country, game randomly selects it now.  I believe that many modern games rely to much on random generation, lazy I guess.  Random generation takes away from the story line and is a disappointing distraction.  Example, you would think you would find books in a library but a random generator will put ammo there instead, sloppy.  Sorry about that, Phoenix Point incorporates elements of the XCOM series but they are bundled so options are limited but it is still a great game but not as good as what XCOM fans are accustomed to, needs more story line and focus.

_childDocuments_.review: Starts off very strong, but the campaign turns into more and more of a slog the further you get. Especially disappointing are vehicles, and that once your soldiers hit max level the upgrades you get from gear are fairly mediocre, so your power hits a plateau while new and improves enemies keep rolling out in larger numbers against you.At a certain point the sheer volume of autogenerated missions you need to fight to do well on the campaign map feels more like work than fun, despite otherwise having some great moments.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played the big update yet, but I hope it fixes the totally broken economy which did not make any coherent sense. I wrote a long review and lost it, but hopefully it is relevant anymore. What I will say is that the core gameplay is the best turn based tactics you're going to find anywhere. It is way better than Xcom 2. It is unfortunate that they got mission creep developing this 4X style economy, which last time I played it was so broken I couldn't even imagine a way of fixing it. Basically, you're supposed to be heroes saving people, but the only way to get resources is to save bases from being attacked, so you end up benefiting from aliens attacking, which means you don't want to clear out the aliens. This turns into some kind of Alex Jones CIA ISIS type thing where in terms of role-playing, you're working with the aliens to extort the havens. (Like when AJ says that the CIA funds ISIS to come in and rescue civilians and play hero.) I guess if you start role playing as a kind of clandestine terrorist group exploiting an alien invasion for profit then it becomes kind of funny. But seriously, that's not what the game was supposed to be. I get that the other part was that you were supposed to go to war with one or two of the factions, and then rob them for resources, but the impulse, and the way most people seem to be playing, is that they try to keep a balance between the factions while extorting all of them using false flag terrorism. Maybe making the wars less easy to avoid would fix this. I don't know. Anyway, I'm excited to play the new update and maybe it all makes sense now. But the point is: the combat is fantastic. Honestly, I would consider it a big update if they just cut down resource scarcity and just focused on tactics, plus some map control. I'm hopeful and will update when I play the new release. I still recommend. Best tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: Edited review: Terror From the Void is the best thing to happen to PP. It's an amazing improvement in story and gameplay.  It captures the spirit of the game, extends the play by reducing the artificial urgency of the original while replacing it with a sense of creeping dread. It does the same thing for PP that Long War did for XCOM.I rarely run mods, and then almost never before I've beat the game on vanilla.  I've never beaten PP, but TFtV gives me hope that maybe, just maybe I will someday. Bravo modders, and props to Snapshot for embracing it.Original review: At first a laggy buggy mess, PP:Y1 has greatly improved.  The DLCs have fixed some strategic gameplay issues, and the patches and hotfixes have improved gameplay from "cross your fingers and hope it doesn't crash" to "about as stable as WotC".A fitting successor to the original XCOM, depth of story + side quests + much better combat mechanics (who here wouldn't donate a body part for free aim in Those Other Games, eh?) = recommendable.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally backed this game long before it was hijacked by Epic and then released for free to me as a Steam key. I'm proud to have played it during its infancy and watch it grow to the game it is today. This is truly an improvement upon the format of the latest XCOM games, but actually developed by the creator of the original XCOM, Julian Gollop. It's a mashup of Terror From the Deep, with a faction system similar to UFO: Aftershock and a combat system leveraging Fallout's VATS. The "aliens" are also truly hideous. I'm looking forward to a solid play-through.

name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace
detailed_description: Inspired by the award-winning board game franchise, Arkham Horror: Mother’s Embrace is an investigation game served with turn-based combat, set in the haunted worlds of H.P. Lovecraft’s Cthulhu mythos. Plunge into an original story written by Fantasy Flight Interactive’s official writers and explore the American Roaring Twenties. The year is 1926: a professor of astronomy is found dead in her mansion and everything indicates that she has been the victim of a heinous murder. Choose from 12 intrepid investigators from the Arkham Horror games, each with a unique set of skills, and assemble your team to shed the light over this mysterious death. Find clues, perform interrogations and progress through nine chapters as the story unfolds. Your investigation will take you to visit shadowed institutions and mysterious locales, ranging from Miskatonic University, the Arkham Asylum, and the bayous of Louisiana.  As the investigators get closer to their goal, your squad will have to face curious science, living nightmares, and a sinister cult, whose mad scheme is to bring about the end of everything. Use a large variety of melee and ranged weapons, as well as powerful items and devastating magic spells to defeat your opponents in turn-based combat; while you attempt to retain your sanity. As you face off against Lovecraftian horrors, your investigators will descend deeper into the depths of madness, affecting their level of sanity and causing traumas that will impact the course of your investigation. Care about your sanity and make the right choices… the Ancient Ones are preparing their return.

_childDocuments_.review: Mild recommendation. There are a few bugs related to inventory and things like searchable objects where if you back out before making your choice, it won't let you access the object again. There are apparently some save bugs, but I never had that problem.Perhaps the biggest issue people will have with Arkham Horror is that it is not a straight digital port of the decades old board game, first put out by Chaosium, then Fantasy Flight and now Asmodee. A lot of Asmodee digital games are direct ports of their popular tabletop titles, but this is not one of them. So be warned, if you go into this expecting an board game or the newer LCG (Livign Card Game), you will be sorely disappointed. THIS IS NOT THAT GAME.So what is Mother's Embrace. It's not quite a RPG, but it is a tactical strategy game. In this game you manager up to three playable characters at a time (from a roster of over half a dozen if you collect them all - even more if you count the list of Starter Characters, although you can only have one of those for the entire game.) and you will manage their health, inventory, and sanity. It wouldn't be a Call of Cthulhu licensed game without it, am I right?The game is divided into nine scenarios. All have some combat, but the majority of most revolve around investigation, solving puzzle and mysteries while avoiding sanity loss. There is also a DOOM CLOCK that really reminds me of the dice game Elder Sign (also by FFG/Asmodee) more than Arkham Horror or even Mansions of Madness. If you do a task slightly wrong, the doom clock moves forward. It can be unforgiving in those early scenarios as you learn how to play, but I rarely triggered it at all in the later ones. So this is a good time to point out the learning curve. Hard at the beginning as you flub up the Doom Clock, click on every interaction icon, which will cause your sanity to plummet, and you play the game like a RPG or point and click adventure game - DON'T DO THIS. It will cause more harm than good. If you lose enough sanity, you get a Phobia. I never developed more than one on a character, but if you keep using the same characters over and over without letting them rest, i suppose you will develop more. One of the big complaints that I see is about the narrator, but I don't get why. She's well (voice) acted and it makes a lot of sense the farther into the game you go. She's an unreliable narrator on account of *SPOILER* but her narration makes more and more sense as the game goes on. Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace is one of those games a lot of people will give up in the beginning for good reasons, mainly frustration, but the reward is there as you go further into the game. I kept playing through the bugs and I'm glad I did. Will I ever play this again? Probably not. it's very linear and it would be a pushover in a second playthrough, knowing what I know now.So let's end this mil recommendation, especially if you like Mythos stuff with some tips on how to get through the game. I never had a character die, and I never developed more than one phobia, so I'd like to think these tips will help you.1) The best starter is the Jazz Musician. His giving the party resistance to Sanity Loss will really help. The first partner you get in Chapter One is the second best character in the game. So use these in every scenario you can. The third best is either the writer, or the character you pick up in Arkham Asylum. No, it's not Batman. The writer will help with the Doom Clock and is a good fighter while the Doctor ups your initiative and has double skills while having no weaknesses. Both are good tertiary choices.2) Guns are your friends. Again, this will become more apparent the farther into the game you go and you finally start to get bullets up the wazoo. Have you ever played Space Hulk, either in tabletop or video game form? Treat combat like that. Shoot and Overwatch. Multiple characters on overwatch is your best defensive move. Enemy takes a step and gets shot. Repeat until all characters' Overwatch is done. It's amazingly effective, even in boss fights.  Good bye Tyranids...I mean Lovecraftian fiendish thingies. 3) Melee is fine, but know three things about it - you have to use action points to move closer to the enemy, it's never as effective as a bullet, and most status effects that your weapons give you aren't actually effective at all. Bosses tend to be immune to them, and using a melee character on them means you just moved a guy into damage dealing range which out setting off the other characters' Overwatch. Unfortunately, in the early goings, bullets are rare so you will need a melee character or two. Just make sure they have healing items on them.4) Magic sucks. There is always a better option to magic - including direct damage and healing. Healing items do twice the hit point repair of magic, and guns do more damage than the one direct damage spellbook. As well, magic has a 50% Wild Cast and that means anything, from doing extra damage to your enemy, to hurting your own guys to healing someone else in the battle - be they friend or foe. With the doom clock ticking down in every round of combat, magic is the least best option. You don't want to freaking heal a boss for 10 damage after you blew up his minion for 3, right? There is one person that negates Wild Casting more or less, but she is the last character you get, and she has an awful initiative and sucks at combat,  Do not be tempted by her. You wouldn't just start casting "Summon Dimensional Shambler" willy nilly in the TTRPG - so don't cast spells here unless you have a choice. 5) Use those Pocket Watches - but use them at the right time. A Pocket Watch resets the Doom Clock to zero, so use them regularly when you find them. However, there is no point in using them if the clock is just at one or two. Wait until it is almost full and then use them - even if it is in combat. This will make your life so much easier. 6) A lot of items take up space. As mentioned earlier, conditions do little to nothing and they go away quickly. This is true for your guys as it is for the enemies, so don't waste an item slot on condition healing items. Use it on weapons, clocks, or something that heals Hit Points. There are a lot of inventory red herrings in the game, and with such a limited inventory for your team (makes Diablo 2's inventory look spacious), you need to min/max like a Pathfinder player.  7) Finally, with the final battle, it can be really, REALLY easy if you just shoot away the part of the battle that isn't the boss. I'm trying to not give spoilers, but it took me three rounds to kill it and I only took damage once using the following method - GUNS ON the NOT-BOSS, and then overwatch. Easy as an Akuma Vs. Dan pairing. 8) Finally, the game is unforgiving. You can't go back and replay any old missions AND once you beat the game your save is deleted. So if you are a trophy hunter (and I'm not), you will have to invest a lot of time (or get lucky) to get the suicide by smoking and Matricide trophies. I never even had a chance to get the former and the latter I misjudged by a fraction of a centimeter and don't feel like playing another ten hours to get it. Just a head's up on those pieces.So that's it. Less a review than a quick mini guide to help newcomers. A mild recommendation though, especially if you like tactical combat and Cthulhu oriented games. Note that there is no Cthulhu in this game, which makes it a bit refreshing for a CoC game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm reviewing this partly because some of the negative reviews are just ridiculous.  Essentially, this is a detective game with simple, but fun, turn based combat.  It does not leave the best first impression and the graphics are okay but nothing to write home about.  However, the deeper you play the more enjoyable the game gets.  The atmosphere and mythos is spot on.  The characters and mechanics are cool.  The combat is entertaining.  Its not a great game but neither is it bad.  Its a fun b movie, not a triple A production.  I would pay exactly 15 dollars for this and feel my money was well spent - and guess what?  Its 15 dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace is a detective adventure and turn-based strategy game. You choose one of seven characters as your main protagonist for the whole game. Every character has different stats, a different trait, a back story, and a unique voice. As soon as you did that, the game starts.Wilhelmina Tillinghast, a professor of Astronomy at Miskatonic University invited you over to her house. As you arrive, no one opens the door but the lights are on.. so you break the window to get into the house. Soon after that, you'll hear screaming from another floor. As you search for her, a detective arrives. Together, you find her body and mysterious man, who you'll need to fight..As you probably know, Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace is set in the world of H.P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu mythos. It's to assume that the story gets supernatural in some kind of way. Your team of detectives will get bigger throughout the story. More people will join you and help you find out what happened to Wilhelmina Tillinghast.The gameplay loop consists of adventure elements and turn-based fights. You'll walk around the environment and search for clues, people, and objects. You'll need to talk to people, break things, and so on. Stats of your characters define how successful your actions are just like in a board game. Many of them also let you choose what you do (e.g. try to break a box, shake it or look at it). Your characters can give you hints to let you know which of those actions will be successful. Some cruel things will happen down the line and your character's mind will suffer from it. The game will automatically roll a dice and if you miss the test, your character loses one sanity point. If your sanity reaches zero, your character gets a trauma that will negatively affect him in some way. Between scenarios (missions) you can leave your character at the bureau. If you do that, his trauma will disappear. Besides sanity, your characters have health points. Just like in most games, your character dies if his HP reaches zero. You can revive them in a fight with items. There is no permadeath in the game. Let's talk about turn-based fights.There is a timeline on the upper screen which shows the order of characters making their move. This gets decided through the individual initiative of every character. You have 5 Action Points. Every action costs one to five AP. Different weapons have different stats and cost different AP to use. There is magic to use as well as some abilities like overwatch. The voice acting is good enough IMO, even if many reviews on steam say otherwise. It may have something to do with me not being a native English speaker but I know some other games with very bad voice acting. The graphics and the sounds are okayish. Some things will get on your nerves early on. For example, almost after every object, you inspect the camera will change and a "cutscene" will start - even if it just for one sentence. It feels unnecessary and disturbs the otherwise fluent gameplay. Well, it would be fluent if your character wouldn't move like a tank or get stuck on edges and these "cutscenes" often feel cheap because what they say and how their mouth moves don't match at all. Animations in general are very generic and repetitive.The camera often feels like it is in the wrong position or too close to the character which is another bad thing they should work on. The adventure elements are very expendable, too. You'll mostly click on everything you can see and find and that's it. There aren't challenging puzzles. There isn't even a mode where you can combine clues to find something out (like in The ABC Murders).Add to that, that the turn-based fights are pretty generic, too, and not too innovative or hard, there is not much left to like you will assume and in some way this is true. Mixed reviews on steam show that there is much to dislike about this game - but keep in mind that this is a 20€/USD game and nothing more (On sale you can even get it for 15,99€). I feel like many people expect way too much for that money. The game offers a pretty interesting story and thanks to the fast-paced switch between turn-based fights and story elements it doesn't get boring at all. If you're into an atmospheric detective adventure with easy turn-based fights and can turn a blind eye to those little things, you should definitely check this out on a sale. If you mainly want a tactical turn-based strategy game, this is nothing for you.
