_childDocuments_.review: A quick first impressions look for the curious since it seems like nobody had a preview copy and that naturally makes anyone wary.  Note that the below is all based on the first half-hour of play through the introductory scenario and does not reflect final thoughts on the game itself.  I mostly put in this time just to see if I liked it enough to keep it.  Short answer - I will keep this 'cause it seems cool.Fans of the boardgame should note that this is an adventure game inspired by it, but by no means does it play like it at all, no matter what edition is your fave.  This is more like the LCG than anything else.  That said, there are very familiar elements here that will please fans should they take the dive.  You will choose from a set of initial investigators that will be familiar to you if you've played the tabletop game or any of its spin-offs and while your favorites might not be there at first, it's very possible they will show up later as NPCs such as (minor spoiler) Roland showing up in the first scenario despite not being a choice for yourself.  It seems like the game is broken up into connected scenarios whereby you search a location for clues (yes, you even use a magnifying glass), encounter enemies and complete your overall objective.  Encountering horrific things cause your sanity to be checked, though at present, it's obfuscated on how these checks work - all I know is that you may or may not lose a sanity point.Losing all of your sanity, unlike the boardgame, will not kill you, but rather introduce trauma.  When selecting a character, you will see that they have three potential traumas they can suffer, though there is no explanation on what these traumas are other than unhelpful names (at least I could not find an explanation at the outset).  Also unlike the boardgame, there is a Mythos Clock that is ever-present and it ticks up when you choose wrong (or when an enemy purposely invokes it) during "complex interactions" which are basically 50/50 choices to make when interacting with hotspots.The game itself, then appears to have been developed with controllers in mind so it is a little wonky with kb+m controls that you  rebind.  Maybe you can through config files, but not in-game.  Helpful tip - if you have a controller plugged in and don't want to use it, you will want to choose it as your control method in order to disable vibration and then switch it back.  You control a single investigator, though you may pick up party members as you proceed, wandering around locations and interacting with highlighted hotspots.  At various points, you will enter turn-based combat which operates on an action-point system.  Movement is not grid-based, but rather focused on free positioning and range indicators around characters.  Otherwise, actions cost points and it's pretty straightforward.  Damage is not set and again, there's probably stuff going on under the hood but it's never really made apparent on what is actually being rolled/checked.  Not a big deal - just swing for the fences.In the short time I spent with the game, I only encountered minor issues.  As an example during combat I tried to move someone into melee range, but could not 'confirm' my placement.  I simply backed out of the action and tried again and no problem.  The option menu is pretty limited as well, giving you the standard low-to-high configs, but not much beyond that.  However, special note for some PC freaks is that you can set the framerate to unlimited, so you won't see complaints on that front.  Like I said above, some stuff like having to enable the controller to disable vibration is counter-intuitive.  If anything, I'd say the negative points (thus far) are more clunky than broken.The art here is simplified (reminds me of Evil Genius for some reason) and textures are pixelated, though that could be a stylistic choice.  It seems that this game is really targeted for multi-platform so don't expect it to put your PC through its paces.  That said, it ran very smoothly and I didn't get any hiccups or weird artifacts while playing, but again, I admittedly haven't put in the time.Narratively, it feels right for an Arkham Horror game.  Some Miskatonic Uni prof is dead and no matter who you are, you'll band up with an unlikely cast of characters (though boardgame fans will know all of them already) to figure out what's going on.  There's no reason for a Fed to take a civilian along, but you know, why would a jazz musician, a librarian and a reformed cultist get together, either?  That's kind of how it always plays out on the table.  In short, this is going to feel more like the Arkham Horror card game than the board game, but the overall atmosphere is correct and that's a big bonus for a fan like myself.In short, I'm willing to put more time into it and explore its depths.  The narrative is typical Arkham fare so it's not like it's going to knock your socks off.  The goal here is to stave off an Old One, I'm sure, but it's not clear which one it is yet so that's enough for me as a fan.  As a casual passerby who knows nothing of the franchise or the Call of Cthulhu RPG, you might find this a middle-of-the-road game as is the general consensus on most Artefact Studio games, but as far as I can tell, it's a capable port and doesn't give me any indication of rough seas ahead; it should be smooth sailing.I will probably throw this out and rewrite it should I make it to the end of this adventure, but hopefully you have a better idea of what's in store for you given that there hasn't been much else said in the past couple of years.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkham Horror: Mother’s Embrace is done and dusted. It’s advertised as being inspired by the Arkham Horror boardgames, and I can see that. A lot of the automatic sanity damage in certain battles and the random seeming choices during investigations (despite it not being random) have a definite boardgame feel to them. It also definitely pulls from actual Lovecraftian lore, which is always nice.From a feel standpoint, this game definitely captures the dark and often visceral horror aspects of Lovecraftian writing and imagery. Sanity factors in heavily, both from a gameplay and story aspect. Sanity is handled in a way similar to Darkest Dungeon inasmuch as it triggers negative personality aspects. Because it’s written into some encounters and in others it’s based on your decisions, it can feel a little unfair at times. However, it never actually gets in the way of the game, and so it still works. And, much like DD, characters can rest for a mission or two to reverse an insanity penalty.The gameplay is a mix of turn based combat without cover or environmental factors; and RPG style inventory management where each character is given four inventory slots. As a result, inventory juggling is a very real thing. In between missions, all items you had on your inventories at the end of a mission go into a chest which is shared by all characters, and as you start a mission, you can assign up to four of them per character to take with them. Weapons and spells degrade with use and can’t be repaired. Everything has a destroy option, but the only things with any benefit to doing this are guns, during missions, as that allows you to put that guns ammo back into the ammo reserve for reloads. There are of course some single use items as well.I thought the graphics looked cool and were quite faithful to a pure Lovecraftian experience with solid design and nice looking still frame cutscenes. The voice acting was also done well and captured that Victorian era feel well, with accents appropriate to the setting as well. The characters were likewise well written and appropriate to the setting. You will add four story characters to your group in addition to your starting character, of which you have a few distinct options.There is a fair amount of reading, so I imagine you could skip through stuff to enjoy in a later playthrough. You do also become pretty OP by the end, so that’s worth mentioning.It took right at eight hours to complete the nine game missions and all sub quests within the levels. I don’t really feel like there is much in the way of replay value unless you just really want to try the different starting characters or rushed through the game and missed a lot of the lore. It is, in my estimation, quite worth a playthrough if you enjoy Lovecraftian game. This is a pretty honest addition to the genre. Perfectly Steam Deck compatible as well.

Why was this pushed forward in place of a digital adaptation of the excellent Mansions of Madness or AH/EH board/card games?  Such a missed opportunity!  It's too bad, really. _childDocuments_.review: It's pretty fun overall. Gameplay is more similar to something like Phantom Doctrine than XCOM; you move freely out of combat and your party follows, and you spend that time finding clues and investigating locations. There are primary and secondary objectives to accomplish, as well as items to gather and stockpile, though exploration isn't encouraged or rewarded as much as I'd like. Combat is pretty standard turn-based combat. As for the controls, I don't really understand the complaints about the M&K controls, and the comparison to mobile games seems absurd to me. The game controls fine, if a little clunky at times, but it's nothing that has actively gotten in my way.As for everything else: art style is simple without overdoing it, and the environments are really well designed. The OST is nothing exciting but that's to be expected of Lovecraftian games--it's mostly ambient music with the exception of boss fights. The story itself is well written although some of the dialogue seems stiff, with characters sometimes repeating things that another character just said (this admittedly only happened a couple of times in my first playthrough). The voice acting is hit or miss but you can always turn voices all the way down if it's bothersome.If you're a fan of the AH board game or LCG, don't go into this expecting the same experience. This isn't a tabletop-to-digital conversion, it's a turn-based game based in the Arkham Files universe, so tempered expectations are good to have going in. But honestly? It's a fun game, and I don't regret my time playing it at all. There isn't much incentive to replay the story unless you wanna choose a different starting investigator, or just make some different choices, but I'm hoping they'll release expansions or something to spice things up.

_childDocuments_.review: Light spoiler - this game sucks.  To begin:  It's 1920 & I've been invited to play some jazz at a professors house.  No answer at the door, so I look around for another way in.  I don't feel comfortable going through the cellar door as "There is nothing for me down there".  So I find a pair of pliers in a wheelbarrow and immediately think - "these will let me smash open a window", why I didn't just use a stone from the garden I don't know, or just go home.... but me smashing my way into peoples houses is probably why I don't get invited back to play jazz all that often.  After murdering a person in a bathrobe - lets call them a cultist if the police ask (they won't) - I find the dead body of the prof!  Add this to the pile of carcasses I'm leaving in the entrance hall, and landing, and bathroom, all dressed in comfortable bath robes like they live here and were just getting changed for dinner and a jazz recital, & I should be worrying less about Cthulhu and more about the cops pinning all these murders on me - a black guy in 1920's America (OK I did murdered them, but not the old lady soooo I'm the good guy right?). OK, this is just the intro level to get the game going so lets give it a pass....The next level should be more thoughtful right?  Nope, its about a school shooting, tasteful.  Also if you are a student coming out of the shower in a bathrobe look out that's all the reason I need to blow a hole in you ... wait I'm the good guy right?OK so a misstep there...  The next level is in an asylum, lots of room to explore the subtle distinction of insanity and knowledge no human is meant to possess.  What IS reality and what a construct of the mind after all? ... Naaaa cue crazy nutjobs with knives coming at you.  The psychologist says things like "We should really work this out in therapy" which made me laugh.That's as far as I have got...A lot of reviewers don't get why some of us really don't like this game.  Here is why. Fantasy Flight make very well designed and well written board games under the Arkham Horror mantle, using the characters depicted in this game.  They are fun and interesting, and sure you kill a lot of people in bathrobes who may have just got out of the shower, and sure their depiction of mental illness is, frankly, disgusting, but the games have meaningful choices that effect the out come of the whole campaign.  There is no choice in this game.  The choice between hitting someone with a knife or hitting someone with a pipe is NOT a choice.  In the board game you are piecing together clues and puzzles that if you manage to solve will put you in an advantageous position for the boss battle.  If you take too long then the baddies have finished their ritual and your game is a lot harder.  In this computer game you just walk along on rails vacuuming up the 'clues' until you get to a final battle.If you wanna play a scary Cthulhu PC game play Song of Horror; if you want to play a shoot'em up play Resident Evil; if you wanna play Arkham Horror go play Arkham Horror the card/board game.'People' make a big deal about HP Lovecrafts prejudiced depiction of races.  His excuse is it was the 1920's.  I have a feeling future us's are going to look back on our depictions of mental health in the same way.  Whats our excuse in the 2020's?  Don't buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't managed to get too deep into the game yet, and that's partially because I got stuck between a telescope and a desk at the Miskatonic University. It must have been one of those odd angles that H.P.L. was always on about.So far, the writing isn't compelling, there's no Lovecraftianness to it and it's poorly edited. There's a disembodied narrator that breaks any semblance of immersion and most of the interactions you have with objects seem completely arbitrary. There's a broken vase on the floor--do you put it back together or "manipulate" it? "Well, I don't have any glue and I'm on a time crunch so...manipulate?" The Mythos clock moves ahead!I realize this is basically a board game, but I fail to see how "manipulating" a broken potsherd attracts the attention of Yog-Sothoth.The combat is a very wordy version of what you get in the Divinity: Original Sin series or Baldur's Gate III, with a lot of obscuring dialog and double confirmation. The very first combat I ran into was a barefoot, raggedy-looking cultist that exclaimed "Wha!" before throwing a punch at me. I opted to beat him up rather than shoot and stab the guy to death, because maybe I'll get some information out of the guy if he survives! Nah, the body just vanishes and you're cleared to unload hot lead into more barefoot, robed assailants.I'll probably play through the game, but it isn't worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: It is unclear which board game this is even based on, as it seems to have grabbed all the worst parts of "Arkham Horror", "Arkham Horror the living card game" and "Mansions of Madness", and that's really saying something because all of those games are decent to great. Exploration is slow, with the "run" button increasing your character's movement speed by a blinding 5%. Camera angle is mostly downward and zoomed in, meaning that you can't see very far around you so that means a lot of extra walking to explore larger rooms. There are no meaningful choices to be made. You interact with objects, and are presented with 2 or more possible interactions. All but one is "wrong" and you are penalized for picking it. There is no indication of logic to which is the correct choice. For example: This time picking the lock on the drawer is correct, but for the other drawer across the room, with the same description, the correct response is to bash it open. There are no visible die rolls, character skills do not have an obvious impact on outcomes because there is no feedback outside of "WRONG, time to raise the doom track!"Combat is likewise so barren it might as well not exist. It's "tactical" in the sense that you move around and have action points, but there seems to be no such thing as cover, and units all move far enough that positioning doesn't make any difference. Attacks don't seem to ever miss, just do regular damage or a critical for more. I didn't experience any technical difficulties so I guess there is that.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves the Mansions of Madness and Arkham Horror board games, this is a let-down.  The controls are awkward.  There are no difficulty settings. Combat is incredibly tedious for the chapters I played - generally characters get one attack action and a bit of movement, and the movement is awkward.  For anyone reading this - just go play Mansions of Madness or Arkham Horror on tabletop simulator instead - you'll have a much better time.

One bit that reflects the board game is that with the Mythos clock advancing, things get only more difficult and sometimes you can feel that you won't make it. But I have never been even near from loosing, making the game too easy and straightforward. And you probably will guess the entire story from the beginning. the main thing lacking from the board game is that investigators are basically interchangeable and differ only on their fighting ability, they do not have specific skills. I'd say they should return to their game and work more on it. Potentially good, but far from good.

Every little thing you touch hurts your sanity! These are some of the most fragile human beings you'll ever meet and they never "get better" at not having an aneurysm over the same stimulus.  If someone comes at you the first time, yeah scary, but when you're fighting your 20th cultist maybe not as earthshaking?  I don't feel that my characters should be driven to multiple aneurysms simply by interacting with every single potential clue.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Arkham Files board games, I had high hopes for Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace, but it falls short in key areas. While the story and characters are true to the mythos, the gameplay itself feels slow and lacks depth. Team composition doesn’t matter, and the sanity mechanic, which should be critical in a Lovecraftian game, is practically irrelevant. You’ll just click around randomly, sometimes getting random sanity effects, but they have no real consequences. Characters move so slow around the map it makes you feel they did it on purpose to make the game longer... With no meaningful strategy or sense of progression, the game ends up being a shallow experience that doesn't do justice to the Arkham Files universe. Play it only if you are an Arkham Files fan for the story.

_childDocuments_.review: OR How to make compelling game that requires you make a sanity check whenever touching the games GUISummary:If you think this is Mansion of Madness or a direct implementation of Arkham Horror you WILL be disappointed. However if you’ve been hankering for a turned based RPG/Squad based game that includes a interesting sanity mechanic with a strong Arkham Horror theme, this flawed gem is definitely worth a lookGameplay:You start the game choosing one of seven characters as your main protagonist but gather more investigators to assist you as you play. Each investigation has different stats, strength and weaknesses, different trait, and their own back storyThe gameplay switches between walking your team through adventure/investigate elements and turn-based battles with 5 action points. Both modes have issues, you walk around the maps looking for glowies that will either be clues, people, or equipment you can salvage. Sometimes you will find things that hurt you, that advance the doom clock or damage or hurt your sanity. They are interesting clue seeking tidbits, and clues you can read, but the log is NO help in summarizing that information which means you can run up the doom clock if you don’t have a great memory or don’t take notes. These kinds of issues are common throughout, and really can be annoying BUT somehow if you can accept them you will find a game that is well better than the sum of its parts, or flaws in this case.The adventure and turn based aspects are not well developed but neither are they that bad, the thing that makes this game unique is how you can lose sanity points along your mission, your sanity reaches zero, your character gets a trauma that will negatively affect the investigator, Their sanity then refills up, but you now have to deal with the trauma they’ve acquired. Between missions you can leave a traumatized Investigator at home so their trauma will be cleared. You can also use equipment you find to help you in your adventures. Cigarettes will cure sanity BUT damage the investigator, guns require bullets, and spell books can help you in fights, bandages can heal damage, and coffee can reset your action points.The interesting thing about this game, is that what is does well it does really well, and the thing it doesn’t, can be outright annoying.StoryThe story will begin including a little bit about the back story of you investigator, and the story is well told, BUT the narration is handled by Wilhelmina Tillinghast, who is the person you are to meet and goes missing, and the handling of it is a little jarring. Sure it results in some humorous dialogue at times, and other times unintentionally humorous dialogue, but seems like a odd choice you just get used and ultimately works if you can get over the odd choices the design team made.GUIOof! This one is a mess. You are constantly fighting things here. From an interface that doesn’t give you a clear indicator of how much moving cost in ap till you spent too much, or the clunky way you move in combat or the clunky way move inventory. This is a low light of the game design, it is definitely a hurdle, but if you can excuse it the game has lots to offer you.Sound All the investigators are voiced and have personality. The music is appropriate, this one is across the board pretty good, but not great.Graphics’ The graphics are good, but the animations and interactions are at times limited and clearly make it clear this was intended as a budget titles. They are decent though, some nice detail included throughout and it worksDifficultyModerately difficulty, turn based battle can be challenging sometimes includes puzzles or civilians you need to protect.ReplayabilityOther than the start with the unique back story beginning and the unique voice actors and skills for the 7 investigators, there is a lot of repeat the same adventure portions in replay, but I could see how combat could play differently.PriceWorth the price of $20 if you like the Arkham Horror theme and/or love turned based RPG/Squad based games!

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Arkham Horror table top game, his is a neat point and click adventure with some light but interesting srpg mechanics tacked on. It's not an adaptation of any of the 928 different board and card games in the setting, but I still find it fun enough for the price. The controls are awkward but in a way you can get used to after an hour, and the graphics aren't terribly special but they're also not the worst ever. I wouldn't suggest this for someone who wants something like the Gloomhaven computer adaptation, or to people who are sensitive to controls, but if you're a fan of the Cthulhu Mythos or the Arkham Horror characters and setting, this is a fun point and click adventure in the setting.

_childDocuments_.review: It's what is says on the tin, a lovecraftian adventure using a turn based combat mechanic, and for the price it's worth it I'd say. With the real challenge being: "What gear/Investigators do we bring along today", It's nice to see the characters from the board-game making an appearance, with every character being fully voiced (in the cut scenes).Graphically it's not top of the line, but looks good enough, staying faithful to the hand drawn aesthetic.The story is engaging spreading over various locals but not something extremely original, although there where a few moment here and there. And the big-bad is something other than Cthulhu for a change, All and all I would recommend Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace.

Game play is very simple, almost walking simulator simple, if that makes sense (but it isn't a walking simulator).What are you getting?  A weird combo b/w a very simple adventure game, and a poor xcom style tactical battle system. _childDocuments_.review: I like it!  It isn't really a video game as much as it is game-ification of the mansions of madness app that accompanies that board game. _childDocuments_.review: I do really like Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace, the game has an interesting story and a charismatic cast of characters set in the H.P. Lovecraft universe. It does have a few bugs though, a few issues with the controller I have had so far, hopefully this will be rectified soon. From a gameplay perspective, AH has turn based combat inter-spliced with the exploration of each scenario, from using pistols to melee weapons and also magic against otherworldly foes; one qualm I have with the gameplay is the insanity checks; when working through the levels reading documents and further clues to aid you lowers your sanity. Menial aspects affect this too much though, you will read a newspaper with a headline and lose sanity, a tad over-dramatic. This affects gameplay when you lose all your sanity points, this turns into a trauma, which decreases your skills such as range to attack an enemy. You can rest your investigators in-between scenarios as you'll have a wide range to choose from.Overall it is a solid and enjoyable game for the price of admission, there are some bugs but nothing too game breaking so far. If you are a fan of story and investigation games it is well worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Inspired to write when the game froze up. More on that later.First impression of game play, this looks and handles like a game from well over 10 years ago. I'm not a cutting edge gamer or anything but the basic look and control is substandard.The game flashed tips, for how to play games in general for some reason. Recommended checking the map if you're lost or whatever. Funny thing though, no matter where I move throughout the few levels I could before failure, the icon of my position on the map is always in the same location.Entering a level the map indicated that a door was locked (why is a map telling me that in advance?) so I went the other way to explore for a key or whatever. The game quickly had my character correct me and tell me that I needed to go to that locked room, and instantly placed me there. Where I "found out" the door was locked and then I was allowed to go back about my exploring. There are times for my character to state an exposition letting me know I'm trying something impossible or whatever. But short of that I expect to have the space to make mistakes. For my character to correct my action like that, it takes the role and the play out of a role playing game.Further on the level was a hall that was illustrated to have 2 doors and had a "this might be something" symbol on each, though the map showed they weren't really doors. Not that something secret is hidden behind a wall that is dressed up like a normal wall in a house, rather a programmer did a half @$$ job. I am betting the story will never go to those not rooms, but that for whatever reason that hall is just there serving no purpose and is visually misleading while the map shows its just worthless.Shortly after the game told me about new data in my ledger so I went to go through it to make the prompt go away, but I cannot close the ledger now. I can flip through pages. There is a row on the bottom of my screen telling me the controls, and telling me the same controls again, over and over.From my first impression up until the game refused to play I was disappointed. _childDocuments_.review: Short version: the game felt shallow, capricious, and plodding.  Requested a refund.Long version:The "correct" decisions during Exploration/Deduction felt capricious and inscrutable.  It does seem that there were keywords related to some of the decisions and that there was a system for certain investigators being able to provide hints for those decisions, but for my choice of initial investigator I never benefited from this system in the opening act and what I played of the second act.  Sometimes the narration of the action taken didn't seem to me to match the name of the selection.  And you're punished for choosing the wrong option.In my (very limited) play I was never able to explore anywhere that wasn't absolutely critical to the plot.  There were interactions that were optional, but they all contained an item or delivered only a line or two of flavor text.  Everything was either directly on the main path or immediately adjacent to it.The dialog and plot felt weird.  For example, in the opening act (minor spoilers) very early on you're given a goal to get to a room on the second floor of the house you're in because you believe your friend is there.  You're in the foyer with stairs going up.  You cannot go up the stairs until you take the time to investigate a broken object on the floor first.  Why?  Because the plot says that while you're investigating the broken object you hear a scream from the person you came to see, who is in the room you were heading towards.  And you can't go up the stairs until you've armed yourself (with a letter opener?), which you can't do until after you hear the scream.Later, you find that person freshly sacrificed/murdered, with your only lead pointing to their place of work, ending the opening act.  The second act opens with you arriving at that place of work to access their office.  You approach a colleague to get the key to the office of your just-murdered friend.  The colleague berates you saying that they don't want to talk because they've already been badgered by police, reporters, and others. What?  Wait a minute?  Weren't we the ones to discover the murder?  How did the rest of the world find out about this and beat us there?  And by long enough that these other people were all gone by the time we got there.  It felt like a contrivance by the writer to avoid us having to break the news of the murder and also give the person a reason to not even want to talk to us, but it didn't make any narrative sense to me.The pace of combat felt plodding, even for a turn-based system, and yet somehow the controls are also still fiddly.  For example, during combat you can change what you have equipped for free as much as you want throughout your turn, and you can have both a melee weapon and a spell equipped at the same time, but if you change your melee option to your fist (the only way unequip a melee weapon) that sometimes will unequip your spell and sometimes it won't.I pre-ordered the game because of the discount.  I was disappointed and requested a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: Apart from the theme and a good degree of atmosphere there is little else to recommend Mother's Embrace.Graphics are reasonably good, voice acting less so. Animations are below standard and controlling the player characters is frustrating. The user interface is long winded, inconsistent and confusing where poorly executed cut scenes can easily break immersion.The game world feels confined and your options are few. It is as if the game plays you as you are thrown from one location to the next with no say in the mater, at least during my first 104 minutes of play. At the start of the game you will enter a mansion where you can immediately go upstairs if you choose. When you attempt to go up the stairs to the landing which you can see, you are instead teleported there making the world round you feel fake. Also and while very rare, it is possible to get stuck behind furniture which will require a reload.Mother's embrace does not feel or play like a PC game and could perhaps be better suited to smart phones and tablets. If you do not have an interest in Lovecraft you may want to give this one a miss.

_childDocuments_.review: Lack of content and pretty much anything that made the Arkham horror games fun to play, A straight forward campaign with a choice gimmick that doesn't really matter. Combat is laughably simple, turn based where your damage is just a range, certain characters use less energy for attacks they are better with based on arbitrary stats, that you can't change. Story was thin and lame. "horror" is a joke the scariest thing is realizing you wasted 15-20 dollars on this game. Bugs are really annoying for how little there is in the game and even the puzzles are only difficult if you just skip through the clues and try to do them blind. _childDocuments_.review: This is a lukewarm recommendation; the game has little to offer.Not an RPG whatsoever, it's in essence a Point n' Click gameplay without much thinking, but with a dose of random choices and a copious serving of turn-based combat.Said combat is tactically lightweight, if not flyweight; minimal thinking required as well.The only connections with Lovecraft are the period, a visit to the Miskatonic University, and sanity checks (as introduced by the original Call of Cthulhu franchise.)The horror itself is run-of-the-mill witchcraft, not Lovecrafted.Said sanity checks occur every minute and for the most mundane reasons; not exactly immersive.Besides, in practice, the consequences of sanity losses are negligible.The interface is 2nd-rate.You can save and reload rather freely, but on one slot only; and unreliably so, because said slot is randomly overwritten by the auto-save (for a double dose of stupidity in reinventing the wheel.)The inventory is limited, tiny, yet a pain to manipulate; at least with a gamepad, as it seems to be designed for pocket phones.(Another sign that the game is a mobile port is the smallness of maps and the simplicity of the visuals.)In essence, you get  a decent, linear story with a decent presentation.There is nothing absolutely wrong with the game, but it's casual in every aspect, and certainly not worth the asked price.And if you're looking for excitement, try elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the Super Mario Bros. movie of video games. Growing up with the original Mario games had me so excited for the movie that even though it was TERRIBLE I watched it a million times and tried to focus on the enjoyable parts and forget the dumb stuff. The world and lore of Arkham Horror is amazing; and the new lore is what keeps me playing Mother's Embrace. Fans with a craving for the the lore of the Arkham Horror universe will be satiated but that's where the positives end. The combat is a less tactical XCom. The investigations are often clicking random dialogue options and hoping for the best, randomly picking the right party member at the onset of the adventure is the only way to get any clues as to the right answer. Focus on dancing elevator Goombas, forget the hobo Toad, and you might enjoy yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually like Asmodee's games: they're simple but enjoyable, so I was very happy to know they were about to launch Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace.I can't explain the disappointment.The story may seem interesting, but IMO the gameplay is awful. - The combat system is extremely cumbersome, but that's the least, you can get used to it eventually- Weapons break in no time and you can't replace them since you don't find them easily - a thing you can expect to balance the gameplay since they break and you won't be able to combat but with your bare hands- Ammo is rare to find (!!!) even if you investigate everywhere taking the risk of losing precious sanity points in the meanwhile- The journal is extremely vague - you would expect to find there nearly everything you learned investigating, but this doesn't happen and you need to take notes- Most importantly, the Italian localization of the UI is a nightmare. I'm a game translator myself so I know what I'm talking about. I don't blame the translator(s) since it might have happened for several reasons, but the tips you get when interacting with an object are too often misleading, and your Mythos Clock ticks. In the third scenario, I even found two identical interaction UIs, which is simply unacceptable! Another time, one of my team suggested an action (investigate), I clicked the "Investigate" action and it wasn't the right option. I uploaded some screenshots for this reason. Many other actions were unclear or worse as well - like when you find two synonyms for two different actions (such as "Guardate velocemente" and "Date uno sguardo"). I don't know why the result was this catastrophic, but the localization needs to be fixed, and urgentlyAt the end of the second scenario, I gave this game a second chance and progressed to the third to see if it would get better, but it didn't. It even got worse and worse. When I ended up with 0 ammo and two broken guns in the middle of combat and had to use bare hands to fight, I decided to give up.I'm deeply sorry because this game has lot of potential, but it's poorly developed. I personally don't think a single patch will be able to fix all these issues any time soon. I will change my review as soon as Asmodee will do something and the reviews will start being positive, but for now, it's a huge NOPE.

_childDocuments_.review: , despite sharing a name with another boardgame, is an attempt to bring the  boardgame to the virtual environment. Even the main game folder is named "Mansions of Madness". If you are familiar with the board games by , you will be familiar with the setting. And, if you have previously played games like  or , you will be familiar with the turn-based combat.If I had to describe  in one word it would be "clumsy". It's inventory management is clumsy. And it's combat interface is clumsy. It also has a lot of useless clues that serve no purpose (just like in the  board games, but still).To move objects, you have to left click them, choose a right click context action "move" and select a destination slot. If you are moving stacked object, you also have to select how many of them you want to move. I think a simple drag and drop approach would have been better and Shift + left click could serve for dividing stacks.Inventory is severely limited, and you can't stack more than 5 items in a slot. It's annoying, but understandable, given that the  board games are also extremely punishing towards the players and the playable characters with the right equipment are much more powerful than the monsters. After each chapter, the equipment is transferred to the party chest; which is comfortable, if you want to choose different investigators, not so much, if you want to continue with the same team.True to the original material, there are a lot of sanity checks, and sanity is the most important stat. You check sanity/lose sanity, whenever the Mythos clock advances full cycle, whenever you encounter a monster or even when you examine a mildly disturbing clue. I would argue that the investigators would adapt to certain things with time and should not get scared every time they see blood or a dead body, but I guess, without the sanity checks and traumas, there wouldn't be any challenge at all. The sanity system serves as an approximation of the cosmic scale otherworldly horrors that the characters encountered in H. P. Lovecraft's stories, so that's the thing with these games. It's a rough approach, but I can live with it.Whereas the skill checks are on a whole different level of absurdity. You're lucky, if you have a character on your team with the right skill to tell which choice to make. However, if you don't, you have to make an educated guess, based on the key words. The problem is that not always those keywords are present, or several choices are equally logical or even the correct choice is not logical at all. So, on your first playthrough, you lose a lot of sanity points simply because of arbitrary skill checks. When it comes to combat, it's the same clunky interface as for inventory. You have to choose an action, then the target, then confirm it. If you are choosing to attack, you have to select a weapon to equip it and then you have to select it AGAIN to attack. Why one click was not enough is beyond my comprehension. A few chapters in the game, you also discover that, when it comes to weapons: firearms > melee weapons > spell books. Also, since attacking is usually the optimal action, in most of the situations, I didn't find spell casting or condition removal (Radithor) worth the action points.There are also some puzzles in the game linked to the investigation. The hints don't always make sense, but, at some point, I stopped caring. has many flaws. Another one that I haven't mentioned are the painted textures that really don't look good on a full HD monitor. And the first impressions are really bad. Oh, and the narration. The game is narrated by an old lady, who . The comic nature of her remarks breaks the immersion and strongly contrasts with the overall atmosphere of gloom and mystery.However, despite all of that, I do like this game. Because it succeeds in two things that matter to me the most: the story and the atmosphere. When I didn't have to listen to the narrator's remarks, I felt immersed in the spooky atmosphere. It was a similar level of immersion, as when playing the original boardgame with my buddies. And the overall story, pulp fiction that it is, is good. It's your typical Lovecraftian horror against the background of prohibition era New England and New Orleans. And, if that's something you're looking for, this game is worth a shot. Just be warned that the first two chapters are pretty bad. If you can get past the first impressions, there is some enjoyment to have. The gameplay is very linear, though. So there’s barely any replay value.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is serviceable, but unimpressive, and disappointing with the high quality experience that its name suggests.Within the first hour and a half, I felt no agency over my character, where no action that I took ever impacted the story in any meaningful way. Not only that, but there weren't options for me to explore other potential solutions or paths.You need to explore to gather resources and main story quest items, but the game arbitrarily punishes you for exploring that you have no way of mitigating or avoiding. Additionally, exploration doesn't feel fun as the exploration you do doesn't ever make you feel like you found a little hidden corner of the world.Combat is dull and ordinary, but functional. My characters in combat didn't feel different from eachother, and there was no strategic element to the combat  besides a meaty slugfest.Voice acting was fine, animations were functional, with all characters obviously having the same rig.The writing was stiff and awkward, especially with the decision to have a narrator, but that the narrator was the professor who was killed? It doesn't make any sense as to why you, the player, are hearing that character's voice.All in all a functional, but unimpressive and non-interesting game with weird decisions that don't live up to the quality that the Arkham Horror name suggests.

_childDocuments_.review: Very hard to get into game, in my opinion this game is only for serious Lovecraft world desiring fans, definitly not deserving full price of course.The problem with the game is that it is trying to hard to be like board game moved to the PC which honestly doesn't fit that well because let's put it plainly I found the game to be very frustrating. I will point out what I disliked and what I liked to make it easier for people to know (PS: I love Lovecraft, I play board games, got even few lovecraftian board games in my home).Let's start with what I liked:* the story - it was actually good* plenty characters to choose from* music, while not at epic level it really helped me to immerse myself* based on H.P. Lovecraft worksWhat I disliked:* although I liked the story the twist was very predictable* although we had plenty of characters to choose from we couldn't use lots of them from the start* pretty short story, 12h to beat the game and I really didn't hurry playing it* no quickload / quicksave* clunky controls for characters (frustrating)* clunky mechanics for insanity (if anyone is familiar with any Cthulhu/Arkham/Eldritch Horror board/card game you probably know this so skip to next point) any action that comes as shocking can 'cause our characters to lose sanity, when we lose enough points we go insane and have some kind of negative effect on our mental health (for example we need to smoke etc.), the thing is in this game we lose sanity points 2 much and 2 fast, we see dead body (not mangled, just somebody killed with weapon) we can lose sanity points, we read a note from some crazy guy we can lose sanity, we see crying student we can lose sanity, it's 2 much and 2 often to the point it is frustrating enough to save game and reload before any interaction so that you use your very limited sanity for what matters most (like meeting enemy), also gonna mention the fact that we meet and killed very early some kind of inhuman being and yet we get scared later on by notes and human corpses sigh... makes no sense* not enough ways to regain sanity during playthrough, we cannot take rest action or something similar we could in board/card games* cut scenes felt really bad* very few item slots per character, just 4 item slot per investigator is just so frustrating, I can find so many items throughout the game and yet I have just 4 slots* cannot revisit old save file after beating the game (for example replaying chapters with different investigators on same save file and keeping inventory) need to start new game after beating itTL:DR I would say that the game tried to hard to be like board game, it is very frustrating to play, I cannot recommend it the way it _childDocuments_.review: The big caveat here is that this game is not worth the asking retail price -- and only really worthwhile if on sale & below the $10 line.What you get is a tactical turn-based story in the 'Arkham Horror' universe, a franchised world set in H.P.Lovecraft's ficitonal "Cthulhu Mythos".  You can start as one of 7 initial investigators, and will pick up more along the way -- from a total pool of 12.The scenarios, encounters, maps, and narrative are always the same, with variation in dialogue alone, based on your character choices.  You can also see the plot's "twist" coming from a playthrough away, if you have half a brain in your head.It's fun enough for what it is, but don't expect to get scared -- 'ARKHAM HORROR" is certainly not a horror game.  It does have a lot of visual flare and genre flavor, though.Sadly, it has seen only one update since its release, and is apparently ignored by the developers -- despite glaring flaws & typos in the game's text; and the need for simple quality of life fixes that the interface could desperately use to help smooth out gameplay.Let that inform your decision on whether or not to purchase.It certainly reflects poorly on franchise-owner, Fantasy Flight Games.

_childDocuments_.review: Takes most of what was interesting from Mansions of Madness and throws it away.  This is very much of the "interactive story" genre where you just click on everything until you've clicked on everything.  At least in Mansions of Madness you have to decide which of your investigators will do what, and there are such things as skill checks and ways to manipulate them, and items that help with things other than combat.  In this, your group of investigators act as a gestalt entity and all real decision-making ends at the point where you choose which investigators should comprise the group for your scenario.  After that, everything is automatic and depends on whether you chose the right people or not.  Add in an overly-long and uninteresting combat system that isn't really what this game should be about, and the result is something that is almost entirely unlike Mansions of Madness.  A big disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a difficult "not recommend". I am really on the fence about this because I definitely don't think it's a good $20 game. But I also don't think it's the worst in the world. The story was interesting enough that I wanted to finish it- but in the last few chapters, I started to very much get annoyed by the fact that everything was very predictable. A lot of the time, you actually got hints and downright explanations for things in secret notes despite the fact that the reveal was coming only a few minutes later. It's about a 6-7 hour game experience, so it's definitely not overpriced game-length wise. I just don't know how many people will be driven to finish it. It doesn't have much replayability. There's a concept that if you reach insanity, which I think is getting 2+ mental afflictions, you get these "bad endings" for the chapters. I got one, it really sucked. We just decided to murder a dude in cold blood, which thematically made no sense. There are items in here that are just completely worthless. The dirty bandages heal you but they cost sanity. And you are NOT going to have enough sanity in this game to waste it on a healing item. There are books and bandages that heal everywhere, so I didn't use a single one. You get a ridiculous amount of items. It becomes a problem near the middle of most chapters that you can't even take your status items because you need to pile in all the new weapons you can handle because you don't want a weapon to break while you're in the middle of combat. So instead of being a survival horror, it's just an inventory organizer horror. At least in Resident Evil, you have a box to put stuff in. This is chapter-by-chapter, so you have to bring things back to your office at the end of the chapter. There's no way to access your inventory otherwise. The story was interesting at first and I really love the theme. But it got boring and predictable later, as I said. This is nothing like the board game. This was clearly inspired by Call of Cthulhu much more than it was inspired by Arkham Horror. A weird distinction to make, I know. But it felt like one of those Baldur's Gate's wannabe games set in the world of CoC. The only thing that was purely Arkham Horror were some of the named characters and the Mythos element. Obviously there are no "action points" in CoC but it's also not in the Akrham Horror board game, either. There were virtually no stakes in this game. I had no problem beating levels and only had to restart once or twice because I lost a battle. The mechanics of combat were fun and everything, but if that's all we're judging it on, you might as well just play Xcom because at least the story is better and there is much more involved mechanically. And the walking is half the game. You're very slow, and you're punished for exploring by the sanity checks that can be complete nonsense. You MUST play this with a controller. If you try to play it with a mouse and keyboard, it is obnoxious. I think it deserves the 6/10 it got. Not bad enough to completely fail, but not good enough to get unless it was on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: If you really like Lovecraft, and this game is deeply discounted, then sure - it will give you a few hours of entertainment.  However, there is little incentive to replay once you've completed this rather short game.  It's also a bit cartoony, in a Cluedo kind of way, that detracts from the theme of the game.  I had hopes that this would be a direct translation of the Arkham Horror table top game that I've been dreaming of for decades.  A multiplayer,. cooperative experience.  But, this ended up being a rather bland, short, and ho-hum game with a cool backstory.

_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited to play this game, but in the end, it was full of issues. The puzzles were fine enough, took some time to get them sorted, but not really that engaging. The gameplay is clunky, that's the best way to describe it. Even if you manage to find things, the inventory slots are so limited that items are near useless. Boss battles are a CHORE, to the point it doesn't feel like you've won so much as mathematically figured out the right numbers to punch into the calculator. It got to a point when I got to a boss battle and found I really didn't even care if I won or not, I was done. Also, the game has some sudden self-harm that is EXPLICIT, which I get, it's Lovecraft, but there was zero indication it was going to happen (or even why it happened?) and left me super concerned about breaking TOS on Twitch. If you are a Streamer in particular, I wouldn't recommend streaming this because I am not certain if some content is allowed on streaming platforms with the way the rules are now (i.e. Twitch).
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: I have played countless hours of Mansions of Madness first and second edition. I was hoping this game would give the same feeling of exploration, and the semi-horror feeling. However, it fails. It is a point and click adventure with some generic FFG story on top of it. The story was not that captivating, game mechanics are terribly slow and frustrating.  After a while I stopped reading the flavor text and the objective as it does not reward you too much to find side quests, items etc. The only good thing was to play with the characters I know from Arkham Horror files of FFG. I wanted to enjoy and recommend the game, but make yourself a favor do not play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: I'm two scenarios into the game so far, and I would recommend fans of the board games to try it out. There is a lot a jank, but there is also a decent system under there as well. Maybe wait for a patch if you're skeptical. Speaking of, I do notice some problems that I hope are patched away pretty soon:- The camera perspective is weird, as other reviews point out- The run function is not all that much faster than the normal walk function, so its weird to insist on holding the run button in. This should be a toggle instead. Running should be a bit faster as well.- It would be nice if the game had an auto-next for dialogue in cut scenes. When the voice actors takes so much time with each line, I get unnecessarily impatient when I'm tasked with pushing the button for continuing.And I have a last point that might be more off a pet peeve than constructive feedback, but why doesn't Jenny Barnes have the social skill? I first suspected that it could've made her unbalanced, but after recruiting the two first team members in the game, another skill would make her some more balanced, not less. Her social skill gives the character more personality in the board games, so it's a shame that it doesn't keep up in the video game.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly I cannot recommend this game.  There is a severe lack of Lovecraftian games that are worth playing, despite the genre being (one would think) so suited to gaming.Graphically it looks like a PS4 launch title.  Surely not up to par with what one would expect in 2021.   I could overlook that if the game was fun though right?   Well no, it's not.   The camera angle is stuck at a Looking Down 3rd person perspective, which I found to be somewhat annoying.  You can move it back and forth but that's it, no way to properly look around like in Every Other Third Person Game.Voice acting is bland.   I'd liken it to new voice actors who don't understand how inflection and tone are so important in voice acting.   Think original RE1 poor voice acting.You can pick characters, but you don't get a lot of detail as to which can do what.  Saying this character is "average" at "physical" doesn't tell me much.  It's like the devs assumed  everyone had played the board game it's based on and didn't bother with details.It also doesn't have a lot of settings for video.  Seriously, just on/off for antialiasing?Refunded.  A good idea of a game poorly done.

_childDocuments_.review: The game certainly has issues. It's buggy - I encountered a major softlock in the Herd Mansion that required me to completely restart the mission, and multiple times I encountered dialogue subtitles that were completely wrong, or interactable descriptions that were outright broken.The game is also a complete pushover to anyone experienced with turn based strategy games - Not once in my playthrough did an Investigator go down, even though the game clearly expected it to happen with how many revive items it was giving me. Additionally certain combinations from about the mid-game can get hilarious powerful in comparison to the enemies (Give Roland a Shotgun and a few Bromo Caffeine pills and he will literally solo any boss fight in the game, or give any ranged character the Semi-Auto pistol and custom rounds and they will be putting out 15-22 damage per turn (depending on Overwatch)). A difficulty selection would be nice so I can properly challenge myself.However - If you're a fan of the Arkham Horror Franchise and want a quaint budget title (Yes - This is very clearly a budget title), it's worth a look, and certainly worth grabbing on a sale. The overall narrative was quite engaging for someone that likes to immerse themselves in game worlds (And no, the voice acting isn't nearly as bad as people were saying, I have no clue what's up with that), and while the gameplay was simple it was engaging enough to keep me through the game's 6-7 hour runtime.If I had to put a number on this game, I would give it a 7/10 - Very flawed, very jank, but if you're able to look past that, it's a nice time. I hope they're able to learn their lessons from this game and make an even better one in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace feeds a niche need for gamers in terms of turn based strategy games and I applaude that! However 20 bucks for it is simply too much to ask compared to all the great indie titles you get for that kind of money. BUY ON DISCOUNT!The game starts of solidly for the most part but unfortunatelly gets worse and worse as you keep playing!Let me elaborate why I feel this way:- very little diverse weaponry: You get firearms, melee weapons and spell books which in theory is fine...however there is   no variety to it whatsoever. For example there is 4 different firearm types: Revolver, Pistol, Shotgun and Rifle...however every   Revolver has the same stats and that's how it works for every weapon in the game!- the difficulty starts of very low which is alright to learn the games' mechanics but it never get's more difficult. Players get    better weapons or trinkets and the game becomes more and more of a joke difficulty-wise.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of the board games and enjoyed playing this game. The story was interesting and the turn-based combat moved quickly. If anything, the game was a bit too easy. I wish there were multiple endings and that the story line could diverge a bit. I enjoyed my time playing the game, but I'm not sure that I'll replay it much.

Sometimes you need a keypress, sometimes an left-click, sometimes an right-click to close some kind of dialog. It feels like the first game from some students. Its somehow nice to have the characters from the games, but they also dont become real personalities. I wanted so hardly that this game is better...but the game design is just bad.

_childDocuments_.review: This is sort of a qualified thumbs-up.It's not a great game, or a super intricate game.  But if you like the Arkham Horror board games and the Lovecraft Mythos, it's a fun little story / campaign you play with familiar names and personalities from the board games.The combat is passable for what it is, the voice acting ranges from inoffensive to decent, although I was personally impressed that the game adapts with actual voice acting since you can bring any investigators on any mission and they'll still say lines.  It's basically about exploring scenes from the lovecraft mythos, fighting baddies in simple turn based combat, and piecing together a classic mythos mystery.So while I wouldn't give the game any awards, I had fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: Light recommend. The developers being cycled out on this project, and redesign, was felt through the plot in that it felt strung together. The combat is turn-based, much like X-COM but without cover mechanics or any depth. There are perhaps a grand total of 4-5 enemy types, two of them just being variations of one another.So far as the writing, it is serviceable. Not excellent, but not terrible. I would say that the most bothersome aspect of both the plot (once you've figured it out) and the writing is the narrator. The narrator serves more to distract and take away from the atmosphere than to help build it. Speaking of atmosphere, there is not much here beyond the typical Lovecraft setup. One level in a mental ward, one level in a bayou, a few in mansions... But it does not capture that Mansions of Madness board feeling.

_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game with many reservations.1.) Give it a chance ONLY if you enjoy the Cthulhu mythos or universe. If you like HP Lovecraft and/or the Arkham Horror LCG or tapletop games, only then does this game have the *potential* to be worth your time.2.) The game is rough at a technical level. Even within an hour, I ran into a bug that required me to restart from the last checkpoint because the game refused to continue to the next phase of combat. Clearly, this is not an issue related to my OS / hardware, but rather just poor coding and testing. 3.) The UI / controls are rough too, though tolerable. They won't prevent you from enjoying the game if you like the universe, but yeah.. The devs clearly lacked the time, experience, and/or concern to polish the experience of playing the game..4.) The combat system is serviceable. It is turn-based tactical and a super light version of what you'd find in the modern X-Com games or Age of Wonders: Planetfall.  5.) The game oozes atmosphere and that is its sole saving grace. The voice acting is fantastic, the setting spot on for Cthulhu lovers, and the art, soundtrack, and writing are all fantastic. I find myself essentially playing for the story, and I hope that the franchise can get the true digital incarnation it deserves, whether that be in following the LCG format or continuing with what has been established with Mother's Embrace.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: It's more of a classic point and click story than an actual game, but that doesn't mean it's bad.As an Arkham fan I enjoyed the story and it was nice hearing some of my favourite characters come to life.The game is very simple and not very difficult, combat seems to of been added just because, it's not great and doesn't add much to the whole experience.But, if you like Arkahm and enjoy point and click adventures you should take a look at this title.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: The controls are rather terrible and leave me bumbling around or entirely pathing over the objects I'm supposed to be interacting with. Also, the fact that I'm stuck looking at my characters in a permanent downward angled view is annoying. However, the gameplay and story are rather fun, and overall the game is a nice solo variant to play in-between Mansions of Madness and Arkham Horror board game plays with friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game that does a good job of bringing the Arkham Horror characters to life with an fun XCOM style combat system and interesting investigation puzzles, helped by the investigators you pick along the way. While not the most stunning graphics or voice acting this still does a solid job of recreating this series in video game form. I look forward to finishing it and any further Arkham releases that come out in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of both Cosmic Horror and The Arkham Files games (from which this game draws it's characters) I liked it.  It was fun to see the Arkham Files characters appear in a video game. The combat felt good.  Though I will say it was weird that the game felt more like a tactical combat game like X-Com than an investigation game, which is what I was expecting.  Something along the lines of a Telltale offering I guess is what I had in my head for an Arkham Files based game.  Also it's a bit unambitious in it's scope.  I show 10 hours as my playtime for the game and I wasn't speeding through it. That said it was also priced as a budget title so that tracks.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: This one is for the fans of the Asmodee and Fantasy Flight board and card games of Arkham Horror. That said, I think this was a positive surprise and not a let down. I hope they make more of it! Some things to consider:-The game is not balanced well and quite easy. Don't expect hardcore difficulty like from the Arkham Horror board game or XCOM. Altough this makes it an easy story driven ride. However I had too many unused items left and never failed once.-The sanity system needs a rework. After some time you get discouraged to explore things. That shouldn't be the case. It's a good thing that the consequences are not that harsh in this video game.-Another difficulty level would be nice.Overall it's alright for this pricepoint and I really wish that they will make more. This game is solid and doesn't need to be a AAA title. If you are a fan of the material: Buy it! If not and you are interessted: Maybe wait for a discount on it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: I was really happy to purchase and play through this game. I play a lot of Arkham Horror LCG and seeing those investigators in game instantly caught my attention. _childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: To start of I preordered this game since I love the board games (both 1st and 2nd edition) so my impression is of someone who got it for 15 euros.The story of the game is pretty standard for a Lovecraft game. There are somethings that feels a bit original but not much. However the atmosphere is very nice. The voice acting are very varying with most of the characters being pretty horrendous and the rest decent. The controls are sadly bad but since its a turnbased game it is managable. The graphics are dated but that was to be expected, just look at the screenshots. The music was really good in my opinion, suited the game really well.After playing it through I can safely say that, except for achievements if you are into that, there is pretty much no replay value. Sure, you could play it through with a different starting character but all that changes are a couple of voicelines and storybeats in the beginning.Overall the game feels true to what its based on. I would like to see more content for it like the board game does, maybe with DLC cases. It felt a bit short but if compare to other prices in society at the moment I feel like I got 6-7 hours of fun for 15 euros which is roughly the same prices as going to a movie. Speaking for myself I dont regret buying it.Can I recommend it?If you like Lovecraft stories and want to sit through a couple of hours of interactive story. - Yes.If you are a diehard fan of the board game that wants a faithful representation of it. - No.If you are neither and is just looking for a decent video game of the genre. - Maybe, but there sure are a lot of better titles out there.As another reviewer here said, I would leave a neutral review on this if I could.
_childDocuments_.name: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed reading Lovecraft and playing the Arkham Horror board games, so I was really excited when I first heard of the game's release. It was a real treat seeing the players of the game come to life! The story is much more different than anything I've read in Lovecraft or played in the board game, and I think that it's really neat that Asmodee puts their spin into the Lovecraft universe.The game itself: Some of the voice acting was a little limited and the game itself had a number of bugs, but none were completely game-breaking. I'm expecting a later patch to fix the bugs. The mechanics of the game were tricky at times and the game seems a little rough, so I can see how it will disappoint some fans. For $20 USD, the price is a little high for what we get, and I would like to see it go down a bit. Gameplay: Guns are by far the most useful items in the game, but the game still offers some versatility with spellcasting. In my play through the game, I relied on a strong spellcaster to deal spells and had everyone else with guns in their inventory. A few things that I had an issue with during the game: Inventory space is pretty limited, so you really have to make decisions on which to keep throughout each scenario and which ones to bring into each scenario. Before each scenario, you don't really know what to expect, so preparation is a little tricky. Sanity plays a really interesting mechanic since it deals trauma to the investigators once their sanity reaches zero, and large trauma can alter the outcome of each scenario. Some sanity loss is unavoidable since you wouldn't know which interaction causes sanity checks, so it does give some replay value in the game to see how trauma level affects the investigator's decision throughout the game.Once you finish the game, your 'continue' option is wiped, so replay means starting a new game. This is a little annoying since there is no way to go back to previously beaten scenarios and inventory will still be limited in the next playthrough.Overall, I was excited by playing Arkham Horror as a videogame and seeing the story unfold, and I recommend anyone to pick it up when the game goes down to a more suitable price.

_childDocuments_.review: Really love this game being a HP Love craft fan. _childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna preface this review by mentioning that "Mansions of Madness," the Lovecraft-inspired tabletop horror game on which Mother's Embrace is based, is probably my favorite. I'm one of those weirdos who collects each expansion, and hand paints all the miniatures. I've had this particular title on my wish list since 2019, and pre-ordered it as soon as it became available. All this to say, I can comfortably claim that I am amongst this game's target demographic. I was delighted to revisit familiar characters and settings from the games I love so much. So perhaps I'm biased, but I feel as though there's plenty here to like. Game play is surprisingly similar to the app-assisted "Mansions," with turn-based combat, punishments from the "Mythos" events, and frequent (sometimes arbitrary) sanity checks. The tone, atmosphere, and lore are all very true to the source material. I also think there's decent variety from chapter to chapter. Some chapters are more combat-based, some contain puzzles, some require interviewing witnesses or gathering clues, and others require a reasonable amount of strategy. The continuous narration of Wilhelmina Tillinghast, the protagonists' mysterious acquaintance, is a nice touch. (The voice acting in general, in my humble opinion, is perfectly competent.)As for the game's weaknesses... There's no way around it. The game seems to have suffered from its troubled development, and I encountered some pretty gnarly bugs during my play through. Some were easy fixes, requiring no more than a reload from my last saved checkpoint. But one bug in particular was significant enough to block any sort of progression in the game, and required a full restart. (I was five chapters in at this point. It sucked.)The tank controls are decidedly clunky, and feel even more so when you're trying to navigate the occasional room with a fixed camera angle. I also had to run the graphics on the absolute lowest setting, because game play was too choppy otherwise. All in all, however, I enjoyed myself. I look forward to eventually playing through the game again with a different primary investigator, once it's patched up a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: For full disclosure, I have to confess that I haven't played Arkham Horror the board game so this review is from the perspective of the computer game itself. Having said that, I have played Mansions of Madness and other board games in this genre and I've very familiar with the Lovecraftian universe too.On the whole this game is pretty good, but hopefully the sequels will be even better as it goes along. The premise of the game is simple - you take investigators to various sites to collect items, solve puzzles and defeat enemies. The story is interesting and the locations and variety of enemies is fine. The combat is turn based which works quite well, and the limiting inventory space and the number of investigators also works well.It does, however, get quite formulaic after a while. Turn based combat with a limit to the number of movement points means that you largely use the same tactics again and again. Also, by the end of the game I found that it was actually easier to kill enemies which were supposedly harder than those which were supposedly easier. Also, the characters don't seem to quite work for me. At least one of them you start with has significantly lower mental stats than others and then many seem to be much-of-a-muchness so there isn't quite the jeopardy there, and nor is there the co-operative play which makes the board games so interesting.I did like the feature of being able to vary my investigators from time to time as by leaving them behind for one mission they can get better health. Also it's possible there will be slightly greater variety if I choose a different starting investigator. However, the game could really have done with some sort of skill tree which would allow you to variegate your investigators further, and really build up your team so you felt you were progressing.On the whole it's a nice start but hopefully there will be further episodes with better features for greater challenge and replayability.
