_childDocuments_.review: Spoilers aheadIt is a good game for several reasons but it is not „Subnautica good“.Below Zero has some nice aspects that make it a fun game but not if you want a scary dark void to dive into with your submarine.Lets begin with the good parts of the game and why i played it:- a beautiful map, most parts of the map didnt blew my mind but they were pretty nontheless- most PDA entries are readable but also avialable as memo- the music, the OST, beautiful, made up alot of the atmosphere especially in the „deeper“ parts- the sound makes a big part in games and in Below Zero some of the fish have a pretty powerful scream that will send a shiver down ur spine.- some new placable blueprints for base building. (But in the end they didnt really do it for me)and now the reasons why I stopped playing mid game:- the story starts with R looking for the lost sibling S, which could have made a good story but instead, R immediatly forgets the lost sibling after finding an alien calling for help and priotizes it- worst part about the story is that the alien keeps bossing you around to find lost alien artifacts- the map is litteraly just built around the story which gives it a really unatural feeling- my personal most hated reason ist that the main char. talks.In the original the main char. didnt say a word because I was the main character! My thoughts about this mysterious planet were what the main character „said“.I decided what to think and what to make of all the informations the PDA gave me.In Below Zero your are litteraly replaced by R, you just do the walking and swimming, but your opinion about what might have happend doesnt matter because R already has a opinion.- the info the PDA gives you about scanable flora and fauna etc, got really poor and boring. No fantasy about big, scrary and dangerous fish and why there are as they are. Most of the flora and fauna i could scan didnt contribute to the game in any way. Couldnt harvest or plant them nor did they tell you something about the surroundings. Early game I still read every entry in hopes of interesting info about this world, than i started reading less concentrated in the end it wouldnt have surprised me to read that this blue plant is in fact a blue plant.- Below Zero is half land, which was interesting but boring. The weather and the cold made it really hard, early game, to explore the land. But as soon as you get the Prawn Suit, you dont freeze anymore and can explore without difficulty. Devs tried to make the land scary by implementig Ice worms. So about that, you can easily outrun them in the prawn suit.In conclusion the land was rather boring and had nothing of interest to contribute to the game.- About half of the underwater bioms were baren. No beautiful scenery or POIs. Not sure but you could probably finish the game without every stepping a foot in these biomes.The other Biomes seemed to lack the certain „pow“ to make them properly interesting. But they were kinda nice to look at.- The not depth.There are probably a lot of players , like me, that enjoyed the fright of the depth and darkness, the unknown. Below Zero has you not covered. Smaller map, even smaller part water. No Cyclops. No dark waters. And most fish were rather polite.- The Seatruck, if seamoth and cyclops had a baby, but an ugly one. As fast as the seamoth but with configurable attachments to suit everyones wishes. Sounds good right? But no building allowed on the inside. So you only get what the attachment offers. And with every attachment the Seatruck gets slower. To be honest I ditched the Seatruck as soon as I got hold of the Prawn Suit and even without the first Depth upgrade (4oom Max) I explored 95% of the map. Not well balanced.- I had a really big issue with ressources, especially lead. I liked that they changes some of the recepies but damn i was short on lead the whole time and couldnt find a drillable deposit.From time to time i did enjoy the game. In some places it did feel like the old Subnautica. Beautiful scenery and the good old grinding runs and the need to go deeper. But it was not even close to be as memoriable as the Orginal. I lost interest in the story immediatly and just tried to force finish it, since i would try to explore the whole map anyway. It wasnt even a bit scary, in the long run, you kinda grew used to all the fauna and they became more like mosquitos, annoying but not dangerous.At first I did wanna call this game on par with the original, but after playing a bit longer I noticed all the missing features for it to be a good successor.

_childDocuments_.review: Up front, I want to say that this game was kind of a disappointment for me but, ultimately, that doesn't stop me from recommending it to others. Certainly, if you've never played the first Subnautica, I enthusiastically recommend you play that first or instead, but this one does have its charms too. If you have played the first game, then I caution you to temper your expectations. Some who have played both games loved them both, but there is definitely a portion of the fanbase that feels letdown like I do for various reasons. It is definitely what I would consider Subnautica Lite. It's not as scary, so if that was a struggle for you playing the first game, the entire atmosphere of Below Zero is much lighter. The game music is more boppy electronic tones and there's even a fun little jukebox that lets you play some pretty great music inside your base for your listening pleasure. They are songs that are about the experience of playing Subnautica, however, which is a little immersion breaking for me and therefore helps alleviate the scariness if that's a problem for you.The sound design which I highly praised in my review for the first game is, sadly, something I feel went too far this time. Everything makes an unreasonable amount of noise which is effective in scaring the daylights out of you when you first start playing and don't know what to expect or if you've played the first game and have leviathan expectations, but once you're brave or desperate enough to swim farther, you find out what's making all that noise and it very quickly becomes annoying. Because of brutesharks, I became completely desensitized to the leviathan next door. It's become annoying to me, not terrifying. It grabs my seatruck, and I'm irritated, not panicking.And the world as a whole is a lot less lonely. There's more remnants of things people left behind (which is fine, that goes with the plot) and there's even another living person to interact with--though she's not that friendly. The map feels so small and claustrophobic. Absolutely gorgeous in some places. Truly breathtaking, but cramped which makes base building a challenge in those places that are so pretty all you want to do is live there. Not impossible, but again, adding to the list of things I find annoying especially with a few new additions to the base building menu.I'm not terrified of the vastness--there isn't any; I'm not afraid of it's dangerous creatures--they're hardly threatening; and I'm not even sad about the eternal loneliness of the situation--I'm not alone. This, of course, is all personal preference. The first Subnautica was not meant to be a horror game. It sort of accidentally had that effect. It's fine if the direction they wanted to take Below Zero was somewhere more accessible for more players. I get that. But the one thing that is really, truly at the heart of my disappointment is I feel like the game lost its soul. Without giving anything away for those who have not played either game, what was so special--to me, at least--about Subnautica, the thing that made it different from other survival games was that it wasn't about conquering the environment in order to survive; it was about finding your place in it. It was about 'going together.' The goal was surviving, the adventure was sort of incidental of that journey, and finding that weird, surprising message at the end was the thing that you carried with you when the game was done. Below Zero feels like its forgotten that. Also, to a lesser extent, no time capsules! That really made me sad. It was such a lovely surprise to receive those messages from other players who had been on the same journey as me, who knew what I was headed for, and took a moment to reflect upon their own adventure, think of the little things they wished they'd had in the deep dark and paid it forward. And when it was finally my time to do the same, it was a fantastic way to really reflect on what I'd been through.But, Below Zero is a fine game. Even a pretty good one. It comes with voice acting which I really liked, base improvements, quality of life changes to menuing for crafting (I <3 pinning recipes to my HUD) beautiful new biomes, adorable little creatures, and a story that's...middling, I'd say. It feels very rushed. It's very front loaded and then back loaded with a bunch of weird empty middle space, but the ending was good. I'm curious. I still want to know where things are headed. I still want Subnautica in my library. It's worth a play, even if it isn't as memorable.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this game is great, it fixed a few problems that I had with Subnautica. It also introduced a few bigger problems though. As a TL;DR for the review: buy Subnautica first, it's the overall better game and the story will make more sense, if you enjoy Subnautica, buy this game. For the people interested in my more in depth review, I've tried my best to write the review without spoiling anything, but there will inevitably be some minor spoilers.Also any positives in the original game I mention in my Subnautica review that I don't mention in this review are still positives in this game, I just didn't have enough room to write them all out.Let's start off with the positives, the game looks absolutely beautiful, it was even nominated for outstanding visual style for the steam awards. Whilst there are less biomes (we'll get into that later), they mostly feel more fleshed out, and nearly all of them look amazing. A much higher portion of the map looks beautiful (though there are some relatively boring biomes like the sparse reef in the original game, there are fewer of them). The textures look a lot nicer as well, compare the starting area of this game, the shallow twisty bridges, to the safe shallows, and the difference is night and day. This makes the exploration in this game far better than the original in my opinion.The game makes a lot of quality of life improvements as well (this might be outdated in a few months, the devs have said they will be backporting some of these to the original), the game adds pins for recipes, showing how many ingredients you have and the ones you still need, along with how many of the recipe you could make, which is amazing. There's also some accessibility features, like hightlighting nearby items and being able to change the size of the UI. When it comes to sound design, this game still checks all the boxes, it's brilliant, the music is also great, sounding just as good as the first game's, Ben Prunty did an excellent job filling in for Simon. There is one issue with the music, but I'll get into that in the negatives. Base building has been improved upon, there's some new base pieces as well as improvements to old ones, overall a better experience.There are some new items that are great as well, such as the recycler which is an endgame item that lets you break items into their components (for example changing a powercell into two batteries + silicone) and he mineral detector, a portable scanner room with smaller range.The ending is awesome, won't get into it anymore to not spoil it, but it's brilliant.Ore veins, these are a very welcome addition. In certain caves you can find bunched up ores and metals, which is a very fast way to get some of the rarer resources. To balance this they're usually somewhat deep down / hard to get to without a vehicle, protected by something dangerous, or require certain tools to access. But once you find them it's so nice filling up your inventory with things like magnetite and gold.The dialogue is well written and quite interesting to listen to, I loved the lifepod and degasi logs in the first game, and this game's dialogue is even better. The dialogue between your character and a certain other one is especially well written, though I can't get into it too much without spoiling the twist.Finally, the optimisation is a lot better, along with there being much less pop in. I get better fps at the same graphics settings, and there's barely any noticeable pop in (I do get lag spikes near some structures, but that's the same as the original game).Now let's get into the negatives:The mood of the game is very different. This isn't necessarily a bad thing but what I and many other people loved about the original Subnautica was it's atmosphere of loneliness, and this game doesn't have that. There's a lot more dialogue and your character even gets to speak to other characters. The game goes for a more exploratory feel, and isn't as scary either. The music ties in with this, whilst not being up-beat it's not as sad or creepy. The seatruck, this is both a negative and a positive really, it's a cool concept merging the cyclops and the seamoth, but I miss the seamoth, it was a lot smaller and more nimble, and in my opinion more fun. However it does do an adequate job replacing the cyclops.The prawn suit grappling has also been changed a bit and isn't as funThe land sections, whilst these are cool the snowfox has really awful handling, and just isn't as fun as exploring the beautiful underwater areas the team created. The land areas are also a bit more bland and less fleshed out, it's all just white, and there are very few creatures. However the new leviathan there is quite cool. The leviathans aren't as good as the original, especially the one that spawns in the shallower areas. In conclusion, it's still an amazing game, and worth the buy, I love the exploration and the dialogue is great, the gameplay has been improved upon in most areas. However the vehicles and land areas aren't anywhere near as fun (though I do still enjoy most of the land biomes). The mood is also drastically different, and not as unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes. You should play this game. People criticize that it would be less "survival" than the first, that resources are more abundant or that it would be too easy. I am round about 7 hours into the game. Yes, I find my way around more easily than in the first game. But that is simply because I already know things I did not. How long I stared at outcrops before I realized I needed to break them to get access. Now I already know I need to keep backup batteries in my backpack.And unrealistic fauna and flora. Yeah, it's an alien planet. I want to explore it and not surface every 30secs to breathe. They made that a little easier. But the game does not suffer for it.I can't say anything about the "horror" aspect yet, they tend to show up in deeper areas that I haven't been to yet. But I find there are more scary creatures early on with large teeth... brute shark I am looking at you. sorta.So all is well then? Well, the one aspect I miss is that the starting biome in the first game was more colorful. I really do miss that. But there are bladderfish and hoopfish and I feel just at home.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that you wish there was a middle option for recommend or not. Ultimately, I will recommend because it was not bad. On the flip side, compared to Subnautica this simply is a worse experience,-Voiced protag is fine honestly. I got tired of silent protagonists years ago, especially in games where you actually interact with other people that can seemingly just read your mind from any distance. Subnautica did silent pretty good but I would have preferred like a journal entry of his wtf react moments or something, Interaction with other NPCs in Below Zero felt just under organic, but overall i think they were done pretty well and the PDA entries are about the same level as Subnautica were.-Gameplay is where things go downhill for me. Is any of it bad? No, I wouldnt say so. However it simply is not on par with Subnautica in the slightest. Quite honestly the map felt much smaller than Subnautica's which is really weird for a direct sequel, whether or not that is the case I dont actually know. Things felt too bunched up and much too close together distance wise. I would dread having to head back to main base because of how long it would take, only to realize that I'm basically at the front door after traveling for barely a minute. Hostile creatures didn't really give me cause for concern at any point outside of Shadow Leviathans, and even them were dealt with once I realized I was just being stupid about using the defense upgrade the game ends up giving you.The biggest problem I had with the entire game was vision. My god, even with maxed brightness I could not see a damn thing 90% of the time, I dont remember that being an issue in most areas of the previous game.-The need for gathering tons of materials was significantly reduced. Considering the irritating inventory management prevalent in both games, I see that as a positive. Any game that does not allow you to stack the same items in one slot is going to give you headaches in the long run, which is why I was using one of the inventory mods for 3/4 of my playthrough and it helped tremendously. There weren't a whole bunch of new items to make, but the few that were new did add interesting twists to gameplay.As most reviews will probably mention, the ending was anticlimactic. Saying it was an open ended ending to pave the way for a third game is not an excuse. End of the first game (spoilers?), you literally cure an apocalyptic virus from an entire planet after getting your colony ship exploded out of the sky and roll out. The end of Below Zero, you just peace out lol.If there is going to be a third Subnautica game, whether another direct sequel or a spiritual successor, its going to have to be truly open world with completely different mechanics, maybe even with online aspects. I got Below Zero hoping for more and better Subnautica, instead I got what felt like less. I have no interest in taking that chance again with a third installment unless it is completely different.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR It's a poor sequel, threadbare, and with some poor design decisions desperately trying to hide a lack of polish, but it holds up just enough to pass muster, especially at a discount. Subnautica: Below Zero is everything Subnautica was except slightly less polished, smaller scale, less fleshed out, and less exciting.  It's a testament to the first game being so good that even this poor, stripped down sequel is good enough.  Below Zero is a DLC that grew just big enough to be big for a DLC, but not big enough to be the full game its being sold as.  The ambition of the developers obviously grew with the success of Subnautica, then deflated as deadlines neared, and it shows.Despite each of the new environments still being bioluminescently gorgeous, their small number and cramped, busy, if not downright claustrophobic nature undercuts the sense of wonder you got with the exploration of the previous game.  It's far too easy to get lost in the same-y twisting tunnels, despite them not being all that big, and there, frankly, just isn't enough to discover to feel like you have much variety.  The devs have tried to compensate by slowing down all forms of movement and making the exploration much less directed (or hand-holding if you will) than the previous game, but that just exacerbates how easy it is to get lost.  I found exploration still enjoyable, but significantly diminished from its predecessor.The enemies are also pale shadows of their previous counterparts.  There are only a small handful of aggressive fauna types, and those are more bothersome than terrifying.  They don’t do enough damage to inspire terror, but their aggro range seems much wider than before, causing them to be more of a bothersome annoyance than a real threat, despite their louder roars.  Overall, it feels more like harrassment than being hunted.  There only 2 leviathans that you will likely encounter that feel like real leviathans, one on the above water ice shelf and the other in the deepest areas.  Technically there’s also one in the abyss beyond the map, but why would you ever meet it?The crafting too has been toned back.  Gone are several gadgets, and most of the new ones are either downgrades or totally pointless.  The robo-penguin is basically a short range drone that lets you pick up crafting materials hidden in otherwise inaccessible areas along with the occasional plot relevant item.  The base construction is slightly improved with a few nice additional aesthetic options, but it’s largely the same as before.  Gone is the seamoth and cyclops, replaced by the seatruck, essentially a seamoth that can tow modules behind it like a long-haul train-semi.  The problem is, most of the modules are utterly useless, and towing them encumbers an already slightly ponderous and slow vehicle.  The prawn suit works for pretty much anything, making the truck a slightly faster but also slightly less nimble option.  Overall, I found that the prawn suit outclasses the truck for basically everything but speed, with the added advantage that it can operate perfectly well on land and has built in storage.The plot for Below Zero starts out strong enough.  You are a new protagonist, here off the record looking for details to your sister’s death, who officially was labeled killed by her own negligence by the evil megacorp that employed her.  It doesn’t take long to learn that there is chicanery afoot again involving the same virus the protagonist of the previous game stamped out, as well as additional alien relics that offer tantalizing clues about the fall of their civilization to augment what we learned in Subnautica.  While all that sounds great, the game is so hands off about directing the player that the A plot can easily become impossible to advance unless you are willing to look up spoilers and location details.  Even the more important B plot can be frustratingly hard to advance since it’s not always straight forward to get to the waypoints you are given.  It seems to be promoting a “no stone left unturned” mentality for exploration, and given the sometimes frustrating nature of the environments, it was not well appreciated.Overall, I’d say for the current full asking price of $30 it’s just barely worth the ride.  Those who haven’t played Subnautica will probably enjoy it more than those returning, but even as a sequel it’s serviceable, if unpolished and tepid compared to it predecessor.  If you can find it on sale for half off, I’d absolutely recommend it.  On its own merits, I still think it was an enjoyable game, it just looks shabby compared to what came before.

_childDocuments_.review: Negative review for this because Steam has no ‘Nyeeehh’ option and most people won’t read any more positive ones. I get the feeling that Below Zero is meant to be more of a ‘spin-off’ or ‘expanded DLC’ rather than a direct sequel, but I will be making a lot of comparisons to the original as I feel it is similar enough to use as a fair frame-of-reference. I LOVE the original Subnautica and I want to support the developer so they continue to make nice things, but Below Zero has a LOT of flaws, bugs and questionable design choices that just pushed it over the edge, for me.The game looks and sounds great. Every underwater biome has its’ own look, feel and colour scheme that really help you tell every area apart. The arctic setting is utilized very effectively to create some beautiful setpieces as well as many of the perils an explorer would encounter within that environment. The first hour of gameplay was great. Swimming around discovering survival tech, scanning new creatures and daring myself to go deeper was the core of what made the original Subnautica great. However -Due to the well-deserved success of Subnautica 1, it seems like the devs wanted to expand on what made the original good. There’s a TON more voice-actors, characters and extra lore which, while impressive, I feel is detrimental to the overall experience. Subnautica 1 has a sense of disquieting isolation to it. By contrast, Below Zero is more character driven. You are constantly being spoken to in the forms of audiologs, other characters can just ‘call you up on the phone’ whenever something relevant happens, plus the main protagonist (Robin) just starts talking to herself sometimes. This is fine in-and-of itself, but for me, it eroded a lot of agency I had to the character. You aren’t alone in the original, but the experience is just lonely enough that when the Sea Empress reaches out and starts talking to you telepathically, it’s a genuinely terrifying moment that makes the player want to explore deeper.Instead of being listed in chronological timeline, every data/audio log is listed in your databank alphabetically by some arbitrary title. As such, if you lose track of what you were reading/listening because a bruteshark started munching on your leg, or another story-related voice clip started playing over the one you were listening to, it’s very easy to completely lose track of the story. It’s like reading a book where the chapters are in alphabetical title order, rather than by order in the narrative. I completely lost what I was supposed to be doing and had to refer to the wiki to work out what the game wanted me to do next.The story is delivered to the player in huge chunks, followed by vast spans of total silence when they aren’t finding anything. In my experience, the purpose of audio logs is to offer an alternative to big blocks of text. Audio logs allow the player to continue playing the game whilst absorbing the story. But when audio logs start playing over the top of one another, this completely defeats their purpose. As if there wasn’t enough water to drown in, now the game is trying to drown me in exposition! This is made doubley-frustrating when 90% of the audio logs you find are just pointless character fluff. However, I knew I’d discovered something important or relevant, because of all the overlapping dialogue being spoken! (Keep this in mind because I’ll come back to it later) There are two maps in-game. Both are difficult to follow and one looks like it was drawn on the back of a napkin with crayons. In Below Zero, it looks like the events are happening a few years after the first game, when Alt-Terra is beginning to expand its colony-building efforts. The game doesn’t have the excuse the original has, where you are a lone survivor stuck on a distant alien planet and the map-making and beacon setting is entirely up to you. Alt-Terra not-having mapped out at least SOME of the terrain above or below sea level for their multi-billion dollar off-world mining/colonialization expedition feels a bit unbelievable.The dry land exploration in this game is AWFUL. It feels like there’s a blizzard every 10 seconds and when this happens, you can’t see anything. Whilst this is realistic, it sucks in a game about exploring and finding things. This gets even worse at night when the world is dark but the snow fx are full-bright white. My entire screen looked like TV static and it made an otherwise gorgeous environment look absolutely terrible. It feels like the environment and the VFX teams had a massive fight during development and both were trying to sabotage each other’s work!When I first encountered the glacier where Robin’s sister works, there’s a large broken bridge that needs repairing at the entrance. What the game WANTED me to do was go over to the Phi robotics center, then notice the entrance to the Glacial Basin and start exploring there. And I would have done that, but 1, it was night, 2, there was a blizzard, 3, it wasn’t artificially lit up to indicate that there might be something of importance over there and 4, none of the voice-acting was indicating that area was important after I had explored the base. However, there was lots of dialogue about the bridge that needed repairing and my other companion character said something important was across the bridge. So that MUST be where the game wants me to go, right?Remember when I said the game indicates when you’re making progress with a barrage of voice-acting? I spent a good hour just bimbling around on the other side of the bridge after I had repaired it. Eventually I just got so frustrated with not being able to see or find anything that I up-ended my sea-truck on the lip of the glacier and did the Arctic Spires location in the Prawn Suit. None of the animals or leviathans pose ANY threat to you as they are only geared up to attack when you’re on the Snowfox, or on foot. In the prawn suit, you can just stomp right past them. Felt like I was ‘Seeing the puppet strings’ a little, at that point.This may be a very subjective opinion, but I didn’t think much of the creature designs for this game. I can’t quite put my finger on it, but I think it’s because all of the dangerous creatures have a similar ‘threat level’ to how they sound. That, and Leviathans will no-longer gobble you up in a single hit. This may have been frustrating to some players in the original, but I found to be a natural incentive to not swim over and hug one, when encountering it. Or get out of your vehicle and chasing it with a scanner. Once I realised most leviathans weren’t deadly in the slightest, all of my fear evaporated and they became more of an annoyance than a threat.I streamed a bit of the game and spent some time examining one of the hoop-fish. One of my friends commented “It’s amazing how many thousands of lightyears you are away from Earth and you’re still finding alien fish that have the faces of conventional Earth-fish.” This comment stuck with me as I feel there’s some truth to it. This is an alien world, I’d expect the way the creatures look, behave and hunt to be almost completely unrecognizable to anything that happens on Earth. I think it would be unfair to say that all the new creatures in this game are uncreative, but their designs might be a little ‘shallow’, it you’ll pardon the pun.I found Below Zero unintuitive and a far lesser experience to the first game, even with all the additional content. I can’t say if I recommend this one or not. Maybe play it if you’re burnt out on the first one and want more underwater survival horror in a different flavour? But don’t bother if you’re a fan of the same isolating tension and mute, contemplative narrative. This is where a hack reviewer would say something like “the amount of tension in this game is BELOW ZERO LOLOLOLOLOLO” but I ain’t doing that. Just play the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start this review by saying that I just barely don't recommend it. The original is one of my favorite games of all time, yet BZ just falls short of it in so many ways. Most of my complaints will hold ties to the original as it's meant to be a sequel.***SPOILERS AHEAD***Let me start with the positives.VISUALS:The visuals are just as great as the original. The night sky changing based on where you are on the map is an excellent feature.NEW WILDLIFE:All the new Fauna and Flora designs are great and fit well with the biomes that they were placed in. The Ventgardens definitely were one of the coolest out of all of them, though.BASE BUILDING:The addition of all the new base-building aspects was a much-needed addition to the game that made base-building more interesting.SOUNDTRACK:Not as good as the original, yet still makes great ambiance for the specific biomes and events that they were composed for.Onto the negatives.STORY: The story felt incredibly rushed, which makes sense seeing as they completely changed it a couple of months into early access. This left them about a year and a half to throw together a story compared to the original's three years which was used to go through with what felt like a well-thought-out vision.The story involving the Kharaa, Sam, and Marguerite was realistically just a side-quest. All you get from it is an explanation as to what happened to Marguerite after the Degasi logs from the original, information on how Sam died (Which WAS negligence, she even managed to kill a colleague in the process), and some backstory behind both of them. After you finish your one quest with Marguerite, there is no more dialog with her which is odd seeing as she was initially meant to be a much larger part of the story.The ending was an odd cliffhanger to say the least. All of the talk between Robin and Alan about whether any other Precursors were still alive or not, and we don't even get to know the answer. Speaking of the dialog, it got stale at times, with a large amount of Robin's lines being some kind of motivational speech.PROGRESSION:Resources are way too easy to find, which takes away from the survival element of the game. Silver/Gold was readily available without needing to explore anywhere beyond 300 meters of your lifepod, and Diamond/Lithium could easily be found not too much further from that.The resource availability ties in with the need for the PRAWN Suit... it's useless. In the original game, it was REQUIRED to reach the Lava Zone due to its maximum crush depth, and the resource gathering abilities of the drill arm was great for end game blueprints and base building. In BZ, the Seatruck can go down to the exact same depth while being much more maneuverable and defendable than the PRAWN Suit.Food/Water was also too easy to obtain. You will find enough nutrient blocks and large filtered waters to last the entire playthrough if you explore the land part of the game early on.The data-boxes that gave you access to equipment upgrades were way too easy to find, being right out in the open and requiring no special tools like the propulsion cannon or laser cutter to reach.BIOMES:The land section of the game was far too long. Finding your way around the maze called the Arctic Spires in order to find a body component was not enjoyable in the slightest. Add in needing to keep warm so you don't freeze to death, and the lack of enough heat sources means you will be filling your inventory with fevered peppers just to make it to the body component. The whole experience takes hours and was definitely the weakest area of the game.The underwater biomes aren't much better, with most monuments and one other body component being trapped behind a maze of tunnels that will damage your ships more than the leviathans do.I believe that the decreased map size was the heart of these issues as it caused the developers to fit as much as they could inside of it.UNNECESSARY CHANGES:Starting with the Seatruck, I'm personally not a fan. It's trying to be both a Cyclops and Seamoth simultaneously, yet instead of bringing all the positives of both, it brings all the negatives. Adding compartments only hinders mobility and doesn't add nearly as much utility as building in the Cyclops did.The Snowfox was neat and helped with the tedious land section but broke way too easily and could only hold one upgrade despite there being two slots on the model!They removed a lot of the upgrades for the vehicles, including Sonar and Hull Reinforcement, two of the most valuable upgrades that would have helped tremendously with the underwater cave exploration.DATA ENTRIES:The Data Entries were lackluster compared to the original, which had entire Wikipedia articles on EVERYTHING you could scan, including all the Fauna and Flora that very few people bothered with. Being one of those few, I greatly appreciated the information as it added to the experience of the game. Too many of the entries in BZ were composed of very few or only a single sentence of information, causing me to not bother with the majority of them.BUGS:Getting stuck behind and inside of objects is a massive issue with this game. It is very frustrating to lose hours of progress just because you glitched behind a box. Unfortunately for me, I used basic console commands just to get unstuck from these locations, and now I am unable to get my last two achievements unless I play through the game again.MYSTERY/ISOLATION:Easily one of the best parts about the original was the mystery behind the Precursors, the Degasi Crew, and the Kharaa. BZ tried to replicate these mysteries through Sam/Marguerite and Mercury II, yet fell short because they were explained through PDAs almost immediately.Isolation was also an excellent tool used by the original to make the game more terrifying, which is completely absent in BZ. You are never alone, and it honestly makes the game less scary.Considering that many developers left the company while the game was in early access and it was only worked on for two years compared to Subnautica's three, it most certainly isn't a bad game. It just has many flaws that really killed the experience for me and won't be fixed this late into development.

_childDocuments_.review: copy-pasted form Psyckosama's review because it's 100% accurate also not worth the price ''Below Zero lacks the charm and engagement of the original game on just about every level save one.First, the map. The original's map was expansive and interesting. The one here feels kind of samey, being in some areas too mixed and without the same degree of layered exploration. In the original exploration felt very layered. Like every time you went deeper you were moving into a new world with a sense of fear and wonder which magnified as you found new strange locations such as the Lost River and below. Below Zero it lacks that. Instead they all just kind of merge together and the layout just comes off as bland. The closest they have is the surface exploration which, while not bad, is feels divorced from the core game play loop and is set up into this mess of canyons that just adds artificial challenge.Second, the vehicle progression. In the original you work your way up from the Seamoth to the Cyclops. There was a sense of progression. In Below Zero you build the Sea Truck and just bolt new pods to the back and give it upgrade upon upgrade. And using the Cyclops vs. the Seamoth felt like a trade off in places. The cyclops was a mobile base, but it moved like a pregnant cow. The Seamoth was speedy and agile but weak and limited. You could bring both (at least until you got to the lava chamber) but that would mean leaving the Prawn behind. There were trade offs.Third is the plot. In the original you were a simple survivor and the plot is discovered largely by vague hints and stumbling around blindly. You discovered it for yourself. It wasn't handed to you, you had to discover and explore and figure out what was going on for yourself. In Below Zero you immediately start with an annoying generic 'strong female protagonist' (not that anything is wrong with female protagonists, as long as being 'strong', 'female', and 'the protagonist' aren't the sole memorable aspects of the character) who basically skydived naked onto an alien death world for 'reasons'. The plot is driven by an endless stream of poorly written exposition that manage to be memorable in only how annoyingly it can kill your immersion and coupled to 'helpful' way points that remove much of the impetus to explore.One thing to note about the plot is that it was completely scrapped and rewritten halfway through development. It's one of the reasons the story comes off as so disjointed. The reason that everyone mysteriously vanished from the planet was because in the original plot the planet was abandoned after a meteor storm caused everyone to evac to an orbital station but Robin was left behind, but the station was severely damaged meaning that they couldn't go back down for her and it went from there. The current plot was shoe-horned into existing map assets, like a DLC of a DLC, and it shows.In general, they missed the simple factor that made the first game great. It wasn't Ryley the Protagonist's story. It was my story. It was your story. It was the players story. The voiceless blank slate character was simply a vessel for the player's experience. Below Zero is Robin's story, not the players, and frankly, she really ain't that interesting.Then you have the creature designs which compared to the original are largely uninspired, drawing far too much from earth lifeforms to the point they seem less like strange and exotic alien lifeforms from a distant planet and more just strange and exotic prehistoric earth creatures. For example, you have the alternative to the Reaper Leviathan, the Chelicerate. It doesn't feel like as alien, instead its just kind of a giant death shrimp. Then you have the penguins. I mean 'pengwings'. Which are penguins.The only improvement over the original is base design, which is largely due to the addition of some additional rooms and decorative elements. A very welcome addition but it kind of falls flat when combined with the everything else.In general, this is an all around inferior product that shouldn't be bought for full price. If you find it for half off, loved the original, and don't mind being lead around the nose by Lady Generica and her boring sidekick, go for it... but don't pay full price. It's not worth the money.Update: The game being finished does nothing to change my opinion.''

_childDocuments_.review: "Subnautica: Below Zero" might have been better left as a frostbitten fantasy, lurking in the shadows of its brilliant predecessor. Far from being the chilling sequel we hoped for, it turned out to be chilling in all the wrong ways, leaving much to be desired in terms of both scope and thrill.First off, the decision to make the protagonist speak was an unexpected—and unwelcome—change. This move stripped away much of the eerie, silent horror of the original, replacing it with unnecessary chatter that felt more intrusive than immersive. The beauty of the first game was the isolation, the haunting solitude that amplified every sound and shadow. "Below Zero" lost that, opting instead for a narrative that feels less like a survival horror and more like a chatty walk in the park.And speaking of parks, let's talk about the map. Calling it 'compact' would be generous. It felt more restrictive than explorative, with boundaries that seemed to close in rather than expand horizons. The thrill of discovering vast, unknown depths was replaced by the monotony of seeing the same icy walls, over and over.Then, there's the building—a feature that should add depth but instead adds drudgery. "Below Zero" seems to believe that more building equals more fun, but this is a misstep. It felt less like an enhancement and more like busywork padded out to mask the game's thinner content and smaller scale.The creatures, few of which truly stand out, swing wildly between being deadly menaces and mere nuisances, lacking the memorable terror instilled by their counterparts in the first game. They seem to be thrown in as an afterthought, a way to justify the 'survival' part of this survival game without truly integrating into the core experience. In conclusion, "Subnautica: Below Zero" feels like a missed opportunity, a sequel that could have built on the eerie, captivating foundation of the original but chose instead to tread water in safer, shallower waters. It's a game that, while it may offer brief moments of entertainment, ultimately leaves you cold—yearning for the depth, mystery, and genuine thrill that made the first game a standout. In this icy sequel, there's no need to dive deep, both literally and figuratively, because frankly, there's not much worth discovering beneath the surface. Wait, it has more building??!!

_childDocuments_.review: They caught lightning in a bottle with the first game and they just couldn't recreate it with this game. The monsters don't feel nearly as threatening, they definitely could use some better designs. The best designed leviathan in the game isn't even alive. The map felt ridiculously tiny compared to the first game, 35 biomes in the first one and only 25 in this one! Usually you go bigger when you get a sequel greenlit, but even with less biomes you'd expect them to make them better in some way but they've gone backwards with that too. There's very little biome exclusive resources so there's always an easier place to go if you need to pick up an item. They just don't feel connected or deep. I wish they would've been able to recreate that feeling of stumbling into the lost river on accident, or falling down a hole and accidentally finding the jellyshroom cave but it just wasn't there.I'm not going to spoil the ending but just, god. It was so bad and lackluster compared to the deep and somber ending of the first game. You have 2 goals in this game, and you start knowing one of those. But that goal doesn't even matter, it's not important to finishing the game. I fully had the chance and option to just end it without ever completing that story but I dragged myself back to get it done. But...They freaking disable achievements if you turn on the console! Which you'll more than likely have to do because this game is a buggy mess, I got locked in my prawn suit because I saved the game? It's such a stupid decision to do that and apparently isn't reversible even if you disable the console again.I'd honestly only get this game if it's on sale at least half off because it's absolutely not worth 30 dollars. I loved the first game and had such high hopes for this one but I was severely let down, it's such a shame. (My playtime was around 16 hours upon completion)

_childDocuments_.review: Lightning didn't strike twice for Unknown Worlds with Below Zero, but the game isn't without its own spark! This sequel is more of the same explore/crafting play cycle as the original, but with far less emphasis on survival and, to me, a weaker emotional through-line. While not quite as compelling, Below Zero does bring a lot of neat backstory and fill in some of the mysteries surrounding Planet 4546B.New creatures (somewhat few, especially on the large-and-scary side), new biomes (some more interesting than others), and a few new mechanics and updates bring a bit of intrigue to the game. I was surprised how charmed I was by the Penglings, and I wish there had been more content for that mechanic. Favorite minor update: usable coffee maker!For huge fans of Subnautica, Below Zero is probably worth your time. But the main thing I felt when I got to the credits was that I'd be more satisfied by a replay of the original--hard to compete with that level of excellence.

_childDocuments_.review: I have 650 hours of game time on Subnautica. It is among my favorite games EVER. I barely had any interest in finishing my first playthrough of BZ and zero interest in ever playing again. It's a pale copy of Subnautica. Most of the the other reviews go into better detail about the pros and cons, however I will mention things that I haven't seen anywhere : Simon Chylinski, the man responsible for the outstanding soundscape that was Subnautica, was sorely missed in BZ. I understand that they got rid of him because he said some stupid racist stuff in social media, but the soundscape in BZ is very much forgettable. The only time I noticed the music was when I was deep in the creepier biomes and thought to myself "Huh, this seems like a rip-off of a Portal 2 soundtrack". On the subject of poor changes, the PDA's voice going from the incredibly endearing, witty, and experience-defining english-accent voice in Subnautica to a completely uninspired indian-girl-just-because-we-wanted-more-diversity that doesn't offer anything interesting was a big mistake. In Subnautica, that PDA was to you what Wilson was to Tom hanks in Cast Away. In BZ, I felt annoyed every time the PDA spoke, both because nothing it said was all that entertaining or insightful (unlike the Subnautica classic : "Multiple Levianthan-class lifeforms detected. Are you sure what you're doing is worth it?") and because I missed the old PDA and kept asking myself why they thought removing the old one without replacing it with an equally interesting one was a good idea. Very, very disappointed all-round.

_childDocuments_.review: I am conflicted. I recently played Subnautica and I loved so many aspects of it. I simply needed to play the sequel. The visuals are better and the environments more complex and colourful. I simply wished there was more of it. The map simply is smaller and there are less biomes.  Blueprints are so easy to come by it's actually frustrating how easy it was to collect them all. There are a few new blueprints and nice quality of life upgrades. The story feels very fragmented. The snowfox needs some serious control overhaul. I loved the sea truck but I missed the sea moth. _childDocuments_.review: Subnautica 1 was such an impeccable masterpiece in every facet. The story, gameplay, immersion, and fear factor have held up so well since its release back in 2014. What subnautica did best, Below Zero has done exponentially better. During the first couple months of this game, you followed Samantha Ayou, a researcher for Altera, trying to find more about the Architects, and the Karah virus. That story line didn't last long, which at first, was disorienting. Since the last big update, the new story follows Sam's older sister, Robin Ayou, finding what happened to Sam. On Robins adventure, she stumbles upon an Aecherect named Ai-an. Without giving too much of the story away, these two characters traverse the frosty land of 4546B, searching for Altera research facilities to reveal Sams fate, along with giving Aian a new body. To a newcomer just now purchasing this game, it's fantastic. The story is rich, it has many critical thinking moments, and it questions the morality of man-kind, a lot like SOMA. While giving you this, it also delivers a great gameplay experience where you can forge your own path and do the story, for the most part, in however you deem fit. They're still a lot of bugs in the game, some more annoying than others, but they're mostly very minor. Purchase this game if you enjoy narrative drivin, survival horror, strategy, and/or psychological horror games. Games similar to this - SOMA, Subnautica 1, Observation, Observer, Amnesia, Narcosis, Bioshock; 1&2.

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica: Below Zero is a fascinating open-world survival game, setting itself apart from the overabundance of survival games on the market with its tranquil ocean setting, addictive exploration, and unique wildlife.If you are a fan of the previous title or survival games in general, then you really can’t go wrong with Below Zero. There is an enthralling world just waiting for you to explore, with gorgeous graphics and beautiful atmospheric sound. With new biomes, creatures, suits, vehicles and mods, there is plenty to see and experience in your journey to explore Planet 4546B.Now with land-based exploration, which in turn brings a whole new mechanic, temperature. Just like your O2 meter, you now have a temperature gauge and have to find ways to keep warm, utilizing caves, thermal lilies, and food to help prevent you from dying of hypothermia.As with the predecessor, there is a strong emphasis on crafting, base building and farming. You can spend hours in between the main story just making the perfect base, ensuring you’re fully equipped with everything you could ever need.While it’s not quite as big or impressive as the original, it’s still a sizable journey and well worth a deep dive. Highly recommended, 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: A Frosty Dive into New DepthsSubnautica: Below Zero is a mesmerizing sequel that plunges players into an icy abyss teeming with life and mystery. As a big fan of the original Subnautica, I found the addition of dialogues to be a refreshing twist, injecting a new layer of narrative depth into the game. However, this departure also alters the atmosphere, trading the intense feeling of isolation and desperation from the first game for a more interactive and character-driven experience.The dialogues in Below Zero offer insight into the protagonist's journey and the world around them, providing context and emotional resonance to the unfolding narrative. Interacting with other beings and hearing their stories adds a human element to the game, enriching the overall storytelling experience.Yet, I can't help but acknowledge that this shift in focus slightly diminishes the sense of isolation that was so prevalent in the original Subnautica. The feeling of being stranded in an alien ocean, utterly alone and vulnerable, was a defining aspect of the first game's atmosphere. While Below Zero still captures moments of solitude and tension, the presence of other characters and their dialogue exchanges dilutes the overwhelming sense of isolation.That being said, Subnautica: Below Zero remains a captivating and immersive adventure. The frozen landscapes and diverse aquatic biomes are breathtaking to explore, filled with awe-inspiring creatures and hidden secrets waiting to be uncovered. The addition of new tools, vehicles, and biomes keeps gameplay fresh and engaging, while the haunting soundtrack sets the perfect tone for the eerie depths.In conclusion, Subnautica: Below Zero may deviate from the solitary experience of its predecessor, but it still delivers a compelling underwater journey filled with wonder and discovery. Whether you're a returning fan of the series or a newcomer to the depths, Below Zero offers an unforgettable underwater adventure that's well worth diving into.I give it a solid 4/5

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: If you loved Subnautica, you will like Subnautica: Below Zero.I must preface this with a fact: Subnautica is one of my favorite games I've played in the past five years. It contains everything I enjoy about survival games, while also blending in elements of marine biology and sci-fi. Somewhere in the endless fabric of time, I created Subnautica so that my present self could enjoy it today.The dialogue was fine. I haven't seen many reviews, but I can imagine many gamers probably hate the dialogue in this game. At times, it seems forced, but honestly, I didn’t really mind. Some might say it was cringey, but I scoff at that idea.The quality of life improvements with the Prawn suit were amazing. Going from Subnautica to Below Zero, interacting with the Prawn Suit is night and day—you get in and out almost instantly. When I inevitably return to Subnautica, I suspect I will miss these enhancements from Below Zero.Leviathans were okay. Subnautica still has the most iconic leviathans, but Below Zero doesn’t hold back either. The Shadow Leviathan and Ventgardens are awesome, especially since they are designed with their biomes in mind. The Shadow Leviathan, resembling a centipede, fits through the tight spaces of the Crystal Caves, which enhances the challenge. The other leviathans, however, were less remarkable.The giant jellyfish tree, aka Ventgardens, was a true spectacle the first time I saw it. Discovering that you could enter them to gather resources blew me away. Unknown Worlds Entertainment must have some insanely passionate biologists on their team because they consistently excel at creating intriguing creatures.The Crystal Cave was a phenomenal biome. It’s not only a beautiful biome, but the progression from purple to red crystals as you go deeper is great. The Shadow Leviathan really makes this biome terrifying to navigate. In my first playthrough, these creatures constantly chased me from 600 meters to 950. I always had at least one near me, heightening the tension compared to the end-game biome of Subnautica.The Sea Monkeys were a creature that kept on giving. Not only adorable, they also gifted you items and their nests contained important blueprints. Being able to visually identify the blueprints in the Sea Monkey nests was a godsend improvement.Al-an was cool. I really enjoyed the lore dumps from him (I’m not kidding). It was interesting to get more context about the Kharaa Bacterium and to learn at the end that he was the reason it escaped in the first place. The sequence where you finally build his body and travel off of Planet 4546B, presumably to his home planet, left me wanting more.Marguerit Maida was the second most memorable character, right next to Al-an. If other crew members had survived and been given a body to their voices, perhaps there would have been more impact. But Marguerit is a stone-cold badass, and the first time you enter her base and see the huge reaper leviathan head on her wall, you just KNOW she’s built different. I also have to mention her custom Prawn Suit and how much I wish we, as players, could do what she did with hers. Maybe in the future.Flora and fauna were obviously amazing—100% blew it out of the park. This is the selling point of every Subnautica game. If they lose sight of that, I think the series will die off. Creating whimsical, yet believable flora and fauna from an alien planet goes hand in hand with Subnautica. Some of my favorites were the Ventgardens, Shadow Leviathans, Sea Monkeys, Lily Paddler, Spinner Fish, Eye Jelly, Grand Cotton Anemone, and Thermal Lily.If you loved Subnautica like I do, then you will enjoy Below Zero. It still hits many of the same notes that made Subnautica so enjoyable, although not as many as you might expect.The majority of the land-based gameplay. I’m just not interested in the cold mechanics and traversing the glacial tundra, especially at night. When I think of Subnautica, I think OCEAN, not jogging around a giant glacier.The Snowfox was a buggy mess. I learned about the Snowfox, gathered all resources for the Snowfox hoverpad and the Snowfox itself, went back to base and built it all. Finally going back to the arctic spires and using the Snowfox, it fell through the floor. I kid you not, this happened three more times throughout my playthrough. The first time, I literally quit the game for a month because I just didn't want to deal with the hassle. The controls for the Snowfox were strange, clunky, and weird. Having this constant worry that unpacking my Snowfox might cause it to glitch through the ground and force me to go back home and make another was just exhausting.The giant glacier was extremely confusing to traverse (maybe a skill issue). The Arctic Spires and Glacial Bay were extremely confusing for me to navigate. I often got lost, to the point where I just looked up where the key pieces were and went there directly instead of circling around the island another ten times.For me, the reason why Subnautica: Below Zero doesn’t live up to Subnautica is because of the heavy reliance on land-based gameplay. If they focused more on ocean-related stuff and less on land, I guarantee this game would be better. But I do respect them for branching out and trying something new; I find that to be a refreshing quality of this game.The Seatruck. Throughout my whole playthrough, I wrestled with the fact that we don’t have a Cyclops anymore. I loved the Cyclops—it was such a cool and giant ship, essentially a moving base. The Seatruck is their evolution of that, but I am unsure if it actually is an evolution or a devolution. The modules that the Seatruck supports are epic. Being able to customize it however you want and put whatever modules you need is great. My setup was the Fabricator, storage, teleport, and docking module. But I still can't shake off the fact that the Cyclops was just so cool. I am all for having more customization, but I want my Cyclops back.Having a protagonist that talks. A character with a backstory and a purpose for coming to Planet 4546B is good, right? Well, I don’t know. For me personally, unless the character has a genuinely compelling story that can be told, having a faceless, mute protagonist is much more fun. I like being able to transport myself into the world and experience it like I am really there. Having a character just makes it feel a little less immersive, and a little more divisive. It was an alright choice, and obviously necessary for the interactions between Al-an and Marguerit and everything else to happen, but I’m still unsure about it.Subnautica: Below Zero is a good game. If you loved Subnautica, you will like Below Zero. There will be moments when you love the game and think, "Man, give me more of that!" Then those moments will swiftly end, and you will be met with ham-fisted mechanics that don't really fit into the game you know and love. Ultimately, I respect Unknown Worlds Entertainment for trying something different with their game. Even if it doesn't land properly, they at least have the balls to innovate or die trying.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the game has not been fully released, I don't suppose much will be added or changed. If they won't decide to redo the entire game, there is very little room for improvement.And so, as it stands, Subnautica Below Zero (let's call it BZ) lacks in so much compared to the original.• Danger and Horror - unlike the first game, BZ's creatures aren't scary whatsoever. Their design is poor and uninspired. The Chelicerate spawns in 1-2 locations far out where you don't even need to travel. Not only that but it makes grumpy noises at a mere Peeper so you'll know its exact position while hugging the sea floor. And as many pointed out, it is just a humongous lobster. Shadow Leviathan has proven to be more annoying than scary. Apart from its territory patrolling, it resembles a black anvil. Take notes from Vsauce, or actual studies, on what makes things actually scary. The areas themselves aren't particularly creepy, the deepest one being situated at ~900 meters below, they all lack the proper atmosphere. The only one scary enough was the edge of the world. Even though I already expected to be killed by a scripted leviathan, the fact that the part was so murky made that the scariest experience of the entire game.Not to mention the ordinary fish. Previously, there were Warpers and Squidcrabs to worry about too. In BZ, there is literally no creature - including leviathans - that could pose any threat to me while I was in my Seatruck or Prawn suit.• Biomes - this is continuation of what I was talking before; there are no interesting biomes. Admittedly, I was kind of excited about the fact that there was gonna be ice and snow and ice. But due to how much smaller the map is, the glaciers stole much of the spotlight and opportunity for some amazing areas to shine. It's called Subnautica. There was no need for walking. There could've been some iceberg cavities which would lead to caches and laboratories guarded by the most dangerous monsters. The strongest defender of the Glacial Bay was the boredom I didn't want to face when I had to go there to fetch something.• Resources - I have to say, that I'm not the biggest fan of grinding for resources. It was very tiring in the first game, that's true. But on the other hand, I think majority of the players don't want to have basically everything handed to them. Which is exactly how it was; I had basically everything handed to me. This is a huge problem when you don't innovate the resources and reuse most of the blueprints from the original: everybody who played the original will know what to search for. I had all the materials needed for the endgame prepared in the first few expeditions.• Sound design - It'd be super lazy to reuse the roars of the Reapers or use the same music, but honestly, the fish sounded pretty bland. Again, even the Squidcrabs had their terrifying charging sounds. I will give props to the voice acting; both the main character and AL-AN sound good enough - although I'm not a native speaker. There is a track that was a bliss to listen to - Permafrost. And the Jukebox is something I always like to turn on. However, as if to compliment the completely unexpected chill atmosphere, there is no tension that the music could provide. I remember stumbling upon the Blood Kelp zone and hearing the Lava lakes track. Those were moments I felt absolutely uneasy. Maybe the music could be more like that or it could just fade into nothingness when exploring the deepest parts - but then again, there aren't that many.• The story and gameplay - It feels really short. Obviously, it isn't finished, but the story is pretty linear and fed to the player. There is also not much of mystery behind anything, because once you acquire AL-AN, you just go from one cache to another, hunting for the parts you are told to hunt for. And even though I do like the interaction you can have with him, I find  very cliche.• Bottom (1000 m) line - The best word to describe the game is 'lacking'. It just feels empty and shallow. Surprisingly even more so than the first game where I didn't have a companion with me at all times. I would personally prefer if they scratched the whole 'surface' gameplay idea and focused entirely on the underwater world. I would welcome deeper parts of the ocean to explore. I wouldn't mind more dangerous creatures. I wouldn't be against waiting for another year or two if it meant the game would go in such direction.

_childDocuments_.review: It is more of  the good stuff. I really loved the original Subnautica and this one is a worthy sucessor (even if I like the original a little bit more for reasons stated below). First of all the environment, the exploration and the ATMOSPHERE is just awesome. The way how sound and light is used to create mysterious environments is just perfect. Suptile details like the way the sound of your vehicle changes with depth shows that the team behind the game is composed of real divers. There is a whole lot to explore and ecosystems can be pretty surprising. Your progress in the game is very intelligently linked to depth. To progress you must go deeper, so upgrade your crafts etc and you're forced to take risks since to gather the materials to upgrade your vehicle you need to go deeper than it can go so you need to leave it behind. The base building is awesome and I waste SO MUCH TIME for choosing just the right angle to have the most magnificent view on the surroundings. The seatruck (the main vehicle of the game) is an interesting take on vehicle progression since you extend your vehicle rather than having new ones (seamoth/cyclops in Subnautica 1). However I have mixed feelings about this since building the cyclops left me with the feeling of a major achievement which isn't so much the case here. I think the map is also a bit wierdly built. I don't know if it's just me but I have a large biais exploring to the south (I almost completely ignore the east and west from the droppod). In subnautica 1 my exploration was smooth and circular which would let me see all ecosystems. In this one I have the feeling of missing something due to the way the geography drives me to explore. Unfortunately there seem to be less (or at least less diverse biomes than in Subnautica 1)I have also the feeling of being more guided by the story than last lime. Randomly "Someone" would tell me to go to a certain waypoint instead of describing a general direction or ecosystem for me to find which is a little bit sad since the game is heavily linked to exploration. But I'm basically nitpicking here. I love this game! But If I would have to reccomend either Subnautica, I would prefer the first one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game - Subnautica as a series has a wonderful survival core, but be warned that this isn't nearly as tight as the original.  It isn't a death blow, but the developers did some brave things, and not all of them paid off.  The original was quiet - the character didn't speak at all, and any recording or evidence of another human being was precious.  The player felt alone, and I found myself hording odd items just to make my base feel "lived in" - but, there was also a strange peacefulness to the silence.  In Sub-Zero, you're a can-do woman with things to say, but she was given some pretty substandard lines by the writers.  Her voice acting is passable, but there is an ongoing dialogue between her and another character (the ancient alien) which is so foolish and flat, it's genuinely bad for the game. The conversation comes through often enough that you lack that feeling of quietude that made the original so special. The overall "quest", however, is interesting - you're on a mission to discover what happened to your sister, who was assigned to a corporate scientific team on a frozen planet, but all communication went dark.  It's good stuff.  Yet, it can be challenging to know where to go next, and this game doesn't guide the player as neatly as the original.  Pacing isn't really a thing, and it can be all too easy to miss something small, but critical, especially when first getting the lay of the land.  Still, this could be a feature instead of a bug if you don't like having your hand held by the designers.  No matter your preference, though, the original should be played first.  This shouldn't be anybody's introduction to Subnautica.The additional items and structures added to the game are only sometimes an improvement on the original - I'm sad but understanding of the omission of the full-base-sized submarine from the original, but the sea-truck cannot hold a candle to the Seamoth (the single seat submarine from Subnautica I) in terms of appeal.  On the other hand, the recent inclusion of a new base structure that allows a truck with multiple modules to dock completely is VERY well done.  Whoever designed that?  Hats off to you.In summary, Sub-Zero was an attempt by the designers to add some fresh ideas to the original, but not everything was an improvement - the dialogue was poorly executed, and navigating some of the three-dimensional mazes are a clinic in frustration, but despite these painful hurdles, Subnautica as well as Sub-Zero are deeply evocative, stirring experiences, and should be explored.  Just, for this title, maybe wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Below Zero is pretty much classic Subnautica with some QoL improvements, a new story and my two least favorite elements -- setting the entire game in an arctic area, and requiring the player to spend a substantial amount of time out of the water.Underwater gameplay is Subnautica's hallmark and it does oceanic exploration better than any game I've played. It's the primary strength of the franchise. While the Snowfox is pretty cool, surface gameplay just isn't as much fun.Mostly you'll spend time zipping through mostly featureless arctic landscapes and trying to negotiate tight caves, which the delicate Snowfox is not well suited for. There's also an incredibly annoying bug that has the Snowfox sinking into the map, much like the Seamoth did in the original Subnautica. If you pack up your Snowfox, save the game before you redeploy it, otherwise you're going to find yourself trekking back a long distance on foot, hopping between thermal vents to stave off hypothermia.Then there's the Cyclops, or lack of it.While the Seatruck does have some good utility, it lacks the wow factor of the Cyclops, you can't customize the interior and two of the modules are pretty much entirely aesthetic. (The sleeper module and the aquarium, which gathers fish for your base aquariums. The sleeper does offer a small amount of additional storage space, but it's negligible.)By removing the Cyclops the devs took away a fan favorite toy, and they also made the map more compact with a greater focus on vertical exploration instead of horizontal. While I do like some of what they've done, much of it is claustrophobic and the biomes lack the wow factor of areas like the Lost River from the first game.If you're a Subnautica fan, you'll probably like Below Zero despite its flaws. I find I'm losing interest in the extended time spent on the surface. Here's to hoping a third game gives us a huge ocean without snow or ice, a proper submarine (perhaps the Atlas?) and the kind of biome, plant and fauna variety of the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the first Subnautica, I can't imagine how you wouldn't love this game as well. The world felt a little more compact than in the first game, but there was plenty to do in the world that was available, and that compactness mostly boiled down to not getting lost as easily on a large scale, and not needing to spend as much time just jetting forward through the open ocean in your sub. The world is beautiful, above and below the ocean's surface. The various biomes melt into each other even more smoothly here than in the first game, it felt to me like less grinding was required for bulk components (or any grinding that was required felt less tedious than the previous installment). The creatures are gorgeous, from the small to the enormous. If this studio continues the series, I hope they will keep making creatures larger and more intimidating to approach. I felt safer in this game than in the first one, except at great depths. This wasn't a problem for me, but I can imagine the reduced sense of challenge might lead some others to disappointment. I'm just here to scuba dive and drink in the visual feasts while giving a wide berth to whomever shows me their teeth.My number one note would be: Make the Glow Whales bigger, please. The herbivorous leviathans from the first game were one of my favorite parts, and the large vegetarian beasts here are just as lovely. But there's an experience I'd love to have in a game someday, where I'm walking along a squelchy grey beach for over a mile, look down and see a gargantuan eye peering at me curiously out of the beach, and realize I've been walking on top of a living being this whole time. It doesn't need to move all that much, I just want 'em big. The whales were stunning, but I'd love to see them big big big. Big enough to swallow my whole seatruck, even if they're too smart to try digesting all that metal. Big boys. That's what we want. Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica: Below Zero is a strong extension to the existing content of the original game, but some elements will leave you unsatisfied.Starting with the pros - Below Zero takes many of the best parts of the precursor and adds to them meaningfully in a way that satisfies its title as a sequel. Completely new biomes and vehicles, and tons of well-designed new plants and creatures were a welcome addition. Some of the problematic aspects of the original are removed or altered in a positive way, such as the previously limited locomotion of the prawn suit and constantly getting beached with the cyclops. The game also massively adds to base-building options, the most memorable being a jukebox that can bring quality funky fan jams surround-sound throughout your base.The game's biggest addition is the existence of a below-zero temperature surface level, hence the title. A temperature meter functions as a reverse oxygen bar, only depleting when you're out of the water, which you'll craft new unique gear and vehicles to traverse. Unlike the fully open spaces in the former map, Sector Zero is tightened, in that the map does not reach as far below the surface, but is accompanied by a number of above ground zones. Much like you'll use geysers, hotsprings, and heated plants to keep your temperature up above ground, the sequel adds oxygen plants and fish to navigate these tighter spaces underwater. These elements combined get some heat in other reviews, but are actually a welcome change of pace to the vehicle-reliance of the original.  More importantly to many, Below Zero expands tenfold to the original story and mystery, with a pretty strong story hook. There's way more voicelog PDAs you'll discover this time around, and a far larger cast of characters, all voice acted terrifically. Those who enjoyed discovering 4546B's history in Subnautica will appreciate how it's expanded in the first half of the sequel.All that said, about halfway through a playthrough, things sadly start to fall apart. Just about all of the PDA logs through which the story is told are discoverable in easy-to-reach locations, which leaves half the game feeling quite lore barren. There are less indications to point you in the right direction once it's announced there's something nearby, so you might find yourself going in circles finding nothing at the most tense moments of the game. The game rewards you for discovering underwater locations, but the rewards end after you find two-thirds of them. Finding something cool is a bit unsatisfying when you have nothing to gain and your PDA won't even provide you with lore.The surface has some issues as well. You need two full sets of gear when exploring the ice - one set of land items and vehicles, and also all your water equipment. This presents some major inventory space conflicts that can be quite irritating to deal with. Worse, however, is the snowy weather thematic to the environment becomes a big problem farther up. 80% of the time, it's either dark or under heavy snow, so even if you can survive the cold, your complete lack of vision makes exploring far less fun. Either you hope to fumble your way into the right place in the dark, or you sit in a cave for five minutes until it's day again.Many of the strides you make for better gear aren't valuable, since the game's recipes are far more reliant on common minerals. Why bother making a drill arm if there's nothing you'll need to drill? Subnautica needed a lot of rare resources to craft all the different equipment modifications and end the game, but in this one you need three or four then you're set for life. Finally finding a rare resource you needed for an important tool is less valuable if you never need that resource again. You'll have to make tons of trips for common minerals, but only once will you go to the lowest depth locations. Below Zero's biggest disappointment sadly is the story in the second half. A character that makes such a strong entrance goes completely blank and useless midway through, and another core character who should have had a larger voice role only provides a few off-topic conversations or predictable reveals. With every piece of lore you pick up, the game seems to be leading you to discovering a particular truth about your sister, only for it to be thrown all away with such a mundane discovery. This made the other main theme of the story all the more unsatisfying, right up to the credits sequence. All in all, Subnautica: Below Zero will have you at peak interest for the bulk of the game, and expands on existing concepts wonderfully, but some gameplay decisions lead to issues below the surface of the ice.
